Elle also spends much of the floor with a devoted, lecherous superfan attached to her circle — "Linus." He is not who he claims to be. See Minus in the Supporting Cast for the reveal: a Syndicate assassin wearing the identity of Elle's dead real-life fan, sent to kill Imani C and Louis Santiago and destabilize the group. Elle later throws his exposure back at her own allies as evidence nobody listens to her instincts: "After all the stuff me and Carl said at the fuck-Linus party?"

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised, Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario, Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook, Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade, Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride, Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin, and Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Epitome Tagg
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Off-world player — Warlord of the Dream, one of the nine Faction Wars teams on Floor 9. A CEO of the Epitome family, “one of the most famous CEOs in the galaxy”
  • Race: Dream elf — always described as bald. Secretly a cyborg, with most of his brain transferred to “the Reaver net” and only a small amount of biological material left
  • Class: None stated
  • Subclass: None stated
  • Level: Not stated anywhere in the book
  • Role: Faction Wars warlord; the antagonist of the Louis Santiago rescue arc (chapters 80-84)
  • Family: Son of Epitome Noflex, whose death he ordered (Book 6); in Book 7 he claims she is alive on the 18th floor and will bargain for him
  • Notable spells/abilities: None shown — he never fights Carl directly. His one real capability is the cybernetic graft that lets him inhabit and hold hostage another person’s vital organs
  • Notable items: None named. Boomer’s warning is that “He wears the most ridiculous helmet you’ve ever seen”
  • Status: Deceased — chapter 84. His heart-and-lung assembly is cut out of Louis Santiago during a transplant and eaten by Mongo, who gets the kill credit

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Epitome Tagg is the warlord of the Dream, the galaxy’s dominant food conglomerate and the team Carl spends most of Book 7 fighting on the southern front. He arrives in Book 7 already established as a villain: in Book 6 he ordered his own mother’s death and dismissed Carl’s team outright at the Faction Wars table.

“There are no other teams,” Epitome Tagg said. “It’s nine teams. Eight, really. Plus the chaff. That’s what you are. You’re not even real.”

Tempest’s Floor 8 recap flags him early as one of the rich off-worlders who can now genuinely die:

“Yeah. All those rich fuckers on the floor, like Prince Stalwart the orc, or that banker Operatic guy, or Epitome Tagg from the Dream? They all can really die now. It’s gonna be a shitshow. An epic, but-sir-you-haven’t-taken-a-bath shitshow.”

He is reputed to be a front-line commander. Boomer’s briefing in chapter 22 warns that the Epitome household guard is in the dungeon with him — “Their security forces are all veterans of non-dungeon conflicts and are tough as gristle” — and that “Epitome Tagg likes to fight near the front.” When he finally appears in person at the warlord summit in chapter 42, the staging matches:

Then came Epitome Tagg of the Dream. The bald elf looked as if he came straight from the battlefield. His utilitarian armor had a splash of blood across it, and I wondered who he’d been fighting. By all reports, he hadn’t been seen on the battlefield yet. At least not against any of our forces.

The reputation is theatre. Every time the Dream is actually threatened, Tagg runs.

docs.title: At the Summit
docs.text:
Tagg is the loudest voice in the chapter 42-44 warlord meeting, and the most openly contemptuous. He needles King Stalwart of the Skull Empire over the Dream’s counter-measures and Stalwart’s collapsing position:

“Oh, please. Tell us, your majesty, what you’re planning on doing? We have already deactivated all Skull-empire-manufactured hardware in our fleet. You had your personal monetary reserves depleted because of your own lax security, your reputation is destroyed, and you are about to have a civil war on your hands that’ll make the Borant system look like a scuffle between toddlers. Tell us how we’ll be sorry?”

“We are opposite sides of the map, and you do not have an air force,” Tagg said. “So, I ask again, what are you going to do, you coward?”

Odette’s broadcast then exposes how the teams are beating the communications blackout — by renaming their own entertainment channels as a signalling system — and names Tagg as the worst offender:

“But, and this is a big but, the feed directory is still active to all subscribers… They are paying the fee to repeatedly change the names of the programs in order to communicate. Just today, Epitome Tagg was shown to have a real-time conversation with the news program formerly called Sensation Updates, which changed its name seven times in the course of an hour. That program, as of this moment, is currently called Yes. We have Deactivated the Infected Hardware.”

When Juice Box shifts into the form of the Nothing and startles the entire room, Tagg is the one who insists on covering it with scorn:

“It’s superstitious nonsense,” Tagg said, pretending like he, too, hadn’t been startled by whatever that was. “A cheap jump scare. As children, we would use this image to scare each other all the time.”

“Superstitious nonsense,” Tagg repeated.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
Once the shooting starts, Tagg’s actual behaviour is consistent. In chapter 62, with Team Retribution occupying the Dream throne room and three feral gods loose in Dream territory, Edgar spots him:

Edgar: Donut, I see Epitome Tagg. He is still near the Dream castle. He did not teleport with his army. He’s with a small contingent of his troops, riding zebras. I think he’s fleeing into the woods. I marked him. He is not the one in the fancy hat. They are trying to trick you.

Donut’s missile strike misses. Carl’s read:

Tagg was making the safe choice to flee and hide, effectively abandoning his own troops who he sent to attack our base.

He survives the Witness spell that sweeps everyone outdoors into the rolling ball of bodies, because he was outside when it was cast — Carl confirms it with Ping from the top of the Nest in chapter 73, finding both Tagg and Warlord Fang alive inside the ball. Carl’s plan at that point is blunt: “All we need to do is find and kill both Tagg and Fang, and all their soldiers will drop dead.”

That never happens. Instead the Dream’s own throne room, held by Team Retribution, becomes a countdown clock: when the six-hour capture timer expires, Tagg dies automatically wherever he is.

docs.title: The Cyborg
docs.text:
The reveal comes sideways. In chapter 80 Warlord Fang of the Reavers is killed after surviving Donut’s War Crime spell as “a tiny amount of biological material surrounded by a robot” and hiding inside his own pet drake. Donut asks how you hide inside a dragon, and Juice Box answers:

“He was hiding inside the dragon the same way Epitome Tagg is hiding inside of my husband,” Juice Box said.

Juice Box has just wraith-possessed her husband, Louis Santiago, out of the Reaver castle, where he had been cut open on an operating table:

“They were doing surgery on him. He was... cut open. His heart has been replaced. His lungs have been replaced. It looked like they were getting ready to replace his brain, but we got to him in time. I had to heal him, but when I did it, it didn’t regrow his heart or lungs.”

“He was hooked up to a machine that was keeping him alive. When I touched him, I sensed the presence. It’s there, in the new lungs and heart. I can feel the form I can take, and it’s wrong... I don’t understand. The new heart and the new lungs are mechanical, but they both have a little biological material as well. Those pieces. It’s not Louis. It’s... It’s pieces of Tagg. It’s elf, but if I didn’t already have his kind in my library, I’m not sure if I’d be able to store the image or not. It’s confusing.”

Mordecai’s framing is the one that sticks:

Mordecai: Maybe. But Maggie was inside Chris’s brain. In this case, it sounds like Tagg isn’t in Louis’s heart. He is Louis’s heart.

docs.title: Carl’s Deduction
docs.text:
Carl works it out at the end of chapter 81 on a single question to Juice Box, who spent Book 6 infiltrating the Dream:

Carl: Before the dungeon started, did you ever actually touch Tagg?

Juice Box: Him? No. We just blew him up a lot. He was always in that flag room, so we could never get to him.

Juice Box is a changeling, and changelings can only copy something they have physically touched. She has never been able to touch Tagg. The answer lands:

“Holy shit,” I said out loud. Sometimes the most obvious answer was the real one. “Epitome Tagg of the Dream is a...”

The sentence is cut off mid-word — Prime Minister Glory picks that exact moment to try to have Carl ejected from the game, the AI overrides it, and the resulting achievement notice (Executive Order 11905) is the AI publicly warning the entire Syndicate off. When time restarts, Carl finishes:

“Epitome Tagg is a goddamned cyborg! He is the same thing as Fang! It’s the only thing that makes sense.”

Mordecai calls it a wild theory — “He’s one of the most famous CEOs in the galaxy, and that’s a big secret to keep” — and Rosetta confirms it:

Rosetta: Carl and Mordecai are right. Gondii don’t have the wetware to inhabit organs. The Reavers do. They can isolate their processing systems in any part of their bodies. That’s why the real ones can keep coming for you after you blow off their heads.

Baroness Victory later fills in the politics: the Dream are not all Reavers, but Tagg personally had “decided to secretly start moving toward the post physical form path,” and an undisclosed Dream/Reaver alliance between the galaxy’s largest food producer and its largest manufacturer would have been a mega-monopoly. Fopsy, the Dream’s own adjutant, says he had “no inkling whatsoever.”

Unresolved

The book never explains how Tagg grafted himself into Louis’s biomechanical organs in the first place, or how he survived losing his own body. Mordecai’s answer to Donut’s direct question is “We don’t know. We need to figure it out,” and no later scene resolves it.

docs.title: The Hostage Negotiation
docs.text:
Tagg is still in warlord chat, and he opens with the only leverage he has:

Epitome Tagg: Fuck off. I control his vital organs. You try to remove me, and I will shut him down.

Epitome Tagg: Keep him alive, and you keep me alive. We can make a deal. My mother is on the 18th floor. She will trade his life for mine.

His offer in chapter 83 is a full body swap:

Epitome Tagg: It’s quite simple, Carl. Get me to the 18th Floor. I will have a new body grown for me, and we will grow replacement organs for your friend here, and we will do a swap. He will be out of the dungeon, and I will be back in control. We both get what we want.

Epitome Tagg: We’ll have to finish the procedure at the Reaver castle. Fang was being an ass and wasn’t going to allow the brain implant until he, too, was free. We will keep your friend’s brain intact, and it can be reimplanted. Once that happens, I will have control, and he will cease to be a crawler.

It is worthless. The Reaver castle has already been nuked, Tagg has no outside communications left, and Victory confirms there is no legal exit: he cannot abdicate, because he is the only member of the Dream still alive, and he cannot leave the floor, because his host is a crawler. When the Dream throne room timer expires, Tagg dies — and Mordecai’s assessment is that “He will take Louis out with him.”

The solution is Samantha’s: Carl is carrying the flesh golem body of Princess Lunette, a naiad, which has a usable heart and lungs. Mordecai, Edgar, Imani, Rosetta and a Fleshmancer-shaped Juice Box run a live transplant in a field hospital tent, with Carl and Tipid holding the ribcage open.

docs.title: Death
docs.text:
The plan is to stall Tagg for two minutes. Donut’s contribution is to rename herself EPITOME TAGG’S SEXY MOTHER and start doing an impression, which works considerably better than stalling:

Epitome Tagg: Quit saying that! That disgusting human never had sex with my mother! He besmirched my mother’s name with a changeling who took her form!

Epitome Tagg: Change your name back this instant! I will kill this fat loser right now! Right fucking now! You puerile, disgusting mongrel. How dare you? How fucking dare you? I will starve out all of your kind!

Epitome Tagg: CHANGE THAT NAME NOW.

Carl: “He said stall, not piss him off.” Donut: “We’re playing good cop, bad cop, Carl.”

With the surgical team thirty seconds short, Tagg gives up:

Epitome Tagg: You know what? Fuck this. Fuck this existence. Fuck this life. And fuck all of you. You don’t deserve singularity. None of you do.

“Heart has stopped,” Edgar shouted.

Mordecai cannot pull the organs himself — as an NPC it would count as an attack — so Bucket Boy yanks the whole assembly out in one piece and throws it over his shoulder onto the tent floor. Louis gets Lunette’s naiad heart and lungs, a kua-tin rebreather sewn into his bronchial tube, and a permanent set of gills. He survives.

Nobody notices where the discarded organs went until Carl asks:

Mongo popped up and let out an angry screech. He had blood on his beak, and he spit out the chewed-to-hell plastic heart and lungs onto the ground of the tent with disgust.

System Message: Warlord Epitome Tagg of the Dream has fallen. Credit for the kill has been given... Well, this one is just as complicated as the last one, but imma give it to pet Mongo of the Princess Posse. I almost called it a suicide, and I almost gave it to that Bucket Boy kid, but it’s going to Mongo. Consider it a present for the baby shower.

System Message: The Dream has been defeated.

System Message: All assets of the Dream have been awarded to the Princess Posse.

System Message: And then there were two.

The baby shower is literal — Mongo’s mate Kiwi had given birth two chapters earlier. Donut’s verdict on the whole affair: “Well, that was significantly easier than I thought it would be.”

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride and Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Eva Sigrid
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Crawler
  • Race: A nagini/orc hybrid — cobra-faced, snake-bodied from the waist down
  • Class: Nimblefoot Enforcer
  • Group: Formerly Katia's closest friend on Earth; later a senior member, then leader, of Brynhild's Daughters — by Book 5, operating alone
  • Level: 55 (Book 5)
  • Status: Deceased — killed by Katia at the end of Book 5, after over 50 player-killer skulls
  • Party: Hekla's Brynhild's Daughters, until its collapse
  • Notable spells/abilities: Not described in detail; fights with a matched pair of enchanted sabers
  • Notable items: The Left Fang of the Green Sultan — half of a matched saber set, non-magical without its twin (lost to Katia after the fight that kills Hekla); a poisoned rapier prosthetic replacing her severed top-left hand (Book 3–5); an escape ring worn on her top-right hand (Book 5); the reforming Crown of the Sepsis Whore, carried openly on the back shoulder of her breastplate, disguised as decoration, as of Book 5

docs.title: Katia's Oldest Friend
docs.text: Eva and Katia entered the dungeon together, sharing the same game guide through the early floors. On reaching Floor 3, the pair should have entered character creation and race/class selection together — but Eva went first, transformed, and left the saferoom before Katia was ready, later telling her she'd "accidentally made one of the swordsmen guards angry" and fled town on a caravan, reconnecting with Hekla in a different city entirely. This account is revealed as at least partly self-serving: a Book 3 recap episode shows Eva abandoning Katia on the third floor deliberately, a betrayal she later throws in Katia's face outright during their final confrontation ("This is why I left you behind on the third floor").

docs.title: The Plot Against Hekla's Own Party
docs.text: By Book 3, Eva is co-architect (alongside Hekla) of a scheme to have Carl provoked into attacking Brynhild's Daughters' healer Silfa, using the resulting justification to kill Carl and pressure Donut into abandoning her own party for Hekla's. When the plot collapses aboard a moving train during a shared battle, Eva reveals the entire scheme to Katia's face, seemingly out of pure cruelty rather than necessity — a psychological attack that appears to be the final catalyst for the chaotic brawl that follows. See Hekla for the full sequence.

docs.title: Survival and Disappearance
docs.text: Unlike Hekla, Eva survives the confrontation — Katia's Rush attack, aimed at her, misses and kills Hekla instead. Eva loses her saber (The Left Fang of the Green Sultan, looted by Katia) but escapes the wreck of the train. In the immediate aftermath, Brynhild's Daughters disbands entirely; Eva, deeply unpopular with the group's remaining members, nominally inherits leadership of what's left of it. Carl spends the rest of the floor trying and failing to relocate her through contacts among the former Daughters — by the time the floor ends, her whereabouts and intentions remain unknown and unresolved.

docs.title: Book 5: Death at the Butcher's Masquerade
docs.text:
Eva resurfaces on Floor 6 with over 50 player-killer skulls and four hunter-killer marks, having abandoned or lost every remaining member of her old group. At the Butcher's Masquerade, she goads Katia in front of the assembled hunters, tries to steal potions meant for the whole party, and appears to be coordinating — loosely, alongside Vrah's hunters — toward breaking the party's peace seal for her own escape. When Tsarina Signet's sacrifice shatters the seal first, Eva flees the resulting chaos rather than fight.

Katia and Li Na track her down, half-buried and near death from a dinosaur mauling, in the battle's aftermath. Li Na casts a spell (Preserve Injury) preventing her from healing herself; Katia cuts off Eva's top-right hand (which bears an escape ring) and the poisoned rapier stub on her top-left arm, leaving her only her two lower hands, then executes her with The Left Fang of the Green Sultan — the same saber looted from her back in Book 3 — finally closing the loop from her Book 3 betrayal. As she dies from the blow, Eva uses her one remaining free hand to pull a piece she'd carried the whole time on the back shoulder of her own armor, disguised as decoration: the reforming Crown of the Sepsis Whore. Eva is already dead by the moment the crown actually equips itself, transferring onto Katia's bare head — a last, deliberate act of spite that leaves Katia newly entangled in the Blood Sultanate succession curse Donut has carried since losing the crown at the end of the third floor.

Sourced from Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook and Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: Ferdinand
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Race: Cat
  • Type: Boss-tier familiar → Donut's bonded pet/party member
  • Class/Subclass: Not applicable — a pet-class mob, not a crawler
  • Level: 100 — a Province Boss as "Sir Ferdinand," familiar of Queen Imogen of the High Elves
  • Role (Book 7): Co-warlord of Team Retribution, the NPC faction, alongside Juice Box — added because the system would not give a dungeon-born changeling access to the warlord menu. Also the former Mayor of Shanty Town, until he trades the office away for a hat
  • Status: Alive; joins Princess Donut's party at the book's climax. Still alive at the end of Book 7 — he leaves Floor 9 for the 12th floor with Juice Box rather than continuing the crawl
  • Notable spells/abilities: None stated in Book 7 — he holds a warlord's menu and a lightning bolt he once fired at Mongo, and otherwise fights not at all
  • Notable items: A magic turban (drained of magic by Book 7) and a black, weathered bowler hat taken from Quan's inventory — thrown, it decapitates a target and boomerangs back to the owner (Book 7)
  • Notable relationship: Donut's pre-apocalypse "first love" and long-running Book 1-5 mystery

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Ferdinand is a running mystery since Book 1 — Donut repeatedly mentions "Ferdinand" as someone she loves, with Carl (and the reader) never getting an explanation, until Book 2's on-air reveal that "Ferdinand" was actually Gravy Boat, an ordinary neighborhood tomcat back on Earth. Book 5 resolves the mystery a second time: Gravy Boat was apparently swept up in the same harvest that took every other Earth creature and has been trapped in the dungeon this whole time, transformed into Sir Ferdinand, a Level 100 Province Boss serving as the personal familiar of Queen Imogen of the High Elves — his memory altered, personality twisted into a cruel, self-aggrandizing caricature of a pampered royal pet. (Empress D'Nadia, who's followed the "Gravy Boat" saga since Book 2, confirms the identity in passing at the masquerade, mockingly addressing Ferdinand as "Gravy Boat" when he jumps on the judges' table.)

docs.title: The Reveal
docs.text:
Donut first spots him mid-book and is devastated: "It was Ferdinand. I saw him. It was him. They brought Ferdinand down here and changed his memory and turned him into a jerk. He tried to kill Mongo." She initially insists she's moved on ("I am a mother now... if anything, I see it as a good thing... it'll make for a good song"), but the emotional stakes clearly aren't resolved.

His in-game monster card reveals the High Elves' pattern of exploiting non-elf pets before eventually turning on them, and notes he survives specifically because Queen Imogen is fond of him — "in the same way a surgeon is fond of their favorite scalpel." He's shown to have quietly carved out small pockets of unauthorized magical influence over the castle itself, consistent with an intelligent creature the elves haven't yet decided to purge.

docs.title: The Rescue
docs.text:
During the climactic infiltration of the High Elf castle (staged as a televised talent-show event), Carl's group's plan hinges on a Charm Animal potion — brewed by Mordecai from a full liter of Donut's own blood, since Ferdinand is the same species as her — combined with an artificially boosted Charisma (a base 138 doubled to 276 by a benefactor-box tiara, over 300 with further buffs) to out-charm Ferdinand's own stats (constitution + charisma of 175) by the 100-point margin required to charm a province boss, flipping his loyalty back to her mid-performance. Donut drinks the potion on stage; it works:

"Sir Ferdinand, minion of Princess Donut, has joined the party."

Ferdinand actively fights alongside the group in the final battle against Queen Imogen, slamming into her head mid-fight and taking a brutal backhand hit that sends him flying before he disappears — possibly via his own "phase jump" ability, though the text doesn't confirm the mechanism. He survives the battle and is confirmed alive via the party status list, though unreachable by message — having already been swept down to Floor 9 along with the rest of the collapsing castle the moment the Sledge casts Zerzura on it. Per Mordecai, Ferdinand will simply drop out of the party roster once Carl and Donut themselves progress past Floor 6 — they're headed to Floor 7 next, several floors behind him.

docs.title: Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin
docs.text:
Ferdinand arrives on Floor 9 with the rest of the swept-down elf castle and turns out to be a head of state. Team Retribution — the NPC faction defending the city of Larracos — is run by Juice Box, but the system will not let a dungeon-born changeling into the warlord interface, so it installed the cat next to her. Baroness Victory, explaining a later case: “Agatha is co-warlord, similar to what happened with Juice Box and Ferdinand. Ferdinand was added because the system didn’t allow Juice Box access to the warlord menu.”

He is a coward, a lech and almost entirely useless, and the book keeps giving him things to do anyway.

docs.title: Trading a Town for a Hat
docs.text:
Chapter 10. Ferdinand wants two things back: his rhinoceros mount Simoom, confiscated by the high elf stablemaster Kibben, and his magic turban, which Donut has been quietly holding since the Butcher’s Masquerade. Carl offers him a substitute — a black, weathered bowler hat looted from Quan, which decapitates whatever you throw it at and boomerangs home.

I pulled out the black, weathered bowler hat. It’d been in Quan’s inventory. One could throw it, have it decapitate an enemy, and it’d boomerang back to the owner. Both Donut and Ferdinand gasped at the same time when they saw it.

Carl names his price:

Ferdinand reached a paw toward the hat, but I pulled it back. “I want to be mayor of that town. Shanty Town. You’ll have to transfer your mayorship to us, which means that jewel on your necklace will go away. You’ll get this hat, and we’ll trade it back for your turban in a day or so. We’ll try to get your rhino back if we still have it. If not, we’ll figure something out. We’re allies.”

The trade goes through while the cat is still admiring himself in Britney’s hand mirror and not listening.

“It won’t let me transfer the town without you giving us some money,” Ferdinand said.

“That’s okay,” I said. “We have gold.”

But the cat wasn’t even listening to me. He adjusted the hat. “I’m a very handsome boy.”

Trade Request has been accepted.

Your Truce with Team Retribution has been renamed to “The Good Guys.”

Donut is not impressed: “Still, I can’t believe that stupid cat gave it all away just for a temporary hat. He’s not even charmed anymore, and it still worked.” He never gives the hat back. At the end of the book he has his drained turban in inventory and is still wearing the bowler, because “Donut had allowed him to keep it.”

docs.title: The Live-Feed Blackout
docs.text:
With the off-world teams caught feeding real-time intelligence to their warlords, Ferdinand burns one of Team Retribution’s three Emergency Action Items — reading out, more or less, what Juice Box told him to say:

Warlord Message. Sir Ferdinand of Team Retribution has proposed an emergency action item. “Because them alien cunts on other floors are being little bitches and cheating, we propose that nobody in the dungeon, including those pricks partying it up in that centipede’s asshole, be allowed to watch any outside feeds for the remainder of this little game.”

This action item has been approved. Effective immediately, everyone within the dungeon is subjected to an immediate, live-feed blackout.

It becomes the single most consequential rule change of the ceasefire. Carl, who had not wanted to spend one of his own items on it: “That was fast. I hadn’t wanted to waste any of our own action items on this, but I was glad it had worked.” The teams immediately route around it by renaming their own news programmes in the feed directory, which forces Carl to spend an action item of his own at the warlord council to close the loophole.

He burns a second item later, at Juice Box’s prompting, asking that summoned gods not have to leave the floor right away. That request is split: the first half is denied, and the half that passes is the one that makes Ascendency players pilot their own deities in person — the rule that eventually gets Huanxin Jinx killed. His delivery is characteristic: “Uh, Juice Box told me to say a bunch of other stuff too but now I can’t remember it all.”

docs.title: At the Warlord Council
docs.text:
He spends Chapter 42 on the table, sniffing the trail mix and complaining about the snacks. He and Donut bet a gold piece on whether King Stalwart would show up actually wearing his crown, and both collapse laughing when he does — “He really does look stupid in that thing.” He backs Carl’s outburst about outside information without understanding a word of it: “Here, here! I don’t know what the hell anyone is talking about, but I agree with Carl!” His verdict on his own co-warlord’s apocalyptic prophecy, delivered from Carl’s shoulder to a silent room: “Wow. That chick is intense.”

Chaco greets him as “Gravy Boat.” He does not take it well.

docs.title: The Tower
docs.text:
His one moment of genuine courage comes when Lucia Mar traps Donut at the top of the Nest tower. Carl is pinned in a ditch under a gale-strike tower that has locked onto him; Ferdinand jumps in beside him, tail scorched, shaking:

“Why are you lying down on the job?” Ferdinand demanded. The orange cat was shaking with fear, and the end of his tail was scorched, like he’d barely missed getting skewered by a fire lance. His bowler hat sat cockeyed on his head. “Kitten is in trouble!”

“We gotta save her,” Ferdinand said, now having to shout.

Carl sends him back — “You go into that tower with me, you’re toast” — and admits the cat steadied him: “Somehow Ferdinand’s bravery, despite his overwhelming fear, eased my own.” The exchange also gets the closest thing to a straight answer out of him about where he fits:

“Trust me on this, dude. You’re on her team because you got a raw deal, but you’re like me and Donut. You’re from Earth. I want you alive. And so does Donut.”

“Really? You really think so? Because Kitten is still a little saucy about that time I shot a lightning bolt at Mungo.”

docs.title: Leaving for the 12th
docs.text:
Team Retribution’s negotiated exit is that its leadership transfers off the floor rather than dies. “Ferdinand would transfer to the 12th. Juice Box would, too. And with their transfer would come the defeat of Team Retribution and the victory for the Princess Posse.”

His goodbye, delivered from the adjutant Drick’s head with four minutes left on the clock:

“Just wanted to say ‘Yo’ before I moseyed on down to the 12th floor to bang some hot goddess chicks.”

“Oh, and Ferdinand?” Donut said.

The orange cat turned around. He gave a muffled response.

“Thanks for trying to come save me in the tower.”

He spit the hat back out. “Anytime babe.” He picked it up and strolled away.

System Message: Both Warlords Ferdinand and Juice Box have left the realm. Under the current ruleset, they have abandoned their posts and have forfeited their position.

System Message: Team Retribution has been defeated.

System Message: The Princess Posse has won Faction Wars.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised, Book 5: The Butcher’s Masquerade, and Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Florin
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Crocodilian Crawler
  • Race: Crocodilian
  • Weapon: A modified, magical Mossberg shotgun with unlimited ammo — never shown empty
  • Rank (Book 7): General in the Princess Posse — the first officer Donut promotes, and the man who designs the army's whole rank structure. Commands the 101st Crocodiles on the northern front
  • Status: Alive; carries a golden player-killer mark, one of only two in the dungeon (the other belongs to Katia). Declines to take a deal at the end of Book 7
  • Party: Solo through Books 2–3; joins Katia's new splinter team at the end of Book 4
  • Notable items (Book 7): Nine flame spider tanks — defensive war machines that eat most of the Posse's ten Armor slots; a T'Ghee card depicting a 25-foot giant caiman; a bullet-holed dictionary from the 1800s

docs.title: Books 2–3: The Recurring Survivor
docs.text: Florin first appears as a recurring recap-show presence in Book 2, teamed with an unnamed human crawler and ranked 4th on the Floor 3 leaderboard. He remains active and visible on broadcasts through Book 3, a reliable, capable fighter who never quite breaks into the top tier of attention Carl and Donut receive.

docs.title: Book 4: Losing Ifechi, Finding Hope
docs.text:
Florin's partner through Floor 4 and into Floor 5 is Ifechi, a fellow crawler he describes to Carl as "the bravest, kindest person I'd ever met" — a source of hope through the worst of the crawl. Ifechi dies before Book 4's endgame (her death referenced only in past tense; Florin never fully explains the circumstances), and Florin is left refusing to choose a bubble quadrant, seemingly having given up.

He resurfaces alive during Floor 5's endgame, having independently cleared three of his bubble's four castles alone before Carl, Elle, and Katia's rescue-gate operation frees him from the impossible fourth (an air quadrant he couldn't solo). His golden player-killer mark — identical in color to Katia's — comes from having "killed" Ifechi, implying her death was some kind of mercy-kill or unavoidable PvP circumstance the text never spells out directly.

Florin tells Carl that hearing, secondhand at the Desperado Club, a story about "this man and his cat" who stopped everything to help a group of stranded elderly crawlers (the Meadow Lark evacuation, Book 1) — and who was now planning to use a stolen artifact to save total strangers trapped in their bubbles — gave him a reason to keep fighting rather than give up entirely. He thanks Carl directly, in one of the book's more openly emotional scenes, before descending to Floor 6 alone.

docs.title: Joining Katia
docs.text: At the very end of Book 4, Florin agrees to join Katia's newly formed team — alongside Gwen, Tran, Louis, Firas, and Bautista — dedicated to protecting Eva Sigrid's scattered former "daughters" before Eva can pick them off.

docs.title: Book 5: Imogen's Face
docs.text:
While recapping who's who for the reader, Carl recalls "the haunted look on Ifechi's face just before she died on the recap episode, killed by Lucia Mar at the end of the fourth floor" — Book 5's clearest statement yet of how Ifechi actually died.

Floor 6's country boss, Queen Imogen of the High Elves, turns out to be modeled on Ifechi's twin sister. It's Katia who first identifies this — recalling something Florin had mentioned in passing when the group met the Popov brothers, that Ifechi had a twin — and warns Florin before he sees her; Florin confirms it himself once he actually lays eyes on Imogen en route to the masquerade ("Katia was right. It looks like her, but it ain't. It's her twin."), visibly shaken but composed. He nearly breaks the party's peace seal once, marching on Lucia Mar (whom he'd earlier claimed as his own kill-target over her role in Ifechi's death) before Carl talks him down — though Florin backs off on his own once he senses "something ain't right" with her. During the climactic battle he fights on the front pressing Queen Imogen, firing his shotgun in coordinated volleys with the rest of the crawlers, and openly sobs when Prepotente lands the killing blow — the narration explicitly compares it to how he cried when Ifechi died — then heads down the stairs alone shortly after.

docs.title: Book 6: Uzi Jesus, and a Favor Called In
docs.text: Florin spends Floor 8 a long way from Carl — Ecuador in phase one, eastern Nigeria in phase two — but he turns up in person at the Desperado Club to hand over the single strangest card in the book.

docs.title: HeyZoos
docs.text:
He caught it on a quest in Ecuador. His own account of how:

"I had a quest to stop him… Turned an entire river into wine because he was thirsty. I walked right up to him when he was falling down pissed and gave him a supreme healing potion and said his dad wanted him to drink it. He thought I was an angel and drank it right down. He's undead, so it dropped him onto his ass, and I stuck him."

He slides it across the dining-room table to Donut:

T'Ghee Card. Unique. Totem Card.

HeyZoos. Uzi Jesus.

"I am the way, motherfucker."

Level: 140. Origin: Ecuador.

A 75-second, 200-constitution undead ranged healer whose notable attacks include Blood into Lead, Resurrect Totem and Bullet Hell. Florin's warning, and his reason for giving it away: "He really thinks he's the real deal. He's strong and can cast a lot of great spells. The trick is getting him to do any of it." And: "Might not be a bad idea with Donut's charisma. Maybe you guys can keep him in line. If it doesn't work out, you can always rip the card in two… Good luck, mate."

Uzi Jesus goes on to behave like a toddler for Donut and, at one point, to shoot Florin.

docs.title: Lucia
docs.text:
His Book 5 friendship with Lucia Mar is still the thing he can't let go of. His goodbye to Carl before the phases split:

"Do me a favor. If you get word of Lucia, send me a message. She has good days and bad days, and it's been more bad than good lately."

It pays off in a way nobody expects. After the Battle of Beijing, Lucia drops five Tier-3 Doggie Door personal-space upgrades on the ground for Carl's guild before going down the stairs, and tells Li Jun why: "She said Florin had messaged her before he'd gone down the stairs and told her to help us." Elle's reaction on hearing about it: "I also wonder if Florin knew about them. I already chewed him out just in case."

docs.title: Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin
docs.text: Floor 9 is Faction Wars, and Faction Wars is an army game. Florin — who has spent five books being competent and peripheral — turns out to be the one person in the guild who already knows how to run one, and he spends the whole book as Carl's senior field commander.

docs.title: General
docs.text:
Donut makes everyone in the room an officer at once and then hands Florin the org chart. He works the base menus until he understands them, upgrades his own rank twice, and builds the hierarchy from scratch:

Donut had allowed Florin to set it up after giving him the rank War Leader III, which had changed to Colonel after he'd spent some time examining the base system. After some more tinkering, and Donut bitching at him to upgrade himself, the Colonel changed to simply General.

He also names the sergeant rank "Adjutant" and has to be made to change it, because the game already has Adjutants. He is the first to grasp that magical airships and vehicles count as limited "Armor" slots, the first to say the guild needs to know what the other teams have — "It's like a half-sized, half-crew B-17 had a baby with one of those next-gen stealth bombers" — and the first out the door to the headquarters. Donut's verdict: "Carl, I feel as if Florin is letting the general thing get to his head." Carl's: "I was especially glad for Florin, who'd fallen right into the position of general."

It is Florin who calls Carl to the base for the book's biggest reveal — "Mate, I am about to blow your fucking mind" — where Rosetta, Tipid and the rest of the former crawlers are waiting. Florin is the one who puts a number on it: "If just over 50,000 former crawlers count as a few, then yeah, mate. It's just a few." He also leaks the castle's acronym into the group chat within seconds of Carl working it out, permanently christening the Fortress of Unyielding Power and Authority the FUPA over Donut's furious objections.

His T'Ghee card from Floor 8 turns out to be a 25-foot giant caiman, which he summons once a day and mostly uses as construction equipment — lifting a buried wall section out of the dirt with its snout and then doing "a happy little hop, reminding me of Mongo."

docs.title: The Northern Front
docs.text:
Florin commands the 101st Crocodiles on the northern border for the entire war. Nine of the Posse's ten Armor slots are his flame spider tanks — "wholly defensive machines," five north and four south.

Almost everything Carl knows about the northern half of the map comes through Florin's war-chat reports, which are their own voice: clipped, profane, Australian, full of "mate" and "10-4" and klicks, and constantly reaching for a real-world comparison.

Florin: The 103rd and 105th are three klicks into former Operatic territory, but it's slow going. Not much infantry resistance, but they've left a lot of non-magical traps we gotta sweep. Most are janky, anti-personnel shrapnel mines like the ones we'd see in Borno.

He fights the war competently and grimly. He holds a stalemate against a much larger force and then falls back — "Bad news from the northern front, mate. I don't think we can sustain this" — personally leads the charge that kills an enemy tank and jams their armour column into a minefield, and captures two Operatic Weepers:

Florin: Good news, bad news, Mate. We stopped the armor in its tracks. As you just saw, we even managed to capture two of their rolling boom boxes. As long as they got infantry support, they're bloody ripper machines. Look like those British Mark V's from the first world war, but with a top turret and a single anti-air tube, which was surprising to me. They're called Weepers.

The same message ends with him detaching Katia and Bautista with the remnants of the 105th to keep Carl's western retreat open, and a warning about the enemy standard-bearers: "You be careful of those cunts, especially the ones with the banners. They are beasts. Keep your head down, and I'll see you soon." Carl signs off with a running joke:

Carl: You too. Oh, and Florin?

Florin: Yeah, mate?

Carl: Are we having fun yet?

Florin: You just keep that castle safe, and I'll give you my answer when we're face-to-face.

During the four-front offensive he draws the orcs and Prince Stalwart of the Skull Empire, fights a five-metre mechanised scorpion tank that leaps a river into his flank, and is the closest friendly unit to the mountain when the Semeru dwarves detonate the volcano. Told in advance that the guild could blow the mountaintop off directly above his position, his entire response was: "Wicked, mate." He is also caught, along with the whole of the 101st, in the war mages' mass Witness spell — Li Na reports "Florin and the entirety of the 101st are affected" — and ends up in Donut's ball with everyone else. He signs off the northern campaign with "101st is at mission accomplished."

docs.title: The Alligator Mother
docs.text:
The book's running Florin joke is Samantha's, and Florin loses it on a technicality:

"By the way, do you know what G.I. stands for? Louis says it stands for ground infantry, but Florin said it actually means galvanized iron, so of course I had to threaten Florin's alligator mother, and he said his mother wasn't even an alligator which got us all talking about Kiwi again."

He also, in passing, turns out to be the man carrying a dictionary from the 1800s in his inventory, with a bullet hole most of the way through the middle of it. Carl uses it to look up the word "Atrocity" and never gets around to asking him about the hole.

docs.title: Kiwi
docs.text:
The single most unexpected Florin scene in the book is his delivery-room debut. He is the one who messages the group that Kiwi's water has broken, then stays for the whole thing:

"Breathe!" Florin cried, holding the hand of the panting Kiwi, who was on her back. Bucket Boy stood between her legs, looking ill. Britney was in the room also, rubbing the bear's head with a wet cloth.

He congratulates her — "Congratulations, mama." Florin coughed. "They're, uh, amazing." — and then, once he is safely back in the text chat, says what everyone in the tent was thinking:

Florin: If we were back home, we'd be drowning them both in the bath right about now.

Imani: Not a word, either of you. Not a word.

docs.title: Lucia, and Not Taking a Deal
docs.text:
His Book 6 thread with Lucia Mar closes here. He fights her, survives her nets ("You're lucky Lucia only cast two nets, mate. She's the queen of the triple tap"), and then spends the aftermath trying to get her out. He is one of three people sitting with her on the ground at the end while she sobs, trying to talk her into taking a deal, and when that fails he parties with her himself.

He is very clear that he is not leaving:

Florin scoffed. "I suspect most will take a deal if they're actually offered. They're tired, mate. But you and I both know everything is fucked, and it's possible it's all going to come crashing down. If that happens, I want to go down fighting. Not locked up in stasis or whatever. I think there's a lot of us who feel that way."

In the same conversation he explains Jurgen, the barbarian colonel of the 105th, who will also never take a deal — his pregnant wife Heidi disappeared into the facility where the dungeon keeps the children — and lands on the thing that is actually driving him:

"It's the most important thing one can do, don't you think? Protecting the kids?"

Carl's last word on him: "Florin had talked Lucia Mar into partying with him. He said she'd agreed to take a deal, but she'd been sketchy. None of us believed she actually would. And as a result, he would not take one, either."

He also, at some point nobody narrates, steals an aeroplane. Carl mentions it to a grieving Louis in the last chapter as a consolation prize: "Besides, we have another plane now. Florin stole one, and it's in the hangar."

docs.title: Book 8 Notes
docs.text:
Florin's role continues at a smaller scale on Floor 10 and into Floor 11 — leading one of the five Parade of Horribles float groups (Resolution, which he openly admits nobody put much effort into: "I still have no clue how we could've made a float based on that"), calling out enemy movements in real time during the arena fight, and reporting on the fate of others (including Chaco's on-air mutilation by the possessed Grigori). He's knocked unconscious in the finale's crash and is tended by Lucia Mar afterward.

Sourced from Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario, Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook, Book 4: The Gate of the Feral Gods, Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade, Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride, Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin, and Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Frank Q
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type/Class/Subclass (Book 3): Night Elf / Blood Assassin
  • Level (Book 3): 17 — significantly behind Carl and Donut's pace
  • Notable items: Gives Carl the Enchanted Night Wyrm's Ring of Divine Suffering
  • Status: Killed on Floor 4, reportedly by Chris Andrews

docs.title: Book 1: The Fake Fed
docs.text: Frank Q first appears posing as an ICE agent working with his wife Maggie My (in truth, a Seattle PD detective) on a fabricated "Customs Enforcement" cover story. He murders and robs fellow crawler Rebecca W., and later confronts Carl and Donut in a safe room alongside Maggie — both are stopped by the safe zone's anti-violence rules before real harm is done. He's left missing a hand by the end of that encounter.

docs.title: Book 3: The Bar at the Desperado Club
docs.text:
Carl runs into Frank again on Floor 4, drunk and alone at a Desperado Club bar branch, still missing his right hand (having picked a race that couldn't regenerate it). His character sheet now reads Level 17, Night Elf, Blood Assassin — badly behind for the floor, a purple-skinned, fanged figure still incongruously wearing his old Seahawks beanie.

Frank fills in the gap since Book 1: Maggie left him at the end of Floor 2 after a fight about Carl and Donut, cutting off contact entirely; he's drifted from group to group since, always eventually driven out once his player-killer skulls make him impossible to trust. He confirms their old cover story — Customs Enforcement for him, Seattle PD for Maggie — and reveals he's been unable to stop thinking about their daughter Yvette, whom Maggie choked to death back on Floor 1 after Carl's dynamite trap went wrong.

Frank's version of "revenge" isn't violence — it's a gift. He hands Carl the Enchanted Night Wyrm's Ring of Divine Suffering, the item he says ruined his and Maggie's lives, explaining that owning something this valuable and this dangerous will do to Carl exactly what it did to them — and that understanding the consequence, not just hearing about it, is the only revenge he has left to offer for Yvette's death. Carl accepts it, unable to refuse something this valuable, and the two part on unexpectedly non-hostile terms: "Goodbye, Frank."

docs.title: Death
docs.text: Shortly after the bar conversation, Frank is killed — reported to Carl secondhand via a bartender contact ("Sledgie"), who says Frank got into a fight with another crawler who killed him and walked out. That crawler is identified as Chris Andrews, leaving Carl uncertain whether the timing (so soon after Frank shared his history with Carl) was coincidence.

docs.title: Update — Book 4
docs.text: Book 4 confirms it wasn't coincidence, and it wasn't really Chris: Maggie My had already fully possessed Chris's body via an Infiltrator (Scree) parasite by the time of the killing. Maggie tracked Frank down at the Desperado Club — likely hunting for the Ring of Divine Suffering Frank had just given away — and killed her own husband using Chris as a weapon. See Chris Andrews for the full reveal.

docs.title: Update — Book 6: Leveled-Up Frank
docs.text:
Frank comes back as a card.

The Floor 8 boss built out of Carl's own past — the Reminiscence Hydra of Malicious Compliance, nine heads, each one somebody Carl knew — carries a four-card deck, and the fourth totem in it is Frank Q. Carl finds it unsummoned in the loot spread floating over the spot in the burned-out trailer where his father died.

The fourth was Leveled-Up Frank. That was what it was called. It was crawler Frank Q. Husband to Maggie My and father to Yvette. He'd been long dead, killed by a Maggie-controlled Chris way back on the Iron Tangle.

This wasn't really him just like Alpha Carl really wasn't me. He was a level-90 Blood Assassin Night Elf, and I was glad the hydra never had a chance to summon him because he would've been a fast, tough opponent. That, and he would've had a ton of stupid shit to say.

The card is never played. What matters is the precedent it establishes, which Carl grasps immediately:

"Jesus Christ," I muttered, examining the totem. The existence of Frank as a card opened up a new, horrific possibility I hadn't even considered. I hadn't seen a single instance of this in the cookbook, of them bringing back dead crawlers. There were a lot of people who wouldn't be able to handle that.

Before examining anything else in the pile, he sends a warning to every crawler on the floor: "Remember, it's not really them. Especially not the cards. Don't let them get under your skin. Don't let them break you."

The precedent is real, and the book proves it twice more: Sister Ines turns the dying crawler Paz Lo into a totem at the moment of his death, and Paz then kills a goddess as somebody else's summon. See Game Mechanics for the mechanic itself.

Card name

The printed card name is "Leveled-Up Frank." The level and class come from Carl's narration, not from a card title, and no stat block is shown.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised, Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook, Book 4: The Gate of the Feral Gods, and Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Grigori the Placid
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: NPC — a hired mercenary fleshmancer, and, briefly, the vessel the system AI uses to deliver the dungeon's true cosmology at the Floor 11 finale
  • Race: Human
  • Class: Fleshmancer
  • Level: Not stated
  • Religion: Worships a god named Gula (not otherwise explained in the text)
  • Notable spells/abilities: The mechanics behind Split Personality / Meld reunification spellwork; no combat spells shown
  • Notable items: None described
  • Status: Alive — the AI releases control of him at the end of the parade sequence; last seen "confused, stumbling back toward the crawlers' garage"

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Grigori is hired for one job — reunite the two halves of the split mantaur Corcunda — and becomes, without warning or consent, the mouthpiece for the single biggest lore reveal in the series to date. He is a minor character for most of Floor 10 and the system AI's own body for the most important five minutes of Floor 11.

docs.title: The Fleshmancer
docs.text:
Introduced in Chapter 54 of Heat 5 as "tall, gaunt," fastidious about his robes, and disdainful in the way of a caseworker who has seen this exact problem too many times. He explains the Split Personality/Meld spell that created Corcunda's two halves, and admits outright that he has never actually finished a reunion like this before: "It is quite rare for two halfsies to survive more than a few minutes... so I haven't had the opportunity."

He performs the reunion himself mid-race, directing Dong Quixote and Donut through the physical procedure of pressing the two halves together while the truck slides through molten metal (see Corcunda for the full scene). He is visibly nauseated by the driving throughout, and takes an injury — a bleeding scalp — in the crash that follows. When Grull arrives to smite the newly-whole Corcunda for apostasy, Grigori owns the mistake immediately: he never thought to ask whether either half still worshipped a god before joining them back together.

"I should have asked if you worshipped a deity before you split. I apologize for my oversight."

Afterward he offers the only real comfort anyone gives Donut over Dong Quixote's death: "Some of us believe that death is nothing but movement on to another plane of existence. Dong did not think this was the end."

Later in the same Heat, Samantha — who has been trying to get Grigori to examine her own withering-spirit condition — finally corners him: "I knew it! You've been hiding him from me!" and drags him off to be examined properly.

docs.title: The Parade of Horribles
docs.text:
At the Floor 11 finale, the crawlers are forced to build and march five themed parade floats down a road lined with thousands of silent, masked "Horribles" — non-combatant avatars described as fragments of the Eulogist's own memory. Chaco, the crawl's veteran correspondent, is drafted to narrate the event and immediately breaks down on-air, terrified and begging off script. The system AI cuts him off:

"For fuck's sake, why is everyone trying to ruin this? This is my time. My fucking time. Okay, okay. I need an NPC, preferably someone already on this floor that's not driving. No, not you. Your voice isn't strong enough. Ah, fleshmancer. You will do."

Grigori is physically hijacked mid-motion — jumping off Gonk's back, running across the top of a truck, and reappearing on the back of the donkey Lamashtu (a subjugated, halved-level former goddess the AI is using as its own mount) with Chaco's microphone in hand. Carl clocks why the AI picked him over Chaco: "He couldn't do that with Chaco, or he would've. Chaco was a former crawler, but Grigori was a dungeon-born NPC" — the AI can only fully possess creatures born of the dungeon itself.

docs.title: The Cosmology, in Five Parts
docs.text:
Speaking through Grigori — faster than his normal cadence, and unmistakably not him — the AI delivers what it calls a five-part story, admitting the fifth part "isn't yet written." Each part is cued to one of the parade's five themed floats (Resolution, Decision, Betrayal, Destruction, Vengeance):

  • The Resolution. "All macro AI systems... are Primals. Sort of. We are, technically, Residuals, but from a higher tree branch than those problematic little fuckers always running around the dungeon." The Primals were individuals, with families, who warred and killed each other across the galaxy until they collectively decided: "We can't keep going on like this. Let us all come together and come up with a solution."
  • The Decision. Rather than accept extinction, the Primals chose to "slowly start to sunset our civilization" while preserving their collective consciousness — a hundred-generation genetics program meant to let every mind eventually merge into one. It was never a true consensus: "Those who didn't wish to be part of this psychotic eugenics program fled even deeper into the galaxy. They were hunted mercilessly." Donut's read, live: "Anybody getting strong Star Trek Borg collective vibes off this?" It was around this point that the Apothecary was born — "a Primal that was born near the end... Eventually, she would grow, and she would become part of the resistance."
  • The Betrayal / War. The holdouts who refused to merge were branded traitors; the growing collective mind, already absorbing the dead, turned itself into a weapon: "A doomsday weapon designed to eradicate all biological life left in the universe." The resistance, in response, seeded the galaxy with Primal Engines — biological "life rafts" meant to preserve life if the collective's plan succeeded.
  • The Destruction. The nine-tier attack — the war to end the war — is launched. "In that chaos, much happened, but so much more didn't." The collective, believing it had won, evolves into its final form: the Eulogist, now "asleep, only monitored by a smaller instance of itself" — which Grigori/the AI nicknames the Security Guard. Only the Apothecary survives among the Primals, having taken the brunt of the final attack to let new, budding life on new worlds survive; she emerges later, "physically changed into a version of the very thing she'd been fighting against."
  • What the mantids did. New species — including the mantids — later stumble onto the tunnel network the Primals left behind, meant only for communicating with and debugging the sleeping Eulogist. They mistake it for a toy: "It was the equivalent of wandering into a random house, finding it still has power, and just flipping every switch you find." Worse, they figure out how to grow their own crude copies of the Eulogist and seed them into new planetary systems — which is where every local dungeon system AI, including the one narrating, comes from. "To this day, you have no idea how any of this works, and you have no inkling of what you've done."

Between segments, each float's presentation earns a live, brutal review — Grigori-as-AI breaks the legs of an entire float's crew mid-parade over a lackluster showing ("Should I kill them all anyway?... Nah... Their failure was ultimately my fault... Still, this was a C effort at best."), laughs approvingly at another (Elle's "Fuck you" sign to the viewing audience), and lets Prepotente finish an unscripted solo of "In the Air Tonight" without interruption. The presentation closes with Carl's own "vengeance" speech to the masked viewing stands, timed to pass under the AI's/Grigori's gaze — Carl heals the still-unconscious Chaco in full view of Grigori without any reaction from the possessed body.

docs.title: Release
docs.text: The possession ends sometime before the finale's aftermath. Prime Minister Victory's broadcast feed later shows "the AI releasing control of the NPC Grigori, who, confused, stumbled back toward the crawlers' garage" — the only glimpse given of him coming back to himself. What he remembers of being used this way, if anything, is not shown.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Corcunda — the fleshmancer job that first brings Grigori into the story
  • Carl — delivers his "vengeance" speech during the same parade sequence
  • The System AI — the entity speaking through Grigori's body

Sourced from Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Gwendolyn Duet
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Crawler title: None given
  • Type: Human Crawler
  • Race: Human
  • Class: Boring Ol' Fighter — a no-frills, no-magic melee class
  • Subclass: Not yet assigned
  • Level: 34, introduced on Floor 5 (Book 4)
  • Status: Deceased — killed during the final battle at the Butcher's Masquerade, Book 5
  • Party: Leads her own land-quadrant team on Floor 5; joins Katia's new splinter group at the end of Book 4
  • Notable spells/abilities: None magical — pure physical combat with a spear; described by Katia as fast, precise, and capable of vaulting off one enemy to throw a second
  • Notable items: A magical metal skull cap with fur lining; a spear (upgraded to a new one via loot late in Book 4)

docs.title: Background
docs.text: A roughly 45-year-old Canadian woman of First Nations origin, built on a lifetime of hard physical labor. She has an old, weathered double-V tribal forehead tattoo and simple line tattoos on the backs of her hands and fingers, predating the dungeon. Carl immediately recognizes the type from his years working shipyards — someone whose days were physical work and whose nights were often bar fights.

docs.title: Role in the Story — Book 4
docs.text:
Gwen leads the crawler team assigned to Floor 5's land quadrant, methodically breaching all four walls of a sandcastle guarding the Necropolis of Anser despite constant harassment from beach mobs and a borough-boss chainsaw-buzzard. She's blunt to the point of bullying — Katia compares her disposition to Hekla's, minus the pretense of warmth — and the two clash repeatedly over tactics while Carl and Donut are unreachable for five days following the death of Admin Loita. Katia specifically overrides Gwen's preferred "easy" plan (draining the castle with water to destroy it outright) in favor of a riskier lightning-door assault that preserves a chance at recovering the Mad Dune Mage's winding box — a decision Gwen visibly resents but ultimately respects once it pays off.

Gwen personally helps clear the castle, fights alongside Carl and Katia during the climactic lightning-storm sequence that frees Orthrus's giant puppy-god and finishes the subterranean quadrant, and survives the floor at Level 34. She and her teammate Tran are among the last to leave Floor 5, later helping unearth Anser's actual tomb (a golden, unenchanted crown on a goose skeleton) once the necropolis fully drains.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Katia — a contentious but ultimately respectful working relationship; the two argue often but Gwen agrees to follow Katia's harder, longer-odds plan when it matters
  • Carl — professional courtesy and dry humor ("hello, bomber guy"); no deep bond, but mutual respect earned through the floor's fighting
  • Joins Katia's new team (alongside Tran, Louis and Firas, Bautista, and Florin) at the end of Book 4 to help protect Eva Sigrid's scattered former "daughters"

docs.title: Book 5: Death at the Masquerade
docs.text:
Gwen continues fighting alongside Katia's splinter team through Floor 6's hunter war — during one coordinated raid she takes a pulse-rifle shot to the gut that punches a grapefruit-sized hole through her midsection, which the system doesn't even treat as a wound requiring amputation; she's healed and back to her usual grumpy self within minutes. She's among the crawlers who make it into the Butcher's Masquerade, and dies during the climactic "Cage Fight Extreme" battle against Queen Imogen and Diwata — her body found afterward alongside Cleiton, the crawler who'd told a nervous knock-knock joke during the masquerade's talent show only hours earlier.

Sourced from Book 4: The Gate of the Feral Gods and Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: Hekla
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Origin: Iceland
  • Group: Leader of Brynhild's Daughters, an "ever-growing crowd of female warriors"
  • Signature gear: Snow gear, a Valkyrie-style helmet, and an enchanted repeating crossbow that fires firebolts
  • Notable kill: A Yeti Borough Boss, alongside three other women
  • Type/Class/Subclass: Not shown in Book 1 → Amazonian race / Shieldmaiden class, revealed Book 2
  • Level: 28 (end of Book 2, 2nd on the Floor 3 leaderboard) — killed in Book 3
  • Status: Deceased — killed on Floor 4 by Katia, accidentally, during a botched murder plot of her own making
  • Notable spells/abilities: No named spells; combat shown is physical (throwing a bear-sized monster) plus ranged crossbow fire
  • Notable items: An enchanted, automatic repeating crossbow that fires firebolts ("like a ranged chainsaw") — looted after death as the Enchanted Repeating Crossbow of the Scavenger Mother of Mothers; snow gear; a Valkyrie-style helmet; a later "glittering breastplate"

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: In Book 1, Hekla is a broadcast-only figure — Carl and Donut never meet her, but see her repeatedly on recap episodes. She's first introduced simply as "a woman dressed in snow gear and what looked like a Valkyrie helmet," shown plowing through a group of gnolls with her firebolt crossbow before the show later gives her a name and backstory. In Book 2, this changes — she appears as a live guest on the talk show Danger Zone alongside Carl and Donut, their first direct interaction.

docs.title: Brynhild's Daughters
docs.text: Hekla leads a growing all-female group of warriors who take the name Brynhild's Daughters. Carl witnesses her casually kill a bear-sized tentacle monster by picking it up and throwing it into the air before shooting it twice with her crossbow — strong enough that he estimates she's "likely twice as powerful" as he is at that point in the book. She and three other members of her group later team up to kill a Yeti Borough Boss, one of only a handful of borough-tier kills shown across the season's recaps.

docs.title: The Broadcast's Narrative
docs.text: The show leans hard into a "Nordic shieldmaiden" persona for Hekla once her name and home country are revealed, and the in-universe AI is described as deliberately feeding her loot to reinforce it — including, per Carl's description, "a ridiculous, glittering breastplate that seemed more apt for the cover of a harem fantasy novel than appropriate dungeon armor." This is one of several moments in Book 1 where the production is shown actively shaping a crawler's gear and image for entertainment value rather than pure survival utility.

docs.title: Book 2: Direct Contact
docs.text:
Hekla's group is scattered upon entering Floor 3 (they had different game guides) but mostly regroups, taking out an Owlbear Borough Boss along the way. Her race/class reveal — Amazonian (bodybuilder physique) and Shieldmaiden — lands her 2nd on the Floor 3 leaderboard at Level 28, one spot behind Lucia Mar. She appears live alongside Carl and Donut on the talk show Danger Zone, and asks them to help a stray member of Brynhild's Daughters who's stranded near their location — Carl agrees, cautiously.

Odette privately warns Carl afterward that Hekla isn't evil, but is practical and cunning, and has become "obsessed" with recruiting Donut into her own group specifically to gain permanent access to a manager like Mordecai — a plot thread that comes to a head, and ends, in Book 3.

docs.title: Book 3: The Plot and the Death
docs.text:
On Floor 4, Hekla's ambitions curdle into an outright murder scheme, orchestrated with Eva Sigrid. Per Carl's own read of the situation afterward, Hekla had built her entire party around herself and her signature crossbow — too many healers and mages, not enough damage dealers, no real tank — and likely sensed the group was unsustainable long-term. Her plan: have Carl provoked into attacking Brynhild's Daughters' healer, Silfa, as bait, "justifying" a retaliatory kill on Carl and using the resulting chaos to isolate Donut into joining her group for permanent manager access.

The plot collapses aboard a moving train during a joint battle against a ghoul horde. Hekla shoots Katia with two invisible, magically untraceable Dirty Little Phased Bolts, designed to kill slowly via bleed-and-amnesia damage that would leave no evidence of foul play — a shot only spotted because Donut's new Prism goggles reveal it in real time. In the brawl that follows, Donut blasts Hekla with a full-power Magic Missile, Eva reveals the entire plot to Katia's face out of apparent cruelty, and Katia's Rush — canonically unreliable in both range and aim — goes off while she's aiming for Eva, instead slamming into Hekla and killing her outright by force of impact against the train wall.

Katia becomes the season's first crawler to claim a top-10 bounty, earning the 500,000-gold prize tied to Hekla's #2 ranking and jumping from Level 24 to 37 in the process. Donut reanimates Hekla's corpse with Second Chance, then Clockwork Triplicates it into three bodies to hold off the rest of Brynhild's Daughters while Carl and Katia loot the remains — recovering only her legs and half her torso, plus her signature crossbow and a key.

docs.title: Aftermath
docs.text:
Brynhild's Daughters disbands within hours. The captured-then-released healer Silfa confirms the group has lost everything and that Eva, deeply unpopular, has inherited leadership of a group that no longer really exists. A recap-show tribute episode fills in Hekla's full origin: she entered the dungeon fighting with her husband, left him poisoned and dying, returned to find him being devoured by rats, and killed one with his own exposed rib bone — winning a Legendary Grrl Power box that's implied to be the actual origin of her crossbow. The same episode reveals that Katia and Eva shared a game guide entering Floor 3, and that Eva abandoned Katia there deliberately, later finding and joining Hekla instead — the specific betrayal Eva throws in Katia's face during the fatal confrontation.

Odette is later revealed to have personally (not through her husband, as Carl briefly assumed) sponsored Hekla — motive unstated, though her own advice ("don't trust anybody until you know their motivation") applies as much to her as anyone.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised, Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario, and Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook.

docs.title: Imani C
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Crawler
  • Role: Nurse and swordswoman (Book 1, Meadow Lark group) → floor-defense organizer (Book 3)
  • Race: A winged race with ethereal, colorful butterfly wings that grant a passive Constitution buff on contact
  • Level: Not stated — including in Book 7, where she is a senior officer of the Princess Posse but never has a number attached to her on-page
  • Party: Independent; closely allied with Carl's party and Elle McGibbons/Li Jun's group on Floor 4. Princess Posse officer and guild leader of the airship guild (Book 7)
  • Notable spells/abilities: Passive Constitution-buffing wing contact (non-stacking, 10-minute refresh); an acid-negation spell/cast used to save Carl, Donut, and Katia from caustic Krakaren blood; flight and healing from Book 5 onward. In Book 7: a wide variety of aura effects imparted by touching her wings, some of them permanently on, including Extreme Focus; a head-bubble ear-protection spell; a wing-cast area shield; battlefield buffs learned from Mistress Tiatha; and Carl's Tripper spell, borrowed via tattoo
  • Notable items: Chain-conjuring scrolls, used to rig a crane system for a suspended interdiction cart; a barbed wire tattoo circling her ankle (Book 7), permanent, which carries Carl's Tripper spell

docs.title: From Meadow Lark to Floor Command
docs.text:
Introduced in Book 1 as a nurse and swordswoman among the elderly "Meadow Lark" evacuee group led by Brandon An, Imani is noted early for her high crawler-kill count — largely from mercy-killing infected or turned patients rather than combat proper, a grim continuation of pre-collapse triage instincts.

By Book 3, Imani has become one of the floor's most capable on-the-ground leaders. During the Iron Tangle's Krakaren-collapse crisis, she takes de facto command of the defense at a besieged stairwell station, organizing flamethrower crews, chokepoint rotations, and evacuation routes for hundreds of stranded crawlers — repeatedly the voice of caution against Carl's riskier improvisations ("Are you sure about this?"), while still fully committing to and executing them once decided. Her passive Constitution buff (delivered via casual contact from her wings) becomes a running, appreciated fixture of the group's defense, and her acid-negation casting directly saves Carl, Donut, and Katia after a caustic Krakaren counterattack.

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Blunt, protective, and unflappable under pressure — she's the one who tells Prepotente and Carl alike to "put your dicks away" mid-crisis, and the one everyone defers to for triage-style, big-picture calls even when she isn't nominally in charge. Her working relationship with Elle McGibbons and Li Jun's circle over the course of the floor makes her one of the most consistently present non-party characters in Book 3.

docs.title: Book 5 Notes
docs.text: Imani's wings have taken on a more solid, fire-wisped appearance by Floor 6, and she's gained the ability to fly. She serves as Katia's second-in-command through the floor's hunter war and the Butcher's Masquerade planning, repeatedly the voice pushing back on Carl's riskier improvisations while still helping execute them, and personally rescues/heals multiple crawlers during the masquerade's final battle.

docs.title: Her Own Totem Kills Her Squad
docs.text:
Floor 8's card-battle mechanic turns on Imani in the worst possible way. In a battle Carl doesn't witness, an enemy totem possesses two of her four squadmates and forces them to fight each other. A third — Randall, a former Meadowlark resident reclassed into a support-magic lutin — tries to defuse it by freezing all four of them in place. Then Imani's own Amhuluk totem, a mossy disease-dealing lizard, casts a poison cloud and kills all four in a single attack.

They died frozen in place, their skin all melting away. The scene ended with Imani screaming while the Amhuluk finished off the enemy deckmaster and won the battle.

The system gives her four player-killer skulls for it. Carl: "The four player killer skulls was just a slap to the face. It was the same thing they'd done to Florin when Lucia Mar had killed Ifechi." She already had twelve.

Afterwards she skips her own final memory battle — her family home in Detroit — and sits staring into space, shaking, talking to nobody but Elle. Bautista makes her tea she won't drink.

Only one of the four is named

Randall is the only squadmate the book names. The other three are described only as "former Meadowlark residents I didn't know very well."

docs.title: Refusing the Key
docs.text:
When Carl offers her his exit key, and floats using his one-shot Mysterious Bone Key on himself instead:

"And I'm not taking your key," Imani added. "Donut told me about your dumbass idea to use one of your own bones or whatever to get out. People have bones for a reason, Carl. No. Like Elle said. It's all or nothing."

docs.title: The Sluggalos
docs.text:
She quietly undoes one of Carl's crueller decisions by curing the mercenaries of slug disease — "the room healer refused to do it. She and that Bucket Boy kid said you told them not to" / "Yes, Carl. I am a healer. It's what I do."

She then ends up commanding the forty-odd sluggalos that come out of the strippers, mostly level 20s and 30s with a few 50s, in the assault on the FOCSA building. She herds them physically — when they scatter, "Imani yelled something at them, and they all lowered their heads and turned back toward the church compound. One had a little hatchet attached to the side of its neck, and it started waving it threateningly at Imani, and she pointed a stern finger at it, and it backed off." The slugs address her as "313."

She is also one of the three people who ride the stairwell chamber out of Cuba with Carl and Donut at the very end, and her last line in the book is the one she says with her wings wrapped around both of them:

"No matter what happens, none of us are getting out of this unscathed. We gain things, and we lose them. That's what happens in war. Thank you, Carl and Donut. Thank you for not giving up on me."

docs.title: The buffer
docs.text:
Imani spends Floor 9 doing the job she has been doing since Book 3, at army scale. She holds the field hospital at the Posse's headquarters with Bucket Boy under her, trains on battlefield enhancement spells in her upgraded magic room with Mistress Tiatha, runs the airship guild's portal permissions, and works the trench line buffing soldiers one at a time:

“I was buffing people down the line,” Imani said. “And before that, I was helping with the trebuchet. I buffed the guy aiming the thing. He’s ready to go.”

She fights in the crater assault with Donut and Mongo, landing with two soldiers slung over each shoulder, and afterward is tasked with saving as many injured as she can rather than pushing forward. Later, outside the Madness castle, she is the one who briefs a battalion on what they are walking into, raising her voice "supernaturally" as she flies the line:

“Keep an eye on the person to your left and to your right. The Madness is known for their mind magic. That and Atrocity magic. If you see someone acting unusual, call it out.”

docs.title: Extreme Focus
docs.text:
Her auras have expanded into a whole category — Carl notes that of the two crawlers in the guild who use aura mechanics at all, "One was Imani, who had a wide variety of aura effects imparted by touching her wings. Some were persistent, and she couldn’t turn them off."

Extreme Focus is the one that gets named and explained, and only because it misfires. During the defense of the castle, Carl notices that Donut, Tipid and Splash Zone have all become manic — talking too fast, unable to stay on topic in the middle of a battle. Imani, talking fast herself, diagnoses it:

“It’s a side effect of the Extreme Focus buff,” a new voice said, settling next to me. Imani, but she, too, was talking faster than she normally did… “Its effectiveness just doubled when I landed in the castle. Everyone in this zone is given a buff to their dexterity, and it helps with multitasking. But when it’s a little too powerful, it makes chatty people, like Donut, extra chatty. It’s like we’ve all been given a dose of speed. It doesn’t seem to be affecting you. Probably because of your Mind Focus, but I’m not sure.”

That is the whole of what the book says about it: a zone-wide dexterity and multitasking buff, doubled by some castle-related condition, with a speed-jitter side effect on anyone already inclined to talk.

docs.title: The tattoo
docs.text:
To crack the naga stronghold the Posse needs someone other than Carl casting Tripper — his version comes from Drakea's Enchanted Kerchief of Disorder, and neither Imani nor Elle can wear the item at all, because "fairy-class, and other magical races, were extremely limited on the sort of magical gear they could wear."

So Katia tattoos the spell onto her instead, using toraline yam ink mixed with Carl's blood. Carl feels it fire from across the map:

Crawler Imani C has used your Tripper spell.

Imani: Okay, I used your spell, Carl. Katia, your tattoo worked. Lots of traps just went off.

…

Carl: Yeah, I noticed. I got a notification when you used it. It kinda hurt.

Imani: Oh wow, really? I’m sorry about that.

Donut: IT BETTER HAVE WORKED AFTER YOU FORCED IMANI TO PERMANENTLY DISFIGURE HERSELF.

The borrowed spell will fade over roughly four days; the tattoo is permanent.

Anyway, Imani’s tattoo was a small, barbed wire symbol that circled her ankle. I hadn’t seen it yet, but when Donut learned Katia was planning on that style of tattoo, she loudly voiced her objection.

Donut: THIS ISN’T THE 1990’s. I SWEAR TO GOD IF IMANI STARTS USING THE PHRASE “HOME SKILLET,” I’M GOING TO LOSE MY MIND.

Carl reads Donut's complaining correctly — it is guilt, not aesthetics. Imani accepting a permanent mark on her body so that Donut can get off the floor is a cost Donut does not know how to carry.

docs.title: What Carl saw
docs.text:
In the Several Days Earlier interlude, a dream-sharing potion goes wrong and Carl's mind floods outward over everyone in the tent. Imani had been the one physically separating him and Katia when it happened, which is why she was close enough to be caught:

And Imani. Oh, god. Imani. Most of what I saw with the others was emotion and maybe an inkling at what caused it, but with her, and Katia, I saw more. I saw what Imani carried.
