The odds of one of my spells inflicting an instakill is higher, too! Oh, oh, I can go invisible at will, and to top it off, I kept most of my spells from the last floor! But best of all, it comes with a hat! And a ghoulie suit! I don't know what that means, but I see a saferoom around the corner, and I must insist we get there straight away so I can collect my accessories. But isn't the name of the class absolute perfection? It's downright terrifying, and I love it."

Carl has to break the news that it is a ghillie suit, which she refuses to wear on sight — "It's like one of Signet's tattoo people fell through a paper shredder. If I put that on, I'll look like a tassel. You know how I feel about tassels, Carl." The kit is a cat-sized colour-changing ghillie suit (jacket slot; Blend into the Background, Cone of Silence) and a boonie hat (Targeting, plus further range). Worn together the bonuses compound, and Carl notes she could "snipe line-of-sight enemies from well over a mile away."

No system class block

Like Master Telephone Psychic before it, Deathbed Hellcat never gets a printed class description. Everything above is Donut's own dialogue and Carl's examination of the gear.

docs.title: The Tiara of a Thousand Lights
docs.text:
Her first celestial benefactor box from Long Haul Biological Waste Management Solutions — opened in Chapter 4, carried over unopened from the end of Book 6 — delivers a spaceship that folds into a mechanical hand holding a pillow and a tiara.

The Tiara of a Thousand Lights and Accompanying Charge Pillow.

This particular tiara is imbued with 99 Absorption Jewels.

The tiara itself has no inherent magical properties, and in its base state it gives no additional benefits or buffs except plus 10 to Charisma. However, it has the ability to be permanently charged with up to 99 different buff items.

Any enchanted hat left on the charge pillow for ten hours is permanently drained into the tiara — the hat survives, stripped, for her collection. The system's own assessment: "With some careful planning, one can turn this tiara into one of the most powerful items in the history of Dungeon Crawler World." The first thing Mordecai has her drain into it is the Deathbed Hellcat boonie hat, which is what makes the rest of the floor possible: with the tiara's targeting she no longer needs a sniper tower at all.

docs.title: The Nest, and sniping a city
docs.text:
Because the tiara covers the targeting, the Posse's great tower — the Nest, built on the lip of Shanty Town — is instead tuned to synergise with Atrocity-class spells, amplifying their area of effect across the whole battlefield. Donut works out of the top of it for the back half of the book, invisible in the ghillie suit, dropping war mages and defence towers with Magic Missile from across the funnel.

It is also where the book stops treating her competence as a joke. Carl finds her mid-shift:

Only then did Donut look up, and I could see her face. I tried not to react. I could see the hollowness to her eyes, as if they were trying to focus on something so far away, she couldn't quite see it. It'd only been a few hours, but the change was stark.

She'd been level 65 when she'd gone up into this tower. She was now level 74.

We gain things, and we lose them.

docs.title: Three Atrocities
docs.text:
Over the course of Faction Wars Donut casts three spells the system classifies as Atrocities. None of them are hers by choice; each one is the least-bad option on the table at the time. The mechanics belong on the individual spell pages — what follows is only when and why.

Rolling Battle Formation (Chapter 65) — with Louis shot down, a feral god loose and thousands of allied and enemy bodies fused into a single writhing pile outside the Madness castle, Donut casts it to roll the entire mass away from the god fight and onto a field of corpses. It sweeps up more than she intended, including the feral god Meatus and the goddess Eris, and holds every creature inside immobile and invulnerable until it breaks. Carl later tells her flatly that it was the right call: "You saved them by casting the Battle Formation spell. If you hadn't done it, half of everyone would be dead by now."

System Message: Warlord Princess Donut has committed an atrocity.

Donut: WELL, I NEVER. THAT WAS VERY RUDE.

You're Not Done Yet (Chapter 69) — a Legendary quest-box spellbook from early in the floor, which Mordecai recognises with genuine fear: "It's similar to Donut's Second Chance, but it's a lot more insidious." Tower-enhanced and cast over a field of thousands of donated corpses, it flays them into fleshers that sail across the battlefield at the Madness army. The AI's commentary elsewhere notes that war mages exist at all as "a result of too many combatants having access to You're Not Done Yet."

System Message: Warlord Princess Donut has committed another Atrocity. Wow. What a naughty kitty. I sure hope she isn't forced to cast a third.

War Crime (Chapter 76) — from the Legendary 1914 box awarded for killing Empress D'Nadia. It can only be cast three times ever, only on Scolopendra levels, and it combines two of the caster's own spells into something "most governments would consider unconscionable"; it also drops the caster to 1% health and cannot itself kill, so a finisher is mandatory. Carl reads the full description early and is horrified, mostly at what casting it might do to her. The plan is to use it to separate out the Reaver and Dream armies as the battle-formation ball breaks. Rosetta's case is that without it "we will lose hundreds, if not thousands," and Carl agrees. The combination she fires is Bijanbi and Astral Paw — a kilometre-wide ethereal cat's claw that catches thousands of soldiers and a god and crushes them into a flesher swarm over Shanty Town, to a world-wide soundtrack of Limp Bizkit's "Break Stuff."

She casts it under protest and mid-panic, with Carl shouting revised instructions at her:

"Okay, okay," I said. "Cast it, but don't pick fire! Pick something else! We need the Nest to stay intact!"

"What? What should I pick!?"

Afterwards she goes rigid, her health draining, and asks: "Did it work... Carl, I don't feel good. I have a new class. I have a bunch of new spells. What's happening?"

docs.title: The Oak Fell, and Champion of Nekhebit
docs.text:
The third Atrocity triggers the rest of it, all at once:

System Message: Warlord Princess Donut has committed a third Atrocity.

System Message: Warlord Princess Donut has received a new class.

System Message: Warlord Princess Donut will now be referred to as The Oak Fell.

System Message: The Oak Fell has been named Champion of Nekhebit.

The Oak Fell stacks on top of Former Child Actor rather than replacing it, and Mordecai and Rosetta both say they have never seen a class awarded that way. Its spells are deity spells and read as druidic — Raise Forest (trees and plants over a square kilometre per spell level), one that turns water to salt water, and Gather Ye, Vermin, which draws every small mammal within ten kilometres to her. Donut is scandalised by the last one and blames the AI.

Champion of Nekhebit is the goddess Odette is currently driving. It is presented as a reward and functions as a leash. Donut's own summary:

"This new Oak Fell class and this champion thing are in addition to my original class. I don't even worship Nekhebit, and it says I don't have to if I don't want to, but I'm not allowed to worship anyone else who's not in her 'court.' Both the class and the title come with a bunch of weird spells. ..."

Rosetta gives Carl the version she takes care Donut does not hear:

"It's similar to worshiping the deity. Enemies of Nekhebit will receive a bounty if they kill her." She'd lowered her voice, making certain Donut wasn't in earshot. "Honestly, it's not too unlike Conscription, but with a lot more autonomy for Donut. Should the goddess want her to do something, she can order her to do it or face a smite."

Milk's theory is that the class is "a side effect of some posturing that's currently happening on the 12th," and that the Champion title in particular "was something that was set in motion by Nekhebit." Rosetta guesses at the mechanism: "Probably something along the lines, 'the first crawler to cast three atrocities on the next floor gets the title and class.'" Carl's reaction is two words: Fucking Odette. Donut's objection is administrative: she spends the next several chapters in warlord chat as The Champion of Nekhebit, unable to change her display name back — "ALSO HOW CAN I CHANGE MY NAME BACK TO WARLORD DONUT? IT DOESN'T DO THIS IN THE REGULAR CHAT."

docs.title: Breaking the stat ceiling
docs.text:
The same moment hands her four benefit choices at once, and she takes them all in a single burst of chat while Mordecai tries to slow her down:

Donut: GOODNESS, I'M NOT GOING TO PICK THE SWOLE BENEFIT. DO YOU REMEMBER WHAT IT DID TO CARL? CAN YOU IMAGINE? I'M GOING TO PICK MUSCLE MOMMY FOR STRENGTH SO MONGO IS STRONGER, AND FOR INTELLIGENCE I PICK BRAIN TRUST SO I CAN MAKE MAGIC MISSILE EVEN MORE POWERFUL. I ALSO HAVE ONE TO PICK FOR MY CHARISMA TOPPING 200. I'M GOING TO PICK ONE CALLED WHOLESALE DISCOUNT.

Mordecai: Uh, are you sure about that Muscle Mommy benefit?

Donut: TOO LATE. I PICKED IT. WOW! HAVE YOU SEEN MY CHARISMA?

  • Base Intelligence and Strength both cross 100 — Brain Trust and Muscle Mommy, the latter adding 25% of Donut's strength to Mongo's.
  • Base Charisma crosses 200 — Wholesale Discount, everything at cost in the store.
  • Mordecai on the result: "I think the Bopcas will be worshiping you again. Your charm and Love Vampire skills are stronger than that of most gods."

A fourth natural benefit, Monologue, arrives separately and on different terms — Carl describes it as "one of several benefits crawlers received when their boosted stats topped 300." It is a charisma-based skill that terrifies the enemy and pays her experience in proportion to how frightened they are. She debuts it while circling Huanxin Jinx in Chapter 86.

Her own verdict on the whole package, delivered while insisting Mongo and Rend be kept caged away from the gore: "As the strongest crawler in the dungeon I have to maintain a sense of decorum."

docs.title: The dog on her flank
docs.text:
To make War Crime work, Rosetta needs Donut to carry a second spell at level 8 or higher within minutes, which means a tattoo. Donut refuses, loudly and repeatedly — "DONUT: ROSETTA AND EDGAR ARE TRYING TO DEFILE MY ASS" — and Carl calls it off rather than force her. Then she tells him the real objection:

"Carl," Donut said, looking up at me. "It's okay... You're right. It'll work. It's just... I hoped none of them would be on the outside."

"What do you mean?"

"The scars."

Carl's answer is that a chosen mark is not a scar, "it will be a badge of honor," and that she can still say no. She agrees on one condition — "I'll only do it if you also get a matching one. A matching ass tattoo" — and Carl accepts.

Edgar the tortoise inks it on her shaved right flank, holding the poker in his mouth, using an ink he has never tried before, refusing to say what he is drawing until the last second ("A dog."). Milk then writes Words of Power over it in two colours of calligraphic ink to force the spell temporarily up to level 15. The result:

It was a simple, rather adorable line art tattoo of a dog. As I watched, the tattoo did, indeed, move. It lifted its leg and started to lick itself.

The spell is Bijanbi — a wide-area variant of Dinner Bell, extracted from a fallen cleric, which drags enemies toward a designated point. It comes from a god called Wepwawet, which delights her for entirely the wrong reason: "Carl, Carl, it says he's in the 'Court of Nekhebit!' and I can worship Odette now, too!" She also picks up two achievements for it, one calling her a traitor and one awarding her a stolen catalytic converter, and immediately announces she is getting it lasered off on the next floor.

docs.title: Killing Empress D'Nadia
docs.text:
Her former sponsor, now warlord of the Prism, dies in Chapter 26 at Donut's direction. Carl has marked her and is on the edge of doing it himself in a state he has never been in before; Donut talks him back over chat ("No, Carl. Please, no. I need you to step back."), then takes the kill herself, in character, out loud:

"Empress, Darling," Donut said. "Mongo would like to express his utmost disappointment at how you judged him during the pet show."

The system credits it to the raptor:

System Message: Warlord D'Nadia of the Prism has fallen. Credit for the kill has been given to pet Mongo of the Princess Posse.

System Message: The Prism has been defeated.

It also earns Carl the Gavrilo Princip achievement and the Legendary 1914 box that War Crime comes out of — so D'Nadia's death is, indirectly, the origin of the spell that reshapes the rest of the floor.

docs.title: Killing Huanxin Jinx
docs.text:
Chapter 86, with eight minutes left before Emberus destroys the floor. Huanxin Jinx, CEO of Icon Industries, has arrived driving the goddess Eileithyia to collect Katia. Donut has arranged for her to be standing on a floor inscribed with words of power, and the moment Huanxin is distracted she is ripped out of the goddess's soul armour and dumped, shielded and furious, into the circle. Eileithyia herself is frozen until Katia makes her choice.

Donut circles her, weaving Monologue, strips her shields with a Claw skill she has trained from level 4 toward 15 ("All cats have it, naturally"), and then introduces the last guest.

The chain of custody on the kill is precise, and every link matters:

  1. The mount is a Quadruped weapon mount — "The scorpion's bite," a non-magical bandolier from a gold benefactor box sent by the Apothecary. It allows ranged weapons to be mounted on her back and fired and loaded by inventory action.
  2. The weapon is the Enchanted Repeating Crossbow of the Scavenger Mother of Mothers — Katia's crossbow, formed onto the mount, "bigger than Donut" and unloaded. Donut notes it is underpowered for her because "I don't have any women in my party."
  3. The bolt is Mordecai's. Plain, unenchanted, and tipped with his mother's ashes:

"No, I can't. Not directly," Mordecai said. He held something up. It was a simple crossbow bolt. There was nothing magical about it. "You see this?" He flicked the tip. "My brother died because of you and because of Odette and because of Chaco. But mostly because of you. Some of my mother's ashes are built into the tip of this bolt. It's a funeral rite in my culture. To make a weapon with the ashes of those you lost. My mother died before the crawl came to my world, and I'm grateful for the opportunity to allow her to avenge her son."

Mordecai — a non-combatant NPC who cannot touch her — loads the bolt into the crossbow on Donut's back and walks out of the tent. Donut finishes her sentence and fires:

"We don't really need to go through all this. But we want to. We want to show those of you on the 12th floor what's coming. You're strong, yes. But we are getting stronger every day. And you know what? We don't need to kill the gods and goddesses to win. No, honey..."

The crossbow on her back fired, and the bolt slammed right between the multiple sets of eyes of the alien.

Huaxin Jinx, CEO of Icon industries rocketed backwards, slid across the floor, and came to a rest at Victory's feet, dead.

"...We just need to kill you."

She undercuts the whole thing herself a chapter later, which is the most Donut thing in the book:

"I feel really bad about pooping in Mordecai's mother's ashes now. Do you think any of it got into the tip thing? I'm never going to not think of that now when I think of Huanxin. It was supposed to be this big, grand gesture, but she was really killed by a cat poop arrow."

docs.title: "They are not going to break me."
docs.text:
Donut ends Book 7 having lost Katia to the twelfth floor, lost the sponsor who sold her, and spent hours doing things she will not be able to un-know. Carl watches her cover it — "I could tell she was struggling, but the fact she was actively covering it was such a relief" — and at the very last moment, walking to the stairwell as Emberus burns Larracos off the floor, asks her directly:

"You doing okay?" I asked Donut as we moved to the stairwell.

"I'm going to miss her," she said. "But you know what, Carl?"

"What's that?"

"They are not going to break me. No matter how hard they try."

I reached up, and I gave her a pat.

Together, we walked into the stairwell, leaving the now-empty battlefield of Larracos behind.

It is deliberately the same sentence Carl has been saying to himself since Floor 1, turned outward and made plural.

docs.title: Other Book 7 notes
docs.text:
• Party leader: Carl takes the role from her in Chapter 27 on base stats and she pretends to be furious about it; she takes it straight back in Chapter 77 — "At least I'm back in my rightful spot as leader of the party."
  • New gear: the Tiara of a Thousand Lights and its charge pillow; the Deathbed Hellcat ghillie suit and boonie hat; a cloak she insists on calling her "champion shawl," which has been quietly training her Claw skill; celestial knee pads passed to her by Katia, carrying an Eileithyia 500% damage bonus against enemies; and the Apothecary's quadruped weapon mount.
  • New spells: You're Not Done Yet, War Crime, Flak, Shield and Sentry from floor and quest boxes; Bijanbi by tattoo; and the Oak Fell deity spells.
  • She collects two more Celestial boxes and a Lorena Bobbitt achievement in the same minute she becomes The Oak Fell.
  • Mongo's burned wing is regrown, and Muscle Mommy leaves him "decidedly more buff." Rend, Carl's inherited meatball, joins the household.
  • Her charisma finishes the book "way above 300" with gear, though not yet at base — the distinction annoys her, since Li Na gets system-wide announcements for maxing base stats and she does not.

docs.title: Claw Breaks the Level-15 Cap
docs.text:
Early on Floor 10, Rosetta fits Donut for claw caps to keep her from accidentally shredding furniture, and casually suggests she check her Claw skill again. It has passed the previous level-15 ceiling entirely:

"My goodness," Donut said a moment later. "It's at level 17! 17! I thought it topped out at 15!"

Mordecai's read is that a divine-tier item is behind it: "It's from the gods, and when it comes to gods, all bets are off... you've gone from a ranged powerhouse to one of the most powerful melee fighters in the game's history. Or you can use your Astral Paw spell to cut through almost anything." (The full mechanics of the upgrade belong on an Abilities-pass page once one exists for Claw; this page notes only that the jump happens and when.)

docs.title: Astral Paw, Twice More
docs.text:
The upgraded claw gets two standout demonstrations later in the book. In Heat 7, three Russian crawlers (the "Tracksuit Troika") try to double-cross an escape pact and make a run for a portal in a shielded Cadillac; once the shield drops, Donut ends it in one line:

Donut cast Astral Paw. She smashed the car where it stood, crushing it like a tin can. The Cadillac simply ceased to exist.

Moments later in the same heat, the drunk, grieving unicorn Dwight — armed with a missile launcher and screaming threats — loses his head "in a single swipe of Donut's claw" the instant the race begins, before he can fire a shot. See Supporting cast for Dwight and Lucienne.

docs.title: Killing Mitch
docs.text: During the Heat 7 Desperado Club ambush, the shadow mimic posing as the casino's croupier ("Mitch") is frozen solid by Carl's Eye of the Bedlam Bride while Carl is transformed into a dog; Donut lands the actual kill with repeated Magic Missile casts while he's immobile. See Carl for the full scene.

docs.title: Facing Down Chandra
docs.text:
When Princess Chandra, Esq. — Donut's newly assigned attorney — presents her with a conservatorship claim arguing Donut's species "was not yet recognized as a legally competent racial entity," Donut dismantles the argument without raising her voice, turns a matching set of Carl's father's own court documents back on her, and drives her out of the guild's safe room in a panic:

"They paint a very distinct picture of who Carl's father was as a person. Much the same way these papers paint a picture of who you are, Princess Chandra... What a sad little snake you are. I pity you."

See Chandra's own page for the full confrontation and its aftermath.

docs.title: The Wrong Biscuit
docs.text:
At the Floor 11 finale, mid-battle, an Eris-triggered inventory scramble scatters every party member's items into everyone else's hotlists. Carl needs Donut to find and combine a specific banger sphere with an enriched pet biscuit meant to turn the boss Scolopendra into a harmless, mindless pet the party can carry in inventory as a fail-safe. In the chaos, she hands him the wrong one — the same kind of "Nothing Special" sapience-granting biscuit already used on Penelope (see Penelope) — and only admits it after the fact:

"So, with the inventory. It was happening so fast, I made a mistake. Like, a really, really bad one."

Instead of a mindless pet, the transformed Scolopendra emerges as a fully sapient, flirtatious crawler — "Sexy Scolopendra," Level 1, Crawler #12,953,456 — who promptly wraps herself around Carl: "Hi, Carl." Carl's own reaction makes the stakes plain: "Donut had given me the wrong pet biscuit." The intended fail-safe — carrying a mindless Scolopendra as insurance against the party's own deaths — is gone; what they get instead is a new, willing ally with no obligation to obey them.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised, Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario, Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook, Book 4: The Gate of the Feral Gods, Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade, Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride, Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin, and Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Princess Vinata
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: NPC warlord — the Sultana, playing the historical role of the Sepsis Whore, leader of the Blood Sultanate in Faction Wars. Outside the dungeon she is the real-life crown princess of the naga, daughter of the king, a war veteran and lead advisor to her father
  • Race: Naga — and an unusual one. Six arms rather than the usual four, “half again as big as any” other naga Carl has seen, with solid red eyes that have no pupils or slits. In-game she is a brilliant, glossy white with gold along the edge of her cobra hood; the white is makeup
  • Class: None stated — warlords are not given character sheets
  • Subclass: None stated
  • Level: Not stated
  • Religion: Worshipper of Khepri, God of Rebirth and the Sunrise, Level 250 — a break in naga tradition, and the centrepiece of her trap
  • Notable spells/abilities: Travel the Path and Welcome Home, the light-god spell pair that lets her vanish instantly from her own throne room; a temporary Immortality boon from Khepri’s presence; Invisibility and Speed potions; glowing daggers in her lower hands
  • Notable items: A golden breastplate embossed with a tree branch bearing a single flower; golden bracelets on each of her six arms, “that jingled and sang with each wave-like movement”
  • Status: Deceased — killed at the end of Chapter 54 in the lobby of Club Vanquisher by a hatchet to the skull from the sluggalette Kandy “Bigs” Newton

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Vinata is the reigning Sepsis Whore: the target Donut has been contractually locked into killing since Book 1, when she put the Crown of the Sepsis Whore on her head before Mordecai could finish reading the warning. She is also, unusually for a five-book payoff, a genuinely frightening person in her own right.

Carl meets her at the warlord council in Chapter 42, where she materialises coiled beside him with no chair, “bigger than I was expecting, like a building had just suddenly appeared to my left,” smelling of sweet flowers.

I’d seen several nagas at this point, but I’d never seen anything quite like this woman. Her very presence was electric, and I had to make an effort to close my mouth. I hadn’t had a reaction like this since I’d first seen Signet on the third floor, but that had been a magical charm. And that had been a physical attraction. Such effects were not active here in this room. Still, I felt this overpowering sense of awe. I felt... small in her presence. This was how a mouse felt when it was placed into the cage with a snake.

Her introduction is a handshake Carl’s hand passes straight through:

“Carl,” she said, her voice sounding surprisingly feminine for such a large creature. It was like we were the only two in the room. “I don’t believe we’ve properly met.” She held out her lowest arm and offered it to me, palm down. “My name is Princess Vinata. But for these games, you’re welcome to call me the Whore.”

The chapter opens with a warning from an earlier cookbook author:

The naga. Beware the naga. They are cunning, and sometimes I wonder if they can read one’s mind. The others say that the mantids are the masters of strategy, but I do not believe this. Even though everything seems to be going wrong for the nagas this season, I cannot shake the idea that this all isn’t part of some grand scheme. Underestimate them at your own peril.

docs.title: The Ghost of Faction Wars
docs.text:
The Blood Sultanate are perennial losers who have never once lost their Sultana. Their castle is almost always the first to fall, at ruinous cost to the NPCs and mercenaries left holding it — and every single season, by the time the invaders reach her inner sanctum, she is simply gone.

Viewers would carefully watch the naga feed to see where she went. They’d watch the castle get invaded while the sultana would remain in her chambers, and when the invaders got close, the veiled naga would calmly get up from her nest of pillows, go through a door, and then she’d simply be gone. And not just her, but her entire elite honor guard of six nagas.

The vanishing act is deliberate branding. The naga’s continued participation in Faction Wars is a tourism campaign: after she disappears, the feed fills with advertisements for the “exotic” naga system, the ancient palace, the ziggurats, the Forbidden Bazaar. Whole tunnel communities argue about how she does it. Nobody has ever infiltrated the naga inner sanctum — not even Juice Box’s changelings, and the awakened NPC Arief will not try:

“The nagas are not very good at mass warfare, and they say they never win this game. It is said theirs is a court of assassins, not warriors. If they are to win, it is with a poisoned blade in the dark, not with the marching of a thousand feet.”

docs.title: “I wonder how you will react”
docs.text:
At the council she spends the meeting whispering to Carl alone, with a polite, serene smile never leaving her face. She opens by telling him a piece of non-public news — that Cascadia’s family have just been killed in the Borant system — and watching him watch the kua-tin fall apart. Asked how she could possibly know that, given adjutants and warlords are cut off from outside information, she does not answer. Instead:

“I wonder how you will react when you learn your entire family is dead as well?”

Carl says his family is already dead. She clarifies, and it turns into the only real offer anyone makes him all book:

“That’s not the family of which I speak, Carl. You and I both know you will have to make your move soon. Perhaps it’s happening now, while we are up here. We are expecting you, and we will be ready. They will all die, and after, what will happen? Will you become catatonic like Cascadia? When you are forced to choose between Donut and Katia, what choice will you make? How will the other survivors, if any, react? Say the word. Simply nod, and we will take care of your Katia problem for you. We do not have to be enemies, Carl. We can both survive this, and perhaps, gain something in the process.”

And then the recruitment pitch:

“I would very much like to make peace with you. I would like for you to join us in our system when this is all done. My father’s court could always use someone like you. We have great plans. We, too, are survivors. That is how we are the same, you and I.”

The whispering is also cover. The council is a stalling operation: while Vinata holds Carl’s attention, Odette blunders into revealing that the Sultanate owns Blood Hunter Holdings, and Carl works out that the missing naga army is not hiding — it is dead, wiped out by Prepotente at the start of hostilities, with the Sultanate quietly pretending otherwise. Donut addresses her directly for the first and only time:

Donut looked Vinata up and down, and for the first time, addressed the naga princess directly. “Oh, honey. And I thought I was going to be the one who killed you.” She licked her paw and groomed herself for a short moment. “In the eternal words of my mulleted friend, Holger. You done stuck your pecker in the wrong beehive.”

docs.title: Operation: Snake Pit
docs.text:
Carl’s plan to free Donut and Katia from the crown runs roughly from Chapters 44 to 55 under the codename Operation: Snake Pit. It required killing the four blood members of the Blood Sultanate’s line of succession out of the eleven naga playing this season:

  1. Princess Vinata herself, the Sultana.
  2. and 3. Two female assistants holding the title Ikbal — in real life, Vinata’s cousins. One is married to Rishi, the temple guard. The AI’s boss-battle commentary describes the pair as a graphic designer and a PR agent.
  3. The male head of her castle guard, also a cousin, and — per rumour reported by Rosetta — her lover. Carl calls him “the Sultana’s real-life boyfriend”; the AI, during the temple fight, calls him her “secret husband.”

No names given

The text never names the two cousins or the head of the castle guard. Only Vinata and Rishi (who is not a blood member and therefore not a target) are named among the naga.

The castle guard dies first, killed by Elle’s squad in the naga stronghold while Carl is still at the council. That leaves three.

The rest of the operation exists purely to make Vinata run on Carl’s schedule — a full-front push by Florin in the north, a feint by Tran in the south, and then a wave of sluggalos sent to swarm the castle “face-first, inexpertly killing and getting themselves splattered like a bunch of idiots.” As Carl puts it: “We just needed the hornet’s nest kicked. We needed Vinata’s escape plan to get triggered on our schedule.”

docs.title: How She Disappeared
docs.text:
Rosetta’s theory, which the whole plan is bet on, turns on a quirk of the light gods.

Fifteen deities of light in the Ascendency pantheon keep temples inside Club Vanquisher. All fifteen grant Travel the Path, a spell that turns the caster into light and lets them follow a path at the speed of light — “It was a dangerous spell to use and oftentimes ended with the caster getting splattered or cut in half by an unexpected shadow blocking their route. It was not considered teleportation by the system.” Six grant it immediately on worship. Four of those six also grant Welcome Home, a once-ever skill that, combined with Travel the Path, lets the worshipper follow a Bijou fairy’s light tendril straight to the strongest connected temple — which is invariably inside Club Vanquisher. It works even if the temple’s physical entrance has been destroyed.

Two of the four gods come with a recruitment quest that can smuggle the rest of her guard in with her: Theia, who turns prospects into motes of light that fit in a pocket, and Khepri, who turns them into literal beetles that the female worshipper must swallow whole and later give birth to on a buffet table. Rosetta’s reading of past seasons — a year Vinata never appeared at all after the Viceroys’ summoned goddess buried the temple entrance, another year she arrived late and two guards short during a demon eviction event near that same temple — points at the club.

Theia is off the board this season because she is sponsored, and by the Pacifist network. That leaves Khepri. Carl’s team uses Edgar the tortoise and his level-15 Sense Movement skill to watch for the upward flick of a Bijou fairy from inside the naga castle. When Edgar reports “Non-corporeal, Coming from below and moving up,” the theory is confirmed and the raid goes.

docs.title: The Trap
docs.text:
It was a trap, and Carl sees it the instant he is inside.

The one thing Rosetta’s model got wrong was who did the worshipping. Traditionally a guard takes the god so that the Sultana never shows any sign of worship. This time:

To my surprise, I saw Vinata was actually the one who’d worshiped Khepri, which was a break in tradition.

It all hit me at once. Vinata knew we’d have to come for her no matter what. We’d assumed that she wouldn’t anticipate we’d find her secret hiding place. But, unlike so many others, she hadn’t underestimated our determination, and she’d prepared for this eventuality. She’d been the one to worship Khepri, and she’d somehow prepared a method to summon him into his own temple. She’d waited to see if we’d find her, and when we did, she’d summoned the bug god, knowing we’d storm right into the deity’s lap. As trespassers into the god’s own temple, we’d be fucked.

It was the perfect trap, and we’d walked right into it.

What she could not price in was that being in the presence of a summoned deity hands Carl a temporary Immortality buff of his own — 90 seconds against her 63. The boss-battle card goes up:

God of Rebirth and the Sunrise. Khepri! Level 250.

The AI also broadcasts what she was actually protecting, which is not the game at all:

Breaking news, folks. Princess Vinata is about to inherit her own solar system. That’s no secret, but what you don’t know is that after a few hundred cycles pretending to be destitute, her entire kingdom was about to surprise everyone. But now her secret husband is dead, and her kingdom’s plans to pull a Fred Johnson and seize all the shipbuilding factories are being leaked. As we speak, all factory owners are moving to protect their assets from the slippery snake folk.

The moment the countdown ends, her three guards charge on Speed potions, the two cousins flee invisible down the endless banquet hall, and Vinata goes invisible and charges. Carl drops The Waffle Maker — a thermos-sized thermobaric bomb that incinerates everything within 100 metres — at his own feet, inside a long, narrow room that acts “like a cannon barrel.”

If not for the Immortality struggling to keep my very atoms together, I would’ve been just gone. There wouldn’t have been anything left.

Both cousins die in the blast. The three guards die. Carl is flattened, burned and turned inside out, and reforms. Vinata, immortal, does not.

docs.title: Death
docs.text:
She had been wrapped around Carl since the explosion blew them both out of the temple portal, and neither of them realised it for the better part of a minute. When he finally works out what is screaming in his ear, she has her middle hands around his throat, her upper hands slamming his skull against the floor of Club Vanquisher, and glowing daggers going in and out of him “like a piston.”

“Everything. You’ve ruined everything,” she cried as she stabbed me over and over, tears streaming down her snake face. She wasn’t white anymore, but a dusky gray.

“We were almost free. We were almost free,” she cried. I had no idea what she was talking about. “You ruined it the moment that fucking cat put that tiara on. We would’ve been gone. We would’ve been done. We were leaving this madness, and you had to ruin it. You killed my people. All of them. Do you think I really want to be here? I was going to have children with him.”

Carl’s shirt had been blown open in the blast.

In my choking, confused, inebriated state, I realized my shirt was open. The eye on my chest was open, and Vinata was staring directly into it.

She had been driven mad by the Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

See the Eye of the Bedlam Bride. She never stops. Khepri is banished by another god; a third god, Hellik, sits down beside them cross-legged and delivers a message to Carl while she is still beating his head into pulp; the immortal burning bugs swarm over both of them. “Even as her body burned, she slammed me over and over.”

What kills her is a level 29 sluggalette bursting out of a slugpox boil on Carl’s back:

I was about to drop the next bomb when I felt the sluggalo burst out of my back. He—actually, a she—slipped out from under my shirt, whooped loudly, and planted a hatchet right between Vinata’s eyes, killing her.

“Yeah, bitch! Right in the nugget!” the sluggalo woman shouted. She looked down at me as Vinata’s lifeless body slipped off of me and to the side. “I wish I had feet. I’d make me some snakeskin boots!”

System Message: The Sepsis Whore of the Blood Sultanate has fallen. Credit for the kill has been given to Kandy “Bigs” Newton of the Princess Posse.

System Message: The Blood Sultanate has been defeated.

System Message: All assets of the Blood Sultanate, as per prior arrangement, have been split evenly with the surviving blood relatives of the Sepsis Whore, Warlord Princess Donut and General Katia Grim, both of the Princess Posse. As per prior arrangement, all assets have been forfeited to the Princess Posse.

Katia’s reaction, in chat, is the joke the whole five-book thread lands on: “Who the hell is Kandy Newton, and where the hell are you, Carl?”

Carl takes her corpse into his inventory, and only then sees what she actually looked like:

Her white scales were actually gray with a hint of red along her neck. The white had been some sort of makeup or effect. An effect that had been eradicated in the explosion.

In death, she didn’t look so big.

docs.title: What Her Death Bought
docs.text:
Killing Vinata completes the four required kills in the Blood Sultanate’s line of succession, which is the hard prerequisite the crown imposed on Donut and, through the succession rules, on Katia. The mechanics of the crown belong on its own page — Crown of the Sepsis Whore — but the book is clear that her death is only half of it: “In order to save Donut and Katia from the Sepsis Whore issue, we first had to kill the entire line of succession of the Blood Sultanate.”

The remainder is the succession problem between the two surviving blood relatives, which is not settled until much later, when Katia eats the Orchid of Eileithyia’s Grace and the deal with Huanxin Jinx has to be forced. “Donut wouldn’t be able to leave until after Katia was whisked away. That was the price of the Crown of the Sepsis Whore.”

The surviving naga, Rishi — married into the family but not a blood member, and therefore never part of the quest — buries himself in the dirt outside the castle, waits out the fighting, surrenders to Donut, and declares himself leader of the new Naga Sultanate. He speaks well of her:

“I agree. And I know you don’t believe it, but Vinata was a firm believer in this philosophy. She’d seen war on alien soil, and she firmly believed it was all for nothing. Her father insisted she participate in Faction Wars. We needed the tourist money. We needed to keep the shipyards staffed and running. We were going to steal the entire fleet and run. We were going to travel, as a whole, for an entire generation, off in a direction that none of the tunnel threads point. Off to a place where it would be a very, very long time before we were found. That was our Great Consensus, engineered by Princess Vinata. To leave.”

That is what “We were almost free” meant.

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Quasar
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Role: Carl's attorney, retained on Floor 6 (Book 5). By Book 7 he is a "volunteered" lawyer for the season, assigned to negotiate end-of-floor exit deals
  • Type: NPC (non-combatant, off-screen legal representative)
  • Race: Nullian ("Null") — a gray-skinned, bulbous-headed, big-eyed alien (a classic "Area-51 gray" look), about four and a half feet tall, appearing as a holo in a tan suit with a tie featuring an animated Nullian hula girl. Confirmed outright in Book 7, whose opening framing device is narrated by his niece Tempest, "the young nullian"
  • Family (Book 7): A brother whose daughter is Tempest; an ex-wife, Nova; his people live "far out in the middle of nowhere," well away from the inner system
  • Class/Subclass: Not applicable — a lawyer, not a combatant
  • Notable spells/abilities: None — operates entirely through legal maneuvering, contract loopholes, and negotiation
  • Notable items: None described

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Quasar is assigned to Carl as legal counsel once Carl becomes a "taxpaying stockholder" of his own new corporation, following the events of Book 4. He speaks entirely in crude, cheerfully vulgar one-liners — professional advice delivered in the cadence of a drunk buddy giving relationship tips — and communicates almost exclusively via chat, with an automated "out of office" style reply implying he spends much of his downtime drinking and womanizing.

docs.title: Role in the Story — Book 5
docs.text:
Quasar negotiates Carl's opening deal with Syndicate liaison Orren: in exchange for temporarily surrendering the Gate of the Feral Gods (usable again once Carl reaches Floor 9), Carl receives four mercenary "cretin" bodyguards — Bomo, the Sledge, Clay-ton, and Very Sullen, good for floors six through eight — plus two bonus spells for two of them: Bomo gets a level-15 Teleport to Stairwell (with a roughly 25-day cooldown), and the Sledge gets Zerzura, which was Quasar's idea. Quasar explains Zerzura in detail beforehand — a town-teleportation spell that sends an entire town, NPCs and buildings included, one floor down per cast, with one exception: on "Scolopendra levels" it skips straight to the next Scolopendra level instead. He cites a past crawler, Remex the Grand, who got the spell on the fourth floor and moved his town down normally, floor by floor, until a cast made from the sixth floor (itself a Scolopendra level) skipped straight over floors seven and eight and dropped his unprepared people onto floor nine — precisely what later happens when the Sledge casts Zerzura from Floor 6 during the Butcher's Masquerade. The caster can't steer where within that floor it lands, though, and it almost always drops the town into the middle of a monster nest or boss room, killing everyone caught in the impact — which is the real danger, not a casting failure: everyone killed this way is instantly resurrected as a powerful "Children of Inpewt" revenant, and every surviving townsperson plus the caster is marked and actively hunted by those revenants until all of the marked are dead. Separately, the spell can only be attempted once — if the casting itself simply fails ("miscasts"), there's no second try. He also:

  • Secures an emergency extension of Vengeance of the Daughter's broadcast license by exploiting an obscure Borant "emergency use" statute (for shows running at lower-than-expected profits), tying Carl and Donut's safety to the show's continued ratings
  • Successfully sues to end the practice of hunters receiving live outside intelligence on crawler locations — a major turning point that lets Carl's Floor 6 counter-offensive succeed
  • Warns Carl, without directly saying so, that keeping Vengeance of the Daughter's ninth-floor extension alive will require Carl to keep the show exciting without outshining its actual star, or the producers may simply let the story kill him off
  • Flags a mysterious "other problem" that will cost about 150 million credits — more than Carl's entire net worth, and a possible bribery/legal risk even if he could raise it — and says he's "working on" an idea, leaving the matter unresolved at the end of the book

docs.title: Role in the Story — Book 6
docs.text: Quasar gets substantial screen time in Book 6, most of it spent working around a hostile liaison standing in the room.

docs.title: Faction Wars Intel
docs.text:
His single most useful scene is a rushed sitrep delivered in a gap during the Shadow Boxer taping, with the caprid liaison Harbinger watching:

"There's only so much I can say, legally that is, with that scary fucker standing over there. I can't answer too many questions, so keep your honey hole closed while I get this out. There's been a lot of movement on the Faction Wars front. Your team's castle landed right in the middle of the Lemig Sortion's battlefield, and it splattered half their army."

The rest: the Zerzura ghouls are still loose but most of Carl's army made it to his own battlefield; the Lemigs are squatting in the wrecked elf castle and "consensus is they're fucked," with their commander still stranded in the Desperado Club; Signet's tattoo golems survived and "People really like the shark"; Tina is still an allosaurus; the changelings have started building Carl's stronghold; and Ferdinand "lost his hat and moved straight to the city."

The legal win buried in that is his: the Lemig Sortion filed a grievance arguing the castle drop was an attack, and Quasar successfully argued it was an AI action. He fights the liaison for the right to say any of it — "Oh, keep your weird goat dick in the bag. There ain't no explicit rules against this. He's a sponsor." — and signs off with: "I hope plenty of you guys survive this floor because you're gonna need as big of an army as you can get."

docs.title: Adjutant Advice, in Mime
docs.text: At the adjutant selection he is not permitted to speak at all, so he conducts the entire negotiation by gesture from offstage: nodding along with Odette, shaking his head vigorously No when Carl challenges the candidate list, an enthusiastic thumbs up for the orc attorney Baroness Victory, and — bafflingly to Carl — "a tepid thumbs down" for Ripper Wonton, the obvious pick. Carl takes the steer: "Again, I looked to Quasar. He was bouncing up and down, pointing at her, giving me a thumbs up."

docs.title: The Residual's Bin
docs.text:
His actual negotiation of the book is the seizure of the Residual's plastic bin, which he opens on precedent — "This is already settled caselaw. Grixist Swarm V. Syndicate Council. He's already picked up the loot. You can't un-lick a butthole that's already been licked." — and then, when Carl blurts out that he'll just trade for it, salvages by stealing the idea: "Shut your titty hole… A great idea just came to me. What if we trade for it?"

Net result: one wand recharge scroll, three Cracker Jack scrolls, and Orren agreeing that the guild keeps the four cretins free of charge for the ninth floor. Carl does not get the Gate of the Feral Gods back. Quasar is "unceremoniously kicked away in the middle of a sentence once the deal was done," and takes his 15%.

Not Quasar's deal

Carl's 990,000-gold interest-free church loan and the Enchanted Pauper's Ring of the Steadfast Emberus are arranged inside Club Vanquisher by the high cleric Pater Coal and a satyr jeweller. Quasar is not present and has no part in it.

docs.title: Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin
docs.text: Quasar bookends the whole novel. He opens it, in a domestic scene that has nothing to do with the dungeon, and he closes it, in a freezing empty room with Carl covered in ash. In between he appears twice, briefly, and both times he is delivering bad legal news from a long way off.

docs.title: Tempest’s Floor 8 Recap
docs.text:
The book’s prologue material is a school assignment. Quasar’s niece Tempest — “the young nullian,” which is the clearest confirmation in the series of what Quasar himself is — needs a recap of Floor 8 for a report on “perceptions of the crawl,” and she has been assigned Carl and Donut specifically because she is related to their attorney. He makes her fix his sink for it.

“Most people love the sound of their own biscuit holes flapping. I am very busy, and my time is valuable. You want information, you should learn to trade for it. It’s good for you.”

“But why have me fix your sink? Why do you even have this thing? I don’t know shit about this old plumbing stuff. Can’t you do it yourself?”

“I could, but I’m teaching you a valuable life lesson. Never give shit up for free because if you do, they’ll just keep coming back to you and will expect more and more.”

His first attempt at the recap is four sentences long:

“Okay,” Quasar said. “Carl fucked shit up. He fucked up a little in the end and now has a spider stuck in his chest. The end.”

Blackmailed into a real answer, he delivers the entire Floor 8 recap in his own register — the card game (“these fights were like a Saccathian orgy”), Quan stealing Carl’s key, Tsarina Tserendolgor’s death and the flamethrower and meatball Carl inherited from her, Sister Ines, Amayon, Paz killing the goddess Ysalte — and then pivots into the setup for Floor 9 that the reader actually needs: that neither Donut nor Katia can leave until all the Naga are dead, that only one of them can leave at all, and that Katia’s exit depends on the Orchid and on Huanxin Jinx. He also teases, without knowing the name, the thing Book 7 will spend its length on: “something else happened after that god died that only us viewers saw, something that’s going to be a big deal later. It has to do with one of the ladies in the party, but I can’t remember her name.”

The scene ends with the recorder switched off:

“Are you in danger? For representing him, I mean? Like, real danger?”

Quasar let out a long stream of smoke. He wanted to lie, but he decided to tell her the truth. The kid deserved it.

“I think we all are, kiddo. It’s the first time in my life I’m glad we live so far out in the middle of nowhere.”

His interjections about Tempest’s skin, her teacher, her mother and her grandmother are all present and all unprintable. Her assessment: “The only lesson I’ve learned today is that my uncle is a colossal prick.”

docs.title: The Third Season Problem
docs.text:
Carl’s first message on arriving at Larracos is Quasar’s status report, and it is the only piece of legal groundwork Quasar lays in the book. The Vengeance of the Daughter third-season guarantee he negotiated back in Book 5 has been bought:

“But remember that contract with Sensation Entertainment, Incorporated? The one for the Vengeance of the Daughter storyline? Yeah. So, even though the main character is dead and gone, that guarantee of a third season we negotiated is about to haunt the fuck out of us. Sensation Entertainment just got purchased by a subsidiary of the Dream, and things are moving. They’re demanding their third season.”

His advice: stay away from every elite Carl meets, expect the worst, and accept that the courts are not the final authority here — “the AI gives zero shits about what the courts say anyway. If it thinks it’s going to be funny, it’s going to let it happen. Just keep your head down and listen to what Judge Victory tells you. She’s a smart one.”

He is also, as ever, outclassed on paper. Asked by Donut whether Quasar went to the same law school as the orc judge Baroness Victory and the Syndicate’s Panford: “Victory let out a surprisingly pig-like snort. ‘I think not.’” And when Carl tries to invoke him against the liaison Orren mid-crisis, Orren shuts it down: “We are beyond lawyers at this point, Carl, and I think you know that.”

docs.title: The Exit Interview
docs.text:
The epilogue is Carl and Quasar alone in a doorless zero-zone cubicle, minutes after the ninth floor burns. Quasar is wearing a tie with Mongo on it. He gives Carl a moment before starting, which Carl notes as uncharacteristic.

“Before we start, buddy boy, on behalf of the Syndicate Intergalactic Bar Association, I’d like to personally thank you. There being just about 20,000 crawlers making it to the 10th floor is quite the accomplishment. Lots of my colleagues getting work today, and some of them are pretty easy on the receptors, if you know what I’m saying.”

The record number of survivors is also why the offers are worthless — “That, unfortunately, is a side effect of having so many survivors. You’d be better off working as a scrub boy at a bathhouse in a dromedarian leprosy colony.” The list runs to fifty seasons undead, the Desperado Club bomber’s guild, and one genuinely interesting option: Chaco’s job, offered jointly to Carl and Donut, still open at the end of Floor 10.

The one real moment between them comes when Carl pushes:

“Do you? Do you know what I’m going through?”

He was silent for a long moment, which was unusual for the attorney.

“Of course not,” Quasar finally said.

He also sells Carl the next floor’s premise, at a cost of one extra season on any future deal: Floor 10 is called “Don’t Come in Last.” Crawlers pick a conveyance, biological or mechanical, make a fixed number of point-to-point journeys with upgrades along the way, and “if you come in last place, the survival containment around your vehicle is removed.”

Carl declines every offer. Quasar writes it down: “I am shocked.”

The book’s last line of dialogue is his. Donut was assigned a different lawyer for her own meeting, which did not go well:

“Her name is Princess Chandra, Esquire. Apparently her and Donut already had their meeting, and now that you’ve officially declined your offers I can tell you she declined as well. I am hearing there were some serious fireworks during their meeting. And not the good kind. We need to have a serious talk about her. Donut’s lawyer, I mean.”

I grunted. “Why? Is she another catgirl?”

“No. Worse, buddy. She’s your new wife.”

docs.title: Book 8: A Parade of Horribles
docs.text: Quasar gets his first full character-POV interlude — opening the transition from Floor 10 to Floor 11 — and it turns his usual comic-relief register into something much more personal.

docs.title: Watching the Ascendency Begin
docs.text: The interlude opens with Quasar at an attorney bar with his old law-school friend Kiki, watching the Floor 10-to-11 transition screens: 203 crawlers reached Floor 11, 172 have already taken exit deals, and rogue, unsponsored gods are teleporting briefly into real space near tunnel nodes, triggering galaxy-wide panic — the same crisis Carl's Plenty of Plenty broadcast helped set off (see Carl).

docs.title: The Attack on His Family
docs.text: Mid-conversation, Quasar gets a video call from his niece Tempest (already established from Book 7 as his equal in casual abuse): Taurin mercenaries have attacked his brother's home. Tempest fends them off herself, killing two with an illegal blaster Quasar had given her.

docs.title: Chandra's Retaliation
docs.text:
Quasar identifies the client behind the hit immediately — Princess Chandra, Esq., Donut's own attorney, retaliating for the "hit" Donut placed on her after their confrontation. He hires Kiki on the spot for both legal and physical protection:

"Both," he said to Kiki. "Fucking both."

He also confirms, in the same interlude, that his own legal fight against Chandra is ongoing but losing ground: a hearing over the legality of Carl's marriage certificate is scheduled, and he expects to lose it, though the filing itself has at least paused several of Chandra's other actions.

Sets up Book 9

Book 8 does not resolve Quasar's vow of revenge against Chandra on the page — it's raised here and then left as a personal subplot, alongside the still-unresolved marriage and conservatorship fights.

Sourced from Book 5: The Butcher’s Masquerade, Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride, Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin, and Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Queen Imogen
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Country Boss
  • Race: High Elf
  • Class: Cleric Sorceress
  • Level: 145
  • Family: Half-sister of Tsarina Signet (same father, King Finian, now deceased); modeled on the face of Ifechi, Florin's deceased partner from Book 4 — specifically her identical twin sister, not Ifechi herself
  • Status: Deceased — killed by Prepotente during the Butcher's Masquerade's final battle
  • Notable spells/abilities: Casts the Butcher's Masquerade ritual itself — a once-in-a-lifetime spell that enforces an absolute peace seal over an invited guest list chosen by the goddess Apito, in exchange for a boon if the party concludes without violence; area lightning attacks; unlimited mana while the ritual is active; immunity to poison and curses; reflects magical fire back at its caster
  • Notable items: A Memorial Crystal: Apito — a rare, information-storing gem normally worn as a necklace, looted after her death by a ranger crawler named Osvaldo (whose race, Curupira, is drawn from Brazilian folklore) rather than by Carl or Prepotente, both of whom wanted it

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Imogen rules the High Elves of Floor 6's Hunting Grounds from a stark white castle nicknamed "the Sugar Cube." She usurped her position after her father King Finian's death, purging half-elf "bastards" (including her half-sister Signet) to secure her claim, and has ruled ever since through a mix of xenophobic religious doctrine (worship of the goddess Apito, who preaches "cutting off the rot" to grow "the perfect tree") and calculated hospitality.

docs.title: The Butcher's Masquerade
docs.text:
Imogen personally casts the titular ritual — a once-per-lifetime spell that invites a goddess-selected guest list (deliberately including one's worst enemies) to a mandatory party under an absolute peace seal, with the promise of an unspecified boon from Apito if the evening concludes without violence. She meets Carl in person before the party to warn him off any scheme, revealing the ritual's full mythological backstory and confirming she genuinely cannot harm him without breaking her own seal — even as she promises retribution the instant anyone else breaks it first.

Her plan collapses when Signet, having been invited into the sealed ballroom by the ritual itself, sacrifices herself to shatter the peace seal from within — dropping the entire party (crawlers, hunters, elves, and the god Diwata, who has infiltrated the castle) into the floor's climactic "Cage Fight Extreme" boss battle the instant Apito withdraws her unseen protection. Imogen fights ferociously — she magically flings one of her own burning, nymph-covered elk mounts into Dmitri and Maxim Popov, killing the two-headed nodling crawler outright — before being worn down by coordinated, blunt-force fire from Florin's shotgun and dozens of other crawlers. Prepotente lands the killing blow, smashing a potion into her face while she's disoriented from an earlier disco-ball attack.

docs.title: Ferdinand
docs.text:
Imogen's familiar is a house cat, Sir Ferdinand — a Level 100 Province Boss in his own right — whom Donut successfully magically charms into betraying her during the party, using a Charm Animal potion brewed specifically for the purpose. Ferdinand fights on Donut's side during the final battle and survives, transferring with the rest of the castle to Floor 9 as a listed minion of Donut's.

Sourced from Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: Rosetta Thagra
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Former crawler — broadcast host and, secretly, an operative of the Open Intellect Pacifist Network; from Book 7 a re-entered combatant fighting on Floor 9 as a mercenary sworn to the Princess Posse
  • Race: Crest — a human-like race distinguished by having no eyebrows; Crests were a common hunter type on Floor 6
  • Class / Subclass: Books 1-6 never state what class she ran; in her own era she was, per Zev, "a big fan of blowing things up." Book 7 gives two answers and reconciles neither — the name over her head on Floor 9 reads "Rosetta Thag. Crest Barn Burner. Level 60," while her own status card lists her original crawl as Class: Gazetteer, Top Level: 91. No subclass is ever named
  • Role: Host of Shadow Boxer; maker of the documentary The Other Side of the Glass; former crawler and former game guide, released from her indentureship only recently
  • Seniority: A former crawler two seasons older than Mordecai
  • Cookbook: Contributor/owner of the 9th edition of The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook — her notes are mostly explosives recipes
  • Level: 60 (Book 7, as a re-entered former crawler); 91 at the top of her own crawl
  • Rank (Book 7): Colonel in the Princess Posse; named "Theater Commander" of Operation Ruin
  • Status: Alive. Went to ground with the Open Intellect Pacifist Network mid-Book 6; resurfaces in the Book 6 epilogue crewing the freighter Homecoming Queen; re-enters the dungeon on Floor 9 and is confirmed alive at the end of Book 7
  • Notable spells/abilities: None described as a spell list. In Book 7 she fights with drop shields, a tech-based invisibility cloak, and tunnelling/ground-collapse effects she never explains
  • Notable items: A neck-worn scrambler that hides her from security sweepers (Book 6 epilogue); a whip (Book 7); a hand-held banking datapad and a credit chit

docs.title: Book 6: Shadow Boxer
docs.text:
Rosetta is introduced when Zev books Carl and Donut onto her interview program, Shadow Boxer — a non-profit show owned by the Open Intellect Pacifist Network that interviews crawlers about their pre-crawl lives in conversations "designed to look like regular conversations." Zev's summary is blunt: "Rosetta Thagra. An Odette wannabe. She's a former crawler and game guide. She's a Crest… Actually, she was more like you, Carl, than Odette." Carl recognizes the name from the cookbook immediately — the 9th edition's dozens of explosives recipes are hers.

She presents as a pale, pretty woman in her early twenties in a professional pantsuit, bald but for a blob of brightly-dyed hair perched at an angle on her head, with a flowery tattoo circling her right leg. Her tell is rubbing the side of her right thigh when she's nervous, which is often.

Her first act out of the dungeon was to make a documentary about her own home planet, The Other Side of the Glass. Its success is what got the Open Intellect Pacifist Network to fund Shadow Boxer. The title appears to echo her own cookbook note about watching Faction Wars victors murder a crawler through a portal: "We watched as the orc and his friends laughed, just there on the other side of the glass."

docs.title: Milk and Potatoes
docs.text:
Rosetta's interview is the episode in which Carl's entire backstory finally goes on the public record — his mother's suicide, his father's abandonment, the Anacortes Boys' Ranch. See Carl for that material.

Underneath the interview she is running a coded message. She puts a photograph on the display of a teenaged Carl chopping a potato in the boys' home kitchen, next to a jug labelled "Milk." Carl clocks the photo as a fake instantly — he was never allowed near that kitchen, the milk jug is shaped like a two-liter soda bottle, and the camera angle is physically impossible, taken from where a wall stood. She then lays in the line: "Apparently Carl needs a proper recipe to do his best work," and repeats the ingredients. Carl plays along:

"Potatoes are very versatile," I said.

"Very," Rosetta agreed. "Most…"

Harbinger cuts the feed mid-word.

The decode: "potatoes" is the toraline root vegetable his mystery sponsor sent him, and "milk" is Crawler Milk's 6th-edition cookbook notes on special inks. The two together make magic ink. Carl recognizes the phrasing because the exchange mirrors a note pair in the cookbook itself — Milk writing about the stew she used to make for her people's children ("I wish to cook a feast for the whole galaxy. I wish for them all to choke on our pain"), answered by Rosetta: "Comrade, I agree. One day, we will make certain they all know. Our words will not be lost. I swear it."

She plants a second message in the same session that Carl only decodes later: every television show they screen for Donut is set in Miami, steering the party's Floor 8 region pick.

docs.title: Banned
docs.text:
The Valtay liaison Harbinger — the same caprid previously bribed by the Skull Empire — kills the broadcast and recalls Carl's attorney mid-sentence: "She and Carl were obviously talking in code… I have banned Rosetta from participating in any future crawler interviews." Zev, furious in a way Carl has never seen from her, says they will be sued and will win. Donut's summary: "now she's not going to be able to do her show any more because she was talking about mashed potatoes!"

Carl's read is simpler: "She'd risked everything to get that message to me."

docs.title: Going to Ground
docs.text:
After the Open Intellect Pacifist Network's Miami scheme fails — a plan that involved getting Carl within earshot of a Residual's recitation, and was willing to spend Carl and the planet to force the Syndicate Council's hand — the whole organization vanishes. Zev: "The box got seized, and the entire charity and everyone involved just up and disappeared. Nobody knows where they went or if something happened to them. They're all gone, even Rosetta."

Not stated in the text

The book never uses the word "fugitive" and never narrates where Rosetta goes between the Network's disappearance and the epilogue. She simply reappears aboard the Homecoming Queen wearing a scrambler to defeat security sweepers.

docs.title: Epilogue: The Homecoming Queen
docs.text:
Rosetta is one of two people in the cockpit of a converted garbage freighter parked in Earth orbit — the largest ship up there, twice the size of a Valtay warship, belonging to Long Haul Biological Waste Management Solutions (the same company that has just become Donut's sponsor). The other is Tipid, a fellow Crest and the 4th edition's cookbook author. Both were recruited by Doctor Hu with a single promise: "I can only promise two things. Eventual death. And eventual justice."

She spends the scene nervous, chewing her nail, watching the news coverage of the Faction Wars rule change. Her verdict on Carl is unsentimental: "I still can't tell if he's smart or if he's been outrageously lucky… It took an NPC to show him how to use the ink to share powers, and I'm still not sure if he gets it." She also confirms it was the two of them who sent Donut her first celestial box.

The ship is renamed Homecoming Queen, and it is full: fifty thousand former crawlers, smuggled into the system as troopers for the Princess Posse. Tipid's intercom announcement — "We are officially all troopers now for the Princess Posse" — is met with cheers through the hull. Her last line before the book ends:

"Comrade," Rosetta said. She reached over and placed a warm hand on his arm. He clasped his hand in hers. Both of them trembled.

They were coming home.

docs.title: Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin
docs.text:
Rosetta comes back into the dungeon. She arrives on Floor 9 in chapter 11 alongside Tipid, already sworn in as a trooper for the Princess Posse — her dot purple with a pink outline, the name over her head reading:

Rosetta Thag. Crest Barn Burner. Level 60.

Colonel in the Princess Posse.

This is a subordinate.

She looks nothing like the woman in the pantsuit. Black shorts, boots, a plain unenchanted leather top, no weapons visible, and the floral tattoo on her right leg now glowing, its tendrils running up her arm. Her tell is unchanged: she still rubs the side of her leg when she is thinking hard.

Text inconsistency: which edition is hers?

Carl's narration in chapter 11 calls her the seventh-edition author:

Rosetta. Rosetta from the Shadow Boxer television show. Rosetta from the seventh edition of the cookbook.

This is an authorial error. Her own status card at the end of her interlude says:

Author of the ninth Edition of the Dungeon Anarchist’s Cookbook.

And the seventh edition belongs to Volteeg, whose status card at the end of his interlude says:

Author of the seventh edition of the Dungeon Anarchist’s Cookbook.

Book 6 also has her as the ninth ("<Note added by Crawler Rosetta. Ninth Edition>"). This wiki keeps 9th edition as the established fact and treats the chapter 11 line as a slip.

docs.title: Killing King Rust
docs.text:
Chapter 34 is a parley. King Rust, leader of the Skull Empire, comes out to the neutral ground between the armies not to fight but to tell Carl that his own daughter, Princess Formidable, has seized a cruiser, is five hours from the monitor station orbiting Venus, and intends to manually trigger the system failsafe — which would ignite the star and kill everyone in the system. He asks Carl to plead with her on behalf of Earth. A deal is struck: the orc armies will withdraw, the Posse will not harass the retreat, and everyone will spend their last hours writing goodbyes.

Rosetta was not party to any of that. She was underground.

...And that’s when Rosetta appeared, rising up out of the dirt like some fiery goddess of the underworld. She’d been wearing one of those tech-based invisibility cloaks as she launched from the ground. She had a whip of her own in her hand. In a movement so fast, she’d clearly been practicing it, she flipped in the air, landing on the back of the yak directly behind the king. She tossed the whip around the neck of the king, and she yanked.

The head flew from his body like a popped champagne cork.

Five seconds of silence across the field, and then tens of thousands of enemy troops charge. The ceasefire Carl had just bought is gone.

Her own reason surfaces later, in her interlude. Rust killed a crawler named Brooks with that same whip, after Faction Wars was over, for sport, through a portal — the scene that gave her documentary its title.

Rust, still laughing, had stepped back through the portal, lassoed Brooks, and pulled him into the glass, which had cut him right in half. It had been so casual, so fast. Brooks had died immediately.

But Rosetta remembered. She would never forget. She relished that moment when she used the whip to decapitate the old orc.

She had nearly missed the chance: Tipid, who did not know about the bank plan, had tried to hide Rust's presence from her. The original target had been Stalwart.

docs.title: The robbery
docs.text:
The killing was a means to an end. Chapter 35 opens with Carl sprinting the wrong way, into the charge, because Rosetta needs the corpse.

“Grab his head!” Rosetta called as we rushed up… She was on her knees, and she had some sort of weird data pad object in her hand. She had King Rust’s fat hand atop the pad, and one of the rings—not the Ring of Divine Suffering—was placed inside the pad. “Quick, I need a retina scan!”

Carl fetches the severed head out of the grass. Rosetta presses it to the pad, something beeps, and she tells him to inventory the head and the body both. The three factors were the family signet ring, the eyeball, and a password — the PIN came from Baroness Victory as her half of the bargain, and the credit chit Carl had looted off an orc hunter on the sixth floor, which Rosetta had quietly asked him about back in chapter 11, is what she loads into the machine.

A Valtay official, overheard later, lays it out exactly:

“…from what I understand, it required the family ring, his eyeball, and a password. We know how she got the first two… Sounds like she used Colloid… that’s the only bank the orcs use… No, sir. It’s not on the chit anymore. She transferred it out…”

The confirmation comes as a cartoon slime hologram over the datapad — “Transfer approved! Thank you for using Colloid Bank.” — and Rosetta drops the pad in the dirt and sobs on the ground, with Carl standing there having no idea what he has just helped do. The same official puts the number at "the theft of a few billion credits." War Chief Stalwart's demand afterward is for "my father’s signet ring, his body, and the credits you illegally stole."

docs.title: Where the money went
docs.text:
Her interlude, at the head of The Peeling of Larracos, is the payoff. Baroness Victory — Rust's own estranged daughter, and the Princess Posse's adjutant — confirms the transfer landed:

Baroness Victory: …there was a transaction more than big enough to suggest your people were able to purchase two ships, despite the apparent chaos in the system. Assuming your Homecoming Queen starship follows your orders and shoots down that yacht, our transaction is done.

The price of the PIN was a killing. The orc yacht the Homecoming Queen was to shoot down carried several orc children, one of whom, with Stalwart dead, had just become king of the Skull Empire. Rosetta hates the orcs without reservation and still "felt ill about the transaction."

The deal had been brokered between Porthus and Victory long before Victory was ever appointed adjutant, and Victory's motives stay opaque to Rosetta. The money buys two ships: Porthus and the families of everyone who went into the dungeon board one, run for the Plenty system, and trade the second ship plus the remaining funds to the goats for passage through the "forbidden" gate at the Impetus Point, the tunnel node reaching the furthest known point in the galaxy — to get as far from the center system as possible and come back only when the wars settle.

Victory keeps the two halves of her life strictly apart:

Baroness Victory: Just because we have dealings together outside the dungeon doesn’t mean I am not taking my duties as adjutant seriously. I told you before I will not cheat nor will I help you cheat.

See Baroness Victory for her side of it.

docs.title: Theater Commander, Operation Ruin
docs.text:
Carl's own summary of the battle plan for the Open Hostilities phase gives Rosetta the top coordinating job:

Florin will deal with the orcs, Boomer with the Reavers, Donut with the Dream, and my task is the Madness. Tipid will remain at the FUPA to defend, and Rosetta is the designated “Theater Commander,” meaning she is in charge of coordinating it all.

Operation Ruin is the Posse's simultaneous multi-front offensive, timed to kick off the moment the Open Hostilities phase begins. Most of the floor's tactical planning is hers and Tipid's — the assault on the Dream artillery, the naga raid, the tunnel routes under the map. She plans Donut's War Crime finisher in chapter 73-74 down to the spell selection, talking Carl out of Laundry Day and into a Dinner Bell variant called Bijanbi extracted from a dead cleric, because Laundry Day would strip the fleshers off the enemy and turn them loose on the Posse's own soldiers. She also confides the rule Carl had not worked out on his own: spells taken from an unwilling owner are stronger, and the owner loses them for good.

docs.title: Doubt
docs.text:
The interlude is the only place in the series where Rosetta's certainty cracks. Her job is done — the money is away, her mother is avenged, Rust is dead — and she finds it has bought her nothing:

Yet, yet... No amount of revenge would ever bring her mother back. It would never bring Brooks back. No matter how many orcs and orc children she killed, her people would still be dead.

Her mother came into the dungeon with her and died on the first day, killed by goblins. Avenge us was the last thing she said.

She is briefly willing to let the war mages win — "It will be quick for us, and all the remaining mercenaries and leaders will be dead, which is beyond what we even imagined" — and Justice Light talks her out of it. She distrusts the Apothecary, the collective mind steering Porthus, and distrusts the residual Agatha more. She is in love with Porthus, "despite his unhealthy obsession with finding a missing crawler from his own crawl. Menerva."

She watched Carl's speech to Donut about masks and wept at how hopeful it was, and pitied him for believing Donut could ever take hers off. Was she wrong? Maybe so.

She chooses the fight anyway:

Maybe it was a mistake, but nobody could ever fault her for fighting for her friends. There was poetry in that. too.

Colonel Rosetta: Comrades, sound off. The fight has moved to the city. The enemy has changed, and they have taken the castle of Larracos. We don’t know how many there are, but we fight. We fight with all we have.

docs.title: Elsewhere on the floor
docs.text:
She assists at Louis Santiago's heart-and-lung transplant in chapter 84, holding the extracted naiad organs with Imani and Elle. She hauls Edgar the tortoise up a siege tower strapped to her back like a rucksack, wheezing, to tattoo Donut in time for the finisher. She is one of the handful of NPCs and former crawlers who declines the Zerzura transfer and stays on Floor 9 with Carl's party at the end of the book.

Her status card closes it:

Worked as a game guide and in the Desperado Club as a merchant renting mercenaries and occasionally was in charge of distribution of the dungeon newsletter. Upon dungeon exit became a journalist and filmmaker of some renown and eventually became host of the documentary series Shadow Boxer. Eventually returned to the dungeon to fight for the Princess Posse and to assist the mysterious Open Intellect Pacifist Network finance their great plan.

Current status: Alive.

docs.title: The Scavenger Storyline
docs.text:
In Heat 5, Carl finally asks Rosetta directly to lay out everything she knows about "the Scavenger storyline" — the mythology behind his own Scavenger's Daughter patch. Her answer is the fullest lore-dump on Scavenger/Apito/Scolopendra mythology given anywhere in the series to that point, delivered in her usual register (comrade, plainspoken, treating the myth as contested oral history rather than settled fact):

"The all-tree is an actual tree in the dungeon, but it's also a metaphor for existence itself. The tree gave fruit to the old gods, including Nekhebit, who is now also called the Scavenger Mother of Mothers. In the old times, she was a life and protector deity, though she was depicted as a vulture, a scavenger... She supposedly wasn't allowed to have children, but she did anyway. She had three kids, including Apito, who in turn got impregnated via either the all-tree or she made herself pregnant. Take your pick. Nekhebit was the last of the old gods to fall, and she was defeated by her daughter, Apito, absorbing the last of the vulture goddess's worshippers."

Carl's follow-up question — is the Scavenger's Daughter Apito, or something to do with Scolopendra — gets a correction rather than a confirmation:

"No. Nekhebit is a scavenger, but she's not the Scavenger. Nekhebit had three children. A son, a daughter, and a centipede."

Rosetta lays out the competing, contradictory versions of the myth without picking one: sometimes Scolopendra herself is "the Scavenger" and the Scavenger's Daughter is her offspring with someone else; sometimes it's an unnamed son who cleans up escaped souls in "the empty plane"; sometimes Apito, Scolopendra and the son are all considered "a divine trinity... just one of them, but they've been split." What she's certain of is what the Scavenger's Daughter actually is, myth aside: "this child... is considered one with the same power that Apito had. An entity that has the power to erase the current pantheon and start again. But this one is even more powerful. She can take the powers of gods and use them for herself."

This is the scene the wiki's eventual Mechanics coverage of the Primal/Eulogist cosmology will build on; Rosetta's version here is the crawler-side, half-mythologized account, distinct from the fuller, AI-narrated cosmology reveal delivered later through Grigori the Placid at the Floor 11 finale.

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride, Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin, and Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Samantha (Psamathe)
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • True identity: Psamathe, a minor deity, banished to "the Nothing" by her father after an affair with a mortal king
