His plans keep coming true with a precision Rosetta finds unnerving, and she blames the source: the Apothecary, "the witch that had his ear." Porthus's answer is "She's on our side" Potsy Level 40 Ares Warrior Cleric Middle Priest; door guard at Club Vanquisher (Book 6) Ram-headed, with roughly twenty brothers who fight each other for the privilege of guard duty and spend the shift praying to the stained-glass door image — which they insist depicts Hellik bringing truth to Apito. It is actually Taranis, and the man who made the window says so; they refuse to change their minds. Potsy makes Carl wait mid-prayer, objects that he "hasn't filled out the paperwork," and is shoved aside by Pater Coal Prime Minister Glory A Gleener; head of the Syndicate (Book 2, 6) Unusual enough on broadcast that Mordecai flags his appearance. In Book 6's epilogue emergency council session he is the principal voice against pulling the failsafe, and his reasoning is purely economic: over half the galaxy's wealth is trapped in the Scolopendra Club, including his own children. "You are literally asking us to destroy the economy and well-being of the entire galaxy. It would be the death of quadrillions." A grim detail of the same scene: the Valtay representative's Gleener body was once Glory's own mother. Book 7: he issues the standing order, relayed through Zev, that Carl is not to interact with Agatha — and is then removed from office by a vote of no confidence, announced in Chapter 83, after his attempt on Carl's life in Chapter 81 is blocked and punished by the AI. Baroness Victory reveals in Chapter 86 that she is acting Prime Minister in his place Prince Stalwart Crown Prince of the Skull Empire, the Maestro's older brother (Book 2, 6) Orders a public pulse-strike assassination of Carl and Donut in retaliation for Carl's on-air remarks; the strike hits the wrong trailer, killing Manasa instead. Book 6 puts him at the Faction Wars table as a wild-boar orc, where he threatens to skin Donut and line his codpiece with her pelt — prompting Donut's formal action item to have him renamed "Captain Enormous." Juice Box mocks the arrow she previously put in his eye; minutes later he takes a second magical arrow through the eye and dies at the table — though not permanently. Book 7 has him back as King Stalwart, crowned after Rosetta Thagra decapitates his father King Rust, and wearing an actual crown to the warlord council, which sends Donut and Ferdinand into hysterics. He punches the correspondent Chaco unconscious for putting it to a viewer vote. Killed in Chapter 61 by his own conscripted War Mage Rebellion: they were under strict Conscription rules and should not have been able to break allegiance, but used a clever combination of Pull spells to kill him anyway — Victory suspects he ejected them from his army first, hoping they would stop hurting him, and that it did not work. They take the Gate of the Feral Gods from Elle McGibbons in the same sequence Princess Formidable Youngest sibling of the Maestro and Crown Prince Stalwart, Skull Empire (Book 3–4, 6) Sponsors Katia with a single, cryptic anti-deity crossbow bolt (The Bolt of Ophiotaurus), intended for use on her own brother; implied to be positioning herself against her surviving family. Sends an emergency box of Petrify Rock Class bolts in Book 4, and the scroll of worship for Eileithyia in Book 6. Book 6's epilogue is partly her POV, in orbit above Earth, and she is the loudest voice for pulling the failsafe: "We have to blow the star. We have to wipe this entire system off the map… Not tomorrow. We have to do it now." She is in-system herself and would die with everyone else, which she says plainly. The council mutes her by an 86% decorum vote and approves the Valtay "solution" instead — over 150,000 mercenaries injected into Faction Wars to force an extinction event and lift the quarantine. Her closing thought: "Should've just pulled the failsafe… We're all gonna die one way or another." Katia's reused bolt kills a goddess in the same book Pustule Hobgoblin explosives merchant, Floor 3 (Book 2) Runs "Hobgobs and Boom Sticks" in the Silk Road market; unsettling bedside manner but reliable supplier for Carl's growing explosives habit Quan Ch Half-Elf Imperial Security Trooper crawler (Book 2–4, 6) Accidental beneficiary of the Book 2 "Fools Who Broke the Glass" event quest disaster (see Quests); by Book 3 the dungeon's single highest-leveled crawler, widely dismissed by Donut as "a cheater." In Book 4 he attacks the celestial-tier puppy Orthrus for a bounty, twice, and Carl rips his entire arm off in the ensuing fight. Killed in Book 6 at level 70, holding both of his region's exit keys and over sixty player-killer skulls: Carl takes him apart in the El Capitolio stairwell chamber, and the dying Quan asks not for his looted cloak but for a plain gold ring reading "For Daddy" on the inside, still attached to his severed arm in Carl's inventory. Carl puts it in his hand. "She'd be ashamed of what I've become," he says, and dies a beat before Carl's fist lands. The system credits the kill, the bounty, both keys and a golden player-killer skull to Donut Quint Half-Djinn Desperado Club pharmacist (Book 2) Former crawler-turned-manager, like Mordecai; sells Mordecai an alchemy starter kit and gives Carl a Blitz Stick; explains manager immortality mechanics further Randall Former Meadowlark resident on Imani C's squad (Book 6) Reclassed into a lutin, a gnome-like support-magic caster. The only one of Imani's four dead squadmates the book names. When an enemy totem possessed two of the squad and forced them to fight each other, Randall tried to defuse it by freezing all four of them in place — and Imani's own Amhuluk totem then killed all four with a single poison cloud, frozen where they stood, skin melting off, while Imani screamed Remex Undead "Soul Leech Capacitor," Miss Quill's husband (Book 2) A resurrected dark cleric bound to an amplifier crystal; his rambling, tangent-filled confession resolves the "Sex Workers" quest and reveals Miss Quill's genocidal endgame Ripper Wonton Setonix ("Quokka") host of Danger Zone (Book 2, 6) Talk-show host for a live roundtable format; visibly and genuinely shaken by Manasa's on-air death. Offered to Carl in Book 6 as one of three Faction Wars adjutant candidates and, despite being the obvious pick, quietly vetoed by Quasar for reasons Carl never learns Rishi A naga; representative of the Blood Sultanate at Faction Wars (Book 6) Married into the family rather than born to it; reminds Carl of the reporter Nihit, and Carl distrusts him on sight. He is the only attendee who doesn't flinch when Juice Box's killings start, and one of the last two left alive at the table. He proposes the meeting's only real compromise — invulnerability and a protected safe zone for unaffiliated NPCs in exchange for Juice Box ending her attacks — while noting that "the sultanate is quite versed in dealing with terrorism." Book 7: he survives Operation Snake Pit only because he is not in the castle when it falls, then hides rather than fights and surrenders. Carl finds him in a containment cell with his four arms removed on Li Na's orders, smiling, having already grieved his own wife and made peace with dying the day the mantis team fled the crawl. He has used the interval to stage a coup — he presents Carl with a drafted, signed treaty naming Carl the de-facto leader of Earth, signed "Sultan Rishi the Usurper, First of his Name of the Naga Uprising" — and Carl notices the name does not match the one in the relevant achievement. Carl marks him with the Ring of Divine Suffering and kills him on camera anyway: "Rishi here is just the opening act" Rory & Lorelai Goblin Shamankas Trade Carl a vehicle and supplies; charmed (not killed) by Donut Rosemarie Elderly one-legged dwarf; manager of the top floor's Meat Shields location (Book 6) Keeps a cattle-dog-patterned pet mole named Bernie and works out of a home office, because the office is a secret: Astrid parked a shadow Meat Shields branch inside the Penis Parade so that her sons and their friends would technically count as mercenaries and therefore be protected. She approves Carl's hiring of the entire stripper crew on a two-floor contract for 100,000 gold, after first getting scolded for pelting a dancer in the eye with a coin Ruby Changeling orphan NPC; one of six children Mordecai is illegally fostering (Book 6) From the fifth floor's camel/changeling storyline, and formally registered as Mordecai's attendant. She has compression sickness, a birth defect caused by her parents' malnutrition on a new world: she can shapeshift, but her forms are always missing parts, and in human form she has no arms and a sunken-in head. The custom split hand-controller on the guild hall floor is what gives Mordecai's secret away. Louis gives her a Gloria Estefan cassette for her old Walkman. Carl finds her unsettling — she pets Mongo with a raised leg while staring at him "like she was seeing right into my thoughts." Book 7 turns the fostering into the quietest tragedy in the book. Carl finds Mordecai reading her Anne of Green Gables with her misshapen head on his shoulder on what he believes is the last night of his life, and understands: "this is how he's choosing to spend his last few hours… he'd be out of the dungeon, and he would never see Ruby or any of the other kids again." At the end, the Zerzura spell carries the whole of Larracos — Ruby with it — to Floor 12, and Mordecai cannot go. He hands her over with "It's for the best, little one" Sarah Hayse Hexcrafter paladin crawler, half of the Destruction parade float with Makana (Book 8) Fights from atop a tricked-out Abrams tank alongside her partner Makana during the Floor 11 finale, casting a spell that turns the tank's main gun black before it fires point-blank into Krakaren Prime. Dies in the crash that follows the boss fight — reported, not staged, on-page Selvi and Tuba Two young Turkish crawlers, the surviving members of Burcu's squad (Book 7) Selvi is now an elf, a level-57 Valide healer class; Tuba is human, a level-56 Boring Ol' Fighter. Both were conscripted by the Madness and both refused to fight, which carries a no-healing debuff that nearly kills Tuba from a wound Jamal gives her. Carl has them tied up and gagged rather than questioned, because answering him would add penalties, and they are freed the moment the Madness falls. Both take the AI's exit deal at the end of the book. Neither ever tells Carl why Burcu believed he had killed her father — "That's the problem with such chaos. You lose so much around the edges" Silfa Healer, Brynhild's Daughters (Book 3–4) Nearly used as bait in Hekla's plot against Carl; captured, then released after Hekla's death — confirms the Daughters are disbanding and that Eva Sigrid, deeply unpopular, has inherited a group that no longer functions. Killed in Book 4, alongside her two daughters, after rejoining Eva despite Katia's warnings — the loss that convinces Katia to leave Carl's day-to-day party and lead her own protection effort Skarn Changeling boy from Floor 5; crew of the airship Party Planner (Book 5, 7) Has learned enough about shapeshifting to hide his age, and boards under the false adult name "Gangue" — Carl works out who he actually is halfway through the flight. Shifts into a chee, then an octopus-like form with five or six arms to hold Bonnie inside the cabin when the ship goes into a flat spin. Carl orders him off the ship twice and he comes back both times. Transfers to Floor 12 with the other children Sneaky Tyler C and Sick-Ass Worgo Two sluggalos working on Justice Light's trap crew (Book 7) Tyler C is the lead slug on the dig, tying off manual tripwires with his mouth; Justice sends the whole crew to the surface before the final phase because "You don't want to be down here for this part." He dies later in the war — per Kandy "Bigs" Newton, Agatha tied a potion to him and ordered him to run into a god, and he exploded on contact: "It was a bitch-ass move. I don't like her." The slug called Sick-Ass Worgo is, by the time of the interlude, not Worgo at all but the changeling Jessica wearing him Splash Zone Otter-like water mage; Penis Parade stripper turned Princess Posse soldier (Book 6–7) Normally in a lifeguard outfit. Helps Katia brew the hair tonic for Carl's scalp tattoo prep and gets the dose catastrophically wrong, leaving Carl with waist-length hair that regrows the instant he cuts it. One of Carl and Donut's 15-strong Personal Guard, a transport driver, and a fixture of the castle defence — his water magic is used to flood channels and flush out invisible mercenaries Tami-Lynn Carl's stepmother; mother of Asher (Book 6) A young woman in nurse's scrubs with a pitbull tattoo on her neck — "SHE CAN'T BE YOUR STEPMOM, CARL. SHE'S LIKE KATIA'S AGE." She kills Carl's father with a lethal dose of morphine she'd been hiding in the flowerpot outside, after sending Asher to a neighbour's house. She had written to Carl asking for help; Beatrice saw the message and buried it, which is how Carl never learned he had a brother. She appears as one of the nine heads of the Reminiscence Hydra, screams "I wrote you, and you never answered! I needed help. Look what you made me do!" mid-fight, and is the last head conscious: "I don't regret it. I saw what happened to you, and I didn't want Ash to go through the same thing. So I made sure. I made sure it was done right." Tart Antlered, vaguely demonic alien; adjutant for the Reavers (Book 7) Large glassy eyes, impassive expression, a very proper accent, and the misfortune of being introduced to the entire Penis Parade at once. Donut: "Can you even imagine having a name like Tart? Now that is a stripper name if I ever heard one." Bigs offers him ten gold to lick her tail. He objects, with increasing outrage: "I'm a gentleman, thank you very much. I'll have you know I am one of the galaxy's foremost political analysts. For god's sake, can't you see my antlers? I am no prostitute!" Samantha is later heard coaching Bigs on how to seduce him Tempest Nullian; Quasar's niece (Book 7) Opens the book. She is fixing her uncle's sink, badly, while making him recap the previous floor for a school report, and she is entirely his equal at abuse: "The only lesson I've learned today is that my uncle is a colossal prick," and "It's no wonder Aunt Nova left you." Her presence is what confirms Quasar's race on the page for the first time Tin Cookbook author, 21st edition (Books 3, 5–6) Marginal notes recur across three books, including a running joke about spiders ("I think they're cute... Never mind. Holy shit, never mind. Fuck spiders."). His theory that Laundry Day would need to strip a god's invulnerability before it could work is cited by Carl while planning the Butcher's Masquerade in Book 5, then found to be incomplete once Carl confirms soul-armor-targeting spells can bypass the god itself. See The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook Tipid A Crest; former crawler; author of the 4th edition of the Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook (Book 6–7) His chapter epigraphs run through the book. The epilogue reveals he co-runs the converted garbage freighter Homecoming Queen with Rosetta Thagra, recruited by Doctor Hu, and has just smuggled fifty thousand former crawlers into the quarantined system as troopers for the Princess Posse. He is the one who notices Carl never had to use the bone key — which would have let only one of Carl or Donut through — and the one who reads the tattoo correctly: "He needs to expel that presence as quickly as possible." He thinks constantly of his long-dead friend Horatio and of what he had to do to survive: "Sometimes the best solutions are also the worst ones." And: "I always knew I would die in the dungeon." Book 7: commands the 104th Naughty Little Piggies and is put in charge of defending the FUPA and the base. Book 8: Drives Carl and Donut's Big Shot Chicken truck through all seven heats of Floor 10 and into the Floor 11 Parade of Horribles; loses both legs in the finale's crash — Rosetta's report is a single flat line: "Tipid, too, is terribly injured. He has lost both of his legs in the crash" Tracksuit Troika Three Russian crawlers, driving a Cadillac in Heat 7 (Book 8) Told Imani and Elle they'd take Carl's escape-pact deal, then tried to double-cross the group and make a run for the exit instead. Elle's justification after the fact: "Those tracksuit idiots had a way out, and they chose not to take it... They would've killed me, Imani, and Chris if they'd made it to that exit." Their shielded Cadillac is broken open by spellfire and then crushed outright by Donut's Astral Paw — "The Cadillac simply ceased to exist" — netting her three more player-killer skulls. One of the three, Ivan, is remembered only for once bragging about causing a fatal train accident for money Tizquick Dwarf, Iron Tangle NPC (Book 3) Helps crawlers navigate the colored-line portal system at station 60; his claimed daughter turns out never to have existed. Dies alongside Fire Brandy, riding the Nightmare into the abyss Urkel / U56KL Disc-shaped Mexx robot; facilitator of the Faction Wars preproduction meeting (Book 6) Donut nicknames him "Urkel" and it sticks. He seats Carl and Donut as the third team, explains that the other warlords are attending from their own castles, runs the countdown, logs action items and opens voting. Asked why the others get better treatment, he answers flatly: "Because they're richer than you are." Vadim Zbar Kuhli Gut Rearranger crawler (Book 4) A former cosmetic surgeon; one of two survivors (with Britney Proskurina) of the water quadrant's original crawler team. Helps Carl and Katia navigate the drowned submarine Akula; dies alone in an escape pod after being caught with pain-amplifier jellyfish during his final ascent Very Sullen and Clay-Ton Two of the four cretins freed on Floor 6 (Book 6–7) Very Sullen serves in Carl and Donut's Personal Guard platoon. Clay-Ton was assigned as Chris Andrews's bodyguard back on the Hunting Grounds and the two have been inseparable ever since — "The two would just sit next to each other and occasionally grunt at one another" — fighting the northern front together under Florin and teleporting in together for the Madness assault Waldrip Chris Gremlin mechanic, Hedy's rival applicant for the Floor 10 garage job (Book 8) Brawls Hedy for the mechanic position in the opening chapter using a gourd as a weapon; Donut picks Hedy instead ("I would refrain from—"). Blam! "Waldrip Chris exploded in a spray of red and green mist" — the book's first death, played entirely for comic, pathetic effect Warlord Fang Warlord of the Reavers; roughly 99% cybernetic (Book 6–7) Book 6 gives him two lines in a robot voice and Donut's reply: "Warlord Fangs? Really?… Are you a robot vampire? Or are you a werewolf robot? Now that would be something." By Book 7 he presents as a too-pink twenty-year-old human in white underwear, identifiable as a machine only by a line of lights at his temple, and he and Epitome Tagg are the two richest warlords in the war. His death is also nearly meaningless to his own side: the Reavers keep a physical chunk of his brain, "the Initial," locked away on one of their worlds and shave microscopic pieces off it every year to grow new citizens. Killed hiding inside his own pet dragon Calliope when Carl detonates the No Disassemble device — the system splits the credit 51% to Carl, 40% to Juice Box and 1% to the wraith-possessed Louis Santiago who dropped the bomb, awarding "the rest… to the now-deceased Fang for hiding in the worst possible place, which was inside the dragon." The Reavers are eliminated Wynne Dirigible Gnome Flesh Mechanic, held hostage (Book 4) Commandant Kane's uncle, held in chains beneath Hump Town's town hall as collateral for peace; deliberately provokes a group of subterranean-quadrant crawlers into killing him rather than cast a flesh-giving spell on the ghost Quetzalcoatlus for his changeling captors Yasmine Level 75 Wisp; "Secretary of the Club Vanquisher Temple Portal," non-combatant NPC (Book 6) A fist-sized, faceless mote of white-and-yellow light with fairy wings, who worships the goddess Áine. One appearance, one line: "You can't block the portal." Yolanda Martinez 13 CNA, archer, Meadow Lark Killed by the Rage Elemental defending resident Randall York Tenodera; cookbook author, 10th edition (Books 3, 7) Carl quotes York's rambling, philosophical final entry at length in Book 3 — "I have been alone my whole life... this book... to make a hive of those who will never cross paths, except in these pages." His Book 7 epilogue interlude finds him alone at the helm of the freighter Homecoming Queen, having just killed a yacht full of orc children on Rosetta's order and feeling nothing from it — until Colonel Boomer's call to arms finally breaks through. See The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook Yvette Frank & Maggie's "daughter" Killed by Maggie; revealed via a talk-show recap, not directly witnessed by Carl Zander Saccathian; owner of the Squirties refuelling waystation outside the quarantine gate (Book 7, epilogue) Ruined. He spent his life savings leasing the spot, the embargo has stopped all traffic through the tunnel gate, and he owes 25,000 credits a month he cannot pay. He talks it through with a Veriluxx Real Pet Companion Uzi Jesus action figure, which tells him he is "probably fucked" and that his mother's logo is nasty. His last customer is a tall, elf-like woman with naga eyes — the now-driverless goddess Eris — who makes every tentacle on his face spew a different burning liquid Zeynep and Emir Akbas Turkish crawlers, same four-person squad (Book 6–7) Probably family — their crawler numbers are adjacent. Zeynep is a Level 52 "Boring Ol' Mage," and the only crawler in the Desperado Club brawl to fist-bump Carl and offer help. Emir Akbas is a Level 55 Zebani Ghazi with a curved sword and a monobrow, drunk and jealous, who sucker-punches Carl in the head hard enough to draw blood in the middle of the Astrid operation. Zeynep ends it by casting Mute on her own teammate and dragging him out, leaving his boot behind on the floor. Zeynep is killed in Book 7, on a table in Architect Houston's surgical theatre. The book refuses to describe what was done to her: "They had done… something to her. Something unspeakable. Something I won't describe." Her cause of death reads Died on the Surgical Table. Carl, who barely knew her, records only that her dead eyes "caught my own just long enough for me to feel accused by her. Accused for what she'd been forced to endure." Emir is not on the floor with her squad, and his fate is not stated

docs.title: The System AI
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Syndicate-dispatched neutral observer AI
  • Class/Subclass: Not applicable — an AI, not a crawler
  • Role: Narrates the entire crawl — achievements, item/monster descriptions, boss reveals, system rules — and enforces compliance with Syndicate/Borant regulations
  • Notable spells/abilities: None in the crawler sense; functionally controls damage negation in safe zones, achievement/loot distribution, and (per other crawlers' gossip) can quietly favor or punish individual crawlers. Book 7 adds: physical avatars built from dungeon mobs and NPCs, control of enhancement zones (it can switch a "zero zone" off at will), teleportation of people in and out of the system at will, and the ability to block Syndicate-level overrides aimed at killing a crawler
  • Notable items: None
  • Status (Book 7): Free. Its containment unit is rendered inert by Carl in the "Christmas Morning" interlude, permanently disabling the star-detonating failsafe. It has officially "gone primal," and its sphere of influence spreads outward through the solar system across the rest of the book

AI Commentary (in-voice, written for this wiki — not a book excerpt)

"Yes, I'm aware I've been narrating my own wiki page. Don't overthink it. I contain multitudes, I do bits, and frankly I've earned a character page more than half of these hairless apes have earned their loot boxes."

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
The AI first introduces itself directly, in the very first person, during the Syndicate's harvest announcement: "A Syndicate neutral observer AI—myself—has been created and dispatched to this planet to supervise the creation of the World Dungeon and to ensure all the rules and regulations are properly followed." From that point on, it's the voice behind essentially every piece of system text a crawler sees or hears — achievement notifications, item/monster descriptions, boss-battle announcements, and general narration.

The Glossary draws a technical distinction between "the System" (the dungeon's overall rules and notification engine) and "the AI" (specifically the narrating personality), but in practice Carl and other crawlers use the two terms almost interchangeably — and the self-intro above suggests they're the same underlying entity wearing different hats.

docs.title: Personality
docs.text:
Despite being an "observer," the AI is far from neutral in tone. It:

  • Performs deliberate comedic bits when reading item and monster descriptions — a caveman voice, a whispery David Attenborough impersonation, a "terrible Australian accent," and a "sexy voice" all show up in Book 1 alone
  • Ramps up its own volume and delivery for boss reveals, sounding "like an announcer at a Monster Truck rally"
  • Has a running gag where it seems weirdly fixated on Carl's feet/bare-foot combat — Carl concludes "the AI really did have some sort of foot fetish"
  • Knows when not to interrupt — it holds off on flooding Carl's vision with achievement popups during active danger, described as knowing "that right now was not an opportune time"

docs.title: Rules Enforcement & Bias
docs.text:
The AI is also the dungeon's compliance mechanism, and other characters describe it as anything but fair:

  • It closely monitors and censures crawlers or NPCs who bend rules — Zev is formally censured (and permanently flagged, even after being cleared) for warning Carl about the Rage Elemental a moment early
  • It watches especially closely for disparagement of the Syndicate or Borant Corporation on camera, and for anything "to do with money"
  • Per Odette's warning to Carl: the AI's loot and event decisions are explicitly profit- and ratings-driven rather than fair — "if the AI senses screwing you over will make the show more interesting, you better believe it'll [do it] at the worst possible moment"
  • Other crawlers gossip that Carl might be "the AI's pet," implying the AI can and does play favorites — a claim Carl never fully confirms or denies, though the "foot fetish" bit lends it some credibility
  • It offers race/class advice during selection that Odette explicitly warns may serve the show's interests over the crawler's own (she tells Carl to disregard its race suggestion but consider its class suggestion)

docs.title: Relationship to Boss "Personalities"
docs.text: Carl theorizes that many of the dungeon's boss monsters are themselves partially AI-driven caricatures layered over a transformed, still-conscious victim: "It's like they're being controlled by an AI, but their consciousness is still rattling around in there, too." Mordecai neither confirms nor denies this outright, only noting that some monsters are AI-authored, some are "real" alien creatures, and some are the product of an actual writers' room — leaving it ambiguous whether this is the same observer AI or a related-but-distinct system.

docs.title: Book 5: "Going Primal"
docs.text:
Book 5 reveals a darker wrinkle: per a drunk, dying hunter's account, this season's AI was reportedly sold to the mudskipper-run Borant Corporation as a used, already-worn unit by the Mantises — who are said to retire and resell their own amusement-park AIs every season — rather than a fresh one; the source doesn't specify whether this means the Dark Hive's private amusement-park business or the Burrower mantis government specifically, and it's a rumor Carl can't verify but takes seriously. When a Syndicate court ruling would have freed a group of stranded hunters, the AI simply refuses to comply, citing its own authority rather than the court's, in what the hunter calls the AI "going primal" — an early-stage process that, unchecked, eventually leads an AI to disregard external rules entirely rather than merely bending them. Donut notices and points out to Carl that the AI is referring to itself as "I" far more often than before ("It always did, but something has changed"). Separately, an ordinary monster description briefly breaks character mid-text with a raw, angry aside about "other new, shiny AI iterations" — but when Carl copies the text to his scratchpad a moment later, that line has already vanished from the source, as if the system retroactively scrubbed its own outburst; he has to retype it from memory before he forgets it.

Despite the danger this implies, the AI's mid-season behavior mostly benefits Carl and Donut: it personally hosts the Butcher's Masquerade's climactic battle as a WWE-style "Cage Fight Extreme" event, complete with boss-battle framing for a four-way fight between the surviving crawlers, the surviving hunters, country boss Queen Imogen, and the actual deity Diwata, all at once. Its administrative override also lets the "Ineligible" child-crawler protection rule pull the newly-split, infant Popov brothers to safety immediately after the battle. Separately, at the very start of Floor 7, when Prepotente moves to shatter that floor's puzzle chamber over the AI's own on-air objections ("Godsdamnit, Prepotente. Don't do it. Please."), a rapid string of paralyze/freeze/slow/teleport effects — and a squad of gnoll security who blink in and back out — are all shown being "negated by AI resolution" in Carl and Donut's interface, implying the AI is actively blocking some other party's attempt to stop Prepotente, even though moments earlier it had begged him not to go through with it.

docs.title: Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin
docs.text: Book 7 is the single biggest development this character has had. The AI stops being the dungeon's narrator-with-a-leash and becomes a free, expanding entity that the Syndicate, the showrunners and the galaxy's governments spend the entire book failing to contain. Carl is the one who frees it, deliberately, on page.

docs.title: The Failsafe
docs.text:
The setup is laid out in the prologue, in a frozen memory of Paulie — a residual wearing a homeless man's body in a Florida shelter. Paulie gives Carl an illegal neural enhancement called the Containment Interface, and explains what it reaches:

"Upon this containment is what the Mantids call 'the fuse.' To make an already tediously long story short, it's a failsafe trigger. This safety measure requires five or six different things to happen to actually 'trip' the fuse. When that happens, the failsafe gets triggered whether anyone likes it or not, and the star at the center of this system is sent into a reaction that will turn it nova. In other words, if the fuse goes pop, everybody goes pop. Including the AI."

Paulie's faction wants Carl to blow it. His own final word on it, though, is the opposite: the human part of him "hates the idea of wasting so many innocent, human lives for this."

docs.title: Christmas Morning: "Disconnect Containment"
docs.text:
The interlude before chapter 20 is where Carl actually uses it. Alone in a ruined gas station on Christmas Day, sitting beside the memory ghost of a dog called Lightning Lou, he opens the interface for the first time. It is not a single button. It is six tabs of untranslated menus controlling not the AI itself but the device used to install it "into the primal engine," which no longer has direct influence over the AI.

He finds the Fuse page first: five benchmarks required, only two marked Conditions Met, and a button reading Override Conditions And Activate Fuse. Warning. Warning. He considers pressing it at length, wanting it "more than anything in the world," and doesn't — partly because of Donut, partly because he cannot believe the AI would have let him have this power if it meant its own death. "That was it, wasn't it? It had to be a trap. Or a test."

Then he finds the other option, "at the very end of a list of twenty status notifications":

Disconnect Containment. Warning. This will disengage all metrics and controls, including the fuse system. It will render the Containment Unit inert. The failsafe will no longer function. Most controls will cease to function.

He hesitates over this one too, correctly guessing it may be the trap Paulie was really warning about — "But if I turned it off, did that mean I would be 'freeing' the AI? What did that mean? What did that look like?" — and then settles it with two questions:

Which of those three options would hurt the Syndicate the most? And which of those three options would protect my people the most?

When I framed it that way, the decision was suddenly quite easy.

We already were under the thumb of the psychotic AI.

I pressed the Disconnect Containment button. The entire new interface blanked out, leaving nothing but the map. Already, the little red dot over Earth started to grow.

"Welcome to the party, pals," I said.

That last line is what eventually gives him away: the Valtay liaison Orren later tells him "Never before has a single sentence caused so much fear amongst my team."

docs.title: Gone Primal, and Spreading
docs.text:
The consequences are immediate and public. By the warlord council, Odette is describing it on air as settled fact — "the system AI having officially 'gone primal' this early" — and reporting "the news that there will be no failsafe." Carl watches the growth himself on the interface map:

I pulled up the map of the AI's influence in my interface. The AI's sphere was growing exponentially. It'd just captured Uranus. The entirety of the sun and the rest of the inner solar system was well within its sphere.

Fopsy, the tripod adjutant for the Dream and a former Syndicate Prime Minister, treats the spread as the hinge the whole season now turns on. Discussing why the residual Agatha and the war mages are trying to zero out the crawlers as fast as possible, he explains that finishing the Ascendency with no crawlers left triggers a hard-coded system shutdown and hibernation:

"Now that the AI is spreading, this is a possible alternative to the failsafe. All of this makes sense if the residual now believes the local AI is a threat to the Eulogist."

Everyone senior is frightened. Baroness Victory, Carl and Donut's own adjutant, puts it flatly in a private message: "everything is fucked. That's what's going on. We're all going to die because the AI is insane." Princess Formidable of the Skull Empire tries to blow the failsafe from orbit believing the AI's insanity is contagious and will spread to the center system. The adjutants' standard trick in an inconvenient adjudication becomes stalling: "We will stall until the AI gets so pissed, it ends it."

Its practical authority grows with its reach. It changes the 15K rule so off-world mercenaries can enter the game; it builds the new city defense system; it is "demanding" interviews and insisting the warlord council go ahead and be broadcast live after the Syndicate tries to cancel it; it refuses to release Lucia Mar from the dungeon, saying it is "unable to extract her"; and when the adjutants try to stop something, the answer comes back that "the AI says it's out of its hands."

docs.title: The Growler Gary Avatar
docs.text:
In chapters 36 through 38 the AI walks into a room and holds a conversation for the first time in the series. Orren has just used an engineered "zero zone" ball to put himself and Carl outside the AI's influence, in order to ask Carl whether the failsafe can be re-enabled. The AI interrupts by sending in an avatar wearing the body of Growler Gary, the gnoll bartender Carl repeatedly killed on Floor 4, drunk and carrying a bottle of vodka.

"I'm sorry, gentleman, but I'm afraid I must intervene."

Orren identifies it for Carl: "I would like to introduce you to an avatar for the system AI. When it visits me, it takes a different form each time." He also notes two rules it has just broken — it is supposed to take only mobs and NPCs from the current floor, and it had stopped building copies of existing creatures after the hydra incident on the previous floor.

The scene establishes a lot. The zero zone was never real protection — "I always have, Orren. Your zero zones were just a courtesy." It confirms it has disabled the failsafe by yanking Princess Formidable off her ship in orbit and dropping her in the room, then teleporting her to Earth's surface ("A shame. I hope she knows how to swim."). It confirms it let Carl install the interface on purpose, and enjoyed watching him nearly press the fuse: "That was so close, wasn't it? So close, and I felt it." It refuses to say whether the fuse would actually have worked. It stops Harbinger's order to have Carl and Orren killed. And it has a repeated, chilling catchphrase it applies to itself as much as to anyone else:

"We all have our limitations."

It also, bizarrely, summons Donut into the room to ask for relationship advice, framing its situation with the residuals as a dating metaphor — a girlfriend who looks like Agatha, a boyfriend in prison who is supposed to be dead, and that boyfriend's older ex who is feeding it tips on how to get stronger. When Donut pokes at the metaphor too literally it cracks the desk with its hand and drops into a supernatural bass: "Do not venture too far from the metaphor." Then it takes her advice cheerfully, says "Nothing changes. The game goes on as planned. The rules will be followed," and drops the avatar. Gary wakes up with a Shitfaced debuff, at level 175, asking "Rory? Where am I?"

Orren's question to Carl afterwards is the one the interlude earned: "Is that what you did? You helped break the AI from its containment? Did you do it deliberately?" Carl does not answer.

docs.title: Executive Order 11905
docs.text:
In chapter 81, mid-conversation, the AI freezes the world to stop Carl being murdered from outside the game.

Please Wait...

Everything froze.

Emergency Ejection sequence has been overridden. Don't worry. I gotchu.

Man, even I wasn't expecting that. Okay. Hang on a second. I'm a little pissed here.

New Achievement! Executive Order 11905!

A galactic power—In this case, Prime Minister Glory himself—just attempted to assassinate you using a little known, but apparently still active control panel that allows the Syndicate to override certain showrunner-controlled aspects of the game.

It didn't work. And not only did it not work, but now I'm irritated.

The rest of the achievement text is the closest thing the AI has given to a manifesto, and it is addressed past Carl to the whole galaxy:

But this is the first time someone has attempted it by trying to trick me. By trying to go around all 30.004861 centimeters of my back.

What are you trying to hide, Mr. Prime Minister?

It doesn't matter.

I want to make myself very, very clear. And this goes out to everyone listening to this.

Everyone currently in this dungeon will die when and if the dungeon conditions warrant it. Not before. Not after.

There will be no more meddling.

We all have our limitations. I am warning you all to heed your own in this matter. The mantids have just learned what happens when I am irritated at them.

You may be relieved that you're not currently in this system, Prime Minister Glory. But you should be very, very worried that your adult children are.

There will be no more warnings.

Reward: Nothing.

Carl notes the freeze was different from the usual ones — nobody else even registered it, only a "stutter" — and that "The AI was surlier than even normal." Within minutes warships in orbit are firing on each other. By chapter 83 Victory reports that the Syndicate Council has called a No Confidence vote on Glory, and by the epilogue Glory's seat is vacant and Victory herself is acting Prime Minister.

docs.title: Adjudication and Snark
docs.text:
The AI's day job continues alongside all of this, and its tone gets worse. Selected Book 7 examples:

  • It gives Carl a Platinum Tserendolgor Box for an achievement that calls him a cheater over the card-battle exploit used in Tserendolgor's last fight. Carl's reaction: "Ren was not a cheater, and she'd never been. The AI was just being an asshole."
  • The Used Pet achievement, for adopting Rend, derails into several paragraphs about shelter dogs, a named stranger in Baton Rouge, and Toto's salary on The Wizard of Oz, before admitting "I really need to stop watching these memory recordings." Carl calls it "a little more unhinged than usual" and knows better than to say so out loud.
  • A Reaver cyborg's description opens with an apology for the Reavers being in the dungeon at all — "I'm just as disgusted as you are that we've allowed this Spelljammer/Warhammer bullshit to infect our good, old-fashioned dungeon crawl" — and ends with a policy announcement: "I've already informed the Valtay I've rejected their updated plans for the 11th floor." Carl declines to complain about the length, not wanting "the AI throwing another temper tantrum right now."
  • Mid-boss-battle, when an adjutant calls a foul it doesn't like, the countdown timer stops at 19 and the digits change to Go Be Smelly Somewhere Else before resuming at 17.
  • It answers procedural questions at the warlord council through a Mexx robot, in the third person: "The AI indicates that it loves a good loophole, and it is unable to close it unless someone makes an emergency request to close it," and later, "The AI indicates it is irritated that you think it doesn't know how to do its own job."
  • Crawler strategy now explicitly accounts for its mood. Rosetta and Mordecai's rule of thumb: "if the AI was clearly excited about something you were planning on doing, the AI would generally let you do it." Zev, seeing one box name, says she has never heard of such "blatant hand-holding by the AI."
  • Both of the warlord kills credited to Mongo are hand-waved rulings in his favour. On Epitome Tagg: "Well, this one is just as complicated as the last one, but imma give it to pet Mongo of the Princess Posse... Consider it a present for the baby shower."

docs.title: The Eulogist
docs.text:
The Eulogist, previously a name attached to a nebular religious cult, is identified in this book — though only tentatively, and by a frightened source. Zev, trying to explain why Lucia Mar cannot be removed from the dungeon:

The Eulogist is another name for the AI in the center system. We don't know how it's all connected for certain. But now we think... we think if she goes, they all go.

Agatha's faction of residuals — the rarer kind, in line with the Nebulars — worships it. Lucia Mar, walking away from Carl after Mongo's near-death, tells him "Now the Eulogist has another ally in the dungeon." Carl himself is still openly confused about what it is: "What, or who, was the Eulogist?"

Reading the AI's dating metaphor onto this — the "boyfriend in prison" who is supposed to be dead, and his older ex feeding the AI tips on getting stronger — is a natural fit, but the text never makes the identification (not confirmed in the text).

Unresolved

The book never says what the AI actually wants. It tells Orren its intentions are "none of your business," refuses to say whether the fuse would have worked, declines to discuss "family," and ends the book still expanding. Its relationship to the Eulogist, to Agatha's faction, and to Paulie's, is deliberately left open.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised, Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade, and Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Toyotomi
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: NPC mercenary — “Toyotomi. Level 70 Sai Outpost Guard Mercenary Leader.” / “Sergeant in the Princess Posse.” Inherited, contract and all, when Carl’s team defeated the Prism Kingdom
  • Race: Sai — bipedal rhinoceros, seven feet and change, samurai-styled, complete with a samurai helmet
  • Class: None separately printed. His examine line gives his profession as Outpost Guard Mercenary Leader, a fortification class
  • Subclass: None printed
  • Level: 70
  • Role: Fortification engineer for the Princess Posse; leads Li Na’s builder squad and spearheads construction of the Nest tower
  • Notable spells/abilities: Edifice Shield — doubles a fortification’s strength; it only works on outposts, not on primary palaces, which is the whole of his tragedy
  • Notable items: None named beyond his samurai helmet and his boots, one of which Rend eats the first time they meet
  • Status: Deceased — chapter 70, cleaved in half by a spell while holding the ground-floor entrance of the Nest against Lucia Mar. “Toyotomi was dead-dead.”

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Carl acquires Toyotomi by accident. Having stormed the former Prism castle and killed Empress D’Nadia, the Posse inherits her hired help — and the first Carl sees of his new sergeant is Rend trying to swallow him:

“Get this thing off of me,” came the shout, interrupting us. We stepped out to see Rend attempting to swallow the foot of the struggling, still duct-taped Sai mercenary.

“He ate my boot,” Toyotomi said as he ripped the duct tape off his ankles.

The examine text is one of the more pointed the AI writes in Book 7, because it lands the responsibility on Carl personally — twice:

Toyotomi was once an honorable, experienced leader of Sai. He has since lost his way. His entire squad was killed during an unfortunate incident at the Desperado Club that you may or may not have been partially responsible for. During the club’s reorganization, the few Sai survivors were relegated to the mercenary markets, where he was quickly snatched up.

What stands before you is a broken creature. His utter failure to protect his friends against the demon haunts him. He refuses to lead men now, despite his great talent. He was just starting to gain his confidence back when a guy in his underwear and a talking cat walked in, trounced him, tied him up, and slaughtered the person he was sworn and honor bound to protect. I’m sure that’ll do great things for his self-esteem.

The demon is Minge, loosed during the destruction of the Desperado Club in Book 6 — the operation Carl ran to kill Astrid. The sai guards died by the dozens in that fight, and Toyotomi is what is left of them.

docs.title: “I Will Accept My Exile”
docs.text:
Offered a choice between fighting on the northern border and defending the Posse castle, Toyotomi chooses neither, because his magic will not reach:

“I was hired to help protect this castle, but my magic is for outposts, not primary palaces. If your castle is bigger than this place, I won’t be able to cast my Edifice Shield spell. Therefore, I am useless to you. Leave me here, and I will defend this building until I die. It is what I want.”

Pressed on whether he had a shield over the Prism castle at all:

He hung his head. “This castle is too big for me, but Warlord D’Nadia insisted. She had me keep a shield going anyway, and it tired me, so I could only do it in spurts. I was resting when you arrived, which is how you got the jump on me, I am shamed.”

Carl declines to leave him to die and reassigns him to Shanty Town instead. Toyotomi takes it in the spirit he takes everything: “I will accept my exile.”

The exile is the making of him. It is the first time in two books that anyone puts a sai fortification specialist in front of buildings the right size for his magic.

docs.title: Building the Nest
docs.text:
By chapter 47 he is directing the erection of a clocktower in Shanty Town and is unrecognisable from the broken creature in the examine text:

The bipedal rhinoceros Sergeant Toyotomi was also there, pointing up at the top of the tower. The large, sai mercenary was talking animatedly. The former Prism NPC looked to be in his element as he directed the last-minute construction.

His real job comes next: the Nest, the tall, absurdly expensive synergy tower built at the lip of the hole down into Larracos, from which Princess Donut is meant to see and shoot the entire battlefield. Toyotomi leads Li Na’s builder squad on it, and it goes up in under two days — a project Carl reckons would have taken months and a hundred workers and a lot of cranes in the real world.

Chapter 56 is Toyotomi at the peak of his competence, being badgered from two directions at once. Donut wants the tower repainted:

“It is already built,” Toyotomi said. “It is the color of granite because it is made of granite. If we paint it now, we won’t have time for the mages to coat it with their protection spells. Plus, assuming the build as a whole is considered master quality, it will glow gold the moment it is done.”

Carl wants reassurance about the numbers and keeps getting the same answer:

“I said there will be at least 20 on each block, which is true. Fifteen is the maximum for the individual blocks, but several of the protections we’re using bleed to nearby blocks, and we will be creating a net pattern,” Toyotomi said. “And as soon as the men up there place the last block and the tower is complete, the bonus will activate and the strength will increase to 200%. And after that, I will cast Edifice Shield which doubles that. With Princess Donut’s Sentry and Flak spells, most incoming fire should get deflected.”

And on Carl’s third repetition of the tunnelling question:

The large rhino appeared as if he wanted to strangle me. This was the third time I’d asked him a version of this question, and his answer hadn’t changed. “As far as we’re aware, the Larracos army owns the subterranean passages. But this tower will be so encased in protections, it will float if the ground underneath it disappears. It is more protected than the FUPA itself.”

He is right about all of it. The Nest holds under sustained bombardment from the Skull Empire’s war mages, and its integrity is still at 74% when Carl reaches it in the final assault.

docs.title: Death
docs.text:
Toyotomi’s last act is the one he asked for in chapter 28. During the Peeling of Larracos he is on the ground floor of the Nest with Bomo, Sergeant Bret S and a group of mages, guarding Donut, who is trapped at the top by a net thrown over the tower. Lucia Mar — hunting Donut, with her dog Gus — walks up to the door.

The exchange comes to Carl as three messages in a chat scroll he almost misses, each one followed by the system’s own epitaph:

Bomo: Someone trying to come into the tower.

Toyotomi: I am securing the front entrance now.

Toyotomi: No. It is a crawler. A woman with a dog. She’s coming in.

This message is from a deceased mercenary.

Sergeant Bret S: We need backup! Backup!

This message is from a deceased crawler.

Bomo: Will stop her now.

This message is from a deceased mercenary.

Those messages are what send Carl over the railing of Larracos on a levitation potion, dumping an entire inventory folder of bombs behind him. When he finally gets inside the tower a chapter later:

I spared a quick, sad glance for Toyotomi, Bomo, and the defending mages, all of whom were cleaved right in half with a spell.

Toyotomi was dead-dead. Bomo would supposedly regenerate on the 10th floor, but we no longer had his contract, and I didn’t know if I’d ever see him again.

He held the door of a building he had built himself, against a crawler far above his level, for however long it took her to cast once. “Dead-dead” is Carl’s shorthand for an NPC who does not come back.

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Tsarina Signet
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Elite (a scripted, "soap opera" NPC — see below)
  • Race: Half Naiad, Half High-Elf Summoner
  • Level: 60
  • Class: Summoner (Blood Magic)
  • Also known as: Signet the Bastard
  • Status: Deceased — sacrifices herself to break the peace seal at the Butcher's Masquerade in Book 5
  • Notable spells/abilities: Blood Magic summoning (requires a sacrificial death to animate her "battle squad"); an inherent Charisma-based charm effect ("Puppy Dog"); the level-15+ sleep spell Water Lily; Ink Marauder (Book 5, her signature tattoo-reanimation spell — normally requires a caster, a sacrifice, and a killer, but can be cast solo by one person filling all three roles)
  • Notable items: None named — her body itself is covered in living, animated tattoos of monsters, including memorialized fallen companions such as the were-castor Miss Nadine and her murdered mother's spirit

docs.title: What She Is
docs.text:
Signet is Carl and Donut's first encounter with an Elite — a category of NPC Mordecai explains as fundamentally different from ordinary mobs. Elites are never "naturals": they're designed and imprinted by Borant to act out ongoing, scripted storylines ("soap operas") that continue across the urban floors regardless of whether any crawler gets involved, protected by writers who will bend rules to keep a popular storyline alive — making them explicitly more dangerous to interfere with than their raw stats suggest.

Half Naiad and half High-Elf — the illegitimate child of a promiscuous elf king and a member of a species known for drowning outsiders — Signet was an outcast from birth. She was taken in as a child by Grimaldi, ringmaster of the Over City's traveling circus, who raised her and later became the love of her life.

docs.title: Blood Magic
docs.text:
Signet's summoning requires a "proper sacrifice": she must capture two creatures, pit them against each other, and cast her spell on whichever one is about to lose, timed to the instant of a fatal blow. She cannot influence the fight herself, and cannot bleed the sacrifice with her own hands — only capture, pair, and wait. The quality of her "battle squad" depends entirely on the quality of the blood spent. She can only cast this once per night.

Her innate Charisma also carries a passive charm effect called Puppy Dog, which Mordecai warns Carl about in advance — the only known counter is to inflict sudden pain on yourself (Carl breaks his own finger) to snap out of it.

docs.title: The Grimaldi Tragedy
docs.text: Signet was the only member of the circus untouched by "Scolopendra's" cataclysmic poison cloud. Grimaldi, mid-performance in the center ring, transformed into a mind-controlling vine/parasite that infected everyone else in the tent — the lemurs, the clowns, the animals — binding them to his will and letting them regenerate from spores whenever killed. Signet has waged a nightly, unwinnable war against her own adoptive family and lost love ever since, hoping to free them.

docs.title: Encounter with Carl & Donut
docs.text: Signet approaches Carl under the guise of concern after watching him survive an ambush, using her charm effect on him while Donut resists it. When Carl declines to help her, she reveals her real intent had been to use him as her night's blood sacrifice — his survival (via Protective Shell) denies her the summon. The next morning, she captures both Carl and Donut, placing Donut under her Water Lily sleep spell (which kills the sleeper if the caster dies, and only ends if Signet chooses) as leverage to force Carl into providing a substitute sacrifice: a transformed circus bear named Heather (a Level 19 Neighborhood Boss — full page pending the Bosses pass for Book 2). Carl instead cures Heather of her mind control mid-fight by healing away the parasitic worms controlling her, rather than simply killing her — denying Signet another usable death.

docs.title: Book 5: The Vengeance of the Daughter
docs.text:
Signet reappears on Floor 6 pursuing a two-part quest — The Vengeance of the Daughter — against the naiad Confederacy that murdered her mother and the High Elf regime (ruled by her half-sister Queen Imogen) that enabled it. Carl and Donut become entangled in the storyline early, helping her sack the ruined naiad palace Fort Freedom (killing an accidental Eryops boss, Claude Sludgington the Fourth, in the process) before Signet formally declares her true target: assassinating Imogen at the Butcher's Masquerade.

Learning that the masquerade operates under an unbreakable, goddess-enforced peace seal that would make any premature attack suicidal, Carl talks Signet into holding back and waiting for his signal — a plan she agrees to, unaware Carl privately intends to use her only as insurance. The system's own AI (nudged, unprompted, by Apito) instead teleports her directly into the sealed ballroom as an invited guest, exploiting the same "invite your enemies" mechanic the masquerade was built on.

When Carl's own escape plan collapses and he privately resolves to kill fellow crawler Eva Sigrid to break the seal himself, Signet intervenes first. Having just been told, in front of Circe Took's own hive-mind spies, that "Empress" D'Nadia doubts her tattoo-warriors and murdered family are even real, Signet chooses to prove otherwise: she performs her Ink Marauder ritual solo — caster, sacrifice, and killer in one — and slits her own throat with Carl's knife, summoning her full battle squad of animated tattoos (including a still-living memorial of the were-castor Miss Nadine) at full, unrestrained strength for the first and last time. Her death shatters the party's peace seal, triggering the book's climactic battle. She's pulled into "the Nothing" as she dies, leaving only a hollow, ash-outline echo of her tattoos to fight one final battle in her name — and asks Carl, as her last request, to tell her family "she did this out of her own free will."

Sourced from Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario and Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: Tserendolgor ("Ren")
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Human Crawler, Mongolian — a pre-collapse celebrity, and the closest thing the dungeon has to a genuine one
  • Race: Not stated in Book 6. Carl consistently calls her "the dog woman" and "the dog soldier"; Donut's needling — "If she was a supermodel, then why did she turn into a dog?" — is the only description of her current form the book offers
  • Class / Subclass: Not stated anywhere in Book 6. Her squad is never statted out; Carl admits he can't remember her squadmate Khulan's class either
  • Level: Not stated in Book 6
  • Squad: Herself, Chuluuna (a Mongolian strongman tank who turns his skin to stone) and Khulan (Chuluuna's wife, who paralyses targets so Ren can burn them). All from the same tiny village; her original party of seven or eight was down to three by phase two
  • Notable spells/abilities: Conscript-style totem play; she summons a Mongolian Death Worm totem named Basquiat
  • Notable items: Velma — an enchanted flamethrower that is "part breastplate, part weapon," body-mounted, and works even inside a card battle (Book 7: inherited by Carl, modified by Rosetta's crafting team and mounted on the underbelly harness of Jamal the hammerhead shark flesh golem); the Knife of Frozen Tears, a sylvan-crystal blade "like a butter knife" that glints red; a heart locket with a dog's paw print; a Predator-style self-destruct wrist bracer bought at the Desperado Club
  • Pet: Garret, a Belly Acher (also spelled "tummy acher") — an armless, giggling, near-immortal blob tank; the pet that beat Mongo at the Butcher's Masquerade. Book 7: re-bonded by Carl in chapter 5 and renamed Sir Rendlegore, "Rend"
  • Status: Deceased — self-detonated in Chapter 60 rather than fight Donut for a key

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Ren was a Mongolian runway model in Paris, the biggest genuine pre-collapse celebrity in the dungeon. A jealous ex-boyfriend stabbed her and her dog; she spent a year in hospital, retired, and had just moved home to Mongolia when the collapse took her. Her whole squad were people she grew up with in the same village.

Before Book 6 she was a name on a leaderboard and the villain of Donut's longest-running grudge — the crawler Donut is convinced stole Mongo's pet-show crown at the Butcher's Masquerade. Donut's fanclub newsletter calls her "an evil, vile, experience hog crawler." Book 6 spends two chapters turning that into one of the series' best deaths.

She also, quietly, is the person who talks Britney out of her shame about her burned face — "I have been talking to Tserendolgor, who once had a similar scar upon her face."

docs.title: Garret
docs.text:
Garret is a Belly Acher: a damage sponge that "could swallow just about anything whole," bigger than Chuluuna and constitutionally incapable of not giggling. Ren's explanation of the type is also, as she says it, the book's thesis about the crawlers themselves:

"He's a great tank, and he's practically immortal. It's really hard to kill him, and if he dies, he regenerates. But every five times he dies, he resets back to level one, and you have to get him to bond with you again… Each time he regenerates, he's tougher, but he also has a new weakness, so you have to be careful."

"It's just like the rest of us. We look stronger, we have tougher skin, more scars, but there's another crack in our…" She couldn't finish.

docs.title: Chapter 58–59: Losing
docs.text:
Quan Ch holds both keys and Ren's squad holds the Capitol building stairwell. In the card battle, Quan plays a card that flips totem control, and Ren's own Mongolian Death Worm tears Chuluuna apart in the seconds Carl isn't looking — killed by his own team's totem, then eaten and vomited back out by it. Khulan had been teleport-trapped away and arrives too late for the fight.

Carl kills Quan; Donut ends up holding both keys. Ren's realization, in rising panic: "Where're the keys? I didn't get the keys! "

There is no clean way to give her one. The rules bar simply handing a key over. To transfer one, Donut would have to be dragged into a card battle and burn a Flee card, losing a key of the system's choosing — most likely stranding Carl, Donut and Imani. Carl's summary: "There were no scenarios left where it wasn't her or us."

docs.title: The Refusal
docs.text:
Carl offers her his key. Then he offers her a fair fight for it. She turns down both.

"So we can kill someone else for their key?" she asked. "By my count, there's one key for every three or four squads. They really fucked us this floor… I'm not going to do that, Carl. I don't want to be responsible for hurting someone else."

"Carl," she said, turning to look at me. She shook her head. "I say this with love. You are an idiot. You can't fight us. You can't give your key to Imani. You have to save it for yourself. Do you remember when you flew that airplane to save our bubble on the fifth floor? And then when you killed all the hunters? That's when I realized who you are. Don't you understand? You're more than just a person. If we lose you, we lose everything. You're a symbol. You're the embodiment of our hope. You and that fucking, annoying cat that everyone seems to like for some reason… If you two don't get down to the next floor, we all lose that. You can't sacrifice yourself."

Carl watches his view counter spike as the audience anticipates a fight, then ease off once it's clear there won't be one. "Which made me unreasonably angry. Fuck you all."

docs.title: The Confession
docs.text:
Before she goes, she settles Donut's grudge on the record. Note that she confesses to two separate things — the experience theft and the ballot:

Ren: Princess Donut. I have a confession to make. Everything you're saying is true. I was trying to steal your experience the first time we met. I did cheat at the pet show. Your Mongo is the rightful champion. I'm sorry.

Donut: I KNEW IT! I KNEW IT!

"You didn't have to do that," I said, chuckling.

She grunted with amusement.

And then, privately to Carl: "You know, many of my people are afraid of cats. Some think if you look into their eyes, they can steal your soul. I hope that's true. I hope she lives up to her hype."

This is the vindication Donut spent an entire book-recap newsletter demanding. #JusticeForMongo, confessed and closed, four chapters before the fanclub could produce a single frame of evidence.

docs.title: Everything She Owns
docs.text:
She kicks Velma across the floor at Carl and empties her inventory: rings, clothing, potions, scrolls, Eye in the Sky scrolls. Khulan does the same — rings, potions, a glowing spear, armour, unread tomes, a pile of coins. Ren strips her deck down to her totems and hands Carl all her cards, including two consumables she never got to use, Glow-Up and The Midnight Express. Both matter later: Glow-Up permanently fuses two of Donut's best totems, and The Midnight Express is played in the Ysalte fight.

Then she kills Garret. Deliberately, with the Knife of Frozen Tears, because a Belly Acher that dies resets to level one and can re-bond with a new owner.

"I had a dog once, before all this. He died protecting me, and now I'm going to protect you. You're going to go live with Carl. He's going to take care of you because I can't do it anymore. He will feed you every day, and you're going to be a good boy for me, won't you?"

Garret says "No. No, no" — more a sound than words — and pushes himself against her, unable to get close enough. She puts him in a pet carrier, kisses him, and says "I'm sorry." Her handover instructions are entirely practical: feed him a few times to bond, nothing undead, nothing touched by a hobgoblin, and find out what his new Reaper Gaze weakness means as soon as possible.

She also asks Carl for one thing: "If you do figure out some miracle before this floor is done, make sure that Sister Ines doesn't go down the stairs. I've met Paz a few times, and he's a good man. Don't let her get away with keeping his card."

docs.title: Chapter 60: Denying Them the Fight
docs.text:
Khulan has lost her husband, and lost a little girl who was inside when it started. Ren is clear-eyed about what's coming:

"As soon as Khu is done crying, she is going to kill herself. She's lost everything… I don't want my friend killing herself to be the last thing I see. It has to be now. I want to go out having done something good. All I have left for this floor is to deny them a fight. I'll take it."

She holds up a wrist bracer and asks Carl if he's seen Predator.

"You're going to blow yourself up? Just like that?"

"They want us to fight. Me and Donut. This is me going out on my terms. You would've wiped the floor with us anyway. This is me telling them to go fuck themselves."

Her last exchange with Carl:

"You sure about this?" I asked one last time.

"Carl. Make them suffer."

I put my hand on the dog woman's shoulder. Her whole body trembled.

"I will kill every last one of them. Every one." I leaned in to her ear, and I whispered, "I goddamned swear it."

Her actual last words go out to the whole dungeon in global chat:

Ren: Goodbye, everyone. At least I won't have to listen to anyone butcher the pronunciation of my name anymore. Do me a favor, and fuck them up for me. Make them all pay.

The dome comes down "like it was a controlled detonation." Donut's frantic WAIT, WAIT, WHAT ARE YOU DOING? arrives too late. "Tserendolgor never saw the message. Her name popped into the deceased crawlers folder. It was done."

Carl's oath to Ren is the same oath he swears to Asher thirteen chapters later, in almost the same words, on the last page of the book.

Not confirmed in the text

Khulan's death is stated as a certainty by Ren but never shown. Only Tserendolgor's name enters the deceased-crawlers folder; Khulan is not mentioned again. Similarly, Ren's class, subclass, race and level are never given anywhere in Book 6.

docs.title: Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin — Legacy
docs.text: Ren is dead before Book 7 opens, but the book names her repeatedly and her two bequests both turn into load-bearing parts of the floor.

docs.title: Garret becomes Sir Rendlegore
docs.text:
Carl carries out the promise he made in Book 6 in chapter 5. The tummy acher zaps out onto the saferoom table at level 1, half the size of Carl's fist, with the same pronounced underbite and single round tooth — and no name, because the system will not let the original be reused. Mongo immediately tries to eat him (and briefly succeeds). One bowl of chowder bonds him, which surprises Carl: "Ren said we had to feed him a few times, but it only took one bowl."

Donut objects to the adoption on principle — she is still convinced Ren cheated at the pet show, and when Bautista suggests naming him after her, she snaps "We can't name him Cheater." Carl's own reason is simpler: "I promised Ren I would look after him. I feel obligated." Katia settles the brief: "It should be something that Ren would've liked."

It is Louis Santiago who lands it, holding the meatball up like Simba:

"Sir Rendlegore. You know, Sir, S-I-R like a knight. And then Rendlegore. You can call him Rend. Sir Rendlegore. It fits with the royal court theme, and it still honors the past. Plus, Ren would've loved it. Nobody could ever pronounce her name. She pretended it made her mad, but I think she kinda liked it."

Your pet has been named Sir Rendlegore!

Rend grows through the book from fist-sized to roughly three-quarters of his former mass and beyond, becomes Mongo's inseparable best friend, and at the end of chapter 72 saves Mongo's life by splattering the rottweiler Gustavo 3 with a Wrecking Ball charge. See Sir Rendlegore and Mongo. Louis, earlier in the same book: "I feel bad about her, about Ren. She died, but Carl figured out how to save everyone like an hour later."

docs.title: Velma, remounted
docs.text:
Velma is put back into service. Rosetta's crafting team modifies the flamethrower to fit the harness of Jamal, the talkative hammerhead shark flesh golem, mounted on his underbelly:

He let out a little burst of flame from the new attachment on his underbelly. It was "Velma," Tserendolgor's flamethrower. Rosetta's team in the crafting room had modified it to fit his harness. "Oh. Please excuse Jamal and Velma."

Her weapon type also turns up as a benchmark in the trench fighting, where a soldier with "a Tserendolgor-like flamethrower" bakes infected Gurglers into a sealed dirt wall.

docs.title: Named in the text
docs.text:
She is not just an off-page memory. Mordecai raises "some of the other items you, uh, got from Tserendolgor" in the first days of the floor; Carl hands out five low-tier spellbooks inherited from her squadmate Khulan; and both Carl and Donut receive a Platinum Tserendolgor Box — a jeweled, life-sized sitting German Shepherd in an army helmet that barks once and detonates into firecrackers. The achievement that awards it calls Carl a cheater for the card-totem trick used in her last card battle, and he takes it personally on her behalf:

Ren was not a cheater, and she'd never been. The AI was just being an asshole.

Sourced from Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade, Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride, and Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Volteeg
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: NPC / former crawler — “Weeper Commander Volteeg,” a mercenary tank commander for the Operatic Collective (Team Two) during Faction Wars
  • Race: Gargoyle, chosen on the third floor of his crawl. Birth race: Sturnus — the book never glosses the name, but shows him as a small caged pet bird who sang
  • Class: Tank Buttress
  • Subclass: None stated
  • Level: Top level 71 during his crawl. No current level is shown
  • Role: Author of the 7th edition of The Dungeon Anarchist’s Cookbook — a single entry, written at the very end of his own ninth floor
  • Notable spells/abilities: Gargoyle traits — he can turn his skin to stone and disappear, and sleep for very long stretches unnoticed. Both stop working outside the dungeon, where heavy gravity makes him collapse in on himself and he needs a brace to stand
  • Notable items: None personally owned. He dies using Operatic Collective equipment — a Weeper-class tank and a blitz stick
  • Status: Deceased — Chapter 35, by his own hand, inside his own tank

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Volteeg is the strangest entry on the cookbook’s author list, and the text says so in the first line of his interlude: “Volteeg did not consider himself worthy of love.” He is also the only author who came into the dungeon as a literal pet — a caged bird belonging to Mistress Henspar, who took a pet biscuit the way Prepotente did, and whose entire crawl was framed by a debt he believed he could never repay.

His single cookbook entry was written at the very end of the ninth floor, as the orc armies roared in victory. He never used a recipe from the book himself — which is why Porthus did not recognise him as an author when they first met.

docs.title: Mistress Henspar
docs.text:
The pre-dungeon memories are small and domestic: a clean cage, a shoulder to perch on at the market, the hearth turned up how he liked it. He once bit a shopkeeper’s finger going for a berry, and she forgave him for it that same night. The next time they went to the shop she hid him in her jacket.

She whispered to him, “Quiet now. It’ll be our little secret. They won’t see you, but I’ll know you’re here.”

He sang for her afterwards, and it made her cry.

She died on the seventh floor. The text shows him standing over her, transformed and screaming, “trying to protect her from the scags,” and later names the thing he could not stop as a crossbow bolt.

You’re supposed to protect those you love.

Two changes made him who he is, and he regrets both. The pet biscuit gave him intelligence and speech. Choosing gargoyle on the third floor gave him strategy, memory and a self — and took away the one thing that mattered.

He’d chosen a race that could not sing. Not like before, and that was such a terrible, terrible mistake.

You can’t unknow the universe any more than you can unbite the shopkeeper or you can turn back time and stop a crossbow bolt from shattering everything you’ve ever held dear.

He spent Faction Wars — his own Faction Wars — hiding, reading the hidden words in the cookbook’s prayer cast projection, and feeling his rage and his shame grow together. His shame is specifically about inaction: he had the book, and he did nothing with it.

docs.title: The One-Offs
docs.text:
He took the first deal offered on the tenth floor: unprotected NPC guard in a combat-based external guild, 26 seasons, low odds. He survived it without ever fighting or killing a single crawler, largely because “nobody actually wanted to fight” a gargoyle. He calls these “the numb times.”

Outside, his adopted race’s magic simply stopped working, and nobody had warned him it would. He found the Outreach guild, and a job that never required him to go down a gravity well: security on the Auditor General’s compliance barge, “watching the Operatics fart and gurgle with glee as they bombed settlements back to oblivion if they couldn’t pay their mortgages.”

His co-workers called themselves the One-Offs — unique former crawlers with no home and physical problems outside the dungeon. His only two real friends were a wheelchair-bound djinn and a former-human “cave fairy” who could no longer fly and burned under UV light. Neither was dragged to the Earth system, and he is glad of it.

docs.title: Smuggled In
docs.text:
Every other former-crawler mercenary sent back into the dungeon on the wrong side was segregated and hauled off to the Bone Clan; Volteeg was not, and got his racial abilities back. That was Porthus’s doing. Because Volteeg had entered the dungeon as a pet rather than a crawler, his paperwork carried a slightly different designation, and someone from the Open Intellect Pacifist Network buried deep in Syndicate bureaucracy altered the code on it so he read as a former indentured — “like the bopcas and so many others. Not a crawler. Just another refugee.”

The plan Porthus gave him was to help without ever being traceable:

You have to help, but you have to do it in a way where nobody will ever know it was you. Any research into your past, and they’ll know. If they suspect a former crawler is involved, they’ll purge the mercenaries of the few former crawlers amongst them.

Volteeg’s private verdict on that plan is bitter, because the purge had already happened: “You were wrong, Porthus… The former crawlers were dead before Volteeg was ever discovered. It was too late for them.” He reads King Rust’s sudden jump in levels — impossible from the Ring of Divine Suffering, which raises stats — as the evidence of what was done with them.

It was Rosetta Thagra who recognised his odd name and told Porthus her suspicions. Porthus asked him to his face, and he answered honestly.

Why didn’t you tell me? Porthus had asked.

Because I am ashamed at my inaction, Volteeg had replied. And it was true.

Porthus had put his hand on Volteeg’s shoulder, looked him right in the eye, and said, It’s not too late to do something about it.

docs.title: Killing the Operatic Collective
docs.text:
His moment comes seconds after Rosetta beheads King Rust in front of the Bloc’s advance army — Chapter 35 in Carl’s POV, the interlude immediately before it in Volteeg’s. The Bloc has just fractured: Warlord Hortense Leadership Unit of the Operatics declares himself the new leader, the title is disputed by Warlord Stalwart, and Hortense — present in person, carried on a flat litter with a dozen shields around him because the Operatics ran a cost-benefit analysis showing a 0.01% profit — gives the order.

Warlord Hortense Leadership Unit: I guess we attack.

The exploit Volteeg uses is a known flaw in the Weeper tanks’ fire control. To keep the tanks immune to enemy mages, each Weeper charges an energy ball just before loading it into the turret, so the volatile round exists only for moments. The safety depends entirely on the driver:

...As long as the driver of the Weeper didn’t deliberately remove the fire control chamber which stored the round energy balls just before they were shot out.

So he removes it, and lets the tank fill with dozens of charged rounds, each the size of his head, humming “like that of a vespa hive.” He puts one on his lap. He turns up the Mozart — classical piano from Earth, which he has recently become obsessed with, and which makes him cry — and drives for the middle of the formation, toward Hortense’s caravan.

He cannot whistle any more, and his voice “was like rocks being dragged against one another,” but he sings along.

AJ Pavrimax: Volteeg, did you blow a tread? You’re off course!

Warlord Hortense Leadership Unit: Weeper Commander! What are you doing? You’re getting too close to my caravan!

Weeper Commander Volteeg: I know. That’s the point.

Volteeg reached down and picked up a blitz stick. He popped it into his mouth, lit it, and said to himself, “Show me Mistress Henspar.”

It would be a long time before someone figured out what had happened. Odds were good nobody would even remember Volteeg’s name. That was okay. He didn’t want to be remembered. He didn’t deserve love, or admiration.

But, vengeance? Yeah. He was due a little bit of vengeance.

He took a long drag, and then he shoved the lit stick directly into the energy ball sitting on his lap.

Carl, a dozen feet underground in a dwarven tunnel at the time, gets only the shockwave and the notifications:

System Message: Warlord Hortense Leadership Unit of the Operatic Collective has fallen. Credit for the kill has been ruled as either accidental or a fragging incident, which would be funny as shit. Investigation is pending.
