  • Emberus — the god this crystal formed from
  • Taranis — the killer, and the loser of a separate memorial crystal
  • Prepotente, Osvaldo, Britney Proskurina — the rest of the Apito-family crystal subplot
  • Tracking Tag ("The Kyryap has claimed you") — found in the same breath

Sourced from Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Enchanted Mongoliensis Saddle
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Princess Donut (rider); affixed to Mongo (mount)
  • Obtained: A fan-sponsored box, Book 3, adjusted to fit Donut's cat species
  • Rider bonus: +15% offensive spell damage, Anti-Piercing Resistance
  • Mount bonus: +20% Constitution, +20% melee damage while occupied

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A garish, tassel-covered saddle gifted by fans, magically self-affixing to Mongo and turning him into a mount:

"Magically affixes itself to the dreaded Mongoliensis, turning everyone's favorite murder chicken into a mount."

It has no straps or reins — just a seat and pommel — leaving Carl and Mordecai genuinely unsure how Donut is meant to stay on or steer. Both Carl and Mordecai flag an obvious tactical problem: the melee/Constitution bonus to Mongo is only active while occupied, but that means Donut has to be sitting on him mid-fight to grant it, making her a much easier target. Mordecai's proposed fix is training Donut to jump out of the saddle the instant Mongo attacks, to get the buff window without staying exposed through the whole engagement.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: No level-based scaling described — all four bonuses (rider and mount) appear to be flat, static percentages tied to whether the saddle is occupied, not to any skill or item level.

docs.title: Future Enhancements
docs.text:
Not yet checked against later books.

Sourced from Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook.

docs.title: Mysterious Bone Key
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Carl
  • Type: Granted benefit of the Scavenger's Daughter back patch
  • Uses: One. Ever.
  • Effect: Creates a one-time key that opens any lock in the dungeon
  • Cost: Destroys the patch and the jacket it's sewn to, and permanently consumes a bone from the user's body
  • Status at end of Book 6: Never used

docs.title: The Description
docs.text:
This benefit may only be used once for obvious reasons.

Creates a one-time-use key to open a lock. Any lock. Any lock in the dungeon.

WARNING!: (Notice how I used ALL CAPS for the warning?) Using this benefit will destroy both the patch and the item it is attached to. That means the jacket and all those ugly little patches inexpertly sewn to it.

Uh, it also uses a bone from the user's body to create the key. The more difficult the lock, the bigger the bone it uses. It might just be a finger. Or your clavicle. Or your femur. No biggie.

This bone will not grow back. So make sure it's a lock you really, really want to open.

Mordecai doesn't know what the benefit is and has to have it read to him. Carl's response is immediate: "We're gonna mark that as a last resort item." He also half-remembers a note about a similar item somewhere in The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook and means to go looking for it — which he never gets around to.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: The only scaling is inverse and unpleasant: the harder the lock, the bigger the bone. There is no level, no training, and no way to improve the odds. The cost side is fixed and total — the patch and the entire Anarchist's Battle Rattle with every other patch on it are destroyed regardless of which lock is opened.

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text:
The Bone Key hangs over the entire back half of Book 6 as the thing Carl refuses to use. Floor 8's endgame turns on stairwell keys: there are fewer keys than squads, Carl gives his to Imani, and the obvious way out for himself and Donut is the one benefit that opens any lock in the dungeon.

His friends find the idea intolerable. Imani's refusal to take his key comes with it attached: "Donut told me about your dumbass idea to use one of your own bones or whatever to get out. People have bones for a reason, Carl. No. Like Elle said. It's all or nothing."

In the end the party solves the stairwell problem a different way — Carl's Build Trench demolition plan to isolate and tunnel under the stairwell chambers — and the Bone Key is never spent. It carries into Book 7 unused, along with the jacket it would destroy.

docs.title: Book 7: Absent
docs.text:
Flag closed — but as a non-event

This page previously asked whether the Bone Key gets spent in Book 7. It is not mentioned at all. A case-insensitive search of the full text of This Inevitable Ruin returns zero hits for "bone key" (and zero for "battle rattle," the jacket it would destroy).

The key is therefore not spent, and it carries forward into Book 8 still unused, along with the jacket and every patch on it. Do not read anything further into the silence: the book does not retire the benefit, re-describe it, rule it out, or have anyone consider using it. It simply never comes up.

Floor 9's problem is not a locked door. Faction Wars is fought over territory, towers and trenches, and the one time the party needs to move a city they use Zerzura rather than a key.

The jacket itself does appear in Book 7, though only obliquely and never by name — see Enchanted Anarchist's Battle Rattle for the two patches Carl gains and refuses on Floor 9.

docs.title: Book 8: Still Absent
docs.text:
Two books running, now — and still a non-event

Floors 10 and 11 give Carl every reason to want an any-lock key — a seven-heat vehicle race followed by a mandatory parade and a Dungeon Boss fight — and it still never comes up. A case-insensitive search of the full text of A Parade of Horribles returns zero hits for both "bone key" and "battle rattle."

The Bone Key has therefore gone completely unused and unmentioned for two books running (Book 7 and Book 8), on top of the back half of Book 6 where it was first introduced and refused. Do not infer a resolution, a retirement, or a reason from this. The book simply never brings it up again — no locked doors force the question this time either, and neither Carl nor anyone else references the jacket, the patch, or the missing bone it would cost.

This remains an open thread. Whoever processes Book 9 should keep checking.

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride, with an absence confirmed against Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin and Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Necklace of Indelible Woe
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Looted from: King Rust, chapter 39, after Rosetta lassos and beheads him mid-parley
  • Effect: Swaps one of the wearer's own spells for one of a target's. Kill the target and you get one of their five highest-level spells
  • Restriction: Works only on crawlers (and on NPCs like Tipid)
  • Status: Informally banned among Faction Wars combatants
  • Used in Book 7: Never. It sits in Carl's inventory for the whole book

Exact-verification note

No system description block exists for this item in Book 7. Everything known comes from Tipid's chapter-32 explanation, quoted below.

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text:
Tipid explains it while working out how King Rust, at level 78, knows dozens of spells with several at level 11 to 15 — including a level-15 Protective Shell, Tripper and Puddle Jumper:

"That's easy," Tipid said. "He likely has a ring of Divine Suffering for the stats—and the levels that come with charging the ring—and a necklace of Indelible Woe for the spells."

"Indelible Woe?" I asked. "Is that like the tattoo thing Rosetta is trying to make us do?"

"Similar. Indelible Woe is in the same collection as the Divine Suffering ring. It trades out a random spell of your own for a spell of a target's. If you kill the target, it'll be one of their five highest-level spells. Like the Divine Suffering ring, it only works on crawlers. And people like me. It's not all that useful unless you're a complete psychopath with a bunch of spells you can afford to lose. The necklace was popular a long time ago, but they all agreed to stop using it because combatants were farming crawlers to power it up, and it was a little... messy."

Two things are established there.

It is a trade, not a theft. Every use costs the wearer a spell of their own, chosen at random. It is only worth owning if you are carrying spells you are willing to lose sight-unseen, which is a narrow and unpleasant profile of person. Tipid's word for it is "psychopath."

It is informally banned. Not by rule — by agreement. Faction Wars combatants stopped using it because the optimal strategy was farming crawlers for their best spells, repeatedly, which made the games "a little... messy." It is one of very few things in the series banned by the participants rather than the system, which says something about both.

docs.title: The Contrast With Tattoos
docs.text:
Tipid draws the comparison himself, immediately after, and it is the cleanest statement of why the toraline tattoo system was worth building:

"Rosetta's tattoos will help you share skills and spells without actually killing anyone. It just needs to brew for a little longer."

Same outcome — moving an ability from one person to another — with the kill requirement and the random self-cost removed. The tattoos are the humane version of this necklace, and the book puts them side by side on purpose.

docs.title: Why It Is Never Used
docs.text:
Carl acquires it by accident. Rosetta kills King Rust in chapter 38, Carl pulls "the entirety of King Rust's heavy, leaking corpse" into his inventory, and finds he now owns a second Ring of Divine Suffering and this.

His verdict, in chapter 40:

Donut: WHAT DID YOU DO WITH KING RUST'S RING AND THE NECKLACE?

Carl: Don't worry. I can only wear one Ring of Divine Suffering at a time. I checked. Besides, it turns out two rings can't mark the same person on this floor anyway. And we don't need that necklace.

The second Ring of Divine Suffering goes to Li Na — Donut privately begs Carl to give it to her. Li Na asks about the necklace too, and turns it down for a specific and excellent reason:

Li Na had also asked about the Necklace of Indelible Woe but ultimately decided she didn't want it, especially now that she had several level-15 dreads that she could possibly lose if she used the necklace. It remained in my inventory for now.

Which is the trade-off arriving exactly as Tipid described it. Li Na has just spent an entire assault grinding four Dreads to level 15. The necklace would put every one of them into a lottery. Nobody with anything worth keeping can afford to wear it.

It stays in Carl's inventory, unused, through the end of the book.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: No level. The only stated variable is the quality of the take: a swap against a living target yields a random spell, while killing the target yields one of their five highest-level spells. The wearer's loss is random in either case.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• The Toraline Ink Tattoo System — the non-lethal alternative
  • Enchanted Night Wyrm's Ring of Divine Suffering — the same collection
  • Li Na's Dreads — what made her turn it down

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Enchanted Necklace of the Haute Bourgeoisie
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Carl
  • Slot: Necklace
  • Obtained: A Platinum Tyrant's Box, awarded for becoming magistrate of the Medium Skyfowl Settlement after Miss Quill's death
  • Type: A "chain of leadership" — the second-smallest tier — that tracks settlements a crawler personally conquers/controls
  • Grants: Talon Strike (Level 5), among other per-gem bonuses

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A simple silver chain with a charm that gains one jewel per settlement the wearer controls. Its official description lays out the mechanic directly:

"Each jewel encrusted upon this charm represents a settlement owned and controlled by the bearer. If one still maintains a settlement's jewel upon the collapse of the level, the holder of this necklace will permanently receive a tax stipend every ten days from that settlement based on size and population. In addition, each gem will impart additional benefits based on the town."

Carl receives it already carrying one gem — a Poor Sapphire for the Medium Skyfowl Settlement (Floor 3), which he inherited leadership of after killing Miss Quill, the settlement's secret ruler.

docs.title: Current Gem: Poor Sapphire (Medium Skyfowl Settlement)
docs.text:
• +5 Dexterity
  • +Talon Strike (Level 5) — see Talon Strike
  • Taxes received: 432 gold every 10 days

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: Per its own description: "In order to upgrade this necklace, one must first conquer a Large-sized Settlement. Upgraded necklaces will also upgrade all existing gems" — meaning both the tax income and the per-gem bonuses scale with settlement size, and a single conquest upgrades every gem already on the chain at once, not just the new one.

docs.title: Future Enhancements
docs.text:
Not yet checked against later books.

Sourced from Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook.

docs.title: Enchanted Nightgaunt Cloak of Stoutness
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Carl
  • Slot: Cloak
  • Obtained: Gold Apparel Box, opened during the Floor 1 tutorial (the same box that produced the Trollskin Shirt)
  • Rarity note: Received alongside the Trollskin Shirt in the same box — Mordecai visibly gasps at both appearing together

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: +4 Constitution. Resistant to poison- and ice-based attacks. Adds Anti-Piercing resistance to all worn armor. Per its in-game description, it also "makes you look like a dollar store Batman," with a warning that an actual Nightgaunt spying the wearer "probably won't be too happy with you."

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: The cloak grants flat bonuses only — the book describes no level-by-level curve for its Constitution boost or resistances.

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text: Along with the Trollskin Shirt, this is one of the two pieces of gear that immediately mark Carl as having gotten unusually lucky with his very first loot boxes — Mordecai's reaction (a gasp) is the earliest signal in the book that Carl is being favored by the loot system.

docs.title: Future Enhancements
docs.text:
Not yet researched

Later books haven't been checked yet for whether this item gets upgraded or replaced.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised.

docs.title: Enchanted Obsidian Bracelet of the Raggle Rouser
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Princess Donut
  • Slot: Leg bracelet (Donut wears one on each of her four legs)
  • Obtained: Looted from a Dream elf hunter (Akland), killed by Carl
  • Rarity note: Already upgraded three times before Carl finds it; a 50% chance to permanently break if upgraded a fourth time

docs.title: Effect
docs.text:
• +10 Constitution
  • +5 Dexterity
  • +15% Fire Resistance
  • Grants the wearer a castable level-10 Fireball spell, usable once every twenty minutes

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: Not described beyond its listed upgrade history (three prior upgrades, unspecified original stats) — its current bonuses are presented as fixed at this upgrade tier.

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text:
Carl gives the bracelet to Donut immediately after looting it, over her initial complaints about its color ("It's black, and it looks like it's made from glass"). It becomes her primary offensive upgrade for the rest of Floor 6 — she uses its granted Fireball spell to finish off the Eryops boss Claude Sludgington the Fourth, blasting him mid-air after Carl's Protective Shell launches the rooted monster skyward, and again during her solo fight against Lucia Mar, slamming a Fireball into her chest and setting the treehouse pub around them ablaze (prompting Mordecai's after-the-fact reminder that it's an outdoor spell).

Note: an earlier draft of this page claimed Donut also fireballs someone during the Butcher's Masquerade's climactic battle against Queen Imogen — this is confirmed false. Katia's own scouted stat readout on Imogen states outright that "she's immune to poison and curses and has an ability to return magical fire. Nobody hit her with fireballs or magic missiles or magic bolts," which is exactly why the crawlers switch to blunt-force weapons (Florin's shotgun, thrown rocks) for that fight instead. Donut's notable spell during the masquerade is Laundry Day, stripping Diwata's divine armor off Circe Took, not Fireball. Separately, Donut also earns an off-page "Did-You-Really-Just-Cast-Fireball-in-a-Room-This-Small" achievement at some unspecified point — Mordecai's irritated aside is the only trace of that particular incident, and it isn't the masquerade fight either.

docs.title: Future Enhancements
docs.text:
Pending

Not yet confirmed whether Donut risks the 50% break chance to upgrade the bracelet further.

Sourced from Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: Party Planner ("Casket in the Sky")
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Army Air General Louis Santiago
  • Type: Tilt-rotor stealth light bomber. Counts as tier-3 Armor against the Princess Posse's Faction Wars vehicle limit
  • Obtained: Chapter 6, Louis's Celestial box
  • Size: ~50 feet, crew of 5
  • Signature stat: +50% yield on every bomb it drops
  • Fate: Destroyed in chapter 66, ripped in half in mid-air by a gravity-magic dragon

Named for Firas's rejected suggestion for the Twister — "I'd told him it was stupid" — and powered, like the Twister, by a silver-encased soul crystal. Elle's reaction on first sight: "This makes Carl's backpatch look like something he picked up at the dollar store."

docs.title: The Description
docs.text:
Only readable with stealth mode off:

Casket in the Sky. Party Planner. Tilt Rotor Stealth Light Bomber.

Vehicle.

This vehicle is classed as tier three Armor for the purposes of Faction Wars and counts against your limit.

This vehicle is assigned to The Princess Posse.

This aircraft is owned by crawler Army Air General Louis Santiago 2.

You may only use this vehicle if you hold the controller.

If one studies the history of all the societies who managed to wipe themselves out before they reached the ability to flee into the stars, there are a few remarkable similarities in all of them… one of the final waypoints on the this-is-how-they-killed-themselves list is almost always the thing you're looking at right now.

A lighter-than-air, long-range death delivery system.

This usually evolves into something unmanned before the fun really starts, but in the meantime, we have this thing. This is a light bomber that's designed for fast in-and-out surgical raids against enemy forward positions. It flies fast and low and relies on speed and its multiple stealth options to keep it safe. The base model includes some forward and aft anti-air guns, but that's pretty much it. That plus some rudimentary shields.

Seriously. It would take a pilot with gonads the size of bowling balls to fly this thing into a heavily fortified area.

But what this flying one-way-ticket lacks in self-defense, it makes up for in pure, passionate, offensive skill. The multi-use bomb bay can be modified to hold all manner of armament, and all bombs dropped from the main model are given a 50% increase in yield. This could be enhanced even further if you happen to know anybody who can build you even better, custom-made bombs.

Warning: Different dungeon floors have different rulesets regarding the use of airships. It is possible airships will not be allowed at all during future floors. So use it while you got it.

"If you happen to know anybody who can build you even better, custom-made bombs" is the AI pointing directly at Carl. See The Waffle Maker and No Disassemble.

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text:
Property Detail Length ~50 feet, "about the length of a medium-sized private jet" Fuselage Squished oval, ~8 feet tall; belly sits ~18 inches off the ground on chopper-style skids Interior "just a hair too small for me to stand fully upright within" Finish Silver metallic; heavily tinted glass nose reminiscent of a B-29; the entire underside appears to be glass Propulsion Four propellers that pop out of the top and sides in flight, stowed as rectangular protuberances. No visible wings, tail or rudder Crew Five — pilot, co-pilot/navigator, tail gunner, ball-turret gunner, bombardier. One person can fly it alone Defences Louis's Protect Aircraft shield, an anti-flak shield, upgradeable stealth. Door guns are a paid upgrade Support Requires a hangar upgrade and a hired mechanic gremlin

Descriptions vary by who is looking at it. Donut: "It looks like a submarine!" Carl: a smaller-sized bullet train car. Florin: "It's like a half-sized, half-crew B-17 had a baby with one of those next-gen stealth bombers." Carl's first reaction: "Jesus, Louis. This thing looks like a death trap."

Other models exist to buy or build; one is apparently called the Dumbassmobile.

It occupies one of the Posse's ten Armor slots. The other nine are Florin's flame spider tanks.

docs.title: Service History
docs.text:
• Chapter 11 — inaugural flight to the base, carrying Katia, Bautista and a stowaway Samantha
  • Chapter 23 — southern-front bombing runs. Louis deliberately craters the ground in front of enemy trenches rather than hitting them directly, showering defenders with dirt and stripping traps and enhancements off the terrain
  • Chapter 25 — ferries Carl, Donut and Mongo
  • Chapter 50 — poison-cloud loitering over the naga stronghold
  • Chapter 59 — the first Reaver bomb run, with Carl and Samantha aboard. Survives a corkscrewing missile barrage despite the stealth failing. Bonnie and Skarn stow away on the door guns in direct violation of an explicit ban
  • Chapter 60 — the bombs-away moment: "several spots on the ship's floor slid open at the same time. Tendrils of freezing mist curled up into the cabin as the airship bucked. Ching, ching, ching, ching. The square, shield and tech-busting No Disassembles clinked as they zipped out of the holders, pulled down by gravity, followed by the round high-yield Waffle Makers, which were shaped like tubes"

docs.title: Destruction — Chapter 66
docs.text:
Killed by the gravity-magic dragon circling the Reaver honeycomb castle. Louis's chat message is the whole of it, and it is a hard read:

Louis: A little busy now, Carl. Feather falling... Party Planner is dead. Ripped in half... Hit the dragon with missiles, and it just pissed it off... It cast a spell, and I tried to dodge. It ripped Party Planner down the middle. Dropped the bombs before they were armed. I'm sorry... They didn't go off. I'm falling through the air right now. Gonna land right on the Reaver castle... I think my door gunners are dead... Glad Bonnie and Skarn weren't here... He was right... That cop's husband. I'm sorry... The feral god is still there a mile west of the castle. I see him just sitting there. Dragon still flying above... I'm going to hit the castle by myself. Tell Katia when she wakes up that I'm sorry to be such a fuckup...

Colonel Boomer had overridden Carl's instinct to call the run off. The unarmed bombs Louis dropped on the way down are recovered by him on the castle roof and become, twenty chapters later, the remotely detonated EMP that kills the Reaver robot force — see The Waffle Maker and No Disassemble.

Louis's last word on it, chapter 87: "I really wish I could've kept Party Planner."

Florin later steals a Reaver replacement aircraft, which is covered elsewhere.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: No level. The two stated upgrade paths are bomb-bay armament (the +50% yield multiplies whatever you load, so better bombs scale the whole aircraft) and purchasable modules — door guns, improved stealth. The warning clause is the real ceiling: future floors may ban airships entirely.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• The Waffle Maker and No Disassemble — the custom payload
  • Carl's Jug O' Boom — the same escalation, eight floors earlier

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Prism Industries Capacitating and Focusing Goggles
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Princess Donut
  • Slot: Eyewear
  • Obtained: Gift from Princess D'Nadia of the Prism Kingdom

docs.title: Effect
docs.text:
A one-of-a-kind gift, personally signed by Princess D'Nadia. Per its own card:

"Protects the eyes from a variety of environmental hazards, including magic-based attacks that render the user blind. Enhances all dark vision effects. Allows for heat vision and other visible-light viewing options. In addition, any energy-based spell that originates from the ocular region is caught and focused by these goggles, which allows for multiple combat and targeting options."

In practice this gives Donut three confirmed uses:

  • Enhanced vision — lets her spot Hekla's invisible "Dirty Little Phased Bolt" ammunition being fired into Katia, which is what exposes the plot in time to save her
  • Multi-shot casting — turns her Magic Missile into an eye-fired laser capable of firing multiple bolts at once (a "Double Shot" headshots two Jikininki ghouls simultaneously in one fight)
  • Charge storage — the goggles can separately hold the energy of one full-power spell cast in reserve and release it later as its own "double shot," demonstrated against an awake province boss during a cart-lift ambush

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: Not described in detail beyond the two confirmed effects above.

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text: The goggles directly expose Hekla's plot against Katia — without them, the attack would have gone completely unnoticed, since the bolts are specifically designed to be untraceable. Donut treats them as a fashion statement first and a tool second, repeatedly drawing attention to how good they look on her before mentioning what they actually do.

docs.title: Future Enhancements
docs.text:
Pending

Not yet confirmed whether the goggles have additional effects beyond hidden-vision detection and spell charge storage.

Sourced from Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook.

docs.title: Rockard's Ring of Sniping
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Carl — looted from Quan Ch's severed arm
  • Slot: Ring
  • Namesake: Rockard, an orcish warrior and one of the dungeon's most infamous crawlers, said to have led his season's top-10 list until his own mother knifed him in his sleep

docs.title: Effect
docs.text:
An amber-stoned ring granting two passive benefits:

  • Ripe: All creatures with less than 50% health are shown on the map. Doesn't extend the map's normal view range, but combines with skills like Pathfinder to make experience-sniping (swooping in late to steal a kill) trivially easy.
  • Loaded: All non-hidden creatures wearing magical gear are shown on the map — useful for finding well-equipped targets to rob or avoid.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: Both benefits are binary detection effects with no stated scaling.

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text: Carl rips this ring (along with two others) off Quan Ch's arm after tearing it from his body during the fight over the celestial-tier puppy Orthrus. Carl notes the ring explains Quan's reputation as a "glory-stealing" opportunist who repeatedly shows up late to steal kills and loot from other crawlers' fights.

docs.title: Future Enhancements
docs.text:
Pending

Not yet confirmed how Carl uses Ripe or Loaded on Floor 6 or beyond.

Sourced from Book 4: The Gate of the Feral Gods.

docs.title: Quadruped Weapon Mount, "The Scorpion's Bite"
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Princess Donut
  • Type: Non-magical bandolier accessory
  • Obtained: Chapter 86, from a Gold Benefactor Box sent by her sponsor, the Apothecary
  • Effect: Allows the mounting of multiple ranged weapons on her back; may fire and load via inventory action

docs.title: Effect
docs.text:
A simple mechanical harness rather than an enchanted item, delivered without fanfare mid-confrontation with the goddess Huanxin:

A strange device appeared on Donut's back. This was from the gold benefactor box she'd received from the Apothecary. A simple gift, but the implication was clear.

Quadruped weapon mount.

"The scorpion's bite."

Non-magical bandolier accessory. Allows for the mounting of multiple ranged weapons. May fire and load via inventory action.

It immediately forms Katia's Enchanted Repeating Crossbow of the Scavenger Mother of Mothers on Donut's back, "bigger than Donut," attached with "an ominous click." Donut carries the weight without difficulty and keeps moving.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: No level or stat values are given; it is a fixed mechanical accessory, not a magical item that scales with a skill or stat. Its only stated limitation is indirect: the mounted crossbow itself is weaker without women in Donut's party, a property of the crossbow rather than the mount.

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text: The mount lets Donut fire Katia's crossbow off her own back hands-free while she circles and menaces the captured goddess Huanxin, stalking her "like liquid across the floor" while showing off her new knee pads, her Claw skill upgrade (via her "champion shawl"), and her Monologue benefit in the same scene. It is a purely practical, non-magical answer to a very magical fight — a strap that lets a housecat carry and fire a crossbow bigger than she is.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Enchanted Repeating Crossbow of the Scavenger Mother of Mothers — the weapon it mounts
  • Enchanted Spiked Knee Pads of Kina — worn in the same scene
  • Cloak of the Benevolent Champion — the "champion shawl" credited for her Claw upgrade in the same scene

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Enchanted Silver Bracelet of the Ab-solar
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Princess Donut
  • Slot: Leg bracelet
  • Obtained: Gold Benefactor Box from the Apothecary, delivered mid-Floor 6

docs.title: Effect
docs.text:
• Protection against Vampirism
  • Protection against Lycanthropy
  • +25% Magical damage against all sapient undead

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: Not described — presented as a flat, one-time set of protections.

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text:
Donut receives this bracelet from a Gold Benefactor Box sent by the Apothecary; in the very same box-opening session, Carl separately receives an identical set of bonuses via a jacket patch (the "Midnight Epicure" patch — see Enchanted Anarchist's Battle Rattle) from a different sponsor's box, a Gold Benefactor Box from the Plenty. Mordecai reads the two sponsors handing out matching anti-vampire/anti-lycanthropy protections to Carl and Donut at the same moment as clear evidence "the Apothecary and the Plenty really are working together" — a coordinated warning about something coming. That warning pays off almost immediately: Miriam Dom — already a vampire since an earlier floor — accidentally infects the boss dinosaur Big Tina with her own vampirism while fighting alongside Prepotente, and the curse spreads floor-wide through the local wildlife from there. Separately, an elite vampire hunter named Viscount Fog (with his flying mount Sierra) specifically hunts Miriam down as the outbreak's source; Sierra herself is injured and infected during one of these clashes, later becoming the undead boss "Sierra – Northropi Vampire" that Carl and Donut kill. The bracelet is never shown activating directly in combat, but its protections likely spare Donut from infection during the vampire-plague sequence that follows, and the matching pair (Werecastors like Clint and Holger are also encountered this floor) suggests both anti-vampirism and anti-lycanthropy protection were deliberately bundled together.

Sourced from Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: Spunky Jefferson the Enchanted Nickel Sock of the Elderly Miser
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: One-handed flail-equivalent — a white tube sock with red and blue stripes, weighted with several dollars' worth of nickels. Old, crusty, and blood-splattered
  • Traits: Sapient (it talks) and incremental-damage (it grows stronger with every kill). Already upgraded twice
  • Origin: Originally awarded to a crawler in a Legendary You-Know-Everybody-Can-See-You- Right? Box on Floor 5
  • Obtained by Carl: Looted from Quan Ch's body in Havana (ch. 60; Quan dies at the end of ch. 58, and Carl strips the corpse after Tserendolgor's last stand)
  • Current wielder: Dong Quixote, the elderly Club Vanquisher dancer turned mercenary, to whom Carl gives it outright

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Jefferson is the life force of a miser who angered the spirit sent to show him the error of his ways, and was cursed to inhabit a sock once owned by a teenage boy named Tanner. The AI's description makes the sock's provenance clear and then moves briskly on: "It's unusually effective, more so than you might think."

docs.title: Effects
docs.text:
This weapon's damage increases by 1.5% for every mob it kills that is no more than 10 levels below the current wielder's level. Current upgrade: 238% damage increase.

Increases wielder's dexterity by 10 points plus 10%

Has a 5% chance to inflict Bonked on any mob struck with this weapon.

All mobs killed with this weapon have a 20% chance to burst into a pile of gold coins upon death. The number of coins is equal to the (value of the items in their inventory)+(level x 10).

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
This is the interesting part. Damage is permanent and cumulative: +1.5% per qualifying kill, with no stated ceiling. The qualifier is the throttle — the kill must be within 10 levels of the current wielder's level, so grinding trash mobs gives nothing and the weapon only grows when it's being used on real threats by someone whose own level is keeping pace.

At the point Carl reads it, the sock is sitting at +238% damage increase — accumulated across at least two previous owners and two upgrades before it ever reached him. Every subsequent qualifying kill Dong Quixote makes pushes it higher.

The gold clause scales with the victim rather than the weapon: (value of items in inventory) + (level × 10) coins, 20% of the time.

docs.title: Sapience
docs.text:
Carl's chat exchange on discovering the tag:

Carl: Is a sapient weapon what I think it is?

Mordecai: Oh gods. Yes. They can talk, but it's usually only in the mind of the wielder. Though some do talk out loud. They tend to be quite annoying. Samantha-level annoying, but luckily they're treated as objects, and you can keep them in your inventory if they won't stop yammering. I suspect Florin's shotgun might be sapient, but he hasn't said one way or another.

Dong Quixote, who had asked Carl for a one-handed flail and gets this instead, receives it reverently — "My lord, you honor me... This is a mythical weapon" — and immediately falls into conversation with it, one side of which the party can hear:

"Yes. Yes. My name is Dong Quixote... Yes. Jefferson? It's nice to meet you... Yes. We are going to. I am a former adventurer turned entertainer turned mercenary... Yes. About five gold coins per dance, but more if we moved it to the cum closet... I do not know what a mutual fund is. Why?"

Katia's only question is why it smells.

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Stayfast Ink and Adept's Fountain Pen
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Carl
  • Obtained: Chapter 75, a parting gift from the crawler Milk, handed over as what looks like a wineskin
  • Quantity: 825 ml — "Enough ink for several chonky books"
  • Property: It never fades. "Nothing. Not even distance or time or the death of a star"
  • Purpose: Explicitly given so Carl can write skills and spells into The Filthy Little Crawler's Book of Voodoo

This is the successor to the toraline ink, and the moment the Book of Voodoo's long-flagged "nefarious purpose" finally becomes legible.

docs.title: Why Milk Gives It
docs.text:
Milk's explanation is a confession before it is a gift. She had once written her recipes in a book, switched to a different ink partway through, and lost everything she wrote afterward:

"There's more than you can imagine. Even with just ink and calligraphy and maps, there are dozens of different methods. It is dangerous, though, attempting to learn too much. There's a lot the right kind of ink can do. But, over the turns, I've learned the danger of using recipes I don't quite understand. Inks and letters that shine the brightest burn out the fastest."

"I had a book once, and I wrote several of my recipes in it. But later, I switched to a different type of ink. It was an attempt to share my knowledge with a wider group, and it wasn't until recently did I learn all that I wrote after I changed methods faded and disappeared.… Some of my best recipes were lost, and it wasn't until they were needed the most did I learn they were gone. It is my fault that I didn't write them properly."

This closes a loose end from chapter 47. Carl had gone looking in the cookbook for Milk's entries on the tattoo mechanic and found nothing: "There was nothing about this in her entries. I'd looked three times." They had been written. They had simply evaporated.

Her people's saying, offered with the wineskin: "No single recipe is a feast in itself." Meaning there is always another way.

docs.title: The Descriptions
docs.text:
Stayfast Ink, 825 ml.

Enough ink for several chonky books.

Warning: this shit stains, so be careful. Nothing will ever make it fade. Nothing. Not even distance or time or the death of a star.

Adept's fountain pen.

The most basic of all the calligrapher's implements. How much grief, how much suffering has been caused by one of these things? Yet, how much joy? That whole saying, the pen is mightier than the sword, is one of the few human world metaphors that I believe to be universally true, especially since swords are terrible, barbaric weapons.

This is the most versatile item anyone can own. What will you do with it? Write a book that changes everything? Come up with a new, titillating take on hucow fiction? (Don't look that up.) Or will you literally stab someone in the neck with it again?

The "again" is the AI remembering that Carl has, in fact, previously stabbed someone in the neck with a pen.

docs.title: What It Is For
docs.text:
Milk says it outright, and she says it looking Carl in the eye:

"He also has another book. One that all of you have. The Book of Voodoo, I believe it is called. Anything he writes in it will be given to everybody who already has the book. Best of luck to you."

Edgar had reached the same conclusion a chapter earlier, working from the other direction:

"Rosetta was just telling Milk and myself about that book of Voodoo you have, and I believe you may be able to share skills and spells that way as well, using the same ink. It will be more temporary."

And the AI had been screaming it at Carl since chapter 57, in the form of an achievement reward box named:

Platinum Have You Goddamned Figured Out How To Use This In Conjunction With the Fucking Voodoo Book Yet? Jesus Christ I Can Only Help You So Much box.

So the chain is complete: the toraline tattoo system proved abilities can be written into skin; Milk's calligraphy proved writing can amplify them; permanent ink plus a book that broadcasts to every crawler alive means abilities can be written and distributed at scale.

The immediate consequence is Carl's Book of Boom in chapter 85 — 30,000 pages of donated skills and spells, written by departing crawlers, distributed to everyone still fighting.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
No level. The quantity — 825 ml, "several chonky books" — is the only stated limit, and unlike the toraline it is not consumed by a ration that runs out mid-plan. The ink's defining property is permanence, which is precisely the property Milk lacked when she needed it.

Donut's contribution to the scene, for the record: "CARL, WHAT THE HECK IS SHE TALKING ABOUT? IS SHE HITTING ON YOU?"

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• The Filthy Little Crawler's Book of Voodoo
  • Carl's Book of Boom — the payoff
  • The Toraline Ink Tattoo System — the predecessor
  • The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook — where Milk's lost entries should have been

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Talisman of the Slate Butterfly
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Princess Donut
  • Slot: Collar charm
  • Obtained: A loot box opened during the Floor 1 tutorial
  • Effect at time of receipt: Raised Donut's Light on Your Feet skill from 3 to 7

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: +4 to the Light on Your Feet skill. +1 Intelligence. Winged fairies are no longer automatically hostile toward the wearer. Per its description: "Those who remember and commemorate the sad tale of the Slate Butterfly are given a boon by the fairies of the world" — the actual "tale" is never explained in Book 1.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: The talisman's own bonus is a flat +4 to the skill, but that skill's effect scales with its total level: Donut's jump height roughly doubled going from a Light on Your Feet of 3 to 7, letting her clear obstacles (like the top of a play structure) she couldn't reach before.

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text: A minor but useful item — the fairy-hostility immunity becomes relevant once the party starts dealing with Rev-Up's Laminak and Clurichaun workers on Floor 2.

docs.title: Book 5: Retired
docs.text: Donut retires the talisman from her collar-charm slot on Floor 6, swapping it out for the settlement-tracking Enchanted Collar Charm of the Effete Bourgeoisie after conquering the town of Point Mongo. The talisman itself is not destroyed, merely unequipped.

docs.title: Book 5: Britney's Jacket
docs.text: Separately, fellow crawler Britney Proskurina builds an entire jacket out of dozens of common-rarity Stuffed Slate Butterfly beanbag figures (sourced from Bautista's collection), each summonable as a live, hand-sized butterfly that instinctively flies to and extinguishes the nearest light source before reverting to a stuffed toy. She uses one to covertly disable a warning light monitoring the Butcher's Masquerade's guards; later, the entire jacket discharges at once when Queen Imogen's own offensive lightning spell — meant for the crawlers assaulting her — gets drawn to the butterfly swarm instead, saving several crawlers' lives at the cost of Britney's face being permanently burned.

docs.title: Future Enhancements
docs.text:
Not yet researched

Later books haven't been checked yet for whether Donut's own talisman gets upgraded or replaced.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised and Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: The Bard's Golden Throat
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Princess Donut
  • Slot: Face accessory — explicitly not a hat (Mordecai: "It's a face accessory. Like your bandana"), so it stacks with whatever tiara she's wearing
  • Obtained: A fan box — the item was voted for by her fanbase, the Princess Posse
  • Appearance: A golden, amethyst-encrusted headset microphone
  • Effects: Auto-tune within 1.5 steps, assistance with all bard songs and spells, up to 5× amplification, +5% Charisma

docs.title: Why It Exists
docs.text:
Donut's Legendary Diva kit from Book 5 has always had one crippling flaw: she cannot hold a pitch, so her songs frequently fail to cast. The Posse fixes it by voting her a microphone.

Her reaction on opening the box is unrestrained — "Oh my god. Oh my god! Thank you! Thank you!... Carl, look! Look what my Princess Posse voted on for me!" — and she is delighted that it has a purple jewel: "I'm going to look just like Britney! The real Britney, not the crawler." Mordecai's reaction is relief: "Oh, thank the gods... It's a good one. Sort of."

docs.title: Effects
docs.text:
The description is a history of Antares Audio Technologies and the 1997 release of AutoTune, credited by the AI as the greatest invention of the twentieth century for curing "the disability" of tone deafness. Then:

The Golden Throat enhancement. Automatically tunes songs within one and a half steps of correct note. Assists in the proper formation of all bard-based songs and spells.

Amplification. While equipped, all spoken words and songs are amplified at twice the normal volume. This can be increased to up to five times of top volume.

Charisma plus 5% when equipped.

The moment she equips it her voice modulates and doubles in volume; her own assessment is "it sounds like I'm talking through a fan."

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
No level scaling. The two numeric limits are fixed: 1.5 steps of pitch correction and 5× maximum amplification. The Charisma bonus is a flat percentage, so it does grow in absolute terms as Donut's already-enormous Charisma climbs — relevant because Charisma governs the casting time and area of Minion Army and the reach of her charm effects.

Mordecai's advice is to keep it in her inventory and equip it only when singing. Carl's is blunter: "let's keep that as a secret weapon." Donut compromises by keeping it in her hotlist "when I need a little extra oomph. Or when you're not paying attention to me properly."

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text:
Beyond fixing her songs, the microphone turns Donut into the party's battlefield PA system. With amplification cranked she can issue orders across an entire street fight, address massed NPC and mercenary forces, and be heard over a hailstorm — a role that matters increasingly as the guild's Floor 8 engagements scale from six-person skirmishes to coordinated assaults with dozens of conscripted troops.

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Carl
  • Slot: Not equippable — a readable/writable book kept in inventory
  • Obtained: A prize-carousel "joke" reward on Floor 3, widely assumed by the party to be worthless
  • Format: A living, crowd-sourced field manual, edited and annotated by a chain of prior crawlers going back at least 24 editions

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: Far from a joke prize, the Cookbook turns out to be Carl's single most valuable item of Book 3: a running compendium of survival knowledge — power-supply mechanics, portal theory, deity-summoning rules, crafting recipes, monster lore — left behind by 24 previous crawlers who owned it before him, each annotating and correcting the last. Carl becomes its 25th author. He also discovers it comes with a hidden, mentally-accessed "scratchpad" feature that lets him add his own notes without physically opening the book, which he uses constantly to record observations he then passes off to Mordecai as his own deductions.

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: No combat stats or equip slot — its value is purely informational. Passages quoted from prior editions (credited to named past crawlers like Coolie, Forkith, Tin, Milk, Azin, and Drakea) cover topics as varied as indestructible "quest-critical" NPCs, portal behavior, and the full rules behind deity summoning (see Enchanted War Gauntlet of the Exalted Grull for how Carl applies that last one).

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: Not applicable — the book doesn't scale with a stat or skill; its usefulness scales with how much Carl reads and adds to it over time.

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text: The Cookbook becomes Carl's primary information advantage for the rest of Floor 4, repeatedly supplying him with knowledge (power cell mechanics, portal classification, deity lore) well ahead of what Mordecai or anyone else on the floor has access to — enough that Elle McGibbons tells him: "Sometimes I think you're cheating, Carl. How do you know all this stuff? It's like you have one of those teacher's editions with all the answers in the back." By the end of the floor, Carl writes his own entry — the book's 25th — closing not with a plan to free NPCs, but with a darker escalation: killing mobs and NPCs is framed as mercy ("actually the best thing we can do for them"), but Carl vows that the 24 crawlers before him all failed to go further than talk — he commits to actively fighting back against the system itself ("They will not break me... I will break them all"), without yet knowing how.

docs.title: Book 5: New Marginalia and a 25th-Edition Log
docs.text:
By Floor 6, the Cookbook is shown being actively annotated by dozens of past crawlers, cited by edition number (e.g. "Crawler Forkith, 20th Edition," "Crawler Everly, 5th Edition") — reinforcing its nature as a living, multi-author artifact rather than a static reference. Several new marginal notes recur across the book, quoted directly:

  • Herot (16th Edition) — contributes theory on manipulating NPC belief systems ("Show them the lie... find the pebble and place it on the path") and on castle typology, both of which Carl applies directly against Signet and while planning the Butcher's Masquerade infiltration
  • Everly (5th Edition) — a multi-part, increasingly bitter entry describing a sponsor who seemed helpful before deliberately steering her toward a broadcast-friendly death; Drakea's 22nd-edition follow-up confirms it was her final entry
  • Ikicha (11th Edition), Milk (6th Edition), Volteeg (7th Edition), Rosetta (9th Edition), and Allister (13th Edition) — shorter entries on love, loss, vampires, and country-boss treasure maps, several marked by Drakea as their authors' final contributions
  • Drakea (22nd Edition) — recurs constantly as the book's most active recent annotator, bridging older entries with fresh Floor 6 observations (elite/hunter dynamics, faction insurance schemes) and consistently urging future authors to document exactly how they die

Still credited as the book's 25th author (a status he earned back in Book 3), Carl opens a new, dated entry midway through Book 5 that documents, in real time, the entire Butcher's Masquerade plan — page by page, with running annotations signed by Katia, Imani, Elle, Donut, Florin, Louis, Firas, Li Na, Bautista, and Chris — explicitly framed (per Drakea's earlier advice) as a record in case the plan gets them all killed.

docs.title: Known Authors & Their Editions
docs.text:
Books 6 and 7 confirm the book's full authorship model. Every marginal note is signed by "Crawler [Name], [Ordinal] Edition," and Book 7 goes a step further: nine of its part-openers are interludes — short chapters narrated in the third person, each from the point of view of one cookbook author, appearing at the moment they wrote (or were about to write) their entry. The table below lists every author confirmed in the text, in edition-number order, with what they personally contributed — a quoted note, a theory later used in the main plot, or a summary of their interlude — rather than a full biography. Where a character already has a full page or a supporting-cast row, the "Who" column links there instead of repeating it.

Two editions before Carl's own are never named on the page (1st and, so far, 23rd and 24th) — the book's status quote to Carl calls it "at least 24 editions," but only 21 distinct predecessors (2nd–22nd) are ever credited by name. Porthus's own note in Book 4 implies there was no author before him at all: he calls himself "the first to receive these words, and now, as the author of the second edition," suggesting the book started as a bare, uncredited set of recipes (an unofficial "1st edition") before he became its first actual contributor.

Ed. Author Who Contribution 1st (uncredited) — No author is ever named. Porthus's own note implies the book began as an anonymous set of bare recipes before anyone signed an entry 2nd Porthus ("Dr. Porthus Hu") Race/class not stated in text; see Supporting Cast Found the book blank of any prior commentary and became its first credited writer. His last entry, written the moment he took a 100-season "game guide" deal rather than search for his missing friend Menerva: "I have decided to accept the deal... one day I will make them pay... This will be my last entry into this book, but I am not yet done with the enemy." Generations later he funds Carl as a secret second sponsor and, per his own Book 7 interlude, is revealed as the head of the Open Intellect Pacifist Network 3rd Dante Crocodilian; class not stated — see Supporting Cast His Book 7 interlude covers his indentureship as a merchant and trap-master neighbor to fellow author Justice Light. Reassigned as an ice-castle guard, he is ordered to kill the castle's gentle ice-elf NPCs; he refuses twice and is executed on the spot by an AI beam ("no third warning... the light simply erased him, as if he'd never existed"). His status card: "Was killed by administrative action for refusing to follow orders." Justice Light later cites him as proof "there is no such thing as the point of no return" 4th Tipid Crest; see Supporting Cast His chapter epigraphs run through Book 7. His Book 7 interlude (Chapter 11's lead-in) covers losing his party to a sentience-plague floor and taking a deal rather than search for his missing friend Kimu/companions further. Co-runs the freighter Homecoming Queen with Rosetta Thagra, recruited by Porthus; loses both legs in the Book 8 Floor-10/11 crash 5th Everly Sward Mantis Explosives Engineer Her Book 7 interlude follows her final minutes on Floor 8, hired an ogre digger crew alone rather than work with the thousands of other mantises who entered the dungeon with her. Whispers the book's title, "The Inevitable Ruin," to herself just before an advertisement-disguised tower's slow-collapsing ceiling crushes her and the ogre both. Status card: "Dungeon Exit: crushed to death on the eighth floor." Book 5 quotes an earlier, "increasingly bitter" entry of hers about a sponsor who steered her toward a broadcast-friendly death, which Drakea's 22nd-edition follow-up confirms was her final note 6th Milk Xenopus/Vesper; full page: Milk Her own entry, quoted directly in Book 6: "I am writing the sixth edition of this book... I wish to cook a feast for the whole galaxy. I wish for them all to choke on our pain." Her Book 7 interlude covers her decades as guildmaster of the hidden Cartography and Calligraphy guilds inside Club Vanquisher, and introduces Words of Power calligraphy magic on the page (see her full page) 7th Volteeg Gargoyle/Sturnus; full page: Volteeg His single, guilt-ridden entry, made only at the very end of his own crawl. His Book 7 interlude ends with him deliberately overloading his Weeper tank's energy-ball chamber and detonating it inside his own faction's formation, killing Warlord Hortense Leadership Unit and 10,000+ soldiers and single-handedly eliminating the Operatic Collective 8th Justice Light Skyfowl; full page: Justice Light His entry on killing an NPC out of anger, reprinted at a Book 7 chapter head, and referenced by Herot's own regret. His Book 7 interlude recounts Dante's execution and his own lost wing, then shows him talking Juice Box's changeling spy down and revealing his trap plan for what becomes Operation Ruin. Currently alive; breaks "the Nothing" and wakes Scolopendra at Book 7's climax 9th Rosetta Thagra Crest; full page: Rosetta Thagra Contributed dozens of explosives recipes and the "watching them through the glass" note that gives her own later documentary its title. Her Book 7 interlude covers looting King Rust's banking credentials after decapitating him. Chapter 11 mislabels her "the seventh edition" — a confirmed text slip; both her own status card and Book 6 give 9th, and 7th belongs to Volteeg (see her page's note on this) 10th York Tenodera His Book 7 epilogue interlude is set alone at the helm of the freighter Homecoming Queen, having just killed a yacht full of orc children on Rosetta's order and feeling nothing from it. Carl, in Book 3, quotes York's "rambling philosophical" final entry at length: "I have been alone my whole life... this book... to make a hive of those who will never cross paths, except in these pages." 11th Ikicha Yenk Marginal notes only (Books 3–7), on the Hunting Grounds' weather, on a lost love turned monstrous, and a final, oft-quoted line: "The burning Yenk needs only to embrace their enemies." Drakea's 22nd-edition follow-up confirms it was his last entry 12th Batbilge Race not stated One surviving note (Book 4), warning that the marketplace interface tags the cookbook itself as a 50-million-gold heirloom item — Allister's follow-up notes it was likely his last entry 13th Allister Race not stated; T'Ghee practitioner — see Supporting Cast Notes recur across Books 3–7 on explosives stability, vampire lore, and Immortality/protection spells, all drawn from his home culture's T'Ghee card-and-meditation tradition. Carl leans on Allister's note that, to him, T'Ghee was a religion — not the card-battle totem game later run by Ren/Tserendolgor — when first encountering it in Book 6 14th Priestly Race not stated Marginal notes (Books 4, 6–7) on Larracos, the ninth floor's inverted city, called "the single best source of info on the ninth floor" 15th Sinjin Race not stated Marginal notes (Books 3–4) on infusing bombs with healing potions to mass-kill undead 16th Herot Skink — see Supporting Cast The book's other most-quoted theorist. His "Worn Path Method" essay argues NPCs should be broken of belief through direct confrontation ("Show them the lie... find the pebble and place it on the path"); a separate note theorizes he can "manifest his own destiny" — that voicing a wish where the AI can hear it causes the AI to make it happen. Believed dead through most of the series; revealed alive in Book 8 as a skink who, with a former crawler named Menerva, secretly built the Pineapple Cabaret — a pocket dimension sheltering escaped NPCs and mobs — sacrificing his own exit to run it 17th Azin Race not stated Marginal notes (Books 3, 5–7) on indestructible "quest-critical" NPCs and on spiders 18th Ossie Race not stated — see Supporting Cast His notes (Books 6–7) theorize that the dungeon's origin stories are painted over, over and over, and that species like the bopca — told the aliens merely "offered" them a place in the dungeon — sit well above their apparent station as constructed NPCs; i.e., they are indentured biological "naturals" rather than printed constructs, a theory Carl finds himself relying on in Book 7 19th Coolie Race not stated Marginal notes (Books 3–4) document a failed assassination of two admins via a bugbear-paste bomb detonated in orbit — "I have failed... Think of me, brothers" — and his death. Carl explicitly draws on Coolie's account when planning his own first move against the system in Book 4 20th Forkith Urgyle Sapper Extensive marginal notes (Books 3–5) confirming and correcting earlier passages; lost his sister Barkith mid-crawl ("Rest well, little sister... Her name was Barkith, and she was all I had left"). Not the unrelated demon named Forkith introduced in Book 8's epilogue (see Supporting Cast) 21st Tin Race not stated — see Supporting Cast Marginal notes (Books 3, 5–6), including a running joke about spiders. His theory that Laundry Day would need to strip a god's invulnerability before it could work is cited by Carl in Book 5, then found to be incomplete once Carl confirms soul-armor-targeting spells bypass the god itself 22nd Drakea A bune, per Drakea's Enchanted Kerchief of Disorder — see Supporting Cast The book's most prolific recent annotator, a survivor of the final naga-controlled season. Theorizes that the system AI is "moving into the minds" of monsters at the point of death, trying and failing to know what it's like to lose everything — "If only I could convince it to move into the minds of one of these nagas." Confirms several other authors' final entries and consistently urges future writers to document exactly how they die. Died, per Mordecai's uncertain memory, on the 11th or 12th floor 23rd (not named in the text) — Not identified anywhere in Books 1–8 24th (not named in the text) — Not identified anywhere in Books 1–8 25th Carl Human; full page: Carl Becomes an author partway through Book 3, closing his first entry with a vow to fight the system rather than just talk. Adds notes and interludes throughout Books 4–7, including a real-time, page-by-page log of the Butcher's Masquerade plan (Book 5) and a note to the dead Drakea after liberating the naga's inner sanctum (Book 7)

Unverified

The text never explains why the ordinal count (24 named-or-implied predecessors) doesn't exactly match 21 credited names between the 2nd and 22nd editions plus an uncredited 1st — the gap is the never-named 23rd and 24th editions. Nothing in Books 1–8 fills it in.

docs.title: Future Enhancements
docs.text:
Confirmed by later books: Book 6 establishes the interlude-free "Crawler [Name], [Ordinal] Edition" marginal-note format as an ongoing device through Floor 8, and Book 7 adds the first-person interlude structure for nine of its authors (see table above). Book 8 confirms Herot (16th edition) survived and is running the Pineapple Cabaret. Not yet confirmed: any further detail on the 1st, 23rd, or 24th editions, or whether the book itself (as opposed to Carl's scratchpad) appears again after Book 7.

Sourced from Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook, Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade, Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride, Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin, and Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Bearer: Carl
  • Type: Tattoo — centre of the chest, just above the sternum
  • Applied by: Shi Maria, the Bedlam Bride, while controlling Carl's body as a summoned totem (chapter 71)
  • Applied with: The Enchanted Prison Tattoo Kit and ink brewed on the spot
  • In-game description: "Tattoo. The Eye of the Bedlam Bride." — and nothing else
  • This is the book's title item

docs.title: How It Was Made
docs.text:
Shi Maria — "The Screamer. Shi Maria. The Widow Endless. The Bedlam Bride" — is summoned as one of Donut's totems during the Ysalte/Amayon climax and seizes control of Carl's body. She is working to a deadline: when the totem times out she returns to the deck, and Donut has every intention of ripping her card. So she uses the time to make herself permanent.

The ink is brewed from scratch, in Carl's hands, out of three things:

  1. Extreme heat — she makes him cast Self-Immolation with the party standing around him, burning Katia and Mongo badly and melting a hole through the floor
  2. A sliver of the toraline root vegetable Carl's sponsors, the Open Intellect Pacifist Network, had given him, dropped into a beaker he'd looted on the first floor
  3. Li Jun's eye. Li Jun slides down a chain to help — "Carl, what can I do?" — and Carl, screaming inside his own head, drives the tattoo stick into his friend's eye, pulls it out on the end of the stick, and eats it.

Then he tattoos his own chest with it, his hand "moving faster and faster, faster than possible." It is a small image, right above the sternum.

docs.title: What She Said
docs.text:
"You have so much power in your hands, Carl, and you don't even know what you have. That's okay. Today, you live. If you won't bring this card to the next floor, I will have to attach myself to something you can't discard so easily."

"There. There. Almost done. You may gain some of your friend's powers, too, with the blood on the needle. Not much. But I am with you now, Carl, until you decide to free me. I will no longer be a card you can abandon, one you can rip away. I am a part of you, and you will have to decide. Keep me with you and gain my power, or set me free. Either way, I win."

A second voice, male, interjects throughout — Shi Maria insists it isn't real and that she didn't put it there; it answers "You did. You killed me, and now I am here." Its parting advice to Carl: "Don't trust her, boy. Get her out of you as soon as you can. Don't ever trust her."

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text:
Nothing stated. When Carl regains control and looks down at his bloody chest, the eye blinks once, then closes and completely disappears against his skin. Pulling it up in his interface returns only the item's name:

Tattoo. The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

That's all it said. It gave no other description.

What he can feel is "a hole inside of me. A bottomless hole." He touches it, hesitantly, and passes out.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: No mechanics of any kind are given — no level, no stats, no activation. The only thing the text establishes is the binary choice Shi Maria framed: keep her and gain her power, or set her free. Neither option's terms are explained.

docs.title: Status at Book's End
docs.text:
Open thread

Donut rips the Shi Maria card the moment the battle ends — "She's not going to hurt Mongo ever again" — which removes the spider from her deck permanently. The tattoo is unaffected. That was the entire point of making it: Shi Maria explicitly moved herself onto "something you can't discard so easily" because she expected the card to be destroyed.

Carl's own summary, two pages later: "I still felt it there, right on my chest. The tattoo. I had no idea what it really was or what it meant."

The associated escort quest — "The Bedlam Bride," a quest to get her "crazy ass to the city of Larracos" — is never formally closed, failed, or updated on-page after the card is ripped. Book 6 does not say what the tattoo does, what "her power" would be, how one would "set her free," or what happens to the quest. Do not resolve any of this from inference.

docs.title: Book 7: The Terms, Finally Stated
docs.text:
Book 6's open thread, answered

Book 6 established a binary choice and refused to explain either half of it. Book 7 explains both, and adds a third party nobody knew about: Hapanzi, Shi Maria's husband, a spider-god. Shi Maria is not merely attached to Carl. She is imprisoned in him, by her husband, and Carl is the lock.

docs.title: What she is
docs.text: Panford, chapter 19: "The entity contained within Carl is basically a special Reaper Spider Minion merchant. Part demon and part demi-god." Baroness Victory adds the complication that explains why Carl half-failed a teleport: "it could also be the duality of the Shi Maria presence. She, in turn, has a god within herself.**"

docs.title: The quest fails first
docs.text:
Book 7 opens with the escort quest still live, and the AI needling him about it:

Quest Update! The Bedlam Bride.

The quest is to get the creepy spider to the city. You're in the city, you have the spider with you, sort of, but you haven't won the quest yet? How is that so?

Did you know that in some cultures, fares for travel aren't paid until the traveler safely arrives at their destination?

The spider is still sitting on the bus, so to speak. You just gotta open the doors and let her out, and you'll win the simple prize. What's the worst that could happen?

Carl declines to open the doors. In chapter 17 the quest reads Quest Failed. The Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: The procedure
docs.text:
Before that, the eye had been active and hostile. Chapter 16: "The eye was open and blinking, angrily looking back and forth, desperately attempting to cast this or that." Every one of those attempts was being blocked by Mind Balance, silently, hundreds of times, logged in a notification folder Carl had suppressed.

Mordecai, Rosetta and Katia construct a shared dream in which Carl must witness Shi Maria's worst memory. Mordecai adds a drug — Removal Order — that gives Carl the option to lock her in the memory permanently at the end.

Inside the dream, Shi Maria's own defence is a scream she repeats in two separate scenes: "I didn't kill you, Hapanzi! I would never kill you!" and later "I didn't kill him! I didn't kill him! I did not, I did not, I did not!"

docs.title: Hapanzi's terms
docs.text:
At the end of the dream, Shi Maria disappears and a second spider takes her place.

I have her now, son, he'd said. She is good and trapped. You can always set her free, if you must. But do not unless all is lost.

And the canonical statement of the mechanic, chapter 19:

He told me that she was gone, trapped in my own body. He told me that I would now have control over the eye and the containment she was within. I could summon her again at will, if I wanted. But I could only do it once, and if I did so, she could choose. She could choose to take over my body or expel herself back into her own form.

In other words, Shi Maria had become yet another bomb in my inventory. An especially dangerous bomb.

I had an uneasy feeling as I watched the replay. She didn't look nearly as trapped as Hapanzi said. Still, I now had control of the eye on my chest. I could feel it there, clenched closed.

So the terms are precise, and they are terrible:

Uses One. Ever. Who decides the outcome She does. Not Carl Outcome A She takes over his body Outcome B She expels herself into her own form Carl's input The decision to open the door. Nothing after that

docs.title: The eye as a weapon
docs.text:
Carl gains conscious control of the eye and can see through it, at a cost:

I could now see from the eye on my chest. It was still a tattoo, but I could feel it when it was open. I had to make a conscious effort to keep the eye closed. Another wave of nausea flooded me.

I tried opening the third eye, but I clenched it shut a moment later. I had to close it. There was power there. So much power. I had to keep it closed.

It is also passively dangerous to anyone who looks into it. In chapter 54, with Vinata crushing him and his shirt torn open, "the eye on my chest was open, and Vinata was staring directly into it. She had been driven mad by the Eye of the Bedlam Bride." The same thing had happened to Warlord Stockade, which Carl only works out on review: "I remembered that moment from the video, when he looked right into my eye. I shook my head. Not my eye. Shi Maria's eye."

The dungeon knows about this. Rishi's cell in chapter 58 has a prismatic containment shield that "would supposedly protect from charm spells and things like the Eye of the Bedlam Bride."

docs.title: The comparison Carl makes himself
docs.text:
Shi Maria wasn't truly gone, but she was trapped. I remembered now. She was like an egg inside of me. One I could break at any time, but I had to do it myself.

Just like Carl's Doomsday Scenario. I was gathering quite the collection of weapons of mass destruction.

That should've been an enormous relief. It was not.

See Carl's Doomsday Scenario for the other one.

docs.title: She keeps asking
docs.text:
Shi Maria spends the book negotiating from inside him, and gets more articulate as she goes:

"I'm still here, Carl. All you need to do is set me free. Use me while you still can. I can save you. Even you can't survive this chaos. It's the end of days." (ch. 54)

"You're always on rails… You're a puppet, dancing on their stage. I'm still here. You just need to untie me." (ch. 62)

Still open at the end of Book 7

Shi Maria is never released. The one-shot is unspent. Carl carries her, and the option, into Book 8.

Also note the friendly voice in chapter 65 that pushes Carl's Mind Balance to 16 — "You're family now, after what you did… She would be proud of you" — is explicitly neither Shi Maria nor Hapanzi. It is never identified.

docs.title: Book 8: Used at Last — Without Releasing Her
docs.text:
The one-shot is still unspent — but the eye itself gets used

Book 7 closed with the one-time release option unspent and the friendly-voice question from chapter 65 unidentified. Book 8 does not resolve either of those. What it does, for the first time since the tattoo was made, is show Carl consciously opening the eye and drawing on its power — without triggering the one-shot release clause at all. Shi Maria is not consulted, not freed, and not heard from on the page.

docs.title: Freezing Mitch, as a dog
docs.text:
During the Floor 10 Desperado Club ambush (see Mitch for the encounter from the mob's side), Carl — transformed into a dachshund by one of Scolopendra's nine-tier-attack curses, with the tattoo relocated to his forehead in canine form — is cornered by the reforming Shadow Mimic. He opens the eye on reflex, and it works as a freezing weapon:

I'd reflexively opened the eye in the center of my forehead, and he froze in place.

"No," Mitch said. His entire form started to sparkle like someone had poured glitter into him. "No. Don't do this. It's too cold... It's too cold!"

Donut finishes Mitch off with a full-strength Magic Missile while he's frozen solid. This is the first time in three books that the eye is used on purpose, as a weapon, by Carl — every prior mention was either Shi Maria trying to seize control from inside it, or the eye's passive madness-inducing gaze (Vinata, Warlord Stockade, both in Book 7).

Afterward, Carl confirms privately that he stayed in control the entire time and deliberately shut the eye again before Floor 11 opened:

"No. You stay where you are. You are trapped, and you will stay trapped. I am in control."

See Carl's own page for the rest of that scene (the Shadow Mimic taxonomy reveal, the Big Six factions) — it is not repeated here.

docs.title: What this does and doesn't change
docs.text:
• Shi Maria herself is not released. The one-time choice from Book 7 — summon her, and let her decide whether to take over Carl's body or expel herself — is never invoked. She does not speak in Book 8 at all.
  • The mechanism behind the freezing effect is never explained. The text does not say whether this is "her power" in the sense Shi Maria offered back in Book 6 ("keep me with you and gain my power"), a property of the eye itself independent of her, or something else. Do not guess at which.
  • This is the clearest on-page evidence yet that Carl has some form of partial, controllable access to the eye that stops short of the all-or-nothing release clause — a capability neither Book 6 nor Book 7 demonstrated.

docs.title: The Book 7 chapter-65 voice: still unidentified
docs.text:
Still open

Book 8 never revisits or explains the mysterious voice from Book 7, chapter 65 — the one that told Carl "You're family now... she would be proud of you" while pushing his Mind Balance to level 16, and which the text explicitly said was neither Shi Maria nor Hapanzi. It is not named, referenced, or followed up on anywhere in A Parade of Horribles. This thread remains fully open for a future book.

docs.text:

  • Carl's Doomsday Scenario — the comparison Carl draws

  • Mitch — the Shadow Mimic frozen and finished off with the eye's help
