docs.title: The Filthy Little Crawler's Book of Voodoo
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owners: Essentially every crawler in the dungeon — Carl, Donut, and the entire surviving field receive one
  • Obtained: A Gold Prepotente Box — a box type named after Prepotente as a joke, because breaking Floor 7 upset the announcer Cascadia so badly
  • Type: Messaging artifact
  • Restrictions: Cannot be traded, cannot be destroyed, cannot be dropped (it returns to your inventory automatically)

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
A heavy, diary-like book of three or four hundred blank pages in a hard black leather cover with no title. When Carl's box opens, it screams.

The name is a joke about pre-cellphone convention message boards: attendees' names were listed on a big board, you stuck a pin next to someone's name to flag that you'd left them a note, and they went to an alphabetical file to read it. "Privacy be damned!"

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
When you meet a crawler who owns this same item, their name will permanently appear in this enchanted book. You may use the book to exchange messages. You may write your message under their name, and only they will receive it. If you write under your own name, everyone who has your entry will see the message.

This book is not retroactively filled with the entries of people you have already met. You must be within close-ish vicinity of them for their name to be added. Works only with crawlers who also own this book.

So: write under someone else's name for a private message, write under your own for a broadcast. Names only populate through in-person proximity, never retroactively. The book buzzes like a phone when a message arrives, and opens itself to the relevant page. You can write manually or through the messaging interface, and copy text out of it.

Carl's first message to Donut is "You have bedhead, Donut." Her reply, in full caps, is a refusal to ever use the thing: "THIS IS A STEP BACKWARD, CARL. THIS IS THE EQUIVALENT OF CHATTING BY LEAVING POST-ITS ON ONE'S LOCKER IN HIGH SCHOOL."

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: None. It has no level, no charges, and no upgrade path. Its only variable is how many names are in it, which grows purely through meeting people face to face — and the book's real utility across Book 6 turns out to be exactly that. It quietly builds a verified, in-person-only roster of surviving crawlers, updating with entries for Sister Ines Quiteria and Quan Ch at dramatically inconvenient moments, and it is what lets Carl broadcast the Build Trench stairwell plan to the entire remaining field at the climax.

docs.title: The Obvious Setup
docs.text:
Flagged — unresolved, almost certainly deliberate

The item description goes out of its way to deny something nobody asked about:

It was called the Voodoo board because of the pins. This book is the same thing. It's called a book of Voodoo because it's named after the message board. Not because it can secretly be used for any sort of nefarious purpose which will become clear later, so just get that out of your head this instant, mister.

Carl notices. His own reaction: "why would they give this to most everybody in the dungeon? The description was a little alarming. You never really knew when the AI was being serious or not."

An undroppable, indestructible object that every crawler in the dungeon is carrying, with their true names written in it, distributed for free, by an AI that is openly telling you it has another purpose. Book 6 does not reveal what that purpose is. Do not guess.

docs.title: Book 7: The Other Purpose
docs.text: The book's other purpose turns out to be skill and spell distribution. Written in the right ink, a page of the Book of Voodoo can carry an ability from the person who wrote it to whoever eats the page. Because the book broadcasts to every owner, that makes it the only mass-distribution channel for abilities in the dungeon — the opposite of nefarious, in the end. What it enables in chapter 85 is thousands of departing crawlers permanently giving up their own skills to arm the people staying behind.

docs.title: The AI shouts about it for twenty chapters
docs.text:
Chapter 57, after Carl kills someone with an ability borrowed via tattoo, the reward box is named:

Platinum Have You Goddamned Figured Out How To Use This In Conjunction With the Fucking Voodoo Book Yet? Jesus Christ I Can Only Help You So Much box.

Carl does not figure it out. Edgar does, in chapter 74:

"Rosetta was just telling Milk and myself about that book of Voodoo you have, and I believe you may be able to share skills and spells that way as well, using the same ink. It will be more temporary."

And Milk states the distribution rule plainly in chapter 75, while handing Carl 825 ml of Stayfast Ink and a fountain pen:

"He also has another book. One that all of you have. The Book of Voodoo, I believe it is called. Anything he writes in it will be given to everybody who already has the book. Best of luck to you."

docs.title: The book splits in two
docs.text:
Chapter 85, at the mass departure ceremony:

Your Book of Voodoo has been updated.

Your Book of Voodoo has been updated with a metric fuckton of entries.

For fucks sake. Finally.

Your Book of Voodoo has been segmented into two volumes. The second volume is entitled Carl's Book of Boom.

Volume two has its own page: Carl's Book of Boom — roughly 30,000 pages, one per departing crawler, each granting that crawler's skill or spell temporarily when eaten. Donut receives her own equivalent volume, A Banquet Fit for a Princess.

Crucially, each donor also wrote a third page onto their own entry in the original Book of Voodoo, which Milk describes as "a first come, first served sort of deal in the original book of Voodoo that anyone can use." So volume one is no longer only a message board. It is now a shared, open armoury for every crawler who owns a copy.

docs.title: Its ordinary use continues
docs.text: The book remains the party's day-to-day comms channel throughout Floor 9 — Donut approves tattoo designs through it, Katia sketches artwork in it, and war chat runs across it. Donut's Book 6 position that it is "A STEP BACKWARD, CARL" does not survive her discovering she can use it to art-direct other people's tattoos in all caps from several kilometres away.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:

  • Stayfast Ink and Adept's Fountain Pen — the ink that makes it work
  • The Toraline Ink Tattoo System — the underlying mechanic

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride and Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: The Scavenger's Daughter
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Carl
  • Slot: Back patch, affixed to the Enchanted Anarchist's Battle Rattle
  • Rarity: Divine, Unique, Fleeting
  • Obtained: A Celestial Predator Box — the reward for the "Apex Predator" achievement, earned for killing the most hunters on Floor 6 and killing the very last one (a Book 5 event; the box is opened at the start of Book 6)
  • Grants: Doubled patch stat bonuses, +25 Dexterity, +25 Strength, deity-proximity alerts, Climb, Soul Reaper / The Daughter's Kiss, and the Mysterious Bone Key

docs.title: The Patch Itself
docs.text:
A thick black rectangle of fabric embroidered with a white pile of skulls from various creatures, stacked into a pyramid. Running across the whole face of it, invisible until it matters, is a layer of clear stitching, "almost like it was sewn with fiberoptic wire" — an image Carl can feel but not see.

Its pre-installation description tells him nothing:

This patch depicts a pile of scary skulls, all stacked up nice and neat. I wonder if there's a story there?

If this upgrade patch is affixed to an eligible garment, it will imbue the following upgrades: (Hidden until it is affixed and then worn.)

Affixing it also earns the achievement "Fashion of the Gods!", which explains what a divine item is: something that "might've once been worn by a god. Or sneezed on by a god." Divine items hide their effects until equipped, and gain new powers — or nasty debuffs, with "no rhyme or reason to it" — in the presence of divinity. Mordecai is unbothered: "Divine items are the best items."

Carl sews it on himself, badly, over Donut's loud objections about his stitching.

docs.title: Base Effects
docs.text:
All patch stat point benefits are now doubled.

Plus 25 points to Dexterity.

Plus 25 points to Strength.

You will receive a notification every time a deity enters the area.

The Climb benefit.

The Soul Reaper benefit.

The Mysterious Bone Key benefit.

This patch will imbue additional, varying benefits when it is in the presence of divine entities.

The Battle Rattle already grants +1 to every stat per affixed patch; doubling that across Carl's five smaller patches, on top of the flat +25/+25, makes this the single largest equipment upgrade he receives in the book. It also adds a new Soul Essence bar to his interface, sitting directly below his mana in the slot the Floor 6 blood bar used to occupy.

Mordecai's reaction to the middle benefit is the tell — he blinks his single eye and says "Oh, shit. Soul Reaper?... it's good all right. But you gotta be careful with it."

docs.title: Divine Proximity Effects
docs.text:
The patch "opens her eyes" whenever a deity or demon prince enters the area, and the effect varies entirely by who shows up. Every instance seen in Book 6:

Entity Effect Ogun, god of blacksmiths (lvl 250) All Smash-related attacks +300% Yemaya, the river mother All healing skills and spells cost no mana and have no cooldown Eileithyia All damage Carl deals to female opponents is quartered; all female party members strike with melee power of 500% ("Girl power, bitches!") Amayon, prince of Sheol All of Carl's fire spells use Sheol Fire instead of regular fire Ysalte, goddess of hopelessness and insanity All potions Carl quaffs or physically handles outside his inventory turn to vinegar — and return as a more powerful version of themselves upon her banishment

Ysalte's is the book's clearest demonstration that a divine "debuff" on this item is usually a delayed gift: Carl deliberately pulls potions out and drops them on the floor mid-fight to be vinegared, earning the "Kombucha!" achievement, and when the patch looks away it announces that "all of your vinegar-infused potions outside your inventory have been enhanced." One of them regrows Mongo's burned-off wing.

Amayon's effect does the heavy lifting at the climax: with every fire attack upgraded to Sheol Fire, Carl's Martyr's Path release bathes a demon prince in hellfire rather than ordinary flame.

When a deity leaves, the buff "fades and will completely dissipate over the next ten minutes."

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: The patch's own numbers are flat. What grows is the Soul Essence bar it adds: the bar's capacity increases every time it is filled and fully drained, so the longer Carl uses it the bigger each charged attack becomes. See Soul Reaper / The Daughter's Kiss for the full mechanic. By mid-book Carl has topped and drained it repeatedly and notes the attacks are "noticeably stronger already."

docs.title: The Hidden Stitching
docs.text:
Foreshadowing — unresolved

The clear stitching resolves on the final page of the book. As Carl and Donut are being lifted off Cuba, Donut sees the jacket glowing and finally makes out the image: "It's not an aardvark like I thought. It's a giant centipede! The image is of a centipede crawling through all the skulls!"

A centipede is a Scolopendra reference — the same entity behind the "Scolopendra levels" of Zerzura and, per in-dungeon rumour, connected to the Bedlam Bride herself ("one dwarf say she is the daughter of the great centipede. Another say she's the sister. Another claimed she's the mother"). Book 6 does not explain the connection.

At the same moment a voice speaks in Carl's mind: "You did not diffuse your soul power from the Scavenger's Daughter. That was a mistake. You should never allow it to linger within you. I need you alive, Carl. I need you reasonably sane. We have so much work to do." The speaker is not named. Carl had indeed forgotten to spend a full essence bar, which the item's own description had warned about in a joke he was told to ignore.

docs.title: Book 7: Soul Poisoning
docs.text:
New mechanic — the warning was real

Book 6 closed with an unnamed voice telling Carl "You did not diffuse your soul power from the Scavenger's Daughter. That was a mistake. You should never allow it to linger within you." Book 7 opens by making that a condition with a name and a progression bar. Letting the Soul Essence bar sit full now actively damages Carl, and it gets worse the longer he leaves it.

The condition surfaces in chapter 1. Carl feels "a sudden pang… like a stomach cramp, but much more burning," and his Emberus ring flashes and warms. The health menu reads:

Soul Poisoning.

The effects of this condition are being partially blocked by your Pauper's ring of the Steadfast Emberus.

This condition is worsening.

This condition causes jolts of pain.

This condition has additional effects that will soon be revealed if you don't do something about it.

You are suffering from a very minor case of stop-carrying-stored-souls-on-your-back. Seriously. Do you know why soul crystals explode when they get overloaded? Do you remember that whole thing on the previous floor when too many souls flowed through Sheol? And you're just walking around, giving a piggyback ride to a bunch of corrupted souls stuck in something made out of fabric? Yeah, good luck with that. You better smush something soon, dumbass.

Oh, and don't try unequipping that jacket while your soul power is full. That won't go well for you or anybody nearby.

That last line converts the jacket from an asset into a hostage: while charged, it cannot safely be taken off.

docs.title: The escalation
docs.text:
Stage Chapter Effect Onset 1 Jolts of pain, partially blocked by the Pauper's Ring Reminder 20 "You are now suffering from Soul Poisoning. Activate the Daughter's Kiss skill to disperse the effect." Worsening 24 "Your Soul Poisoning is worsening. You will now suffer from Post Coital Blues." Carl's entire reaction: "What the hell does that mean?" Worst 25 Post Nut Clarity — using the Daughter's Kiss now knocks Carl unconscious

Imani, over chat, after he buries the squad in dirt:

"The second you did that attack, you had a debuff called Post Nut Clarity. You were out for 25 seconds. You buried us in dirt. Don't do that again when we're that close."

Carl's own summary: "The Post Nut Clarity was, apparently, a debuff from my soul poisoning that knocked me out once I activated my Daughter's Kiss. That was dangerous as fuck. I needed to make certain I used the skill from now on before the debuff activated."

So the patch's incentive structure inverts. In Book 6 the bar rewarded patience — hold the charge, hit harder. In Book 7 holding it invites a condition that makes the very act of spending it dangerous, and the correct play becomes discharging early and often, on whatever is nearest. Chapter 1's discharge is on an already-dead Concierge Shark, which earns the achievement "Sushi Smoothie" and the system's note: "Next time use your foot."

Exact-verification note

Post Coital Blues is never defined. The system names it, Carl asks what it means, and the book never says. Post Nut Clarity is a consequence of the worsened condition, not a baseline cost of every Daughter's Kiss — it only appears once the poisoning has escalated.

docs.title: Divine proximity on Floor 9
docs.text:
The deity-proximity mechanic is unchanged and fires constantly — Floor 9 has gods walking around in the open — but Book 7 clarifies its duration rules. The patch "opens her eyes" when a deity is in range, and closes them when the deity leaves, at which point "your boon is timed and will run out on its own." There is also an explicit range limit: "This deity is too distant to activate your Scavenger's Daughter," and a partial state, "The Scavenger's Daughter has blinked her eyes, but she does not know what she sees."

Every effect seen in Book 7:

Entity Chapter Effect Khepri 52 "Uh, please wait while I look something up…" → immortal for the next 90 seconds Harpocrates 70 Level 15 Pied Piper skill (later made permanent by Eris — see Pied Piper) Yarilo 72 "Temporary Effect from Yarilo: Please wait. / Oh shit, we hadn't fixed that one…" Meatus, a feral god 76 "Your dick will fall off if you get an erection." Made permanent when Meatus is "slap-chopped all over the realm" Eileithyia 86 Damage against female opponents quartered; all female party members strike at 500% melee power. "Girl power, bitches!"

Chapter 54 is where this becomes a liability rather than a lottery. With gods appearing all over the battlefield at once, Carl works out why he has worms coming out of his nose: "My Scavenger's Daughter patch. Every new god gave me either a buff or debuff." The simultaneous stack — Never-Ending Mana, Shit-Faced, Stiff Legs, suction cups on his fingers, screaming worms — is what finally overloads the Pauper's Ring.

Still unanswered

In chapter 78 Carl asks Mordecai outright who the Scavenger and the Scavenger's Daughter actually are. Mordecai deflects — "in-dungeon one or the fairy tale?" — and the question is never answered. The Book 6 centipede/Scolopendra stitching is likewise not explained in Book 7.

  • Mysterious Bone Key — the granted one-use lockpick

docs.title: The Waffle Maker and No Disassemble
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Maker: Carl
  • The Waffle Maker: A thermobaric bomb the size of a thermos. Incinerates everything within 100 metres. The direct descendant of Book 5's "Just Wait Until Your Daddy Gets Home"
  • No Disassemble: The dungeon's EMP equivalent — square, shield-and-tech-busting, with a pulse radius considerably wider than its blast
  • Delivery: Both are the standard payload of Party Planner, which adds +50% yield
  • Body count: Between them they take the Khepri temple guard, the Reaver honeycomb castle's robot force, and Warlord Fang

Exact-verification note

Neither device has a system description block. Both are player-built, and everything below is Carl's narration.

docs.title: The Waffle Maker
docs.text:
Carl's lineage of increasingly portable atrocities reaches its most compact form here:

The bomb was something I'd been tinkering with for a while now, and it was currently the second-largest explosive I had in my inventory. The first version of this thing had been called "Just Wait Until Your Daddy Gets Home," and we'd used it on the sixth floor.

This version packed about the same punch, minus the addition of Fear. The tradeoff was this version was self-contained in a much smaller device. The first had been so big it had to have wheels. This one was the size of a thermos. The result was a thermobaric explosion that would absolutely incinerate anything within 100 meters. Louis currently had fifty of these things on Party Planner. The only reason he didn't have more was because the explosive dust was a pain to make.

The AI had helpfully called the bomb The Waffle Maker.

Same yield, one wheeled cart's worth of hardware compressed into something that fits in a jacket pocket. The trade was dropping the Fear component. The binding constraint on production is the explosive dust, not the casing.

Physically it is round and tube-shaped, and it makes a heavier clunk than a No Disassemble when it drops.

First use, chapter 54: detonated inside Khepri's temple against three of the god's guards. The blast also flattens Carl into "a boxer-clad amalgam of flesh and hair," which is not a figure of speech — he survives it on invulnerability and healing, not on distance.

docs.title: No Disassemble
docs.text:
Square, and built for a completely different job: killing electronics and shields rather than people.

The No Disassembles were basically the dungeon's equivalent of an EMP. They exploded, and you couldn't just drop one at your feet, but the real damage came from their pulse, which had a much wider range than the explosive itself.

Which is the tactical distinction between the two weapons in one line. The Waffle Maker's radius is its blast. The No Disassemble's radius is its pulse, and the pulse is much bigger than the bang.

Colonel Boomer's reason for pushing the disastrous chapter-66 bomb run in the first place was the absence of these: "We don't have No Disassemble missiles to kill their electronics."

docs.title: The Reaver Honeycomb Castle
docs.text:
This is the payoff, and it takes fourteen chapters to arrive.

Chapter 66. Party Planner is torn in half by a gravity-magic dragon. Louis dumps his bombs unarmed before he goes down and crash-lands on the flat roof of the Reaver honeycomb castle.

Chapter 67. He collects what he can from the roof — "a handful of unexploded No Disassembles and Waffle Makers into his inventory" — and Carl notes the problem: "He had no way of setting them off without blowing himself up. They had to be unstable as fuck. Louis did not have invulnerability."

Chapter 68. Louis, trapped inside the castle and being shot at by Reaver sentry dogs: "They have these little dog robot things that shoot darts… I have some No Disassemble robot killers, but the explosions are too big. I can't do it where I'm stuck."

Chapter 80. Carl solves it from outside. Louis still has "a ton of no disassembles and waffle makers" in his inventory. Carl tells Juice Box: "Louis has No Disassembles in his inventory. Drop them and leave! They'll kill the robots!" — and then opens his own crafting menu, finds the No Disassembles page, sorts by unexploded, and triggers them remotely. He built them, so he can set them off from anywhere.

The pulse wipes the Reaver robot force. The collateral is instructive:

  • Jamal's mechanical legs are destroyed — they were unshielded and sat on the edge of the pulse radius
  • Louis's replacement heart and lungs are shielded, and survive. Carl's note afterward: "if we figure this out and he has to keep those organs, we can't use those bombs anywhere near him ever again"
  • The transport is wrecked by a separate Mini Tactical Nuke, not by the EMP

Warlord Fang dies in this sequence. He survived Donut's War Crime in chapter 76 specifically because he is biological material inside a robot; the No Disassembles are the thing that finally reaches him.

docs.title: The "Shit Just Hit" Folder
docs.text:
Chapter 71 contains the clearest single illustration of Carl's late-book inventory, dumped all at once toward the Piccadilly Theater:

approximately 20 waffle makers, two no disassembles, a pair of the anti-personnel cheese cutters, approximately 500 impact hob-lobbers, and more sticks of dynamite than I could count

He keeps them pre-sorted into a folder named for the circumstance in which he would need all of them simultaneously.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
Neither device has a level. The relevant multipliers are:

  • Party Planner's +50% yield on anything dropped from its bomb bay
  • Production limits — the Waffle Maker's explosive dust is the bottleneck, not the design
  • Remote detonation via the crafting menu, available to Carl as the builder, for any unexploded unit anywhere in the world

docs.text:

  • Carl's Jug O' Boom and Carl's Doomsday Scenario — the rest of the escalation

docs.title: The Tiara of a Thousand Lights and Accompanying Charge Pillow
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Princess Donut
  • Slot: Head
  • Rarity: Celestial Benefactor Box, unique
  • Obtained: Chapter 3, from Donut's sponsor Long Haul Biological Waste Management Solutions — a crest-owned company Mordecai has never heard of sponsoring anyone
  • Base effect: +10 Charisma. That is all.
  • Real effect: 99 Absorption Jewels — a permanent buff-storage battery, filled by draining other enchanted hats on the accompanying red charge pillow
  • Second pillow: A purple universal charge pillow from a separate Platinum Apothecary benefactor box, same chapter, which drains any magical item but only transfers to a like item

This is Donut's third tiara, and it does not replace either of the first two in the way one might expect. It is a container. The Enchanted Tiara of Mana Genita stays in inventory, and the Enchanted Tiara of the Inebriated Dragonfly is deliberately destroyed as an enchanted item on the purple pillow so that its powers can be poured into this one.

docs.title: Delivery
docs.text:
The benefactor box arrives as a box-shaped spaceship covered in flashing lights, with the Long Haul logo on its side, which then folds in on itself:

The ship started to move, folding in on itself like it was a giant robot. Donut squealed with delight as it turned into a massive, mechanical hand. And sitting upon that hand were two items. A red, fluffy pillow with a glittering, shining, opalescent tiara placed upon it.

Mordecai's reaction is split between suspicion and approval — "That's a crest-owned company. I've never even heard of them sponsoring anybody. Much less giving a Celestial Benefactor box. It doesn't make any damn sense" — followed immediately by "Wow. That's a lot of absorption crystals. Good. This is a good one."

The pillow is velvet-textured and much heavier than it looks. The tiara is "covered in about a hundred, tiny jewels, each sparkling a different color."

docs.title: The Description
docs.text:
The Tiara of a Thousand Lights and Accompanying Charge Pillow.

This is a unique item.

This item was made especially for Crawler Princess Donut by her sponsor, Long Haul Biological Waste Management Solutions.

This particular tiara is imbued with 99 Absorption Jewels.

The tiara itself has no inherent magical properties, and in its base state it gives no additional benefits or buffs except plus 10 to Charisma. However, it has the ability to be permanently charged with up to 99 different buff items.

Any single enchanted hat item of any quality you place upon the accompanying charge pillow for a period of ten hours will lose all of its magical properties. These properties will be stored in the pillow until the tiara is placed upon the charger, upon which time, all of the buffs and magical enhancements will be instantly transferred to the tiara. If a hat item contains five separate buffs, it will use up five of the 99 jewels. Similar buffs from different hat items, like two different intelligence boosts, will not combine and will take up two jewels.

With some careful planning, one can turn this tiara into one of the most powerful items in the history of Dungeon Crawler World.

The item's lore section is a Long Haul origin myth about a lost crest habitat, a scavenging young engineer and "a bioengineered farm animal called a cockrent — basically a space chicken that breathes methane," whose jettisoned spheres exploded into colored light and drew a Syndicate rescue squad. The joke is buried in a parenthetical, and it matters for reasons the book does not flag until much later:

(They, of course, were fined so much money that the habitat was eventually repossessed and the vast majority of the adults were forced to indenture to pay off the debt, but this part is usually left out of the retellings of this legend.)

docs.title: The Warnings
docs.text:
These are the operative rules, quoted in order:

Warning: Temporary effects will remain temporary, and upon expiration will burn out the absorption jewel.

Warning: Items with curse effects may or may not transfer to the tiara depending on multiple factors, so be wary. As such, curse effects may or may not be removed from items that have been drained of their magical properties.

Warning: Certain Celestial, god-blessed hat items may or may not be properly drained or transferred.

Warning: Items carrying a debt cannot be absorbed into the pillow.

Warning: This is a big one. Hat items placed on this pillow take ten hours to fully transfer, however if you remove the item after one hour, it will still lose its magical abilities.

Four things follow from that list and they are all load-bearing:

  1. A temporary buff is worse than useless. It occupies a jewel, expires, and burns the jewel out.
  2. There is no safety window. Pull a hat off after one hour and the hat's magic is gone anyway, with nothing stored. The ten hours is the transfer time, not a trial period.
  3. Curses are a coin flip in both directions — they may ride across into the tiara, and they may or may not be scrubbed off the drained item.
  4. Debt-bearing items are categorically excluded. See the debt cross-reference below.

There is also no completion notification, which Mordecai calls a long-standing bug — you have to set your own timer, and you cannot tell whether it worked until you peel the drained item off. Items "click" audibly onto a pillow and then stick like a magnet.

This is the third tiara referenced on Magic Missile and Tiara of Mana Genita — its "advanced targeting" doesn't originate with the tiara itself, but is absorbed into it from a hat; see Where the "advanced targeting" actually comes from.

docs.title: The Second Pillow — Purple, Universal
docs.text:
Minutes after the Long Haul box, a Platinum benefactor box from the Apothecary arrives in the same chapter. Donut expects a hat; it is a second charging pillow, nearly identical to the first but purple instead of red, with the same ten-hour transfer and the same one-hour point of no return. The difference is a single appended clause:

Warning: This will drain any magical item, but it will only transfer to a like item. If you drain a ring, the stored buff will only be transferred to an absorption crystal affixed to a ring. If you attempt to transfer to an incompatible item, the buff will be lost.

Carl's read on it:

"So, this one is almost like a universal charger," I said, turning the purple pillow over in my hand. "Be sure they're listed as hats before you use it, Donut. But now that you have two, you can fill up your new tiara twice as fast. We'll need to start cataloging all your magical hats ASAP and see what buffs we want to transfer over."

In practice the purple pillow serves two roles: it doubles the party's charging throughput (two hats can cook at once, even though only the red pillow feeds the tiara), and it is the tool used to strip non-hat gear.

docs.title: The Inebriated Dragonfly Is Sacrificed
docs.text:
Donut loads both pillows for the first time in chapter 3: the new boonie hat on the red pillow, and the Tiara of the Inebriated Dragonfly on the purple one.

Donut grumbled as she put the pillows on the counter. She placed her new boonie hat on the red pillow and her Tiara of the Inebriated Dragonfly on the other. Each item made an audible click the moment they touched the pillow. There was no other notification.

The dragonfly tiara is therefore deliberately and permanently drained — its 50% potion cooldown reduction, +10 Intelligence, poison protection, inebriation clause and level-10 Hover stripped out of it — so that those buffs can be re-housed in the Thousand Lights tiara. The physical tiara survives; Donut keeps all her drained hats for her collection, which she considers the best part of the whole arrangement:

"Do you know how many hats I have with magical abilities, but I can't wear them because they only have one or two? Or because they're ugly? And you know what the best part is? Even though it drains the original item of all its magic, it doesn't destroy it! So I can keep the hats for my collection. It is just divine."

Hover survives the migration — confirmed to chapter 75

Mordecai briefly argues against spending a jewel on Hover when the party is deciding which single skill to push to level 15 ("Hover is a little different, and I don't think it would be worth it"), but Donut does have it afterward, while wearing the Thousand Lights tiara. Chapter 75, planning the Nest collapse: "I also have Hover, Carl. If the tower falls, I won't. But in case I do, I have the potion," and in narration, "would it break in time for her to use her Hover to save herself?"

Exact-verification note: the book never prints a "Hover transferred" notification, and chapter 75 is the last mention of Hover in Book 7. Continued possession at the very end of the book is an inference from the tiara still being worn in chapter 86, not an explicit statement.

docs.title: Where the "Advanced Targeting" Actually Comes From
docs.text:
The Book 6 flag pointed at "a tiara granting advanced targeting." The chain is longer than that.

Donut's Floor 9 class is Deathbed Hellcat, a long-range sniper/assassin class she picks off-page during the floor transition. It quadruples the range of all her existing spells, raises her Dexterity, improves her instakill odds, grants at-will invisibility — and it ships with an accessory kit containing a ghillie suit and a boonie hat. The hat is what carries the skill:

The floppy hat added a Targeting skill, which allowed her to zoom in and examine mobs from afar. It was similar to the gnomish farseerer, but a lot less awkward. It also increased the range of all her spells, even more than they were already buffed.

Worn together with the ghillie suit, the two stack: "She'd be able to snipe line-of-sight enemies from well over a mile away."

Mordecai's very first instruction on receiving the pillow is to drain that specific hat first:

"The first thing you'll want to put on that pillow is that hat you just got with the targeting ability. And set a timer in your own interface. I know these things, and they don't give any sort of notification when the transfer is complete. It's been a bug for a very long time. So set a timer for like ten and a half hours to be safe. You can't see if it worked until you pull the drained item off, so you have to be extra, extra careful."

By chapter 32 the transfer has landed — "Donut was examining the orc prince via her new Targeting skill which had just been added to her crown" — and by chapter 61 it produces the exact line the Book 6 flag was reaching for:

Crack! That was a new sound, and it took a moment for me to realize what it was. It was Donut casting Magic Missile. With her tiara's advanced targeting skills and Donut's elevated position, along with her Deathbed Hellcat class, she could hit anything she could see with any of her long-range spells. It was louder than expected.

That single capability changes the party's siege engineering. The Nest tower was going to be built as a dedicated sniper tower to give Donut exactly this; because the tiara already provides it, the tower's synergy slot is freed up and reassigned to Atrocity-class spells instead — which is what makes War Crime viable from the top of it.

docs.title: Fill Rate and the Running Tally
docs.text:
Chapter State of the tiara 3 Received. Empty — "The tiara didn't have any powers yet, but it glittered magnificently." 32 Targeting confirmed transferred and in use 40 23 of 99 jewels lit. This session adds +10 Constitution, a +2 Dodge upgrade (taking Dodge to 15), and a 1% Intelligence buff. Steady is queued on the pillow via a plastic baseball hat 56 35 of 99, with Perfect Night Vision newly added, and "two more by the time the timer expired" 73 Glowing "like a lighthouse beacon"

The chapter-40 passage is also the clearest illustration of the mechanic's waste problem — Katia is running the swaps, and one jewel is spent on nothing useful because it rode in on the same hat as something Donut wanted:

On the tiara, three of the absorption jewels started to sparkle, joining the twenty other sparkling gems. Twenty three buffs added, 76 to go. The tiara had just gained another 10 to Constitution, a plus two enhancement to Donut's Dodge skill—which should bring it to 15—and a 1% buff to her Intelligence. The intelligence buff was a waste of a crystal, but it was on the same hat that had the Dodge upgrade and couldn't be avoided.

Exact-verification note

The figure 37 does not appear in Book 7. The only number after 35 is the forward-looking "two more by the time the timer expired" in chapter 56, from which 37 can be inferred but is never stated. No final count is ever given.

docs.title: The Liability
docs.text:
The tiara's brilliance is a tactical problem, and Carl says so as soon as it becomes obvious:

The tiara itself glittered brilliantly like a star upon Donut's head, which I didn't like. She, predictably, loved it.

The concrete version, same chapter: "Especially since she wore a glittering, here's-where-my-head-is tiara." By chapter 73 the contrast is absurd — Donut is in the top level of the Nest tower wearing a ghillie suit, the single most camouflage-oriented item she owns, with a tiara that "glowed like a lighthouse beacon" on her head, marking the exact position of her skull for every enemy gunner on the field.

docs.title: The Only Hint About Debt-Bearing Items
docs.text:
The fourth warning — "Items carrying a debt cannot be absorbed into the pillow" — is the only place anywhere in Book 7 where debt-bearing items are acknowledged as a mechanical category.

That matters because Carl is still carrying one. The Enchanted Pauper's Ring of the Steadfast Emberus has an explicit "This ring has a debt attached to it" clause and a 990,000-gold Temple of Emberus loan outstanding since Book 6. Book 7 never mentions the loan, the asterisk on "interest-free," the curse clause, or Pater Coal. This warning line is the closest the book comes to touching the thread at all, and it does so sideways, in a different item's fine print, about a different character.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
The tiara has no level. Its power is a pure function of how many of the 99 jewels have been filled and with what — which makes it the only item in the series whose ceiling is set by logistics rather than by loot. The constraints on filling it are:

  • Ten hours per hat, one hat per pillow, and only the red pillow feeds the tiara
  • One buff per jewel, with no stacking of duplicates
  • No partial-drain recovery — an aborted charge destroys the source hat's magic for nothing
  • Temporary buffs self-destruct their jewel on expiry
  • Donut's supply of hats, which is the one resource she has in genuinely absurd abundance

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Enchanted Tiara of the Inebriated Dragonfly — deliberately drained on the purple pillow to feed this tiara
  • Enchanted Tiara of Mana Genita — Donut's Book 3 tiara, kept
  • Hover — migrated skill
  • Targeting — the absorbed skill the Book 6 flag was pointing at
  • Magic Missile — the spell the targeting most visibly serves
  • War Crime — enabled from the Nest tower by the freed synergy slot
  • Enchanted Pauper's Ring of the Steadfast Emberus — the debt-bearing item the fourth warning implicitly excludes

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Enchanted Tiara of Mana Genita
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: A Book 3 loot box, replacing her lost Crown of the Sepsis Whore
  • Effect: +3 Intelligence, increased mob-detection range, removes automatic hostility from worshippers of the goddess Mana Genita

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A white-jeweled tiara that replaces Donut's lost Crown, described with characteristically dark in-universe humor:

"A crystal tiara fit for royalty. Made in honor of all the lost children of the world. Because nothing helps sooth the tears of grieving parents like watching someone else dress up all fancy."

Mordecai admits he barely knows anything about Mana Genita herself — "a pretty obscure" goddess, apparently associated with spells, one of thousands of deities the dungeon can reference, most of which "never leave the 12th floor." Her identity and relevance remain unexplained as of the end of Book 3.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: No level-based scaling is described — the tiara's three effects (Intelligence bonus, detection range, and the worshipper-hostility removal) all appear to be flat, static bonuses.

docs.title: Book 6: Benched, Not Replaced
docs.text:
The Mana Genita tiara is confirmed as Donut's standard everyday headwear right up to the middle of Floor 8 — "That's what she usually wore, and that was what she was wearing right now" — sitting alongside a collection of literally hundreds of unenchanted hats in her inventory.

Midway through the floor she builds the Enchanted Tiara of the Inebriated Dragonfly from a blank tiara and a Flawless Jeweler's Gem, and the dragonfly becomes her new daily wear. Importantly, the Mana Genita is deliberately kept rather than traded in — Carl notes it "might end up useful one day" — and Donut continues to swap tiaras situationally, explicitly "switching into her dragonfly tiara" when she wants the Hover skill.

docs.title: Book 7: A Third Tiara Arrives, and It Is Neither of These
docs.text:
A third tiara arrives in chapter 3: The Tiara of a Thousand Lights and Accompanying Charge Pillow, a Celestial benefactor box from Donut's sponsor Long Haul Biological Waste Management Solutions.

It is neither a replacement nor an upgrade of Mana Genita or the Dragonfly tiara in the ordinary sense. On its own it grants +10 Charisma and nothing else; its value is 99 Absorption Jewels that can be permanently charged by draining other enchanted hats on an accompanying pillow. The tiara's own "advanced targeting" doesn't come from the tiara itself — it's absorbed into it from a boonie hat that ships with Donut's new Deathbed Hellcat class. See Targeting and Magic Missile.

The Mana Genita tiara is not drained and not mentioned in Book 7. The sacrifice goes the other way: it is the Enchanted Tiara of the Inebriated Dragonfly that Donut deliberately places on the purple universal charge pillow in chapter 3, permanently stripping it of its magic so the buffs can be re-housed in the new tiara.

Exact-verification note

Book 7 gives no on-page statement of where the Mana Genita ends up. Carl's Book 6 reasoning for keeping it — it "might end up useful one day" — is not revisited, and it is not among the hats shown being drained. Treat its status as unchanged and unaddressed, not as resolved.

Sourced from Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook and Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride, with Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin resolving the open flag.

docs.title: Tier 3 Doggie Door
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Personal space upgrade module
  • Tier: 3 — per Mordecai, these "shouldn't be available until the ninth floor"
  • Obtained: Lucia Mar dropped five of them on the ground and walked down the stairs (ch. 63)
  • Effect: Turns your personal-space door into a selectable exit to any door you have previously used on that floor — a fast-travel waypoint network, shareable with guests and party members
  • Cost to extend guild-wide: 25 million gold

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Personal Space Upgrade. Tier 3 Doggie Door.

So, you're out adventuring, and you suddenly have a hankerin' for those sweet pancakes you had two weeks back at some dive that's now over two hundred kilometers away. What are you gonna do? Travel for several hours in the wrong direction just to get another taste? Psshh. Okay, loser.

The cool kids use the doggie door.

Upgrades the door in your personal space to allow a selectable exit via any door you have previously utilized on this same floor, effectively creating a fast travel waypoint system. Allows shared gated access amongst guests and party members.

A module from a box arrives as a physical object that must be placed in inventory and activated through the personal-space tab; a bopca-purchased one would simply be installed into the room for you.

docs.title: How the Guild Got Them
docs.text:
Li Jun hands the first one to Carl and can't explain it. Lucia Mar — fresh from what the broadcast is calling the Battle of Beijing, where she killed her way through a building full of keyless crawlers — was waiting for Li Jun's group at the stairwell. She had messaged with Florin before he descended, and he'd told her to help them. She dropped five Tier 3 modules on the ground, said nothing useful, and left.

"She was really friendly, too, which was unsettling. My sister wanted to fight her."

Katia's assessment: "She shouldn't have had one, let alone five of them. It's a tier-3. Mordecai says these shouldn't be available until the ninth floor... He thinks Lucia stole them when she went on a show or something."

docs.title: Scaling and Limits
docs.text:
"Tier 3" is the scaling. The tier is what makes it a floor-wide waypoint network rather than a single fixed exit, and it is what makes it expensive and out of season. Three limits apply:

  1. Same floor only — the door network resets when the floor does
  2. Previously used doors only — you can only travel to a door you have physically walked through already
  3. One module, one room — access is shared with that room's party and guests, so one installed module covers a whole party but not the whole guild

The guild installs the first in Imani's room, which immediately gives the entire Meadowlark party door access to the church, Washington, Detroit, and Belgium. Four modules remain unspent at book's end. Upgrading the whole guild so that every member's own door joins the network costs 25 million gold, which they cannot afford — they had just pooled everything they had to buy the five-million barracks upgrade.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
This is a capability the guild has been chasing for several books: a way to move a distributed, multi-squad organisation around a floor faster than the floor can kill them. Arriving mid-Floor-8, two floors early, via the dungeon's most feared player killer, it changes the shape of the endgame — and quietly raises the question of how Lucia Mar came to be handing out ninth-floor infrastructure for free.

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: The Toraline Ink Tattoo System (Skill and Spell Transfer)
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • What it is: A method of copying a spell or skill from one person to another by tattooing them with ink made from toraline root and the donor's blood
  • Built from: The leftover ink Shi Maria brewed in Book 6 with the Enchanted Prison Tattoo Kit, plus the remaining toraline root Carl's sponsors (the Open Intellect Pacifist Network) gave him
  • Developed by: Rosetta, Edgar the shell-mage tortoise, Mordecai, and later the crawler Milk
  • The core rule: Blood freely given lends a spell temporarily. Blood taken by violence steals it permanently
  • Status at book's end: The toraline is used up; Milk supersedes it with a new ink and gives Carl Stayfast Ink and an Adept's Fountain Pen

This page covers the mechanic. The physical kit that applies it has its own page at Enchanted Prison Tattoo Kit, and the three tattoos actually inked in Book 7 are detailed below.

docs.title: Origin: Rosetta Asks for the Ink Within Minutes
docs.text:
Book 6 ended with Shi Maria's parting note that Carl "will likely be doing more of this soon with the remaining ink." The payoff lands almost immediately. In chapter 11, minutes into the party's first real negotiation with Rosetta on Floor 9, she examines Carl, reaches down his shirt to touch the Bedlam Bride tattoo, and asks a question with no preamble:

"How much do you have left?"

"Of what?"

She pulled her hand free. "The toraline. Give it to me, and give me the ink the spider used to make that tattoo."

What Carl has left is thin: "a finger-sized slice" of the vegetable and "only a few thimblefuls" of Shi Maria's ink, still hot to the touch in its glass container. Mordecai has a little more toraline, "but not much." Rosetta's asking price for her part is saferoom access, access to the bomber's studio, and four million gold.

Rosetta already knows what this ink is for before anyone else does. It takes the party the better part of forty chapters to catch up.

docs.title: Consent determines everything
docs.text:
The single rule the whole system turns on is intention. Katia lays it out in chapter 40, after Li Na donates blood for Carl's first transfer tattoo:

"She says it didn't hurt at all. It's not permanent, unlike what happened with her brother. She lost five levels temporarily, but she can still use it. Intention matters. You pulled out his eye with violence when you were under control of that thing. If the blood is freely given, the potion allows you to choose the spell or skill. The tattoo itself, unfortunately, is permanent."

Rosetta's version, chapter 47, is blunter:

Spells and skills taken against the owner's will were much more powerful and resulted in the owner losing them permanently. My Walk on Air skill, stolen from Li Jun, was proof of that.

And Edgar's, chapter 74, is the cleanest one-line statement of the system:

"The ink Carl had from the toraline allows one to borrow spells and skills temporarily from willing subjects. It allows one to take them permanently from unwilling subjects."

docs.title: The Walk on Air revelation
docs.text:
This is the mechanic's retroactive gut-punch, and it lands in chapter 4, long before anyone explains the system. Reading the description of his new Enchanted Toe Ring of the Well-Balanced, Carl hits a line that does not make sense:

Physical Balance, Level 5. At level five, this skill imbues both the Extra Steady Balance skill and the Walk on Air Skill (already obtained.)

"Already obtained?" I asked out loud. That didn't make sense. I moved into my menu. I knew what Walk on Air did, but I didn't have that skill. It was what Li Jun…

I swallowed, suddenly feeling very, very dirty.

It was what Li Jun used when he fought.

The memory that follows is the taste of Li Jun's eye — which Shi Maria forced Carl to gouge out and eat with this very tattoo kit's stick in Book 6, telling him at the time that "you may gain some of your friend's powers, too, with the blood on the needle." Carl has had Walk on Air since that night and never noticed. Li Jun lost it permanently; his brother "got Walk on Air back, but they had to buy a book." The eye itself is unhealable.

So the system's first documented transfer was a mutilation, and the party learns the rules by working backward from it.

docs.title: Decay, re-energizing, and levels
docs.text:
Property Rule Donor cost The donor temporarily loses levels in the donated ability. Li Na lost 5; Carl lost 6 on Tripper Donor recovery The ability "heals" back over roughly four days Recipient decay The borrowed copy "slowly loses potency" and eventually disappears entirely Re-energizing A faded copy can be restored: the donor drinks the yam potion again, selects the spell, and the existing tattoo is re-charged. No new tattoo needed The tattoo Permanent, regardless of whether the ability inside it has faded Size Scales with the level of the ability. Li Na's level-13 skill "has to be pretty big" and consumed nearly a full vial; Tripper needed only a small one Theming "The tattoo doesn't have to actually be a specific image, but if it's 'properly themed,' it'll last longer" Artistry "And if it's drawn well, it could possibly be even stronger than the original version"

Katia's full statement of the sizing and quality rules, chapter 40:

"So, it depends on the level of the spell or skill. Since this is a level-13 skill, it has to be pretty big. I have to use almost all the ink in the vial, otherwise you won't get it at full strength. It took up a third of the potion already just to make the ink. We'll have just enough to do Imani's small tat next. Rosetta says the tattoo doesn't have to actually be a specific image, but if it's 'properly themed,' it'll last longer. And if it's drawn well, it could possibly be even stronger than the original version."

The system grades the artwork. Katia's chain dragon comes back rated expert quality — "Edgar said that's the second highest one can get" — which is a notable result given she had never tattooed anyone before and was only doing it because Edgar was away scouting naga territory.

docs.title: The achievement that confirms it
docs.text:
Chapter 57, after Carl kills with a borrowed ability:

New Achievement! Hey Larry, can I borrow your chainsaw?

You have utilized a borrowed skill or spell in battle. You have used this borrowed ability to kill an opponent. Oh, man. This opens up a whole new possibility of fighting styles, don't you think? Just keep those tattoos above the knee.

Reward: You've received a Platinum Have You Goddamned Figured Out How To Use This In Conjunction With the Fucking Voodoo Book Yet? Jesus Christ I Can Only Help You So Much box.

The AI is, characteristically, yelling the answer at Carl a full twenty chapters before he works it out. See The Voodoo Book Connection below.

docs.title: How it differs from the Necklace of Indelible Woe
docs.text:
The dungeon already has a device for taking someone's spell: the Necklace of Indelible Woe, which swaps one of the wearer's spells for one of a target's and works best if you kill them. Tipid's comparison in chapter 32 is the cleanest statement of what the tattoos are for:

"Rosetta's tattoos will help you share skills and spells without actually killing anyone. It just needs to brew for a little longer."

docs.title: 1. The Chain Dragon — Carl's right forearm (chapter 40)
docs.text:
• Artist: Katia, her first tattoo ever
  • Donor: Li Na, blood freely given
  • Ability: Profane Iron, level 13
  • Design: "It has to be a chain. A chain shaped like a dragon." Rated expert quality

Donut, following remotely by Voodoo book, demands design approval in all caps — "KATIA MAKE SURE YOU DRAW IT IN THE VOODOO BOOK FIRST SO I CAN APPROVE AND SUGGEST CHANGES TO THE DESIGN" — and when she finally sees it: "You're starting to look like one of those white rapper doodle notebook guys, Carl. And it's a little crooked!"

See Profane Iron for the ability itself.

docs.title: 2. The Barbed Wire Ankle Band — Imani (chapter 47)
docs.text:
• Artist: Katia
  • Donor: Carl, blood freely given (he loses 6 levels of the spell)
  • Spell: Tripper
  • Design: "a small, barbed wire symbol that circled her ankle"

This one exists because of an equipment restriction, not a tactical preference. Carl's Tripper is level 15, but it is item-based — it comes from Drakea's Enchanted Kerchief of Disorder. The plan was simply to lend Imani or Elle the bandana, "but it turned out that neither of them could wear it. Apparently fairy-class, and other magical races, were extremely limited on the sort of magical gear they could wear." The tattoo is the workaround.

A useful side-discovery: taking the bandana off revealed that Carl's own underlying Tripper had trained itself to level 7 independently of the item, which set off "its own, mind-numbing conversation with Mordecai" because the spell version has a 10-minute cooldown and the item version a five-hour one, and the two cannot be mixed.

Donut's objection is sustained and entirely about aesthetics: "I'M SORRY, BUT A PAMELA ANDERSON TATTOO IS MOST CERTAINLY A DISFIGUREMENT. I KNOW THIS IS IMPORTANT, BUT SOMETIMES I WORRY ABOUT THE COST." And: "THIS ISN'T THE 1990's. I SWEAR TO GOD IF IMANI STARTS USING THE PHRASE 'HOME SKILLET,' I'M GOING TO LOSE MY MIND."

Carl's own reaction is guilt, and he traces it all the way back: "All of this stemmed from her putting that goddamned tiara on her head way back on the very first floor."

docs.title: 3. The Cartoon Dog — Donut's right flank (chapters 74–75)
docs.text:
• Artist: Edgar, working at speed
  • Donor: A fallen cleric of the god Wepwawet who died defending the FUPA — the ability is extracted from a corpse, using Edgar and Milk's new ink rather than toraline
  • Spell: Bijanbi, originally called Heel
  • Design: "a simple, rather adorable line art tattoo of a dog," which then "lifted its leg and started to lick itself"
  • Overwritten by: Milk, with Words of Power calligraphy

This is the one with real stakes attached. The endgame plan requires Donut to have a mass-drag spell at level 8 or higher to combine into War Crime from the Nest tower, and she does not have one. Rosetta explains the substitution:

"We were going to go with Hamzo, but even with the Synergy tower's effect tied in with the bonus from the War Crime spell, it won't be a wide enough area. So we went with a Dinner Bell variant from a cleric who fell defending the FUPA. It's a spell that came from him worshiping his deity, but it appears it's going to work. Edgar extracted it properly, and with some ink tips from Milk, we don't need the toraline anymore to do what we need." She eyed Donut nervously. "It used to be called Heel, but apparently the translation makes it sound like another spell, so this season it's called Bijanbi."

Edgar picks the placement — "Best would be on her right flank, I think. Rosetta, quickly now. Shave her. I need a spot about as big as my foot" — and Donut's protest is immediate and sustained: "You will not be shaving my ass!"

The transfer works, but lands at level two, far short of the required eight. Milk fixes it by inking calligraphy over the finished tattoo:

"Not quite yet, child. We must get it temporarily above level eight. This may sting a little," Milk said. She came forward and produced a pen, dripping with black ink… She wrote some words atop the tattoo with a flourish as Donut hissed with pain. I didn't recognize the script, but when I examined the characters, the system simply said, Words of Power.

"It's a magic style that I haven't seen used often in the dungeon. The calligraphy guild teaches it."

The result overshoots the requirement badly: "The spell went up to level 15!" Milk's caveat is that it is temporary — "As the ink fades, the power will decrease, but if you practice using the spell at that high of a level, it will assist greatly with training." Edgar confirms the moving artwork is not alive: "I do not believe the art is sentient, as it hasn't been imbued with anything other than the spell itself."

Donut also picks up two achievements she does not appreciate — one calling her a traitor, one awarding "something called a stolen catalytic converter" — and the option to worship Wepwawet, who turns out to be in the Court of Nekhebit, which also unlocks worship of Odette.

docs.title: Donut's condition
docs.text:
The negotiation that gets her into the chair is one of the book's better quiet scenes. Her objection is not vanity; it is that this one will be visible:

"Carl," Donut said, looking up at me. "It's okay... You're right. It'll work. It's just... I hoped none of them would be on the outside."

"What do you mean?"

"The scars."

I closed my eyes. "Donut, if you decide to do this, it won't be a scar. It will be a badge of honor. … This is no scar, Donut. Not even close because it was your choice. And, you know what? You can still say no, and we'll find another way."

She looked at me, eyes shining. "I'll only do it if you also get a matching one. A matching ass tattoo."

I smiled. "Absolutely. But it'll have to wait a day or two."

She holds the line on placement, though — "So help me God, Carl. I will not have a tramp stamp on me" — and after the ink sets: "Now, cover it up. I don't even want to look at it. We'll get it lasered off on the next floor."

Unpaid setup

Carl's promised matching tattoo never happens within Book 7. There are no further references to it after chapter 75. The promise carries forward unresolved.

docs.title: Running Out, and the Replacement
docs.text:
The toraline supply is a hard constraint from the moment Rosetta takes it. Katia's chapter-40 accounting — "We'll have just enough to do Imani's small tat next" — turns out to be exactly right, and by chapter 47 Carl notes "we were just limited by the fact we had barely any of the vegetable left."

The bottleneck is broken in chapter 74 not by finding more toraline but by replacing it. Edgar, working with Milk, develops a different ink that does something the toraline ink could not:

"This is a different kind of tattoo," he said… "The ink Carl had from the toraline allows one to borrow spells and skills temporarily from willing subjects. It allows one to take them permanently from unwilling subjects. With help from Milk, I have learned a few new tricks. This ink is similar to that made with the toraline, but not identical, and I don't know how it'll form. It captures the essence of the fallen crawler in a unique way, and it allows you to learn one of their spells or skills."

That is the third category: the dead. Toraline ink needed a living donor, willing or not. Edgar's new ink extracts from corpses.

Edgar also notes one hard limit, chapter 78: "He's a rock monster. I can't tattoo a rock, let alone extract anything from him. Not with my tools."

docs.title: The Voodoo Book Connection
docs.text:
The AI had been screaming about this since chapter 57. Edgar works it out at the end of chapter 74:

"Rosetta was just telling Milk and myself about that book of Voodoo you have, and I believe you may be able to share skills and spells that way as well, using the same ink. It will be more temporary."

Milk confirms the distribution mechanic in chapter 75:

"He also has another book. One that all of you have. The Book of Voodoo, I believe it is called. Anything he writes in it will be given to everybody who already has the book. Best of luck to you."

Which is precisely why her parting gift is 825 ml of Stayfast Ink and an Adept's Fountain Pen — see Stayfast Ink and Adept's Fountain Pen and The Filthy Little Crawler's Book of Voodoo. The book's "nefarious purpose which will become clear later," flagged as obvious setup since Book 6, is this.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
The system has no level of its own. Four independent variables govern output:

  1. The donor's level in the ability — the copy cannot exceed the original except through exceptional artwork
  2. Consent — violent acquisition produces a more powerful and permanent copy, at the cost of permanently stripping the donor
  3. Ink volume, which scales with the ability's level and is the binding constraint all book
  4. Artistry, graded by the system, which affects both duration and raw strength — and can be layered over afterward with Words of Power calligraphy for a temporary, decaying boost

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Enchanted Prison Tattoo Kit — the physical kit
  • The Eye of the Bedlam Bride — the tattoo that started it
  • Stayfast Ink and Adept's Fountain Pen — the successor
  • The Filthy Little Crawler's Book of Voodoo
  • Profane Iron, Bijanbi, Tripper — the three transferred abilities
  • Necklace of Indelible Woe — the lethal alternative

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Tracking Tag ("The Kyryap has claimed you")
docs.text:
Open Book 9 setup — do not speculate about what the Kyryap is

This page documents only what Book 8 states on the page. The Kyryap's true nature is never explained, and this entry should not guess at it.

Quick facts

  • Bearer: Carl
  • Type: Enchanted dart / tracking tag
  • Planted: Somewhere during the Floor 11 arena climax, unnoticed until the very end of the book
  • In-game description: "Tracking Tag. The Kyryap has claimed you. Fucked = you."
  • Status: Unresolved — carries into Book 9

docs.title: The Discovery
docs.text:
In the arena's aftermath, moments after looting Emberus's Memorial Crystal, Carl notices something odd:

As I shifted, I stepped on something in the dirt... I had a dart sticking out of my leg. I hadn't felt it, and I couldn't feel it now. I didn't know when I'd received it or how. I gently pulled it out.

Tracking Tag.

The Kyryap has claimed you.

Fucked = you.

"The shit?" I asked.

Carl checks his debuffs, finds nothing else new tied to it, and — distracted by an unrelated new effect involving his Emberus ring — shelves the question entirely:

Hopefully, this Kyryap thing would be dead in the floor collapse.

Nothing further happens with the tag on the page. Book 8 ends without revisiting it.

docs.title: Earlier References to "the Kyryap" in Book 8
docs.text:
The name isn't new by the time the tag appears — Book 8 itself plants it twice earlier, both times tied to the same location: the deep interior of Club Scolopendra, reached via Oozy Form during the Floor 11 climax.

On the caprid interview show Plenty of Plenty (ch. 28-ish), a goat judge explains what Justice Light's trap unleashed onto three separate floors when it broke the in-game Nothing:

"We have no vision of what's happening on the fifteenth, and we only saw brief snippets of the ongoing slaughter and torture within Club Scolopendra. The dread Kyryap is there. As is Krakaren Prime."

Inside Club Scolopendra itself, while Carl and Penny move toward Emberus:

A level 13 snare trap sat in the middle of the hallway ahead. Something set by "the Kyryap." I deactivated the trap and hesitantly moved to the stairs.

So by the time the tracking tag turns up on Carl's own leg, "the Kyryap" has already been established within Book 8 as a named, dreaded, trap-setting presence loose in Club Scolopendra — grouped in the same breath as Krakaren Prime, another Dungeon-Boss-tier threat. The tag suggests whatever it is took a direct, personal interest in Carl specifically, sometime during the arena fight.

The brief's earlier guess was wrong — corrected here

An earlier draft of this catalog's brief guessed the Kyryap might trace back to Book 7's Floor 9 or an earlier caprid conversation. It does not. A full-text search of This Inevitable Ruin and all earlier books turns up zero hits for "Kyryap." The name originates entirely within Book 8 itself, first via the Plenty of Plenty goat panel and the Club Scolopendra snare trap, both earlier in the same book as the tracking tag payoff.

docs.title: What Is Not Known
docs.text:
• What the Kyryap actually is (species, individual, faction, or something else) — never stated
  • Why it tagged Carl specifically, or when during the arena fight it happened
  • Whether "Fucked = you" is a literal mechanical effect or purely flavor text — no debuff, stat change, or further notification is shown resulting from the tag
  • Whether the Kyryap survived the Floor 11 collapse

Treat all of the above as deliberate, unresolved Book 9 setup.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Memorial Crystal: Emberus — found in the same moment
  • Oozy Form — how Carl reached the interior of Club Scolopendra where the Kyryap's snare trap was found
  • Scolopendra — the dungeon boss whose body and club the Kyryap apparently occupies

Sourced from Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Enchanted Trollskin Shirt of Pummeling
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Carl
  • Slot: Under-armor shirt
  • Obtained: Gold Apparel Box, opened during the Floor 1 tutorial
  • Rarity note: Mordecai calls it something that would normally come from a Platinum or Legendary box — an early sign the loot system is quietly favoring Carl

docs.title: Effect
docs.text:
+7 to the Regeneration skill. All melee-based damage debuffs — Stun, Knockback, Disarm, and Out-of-Breath — are automatically negated.

The in-game description notes it will not provoke a negative reaction from trolls despite being made from troll skin — the opposite, in fact ("lady trolls might just want to haul you away").

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: The shirt grants a flat +7 to Regeneration rather than scaling with anything Carl does — the book doesn't describe a level-by-level curve for the Regeneration skill itself, only the effect at the level this item happens to grant: per Mordecai, a level-7 Regeneration means Carl is back to full health in as little as two minutes after taking damage, making it one of the best under-armor tanking pieces available this early in the game.

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text: This shirt is one of the two pieces of gear (alongside the Nightgaunt Cloak) that immediately mark Carl as having gotten unusually lucky with his very first loot boxes. Its regeneration bonus is what allows him to survive repeated brutal hits throughout Book 1 — including broken bones from punching bosses barehanded — without needing to burn through healing potions as fast as he otherwise would.

docs.title: Future Enhancements
docs.text:
Confirmed — Book 3

In Book 3 (The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook), Carl applies a Scroll of Upgrade looted from a boss box directly to this shirt, permanently adding +3 Dexterity on top of its existing Regeneration and status-negation effects.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised and Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook.

docs.title: Velma (Tserendolgor's Enchanted Flamethrower)
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Original owner: Tserendolgor ("Ren"), the Mongolian crawler and CrawlCon pet-show entrant
  • Current owner: Carl, by bequest
  • Type: Enchanted flamethrower — "part breastplate, part weapon," worn as a snap-on attachment rather than carried
  • Obtained: Chapter 59, in the collapsing stairwell chamber at El Capitolio Nacional in Havana, as Ren's dying gift

docs.title: The Weapon
docs.text:
Velma is not a hand weapon. It is an apparatus Ren wears: a breastplate with a flamethrower built into it, unsnapped and dropped as a single unit. Carl only registers what it actually is when he loots the rest of her gear afterward — "the enchanted flamethrower, which was really part breastplate, part weapon."

It is her entire fighting style. Her tank Chuluuna could turn his skin to stone specifically so he could withstand it; her teammate Khulan paralysed targets so Ren could torch them; and she can use it even inside a card battle, where Carl hears "the whoosh of Tserendolgor's flame thrower [go] off, followed by an unholy screeching and a wave of heat."

Ren did not name it. Her only comment on handing it over is: "My flamethrower is named 'Velma,' by the way. I didn't name it that."

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: No stats, levels, or mechanics are given on-page. Carl loots it in the middle of a building collapse and never gets to a saferoom to read the description before the book ends — his own inventory note lists "Velma the Flame Thrower" among the best prizes taken from that fight, alongside the Eye in the Sky scrolls, the magical tomes, Spunky Jefferson, and Quan's celestial cloak, all of which he still needs to examine properly.

docs.title: The Bequest
docs.text:
The scene is one of the book's bleakest. Ren, out of keys and out of options, refuses to fight Carl for his, tells him "You are an idiot... You're a symbol. You're the embodiment of our hope," and then starts emptying her inventory onto the floor one item at a time: rings, clothing, potions, scrolls, and a stack of the very rare Eye in the Sky scrolls.

"I'm donating to the war effort," she said.

Carl recognises the gesture immediately and it lands hard — he flashes back to Miriam Dom doing exactly the same thing in a forest clearing, and to his own mother: This is my birthday present to you. I am giving you a chance at life.

The last item out of her inventory is the Knife of Frozen Tears, a sylvan-crystal blade that is the only thing capable of permanently killing her regenerating pet, Garret. She breaks while explaining it.

Velma is later put to an unexpected use: during Shi Maria's possession of Carl's body in chapter 71, the spider examines "Ren's flamethrower" as a possible heat source for brewing tattoo ink, before rejecting it in favour of forcing Carl to cast Self-Immolation instead.

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Wand of Nighty-Night
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Carl
  • Type: Wand, 10 charges
  • Obtained: Chapter 49, from an unnamed "wand box" opened alongside a batch of other Floor 8 loot boxes
  • Effect: Casts a level-10 Sleep on a single non-boss target for five minutes

docs.title: Effect
docs.text:
A gnarled wooden wand. Its description is short and specific about its one trick:

Wand of Nighty-Night. 10 Charges.

Knocks an opponent out onto their ass. Casts a level-10 Sleep on a non-boss, single target for a period of five minutes. Opponent will reawaken if they sustain physical damage. Multiple casts compounds the effect, which is why this wand is so fancy. If you don't know what that means, ask a math nerd.

The target wakes up early if it takes physical damage, and stacking multiple casts on the same target compounds the sleep effect rather than simply refreshing it — the wand doesn't explain how, leaving it as one more "ask a math nerd" joke at the crawlers' expense.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: No level-up path is given; it is a fixed level-10 effect with a flat 10-charge pool, not a skill Carl trains.

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text:
Carl draws it, unused, at the climax of the hunt for Sister Ines Quiteria in chapter 65. She comes around the corner already glowing and charging, screaming "Sinner!" and closing too fast for any other plan:

I pulled my new Nighty-Night wand. I opened the door to reveal a glowing Sister Ines, running full tilt down the hallway directly at us, screaming "Sinner!" at the top of her lungs. She was already too close.

"Gah!" I zapped my wand, and she instantly went unconscious. She dropped and slid, coming to a stop at my feet.

The wand ends the fight before it can start — Sister Ines is executed unconscious a moment later by Louis, which is what triggers the goddess Ysalte's entrance into the realm.

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Enchanted War Gauntlet of the Exalted Grull
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Carl
  • Slot: Right hand (wrist bracer that transforms on command)
  • Obtained: Gold Brawler Box, awarded at a training guild right after The Juicer fight
  • Deity link: Grull, a war god worshipped by equine-class creatures (centaurs, tikbalang, and — after Floor 3 — the Bad Llama's kin)

docs.title: Effect
docs.text:
• +3 Strength (fist mode only)
  • +1 Dexterity
  • +2 skill levels to Iron Punch
  • +1 skill level to Powerful Strike
  • 2% chance to Stun an enemy on a successful hit
  • Does not negate Carl's bare-knuckle skill bonuses — it stacks with them rather than replacing them

The item is worn as an ordinary wrist bracer and takes about two seconds to transform into a spiked, black orcish-steel gauntlet when Carl clenches his fist or holds a weapon for more than two seconds. It reverts to bracer form when released.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
The gauntlet's own bonuses (+3 Strength, +1 Dexterity, 2% Stun chance) are flat and don't scale — but the skill levels it grants feed into skills that do scale on their own:

  • Powerful Strike: per Mordecai, each level of this skill multiplies unarmed damage — at level 3, for example, every kick or punch does three times normal damage. The gauntlet's +1 skill level is a direct, permanent boost to that multiplier.
  • Iron Punch: the book doesn't state an explicit per-level formula, but Carl's own natural Iron Punch level climbs independently through combat (observed at levels 3 and 5 elsewhere in Book 1), so the gauntlet's +2 skill levels stack on top of whatever he trains up separately.

By late Book 1, the combination of Iron Punch, Powerful Strike, natural Unarmed Combat, and Pugilism lets Carl's bare fists match a weapon as strong as Brandon's lightning maul.

docs.title: The Grull Warning
docs.text: The item carries an unusual warning: striking a worshipper of Grull with it carries a 1.5% chance of transfiguring the target into the god Grull himself. Mordecai clarifies that Grull "isn't a real god" — a rare moment where an NPC volunteers that the dungeon's "deities" are constructs rather than literal beings, at least as far as he's willing to say on the first couple of floors.

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text: This becomes Carl's signature weapon for the rest of Book 1 — the piece that finally gives his bare-knuckle build a proper offensive multiplier without abandoning his refusal to carry a traditional weapon. It's directly responsible for one of his first successful Stun procs, which lets him land a killing blow on the Frenzied Gerbil boss "Ralph."

docs.title: Book 3: Deity Summoning Rules and the Death Challenge
docs.text:
Book 3 finally lays out the dungeon's full deity-summoning mechanics, explained to Carl by Mordecai after Carl starts asking pointed questions about the gauntlet's involuntary-summon warning. There are three summon types — celestial boons (a worshipper prays and the god fights for them), indentured summonings (a mage compels a god against its will), and involuntary summonings (accidental, via a trap, spell, or item like this gauntlet). All require a physical "vessel," usually a mob of the god's own worshipper race. An involuntarily summoned deity lasts a number of seconds equal to the vessel's level plus the god's own level, and grows until it fills the chamber it's summoned into; a captured or re-triggered summon can be "stolen" from one vessel to a second one with no cooldown.

Carl deliberately exploits this on Floor 4, beating a captured mantaur neighborhood boss into vessel status and pushing it through a portal to summon Grull directly in front of a threatening city-boss mimic — turning the whole encounter into a broadcast Death Challenge gambling event, since the "god" is secretly being sponsored and piloted by the previously presumed-dead Prince Maestro. Carl survives by decoying Grull with a body double and re-summoning a second mantaur at the last possible second to yank Grull (and Maestro) out of the fight and into the abyss — winning the encounter without the gauntlet, or any weapon, landing a single blow on either monster. See Carl for the full sequence.

docs.title: Book 4: The Platinum Sharpening Stone
docs.text:
After Carl and Katia detonate the Wasteland from a hijacked ambassador's balloon, Carl's platinum quest box reward includes 5,000 gold, twenty healing scrolls, and a Platinum Sharpening Stone. Mordecai identifies it immediately as a Book-4-era enhancement item — "you're starting to get items that will enhance your existing items" — and directs Carl to apply it right away, since it carries a short shelf life. Its full description:

"Apply this to any spiked offensive weapon to receive the following buffs. Plus (2 x current level)% damage to all attacks. Plus 1 to all current stat buffs. Does not add new buffs if they do not exist. It also makes the weapon look extra oily and mean looking."

Carl rubs the stone along the gauntlet's spikes immediately (in the desert outside Hump Town, mid-mission). The spikes visibly lengthen and the gauntlet glows; the effect resolves as +1 Dexterity and +1 Strength on top of its existing bonuses, plus the scaling damage buff. This remains the gauntlet's most recent confirmed upgrade as of the end of Book 4.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised and Book 4: The Gate of the Feral Gods.

docs.title: Enchanted Xistera Extension (Head-Throwing Attachment)
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Carl
  • Slot: Xistera attachment (see Xistera)
  • Obtained: Emergency Platinum Benefactor Box, from Carl's mysterious second sponsor, The Open Intellect Pacifist Action Network, Intergalactic NFC
  • Unique item: One-of-a-kind, custom-built specifically for Carl

docs.title: Effect
docs.text:
A wicker attachment that slots onto the end of Carl's xistera, purpose-built to throw decapitated withering-spirit heads:

"Attaches to the end of a xistera. Allows for the tossing of a head. This special edition head tosser is custom made to fit decapitated love doll heads. When tossing a head of a withering spirit, the distance traveled will be greatly enhanced. (500 meters x Strength.)"

The tossed head is magically returned to Carl's inventory once the extension is removed from the xistera.

docs.title: Scaling
