docs.text: Throw distance scales directly with Carl's Strength stat, multiplied by 500 meters — at his Book-4 buffed Strength (over 100), this is enough to hurl Samantha more than fifty kilometers in a single throw.

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text: The item arrives moments before a feral demon (Slit, hunting Samantha specifically) reaches Carl's location — the sponsor's emergency, extravagantly expensive box turns out to have been built for this exact purpose. Carl uses it to hurl Samantha's head away from the fight as a distraction/weapon, luring the demon off; a summoned god intercepts and kills the demon moments later. Carl concludes the item was originally intended as a future-floor sponsor gift, rushed out early because protecting him and Donut mattered more to the sponsor than the original timeline.

docs.title: Future Enhancements
docs.text:
Pending

Not yet confirmed whether Carl uses this attachment again on Floor 6 or beyond.

Sourced from Book 4: The Gate of the Feral Gods.

docs.title: Xistera
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Carl
  • Slot: Right wrist/forearm (retracts into a bracer, compatible with the War Gauntlet)
  • Obtained: A Gold Fan Box (voted on by Carl's own viewers) after passing 1 quadrillion views
  • Type: Non-magical, mechanical throwing tool

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: A xistera is the curved wicker scoop used in the real-world sport of jai alai (Cesta Punta) — Carl only recognizes what it is and how to use it because of the random skill granted by his Earth Hobby Potion. Strapped on with two buckles, it lets him catch an item from his inventory directly into the scoop and hurl it far harder and farther than a bare throw, using a full-arm swinging motion. A pull-ring on the strap retracts the entire scoop into a metal bracer that his War Gauntlet fits over cleanly, so he can switch between throwing and punching without removing either item.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: Not an enchanted item, so it has no spell-style level curve — but its usefulness scales directly with Carl's own physical stats (Strength, and later Dexterity for accuracy) and with the Explosives Handling/Dangerous Explosives Handling skills he trains alongside it. By his own account, accuracy improves the more he practices, and small, dense projectiles (a hob-lobber bomb) work far better than irregular ammo like slingshot pellets, which the scoop can't properly grip.

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text: The xistera immediately replaces Carl's clurichaun slingshot as his primary ranged option, letting him hurl hobgoblin "hob-lobber" bombs at roughly 250 mph — turning him into a genuine ranged threat for the first time, not just a bare-knuckle brawler. Zev confirms on Carl's behalf that "no more slingshot" is now official.

docs.title: Future Enhancements
docs.text:
Not yet researched

Later books haven't been checked yet for whether this item is upgraded or replaced.

Sourced from Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario.

docs.title: Zhang's Cape of Odds
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Zhang
  • Rarity: Celestial, unique
  • Obtained: Zhang's Celestial box from the Club Vanquisher assault
  • Passive: +15% to all stats and a level-10 Dodge skill
  • Active: Roll the Dice — once an hour, one of 333 outcomes, 66 of which are bad
  • The catch that makes it Celestial: After 19 spins, you may pick the outcome instead
  • Never voluntarily used

Exact-verification note

No system description block exists for this item in Book 7. Everything below is Carl's narration on seeing the cape, quoted at length because it is the only account there is.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text: White, with the standard black, blue, red and yellow concentric circles of an archery target on the back. Zhang wears it proudly. It was first mentioned a chapter earlier, on a broadcast, simply as "Zhang's new cape with the target on the back."

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text:
It was a great, but dangerous, item. It was a unique item called Zhang's Cape of Odds. When it wasn't activated, it gave him plus 15% across the board for all his stats plus a level 10 Dodge skill. His skill in that was already 11, so it brought it to 14.

But it also came with a once-an-hour skill called Roll the Dice, which reminded me of the Wheel of Fortune game at the casino. If he activated the skill, one of 333 different outcomes could appear. Most of the outcomes were great, such as doubled strength for ten minutes. The ability to fly for an hour, etc. There were a few really epic outcomes, as well, such as Death Ray and several various summons.

But there were 66 outcomes that were bad. None of them killed him outright, and all were temporary, but there was paralysis, all stats are now 5, and something called "It's been four hours and I think it's time to call the doctor" which sounded ominous as fuck. The worst was "Summon the God Who Hates You Most."

But, and here was where the cape was especially insidious—and a true Celestial item—was that after 19 spins, you could manually pick one of the choices.

Zhang wore the cape proudly, but he said he wasn't going to actually use it unless absolutely necessary.

docs.title: Why Nobody Uses It
docs.text:
The maths is the trap. 66 of 333 is just under one in five. Reaching the 19-spin threshold that unlocks manual selection means accepting, on average, roughly four bad outcomes along the way — and one of the possible bad outcomes is Summon the God Who Hates You Most, on a floor where gods are already walking around in the open killing people.

So the cape's best feature is gated behind a gauntlet nobody in a war zone can afford to run, and its passive alone (+15% all stats, +3 effective Dodge) is already excellent. Zhang wears it and does not touch it.

Note also the stacking rule the Dodge grant demonstrates: Zhang's own Dodge was 11, and a level-10 item skill takes him to 14, not 21. Item-granted skill levels are added to the base as a partial bonus, not substituted — and consistent with the series-wide behaviour, the total stalls just short of 15.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
No level. The only progression is the spin counter, which is cumulative and one-way:

Spins State 1–18 Random. Roughly 80% good, 20% bad 19+ The wearer may choose the outcome

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Deflection — Donut's Dodge-derived passive, for comparison
  • Cloak of the Benevolent Champion — the other Celestial cloak in the party, and the opposite design: no gamble, all timers

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Area 52
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Floor: 9 ("Faction Wars")
  • Where: The forested region of the Princess Posse's territory (spot 3), on the Plains of Larracos
  • What it is: The Posse's rear-area airbase, missile battery, and saferoom
  • Named by: The Princess Posse, in the obvious joke on the Nevada original

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Area 52 is the Princess Posse's second base — not a fortress like the FUPA but a working rear installation tucked into the woods, well back from the corridors. It does three jobs.

Saferoom. It holds one of the handful of true saferooms inside Posse territory: "There are a few out in the forested region, including the one at the Area 52 base." Late in the book it is also wired into the party's doggie-door fast-travel network — an escape route teleports the party "all the way to just outside the safe room at Area 52, where we could go in and use the doggie door to go anywhere we wanted."

Missile base. The Posse's missile batteries are fired from Area 52 rather than from the front, operated remotely through a pair of controllers the system calls a Trollish Portable Control Room — a repurposed oversized video-game controller. The Sledge is one of the operators.

Airship dock. Louis's airship Party Planner docks, reloads, and repairs here between sorties; on one return Louis burns "a precious Emergency Repair scroll to speed up the repair of Party Planner" after unloading evacuated children.

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Chicken and Waffles and Upgrades (C&W&U)
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Floor: 10 ("Don't Come in Last," Book 8), Hungry Eyes Village's vendor strip
  • Cover story: An ordinary 1950s-style roadside diner with a novelty kids' menu
  • True nature: A hidden upgrade shop concealing the war mage Akuma's personal hideout
  • Staff: Darla-Dean, an imp hostess; Hickster, the shop's actual upgrade dealer — already dead by the time Carl finds the place, killed by Akuma

docs.title: First Sighting
docs.text:
The storefront is noticed well before it opens, as an unmarked space with no signage at all:

A blank storefront with no sign. The moment my eyes passed over it, a notification popped up. C&W&U Location. Illegal Modifications and More. Grand Opening Soon.

It opens on schedule, exactly as its own promotional invoice promises — "Shop opens after the third heat" — and Carl's group visits soon after on Akuma's own written invitation (see Akuma for the note and the interrogation that follows; this page covers only the location itself).

docs.title: The Diner
docs.text:
Walking in reads as an ordinary meal stop, deliberately clashing with the rest of town's aesthetic:

Entering Chicken and Waffles and Upgrades. The place was a typical diner. Even though the whole town had this aesthetic from the 1980s film Blade Runner, the restaurant gave the 1950s, at least at first glance. There was an overabundance of neon within. The jukebox was playing that "Fame" song from the movie.

Staff are flightless imps rather than the gremlins running the rest of town. The hostess, Darla-Dean, plays her cover completely straight — gaudy rockabilly wig, gum-chewing patter, menus that flip open to a "kiddie menu" secretly stocked with adult buff-food items rather than children's fare.

docs.title: The Hidden Door
docs.text:
The shop's real entrance is the jukebox itself. Playing the right track — Peter Gabriel's "Sledgehammer" — slides it aside to reveal a passage behind it:

Darla-Dean nodded. She pointed to the jukebox. I could already see that there was a hidden door and hallway past it. "Just push the music machine. Don't push too hard, though. We just opened, and we don't need it scratched."

The door reveals "a short hallway with a blinking neon sign that read 'Upgrades' with an arrow," sealing itself shut behind visitors and cutting off the diner's noise entirely.

docs.title: The Back Room
docs.text:
Beyond the hallway is a legitimate-looking upgrade counter — "a dusty counter lit with flickering yellow light," vehicle posters on every wall, and a heavy binder of laminated upgrade options — that turns out to be a crime scene. The shop's actual upgrade dealer, an imp named Hickster, is already dead on the counter, killed by Akuma, with a note left in his place. A second, genuinely hidden door sits behind a poster of yak armor, itself booby-trapped:

Attached to the door itself was a hidden disintegration trap.

Carl disarms the trap before opening the final door onto a small storeroom — Akuma's actual hideout, where the war mage is waiting. See Akuma's own page for what happens once the party is inside.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Akuma — the war mage hiding here, and the interrogation that follows
  • Hungry Eyes Village — the vendor strip C&W&U is tucked into
  • The Pineapple Cabaret — the escape route Akuma is trying to broker access to from this same back room

Sourced from Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Club Scolopendra
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: A luxury resort literally built inside the living body of the dungeon boss Scolopendra — not a separate structure
  • Floor: Physically wherever Scolopendra herself is. Established on the 18th floor across Books 6–7 (see Mechanics: Post-Crawl Economics); reached again at the Floor 11 arena climax in Book 8, mid-battle, via Oozy Form
  • Judgment call — same venue, not two: This wiki treats Book 8's "Club Scolopendra" as the same facility as the "Scolopendra Club" named in Books 6–7, rather than a coincidentally similarly-named second venue. Book 8 is simply the first time the club's actual mechanism — built inside its host boss, and therefore relocating wherever she goes — is shown on the page. See Continuity with the 18th-Floor Club below for the reasoning; treat this as an editorial judgment call, not something the text states outright in so many words.
  • Notable residents/threats found inside: Emberus, Taranis, a tortured tourist named Cerni Pinta, and traps set by the unexplained "the Kyryap" — see Tracking Tag: The Kyryap

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Club Scolopendra is one of Book 8's stranger pieces of worldbuilding, and it resolves a question the series left open since Book 6: what the "Scolopendra Club" — the members-only VIP resort holding over half the galaxy's wealth, cited since Book 6 as leverage against pulling the failsafe — actually is. Book 8 shows it directly for the first time: a functioning, staffed resort built physically inside the dungeon boss Scolopendra's own body, complete with numbered guest rooms, an automated PA system, and paying tourists — all of it apparently normal enough to run day to day, even while its host is actively rampaging through the Floor 11 arena. Carl and the sapient pig Penelope reach it mid-battle by tunneling directly into Scolopendra's flesh with Oozy Form, using her body as a shortcut to a private meeting with the gods Emberus and Taranis — see Timeline for how that confrontation plays out.

docs.title: Continuity with the 18th-Floor Club
docs.text:
Books 6 and 7 already established a "Scolopendra Club" on the 18th floor — see Mechanics: Post-Crawl Economics for that account in full, not repeated here. Nothing in that earlier material spells out what the club physically is; it's introduced only as a members-only viewing facility "programmed from orbit." Three details point toward this page's club being the same facility rather than a second, differently-located one:

  • The Book 7 evacuation warning is phrased as tied to the boss's own location, not a fixed floor: "when the Nothing drains into Scolopendra's Lair, the planetwide message reads 'It is advised all current guests at the Scolopendra Club evacuate immediately.'" The club empties out precisely when her lair is disturbed.
  • Book 8 opens with Scolopendra already loose and rampaging across the upper floors, and — in the same breath — "the 18th floor's Scolopendra Club has already gone dark, its guests forced through a gauntlet to reach safety" (see Scolopendra). A club that "goes dark" the moment its host boss physically leaves the 18th floor reads as a venue whose power/access literally depends on her presence, not an unrelated fixed building she happens to share a name with.
  • By the Floor 11 climax, a fully staffed, functioning "Club Scolopendra" is again reachable — specifically by tunneling into her body — with guests checked into numbered rooms exactly like a standing resort operation, not a hastily-built pop-up.

Treat this as this wiki's own inference connecting the dots across three books, not a fact the text states in a single sentence.

Reaching the club requires physically boring through the boss's own flesh:

I activated Oozy Form... We lost our eyes and our ears, and my vision was suddenly all around, and I could see perfectly in the dark... I aimed for the building wall and slimed my way toward it, pushing through and around and over strange, giant, pulsing organs.

Entering Club Scolopendra.

docs.title: A Working Resort, Mid-Rampage
docs.text:
Despite being lodged inside a berserk Level 500 dungeon boss, the club continues operating on autopilot, complete with an automated, cheerfully oblivious PA announcer smoothing over the building's own violent shaking:

Automated resort announcement, Book 8

"Honored guests, not to worry. That is nothing but Scolopendra settling as she slumbers. Rest assured such movements are perfectly natural, and the resort's centrifugal dampeners are more than up to the task of keeping you safe."

The interior is a long hallway of numbered guest doors, some broken open onto "opulent, bigger-on-the-inside rooms," soaked in blaster scoring, spell fire, and a sticky orange webbing that isn't otherwise explained. Deity auras outside are blocked for anyone standing inside the club's walls — Carl briefly gains an Immune to Sheol-based attacks buff purely from Emberus's proximity once inside — though the club's protections do not extend to Scolopendra's own nine-tier attacks, which reach guests and intruders alike regardless of location. See Mechanics: Scolopendra's Nine-Tier Attack for that mechanic in general.

docs.title: Cerni Pinta and the Tortured Tourists
docs.text:
The club's darker side surfaces immediately: hanging in the hallway webbing is a tortured guest, a quill-covered alien named Cerni Pinta, examined as:

Cerni Pinta. Non-Player Tourist. Guest of Club Scolopendra, and she is currently checked into room #422 along with her three husbands. Pinta is a type of alien called a bristle. She is the vice president of Nova Client Services, LTD., a notorious medical collections agency whose primary client is the Viceroy system.

She begs Carl to kill her outright rather than let whatever tortured her return. He can't bring himself to, and the choice is taken out of his hands moments later: Scolopendra's second nine-tier attack (Sin of Consumption) fires while they're still talking, and Pinta rolls red where Carl and Penny both roll green — worms burst from her body and she is devoured on the spot. See Scolopendra for the attack itself.

docs.title: "The Kyryap"
docs.text:
Twice within the club, the party encounters evidence of a named, dreaded presence loose in the building well before Carl himself is later marked by it: a caprid news panel elsewhere in the book places "the dread Kyryap" inside Club Scolopendra in the same breath as Krakaren Prime, and Carl personally disarms a snare trap here credited to the same name:

A level 13 snare trap sat in the middle of the hallway ahead. Something set by "the Kyryap." I deactivated the trap and hesitantly moved to the stairs.

Nothing more is learned about the Kyryap here or anywhere else in the book — see Tracking Tag: The Kyryap for the full, deliberately unresolved thread, including Carl's own tracking tag found on his leg after the arena fight. This page should not be treated as resolving that mystery; it only confirms Club Scolopendra as the place the Kyryap is first established as active in Book 8.

docs.title: Status After the Battle
docs.text:
When Scolopendra is transformed into a Level 1 crawler by the enriched pet biscuit mix-up, the club and everyone inside it "blinked out" instantly — Prime Minister Victory's epilogue account confirms the guests died but then regenerated, exactly as tourists elsewhere in the dungeon always have, implying the club exists inside some kind of protected dimensional space of its own rather than the ordinary playing field:

"The moment that transformation happened, all the non-protected entities within the club had blinked out. The guests had also all died, but they had regenerated, just like always. She was waiting to hear how that was possible. Likely some sort of dimensional space."

Whether the club (or Scolopendra's body itself) persists in any form after Book 8 is not addressed.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Scolopendra — the dungeon boss whose body hosts this resort
  • Tracking Tag: The Kyryap — the unresolved threat first established here
  • Mechanics: Post-Crawl Economics — the other, unrelated "Scolopendra Club" on the 18th floor
  • Timeline — the arena battle this detour happens during

Sourced from Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Club Vanquisher
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Members-only social club, Over City floors — the Desperado Club's rival
  • Access: Mutually exclusive with Desperado Club membership — holding one pass generally blocks the other

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Club Vanquisher is the Desperado Club's upscale counterpart. For four books it exists as a single line of Mordecai's, drawn as a contrast while he walks Carl and Donut into the Desperado Club itself; the interior isn't shown until Floor 8 (see below):

"There are two main clubs in the Over City. The Desperado Club and Club Vanquisher. Generally, once you have access to one, you're not allowed in the other. This one is easier to get into. Club Vanquisher is more like a country club where old clerics sit on leather chairs and smoke pipes and occasionally tell racist jokes."

Neither Carl nor Donut visits it in Book 2, and for three books afterward everything known about it is contained in that single comparison — a genteel, clergy-heavy counterpoint to the Desperado Club's Vegas-meets-Mardi-Gras atmosphere. Access to it is also implicitly why the Desperado Pass locks a crawler out of Cleric and Paladin classes (see Desperado Club: Overview) — those "goody-two-shoes" classes appear to be Club Vanquisher's natural clientele instead.

docs.title: Inside, at Last (Book 6)
docs.text:
Floor 8 is where the book finally walks through the door. Carl goes in cold — "The cookbook held precious little about Club Vanquisher… I was going in blind" — having gained access not through a pass but through his worship of Emberus, via the temple entrance inside the Colón Cemetery. Havana's second entrance is in the Kuraokami temple on the grounds of the Iglesia de Jesús de Miramar.

The greeting sets the tone:

Entering Club Vanquisher. Members Only.

Heathens will find no solace here.

The vestibule is small and clean, with a stained-glass door showing a winged angel rising toward an inverted tree. The Ares-worshipping ram-headed guards insist the figure is Hellik; it is in fact Taranis, Hellik's brother.

The lobby reads, unexpectedly, as "the lobby of a ski lodge": a brick fireplace, leather chairs, dwarves playing chess and served by an elf waitress, and trophy monster heads on the walls including a giant black dragon's. "A dozen stairwells led up and down to different places." Mantaur guards work the room, and security is on heightened alert "especially since the caprid incident" — Prepotente's hellspawn familiar attacking clerics in the Pandinus branch on Floor 5.

The upper level holds a market called Comforting Supplies, a guild hallway, a jeweller ("Blessed Sun Enchantments," one visit per day for members), and the fairy receptionist Yasmine, a level-75 Wisp with the title Secretary of the Club Vanquisher Temple Portal.

docs.title: The Emberus High Temple of the Ending Sun
docs.text:
The club's marquee venue, and the closest thing Carl has to a church.

Entering the Emberus High Temple of the Ending Sun.

Welcome home, Initiate.

You are protected in this place.

"We stood upon the sun." There is no roof and no walls except the one the entry door sits in; the sky is black and the floor is a burning field of fire that is warm rather than painful. Perhaps two dozen worshippers lie prostrate toward a distant glow. A marble fountain and a charred tree stump rise out of the fire for a foot-washing ritual.

Its clergy are Pater Coal, a Hobbledehoy High Cleric Supreme of Emberus (level 101), and the openly hostile Ares cleric Potsy. Carl, admitted only as a limited-access worshipper, is treated for slugpox here, learns of the murdered god Geyrun, and buys a ring he would rather nobody knew about. The temple recurs across the book, and Carl's promotion to Devotee — the ceiling rank for a non-Cleric — is an Emberus rank earned in its service. See Deity Mechanics.

Sourced from Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario, and Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Colón Cemetery / The Temple of Yemaya
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Floor: 8 ("The Ghosts of Earth") — see Level 8
  • Region: Havana, Cuba
  • System designation: Medium Ghommid Settlement — corrupted, and unclaimable until the corruption is removed
  • Renamed: Club Vanquisher Entrance Temple, The Temple of Yemaya, after Carl repairs Yemaya's shrine
  • Contains: A Club Vanquisher entrance, and a saferoom pub called The Yellow Zone

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The real Colón Cemetery is, as Paz Lo puts it, "one of the largest cemeteries in Latin America… it's like a park filled with monuments." The dungeon's version is walled behind a black spiked fence and a gothic archway, permanently fogged, with a church hidden at its centre — and the system tags it not as terrain but as a settlement:

Entering Medium Ghommid Settlement.

Warning! This town has been corrupted. You may not claim or repopulate the town until the rot has been eradicated.

The residents are ghommids, creatures that settle "where the veil is thin. Like cemeteries." Entering triggers the quest Pueblo de los Olvidados — the village of the forgotten.

docs.title: The Corruption
docs.text:
The settlement's rot has a cause with a name: the orisha Asojano, Lord of Smallpox, squatting in the cemetery and sickening its population. The ghommids are hostile on arrival because they are dying, not because they are malicious — a distinction the floor's design does very little to make obvious.

Notable ghommids include Kipper, a level-30 unsettled ghommid, and Skylar Spinach, a donkey-headed "Two-Thirds of an Enraged Ghommid Splitter" who later becomes one of Carl's totem cards (see Splitters).

docs.title: The Thorn Room
docs.text:
At the settlement's heart is a Celestial Thorn Room holding seven broken shrines — Ogun, Legba, Shango, Oshun, Asojano, Inle, and Yemaya — of which exactly one may be repaired. Each god is present as a ghost, whispering at the crawler to choose theirs.

Repairing Asojano's shrine would cure the ghommids and win the quest outright, at the price of returning a god the pantheon considers "too much of a dangerous asshole to let back into the Halls." Acting on a private warning from Katia, Carl repairs Yemaya's instead. The quest is won anyway, and the cost lands on other people: Ogun, passed over, kills Anton Lopez outright and lays a permanent unhealable smite on Paz Lo.

docs.title: The Temple of Yemaya
docs.text:
The liberation sequence rewrites the location wholesale:

Medium Ghommid Settlement has been liberated.

The surviving ghommids have been cured.

Entering Club Vanquisher Entrance Temple, The Temple of Yemaya.

Welcome, Friend of Yemaya.

System Message. The Goddess Yemaya has re-ascended. She is welcomed into the family by all.

Afterward the six unrepaired shrines vanish, leaving only Yemaya's. The ground becomes tiled and threaded with blue tributary fountains, the tombs convert into shops, and the surviving ghommids turn friendly and settle in as NPC residents. Yemaya herself appears as a level-250 two-tailed mermaid goddess — see Deity Mechanics for the temple-appearance rule that makes a goddess standing in her own temple so dangerous.

docs.title: The Yellow Zone
docs.text: The cemetery's saferoom is "a crumbling, marble, gothic-style crypt with a little neon sign hanging on it that read 'The Yellow Zone.'" The book never takes the reader inside — the pub exists in the text as an exterior and a name only.

docs.title: Club Vanquisher
docs.text:
The temple at the cemetery's centre doubles as one of Cuba's two Club Vanquisher entrances, which is how Carl — a worshipper of Emberus rather than a Desperado Club regular — gets access to the rival club at all. The other Havana entrance sits in the Kuraokami temple on the grounds of the Iglesia de Jesús de Miramar.

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Dallas County, Iowa (on the Florida Keys)
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Floor: 8 ("The Ghosts of Earth"), phase two — see Level 8
  • What it is: A slab of Iowa farmland physically transplanted onto Monroe County, Florida by a placement glitch
  • System designation: Entering Dallas County, Iowa — while standing in the Keys
  • Notable features: A commercial farm, a trailer park, a turkey barn, and Carl's father's trailer, spliced in from a different broadcast season

docs.title: The Glitch
docs.text:
Phase two is supposed to offer each squad leader three destinations: "One chosen by us, one by the AI, and one randomly selected spot." The transfer misfires dungeon-wide. Zev's account:

"You should have only received three choices for a new location… You received four, and we don't know why… Some crawlers had four choices. Some only had one. A few didn't have any at all, and one squad leader had the whole globe to choose and dropped herself into the middle of the ocean for some reason."

Donut, given four options, picks Miami — and the party lands in a dark Victorian mini-mansion in the Florida Keys, tagged by the system as Monroe County, Florida. Then the system pauses ("Please wait" / "Thank you for your patience"), a small earthquake moves the key marker, and a chunk of Iowa terrain is dropped bodily onto the map. Katia's squad suffers the same class of error, choosing Ukraine and arriving in a Ukraine/Vietnam hybrid with its key in Da Nang.

docs.title: The Mound
docs.text:
What lands is a mesa of Iowa farmland about 700 feet high, surrounded by ocean and already eroding into it. It has to be climbed: Carl scales the cliff face and picks up an achievement ("Cliffhanger") for it. Cross the ridge and the system announces Entering Dallas County, Iowa, and it is abruptly winter — snow, Christmas, and Midwest farmland, sitting on top of a subtropical island chain.

The terrain on top:

"a street dotted with farm-style houses followed by a sparse trailer park. Immediately to our left was half of a commercial farm. A few large buildings dotted the property along with a corrugated silo that stood precariously close to the edge."

docs.title: The turkey barn
docs.text: "A large, corrugated building… looked like an airplane hangar, but much longer," packed wall to wall with level-5 turkeys. They turn hostile and then undead — the "zombie turkey barn" — and the infection spreads outward into the rest of the farm's animals. Carl's extinction sigil charm normally pacifies turkeys (they are the natural predators of a lizard species he wiped out on Floor 4), but the effect is negated the moment a boss-tier deckmaster is involved. The sequence's reward is the turkey-shaped Gold Gobble box.

docs.title: The trailer park
docs.text: Site of a deckmaster fight against a hydra that summons the giant Christmas cat Jola. It is also where Carl starts recognizing the dead: real people from his own life, fed into the dungeon's monster roster — his landlord, a friend, possibly his own former neighbours.

docs.title: Carl's father's trailer
docs.text:
A roughly twenty-foot rectangle of summer sitting inside the snow — dry grass, green leaves, untouched by the Christmas weather around it. Carl works out what he is looking at immediately:

"This yard and trailer is not from Christmas. They are cheating. This little spot is from a different time… It's spliced in."

The system confirms it with three stacked warnings: a forced 42-minute-30-second delay before the fight commences, "This area exists in a different time instance than the remainder of this floor," and "Physical interactions in this area act differently than other locations on this floor." The seam is visible — a bicycle, a fence, and a minivan are all cut cleanly at the boundary.

Inside the pocket: Carl's father's 1965 Harley-Davidson FLH Electra Glide Panhead (which still runs, and which Carl later rides to the Shepherd's House), a Ford truck, a shed, and a flower garden planted in unfamiliar, feminine handwriting — evidence of a woman who lived there after Carl left. Vehicles looted here file into a dedicated "Shitty Transportation Items" inventory category.

This is where Carl watches his father die of a morphine overdose administered by his stepmother Tami-Lynn, and where he learns he has a six-year-old half-brother, Asher. The book never names his father.

docs.title: Nine Deckmasters
docs.text:
The mound is a gauntlet: Carl and Donut beat nine deckmasters in sequence across it, ending with the Reminiscence Hydra of Malicious Compliance — built from the faces of everyone they have known, Asher's included, and the first boss the system AI ever built from nothing. Killing it wins the phase key and raises Carl to Devotee.

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Desperado Club
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Cross-instance nightclub, bazaar, and members-only social venue — not a faction or organization; nobody in the text is shown running it or acting on its behalf
  • Access: Via a Desperado Pass neck tattoo, awarded from certain loot boxes (or, for at least one NPC, promised as payment for a job)
  • Structure: Exists as a shared instance across every Over City location — enter through any local branch, and you're in the same room as crawlers and NPCs from anywhere on the floor. Confirmed (Book 3) to also maintain entrances on non-Over-City floors like the Iron Tangle, so it isn't strictly limited to Over City levels
  • Rival club: Club Vanquisher — access to one generally excludes the other
  • Notable staff: Clarabelle (Crocodilian bouncer), Quint (Half-Djinn pharmacist)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
First introduced in Book 1 as a mysterious tattoo with no explained purpose, the Desperado Club turns out to be a massive, cross-instance nightclub/bazaar complex, physically marked by a tower with a rotating knife sign reading "So fun it hurts" and "Members only section + public pub." Per Mordecai, it's the wilder of the Over City's two major clubs: "This place is like your Las Vegas Strip mixed in with Mardi Gras and the discos of the 1970s," in contrast to Club Vanquisher — "more like a country club where old clerics sit on leather chairs and smoke pipes."

The club won't admit "goody-two-shoes" crawlers — holding a Desperado Pass locks a crawler out of Cleric, Paladin, and several Monk classes entirely during race/class selection. Mordecai repeatedly warns Carl and Donut never to go without an escort.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
• Public pub (first room) — open to anyone, no pass required, always busy
  • Main room — members-only; a 200-person dance floor with a retro-futuristic, Blade Runner-style aesthetic, populated mostly by disposable "bot" NPCs that vanish the instant a real crawler or NPC takes their place, plus a handful of roaming Elites
  • Bitches / Penis Parade — brothels (female- and male-clientele respectively); crawlers are discouraged from visiting either, for safety and for the on-air ridicule that follows
  • Jobs — a quest board, mostly NPC assassination and theft contracts
  • The Silk Road — a marketplace mirrored on the floor below, selling higher-end magical goods than general stores, including a booth run by the hobgoblin explosives dealer Pustule
  • Guild-O-Rama — houses several rogue-themed guild rooms (an explosives guild among them)
  • Playroom — a familiars/pets area (no pets otherwise allowed inside); safety not guaranteed
  • Casino — not yet open on Floor 3; features a High Roller's Roulette Table and a Wheel of Fortune, playable only with non-transferable comp chips won as loot
  • The Hunting Grounds — a staircase down, accessible only once a crawler reaches Floor 6
  • Casino — open by Floor 4, with a working High Roller's Roulette Table and Larracos card tables, playable with non-transferable comp chips

docs.title: Scale and Access (Book 3)
docs.text: The club's physical scale varies enormously by branch — the Iron Tangle's Station-131 location is noticeably smaller and quieter than the Over City flagship, staffed by a skeleton crew including Astrid, a Bloodlust Sprite assistant manager (Level 125). Entrances are tied to specific station numbers ending in 1 (members-only, guarded) versus 9 (public pub only) along a given line — a pattern crawlers use to predict which stops are worth a detour. Every branch maintains its own private security/bodyguard system regardless of scale; hired cretin bodyguards (see Species) can be purchased outright by a patron to protect a specific person for the duration of a visit, as Donut's party does at Station 131.

docs.title: The Recruitment Pipeline (Miss Quill Connection)
docs.text:
The club has a genuinely dark undercurrent that ties directly into Book 2's main quest. Local elves recruit women from other settlements with the promise of club jobs — bar and brothel work — and the rumor that working there is a path toward eventually descending through the Hunting Grounds to safety. It's a lie: recruits are instead delivered to Remex, Miss Quill's undead husband, who "twists" them. Most die outright or become the krasue terrorizing the settlement; a rare few, like the dying woman Burgundy, survive as day-human, night-monster hybrids. This recruitment pipeline is the actual answer behind The Sex Workers Who Fell from the Heavens quest — the dead women found in the alleys every morning are club recruits who didn't survive Remex's transformation.

Separately, a member of the 201st Security Group reveals he was sent to assassinate a target specifically as payment for a promised Desperado Club membership — club access is valuable enough in-world to be traded as a reward for contract killing.

docs.title: Floor 6 (Book 5)
docs.text: Carl's opening-day raid on Zockau, Floor 6's capital city — blocking off the club's entrance bar mid-battle — strands a group of hunters inside the Zockau branch's Hunting Grounds level, unable to leave until the mayor (a mantis, eventually revealed to be Vrah) approves rebuilding the entrance. Management responds by permanently segregating the two groups: each floor of the dungeon a crawler has reached maps to a corresponding physical floor inside the club (crawlers enter and exit on their own floor; hunters are confined to theirs), with no more mixing between them. A concealed stairwell — reached by removing the tank lid of a toilet in the last stall of the women's restroom and pulling a hidden latch — connects the floors for anyone willing to sneak past the rule, which is how Carl and Donut reach the Hunting Grounds level directly to meet with changeling contacts hiding there. That level includes its own restaurant, casino, "Silk Pavilion" market, and skill-guild hallway, staffed by assistant manager Astrid (see Bloodlust Sprite), the same rank/role Book 3 introduces at the Iron Tangle's Station-131 branch.

docs.title: Notable Incidents
docs.text:
• Lucia Mar's rampage: banned from the club after her two rottweilers kill two attendants and another patron's pet in the playroom; she then freezes the entire room with an unexpectedly powerful spell, robs the bar, and kills an elite gnoll — all in one visit. The playroom closes for a week afterward, and the System AI is later implied to be deliberately buffing enemy difficulty in response to "high performers" like her getting too strong too fast.
  • The wild magic burst evacuation: during the climax of The Fools Who Broke the Glass, the club's back room — the safest nearby evacuation point — is sealed off by Borant to insulate the venue from the incoming blast, forcing Carl to reroute everyone without club access to a different stairwell entirely.

docs.title: Book 8: Shadow Mimic Infestation
docs.text:
By Book 8, the club is under new management — Hamed, the Night Wyrm, husband of the late Astrid, banning all crawlers on taking over (see Dungeon Factions). The casino itself has been rebuilt more ornately than before, with a new Wheel of Fortune croupier standing in for the previous one, Tito.

That croupier, "Mitch," turns out to be an Adolescent Shadow Mimic — see Species: Shadow Mimics — running a long-planned ambush with the casino's entire furniture set (tables, chairs, chandeliers, slot machines) revealed as more mimics the moment the trap springs. See Mitch for the fight itself.

The aftermath permanently changes the club's status:

Mordecai, Book 8

"If the Desperado Club is infested, you guys can't go back. Those things are almost impossible to root out. The whole place will need to be fumigated. They have a special ability to avoid most detection spells. They're like one of Carl's level 15 traps. All but invisible. You should all devise safe words and quiz each other every day from now on. They can mimic crawlers, and the system will label them as such until you discover them."

The club is left effectively off-limits going forward: even setting aside Hamed's standing ban on crawlers, the party itself has no safe way back in until (if ever) the infestation is cleared. Several of Hamed's own stripper-band employees — Splash Zone, Gluteus Maxx, and Doctor Bones — go missing inside the club on an errand to see Hamed shortly before the ambush and cannot be reached afterward; the book does not resolve whether they are casualties of the same infestation or a separate incident. Whether Hamed's own leadership knew about the mimics in advance is not addressed.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised, Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario, Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook, Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade, and Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: El Capitolio Nacional de Cuba
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Floor: 8 ("The Ghosts of Earth") — see Level 8
  • Region: Havana, Cuba — Carl and Donut's phase-one and phase-three region
  • Role: The floor's starting chamber, and one of the region's two stairwells
  • Fate: Its stairwell doorway is destroyed during phase three, sealing the exit permanently; the building itself collapses shortly afterward

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Every crawler on Floor 8 begins inside "a large structure within your starting area." In Cuba, that structure is the historic capitol building in downtown Havana. The system announces it plainly — "Entering El Capitolio Nacional de Cuba" — and the room Carl and Donut step into is a marble rotunda deliberately reminiscent of the US Capitol: blue and magenta floor tiles running in both directions, enormous arched windows at regular intervals, a curved half-pipe ceiling tiled in relieved bronze squares, and a round divot at the centre opening into an enormous cupola. The light comes from what look like street lamps — warm and yellow, and entirely wrong for the hour.

Two details establish the floor's rules immediately. The windows show nothing on the minimap, because the outside world hasn't been explored yet. And the brass lamps are hung with red and green ribbon: it is December 10th, and the Earth being replayed around them is decorated for a Christmas that already happened.

docs.title: As a Stairwell
docs.text:
The Capitolio holds one of the region's two stairwells — the one Carl and Donut are generated beside, and therefore the one their phase-two key will be cut for. Several of the building's doors are locked, and the stairwell itself needs a key that cannot be obtained until phase two begins.

Carl treats the building as a fortification from the first week, ringing the exit with alarm traps and teleport traps long before there is anything to defend it against. That groundwork is what makes the phase-three fight survivable.

docs.title: The Battle for the Keys
docs.text:
Phase three drops keyless squads directly onto keyholders' doorsteps, which makes the Capitolio a killing floor by design. The battle that follows runs across several chapters and involves the rival crawlers Quan Ch and Tserendolgor ("Ren"):

  • Quan Ch strips the phase keys from Sister Ines and then from Donut before Carl and Donut ambush and kill him with teleport traps smuggled inside Samantha, recovering both.
  • A Mongolian death worm summoned mid-fight cracks the ceiling and tears open the structure.
  • The stairwell doorway is destroyed, and the system's notice is final: "The Stairwell Exit at El Capitolio Nacional de Cuba has been rendered inaccessible. All available keys through this exit have been destroyed." See Stairwell Chambers for why the doorway can be destroyed when the stairwell itself cannot.
  • Tserendolgor, refusing to fight Donut for the last remaining key, hands Carl her gear and her pet Garret and detonates a bomb rather than let the space be used — denying the building to everyone.

Carl flees as the Capitolio crumbles behind him. With its exit gone, the region's other stairwell — at the Iglesia de Jesús de Miramar — becomes the only way off the planet, which is what forces the endgame plan.

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: The FOCSA Building
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Floor: 8 ("The Ghosts of Earth") — see Level 8
  • Region: Havana, Cuba
  • Shape: Green and tan, Y-shaped, 32 storeys of regular residences plus penthouses and a roof
  • Role: Site of Book 6's final battle, and of the deaths of Sister Ines and the goddess Ysalte
  • Fate: Destroyed floor by floor during the fight

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Havana's FOCSA tower becomes the endgame's fixed point for a simple reason: during the planet-wide Demon Eviction, the demons converge on it "as if they knew their best chance at getting home was there." What roosts on top of it is the demon prince Amayon, riding the city boss Madre de Aguas — a snake reared vertical like a spire, pouring fire into the sky at the centre of a tornado of bird and bat demons, visible from across the city.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
The tower is a genuine mixed-use building, replayed intact from the Earth memory:

  • Ground floor — an open-air shopping mall wrapping the perimeter: grocery stores, electronics shops, bakeries, all of it populated by memory ghosts going about a December day they have no idea is being watched.
  • Residential lobby — elevators and a stairwell leading up.
  • Floors up to 32 — ordinary apartments. The 32nd is "the top floor of the regular residences. Everything above here was through a separate stairwell and consisted of expensive, penthouse apartments."
  • Penthouses and roof — reached by a separate service stairwell.

The Y-shaped floor plan matters in the fight: three wings radiating from a core means no single sightline covers the building, and collapsing one wing does not immediately drop the others.

docs.title: The Final Battle
docs.text:
The battle spans the roof and works its way down through collapsing floors.

  • Louis kills Sister Ines, which summons her divine patron Ysalte, a goddess native to Larracos and known as "The Downward Spiral."
  • Amayon is freed from the Madre de Aguas shell but remains enslaved to Ysalte, who must hold control against a ten-minute timer or lose him.
  • In the last T'Ghee card battle of the book, Paz Lo — Ysalte's own stolen totem — kills the goddess with Katia's reused Bolt of Ophiotaurus and his own self-destruct. See Deity Mechanics: gods are invulnerable on this floor except to their own summoned totems.
  • Carl teleports himself inside Samantha to drive his health down and trigger The Martyr's Path, bathing the tower and Amayon in Sheol Fire — which, per the cookbook's own warning, makes a demon exponentially stronger. That is the point.
  • Donut ends the sequence stranded on "maybe the 25th or 26th floor" amid falling girders as the building comes apart around her.
  • Escaping the wreckage, a misfired Golden Combo fuses Carl with the boss Shi Maria, who takes control of his body long enough to tattoo the Eye of the Bedlam Bride into his chest.

By the time Amayon casts his homecoming spell, the tower is effectively gone.

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Fort Freedom
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Floor: 6 ("The Hunting Grounds")
  • Formerly: The Naiad royal river palace
  • Occupied by: The Naiad Confederacy (see Naiad), then squatted by Claude Sludgington the Fourth in its throne room
  • Liberated by: Tsarina Signet's forces, with Carl and Donut's help — Part One of the Vengeance of the Daughter quest

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Fort Freedom is the submerged former seat of Naiad royal power — a decaying castle standing about a quarter-mile offshore in the river dividing Floor 6's human and High Elf territories, its ramparts crumbling and its stained-glass windows shot through with holes. The Confederacy that seized it generations earlier never bothered to maintain the place, leaving huge sections flooded and abandoned; by the time of Book 5, its own throne room has been quietly overtaken by an unrelated boss monster (see Claude Sludgington the Fourth) that the Confederacy's remaining leadership either couldn't or wouldn't deal with.

docs.title: The Assault
docs.text: Signet's forces — a mixed group of bush elves, were-castors, pixies, a shell-mage tortoise (Edgar), and paper "blood and ink elemental" tattoo-warriors summoned via her Ink Marauder spell — stage a coordinated amphibious assault: Carl distracts the castle's guards by launching the possessed head Samantha into the water as a loud, indestructible decoy, drawing the defenders toward the front gate while Signet's real strike team slips in from the undefended air/water approach. The castle falls with minimal resistance once its guards are lured away, but the operation costs the lives of Nadine and Clint (see Were-castor) when Claude Sludgington is accidentally summoned into the middle of the fight.

docs.title: Aftermath
docs.text:
With the Confederacy defeated, Signet declines to rule in her murdered mother's place, citing her own curse (water will not touch her skin). The quest immediately pivots — see Timeline — toward Signet's real target, her half-sister Queen Imogen.

Sourced from Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: Gasworks Screw Factory, Steel Mill, and Doll Workshop
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Floor: 10 ("Don't Come in Last," Book 8) — Heat 5's track
  • Full name: "Gasworks Screw Factory, Steel Mill, and Doll Workshop That Is Totally Not a Front for Anything Else"
  • Type: A single combined industrial track, run as one connected factory building rather than several separate locations
  • Notable events: Dong Quixote and Corcunda's reunion and double death fighting Grull

docs.title: One Building, Not Several
docs.text:
Despite the four-part name, the text is explicit that this is one track through one dilapidated multistory building, not a cluster of separate locations — the full name appears as a single neon sign, with its own punchline underneath:

A flickering neon sign hung from the top of the dilapidated multistory building. It read, "Gasworks Screw Factory, Steel Mill, and Doll Workshop." And under it, a smaller sign read, "There's no cocaine in here." Sparks flew from the sign.

The system's pre-race announcement confirms the combined, single-track nature and its brutal physical rules:

Track: Gasworks Screw Factory, Steel Mill, and Doll Workshop That Is Totally Not a Front for Anything Else. This track will require vertical climb, inverted racing, and gap coverage of up to 100 meters. There will be multiple paths to the exit.

Tasks required to complete: Don't get squished. Don't get melted. Don't get screwed.

Environment: Extreme heat. Containment field will protect from heat and molten metal.

Hazards: Containment theft is now enabled. If your containment touches another containment for more than 5 seconds, you may lose it upon separation.

Racers pass through a sequence of connected rooms inside the same structure: a receiving bay piled with metal balls, a conveyor-belt jump room, a molten-vat steel-mill chamber, a doll-packing room, an inverted ceiling-track section flooded with molten metal, and a final crate room leading to the exit. All paths are only wide enough for two vehicles at a time, and the track is shared simultaneously with eleven other heats.

docs.title: The Creepy Dolls
docs.text:
The steel mill's own manufacturing accident is the track's other running joke and its real hazard. The factory's knocker workforce (see Species once a dedicated Knocker page exists) had been using the mill to cook a recreational drug nicknamed "Toddler Cocaine" ("Daddy's Little Snow Drops"); casting the elemental-summoning spell needed to generate the track's intended boss monsters let some of that same drug-infused magic leak into the factory's inventory of Barbie/Bratz/G.I.-Joe-style dolls sitting nearby:

Toot-Toot doll. Level 12 Grape-flavored Cocaine Elemental.

So, the dolls were a mistake. In preparing to defend their factory, the knockers got a little enthusiastic with the elemental magic. The metal frames of these dolls are infused with their special blend, and when they cast the magic spell in the steel mill to create the elemental boss monsters you'll probably face in a few minutes, some of that magic accidentally leaked. And now these creepy little fuckers are everywhere.

Named doll elementals include Toot-Toot, Sally Speedball, and Belushi — animate, corrosive, shield-piercing toys roaming a sealed room that only opens once racers break its containment.

docs.title: Dong Quixote and Corcunda's Reunion
docs.text:
The track is also where the floor's longest-running NPC subplot resolves. Corky, half of the mantaur Corcunda split by a Split Personality spell, is thrown into this same factory when the Lady Dominators' car crashes through a trap floor into the doll room; his other half, Porky, is recovered separately from the hidden Stage Performance Guild inside the Lollipop. The fleshmancer Grigori the Placid performs the reunion mid-race — both halves unzipped from their containment gimp suits, heads sealed in plastic wrap, organs floated in place by spell — while the truck itself races upside-down along the track's inverted ceiling section. Dong Quixote holds the two halves together bodily throughout, repeating "I have you... I got you" until their separate health bars merge into one and the name Corcunda reappears whole.

Reunification comes with a fatal cost: while split, one half of Corcunda had quietly kept worshipping Grull, and the god arrives the instant the reunion completes to punish the whole for the apostasy of the half that raced for a rival team:

System Message: Grull has entered the realm.

Corcunda accepts the smite willingly rather than let Grull turn on the truck, and Dong Quixote — who had kept a long-hidden lance since the earliest days of the floor — charges the war god at his side rather than be parted from him again:

"It's been a long time since I've tilted a giant."

Both die in the charge, screwed to death by Donut's Big-Ass Magnet spell dragging thousands of loose factory screws through them and into Grull, who is unharmed (gods on this floor cannot be killed by crawlers) but departs satisfied: "A good death... A good death indeed." Dong Quixote's own farewell to the party — "Goodbye, Carl. Goodbye, Princess Donut... it was my pleasure to serve with them" — closes out one of Floor 10's most sincere relationships. See Corcunda and Grigori the Placid for both NPCs' own character arcs in full rather than duplicated here.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Corcunda — the reunited mantaur's own page
  • Grigori the Placid — the fleshmancer who performs the reunion
  • The Heats — Floor 10's Race Ruleset

Sourced from Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: High Elf Castle
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Floor: 6 ("The Hunting Grounds"), extreme southeast corner of the map, against a rocky bluff
  • Nickname: "The Sugar Cube" (per Elle McGibbons)
  • Ruler: Queen Imogen of the High Elves
  • Notable event: Site of the Butcher's Masquerade and the book's climactic battle

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The High Elf castle is a stark, roughly cubic structure — about 150 meters to a side, seven visible stories plus several sub-basement levels — built from a single, living white wood carved all over with a fine acorn pattern, giving it the look of white marble or stone from a distance. Donut calls it ugly on sight, expecting elven architecture to favor waterfalls and flowing lines; instead it reads as a "Bauhaus art installation blown up to ridiculous proportions." Four thin towers stand at each corner, each housing a small garrison of magic-wielding guards, reachable only from the third floor (or the very top). An empty moat, drained by royal order because it "smelled funny," surrounds the base. Caves in the surrounding rock bluff house a population of trolls in a running, unresolved conflict with the castle's guards.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
Per a map supplied by Edgar the tortoise, the castle is divided into three functional sections:

  • The public/guest wing, including the visitor stairwell (which only reaches the fifth floor) and the two mirrored "goodwill ballrooms" used for the Butcher's Masquerade
  • The royal wing, all of it restricted, culminating in Queen Imogen's private seventh-floor ballroom and living quarters, and a sealed dungeon-level stairwell to Floor 7 that only unlocks once Imogen (a country boss) is dead
  • A hidden underground level, accessible via a secret entrance in the troll caves, used by Signet's forces to infiltrate during the climax

The domed ceiling above the main ballroom bears a massive, slowly moving mosaic depicting Scolopendra, described in-game only as "dreaming... it is said when she finally awakens, she will destroy everything and free us all" — with a living white tree, roots in the mosaic, growing downward from the center of the dome.

docs.title: The Goodwill Ballroom System
docs.text: For the Butcher's Masquerade, the castle's magic splits attendees into three functionally separate but visually merged spaces: Ballroom A (crawlers, fourth floor), Ballroom B (hunters, second floor), and the Queen's ballroom (seventh floor, unprotected, hers alone). Everyone appears to share one room, and can speak, dance, and lightly touch across the barrier, but cannot meaningfully attack anyone in a different physical ballroom — the illusion is powered by five soul crystals in a control room on the castle's third floor, four for the individual ballrooms and one larger crystal maintaining the overlay connecting them. See The Butcher's Masquerade for the full mechanic and how it's ultimately broken.

docs.title: Destruction
docs.text:
During the Masquerade's climactic battle, the castle — badly damaged by simultaneous mantis, changeling, and elf fighting throughout its towers and halls — is teleported away in its entirety partway through the final boss fight, relocating (along with everyone still physically inside it, Ferdinand included) to Floor 9, while everyone outside its walls is left behind to finish the fight in the open crater it leaves behind.

Sourced from Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: Hump Town
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Floor: 5 ("The Bubbles"), bubble #543, Air Quadrant
  • Run by: The Dromedarian population, secretly infiltrated by the Changeling Principals
  • Notable features: "Bang twice to enter" entry policy at the main gate; a toll paid in gold, drugs, or "pleasure"

Hump Town is the last surviving camel settlement in Carl and Donut's bubble on Floor 5, home base for the entire Air Quadrant campaign. It's a Dromedarian brothel town — the name is not subtle — protected from the desert's twin suns and sandstorms by a magical, balloon-fabric shield that has to be manually re-stretched by the town's residents after every storm.

docs.title: Layout & Notable Areas
docs.text:
• The Toe — the town's central tavern and the location of Carl's personal-space pub entrance; badly damaged when a chunk of the Wasteland crashes into the surrounding block, though the entrance to the personal space survives
  • Weird Shit Alley — the street everyone in town is a little afraid of; home to the only true saferoom tavern available to crawlers without their own personal space
  • The Acrotomophilia Oasis ("the A.O.") — the saferoom tavern in Weird Shit Alley; unpopular with most crawlers despite (or because of) its name
  • The Spit and Swallow — a second tavern, used by Juice Box to discuss changeling business away from prying ears
  • City Hall — houses the basement chamber where the gnome hostage Wynne is kept and drugged; burned down and collapsed after Carl's party stages a fake "grulke toad" break-in to rescue him
  • A branch of the Desperado Club — present in Hump Town as in every transfer-station-sized settlement; features the usual Penis Parade, Silk Road, and casino areas

docs.title: The Siege
docs.text: Hump Town survives two separate near-destructions in Book 4: first the initial bombing threat after Wynne's collateral status is compromised (averted via Carl's decoy-negotiation ambush on the Wasteland), and later a mass swarm attack by thousands of regrouped Frenzied Gerbils released from the wreckage of the destroyed dreadnaught. Both crises are survived with the help of Carl's personal space, which briefly shelters dozens of Dromedarian and Changeling children (plus several fellow crawlers) during each attack.

docs.title: Notable Residents
docs.text:
• Juice Box — a Changeling sex worker who becomes Carl's party's main source of information on the town's hidden faction politics
  • Skarn — an orphaned juvenile Changeling child who runs a small telescope-rental business and later helps organize the town's children during the sandstorm evacuations
  • Bonnie — the young Dirigible Gnome daughter of Commandant Kane, taken in by Juice Box after the destruction of the Wasteland

Sourced from Book 4: The Gate of the Feral Gods.

docs.title: Hungry Eyes Village
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Floor: 10 ("Don't Come in Last," Book 8)
  • Type: The race floor's central hub town — garage row, vendor village, mercenary market, and finish line, all in one
  • Aesthetic: A "1980s neon-infused, cyberpunk fever dream" — deliberately contrasted against the "faux-medieval style" of most other dungeon towns
  • Notable NPCs: Hedy, Carl and Donut's garage-attendant gremlin; the bugbears Jasha and Radoslav; Darla-Dean, the imp hostess at C&W&U

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Hungry Eyes Village is Floor 10's one constant. Every one of the floor's seven Heats starts and ends here, and it's the only place on the floor where a team can safely repair, shop, hire mercenaries, or simply catch its breath between races. The dots that first appear on Carl's GPS as he closes in on the finish line are labeled, simply, "Hungry Eyes Village and Finish Line."

Its look is a deliberate departure from the rest of the series. Most dungeon settlements go for a "faux-medieval style"; Hungry Eyes instead reads as "straight out of a 1980s neon-infused, cyberpunk fever dream" — gaudy flashing signage, a skyline of glowing temples, and streets full of shouting vendors. Donut's own review: "You would think this pink-and-teal-and-purple aesthetic would be right up my alley, but it's quite garish, don't you think? Like I'm trapped in a clearance rack at a Claire's."

docs.title: The Team Roundabout
docs.text:
Each racing team is assigned its own numbered garage inside a private cul-de-sac called the Team Roundabout — entering it, or the garage itself, is announced as ordinary Safe Zone territory ("Safe room rules apply"). Carl and Donut's own arrival:

Welcome to Hungry Eyes. You are standing in your Team Roundabout.

The Roundabout itself is an incongruously suburban pocket: "a large asphalt cul-de-sac ringed by nine garage doors painted with numbers... Above, a blue sky with a red sun blazed, and the air was a little hot. Tall trees ringed the small neighborhood, and the spaces between driveways were filled with manicured green grass... The whole place even smelled like recently cut grass." A garage numbered with a team's most recent finishing position sits open to the circle; a narrow walking path connects the Roundabout to the neon vendor village beyond, through a shimmering arched portal too narrow for any vehicle to pass. Eliminated teams' garages are marked with a painted skull.

Lawn-chair life along the Roundabout is where most of the floor's cross-team socializing happens — this is where Carl and Donut first meet the bugbear musicians Jasha and Radoslav, the razor fox mercenary Chiyome, and the womantaurs Genesis and Rapture, all trading beer and gossip between heats.

docs.title: The Vendor Village
docs.text:
Past the portal, the tone flips entirely from suburban to neon-lit strip: "Another street was full of flashing shops of all kinds with dozens and dozens of NPCs moving about. Shouting street vendors with food carts and what appeared to be glowing souvenirs littered the sidewalk." Staffing is mostly gremlin, with a smattering of Draconians. Unlike the Roundabout, the main square is explicitly not a protected Safe Zone:

Entering Hungry Eyes Vendor Village.

Safe room rules do NOT apply in the main square.

Even in safe room areas, poisoning rules do not apply. Eat at your own risk.

Food carts sell unlabeled meat-on-a-stick under a blanket system warning — "No food in Hungry Eyes may be examined. Good luck." — and a cluster of temples forms the skyline, one of them marked with a hanging black "X": the entrance to Club Vanquisher, which Carl remains banned from.

docs.title: The Hairpin and the Lollipop
docs.text: Two named bars anchor the strip. The Hairpin advertises itself with "a Formula 1–style race car in pink-and-purple neon" and doubles as a Desperado Club entrance ("Desperado Club entrance in the back"). The Lollipop, marked by a neon gremlin waving an oversized candy, is an 1980s-only karaoke bar — and secretly conceals the entrance to the Stage Performance Guild, reachable only by singing a marked song to a perfect score the whole way through.

docs.title: Mercenary Market
docs.text: Hungry Eyes is also where every team hires its allotted mercenaries for the heat ahead — "You can add up to three mercenaries each heat. There's a bar out there in Hungry Eyes where you can hire 'em." Carl's own hires are negotiated through Rosetta and Tipid, and prices climb every time a team loses a previous hire in the field.

docs.title: Hedy the Garage Attendant
docs.text:
Carl and Donut's own garage manager is decided within their first minute on the floor, in a job interview that turns violent between two rival gremlin applicants — Hedy (a mechanic) and Waldrip Chris (an animal trainer) — brawling over which discipline the team will need:

Hedy. Gremlin. Level 30 vehicle mechanic. This is an applicant to be manager of your garage... Hedy is an expert in all things mechanical... If you can limp your vehicle back to the garage, rest assured it'll be good as new by the time the next heat starts.

Warning: Just because Hedy is a non-combatant NPC, it doesn't mean she's invulnerable. If something happens to her, your vehicle will not get repaired between heats. Hedy is not allowed to enter your safe room.

Donut picks mechanical (and Hedy) specifically so a mechanical vehicle "won't ever try to eat" Mongo; Waldrip Chris explodes on the spot the instant he's passed over. Hedy remains Carl's garage attendant for the rest of the floor — patois-heavy, endlessly harried, and the one constant NPC presence guiding the team through every upgrade choice. She is confirmed killed during the Floor 10 evacuation into the arena at the very start of Floor 11, when the Team Roundabout's own "ice-cream truck" garage is destroyed.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Locations & Places to Go — the general index this page hangs off of
  • The Heats — Floor 10's Race Ruleset — the mechanics this town exists to service
  • Chicken and Waffles and Upgrades — the hidden shop tucked into the same vendor village
  • Jasha and Radoslav — the bugbear musicians met on the Roundabout lawn

Sourced from Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Larracos, the City of Dreams
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Floor: 9 ("Faction Wars")
  • Shape: A funnel-shaped city sunk into a pit in a volcanic plain, built as concentric rings terraced down the inside of the hole
  • Rings: 66, numbered from the bottom up — "We say there are 66 levels, but that's not true. Not all rings completely circle the city … We number from the bottom up."
  • Held by: Team Retribution, the all-NPC tenth Faction Wars team — the only team that defends the city instead of holding a slice of the Plains of Larracos
  • Status at book's end: Transferred bodily to the 12th floor by a second casting of Zerzura, leaving nothing on Floor 9 but an empty pit

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Larracos is the ninth floor's capital and the prize the whole of Faction Wars is fought over. It is not a city on a plain but a city in a hole — a vast funnel sunk into the volcanic ground, with its streets, districts, and temples built as rings stacked down the inside wall. Carl's first proper look at it from ring 49 puts the top lip "maybe 3-400 feet up," and the text is blunt about what the place actually is: "This funnel was nothing more than a hole in the ground."

The counting convention is the thing to keep straight: ring 1 is the bottom and ring 66 is the top lip. The higher the number, the closer to the surface. Ring 66 is the outermost defensive ring, "normally occupied by barracks and soldiers"; the Semeru dwarves' castle sits at the very bottom.

Larracos has appeared by name since Book 4, when Carl dumped a feral god through a portal into its marketplace and flooded the city. The damage is still visible throughout Book 7 — the adventuring shops "got ruined when you guys flooded the city," and the floodwater, which once stood at ring 39, has drained to ring 3, "just enough to cover the highest tower of the castle." Several NPCs the party wanted are simply gone, drowned or vanished in that flood.

For the floor as a whole, see Level 9. For the territory outside the funnel, see The Plains of Larracos.

docs.title: The Rings
docs.text:
Only a handful of the 66 rings are described in any detail. Those that are:

Ring What's there 66 The top lip and outermost defensive ring — barracks and soldiers. The new Shanty Town settlement grows in a band immediately outside it. 50 The uppermost of Larracos's three cultural-district rings. The Larracos College of Magic takes up a third of the ring (elsewhere described as a quarter); the rest is the high cultural district and the museums. The arts district — theatres, restaurants, shops — sits just outside the college. 49 The ring immediately below, and the party's entry point on their first tour of the city. 9 The Piccadilly Theater and its surrounding bars, several of them true saferooms. 4 The Desperado Club. 3 The current waterline of the Book 4 flood. Bottom The Semeru dwarves' castle, built along the roots of the All Tree.

The other two cultural-district rings are never numbered or named.

docs.title: The Larracos College of Magic
docs.text: "Entering The Larracos College of Magic." The college occupies a large fraction of ring 50 — the text gives it as a third in one place and a quarter in another — and is the city's academic heart, sitting alongside the high cultural district and its museums. It is used late in the book as a staging point for the assault on the war-mage-held castle, with Britney coordinating from inside it.

docs.title: The Piccadilly Theater
docs.text:
Larracos's biggest theatre, down on ring 9, and one of the most distinctive pieces of architecture in the series:

"The floor contained the massive Piccadilly Theater, surrounded by bars, including a few true saferooms. The large theater building sat right underneath the waterfall, and the sculpture- covered roof doubled as the step for the water from above to land and cascade off the edge."

The river that crosses the plains drains through Shanty Town and plunges into the funnel as a waterfall; the Piccadilly's roof is the landing it breaks on. Ring 9 was under water after the Book 4 flood — Arief's uncle drained the theatre and found it "filled with jellyfish," and it is "still a little wet" when the party arrives.

By the Peeling phase the Piccadilly has become a military target rather than a venue: it houses the generator spawning the floor's zarogoth mobs, and Donut bombs it from the air — "I can start tossing bombs on the Piccadilly Theater!"

docs.title: The Desperado Club (Ring 4)
docs.text:
The ninth floor's Desperado Club branch, reopened after Book 6's demolition of the club by the demon Minge — and reorganised in the process, with every sai and cretin guard fired and replaced (which is how Toyotomi ends up on the mercenary market). Architecturally it is the odd one out:

The Desperado Club stuck out amongst all the other buildings on the fourth floor … The square, concrete building stood on a group of pillars, looking like someone had taken a modernist building built in the 1960's and dropped it right into the middle of renaissance France. A Las Vegas-style neon sign stood above the large building, but only the red, bottom half of the arrow was lit.

Ring 4 is small, and the hole at its centre is still full of water from the rings below. The club's entrance bar this season is The Headlamp Colonnade. Three sub-venues matter:

  • The Cosmic Lounge — in the basement, and the one place a non-warlord can teleport directly to the 18th floor.
  • The Midnight Market — "a special bazaar hidden in the bottom regular floor of the Desperado Club," entered under the warning "Access to the Midnight Market. Safety or Sanity not guaranteed." Run by the merchant Paca, an agent for Krakaren Prime — which is where the hell-kissed Conscription potions come from.
  • The Gray Market — a second hidden market on the middle floor, which Carl never manages to get into at all.

Access to the club is precarious in wartime: Ferdinand spends part of the Peeling phase locked out of it and being chased through the city.

docs.title: The Semeru Castle and the All Tree
docs.text:
At the very bottom of the funnel, beneath everything, the Semeru dwarves built their castle on a mat of enormous roots:

"These roots traveled through everything, and they were attached to something they called the All Tree. A great tree that is so vast, it connects everything."

The dwarves had dug looking for the gods and found the roots instead. What they built there is explicitly not a fortification:

"They built their castle at the very bottom, along the thick roots. But it's more than a castle. It's a monument. An apology."

Originally grown from living wood and since "encased in intricately carved stone," the castle is wrecked in the fighting. The Semeru themselves numbered in the millions before Scolopendra's nine-tier attack; fewer than 10,000 remain.

docs.title: Temples and Other Venues
docs.text: Venue What it is Temple of the Dagda The season's Club Vanquisher entrance temple. Each floor gets two Vanquisher entrances — one inside Larracos, which "would almost always get trashed," and one outside the city limits, which is usually left alone. This season's is dedicated to Dagda (or the Dagda), "a weather and 'masculinity' god" whose only membership requirement is growing a beard. The outside-the-limits temple is where the party bases its Vanquisher operations. Temple of Khepri The endless-buffet temple of Khepri, God of Rebirth and the Sunrise (Level 250), reached by a ritual in which female adherents swallow his beetles. "this 'endless' temple is just a room with a door that leads to one long table covered with a never-ending feast. And that feast is covered with 433 different kinds of bugs. Some of those bugs are quite unpleasant in their own right." After Khepri himself is dealt with, "His flaming, immortal bugs" remain. The Midnight Market See the Desperado Club above — the hidden bazaar on the club's bottom regular floor. The Calligraphy and Cartography guilds Two adjoining hidden guildhalls, both run by the same guildmaster, Milk, who has not had a one-on-one with a floor supervisor in over fifty seasons. The calligraphy guild is where the Words of Power system is taught. The text never states which ring or building either guild occupies — only that both doors are hidden and that nobody ever enters.

docs.title: The Peeling of Larracos
docs.text: Once only four teams remain, the floor's fourth phase triggers automatically and the city physically opens up, exposing the throne room to whoever can reach it. Holding it for six continuous hours wins Faction Wars; holding it for a full week makes the win stick. See The Four Phases of Faction Wars.

docs.title: Fate: The Second Zerzura
docs.text:
The Princess Posse never storms the throne room. Instead, with the floor under a doomsday countdown, they cede Shanty Town back to the NPCs so that the two settlements register as one town, and the Sledge casts Zerzura for the second time in the series — the first casting having dropped the High Elf Castle from Floor 6 to Floor 9 back in Book 5.

Rosetta: It worked. Shanty Town is included in the glow. It successfully combined the two towns …

The entire funnel city, plus the Shanty Town ring, transfers to the 12th floor — the Court of the Ascendency. Because Team Retribution's city is no longer on Floor 9 to be taken, the Princess Posse wins Faction Wars by default. Hired mercenaries do not transfer; thousands of them are simply removed from the dungeon the moment the spell fires.

What's left behind:

"Larracos was gone. All that was left now was a massive pit. A few saferooms remained, just doorways against the sloped pit of Larracos, including one, thankfully, at the very bottom."

Tree roots cover a giant hole at the lowest point of the empty pit.

docs.title: Unverified / Not Stated
docs.text:
• No population or diameter figure for Larracos appears anywhere in the text. The only dimension given is the ~300–400-foot distance from ring 49 up to the lip.
  • The two remaining cultural-district rings are never identified.
  • The calligraphy and cartography guilds' physical location inside the city is never stated.

Sourced from Book 4: The Gate of the Feral Gods, Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride, and Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: The L'Engle Building
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Floor: 10 ("Don't Come in Last," Book 8) — Heat 6's track, revisited in reverse for Heat 7
  • Type: A seven-floor human apartment building, raced through at drastically shrunk scale
  • Named for: Madeleine L'Engle, author of A Wrinkle in Time — never explained in-text beyond the name itself
  • Mechanic showcased here: The "what-if" predictive-modeling simulations — documented in full at Mechanics: The What-If Apartment Simulations; not repeated on this page

docs.title: The Track
docs.text:
Announced simply as "Track: The L'Engle Building," the race requires travelling from the top floor to the bottom for Heat 6, then back up for Heat 7:

Tasks required to complete: Multiple. This track has nonlinear paths, meaning there is no direct route to the finish line. You must get from the top floor to the bottom floor for this sixth heat. For Heat 7, you will return.

Special Rules: All remaining heats will be competing on the same track. As we have over 300 heats remaining, this means the racers will be shrunk to accommodate the track, which is the interior of a human apartment building.

Environment: It's a 7-floor apartment building. You may not exit the building during the race except through the front door.

Hazards: Black Lung Smog. Different apartments may have additional hazards... assuming this is an accurate depiction of a human apartment, there'll be fleas and poorly trained Yorkshire terriers and the loudest, most annoying, most selfish people you've ever met...

docs.title: Scale and Atmosphere
docs.text:
