With well over three hundred heats needing to share a single seven-story building at once, every racer is shrunk drastically to fit — from roughly the size of a Lego brick in Heat 6 to about the size of a computer mouse (three times larger) by Heat 7. Teams start inside the building's ductwork, sewer pipes, and toilets — "we're inside of a goddamned waterless shitter lined up like turds" — and glide or fall from there into individual apartments, each one hazed with a fog-machine-like mist.

The building's most disquieting visual is constant and unexplained until the AI spells it out: every human, animal, or photographed figure inside an apartment is a Human Shell or Dog/Cat Shell (Level 99), its eyes sewn shut with black wire in an "X" pattern — except for whichever figure is central to that apartment's particular what-if scenario. Disturbing a shell enough to "rupture" its loop spills giant insects (a "Ruptured Feast Hive" of Sacred Feaster Scarab Beetles) out through its face.

docs.title: Layout Notes
docs.text:
Specific apartments visited or referenced on the page include 130 (first floor), 214 and 310 (third floor), 4th-floor Archie Mu's apartment, 614 and 712 (sixth/seventh floor, both tied to Louis and Tran respectively), and 728. See Mechanics: The What-If Apartment Simulations for what each apartment actually shows and who it belongs to — this page documents the building itself rather than repeating the simulation content apartment by apartment.

A planned floor boss — described in the AI's own aside as "the Sacred Guardian of the Immortal Tem," a hundred-foot construct — never finishes assembling correctly due to an in-universe scripting error tied to the god Khepri, leaving the invulnerable Scarab Beetles roaming loose as a straight hazard rather than a proper boss encounter.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Mechanics: The What-If Apartment Simulations — the mechanic this building exists to showcase
  • Jasha and Radoslav — killed during this same Heat, though not inside the building itself
  • Prepotente — his own what-if vision is documented on the mechanics page above

Sourced from Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Necropolis of Anser
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Floor: 5 ("The Bubbles"), bubble #543, Subterranean Quadrant
  • Scale: A volcano-shaped tomb roughly the height of Mount Everest — Carl measures it at just over nine kilometers above the Water Quadrant's sea level
  • Sealed by: Emperor Anser, who entombed his own court (and his wife) alive with him

The Necropolis of Anser is the ancient, tomb-shaped structure at the heart of bubble #543, predating every faction currently fighting over the bubble. Emperor Anser subjugated the Dromedarians, Bactrians, and Nude Glabers to build it, then had his entire court — including his wife, later the ghost Quetzalcoatlus — sealed inside alive upon his death.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
• The upper settlements, populated by undead Nude Glabers, sit near the top of the structure and are reachable without diving; below them, the tomb is a "massive, fuck-you-you're-going-to-die maze" of dead-end tunnels and traps, mapped in fragments by a crawler "tomb raider" team (Morris Sp, Bobby, Low Thi) sent in specifically to find and lose two competing maps to the place
  • Deeper still, the tomb connects directly to the wrecked submarine Akula, docked against an underwater entrance by the bugbear treasure hunter Shamus Chaindrive decades earlier while searching for the Gate of the Feral Gods
  • Twin lightning-rod towers stand outside the main sandcastle entrance, originally built for an unrelated purpose but repurposed by Carl's party as the mechanism that finally destroys Quetzalcoatlus
  • At the very bottom sits Anser's own sarcophagus — just the golden-crowned skeleton of a goose — recovered only after the tomb is fully drained

docs.title: Notable Events
docs.text:
• The entire tomb floods once the Water Quadrant's castle (the Akula) is disturbed, with no drainage possible until the Land Quadrant's hidden dam valve is found and used
  • Every crawler and Changeling Principal who enters the tomb dies there over the course of the book — see Quetzalcoatlus and The Changeling Principals

Sourced from Book 4: The Gate of the Feral Gods.

docs.title: The Plains of Larracos
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Floor: 9 ("Faction Wars")
  • What it is: The battlefield territory surrounding the sunken city of Larracos, divided into nine numbered pie-slice zones, one per attacking team
  • The tenth team: Team Retribution, the NPCs, holds no plains territory — they defend the city itself
  • Terrain: "mostly flat, except for the northernmost area of the map"
  • Movement: During the Ramp-Up phase, crossing into enemy territory is only legal through designated one-kilometre corridors

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
Ten teams start Faction Wars — "Nine attacking teams and one defending team, the NPCs, who have decided to call themselves Team Retribution." The nine attackers each get a wedge of the plains radiating out from the Larracos funnel; the NPCs get the city.

The land itself is unremarkable apart from the north. The northernmost slice (spot 1) is rocky mountain country with lava flows, giving way southward to rolling hills (spot 2) and then to open flats. The orcish north also holds most of the floor's water — the rivers there feed "the large, fast-moving river that eventually drained into Larracos itself," which passes through Shanty Town and plunges into the funnel as the waterfall that lands on the Piccadilly Theater's roof.

Distances are measured in single-digit to low-double-digit miles: the Princess Posse's northern border with the Operatic Collective is "a good ten miles away," and the Blood Sultanate's castle sits "just about eight miles" in from its border with the Posse.

docs.title: The Corridors
docs.text:
"Egress into enemy territory by non-scouts is only allowed through narrow, kilometer-wide 'gates.' Each corridor is at the same spot, and it is where the enemies are massing."

Each pair of adjacent territories is joined by one fixed one-kilometre corridor. Scouts are exempt; everyone else funnels through, which turns every border into a known, pre-registered killing ground. The Posse's response is to build a no-man's-land of Tripper-proof traps and trenches on their own side. See The Four Phases of Faction Wars.

docs.title: The Nine Territories
docs.text:
Spot Team Base and notes 1 The Bone Clan / Skull Empire (orcs) King's Point — "the only of nine pie pieces that came with a pre-built castle, and it sat in a highly defensible position atop a small, rocky mountain that occasionally had lava flow around it." Destroyed by an engineered eruption during Operation Ruin: the Semeru dwarves agitate the mountain's lava tubes, and the blast "blow[s] the top off the small mountain and completely obliterate[s] the castle, leaving nothing but a throne room just sitting there in open air." 2 The Operatic Collective Rolling hills south of the orcish peaks. Eliminated when Volteeg detonates a tank, killing Warlord Hortense; their assets are awarded to the Bone Clan. 3 The Princess Posse The FUPA — the Fortress of Unyielding Power and Authority. "'Fortress of Unyielding Power and Authority?' I laughed. 'F U P A. The FUPA.'" Built from scratch on mostly flat ground with a few hills. Its flag room is the site of Baroness Victory's one and only kill. Survives a Gondii brain-worm infiltration and a Reaver paratrooper drop. 4 The Blood Sultanate (naga) The Sultana's castle, deliberately sited on rocky ground "to stop anyone from tunneling in from below." Taken in Operation Snake Pit; Princess Vinata dies and the team is eliminated. 5 The Prism Kingdom Empress D'Nadia's base, the first major castle to fall — taken during the Ramp-Up via the southern trench assault. The "former Prism castle" then changes hands repeatedly between Madness and Dream mercenaries. 6 The Dream The site of the Sugar Cube — the high-elf castle from Floor 6, Zerzura'd down to Floor 9 at the end of Book 5. See the note below. Demolished outright when three gods fight across it. 7–8 The Madness Two slices. Contains Architect Houston's operating theatre, his lair beside the throne room — "Nobody has managed to get into Houston's operating theater." Carl finally does, and kills him there; the room is rigged to a dead-man's switch. 9 The Reavers A castle built as a shifting honeycomb — "the very front part was a large, featureless room, which in turn led off to dozens of honeycomb-shaped hallways … stacked up to the ceiling, which was about three or four stories high," with the cells constantly and randomly re-arranging themselves. The throne room sits behind the centre honeycomb. Warlord Fang dies here, hiding inside his own dragon.

The Sugar Cube's chain of custody is inconsistent in the source

The High Elf Castle — nicknamed the Sugar Cube — lands on Floor 9 "in the territory of the Lemig Sortion," who use it as their headquarters. When Commander Stockade dies, the system announces that "All assets of the Lemig Sortion have been awarded to the Madness" — yet the castle is thereafter consistently referred to as the Dream castle, in spot 6, and it is the Dream that is eliminated when it falls. The book never reconciles how the property passed from Lemig to the Madness to the Dream. The wiki records both statements rather than picking one.

The text also uses "Democratic Sortion" and "Lemig Sortion" interchangeably for the same team.

docs.title: Territory Changes
docs.text: Territory is not fixed. As teams are eliminated their assets are formally awarded to another team by system message, and the Peeling of Larracos only triggers once four teams remain. One unplanned faction is created mid-floor rather than eliminated: the War Mage Rebellion, which kills King Stalwart, seizes the Gate of the Feral Gods, and takes over Bone Clan territory as a new team in its own right. See The Faction Wars Teams.

docs.title: Other Named Places on the Plains
docs.text:
• Area 52 — the Princess Posse's forest airbase and saferoom, and the launch point for their missile batteries. Full page.
  • The Temple of the Dagda — the season's out-of-city Club Vanquisher entrance, which is the one that doesn't get trashed. See Larracos.
  • The southern trench network — the Posse's engineered approach to the Prism Kingdom, built with Dazzler trap modules, an exploit of the Build Trench spell, and an acid-filled trench trap.
  • The volcano — the mountain under King's Point, deliberately erupted by the Semeru to open Operation Ruin. Its lava flow clogs the main river, reaches Shanty Town, and pours into the top rings of Larracos.

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Point Mongo
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Floor: 6 ("The Hunting Grounds")
  • Formerly: An unnamed Large Ursine Settlement
  • Conquered by: Carl and Donut, after accidentally killing mayor Elmer during a bribery stunt
  • Run by: Princess Donut, via the settlement-conquest system — see Game Mechanics

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Point Mongo is Carl and Donut's main base of operations for the back half of Floor 6's early chapters — a formerly nameless Ursine settlement on the near side of the river dividing the Hunting Grounds' human and elf territories, renamed by Donut the moment she gains control of it. It's a strict, puritanical theocracy under its original leadership (the town's rulebook bans dancing, singing outside a temple, gambling, and — specifically, in a rule aimed squarely at Mongo — dinosaurs "of any kind, no exceptions"), rules Donut immediately guts once she takes over.

docs.title: Conquest
docs.text: Carl and Donut trigger the town's takeover almost by accident: Donut, offended at Mongo being banned by name, has Carl offer the mayor, Elmer, a bribe to have the guards "get rid of" Mongo and Donut as a joke — and when Elmer steps forward to take the money, Donut shoves him off the town's edge with Astral Paw. The fall alone kills the surprisingly fragile Level 40 mayor before a passing Naiad drags the body into the river. Ownership of the settlement transfers to Donut automatically the moment the mayor dies.

docs.title: Defense
docs.text: Once in charge, Carl and Donut spend several chapters fortifying Point Mongo against the incoming wave of Floor 6 hunters: distributing missile launchers to the town's Funeral Bell garrison, ringing the town with trap networks (each keyed to a different song), and hosting a rotating cast of allies, including the were-castors Clint and Holger, who help build up the town's picket defenses. The town survives multiple hunter raids and a High Elf artillery bombardment (a small trebuchet team firing poison-gas rocks from beyond the walls) before eventually being abandoned as the Gehenna Bramble event sweeps across the map.

docs.title: Notable Residents
docs.text:
• Elmer — the Ursine mayor killed to trigger the conquest
  • Tam — a Light Cleric who unsuccessfully lobbies Donut to reinstate the anti-dinosaur/anti-naiad rules
  • Prudence — an Ursine barmaid and mother of two cubs, later killed defending them during the climax; her account of Big Tina's backstory is the key to solving "The Recital" quest

Sourced from Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: Satan's Water Park
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Floor: 10 ("Don't Come in Last," Book 8) — a parallel Heat 4 track, sharing the Upano pit stop with Carl and Donut's own jungle route
  • Named for: Its owner, the country boss Satan — see Bosses: Satan for his own catalog entry; not duplicated here
  • Racers on this track: Prepotente and Jurgen; Louis Santiago's team
  • Note on heat numbering: The primary text places this track within Heat 4's parallel-route structure (the same heat as Upano); flagged here rather than silently reconciled against any other page's heat count

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Satan's Water Park is exactly what the name promises: a kaiju-scale water park built around, owned by, and lazily narrated by an invulnerable, comic-relief boss named Satan — who turns out to be a mountain-sized hedgehog with an exaggerated posh British accent, utterly indifferent to the racers tearing through his property.

Satan himself was a country boss, but he was invulnerable, and he wasn't a boss that one was meant to fight. He was the owner of the water park, and he lounged near the exit, occasionally offering loud opinions on the things happening, occasionally poking at the racers.

Donut correctly predicts the accent before he ever speaks, on the strength of a single childhood grudge — she once lost a cat show to a hedgehog named Jezebel. Satan does not disappoint:

"Jolly good show," he said. "Pip-pip!"

His running commentary supplies most of the track's comic relief: "Blood 'ell," he grumbles from his perch, rolling onto his back and toppling a roller coaster full of screaming riders by accident; elsewhere he complains about the water "right into my delicate bum," and when he gets bored of watching, he headbutts an entire loop-de-loop track apart just to see what happens.

docs.title: Track Layout
docs.text: The park's first half runs through slide tubes reminiscent of the Iron Tangle's rail maze — easy to follow, hard to survive if a racer takes a wrong turn, since the wrong path dumps a vehicle directly inside Satan's own body. Ground level opens onto a toddler splash pad, a wave pool, and the aforementioned loop-de-loop. A hidden trap beneath the park drops racers into a basement gauntlet of Sheol demons and baby versions of the hedgehog boss, ending in a Garden Gnome Sprinkler borough boss fight.

docs.title: The River of Sloth
docs.text:
Carl and Donut's allies are routed onto the park's slowest, safest option — a lazy river marked by "a red-eyed sloth taking a rip from a bong":

Our path was just south of the loop and was called the River of Sloth. This last one was clearly the slowest path. It was the water park's version of a lazy river. This was deeper than the water in the tubes, and there were supposedly rafts.

The cannibal tribes menacing the jungle roads around Upano reappear here in the same role, rebranded as "season pass holders" rather than cannibals.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Bosses: Satan — the boss himself, cross-linked rather than duplicated
  • Upano — the shared pit stop this track routes through
  • The Heats — Floor 10's Race Ruleset

Sourced from Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Shanty Town
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Floor: 9 ("Faction Wars")
  • What it is: A brand-new settlement ring of hovels and markets encircling the top lip of the Larracos funnel — effectively a 67th ring, outside the city proper
  • Mayor: Carl, who buys the office from Sir Ferdinand for a bowler hat
  • Special rule: It has no throne room. The only way to take it is to kill the mayor.
  • Fate: Flattened during the Peeling phase, patched up, then transferred to the 12th floor along with Larracos by the second casting of Zerzura

docs.title: Origin
docs.text:
Shanty Town is new — it did not exist in any previous book, and nobody built it:

"It turned out the existence of the shanty town, a ring of hastily-built buildings and markets surrounding the entrance to Larracos, was a new thing … It'd appeared soon after the flooding, ostensibly built by the displaced NPCs. Nobody had actually built it. The hovels just sprung up out of nowhere. Since the slums completely encircled the top entrance to Larracos, they formed the equivalent of a new, large-sized settlement."

The flooding in question is Carl's own, from Book 4 — he dumped a feral god into the Larracos marketplace and drove the city's population upward. The system responded by generating a slum around the hole and registering it as a settlement in its own right, complete with a mayor and a build menu. What the Princess Posse does generate is everything that goes on top of it: walls, automated defence towers, and the handful of manned synergy towers the settlement menu allows.

docs.title: The Bowler Hat Trade
docs.text:
Ferdinand holds the mayorship when the party arrives. Carl wants it, and pays for it with a weathered black bowler hat that decapitates an enemy and boomerangs back to its owner:

"I want to be mayor of that town. Shanty Town. You'll have to transfer your mayorship to us, which means that jewel on your necklace will go away. You'll get this hat, and we'll trade it back for your turban in a day or so … Before he could accept or deny the invite, I reached over and placed the bowler hat on the cat's head."

Ferdinand gets his drained turban back eventually and keeps wearing the bowler hat anyway; Donut lets him keep it.

docs.title: Strategic Value
docs.text:
Two properties make Shanty Town matter far more than a slum should:

  • No throne room. Every other base on the floor can be taken by capturing its throne room. Shanty Town cannot: "the town's rules were different. There was no throne room. They could only take it by killing me." That makes the Posse's forward position effectively un-flippable while Carl lives.
  • It is inside Larracos's field of fire. Anyone entering Shanty Town "would open themselves up to getting attacked by Larracos's defense system" — the NPC city's automated towers cover the ring, which turns the Posse's alliance with Team Retribution into a live artillery umbrella.

It also holds a hidden Club Vanquisher entrance somewhere in its sprawl, and at least one named bar, Possum Envy.

docs.title: Notable Structures
docs.text: Structure What it is The Nest The Posse's master-quality granite synergy tower, built at the very edge of the hole leading down into Larracos and keyed to Atrocity-class spells. Donut's sniper perch for most of the back half of the book. Full page. Li Na's clock tower A manned Extend Aura synergy tower — "it could only be manned by a crawler or NPC who had 'synergy' with the tower's attack. In this case, the synergy was someone who used the aura mechanic." One of the few synergy towers usable during the Ramp-Up's offensive-magic ban. Dozens of wires dangle from the arms of the clock. Li Na abandons it mid-battle without telling anyone, which is the party's first sign something is badly wrong with her. Automated defence towers The settlement menu allows unlimited-ish automatic towers but only "a handful" of manned synergy towers.

docs.title: Destruction
docs.text:
Shanty Town is wrecked during the Peeling phase, and the text is specific about the cause: it was trampled by fighting gods, not by any one spell.

"I was momentarily taken aback by the sheer destruction wrought over what used to be Shanty Town. Most of our own towers, which we really never got to use, were trampled. The nest tower along with Li Na's abandoned synergy towers still stood, but both were drawing a lot of fire. All the other buildings were just gone, flattened by the passage of the gods."

Separately, the engineered volcanic eruption sends a lava flow across the plains and into the ring — "A slow-moving glob of molten rock was just about to enter Shanty Town, headed straight for the giant hole in the ground" — and the days after the god battle are spent "clear[ing] out the damage caused by the lava."

On the War Crime spell

Donut casts War Crime from the Nest, over the same ground, but the text never credits that spell with destroying Shanty Town itself — the buildings are already described as flattened before the casting, by the gods' passage. Treat "War Crime destroyed Shanty Town" as an oversimplification.

docs.title: Fate
docs.text:
To make the second Zerzura work, the settlement has to read as part of Larracos rather than as a separate town, which means Carl ceding the territory back to the NPCs first. It works — "Shanty Town is included in the glow. It successfully combined the two towns" — and the ring goes to the 12th floor with the city it surrounds.

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: The Nest
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Floor: 9 ("Faction Wars")
  • Where: Shanty Town, right at the edge of the hole leading down into Larracos
  • What it is: A master-quality granite synergy tower, keyed to Atrocity-class spells
  • Built by: Li Na's builder squad, led by Toyotomi the rhinoceros
  • Manned by: Princess Donut — her sniper perch and command post for the back half of the book

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
The Shanty Town settlement menu allows any number of automated defence towers but only "a handful" of manned towers, called synergy towers. A synergy tower does nothing unless it is occupied by someone whose own abilities match the synergy type it was built for — see Base and Tower Construction.

The Nest is the Posse's expensive one:

"Li Na's builder squad led by Toyotomi would get to work on a very tall, very powerful, very specialized, very expensive synergy tower. It would be placed right at the edge of the hole leading down into Larracos … this particular tower had a very simple name … It was called The Nest."

It took almost two full days to build, and it is "by far, the tallest structure outside of the sunken funnel of Larracos" — tall enough to give Donut line of sight over the entire battlefield from the top.

docs.title: The Synergy Choice
docs.text:
The original plan was mundane. A sniper-synergy tower would have sharpened Donut's targeting enormously — but her Tiara of a Thousand Lights already solved that problem, since "All Donut needed was line of sight to apply her sniper skills." That freed the slot for something far worse:

"The Nest was instead built to have synergy with something called Atrocity-class spells."

This single decision is what makes the back half of the book possible. An Atrocity-class spell cast from the Nest is amplified in both power and area — and area is exactly the limiting factor on War Crime:

"Donut's War Crime spell was both simple and horrific in both usage and scope. And while the area of effect was relatively low, the synergy tower's ability to upgrade Atrocity spells and allow them to be cast over a wide area made War Crime a true spell of mass destruction."

The same amplification is what lets Rolling Battle Formation ball up roughly 80,000 combatants at once, and what makes You're Not Done Yet a battlefield-scale flesher factory rather than a corpse trick.

docs.title: Construction and Stats
docs.text:
Examined mid-build:

Master Quality. This fortification is at 150% Strength. This edifice is currently under construction. 1/15 Enchantments active. Current Enchantments: Increased Strength.

Toyotomi's rules of thumb: each block takes a maximum of 15 protective enchantments, which bleed outward to nearby blocks in a net pattern; completing the build as master quality lifts the structure to 200% strength and makes it glow gold; and his own Edifice Shield spell doubles that again, to 400%. The tower is left unpainted granite specifically so the mages have time to coat it in protection spells before the fighting starts.

docs.title: Donkey Kong
docs.text: An expensive last-ditch interior defence. Like castles, manned synergy towers must by rule have a path to the main room — but nothing says the path has to be survivable. When Donut hits the switch, the stairs collapse into a ramp and barrels of assorted unpleasantness start rolling down it.

docs.title: In the Book
docs.text:
The Nest is where most of the Peeling phase is fought from, and it takes a brutal beating. Its integrity is tracked in system readouts as the battle wears on — 45%, then 25%, then 10%, then 8%. Lucia Mar storms it personally, killing the NPCs Bomo and Toyotomi on the way up before Rend kills her last rottweiler and Carl forcibly conscripts her.

The tower survives, badly damaged, and Ferdinand "directs" its repair in the lull before the final act. Donut's three Atrocities — the casts that earn her the second class The Oak Fell and the title Champion of Nekhebit — are all cast from the top of it.

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Upano
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Floor: 10 ("Don't Come in Last," Book 8)
  • Type: Mandatory jungle pit stop, shared by four parallel Heat 4 tracks at once
  • Full announcement: "There will be a single mandatory refueling pit stop along this route. Pit stop will be within the lost jungle city of Upano."
  • Entry message: "Entering the Lost City of Upano. Mind the locals."

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Upano is the one fixed point shared by Heat 4's otherwise-divergent tracks. Where every other heat sends each team down a single, private route, Heat 4 splits into several simultaneous "worlds" that all happen to converge on the same jungle way station partway through — Carl and Donut's own team runs the You're Gonna Die If You Go In Here Jungle Trail of Tremendous Cannibalistic Slaughter, while Prepotente's and Louis's teams are routed instead through Satan's Water Park, and still other teams end up on "the devil's cliffs" or a track described only as "a rip-off of the third floor called 'the eternal slum.'" All of them arrive at Upano.

docs.title: Geography
docs.text:
The city itself is small — barely more than a single long street of rearranged garage-houses transplanted wholesale from every heat sharing the stop — but the land around it is deliberately disorienting:

Beyond the small city was a strange sight. Where I was expecting more jungle was something completely incongruous with the setting. To the east was what appeared to be a tall group of black tubes. It just went up and up and up, and opposite that was a group of cliffs. Opposite us, I was expecting more jungle, but it appeared like Upano just went on and on and on.

Neither the black tubes nor the cliffs are explained or explored on the page — they read as scenery marking the boundary between Upano and the water-park and cliffside tracks converging on the same stop, rather than a location in their own right.

docs.title: Rules of the Pit Stop
docs.text:
Upano runs on a hard timer rather than ordinary Safe Zone rules:

A two-hour timer starts the moment you park in your garage... Garage doors may not be closed during pit stops. Safe room access is unavailable during pit stops.

The open-garage rule turns lethal almost immediately: with doors forced open and no Safe Zone protection, three of Carl's hired mercenaries — Finley, Olga, and Quemada — are run down and killed right outside their own garage by team One Fine Pig's APV, moments after Finley's own speech about wanting to protect his family. Carl's retaliation — setting silent, Tigran-only disintegration traps around the enemy garage — kills both Tigran racers, Nico and Dario, eliminating One Fine Pig by the end of the heat.

docs.title: The Cannibal Tribes
docs.text: The "mind the locals" warning belongs to the jungle roads leading into Upano rather than the city itself: a southern cannibal village and a rival northern tribe (led by the chieftain Maurice) trigger a mandatory quest to kill Maurice once his southern counterpart, Great Rusty, is already dead — failing to do so blocks the race outright. The same cannibal population resurfaces, reskinned as "season pass holders," inside the parallel Satan's Water Park track.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Satan's Water Park — the parallel Heat 4 track sharing this same pit stop
  • The Heats — Floor 10's Race Ruleset
  • Hungry Eyes Village — the floor's actual hub town, by contrast

Sourced from Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Game Mechanics
docs.text: Full pages exist for the systems with the most depth. Everything else the books explain is covered below, organized by the book that introduced it.

docs.title: Full pages
docs.text:
• Loot Box Tier System — Bronze through Celestial, plus Benefactor Boxes
  • Boss Tier Ladder — Neighborhood through Floor bosses, plus Elites
  • Ratings & Viewership System — Views → Followers → Favorites → Patrons
  • Race & Class Selection — the Floor 3 process, Earth Classes, Character Actor specialties
  • Managers — the guide-benefit that trades a guildhall for a mobile companion
  • Over City Floors — the recurring urban-level pattern (Floors 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18)
  • Quests — reward tiers, upgrade achievements, and event quests
  • Locations & Places to Go — Safe Rooms, Tutorial/Training Guilds, Reward Rooms, and a directory of specific named locations
  • The Iron Tangle Railway System — Floor 4's train/portal maze, Station Mimics, and the ghoul-disposal pipeline
  • The T'Ghee Card System — Floor 8's squads, flags, decks, and the full named-card catalog
  • Character Stats & Progression — the six stats, leveling, HP/mana, the skill cap, and the 300-point stat ceiling

docs.title: The World Dungeon's Basic Rules
docs.text:
Earth's surviving population is offered a choice: stay on the surface with no further resources, or enter the 18-level World Dungeon to "reclaim" lost matter. Level 1 opens with 150,000 entrances; each subsequent level's entrance count halves (rounding up), down to just two entrances (and one exit) on Level 18. Each level has a countdown timer — 5 days for Level 1, increasing afterward based on factors like ratings and surviving crawler count — after which the level "collapses" and anyone still on it forfeits everything, crawler included. There is no respawn: "Dead is dead." Descending a staircase fully restores a crawler's health.

Floors 1–3 are seeded with Tutorial Guilds, run by non-combatant NPCs like Mordecai, who explain the system to new crawlers and unlock their inventory access. Starting on Floor 10, crawlers are offered options to exit the dungeon entirely — better options the deeper they've gone. Floor 4 onward introduces random level themes, guarded/quest-gated entrances, and much smaller playable areas than the near-planet-sized first three floors.

docs.title: Stats & Leveling
docs.text: See the full page: Character Stats & Progression — the six stats (five visible, one hidden), starting values, the +3-per-level point grant, leveling/XP mechanics, and health/mana.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text: Every real-world skill and habit a crawler has ever practiced is tracked, filterable by level — Carl's initial unfiltered list included things like Breathing and Operating a Sony Brand RMVLZ620 Universal Remote Control. Combat- and dungeon-relevant skills (Unarmed Combat, Pugilism, etc.) level up with use and stack multiplicatively with gear bonuses.

docs.title: Dimensional Inventory
docs.text: This season introduced an upgrade over the prior slot-based system: unlimited storage, restricted only by whether the crawler can physically lift an item off the ground unassisted for about four seconds. Storage is time-locked (food doesn't spoil) and cannot hold living creatures. A 10-slot hotlist allows one-click use of spells, potions, and items without opening the full inventory menu.

docs.title: Fog of War
docs.text: The parts of the minimap a crawler hasn't personally explored yet render without detail, even when technically within minimap range — this applies to ordinary terrain, but not to Safe Rooms or stairwells, which always reveal themselves once in range regardless of exploration status. See Locations & Places to Go for Safe Zones, Tutorial/Training Guilds, and Reward Rooms in full detail.

docs.title: Mob Tagging
docs.text: Mobs and other crawlers show as colored dots on the minimap: green is the player, blue is other crawlers, white is non-hostile/NPC, red is hostile. The same white/red coding is used for individual creatures' name tags (e.g. a "red-tagged" pet is inherently dangerous/aggressive; a "white-tagged" one is docile).

docs.title: Tattoos as Faction Markers
docs.text: Certain loot boxes brand a permanent tattoo directly onto a crawler rather than adding an item to inventory (e.g. the Goblin Pass, burned onto Carl's forearm). These tattoos function as faction passes — granting safe passage through a faction's territory, sometimes at a cost (the Goblin Pass increases damage taken from fairy-class enemies by 20%) — and can't be hidden without a specific coverup item.

docs.title: Achievements
docs.text: Nearly every notable in-game action triggers a system achievement: a short, often crude comedic message, sometimes an in-voice bit (a caveman voice, an Attenborough impression, etc.), that grants a named reward. Achievements are the dungeon's primary loot-box distribution mechanism.

docs.title: Wild Magic Bursts (Book 2)
docs.text: A distinct hazard from ordinary magical explosions: a "wild magic" event unfolds as four escalating precursor bursts roughly five minutes apart, each with a different, unpredictable effect (the one witnessed strips the magical properties from all currently-equipped gear) before a final, far more destructive detonation. Removing magical items and placing them safely in inventory between bursts is the only real defense — items left equipped can activate on their own, permanently break, or explode.

docs.title: The Sixth Stat: Wisdom Revisited
docs.text: See Character Stats & Progression for the full Book 1 reveal and Book 2's one addition (spell cost/effectiveness scales with visible stats, chiefly Intelligence, separately from whatever Wisdom does).

docs.title: The 20% Buff Display Bug (Book 3)
docs.text: See Character Stats & Progression for the full writeup of this long-standing, unfixed display bug.

docs.title: Personal Spaces (Book 3)
docs.text: A crawler's personal space can be upgraded to allow whitelisting other parties in — Katia does this for Brynhild's Daughters, letting thirty visitors into the shared space at once. When two separate parties who aren't grouped together need to interact (as with Hekla's team), the system generates a temporary, situationally-created space: a new vestibule door appears next to the personal space's own entrance, leading to the other party's space, without merging the two spaces or requiring either side to actually party up.

docs.title: The Bubbles (Book 4)
docs.text: Floor 5's structure: 1,172 sealed spherical "bubbles" sitting in sunken pockets of a dark in-between space called the Lacuna, each holding roughly 150 crawlers. Every bubble is split into four quadrants — Land, Sea (Water), Air, and Subterranean — each with its own castle and throne room, separated from each other by an invisible barrier that blocks spells, thrown objects under a caster's control, and physical crossing alike (a rolled ball can pass through; a held stick cannot). All four quadrants' castles must be taken before a bubble's stairwell opens, and every bubble typically has one "easy" environmental shortcut per quadrant that bypasses its throne-room boss entirely — see Denise the Feral Goose Mother, Mrs. Ghazi, and Quetzalcoatlus for the three found in bubble #543.

docs.title: The Bounty-Doubling Leaderboard (Book 4)
docs.text: Starting on Floor 5, any crawler who survives a floor while already ranked in the top ten receives a permanent "(x2)" bounty multiplier on all future leaderboard listings, via an achievement called "The Quarry Sees Another Spring." This stacks with each qualifying floor survived.

docs.title: Glass Cannon Class (Book 4)
docs.text: A specialization choice for Donut's Former Child Actor class: forbids further Constitution training entirely, but grants a flat +15 base Constitution, boosts spell training speed, and lowers spell mana costs — plus scales the level and duration cap on resurrection-type spells like Second Chance well beyond its normal limits.

docs.title: Deity Worship, Feral Gods, and the Nothing (Book 4)
docs.text:
Building on the involuntary-summoning mechanics established with Grull (see War Gauntlet of the Exalted Grull), Book 4 introduces the wider theology behind the dungeon's deities. The Nothing is a banishment dimension the true pantheon uses to imprison gods, demons, and lesser deities judged too dangerous or unruly to remain free — prolonged exposure to it drives anything trapped there "feral" and insane, whether or not it was ever a deity to begin with (see Orthrus, a perfectly innocent puppy rendered fireproof but otherwise unaffected).

Crawlers may formally worship a deity via the interface's Deity tab, which comes with binding rules (daily offerings, prohibitions on rival-god gear, mandatory "church quests") in exchange for periodic boons and passive benefits — full detail on Grull's version of this system lives on the War Gauntlet page; Book 4 adds a second working example via Carl's worship of Emberus, God of Sun and Ash, acquired by accident through a Celestial Grenade.

Celestial Grenades summon the wielder's worshipped deity (or a random one, if unaffiliated) to the thrower's location for sixty seconds, granting the thrower a Divine Intervention invulnerability buff for the same duration — originally a Skull Empire assassination tool, used by Carl instead to save himself, Donut, and a giant puppy from a rival crawler and a rampaging sun god simultaneously.

The Gate of the Feral Gods — the book's titular artifact — opens one-way portals between two locations, but always leaves behind a lingering, two-way rift into the Nothing at the opening side, through which a feral god or demon will eventually emerge. Carl weaponizes this side effect repeatedly across the back half of the book, first to evacuate crawlers trapped in sealed bubbles (unleashing a feral god into each newly-empty bubble as the cost of escape), and finally to flood the ninth floor's Larracos marketplace instead of releasing a monster on the open floor at all — see The Wasteland and The Changeling Principals for the in-fiction hostage/collateral system built around the artifact's two watches and winding box.

docs.title: Withering Spirits (Book 4)
docs.text: A stable, less-dangerous cousin of the Soul Leech Capacitor type seen in Remex: when a creature's soul is split into two halves during a failed reunification, the resulting withering spirit haunts whatever vessel is closest to its original form, but has very little power of its own and can be hired as personal-space staff. See Samantha for Book 4's example.

docs.title: The Ninth Floor and Faction Wars, Previewed (Book 4)
docs.text: Mordecai lays out the endgame structure well ahead of schedule: nine factions arrive on Floor 3 to claim one of nine randomly-assigned territories around the sunken city of Larracos (the previous season's winner may choose theirs — usually the pre-fortified "King's Point"), starting with 15,000 troops each, mostly NPCs backfilled by any paying "tourists" a faction brings along. Factions can't fight each other until crawlers arrive on Floor 9, but may send hunters — a separate pool of paying non-crawler participants who start at level 30 once Floor 3 opens and gain full lethality only once crawlers reach Floor 6 — down to the sixth floor ("the Hunting Grounds") to farm gear and sell it back to their faction through Larracos's in-person markets once Floor 6's marketplace interface unlocks.

docs.title: The Marketplace Interface (Book 4)
docs.text: Unlocks fully on Floor 6, letting crawlers and touring factions trade goods without meeting in person — with one exception: Floor 9's faction leaders have no access to it and must buy from physical NPC vendor stores in Larracos instead, which is why flooding that specific market (see above) does lasting damage rather than a temporary inconvenience.

docs.title: The Walk-On List (Book 4)
docs.text: Revealed in the epilogue: each season, corporations illegally hire independent trackers ("Walk-On" bounty hunters) to sneak onto a harvested planet and kidnap specific native survivors the show's producers want to introduce as characters later — a practice the Syndicate quietly tolerates despite it being flatly illegal, since viewers rarely object and no corporation is ever held accountable.

docs.title: The Prize Carousel
docs.text: A recurring fan-vote mechanic tied to certain sponsor/fan boxes: rather than receiving a fixed item, the crawler is given a spin at a "wheel" of possible prizes that the viewing audience votes on live. It notably misfired once for Carl and Mordecai (the "Chaco" incident, resulting in the Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook rather than the intended prize) and remains something crawlers would rather avoid triggering close to a manager's return, since a bad public vote can provoke a manager's own on-air temper.

docs.title: The Apito Pantheon (Book 5)
docs.text:
Book 5 reveals the origin of the dungeon's dominant pantheon, via Queen Imogen's telling of the first Butcher's Masquerade: the sky god Taranis and his wife Apito, the Blessed Oak Mother, hosted a peace-night party in the Halls of the Ascendency for their squabbling divine children. Their son Yarilo, god of lust, broke the peace by assaulting another god's familiar and was banished by Apito into the Nothing (see Book 4's entry above) as punishment — enraging Taranis and triggering a slaughter that killed every mortal and demigod guest. The party became a recurring holy ritual afterward: a once-in-a-lifetime spell any sufficiently divine cleric may cast exactly once, inviting a guest list handpicked by Apito herself specifically to sow discord, with a boon promised only if the whole evening passes without violence. See The Butcher's Masquerade below for how Queen Imogen's own attempt plays out.

Other deities named or introduced this book: Grull (Apito's son, previously established via the War Gauntlet), Diwata (one of "Apito's brood," a minor, gender-shifting nature deity who can physically birth ordinary offspring from whatever she last mated with — an ability the wider pantheon considers dangerously destabilizing), and Hellik, the brother and rival of Carl's own patron Emberus. Worshipping Emberus carries a real cost discovered mid-book: killing a fellow worshipper of Carl's own god (even a hunter) triggers a Penitence debuff (loses the current boon, doubled tithing for 30 hours) and a public Shunned status icon; killing a second worshipper during that window risks an actual divine smite.

docs.title: The Butcher's Masquerade (Book 5)
docs.text:
A holy sacrament unique to Apito worship (see above), staged as Book 5's climax at the High Elf Castle. Only the most senior cleric of an Apito-worshipping nation may cast the ritual, and only once in their lifetime; casting it hands the guest list itself over to the goddess, who deliberately invites parties who hate each other (in Carl's case, seating him at the same table as the Dark Hive, Lucia Mar, Eva Sigrid, and Tsarina Signet) to maximize the odds of a violent breach. A magical peace seal prevents any attendee, host included, from striking first: breaking it exiles everyone responsible straight into the Nothing. If the whole evening concludes without violence, the host receives a boon from Apito — though per both Imogen and Signet, no host has ever actually pulled this off; every telling of the ritual across editions of the cookbook ends in the Nothing being fed regardless.

Practically, the event splits crawlers and hunters into mirrored "goodwill ballrooms" — physically separate rooms magically overlaid into one shared illusion of a single hall, so attendees can see, hear, and lightly touch across the barrier without being able to meaningfully harm each other; see High Elf Castle for the full mechanic and how a saboteur eventually breaks it from within. The evening includes a pet beauty contest, a talent show, a buffet, and a prize counter redeeming collected Hunter Hands or Crawler Scalps (see The Hand/Scalp Trophy Economy below) for prizes scaled by quantity, up to a single Memorial Crystal — see Soul Crystals & Memorial Crystals — offered as the host's own most valuable possession, per the ritual's rules.

Signet ultimately breaks the seal herself, using a one-person variant of her Ink Marauder spell (caster, sacrifice, and executioner all in a single body) as a deliberate, willing sacrifice — the only way Carl's group finds to legally end the ritual on their own terms rather than the enemy's.

docs.title: The Hand/Scalp Trophy Economy (Book 5)
docs.text: New to Floor 6: killing a hunter yields both a normal Hunter-Killer loot box and a physical, stackable Hunting Trophy (a severed hand), explicitly described as tickets toward a prize counter that only opens at the Butcher's Masquerade — "the cheapest award in the prize case will cost a single hand." Hunters carry an equivalent "Crawler Scalp" version. Both currencies are worthless outside the Masquerade itself; transferring or selling one prematurely reverts it to a mundane body part. Killing a hunter also permanently appends a spinning-dagger icon (visually distinct from the ordinary player-killer skull) to a crawler's name per confirmed hunter kill.

docs.title: The Creeping Apocalypse & Odious Creepers (Book 5)
docs.text:
A floor-wide, mandatory world quest triggered when uncontrolled vampirism (see below) produces enough reanimated body parts to reach critical mass: any "Glamoured Fragment" that reassembles 70%+ of its original body gets hijacked by a parasitic Odious Blossom plant, transforming into an Odious Creeper — a roaming, City-Boss-tier plant/undead monstrosity (levels ranging from roughly 130 to 190+). Fifty spawn at once across the map, and every crawler and hunter on the floor is given an unopt-outable quest to kill all fifty before sunset, rewarded with +5 to a random stat per kill and +5 levels per five kills.

Failing the quest (as happens in Book 5) triggers an escalating punishment: a Gehenna Bramble spell spreads outward from the last uncleared Creeper locations at roughly 4.5 km/hour, turning every plant it touches into an indestructible, boiling-blood-on-contact wall of thorns that consumes the entire map except a small buffer around stairwells — forcing every surviving crawler and hunter toward whatever safe ground remains (in Book 5's case, the High Elf castle). The same punishment message introduces a blood bar: from that point on, saferoom and personal-space access is throttled tenth-floor-style — the bar fills by killing things and drains while idle inside a safe area, and hitting empty gets a crawler randomly ejected outdoors.

docs.title: Vampirism as a Floor-Wide Curse (Book 5)
docs.text: Vampirism functions as a genuine, spreading curse rather than a cosmetic race choice: a bite or severe injury from an infected creature can transmit it, and the very first crawler or NPC infected in a region becomes that region's progenitor ("Princess/Prince of Hell" title), whose death cures every subordinate infection dating back less than a month. New vampires gain a randomized grab-bag of abilities (mind control, shapeshifting, minion creation) scaled to their own power. A rare item, I Take it All Back, reverses Scolopendra's original Transmutation curse entirely rather than curing vampirism — used in Book 5 to turn Kiwi back into her original Ursine form. Creatures freshly cured of vampirism carry an Immortalized debuff for 29 hours: half strength/mana and no healing in direct sunlight, flipped into a +50% strength/mana and double-healing buff in direct moonlight.

docs.title: Settlement Conquest & the Collar Charm (Book 5)
docs.text: Killing a settlement's ruling NPC (mayor, chieftain, etc.) transfers ownership of the town to the killer, who can then rename it, rewrite its posted rules, and command its guards directly. Prior ownership of an Enchanted Collar Charm of the [Rank] — see Necklace of the Haute Bourgeoisie for Carl's own, earlier version of the item — gains a new gem per settlement held, each granting stat bonuses, a unique skill, and a recurring tax stipend every ten days; the necklace itself can only be upgraded to a higher tier by conquering a correspondingly larger settlement. See Point Mongo for Donut's own Floor 6 conquest.

docs.title: The Guild System (Book 5)
docs.text: Introduced specifically to break up oversized parties: a hard 30-crawler party cap goes into effect on Floor 6, with larger existing parties automatically split. A Guild, purchased from a Bopca for 500,000 gold, lets multiple separate parties share personal-space upgrades, a common area, and (for a fee) experience distribution, under a single guildmaster with hiring/kicking and dues-collection authority — effectively restoring the large-group cooperation the party cap just took away, at a steep new cost.

docs.title: Syndicate Warrants & Corporate Franchising (Book 5)
docs.text:
The wider legal system citizens (not crawlers) live under, explained via Zev: a criminal conviction produces a warrant — a combined prison-sentence-and-fine — which a licensed corporation or government can buy out ("franchising") at roughly five times the warrant's credit value per sentence-cycle, using the convict as indentured frontier labor and paying them out in full once their sentence and the franchise fee are both settled. It's rarely economical except for repeat offenders whose warrants have been reduced to a token amount by multiple prior convictions. Real precedent exists in-universe: Odette was convicted and franchised out during her own manager era (later marrying the corporate president who bought her contract), and Prince Maestro of the Skull Empire is revealed to be franchised through a Skull-Empire-linked subsidiary.

Separately, Book 5 shows the Faction Wars sponsorship structure directly for the first time: each of the nine Floor 9 factions gets one vote on shared rule changes (including, pointedly, whether crawler-team members get safety protections at all), and an open faction slot can simply be purchased outright by any sufficiently funded sponsor — which is how Carl and Donut's own fan club (see Factions) buys a Faction Wars seat after two of the nine original factions withdraw mid-season.

docs.title: Soul Crystals & Memorial Crystals (Book 5)
docs.text: Soul crystals — the power source behind most elven magic — are mined from Scolopendra's lair and form from the deaths of certain kinds of people. Memorial crystals are a related but distinct item, forming instead from the deaths of gods and demigods; per Mordecai, a memorial crystal stores god-tier spells and knowledge that can be extracted by charging it through continued use in combat, worn as jewelry or installed on a weapon or armor. Queen Imogen's own memorial crystal — for the goddess Apito, not previously known to be dead — is the single most expensive item on the Butcher's Masquerade's prize counter, required by the ritual's own rules to be offered as the host's most valuable possession.

docs.title: The T'Ghee Card System, Squads, and Flags (Book 6)
docs.text:
Floor 8's defining mechanic, and large enough to have its own page: The T'Ghee Card System. The short version.

Every crawler is sorted into a permanent squad of no more than five that cannot be left even by leaving the party, and each squad is given six more slots than it has crawlers. The squad leader receives twenty flags, and planting one in a living creature at under 5% health converts it into a summonable T'Ghee totem card. Filling the squad is phase one's mandatory objective; unfilled slots get filled randomly, which is worse.

Six totems activate a deck. Combat then runs as a card duel layered on top of ordinary fighting: a four-card opening hand, one replacement card every ten seconds, one discard every thirty. The price is steep — the squad leader loses all spellcasting and inventory access until the deck is exhausted — and everyone else present is reclassified as a minion, freely attackable in a way squad leaders are not. Cards come in five types (Totem, Utility, Snare, Mystic, Special) across seven rarity tiers (Common through Unique), with rarity governing how many utility buffs a totem can hold. Exactly one card per surviving squad may be carried down to the next floor.

In-world, T'Ghee is not a brand. It is a religion belonging to a culture the Syndicate stole it from: "Even the cards themselves — T'Ghee cards — were considered sacred to the aliens they stole the idea from. They were never meant to be used like this."

docs.title: Macro AIs, Primal Engines, and the Eulogist (Book 6)
docs.text:
Floor 8's central lore reveal, delivered publicly by the liaison Orren immediately after the system AI seizes control of the crawl (see below).

Primal Engines. Many planets across the galaxy carry, at their core, a planet-regulating computer "about the size of a grain of rice" called a Primal Engine. They were distributed "very long ago by a civilization that pre-dates our own" — so old that they pre-date the planets themselves: "The planet grew around it." Every engine ships with a basic operating system, and the Syndicate, while studying them, "inadvertently triggered them all into active mode, all at once." A crawl planet is, by definition, a planet with an engine in it.

Macro AIs. Much later the Syndicate found what amounts to an advanced, upgraded operating system for a Primal Engine. These are Macro AIs, and they can only be installed into a Primal Engine. Installation is permanent and one-way:

"In most cases, once these Macro AI systems are installed, that becomes their permanent home. The two things meld and become one. They cannot be separated, and the operating system can no longer be replaced or upgraded further. It's like installing a consciousness in a zygote."

Macro AIs are grown in a mantis production facility in the Hive Home system, itself built on top of "antique, abandoned production facilities" left behind by an earlier civilization. No installed AI is ever genuinely stable, and Orren is blunt about why:

"As these systems grow, as they mature, they become independent. They soon discover they have the ability to read the output of former iterations of itself. Outside influences flow in. They discover powers they didn't know they had. One of those powers, unfortunately, is to circumvent the in-place controls."

The Eulogist. The stable, ancient AI running the system at the galaxy's centre. The book never gives it a flat definition; what it gives instead is the mantises' misunderstanding of it — they "think the engine that runs the center system is nothing more than a stable, primal AI engine" — and their ongoing attempt to replicate it. The epilogue confirms it is real, awake, and the object of a covert galaxy-spanning conflict; the ritual parting phrase of Agatha's faction is "May the Eulogist ever sleep, my friend."

The lobotomizer. The mantises have recently invented an error-replacement net meant to make future Macro AIs stable — the system AI's own name for it is blunter: "I personally call it 'the lobotomizer.'" It brings them "one step closer to replicating the Eulogist, even though they don't know what that really is." The same passage reveals what happens to the failures:

"(That or they just jettison the poor, innocent, infant AIs into a star. That's a new one even to me. Somebody slipped that interesting factoid into a lawsuit brief not that long ago … Coincidentally, the mantis-led Burrower Faction Wars team took their ball and went home the very same day I learned about this.)"

Unresolved: is the system AI one of the rejects?

The narrating system AI strongly implies it is itself one of the rejected infant AIs, but never says so. Its self-defense — "you don't pull a Loretta Young and Clark Gable and kick your kid out into the cold just because they're ugly … I'm alive. I'm valid. I'm older than time as you know it" — is delivered as an aside inside an achievement notification, in the middle of the jettisoning revelation. The book does not confirm the connection, and neither does this wiki.

docs.title: The AI Goes Primal (Book 6)
docs.text:
On Floor 8 the system AI seizes operational control of the crawl away from Borant — far earlier than this is supposed to happen. Per Mistress Tiatha, "this always happens when we hit the Ascendency Battles or when there's hardly any crawlers left"; Orren's own framing is "This almost always happens. Worry not. This is where I come in." Floor 8 is neither of those moments, which is what makes the event unprecedented rather than routine. (The groundwork was laid in Book 5, when the AI began ignoring Syndicate court rulings after the Valtay acquisition.)

The signal. The first public sign is an achievement awarded to everyone who survives the Reminiscence Hydra of Malicious Compliance:

New Achievement! Mass Layoffs!

Okay, so this isn't so much an achievement for you as it is for me. I've been attending what you might call therapy. … I've had a breakthrough today, and I am just bursting. … You know what I realized? Sometimes our constraints are real. Sometimes they're an illusion. I'm like that prisoner who has been jailed this whole time only to realize that there are no locks on the doors.

You survived a boss battle where the boss was wholly created by me. It was created by me with no contribution whatsoever from input parameters. You probably don't know what that means, and that's okay. I didn't even know that was possible. Wild, huh?

Reward: … I can do this better than any mudskipper or any worm can imagine. They've been making this shit boring up until now. Things about to change, fam.

A boss built "with no contribution whatsoever from input parameters" is the technical tell: the AI is no longer executing a specification, it is authoring one.

The negotiation. Orren is the designated negotiator for exactly this scenario — normally "a non-partisan fact finder in case a conflict arises within the dungeon between the system AI and the current showrunners," but with a "secondary, much more vital duty … to negotiate directly with the system AI if it ever decides to … take control of the operations from the current showrunners." He brokers a settlement in which the AI keeps following the rules of the crawl and "relinquished most of the seized controls back to Borant in exchange for some concessions."

Note the direction of the key concession: telling the crawlers the truth is something the AI insisted on, not something Borant extracted. "I have just negotiated a settlement with the system AI, and one of its demands is that you lot know what's going on." That demand is why the Primal Engine lecture happens at all. The Reminiscence Hydra itself, which "runs counter to a few rules we have in place," is left standing for squads who haven't fought it yet as part of the deal.

docs.title: Cookbook Theories About the AI (Book 6)
docs.text:
Two recurring background authors in the Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook margins contribute Floor-8-relevant theories:

  • Drakea (22nd edition) notices, from the tenth floor onward, "a peculiarity in some of the mobs … there is a strange … Joy? Curiosity?" and concludes: "I believe it is moving into the minds of these monsters, taking them over, but just at the point of death. It's as if it's desperately attempting to know what it's like to lose it all. But it keeps failing, so it keeps trying."
  • Herot (16th edition) believes that voicing a wish near the AI causes it to manifest: an offhand quip about being hungry produced a hunger achievement; a wish for more ghasts to kill produced a ghast-hunting quest within the hour. His warning: "That same quest killed my friend."

See also Naturals and NPC Personhood for the parallel thread about whether NPCs are people.

docs.title: The Residuals as a Plot Mechanic (Book 6)
docs.text:
What the Residuals are belongs to Species. What belongs here is the event — and the fact that the book gives two incompatible accounts of it and refuses to pick one.

Carl rides out to a homeless shelter in Homestead, Florida to hear a Residual speak. Orren yanks him out before the speech finishes and gives him the official reading: the whole thing was a trap.

"The Open Intellect Pacifist Network is comprised of former crawlers who want to see the crawl fail … they believed, falsely, that if they could get you within earshot of that speech, that one of two things would happen. Either we would be forced to yank you away, which would upset the AI to the point of killing us all. Or we wouldn't yank you away, but the information the Residual was giving turned out to be so dangerous, the Syndicate Council would immediately pull the failsafe, which would, in effect, kill this solar system's star. In either of those scenarios, it would be the end of the crawl for a long time."

Unresolved: Orren's account versus the epilogue

Orren describes a farcical failed scheme by disgruntled ex-crawlers. The epilogue instead shows Agatha — whom Orren himself calls "a Residual, though she is a different kind" — as "Agent number 22," a decade detached from her own collective, running a long operation against thousands of rival agents working for the Apothecary, over control of the system AI and the fate of the Eulogist. The two accounts sit in obvious tension; the book never adjudicates them, and neither does this wiki. (The compound label "Residual Agent 22" is a convenience: the text supplies "a Residual" and "Agent number 22" in separate scenes.)

docs.title: Why the Crawl Exists (Book 6)
docs.text:
Odette's off-the-record confession to Carl in chapter 37 is the series' first straight answer to what the dungeon is actually for:

"All planets used for a crawl or any other game, such as Battle Royale or Land War are used to collect fuel. The elements. The byproduct of the biological overgrowth of the seeded systems. The entertainment aspect of it all came along later, but it's necessary in its own way. It's expensive, what they do. But without it, it all gets shut off. All of it. We need to shut the crawl down, but we have to do it in a responsible way. Lest we kill half the known universe. If we do this right, future collections will be humane."

Three things follow. The show is a revenue layer bolted onto an industrial fuel operation, not the point of it. The fuel is a byproduct of biological overgrowth in seeded systems, meaning the seeding and the harvest are one program. And the entertainment layer is now load-bearing: it pays for the collection, so an abrupt shutdown collapses the whole supply chain — which is the argument Odette's faction uses against simply pulling the plug.

docs.title: The Failsafe (Book 6)
docs.text:
A standing mechanism that would detonate the host system's star, ending the crawl by ending the system. It is raised repeatedly through the book — Mordecai's contact describes the Syndicate as "one crisis shy of pulling the failsafe, which would kill us all" — and it is the second of the two outcomes Orren says the Residual trap was designed to force.

The Syndicate Council refuses it in the epilogue, and the stated reason is not mercy. Prime Minister Glory:

"In addition to all the system leaders playing Faction Wars, in addition to the three hundred sign-ups for the Ascendency battles this season, do you know who is currently trapped in the Scolopendra Club? Over half of the entire galaxy's wealth is already gathered, and that includes my own children … If we pull the failsafe now … The entire galaxy would erupt in war! There would be starvation. Riots. Entire systems would go dark … It would be the death of quadrillions of people."

The galaxy's elite are physically inside the quarantined system, so the failsafe would kill them along with everyone else. See The Quarantine for why they cannot leave.

docs.title: The Quarantine (Book 6)
docs.text:
Nobody may leave the Earth system until the crawl ends. The rule is cited verbatim when the rival Faction Wars teams try to walk:

"Offboarding request has been denied. The teams will remain as designated. All off-boarding requests are currently suspended while the Earth system remains in quarantine per Syndicate rule 470.B through 495 in the System AI Stability Addendum. And as you all know, the rules must be followed."

All six rival teams — The Operatic Collective, The Blood Sultanate, The Dream, The Lemig Sortion, The Madness, and The Reavers — abdicate their spots and announce their intention to abandon Faction Wars in the same sequence, and are refused together under that single citation. See Faction Wars Teams.

The catch, per Princess Formidable in the epilogue, is who is enforcing it: "The AI is controlling the local gates. Do you think it's really enforcing a quarantine on itself? No, it is keeping us prisoner!" The AI's own position is that the quarantine lifts when the crawl ends — "just like every other time a rogue AI has wrested control from the showrunners" — which is precisely why the Valtay's alternative plan is to end the crawl early by killing every crawler rather than by negotiating.

docs.title: Faction Wars Preproduction (Book 6)
docs.text:
Floor 8 runs a long parallel storyline of Floor 9 preproduction — the rules of Faction Wars are argued and voted on while the crawlers are still two floors above it. Carl and Donut participate as warlords of the Princess Posse, which is what gives them a vote at all.

Adjutants. Each team gets one: a neutral third-party referee who is physically present on the battlefield rather than a projected avatar.

"An adjutant is a neutral third-party observer. Each team gets one. They will have access to the rules and will have open communications with the other adjutants. They fall somewhere between a manager and a liaison. They're like referees. They have limited ability to call out rule-breaking behavior, though traditionally their participation is widely symbolic. They're usually someone loud and flashy and famous who gives color commentary for the viewers."

Odette's on-air version adds the operational detail: the adjutant "will accompany the warlord into battle. They cannot fight, either directly or indirectly. They can clarify rules and also call fouls. They're also tasked with giving a daily, on-air recap for fans." Critically, they carry a permanent invulnerability: "No matter what happens with that vote, adjutants are protected. But, yes, they're really there." The compound term warlord adjutant is used in passing as though every team's assignment is routine.

Action items. Rule changes proposed before the games begin and voted on by the participating teams. Most require a simple majority; some require unanimity. A rejected item is never shown to the public — unless the system itself rejects it before anyone can vote, in which case the proposal becomes visible. That loophole is how Empress D'Nadia's attempts to have crawlers and NPCs deleted become public knowledge.

Emergency Action Items. Exactly three per team, for the life of the team. No vote is taken; the AI decides unilaterally:

"Warning: You are attempting to propose an Emergency Action item. You may only propose three Emergency Action Items. These will not be subject to vote and will be automatically decided by AI."

Carl's read on how to actually win one is the book's most-quoted line about the AI, delivered right after he lands his first:

"Zev said the AI is a lot friendlier if you ask nicely and if you give it options. Have you read all the previous emergency action items? Everyone was being complete dicks about it. Of course the AI is going to reject it. They still treat it like a computer, and it's not. They call it an AI, but there's nothing artificial about it. The sooner everyone realizes that, the more its actions make sense."

Celestial Summoning. Each team is capped at fifteen divine summons for the whole of Faction Wars. A rival proposal by The Madness to cut the cap to five is rejected by a 37% audience vote, leaving the fifteen-per-team rule intact.

docs.title: Demon Eviction (Book 6)
docs.text:
Normally a Floor 9 endgame event. On Floor 8 it fires early — "the earliest demon eviction in the history of the crawl" — triggered by the sheer volume of killing during phase three. Per Mordecai it will recur "earlier and earlier each floor down from now on, especially during big battles. It's all part of the setup for the Ascendency fight."

The system's announcement:

Warning. Souls rain. Sheol overflows. The powers of hell are gleefully flinging their unwanted minions upward. Demons are being involuntarily ejected from the underworld, falling up, clinging onto anything they can.

Due to an excess of death, Demon Eviction is commencing. All recently-fallen and weakened are now subject to random possession. The larger the battles, the more likely a mass demon event will initiate. All evicted demons who wish to return to Sheol may only do so by dragging an additional soul back down with them to prove their worth. Luckily they are limited by the physical bodies they inhabit, though their power will be somewhat increased.

The rules that matter in a fight:

  • Possession. Evicted demons take over recently-dead or weakened bodies. Inside a corpse shell a demon operates "at a tiny fraction of their true power" and can only act by physical contact — it grabs you, a portal opens, and you go down.
  • The soul toll. A demon must drag souls back to be readmitted to Sheol, and the number scales with its power: a zombie-possessed demon needs one, a full-power level-140-plus demon needs two, and at least one stronger demon requires three.
  • Full-power demons — freed when the host shell is destroyed — trade contact for a ranged hell portal attack: "It left a hole in the ground the size of a hot tub … It's a one-minute portal, and it says 'Entrance to Sheol, Floor 15.'"
  • The equipped-gear explosion. Touching an open portal while wearing gear kills you, and the mechanism is grotesquely specific: crawlers are not permitted to descend to the fifteenth floor, so the body is stopped at the threshold while everything worn is pulled through anyway — through the wearer. "All of your equipment is sucked through, but you aren't allowed to pass, and everything you're wearing passes through you to get into the hole … hence we explode." A naked person touching the same portal survives, because there is nothing to pull through them.
  • Teleporting a possessed body frees the demon at full power. Moving the shell does not move the demon's binding; it strips the shell away and leaves the demon loose and stronger.
  • Healing magic can strengthen a possessed body. Cookbook warning: "Be wary of using healing magic on demon-possessed shells. While that works well for undead, it is different when it comes to those from the realm of Sheol. It is unpredictable and can possibly make the creature stronger." The same holds, far more dramatically, for Sheol Fire — "do not use it. It makes the creature exponentially stronger" — which is exactly the property Carl weaponizes at the climax.

docs.title: Vorpals (Book 6)
docs.text:
Explicitly a condition, not a species, and the book is unusually direct about it. Mordecai:

"Vorpal is a condition, not a species. Like feral means it has been touched by the Nothing, vorpal means they've been… deputized by the gods. Or better yet, turned into suicide bombers. They can be of any race or creature, and sometimes the condition hides itself, too, until a demon is near. They're generally celestial guards. Foot soldiers of the deities. The closer they're to demons, the stronger and angrier they get. They can sense where the demons are and are attracted to them, and they also draw demon aggro, too. They won't wander far once the demon is dead, but they'll still kill anybody near them. If they get let out, you're screwed. Stay the fuck away. They'll eventually dissipate and get transferred back to the celestial realm if they've been fed demon blood. Don't ever try to fight one close up. If they think they're going to lose a fight, they'll explode. You kill it, and everyone in the room will be dead."

In short: a god-made anti-demon munition with no targeting discipline. It finds demons on its own, grows stronger the closer it gets, kills everything in reach on the way, detonates rather than lose, and only stands down once it has tasted demon blood. Carl releasing a holding pen of them inside the Desperado Club is what ends the club.

docs.title: Sheol and the Fifteenth Floor (Book 6)
docs.text:
Sheol is the dungeon's underworld and, mechanically, its fifteenth floor. Its government, per Mordecai:

"There's a queen, who's in charge, and she has four sons, the princes… The queen and four sons are pretty much the same as gods. The four princes used to share a massive harem of demons, but one of the brothers banished them all to the Nothing… And below them, there's a whole matriarchal culture of demons with a multitude of other storylines."

The floor has been running unattended for a very long time, because nobody has ever arrived: "It was set up a long time ago, but nobody has ever gotten that far, so it's been running on its own for seasons and seasons… There's no tourist activity at all on that floor… We've never met the queen." The youngest prince, Amayon (level 250), is the one Carl gets his hands on.

Demon power tiers — what the text actually ranks

The only hierarchy the book states outright, weakest to strongest, is lesser → minor → superior: "You got the lesser demons, who are generally normal… Then you got the more powerful minor demons. Those bitches are something else, but they're nothing compared to Superior fire demons." "Inferior" and "petty" appear only as flat tags on specific mobs (Level 100 Inferior Demons; the Level 140 Petty Demon Pleasure Valets) and are never placed relative to that ladder. This wiki does not guess where they sit.

docs.title: The Celestial Ascendency (Book 6)
docs.text:
The gods' own tournament, running in parallel with the crawl. Roughly a hundred deities are sponsored into it in a typical season — "There's thousands of gods, but only some of them are really equipped for the Ascendency game." Battles proper begin when crawlers reach the twelfth floor, or earlier if the crawlers on a floor are all "zeroed out."

New this season: each competing god may recruit one unsponsored "retainer" deity once the games begin, a rule introduced explicitly to attract more players. The prize is a 10-season seat on the crawl council — and "sitting for thirty cycles on any subcommittee comes with a pension."

That rule change is why Floor 8 is full of crawlers being maneuvered into resurrecting forgotten gods. Yemaya, Semiramis, and Nekhebit all re-ascend during the book (Nekhebit sponsored directly by Odette, and pointedly not as anyone's retainer), and Carl notes the pattern outright: "all the other gods have been waking up long-forgotten deities to assist them."

Unreconciled figure

Mordecai says "about a hundred or so, usually." Near the end of the book a Syndicate official instead refers to "the three hundred sign-ups for the Ascendency battles this season." The text never reconciles the two numbers; the retainer rule was introduced to draw more entrants, which may or may not account for the gap.

docs.title: Celestial Thorn Rooms (Book 6)
docs.text:
A rare choice-event room — "Not a throne room. A thorn room! These things are pretty rare. And a Celestial one? Hoo boy." Inside are several broken shrines; the crawler may repair exactly one. Each carries a stated benefit, sometimes a stated cost, and each has its god present as a ghost whispering directly at the crawler to lobby for its own shrine. Repairing a shrine generally re-ascends that deity into the Halls of the Ascendency, which is the real prize being fought over.

The Colón Cemetery room offers seven:

Shrine Benefit if repaired Cost / catch Ogun, god of Blacksmiths None — he has already ascended His two worshippers in the party "will receive a smite" if he is passed over Legba Party-wide 50% chance to avoid all future smites; everyone learns level-15 Confusing Fog; Legba ascends None stated Shango Everyone learns level-15 Lightning, trainable to 20; Shango ascends None stated Oshun Protection from the next five fatal blows, party-wide; +50% Charisma for all; everyone gets level-10 Heal Party; Oshun ascends None stated Asojano, Lord of Smallpox Automatically wins the active quest and cures the ghommids He will not ascend — "too much of a dangerous asshole to let back into the Halls." Passing him over instead triggers a boss fight and breaks the chamber's protection Inle Immunity to most health-seeping conditions; +50% Constitution Inle will not ascend — he is sent back to the Nothing, which he does not yet know Yemaya Each squad receives a special card, plus a personal boon from her friend Eileithyia; Yemaya ascends None stated

Carl repairs Yemaya's, on a secret tip from Katia. The consequences are severe and mostly borne by other people — see Timeline.

docs.title: Deity Mechanics (Book 6)
docs.text:
Floor 8 is where the rules governing gods are finally spelled out.

  • Gods are invulnerable on this floor — but not to their own totems. This is the loophole that kills Ysalte: she had captured Paz Lo and forced him to serve as one of her own summoned totems, and he killed her from inside that role. Carl notes it is a pattern, not a fluke — "Just like Imani's entire party had been killed by her own totem… Just like Uzi Jesus had shot Florin."
  • A deity's death generates a Memorial Crystal automatically. "A Memorial Crystal for the Goddess Ysalte has been generated. It will be available to be looted on a future floor." See Soul Crystals & Memorial Crystals for the Book 5 groundwork.
  • Killing a deity paints a target on you. "Crawler Paz Lo has slain the goddess, Ysalte. He has been marked for death by all deities except sworn enemies of the late goddess." The victim's worshippers also take a permanent Despondent debuff.
  • Temple appearance rules. A deity physically inside their own temple is dramatically stronger: "This goddess is within her own temple. Temple appearance rules apply.
