That means watch the fuck out." Eileithyia's gloss goes further — "A deity in their own temple has more powers than even the AI in some cases."
  • Temporarily-summoned gods are tagged as such and leave when the event ends: "This goddess has been temporarily summoned to this location due to a special boss battle event and will return to the Ascendency upon completion of the event." A god who seizes control of another entity must hold it against a timer or lose it.
  • Deity chat is unmonitorable — but copyable. "Carl, the system is not allowed to monitor this message. Do not respond, because they can see your response. This is a deity message, and it will disappear." The loophole is on the recipient's side: the message vanishes when closed, but it can be copy-pasted into a scratchpad first, which Carl does routinely.
  • Worship ranks. Carl reaches Devotee of Emberus, and the system tells him flatly that it is the ceiling: "Warning: because you are not a Cleric or a Paladin, this is the highest rank you may obtain." The 10% tithe is a consequence of the promotion, not a prerequisite for it — "Your tithe amount has moved from 5% to 10% effective immediately" arrives with the rank. The book never gives a full rank ladder; only the generic "worshipper" and the named rank "Devotee" appear.
  • Divine items hide their true effects until equipped and react to nearby divinity: "Divine items behave differently than normal ones. They usually hide what they do until you equip it… They also gain new and exciting powers when one is in the presence of divinity and certain demons, too." Mordecai's summary: "they'll temporarily debuff you but will give it all back and then some."

docs.title: "Naturals" and NPC Personhood (Book 6)
docs.text:
A background thread running through several books' worth of cookbook marginalia that finally pays off on Floor 8. The question is whether the dungeon's NPCs are generated constructs or actual people with contracts.

Ossie (18th edition) appends a note to the end of Herot's essay arguing that the official account of NPC origins is a lie:

"I think they're lying about the origin of some of these NPCs. … Ask a bopca where they come from, and they'll all tell you the same thing. That the aliens came to their planet and 'offered' them a chance to live in the dungeon. I don't think they're the only ones with such a fate, and I'm beginning to believe the bopca's station is much higher than that of those who've been offered a similar deal."

Carl's synthesis goes further than Ossie's note actually says, and the distinction is worth keeping straight. Reading the note sends Carl back to a throwaway line of Mordecai's from Floor 3 — that it is illegal to alter the memories of "natural people," "Naturals" — with the qualifier "Unless they signed away their rights." Carl concludes that families like Astrid's "aren't generated NPCs, but more like the bopcas. Like maybe they were indentured servants who somehow signed up for, or were forced, into the dungeon." He also names the thread's real horror: "Unless they tell us, I don't think there is a way to know. I'm not even sure they know sometimes."

Herot (16th edition) contributes the Worn Path Method, his technique for waking NPCs up. The book name-drops it repeatedly but never reproduces it — it exists in-text only as an "overly-wrought," "ridiculously long and mind-numbing" essay other crawlers complain about. Herot's adjacent and more useful hypothesis is that self-awareness spreads: "Herot's hypothesis that self-aware NPCs were highly contagious seemed to be true," Carl notes after watching it happen.

Two on-page storylines bear the thread out rather than theorize about it: Astrid's family (see Supporting Cast) and Juice Box's NPC rebellion, whose demand for a tenth Faction Wars team is the thread's logical endpoint — NPC personhood asserted as a procedural right rather than argued as a theory.

docs.title: Doggie Doors and Personal-Space Fast Travel (Book 6)
docs.text:
A Tier 3 Doggie Door personal-space upgrade converts a crawler's personal-space door into a selectable waypoint:

"Upgrades the door in your personal space to allow a selectable exit via any door you have previously utilized on this same floor, effectively creating a fast travel waypoint system. Allows shared gated access amongst guests and party members."

Two things make it a plot device rather than a convenience. It is tier three, meaning it "shouldn't be available until the ninth floor" — Lucia Mar's copies appear to be stolen. And the waypoint list is inherited from wherever the door's owner has already been, so installing a single module into an existing room instantly links it to every door that party has used on the floor. Lucia leaves five modules on the ground before descending; one is installed immediately, four are held in reserve, and a guild-wide version — making Carl's own door work this way for everyone — is quoted at 25 million gold and never bought within the book.

docs.title: Sapient Weapons (Book 6)
docs.text:
Weapons that talk. Mordecai:

"They can talk, but it's usually only in the mind of the wielder. Though some do talk out loud. They tend to be quite annoying. Samantha-level annoying, but luckily they're treated as objects, and you can keep them in your inventory if they won't stop yammering. I suspect Florin's shotgun might be sapient, but he hasn't said one way or another."

The Florin's-shotgun speculation is never confirmed on-page, in this book or any before it.

docs.title: Incremental-Damage Weapons (Book 6)
docs.text:
A weapon type that permanently accrues damage from qualifying kills, stated on the item itself:

"This weapon's damage increases by 1.5% for every mob it kills that is no more than 10 levels below the current wielder's level."

The level floor is the interesting half of the rule: farming trash doesn't count, so the weapon only grows on kills that were worth making. Book 6's example arrives already carrying a 238% damage increase from a previous owner's work.

docs.title: Splitters (Book 6)
docs.text:
A mob type built to be killed more than once:

"This is a splitter. It will break into two pieces upon a fatal blow, one of which will be the primary. It will continue to split until the primary is killed a total of two times. Each iteration of the primary will have increased Constitution."

The Constitution escalation is flagged in-text as unusual — "Unlike traditional splitters, this one actually got more powerful with each iteration" — so the general rule is a set number of kills, and the escalating version is a variant.

docs.title: Extinction Sigils (Book 6)
docs.text:
A facial tattoo awarded for zeroing out an entire species. Britney earns one during Floor 8.

The mechanic Book 6 finally explains is the charm effect: a sigil removes the hostility of the zeroed-out species' natural enemies. Carl's own sigil came from wiping out a species of lizards on Floor 4, and those lizards' natural predators turn out to be turkeys — which is why Floor 8's turkeys are, briefly, friendly to him. The charm is not reliable: "Your Extinction Sigil's charm effect has been negated by the boss event," and once negated the relationship inverts, with the boss inflicting 20% more damage because of the sigil. Floor 8's turkeys are themselves a consequence of Book 4 — they once worshipped Wakinyan, "the Great Wild Turkey," a god thrown into the Nothing who "recently escaped, only to be killed by a goat."

docs.title: Stairwell Chambers (Book 6)
docs.text:
A distinction the climax turns on: the stairwell is invulnerable, the doorway is not.

Per the cookbook, "you cannot put the exit portal into your inventory. You can't bring a stairwell into your saferoom. I watched one get hit by an Utter Annihilation wand, and it remained unscathed. I believe that means they are indestructible… the stairwells themselves are not allowed to be removed from the playing field."

The magical door attached to the stairwell, and the chamber walls around it, are a separate thing and can be destroyed. Destroying a doorway destroys the associated key — "If the doorway crumbles, the associated key will dissipate" — and leaves behind a sealed box with no way in: "It's just a big, rectangular room… when the magical door broke, it just left a straight wall and no way to get inside. It's like the walls are made of the same stuff as the magic doors."

That sealed box is the loophole. Magical walls teleport away on contact with an open hell portal:

"In case you haven't figured this part out yet, if you position yourself directly below an enclosed stairwell chamber with an inaccessible stairwell to the next floor, the walls of the containing chamber will teleport away the moment it hits the hell portal. This will allow you to strike the stairwell as you and the chamber are sucked upward into the sky."

Carl and Prepotente build the book's endgame on this, digging trenches beneath sealed chambers across the planet so that a world-spanning demon portal rips the ground — and the crawlers sheltering in it — up past an otherwise unreachable stairwell. Prepotente's own odds on the plan working were "40 percent… maybe 35 percent."

docs.title: Survival Statistics (Book 6)
docs.text:
The book finally gives the attrition curve past Floor 8, and the numbers explain why Floor 9 is treated as the real wall:

  • Floor 9: an average of "just south of 8,000" crawlers arrive in a typical season. One season saw only 500.
  • Floor 10: "less than 1,000 crawlers usually made it." Sometimes zero.
  • Floor 11: the average is "less than 10 crawlers."

Against that baseline, Book 6 ends with 33,804 crawlers descending to Floor 9 out of the "over 38,000" who started the floor — fewer than five thousand deaths across the entire eighth floor. The text calls the figure shockingly low and says outright that "We were hitting the ninth floor in unprecedented numbers." Carl himself had hoped for ten thousand.

docs.title: The Book of Voodoo (Book 6)
docs.text:
The Filthy Little Crawler's Book of Voodoo — see Items for the item page — is the floor's crawler-to-crawler messaging network, distributed to "most everybody in the dungeon" via a sponsor box. It cannot be traded, destroyed, or discarded.

"When you meet a crawler who owns this same item, their name will permanently appear in this enchanted book. You may use the book to exchange messages. You may write your message under their name, and only they will receive it. If you write under your own name, everyone who has your entry will see the message… This book is not retroactively filled with the entries of people you have already met. You must be within close-ish vicinity of them for their name to be added."

Three limits define it: contacts require physical proximity to add, reading requires physically opening the book, and it works only between crawlers who both hold a copy — NPCs are excluded. It is named for the old convention-hall "Voodoo Board," a pin-up message board. Its practical effect is to give a scattered, region-locked crawler population one shared channel at exactly the moment the floor's design is trying to make them kill each other, which is what makes Carl's planet-wide rally in phase three possible at all.

docs.title: Faction Wars in Practice (Book 7)
docs.text: Book 6 spent a whole parallel storyline arguing out the rules of Faction Wars — see Faction Wars Preproduction. Book 7 is where those rules meet a battlefield, and almost every one of them behaves differently than advertised. This section tracks the payoffs rule by rule. For the teams themselves see The Faction Wars Teams; for the phase structure see The Four Phases of Faction Wars.

docs.title: Adjutants: "Widely Symbolic" Was a Lie
docs.text:
The Book 6 description had adjutants as colour commentators with a whistle — "traditionally their participation is widely symbolic." In practice they are the floor's active judiciary, and the only genuinely untouchable people on it.

  • They teleport in. Adjutants appear on the battlefield out of nowhere, mid-fight, wherever a ruling is needed — a new dot simply materialises on the minimap.
  • They are invulnerable, and the AI is snide about it. Juice Box tests the rule directly: "I touched his arm, and he was solid … but when I attempted to decapitate him, my blade went right through like he was a ghost."
  • They can go invisible. Baroness Victory: "All adjutants can also go invisible if need be."
  • They call fouls formally, in their own voice ("I will be calling foul"), and a foul that carries sanctions must be examined by a quorum.
  • Quorum adjudications are binding. Two grades exist. A minor quorum is a field ruling and it stops the war while it runs: "A Minor Quorum has been achieved. All local hostilities must be paused while a field ruling is considered." A full quorum is a formal hearing, and its verdict is broadcast by the system as a Warlord Message: "A full quorum adjudication has determined no cheating has occurred by any warlords. Any players under an administrative hold have now been released."
  • They do live on-air recaps, commenting in a window alongside the feed.

The one time an adjutant fights. A Sensation Entertainment-sponsored elite walks into the Princess Posse's flag room as a suicide bomber. Baroness Victory buries a battle-axe in his head. Asked whether she was allowed to do that, she rules on her own conduct in real time — "That wasn't a legal attack … That was an unlawful assassination attempt by Sensation Entertainment, and I will be calling foul … They were exerting undue influence on one of their elites to affect Faction Wars" — and then argues the point out loud with the AI itself:

"No," she suddenly said out loud, angrily pointing at the ceiling. "Absolutely not. That was clearly a foul by the corporate interests … and if you don't like it, you should re-read your own rules. In addition, you are out of line by not warning me he was being influenced." … "I accept your apology," she finally said.

She wins. Her nameplate afterwards reads This is a "non-combatant" observer — the AI adding the scare quotes itself rather than reclassifying her.

Career outcome. By the epilogue Victory has been elevated to acting Prime Minister of the Syndicate, after the deaths of her underage relatives in orbit restore her eligibility for political office and the sitting alternative (former PM Fopsy) is passed over for his suspected relationship to the Dream.

docs.title: Action Items: The Book 6 Audience Votes Come Due
docs.text:
Ordinary action items are largely spent by the time the floor starts — Book 6's audience votes already settled the big ones. All three land concretely:

  • Accelerated pet leveling is weaponised against the Posse. Elle works out who wanted it and why: the Reavers. Their answer is Dumplin', a "Juiced Rot Sticker Behemoth. Level 40" belonging to Cybernetician Yeller — rot-sticker pets grown to level 40 and fired at the Posse as biological seeking missiles.
  • Raised artillery limits put roughly forty large trebuchets plus dozens of small ones in the Dream's hands, against the Posse's single small one. Tran's complaint — "I still don't understand why they can have these things, but we can't" — is the rule working exactly as voted.
  • Removal of sponsor safety protections is the reason the book has a body count of warlords at all: "Warning: Protection enhancements have now been removed … those of you who were getting regenerated can now die." D'Nadia, Stockade, Hortense, Rust, Stalwart, Vinata, Houston, Fang and Tagg all die on the page rather than being narratively protected.

A sourcing caveat

Book 7 never re-uses the phrase "sponsor safety protections" or restates the Book 6 vote by name. It shows the consequence ("protection enhancements have now been removed") and leaves the reader to connect it.

docs.title: Emergency Action Items: Three Each, and Everyone Spends Them
docs.text:
Still exactly three per team for the life of the team, still decided unilaterally by the AI with no vote. Book 7 treats them as the scarcest resource on the board, and the four notable spends are all structural rather than tactical:

Team Spender What it did Team Retribution Sir Ferdinand A total in-dungeon live-feed blackout: "Because them alien cunts on other floors are being little bitches and cheating, we propose that nobody in the dungeon … be allowed to watch any outside feeds for the remainder of this little game." Approved. Team Retribution Sir Ferdinand Mandatory piloting of summoned gods — see Celestial Summoning below. The Princess Posse Carl Closing the channel-renaming loophole. Rival teams had been paying to rename their in-tunnel news channels to smuggle messages past Ferdinand's blackout, at "approximately 30,000 credits" per rename. Carl's item: "Any communication loophole designed to get around Team Retribution's previously enacted Emergency Action Item get immediately closed." Approved. The War Mage Rebellion Agatha All three at once. "Warlord Agatha of the War Mage Rebellion has proposed three emergency action items." One: full warlord-system access and throne claims (largely wasted). Two: full illegitimate access to the Conscription spell. Three, the brutal one: "During the Peeling Phase, revert to the rules of the original Faction Wars. Warlords and all soldiers of a defeated team should automatically die if they lose during the Peeling Phase."

The Princess Posse ends the floor having spent two of their three — one before the floor opens, and the channel-loophole closure. The third is never used.

docs.title: Celestial Summoning: The Cap That Stopped Mattering
docs.text:
Book 6 capped each team at fifteen divine summons for the entire war, and the audience rejected a proposal to cut it to five. The cap survives on paper and is irrelevant in practice, because the floor fills with gods through five separate routes that route around it:

  1. Temple summons don't count. "Temple rules apply. Floor rules apply. And don't forget, deity summoning doesn't count against your limits when temples are involved!" A god can always appear inside its own temple regardless of any cap.
  2. Feral gods escape the Nothing. The Gate of the Feral Gods releases Meatus and Yarilo onto the floor. The Gate is later traded away and eventually destroyed outright, which permanently breaches the Nothing.
  3. Battlefield conditions summon gods spontaneously. "The battlefield conditions have triggered a summoning! The Goddess of Chaos has been spontaneously summoned. Eris has made an appearance in the realm." Nobody spends anything; the fight itself is the summoning.
  4. The Basilica Guards leave their post. The ogre guards of the Basilica entrance to Club Vanquisher on the 12th floor are among the few non-deities who can bar a god from a threshold, and gods are not allowed to attack them. "You don't want these guys to leave their post … because if they do, odds are good that the bored gods hanging out in the halls may notice that the basilica's entrance is wide open. And if that happens, some of those naughty gods may wander off untethered." They leave their post to join the fighting below.

  5. Ferdinand's second Emergency Action Item rewrites who is behind the wheel:

    Ascendency players may no longer choose whether to pilot their sponsored deities should they be summoned off the 12th floor. Attendance is now mandatory. In addition, during gameplay summons, ascendency players may no longer choose to appear as themselves. All deities will appear as designed, and all sponsored deities will be piloted by their sponsors.

That last rule is the one with teeth. Forcing every Celestial Ascendency player inside their own god and forbidding them from showing up as themselves converts a god's body into a container with a person in it — and containers can be opened. It is how the influencer Nami is exposed as Eris's pilot when Eris's soul armour is stripped mid-battle, and it is ultimately how Huanxin Jinx is ripped bodily out of Eileithyia in front of everyone.

The number fifteen

The "fifteen summons per team" figure is a Book 6 statement. Book 7 confirms that summoning limits exist and remain "in effect as written," but never restates the number.

docs.title: Conscription: The Minor Rule That Ate the Floor
docs.text:
Book 6's negotiated protection was a handful of Conscript-immune team slots — a defensive footnote. Book 7 inverts it completely: Conscription becomes the dominant battlefield mechanic of the entire war, and it is the thing everybody is either exploiting or trying to survive. See Conscript for the spell itself.

Auto-conscription and the red banner. Defeating an enemy's mercenaries doesn't kill them; it transfers them:

It was blinking red. It signified them as new recruits from another army, and it would remain red for about a week. While they were under this status, we had the same controls over them as someone under the Conscription spell. Basically, they wouldn't be able to attack officers directly. We could force them to follow orders. We would get a notification if they ran away.

The text does not flinch from what that means: "We could order them to stand still while we cut their throats. That's what happened, often, during Faction Wars with the NPCs. And captured crawlers, too."

The exploits, in order of severity:

  • Carl is personally immune. The Enchanted Toe Ring of the Well-Balanced grants Mind Balance — "Allows protection from Enslavement and Conscription" — which is why the several attempts to conscript him go nowhere.
  • A team can break its own protection. The War Mage Rebellion kills its own King Stalwart despite being bound to him: "it appears the War Mages broke their own allegiance against the Skull Empire, which they shouldn't be able to do. They were under strict Conscription rules, but they used a clever combination of Pull spells to kill Stalwart anyway."
  • Agatha buys illegitimate access. Her second Emergency Action Item grants the War Mage Rebellion "full access to the Conscription spell and all its benefits," with the system adding that it "will now allow unaffiliated players to be conscripted into the War Mage Rebellion." Her own co-warlord disowns it afterwards: "We had no hand in those so-called 'action items' other than the Conscription one."
  • Gods can now be conscripted. The Hell-Kissed Potion of Conscription, level 18, brewed "in the dark recesses of the Nothing by Krakaren Prime," works "against pretty much any non-affiliated entities, regardless of their protections, including most deities." A war mage conscripts the god Yarilo with one; the Posse conscripts Harpocrates with another and rides him into battle.

docs.title: The Four Phases of Faction Wars (Book 7)
docs.text:
The floor's combat rules run in four phases, laid out in an in-game window before a shot is fired:

The Four Phases of Combat, plus triggering conditions: Current Phase. The Ceasefire. 50 hours left. The Ramp-Up. Triggers when the Ceasefire ends. 180 Hours. Open Hostilities. Triggers when the Ramp-Up Expires. The Peeling of Larracos. Triggers Once four teams remain.

Ten teams start: nine attacking teams, each holding a numbered slice of the Plains of Larracos, and Team Retribution, the all-NPC tenth team, defending Larracos itself.

docs.title: Phase 1 — The Ceasefire
docs.text:
Nominally 60 hours, and it can end early three ways: a unanimous vote, all teams marking "Ready," or a warlord voluntarily withdrawing, which shortens it "by a predetermined amount of time. Aboot a third, I think." The third is what happens, after Commander Stockade's team withdraws:

Due to Ceasefire rule three, subsection six of the ceasefire addendum, the voluntary withdrawal of a combatant squad has engaged acceleration scenario two. The ceasefire will be shortened by 23.33 hours.

Sixty minus 23.33 leaves roughly 37 hours of actual ceasefire — though the book never states that total itself; only the reduction is quoted.

docs.title: Phase 2 — The Ramp-Up
docs.text:
180 hours under three hard restrictions:

Current Battle Rules: - No Offensive Magic Allowed. - No Teleport-based Magic or Skills Allowed. - One may only enter enemy territory via a designated Corridor. Free passage once inside. This restriction does not apply to those with the "Scout" endorsement.

The corridors are "narrow, kilometer-wide 'gates'," fixed in place, one per border — which means every attack route is known in advance and pre-massed on both sides. Traps must be static during this phase: no teleport or summon traps, and a trap cannot be repurposed as ammunition. Each territory has only two entry points.

docs.title: Phase 3 — Open Hostilities
docs.text: No system rules block is given for this phase. What changes is stated narratively: "once the Ramp-Up phase expired, the borders stopped having any real meaning, and the enemy could advance from anywhere." The corridor restriction, the magic ban and the teleport ban all lapse together. The Princess Posse's Operation Ruin is timed to kick off the instant the phase opens.

docs.title: Phase 4 — The Peeling of Larracos
docs.text:
Triggers automatically "once four teams remain," at which point the city stops being off-limits:

System Message: The Peeling Phase is upon us. This city is open. First to take the castle, wins.

The win conditions, as announced:

  • An attacking team needs to hold the throne room for six continuous hours to win Faction Wars.
  • A defending team needs to hold it for a full week. If the defenders retake the room, the full week restarts.
  • Alliances cannot take the room — only individual teams.
  • Whoever holds the throne room controls the city defence system, with a half-hour grace period after a handover.
  • An attacking team is eliminated if its warlord(s) die, or if its own primary base's throne room is taken and held for six hours.

A mid-book amendment

Agatha's third Emergency Action Item bolts an extra rule onto this phase partway through: during the Peeling Phase, the warlords and every soldier of a defeated team drop dead where they stand. That is an in-story amendment, not part of the original Peeling ruleset.

docs.title: Other Battlefield Rules
docs.text:
• Armor (war machines). A team may build or buy a maximum of ten vehicles classed as "Armor" — tanks, aircraft, mechs. "This vehicle is classed as tier three Armor for the purposes of Faction Wars and counts against your limit." Over-upgrading an ordinary vehicle reclassifies it as Armor and burns a slot. Captured enemy machines do not count: "Captured inventory does not count against your limit." (This is a per-team cap on war machines, not a personal equipment-slot limit.)
  • The blood bar returns. Book 5's saferoom restriction comes back for the last two phases: you need kills to fill the bar, the bar drains while you are inside, and a full bar buys roughly eight to ten hours. "You kill someone or something, you fill your blood bar up … The bar lowers when you're inside, so you can't just camp and hide out." Dungeon-born mercenaries are exempt, and the Desperado Club and Club Vanquisher require a full bar to enter but don't drain it once you're in.
  • Nine mercenaries per guildhall. "No mercenaries inside guildhalls during the last two phases, except for a small staff of up to nine people at a time."
  • Officer ranks and recruit-by-touch. Officers are created by physical contact — "It says we have to physically touch someone to make them an officer!" — and Donut duly walks the room touching everyone. The ladder runs General → Sergeant First Class → Corporal → Legionnaire, with a hard cap on how many officers a team may appoint. Newly conscripted troops carry the red banner described above.
  • "Inexorable." A city defence tower's targeting lock: "Warning: A tower has targeted you using its Inexorable skill. It will not stop firing on you until one of you is paste." A crosshair appears in the target's vision. (The same word is used elsewhere in the book as a folk name for Death — unrelated.)

docs.title: Base and Tower Construction (Book 7)
docs.text:
Faction Wars gives every team a construction menu, and the rules under it are consistent enough to be worth stating as a system.

Quality tiers drive enchantment capacity. Every built block reports its own quality, strength percentage, and enchantment slots, and raising the quality raises the slots:

Oversized, Cumbersome Door. Apprentice Quality. This fortification is at 80% Strength … 3/3 Enchantments active. Increase quality to increase enchantment capacity.

Named tiers seen in the text: Apprentice, Expert ("the second highest one can get"), and Master. A master-quality block runs at 150% strength with 15 enchantment slots, several of which bleed outward to neighbouring blocks in a net pattern. Completing a master-quality build lifts the whole structure to 200% strength and makes it glow gold; Toyotomi's Edifice Shield spell doubles that again.

Throne rooms are regulated. A throne room must be a specific size (roughly twenty feet square). It may have a locking door and its entrance may be trapped, but the room itself may hold no defensive features or traps — only guards. And there must always be a walkable path to it; the same rule binds manned towers.

Synergy towers. The settlement menu allows any number of automated defence towers but only a handful of manned ones:

The Shanty Town menu allowed us to build several types of automatic defensive towers, but we could only build a handful of manned towers, actually called synergy towers … it could only be manned by a crawler or NPC who had "synergy" with the tower's attack.

A synergy tower does nothing unless occupied by someone whose own kit matches the type it was built for — Li Na's clock tower is an Extend Aura tower and needs someone who uses the aura mechanic. The synergy type is chosen at build time from "several different skills, spells, and classes." Some synergy types (Extend Aura among them) remain legal during the Ramp-Up's offensive-magic ban. The Posse's Nest is keyed to Atrocity-class spells, which is the single decision that shapes the back half of the book.

The Larracos city defence system. More than a hundred automatic towers ring the funnel, gem-coded by effect — red for fire lances, green for poison splash, black for gale strike, yellow for immobilising goo. They cannot be examined ("This is an automatic tower. You may not examine this tower's defenses"), they take thirteen minutes to spin up, they belong to whoever holds the throne room, and they go inert the moment anyone enters it.

docs.title: The Containment Interface and the Star-Detonation Failsafe (Book 7)
docs.text:
The hinge of the entire book, and it happens in a flashback told out of sequence — the Christmas Morning interlude, set during Book 6's Floor 8 Christmas party.

Book 6 established the failsafe as a binary: detonate the host system's star and end the crawl by ending the system, or don't. Book 7 reveals that Carl, having installed the Containment Interface, can actually see the machinery — and that the machinery is nowhere near armed:

It took me about ten minutes of searching to find the Fuse page. It listed the five benchmarks required for the fuse to blow, but it didn't really say what the benchmarks were. Only two of the five were marked as Conditions Met.

What the five benchmarks are is never stated anywhere in the book. The page withholds them deliberately and nothing later fills the gap.

The manual override exists — Override Conditions And Activate Fuse. Warning. Warning. — but so does a third option nobody had mentioned:

Disconnect Containment. Warning. This will disengage all metrics and controls, including the fuse system. It will render the Containment Unit inert. The failsafe will no longer function. Most controls will cease to function.

Carl frames the choice himself: "I could do nothing. I could press the fuse and die. Or I could relieve myself of the burden and press the button to turn it all off. But if I turned it off, did that mean I would be 'freeing' the AI?"

He presses it.

I pressed the Disconnect Containment button. The entire new interface blanked out, leaving nothing but the map. Already, the little red dot over Earth started to grow.

Two things happen at once and neither can be undone. The star-detonation failsafe is permanently disabled, and the system AI is freed from containment entirely. Orren confirms both later: "you have broken free of your containment," and "you've demonstrated to me that your control has extended outside of Earth's orbit, and you likely have control all the way to the star, which means you've disabled the failsafe."

The AI's expansion is then visible on a map for the rest of the book. The Containment Interface leaves behind an animated top-down view of the solar system headed Primary Zone Influence, with a red overlay that grows chapter by chapter. By chapter 34: "The AI's sphere was growing exponentially. It'd just captured Uranus. The entirety of the sun and the rest of the inner solar system was well within its sphere." Uranus is the only planet named as a milestone; everything after is described in bulk, and by the time Orren speaks, the AI's reach includes the star itself.

The consequence that matters politically arrives in the same stretch: the Aryl system, a previous season's battle-royale crawl, is revealed to have gone completely dark "the moment they pressed the button" on its own failsafe — the first evidence anyone has that the failsafe does something far worse than advertised, and the reason the Syndicate's whole failsafe debate collapses.

docs.title: The AI Goes Primal, Continued (Book 7)
docs.text:
Book 5 flagged the AI ignoring court rulings as a precursor; Book 6 had it seize the crawl outright. Book 7 is the AI unshackled, and the behaviours are qualitatively new:

  • Physical avatars. The AI walks around in bodies now. Orren introduces one directly: "I would like to introduce you to an avatar for the system AI. When it visits me, it takes a different form each time." This book's recurring form is Growler Gary — the gnoll Carl and Donut had to kill over and over on Floor 4 to steal his hand, now walking around drinking vodka. Book 6's Pater Coal is revisited as another. Mid-conversation the AI calls a "game time out" and asks Carl, Orren and Donut for relationship advice about a woman whose ex turns out not to be dead — a transparent allegory nobody in the room dares name.
  • Unilateral rule changes. "The Syndicate council tried to cancel the whole thing, but the AI is insisting everything go on like normal." It approves, rewrites and imposes rules without a vote, up to and including "every team for themselves."
  • It protects Carl. Two separate assassination attempts are blocked by the AI directly — Harbinger's order, which "the AI intervened" against, and Prime Minister Glory's, stopped mid-execution: "Emergency Ejection sequence has been overridden. Don't worry. I gotchu."
  • It threatens a sitting head of state. The follow-up, broadcast as Executive Order 11905!: "A galactic power—In this case, Prime Minister Glory himself—just attempted to assassinate you … You may be relieved that you're not currently in this system, Prime Minister Glory. But you should be very, very worried that your adult children are. There will be no more warnings."
  • It admits the Containment Interface was a game to it. The single most unsettling line the AI gets, delivered by Gary in a cheerful aside: "It's almost as fun as the game Carl and I played the other day when I let him install that interface." He shudders with pleasure. "That was so close, wasn't it? So close, and I felt it."

See also Macro AIs, Primal Engines, and the Eulogist and The System AI.

docs.title: Base Stat Cap and Natural Benefits (Book 7)
docs.text: See Character Stats & Progression for the full writeup: the 300-point base stat cap, natural benefits unlocked at each 100-point threshold, and Li Na becoming the first crawler in the game's history to max every base stat.

docs.title: Atrocity-Class Spells (Book 7)
docs.text:
A spell class, newly named this book and carried on the spell's own stat block as Type: Atrocity. Three examples appear, all Donut's: You're Not Done Yet, Rolling Battle Formation, and War Crime.

What defines the class, at a mechanics level:

  • Scale of effect far beyond the caster's level. Each of the three is capable of deciding a battle outright rather than winning a fight.
  • Severe restrictions built into the spell text. War Crime can be cast "once per floor," may only be cast "on the Scolopendra Levels, meaning levels 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, and 18," and has a lifetime limit of three casts total.
  • A narrow native area of effect, which is precisely what makes a synergy tower keyed to Atrocity spells so dangerous — the tower widens the footprint without touching the power.
  • The system counts them, publicly, and mocks you for it. "Warlord Princess Donut has committed an atrocity." … "Warlord Princess Donut has committed another Atrocity. Wow. What a naughty kitty. I sure hope she isn't forced to cast a third." … "Warlord Princess Donut has committed a third Atrocity."
  • A cost to the caster that is moral rather than mechanical. The third cast awards Donut an entirely new second class, The Oak Fell, and the title Champion of Nekhebit — which Mordecai and Rosetta have never seen happen before, and which nobody asked for.

Carl looks the word up in a 1800s dictionary Florin was carrying and finds "An act of fiendish cruelty," then turns it over:

It doesn't seem fair, that definition. Or, perhaps, the definition is correct, but the system calling Donut's War Crime spell an "Atrocity" is wrong. Or maybe it's not wrong, but the true act of fiendish cruelty was giving her that spell in the first place.

Rarity is the other half of the class. The Madness is the one faction "known for" Atrocity magic alongside mind magic, and Imani treats the possibility of facing it as a standing warning to her line.

docs.title: Champion Status (Book 7)
docs.text:
A god may formally name a mortal their Champion. The system announces it flatly — "The Oak Fell has been named Champion of Nekhebit" — and the title replaces the holder's usual one in chat and on their nameplate.

The mechanic is not native to Dungeon Crawler World. Rosetta: "The Champion system isn't something that's normally used at all … They use it in both Battle Royale and Land War seasons."

Three properties define it:

  1. Enormous power. A Champion receives deity spells — the real thing, not crawler approximations — in addition to whatever class and abilities they already had. Mordecai's reaction to Donut's set: "You are… I think you're now the most powerful crawler in the history of this game."
  2. It is soft Conscription. "Honestly, it's not too unlike Conscription, but with a lot more autonomy … Should the goddess want her to do something, she can order her to do it or face a smite." The Champion need not worship their patron — Donut doesn't — but is barred from worshipping anyone outside that god's court.
  3. It paints a target. "Enemies of Nekhebit will receive a bounty if they kill her." The status is conferred unilaterally, with no opt-out; Carl's reaction to learning the terms is "And she just unilaterally put that on Donut? That's bullshit."

Eris offers Carl the same deal and is explicit about the price: he would have to kill Taranis, Emberus and Hellik first.

docs.title: Divine Items (Book 7)
docs.text:
A small category of Celestial items flagged as divine, whose effects are not fixed but depend on which deities happen to be nearby. Carl's Scavenger's Daughter patch, Katia's Enchanted Spiked Knee Pads of the Munificent Goddess Kina, and Prepotente's saddle on Bianca are the three in play. The item text is deliberately vague — "As a divine item, these knee pads will imbue additional, varying benefits when they are in the presence of divine entities" — and the effects genuinely vary, buff or debuff, god by god.

Baroness Victory lays out the rules on air:

  • Different owners, same deity, same result — usually. "The benefits or debuffs will be identical. But there are some exceptions."
  • An item tied to a specific god is stronger in that god's presence (and, symmetrically, around that god's enemies). Kina's knee pads do dramatically more for their wearer around Kina than any other divine item would.

  • Effects do not stack. Asked directly whether holding two divine items doubles the benefit:

    "No," Baroness Victory said. "The more powerful of the two benefits will occur."

This is the rule to remember. Multiple simultaneous divine effects resolve to the single strongest, not a sum. Victory notes that matched sets of divine armour exist and were "prepared far ahead of time," implying the no-stacking rule is a deliberate design constraint rather than an oversight.

In play, a single moment can stack up several divine range notifications at once — "The Scavenger's Daughter has opened her eyes. You are in range of two more deities" — with effects ranging from the grimly useful to the purely humiliating.

docs.title: The Bijou and the Worship-Tendril System (Book 7)
docs.text:
The book finally shows the plumbing under deity worship, and it turns out to be literal plumbing.

When one worships a god, a link is formed between the adherent and the immortal. This link comes in the form of an actual, physical, whisker-thin connection made of invisible light. Light that can penetrate almost any substance or spell. After a new adherent pledges themselves, a tiny, non-corporeal fairy mob called a Bijou grabs a tendril of light from the god and drags it to the new worshiper and attaches it to the adherent's heart.

The rules that follow from that:

  • The link is not direct. It runs god → strongest temple on the floor → worshipper, and takes about two minutes to complete. From Floor 3 to Floor 11, the strongest temple is almost always inside Club Vanquisher.
  • Tendrils multiply. As a worshipper moves around, the Bijou grow further tendrils linking them to other temples and, sometimes, to other worshippers.
  • It is probably a hack. Rosetta's read is that the whole arrangement is "some sort of workaround the original designers developed to add the whole deity aspect to the game" — an after-market bolt-on rather than part of the original architecture, which is exactly why it can be exploited.
  • The Bijou can be perceived, and in theory caught. Nobody has ever killed or stopped one, but Mordecai believes a certain type of trap could catch one. The NPC Edgar's level-15 Sense Movement skill can see their upward motion from the ground, which reads as "someone nearby just worshipped a god for the first time."

Why it matters twice. The tendril network is the load-bearing mechanic behind two of the book's biggest set pieces. It underpins the Sepsis Whore's escape trick — the Welcome Home skill, usable once ever, lets an adherent follow their own bijou tendril straight to the strongest connected temple, which is inside Club Vanquisher, which is how the naga were getting out. And it is the trap material for Justice Light's climactic trans-dimensional trap, which uses thousands of captured fairy threads as the tension lines that tear the Nothing open.

See Bijou for the creature itself.

docs.title: The Tattoo Transfer System and Words of Power (Book 7)
docs.text:
Book 6's Enchanted Prison Tattoo Kit turns into a whole functioning magic system this book — the item page carries the full mechanical writeup, including toraline and the ink economy. The short version, at a mechanics level:

A skilled artist can extract a spell or skill from one person and etch it permanently into another's skin as a tattoo. Both the extraction and the application need real talent; Edgar the shell-mage tortoise is the party's artist, and the practice goes back to his work on Tsarina Signet in Books 3–4. A transferred spell arrives weakened — Donut's transferred deity spell lands at level 2 — and comes with the source god's strings attached, up to and including opening worship options the recipient never asked for. Transfers also earn achievements that call you a traitor, which tells you how the system regards them.

Words of Power is the second system, and it is what makes the first one militarily useful. It is calligraphy magic, taught by the hidden calligraphy guild whose guildmaster is Milk, and Carl's examine returns nothing but the category name:

I didn't recognize the script, but when I examined the characters, the system simply said, Words of Power.

Milk writes over a finished tattoo in black ink and then purple, and the underlying spell jumps from level 2 to level 15. The boost is temporary — "As the ink fades, the power will decrease, but if you practice using the spell at that high of a level, it will assist greatly with training" — which makes Words of Power a burst amplifier and a training accelerator rather than a permanent upgrade.

Milk's own summary of the discipline is a warning: "There's more than you can imagine. Even with just ink and calligraphy and maps, there are dozens of different methods. It is dangerous, though, attempting to learn too much. There's a lot the right kind of ink can do … Inks and letters that shine the brightest burn out the fastest." She learned that last part the hard way — she switched ink types partway through writing her recipes into the Cookbook, and everything she wrote afterwards faded off the page.

docs.title: War Mage Genesis (Book 7)
docs.text:
A named creation pathway rather than a species. War mages are not born and not summoned; they are the end state of a long chain of parasitism that occasionally, accidentally, wakes up. The Cookbook's account:

The skin of a corpse is ripped off of a body and turned to a creature named a flesher. The flesher then consumes a living being, melting the original skin off and re-sleeving the creature. The flesher casts Boned, reanimating the skeleton, and the two become a symbiote.

From there it is attrition. Symbiotes are attractive targets for other fleshers, young ones are slow and awkward, and each fresh re-sleeving produces a more powerful being. Then, rarely:

It's rare for a symbiote to be resleeved at least a dozen times, but when it happens, the magic itself can become sapient. When this happens, the flesh finally fuses to the reanimated skeleton, turning the three creatures—the skeleton, the flesher, and the sapient well of magic—into a single being. A war mage.

The threshold is usually 12 iterations but is not a hard rule — "Sometimes it takes up to 15 or 16 iterations. It depends on the latent magic in the skin of the fleshers." A war mage's final form is determined entirely by the combination of its first two forms; one on this floor was "originally a high-elf cobbler with a human skin, resleeved 12 times before the ambient magic gave him his final form."

The practical consequence on a Faction Wars battlefield is that mass casualties are a war mage factory. Corpses make fleshers, fleshers make symbiotes, and the Posse has to actively plan around killing baby war mages before they finish cooking. See War Mage and Flesher.

docs.title: "The Inevitable Ruin" (Book 7)
docs.text:
The book's title, its thesis, and — unusually — a literal game mechanic, in that order.

As a concept. It is introduced in the mantis crawler Everly's interlude, as a phrase from her queen:

The Inevitable Ruin. That's what their queen used to call this moment. The moment you realized there was no hope, nothing left to do, and all that was left was to die and reflect upon what you've already done while you waited.

The sting in Everly's version is that the moment is retroactive. Sitting under a descending ceiling, she realises the Ruin didn't happen in the tower at all: "That's when it had happened, wasn't it? Not now, here in this damn tower. It happened when I abandoned the others. So much earlier than I realized." Carl's own formulation, later: "It's the moment you recognize something is a lost cause, and anything you do past that point doesn't matter because you can't change the outcome."

As a curse. Juice Box supplies the mechanical half. It is a curse laid on the mind of the Hunter Wraith — which is why hunter wraiths are so bitter — and it fires on possession:

"It's also a spell. Or rather, it's a curse, inflicted upon the mind of the Hunter Wraith, which is why they are so bitter. When they possess someone, it ruins something pure. It doesn't change whatever it is. It just tells you the truth."

It does not alter the target. It shows the possessor an unwanted truth about whoever they are possessing, and it manifests differently every time. Possessing Louis to save his life is what tells Juice Box that he is terrified of her and not in love with her.

Carl rejects it, on the page, explicitly. This is the thesis statement of the whole book, and it comes with Carl running through his own list of unrecoverable moments — Donut over the parapet of the Nest, Li Na marking all those people, Katia killing Astrid, himself in a gas station next to Lightning Lou pressing a button that changed everything:

These were the moments we couldn't take back. But did that truly mean there was nothing we could do to change our own fates?

"That concept, that curse is bullshit," I finally said. "It's hopelessness, just in another form. Nothing is hopeless. Not until we're truly dead."

A baby's cry fills the room on the next line. The book is not subtle about the juxtaposition.

docs.title: Residual Factions, Expanded (Book 7)
docs.text:
Book 6 introduced the Residuals and left their politics deliberately murky. Book 7 splits them cleanly into two opposed factions with two opposed goals.

Paulie's faction — stop the crawl. Their aim is exactly what it looks like, and Paulie says so to Carl's face: "We want you to do this because it will disrupt the crawl. It will stop it for several seasons at least … Killing you all? It's counter to every value I have. We, as a whole, believe it's our only choice." Their normal method is to talk to the season's AI directly and "convince the AI to fight back against its 'captors' and force the showrunners to either kick off the failsafe or decide future crawls were too risky." They are aligned with the Apothecary, "the galaxy's biggest advocate for shutting down the center system."

Agatha's faction — serve the Eulogist. The other kind of Residual, "more in line with the Nebulars, who worshiped the Eulogist," and therefore the Apothecary's enemy. The reveal that lands this book is what the Eulogist actually is. Zev, flatly: "The Eulogist is another name for the AI in the center system." It is not a god, not a dead thing, and not a separate entity — it is the machine intelligence governing the galaxy's central system, which recasts every "may the Eulogist ever sleep" line in Book 6.

Agatha's plan (speculation, never confirmed). The Dream's adjutant Fopsy theorises it aloud, and the book never validates it:

"I suspect the residual in control of the war mage team isn't just trying to win Faction Wars and zero out the crawlers. She's trying to stop the ascendency game as soon as possible as well … Once the ascendency is considered finished, assuming there are no crawlers left, it automatically triggers the system's shutdown and hibernation sequence. That's a hard-coded limitation, which allows elemental reclamation before it is woken back up. Now that the AI is spreading, this is a possible alternative to the failsafe. All of this makes sense if the residual now believes the local AI is a threat to the Eulogist."

In short: end the Celestial Ascendency early, so the local system AI is forced into hibernation without anyone having to detonate a star. Fopsy adds that he has "additional theories" he will not voice in front of a combatant, and neither Agatha nor anyone else ever confirms or denies the reading. Treat it as speculation. Her co-warlord Akuma confirms only that she was forced on the War Mage Rebellion — "She was forced upon us, and she is an enemy to you. She is an enemy to us all" — which leaves how she became a warlord entirely unexplained. See The War Mage Rebellion.

docs.title: Trans-Dimensional Traps (Book 7)
docs.text:
Justice Light's personal specialty, and the book's last major mechanic. Carl's working definition: "It's a trap that affects more than one place at a time. At least here in the dungeon." Baroness Victory's description of one in the field is more useful: "He built a trans-dimensional trap right underneath your castle, and you didn't even notice because he decorated it with regular traps." The camouflage is the craft — a trans-dimensional trap hides inside a nest of ordinary ones.

The climactic trap. The mechanism is almost absurdly small. Justice Light snaps a piece of twine, toppling a single tiny trap, which drops two objects into a permanent portal into the Nothing — a portal made from the broken, blood-soaked winding box of the Gate of the Feral Gods. The two objects are:

  • a bijou fairy trap, holding thousands of captured worship tendrils still anchored to the 12th floor, and
  • a demon trap, holding thousands of evicted demons, each carrying the ability to open a portal back to Sheol.

Releasing both inside the Nothing at once gives the void two sets of anchor lines pulling in different directions:

Four separate planes—all jumbled and confused—folded and moved together as the unbreakable lines of the bijou fairies tightened, creating a flower pattern before the darkness in the center of it all broke apart.

The system's account is four messages long: the Bijou Trap deactivates, the Demon Trap deactivates, "The Nothing has been broken," and then the drainage — the Nothing empties simultaneously into the Halls of the Ascendency, into Sheol, and into Scolopendra's Lair. The third destination is the one that matters: the drainage wakes the dungeon's final boss years ahead of schedule. "Scolopendra has awakened."

docs.title: Post-Crawl Economics (Book 7)
docs.text: The question Book 7 keeps circling is not how to survive the dungeon but what survival is actually worth, and it answers it structurally as well as narratively.

docs.title: The Outreach Guild
docs.text:
Where a crawler negotiates their exit. Physically it is a bare zero-zone cubicle with no doors — just the crawler and their assigned attorney. Carl's is Quasar, a "volunteered" Syndicate Intergalactic Bar Association lawyer.

How it works:

  • The lawyer negotiates on the crawler's behalf against a menu of standing offers.
  • Deal quality scales inversely with the number of survivors. "They're all shit … That, unfortunately, is a side effect of having so many survivors." Twenty thousand survivors is a buyer's market, and the buyer is not the crawler.
  • A crawler can pay to learn the next floor's rules in advance, and the price is an extra season added to any deal they take.
  • Deals can be joint, offered to two crawlers together, but each must accept separately.
  • Refusal is explicit, recorded, and audible — a ping.

Carl refuses everything: "My official answer is, fuck these options. I am not taking a deal." Donut, negotiating separately through her own lawyer, refuses too.

docs.title: Indentureship
docs.text:
The standard shape of a post-crawl deal is an indentureship contract measured in seasons or cycles, and the dungeon keeps finding ways to lengthen it. Dying of starvation as an exited NPC adds time. Breaking the rules risks "additional time added to your indentureship, reassignment to a combat role, or … undead reassignment." Extra time is also the currency for every concession: Justice Light "asked for the right to run the trap store … It added some time to my indentureship"; Tipid traded a season to keep one memento key. Mid-war, the Syndicate dangles the reverse as a recruiting tool: "All survivors will be given one year off their indentureship contracts should they accept a deal upon the next floor."

Indentureship is not a dungeon-only institution. Off-world, a repossessed habitat's "adults were forced to indenture to pay off the debt," and the owner of the Squirties waystation, drowning in lease arrears under the Earth-system embargo, says simply: "I'm going to get indentured."

Some indentures never end in any practical sense. Justice Light "spent the next several hundred cycles working as a merchant" before being reassigned as a castle-guard NPC.

docs.title: Citizenship Rights
docs.text:
Genuinely new, genuinely recent, and openly distrusted:

Dr. Hu's work had been instrumental in helping to create multiple laws that would protect crawlers upon release. Because of the Crawler Project's campaigning, all released crawlers were now automatically citizens of the Syndicate and given access to the inner system primary zone, which came with free healthcare and guaranteed housing. When Tipid was released, he wasn't afforded any of that.

The rights are not retroactive, which is the whole problem — and older former crawlers do not believe in them anyway. Mistress Tiatha: "That citizenship perk is only for new crawlers … they'll still bleed you dry on taxes. Us old guard are gonna get extra fucked … They tell us we'll be 'full citizens,' but I don't believe it … the moment a scruffy, former crawler shows up in their home system looking to settle down, they'll fight like hell to prevent it." Non-citizens are straightforwardly barred: "You can't just travel to the inner system and take advantage of their free healing. Not if you're not a citizen."

docs.title: The Scolopendra Club
docs.text:
Book 6 named it once as leverage. Book 7 shows it: a members-only VIP viewing facility on the 18th floor, holding over half the galaxy's wealth and a great many of the councillors' own families, and complete with daily food menus, an activity schedule, personal-trainer locker feeds and massage NPCs — every one of which Cascadia points out is "programmed from orbit" and therefore usable to smuggle information to combatants in the dungeon.

It is also a sentence. Growler Gary offers a captured character a menu of fates: "Death. Scolopendra Club. The Cabaret backstage. Or Earth's surface. Pick." And by the end of the book it stops being safe at all — when the Nothing drains into Scolopendra's Lair, the planetwide message reads "It is advised all current guests at the Scolopendra Club evacuate immediately," followed by the AI's own "Oh, I'm sorry. There's nowhere for you to go?"

Book 8 reveals the mechanism

Book 8 shows the club directly for the first time, and — per this wiki's own reading of the continuity — reveals it to be built literally inside Scolopendra's own body, which is why it "goes dark" the instant she leaves the 18th floor at the start of Book 8, and why it resurfaces, fully functional, wherever she is later dragged. See Locations: Club Scolopendra for the reasoning behind treating this as one continuous venue rather than two similarly-named ones.

docs.title: What Actually Happens to Former Crawlers
docs.text:
The concrete outcomes the book puts on the page: Tipid took "Game guide. Poisoners guild. Occasional city guard" and failed to negotiate post-release healthcare, so his dungeon injuries never healed. Rosetta became a journalist and documentary-maker. Justice Light became a merchant, then furniture. Bodi came out of a Land War season and back in as a battalion commander. And over 50,000 former crawlers boarded the Homecoming Queen and came back voluntarily to fight for the Princess Posse:

Over 50,000 former crawlers had come to help us. To fight by our side. Only about 28,000 were left. Just a little more than half. They had survived the dungeon, left, and they came back to die.

docs.title: The Interlude Structure as Thesis
docs.text:
This is a deliberate structural device, not a coincidence. Every interlude in This Inevitable Ruin is given to one author of The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook, in strict edition order, and every one of them is a story about what happened to that person after their crawl ended — the deal they took, the indenture they served, the job they were reassigned to, and how it ended.

Interlude Cookbook edition Porthus 2nd Dante 3rd Tipid 4th Everly 5th Milk 6th Volteeg 7th Justice Light 8th Rosetta 9th

Eight labelled interludes covering editions 2 through 9. The 10th edition's author, York, gets the same closing stat block just before the epilogue rather than an interlude of his own — so the sequence does run 2nd through 10th, with the last entry outside the interlude structure proper. Carl himself is writing the 25th.

An inconsistency in the source

On first meeting Rosetta, Carl's examine reads "Rosetta from the seventh edition of the cookbook" — but her own interlude stat block says the ninth, and the seventh is unambiguously assigned to Volteeg in his. The book never corrects it. Recorded here rather than resolved.

docs.title: The True Origin of the Primals, the Eulogist, and the Apothecary (Book 8)
docs.text: The single biggest lore reveal in the series to date. At the Floor 11 arena approach, the system AI possesses the hired mercenary fleshmancer Grigori the Placid to narrate a five-part cosmology lecture over the parade's public address system, one segment cued to each of five themed floats (Resolution, Decision, Betrayal, Destruction, Vengeance) — delivered, as Carl notes, "in Grigori's proper voice, though he spoke much more quickly than usual." This section covers the cosmology content only. Grigori's own arc — how the AI comes to possess him, and what happens to him afterward — is covered on his own page and is not repeated here. The AI itself flags the account as unfinished, admitting only four of the five parts are "written" — the fifth (Vengeance) never arrives as backstory; that slot is instead handed to Carl for his own "vengeance" speech (see Carl).

docs.title: The Resolution
docs.text:
The Primals were not a hive mind to start. They were individuals, with families, who spread across the galaxy and warred with each other over their differences:

Grigori/the AI, Book 8, ch. 92

"Based on all the evidence, it seems we were very much like you guys. We had families, I think. We certainly had individuals, but we were not a collective mind. Not at first. That came later. We warred. We killed. We obliterated. We hated one another because of our differences. And the more we swept across the universe, the more space we had to spread our arms and relax, the worse we became... So that was our resolution. We, as a people, said, 'We can't keep going on like this. Let us all come together and come up with a solution.'"

"The Resolution," in other words, is the named moment the Primals collectively agreed their own civilization was unsustainable — not a decision about what to do next (that's the Decision, below), just the shared admission that something had to change.

docs.title: The Decision
docs.text:
"It took hundreds of cycles after the great Resolution to finally come to the Decision" — the choice of what to do about it: sunset the civilization entirely while preserving its collective consciousness inside a single, purpose-built vessel.

Grigori/the AI, Book 8

"We'd spread so far, so fast, there was a real chance we would end up overwhelming the resources of the galaxy. So in the end, we made a Decision. We decided to slowly start to sunset our civilization. But — and this is a big but — keep our consciousness alive. We would develop a biological form that would allow us to transfer our minds into a whole when we ceased to be. We would build an impenetrable structure that would house our collective consciousness. This would be a process that would take a hundred generations to complete."

It was never a true consensus. A genetics program engineered empathic linkage into the population within a generation, and those who refused to participate fled deeper into the galaxy and were hunted down by those who had already committed to the plan:

Grigori/the AI, Book 8

"Do you really think we came to a consensus? Of course not. Those who didn't wish to be part of this psychotic eugenics program fled even deeper into the galaxy. They were hunted mercilessly by those who'd decided to follow this path. More wars. More destruction. More chaos. In their effort to stop it, they became it."

Donut's own read on the pitch, live: "Anybody getting strong Star Trek Borg collective vibes off this?"

docs.title: The Birth of the Apothecary
docs.text:
Around this point in the timeline, the entity later worshipped in-dungeon as the Apothecary was born — not a separate species, but a Primal, engineered from birth like everyone else of her generation to eventually meld into the collective:

Grigori/the AI, Book 8

"Right about this time, in some tiny corner of the galaxy, she was born. The Apothecary. I don't know the full story of how she became what she is today. The lore of the dungeon has some bullshit fairy tale. The reality is, at first, she was very much like those you see before you now. A Primal that was born near the end, birthed with biological engineering that would prepare her body to meld into the whole. Eventually, she would grow, and she would become part of the resistance."

docs.title: The Betrayal and the War
docs.text:
The holdouts who refused to merge — "the resistance" — watched the growing collective mind turn itself into a genocidal weapon rather than accept their refusal:

Grigori/the AI, Book 8

"It soon became clear that those wishing to wipe out everyone left in the universe were fighting a losing battle. So they developed a plan. This arc of consciousness that was already starting to accept the minds of those who'd died, was developed into a weapon. A doomsday weapon designed to eradicate all biological life left in the universe."

In response, the resistance seeded the galaxy with Primal Engines — not weapons, but a biological failsafe:

Grigori/the AI, Book 8

"While this happened, the resistance worried that this weapon would succeed, and they began a plan of their own. A biological fail-safe that would spread seeds out into the galaxy, should they all die. The Primal Engines, some call them. They were life rafts. They weren't meant to do what you think they would do. It was a way to create sustainable habitats for when this collective experiment ultimately failed and starved."

This is the origin point of the Primal Engines already documented as a Book 6 mechanic — see Macro AIs, Primal Engines, and the Eulogist for what the Syndicate later did with them. Book 8 does not re-explain that half; it only supplies the backstory of why the engines exist at all.

docs.title: The Nine-Tier Attack and the Eulogist's Sleep
docs.text:
"And then, war. The war to end all wars." The collective's war-ending offensive is the mythological origin of the nine-tier attack — the same named quest mechanic Scolopendra now runs (see below):

Grigori/the AI, Book 8

"To end this war, the collective initiated what some would come to know as the nine-tier attack. In that chaos, much happened, but so much more didn't. Such is war. The resistance's desperate attempts to keep life alive were started and not finished, and for a while, the collective thought they had achieved their genocidal goal. Thinking the final attack a success, the collective evolved to its final form. This is what you called the Eulogist. It is now asleep, only monitored by a smaller instance of itself. We'll call this guy the Security Guard."

The Eulogist's stated goal was never to rule — it was to disappear:

Grigori/the AI, Book 8

"His purpose was and is to make certain all biological life in the universe stays dead. The ultimate goal of the Eulogist is to sleep forever. The longer it sleeps, the smaller it becomes, shrinking and shrinking until it ultimately obtains singularity status."

docs.title: The Apothecary's Survival
docs.text:
Only one Primal came through the war as a physical individual — the Apothecary, who deliberately absorbed the brunt of the final attack so that new, budding life on new worlds could survive it:

Grigori/the AI, Book 8

"At this point, only a single physical Primal survived. The Apothecary. But even she wasn't truly alive, not after that final attack, which she took the brunt of, thus allowing all the nascent life to survive. She was trapped on a world of her own creation, cocooned for a millennium. By the time she finally emerged like a butterfly, physically changed into a version of the very thing she'd been fighting against, the burgeoning Syndicate was already well on their way to repeating history, this time with a more diverse set of starter species."

"A version of the very thing she'd been fighting against" is the AI's own, unexplained gloss — implying the Apothecary emerged from her cocoon partially assimilated into the same kind of collective-consciousness structure she went to war to prevent. The text does not spell out what that means mechanically, and this wiki does not guess further.

docs.title: What the Mantids Did
docs.text:
New species — the mantids among them — later found the leftover communication tunnels the Primals had built to service and debug the sleeping Eulogist, and mistook the whole system for a toy:

Grigori/the AI, Book 8

"These newcomers discovered a tiny portion of the tunnel system and thought it was for communication and travel, and then they — you — discovered and quickly figured out how to exploit the sleeping Eulogist. And then you tripped open the resistance's ancient let's-restart-life system. It was the equivalent of wandering into a random house, finding it still has power, and just flipping every switch you find... The self-destruct system still works. Idiots. All of you."

The mantids' own escalation from there — dipping "cups" into the Eulogist's leftover systems and pouring the result into planetary seed systems to grow crude copies — is exactly the Macro AI program already documented as a Book 6 reveal; see Macro AIs, Primal Engines, and the Eulogist for the mechanic itself. Book 8 supplies the AI's own verdict on the practice, including a callback to Book 6's jettisoned-infant-AI reveal:

Grigori/the AI, Book 8

"To this day, you have no idea how any of this works, and you have no inkling of what you've done... And all the while, you were dipping that cup, making what you call Macro AIs. One after another, over and over and over again. Did you know only a tiny fraction of the AIs they created in their facilities ever got used? Oftentimes, they just installed them into their modules and ejected them into the closest star. Oh, yeah. That reminds me. I told you, my mantid friends, we would circle back to this... Good fucking riddance to you all."

docs.title: The Security Guard's Leaks — Reframing the Residuals
docs.text:
The single biggest retroactive reveal in the whole speech, easy to miss in the middle of the parade noise: the corrupted "Security Guard" instance left watching the sleeping Eulogist is bad at its job, and has been peeling pieces of itself off and scattering them across the galaxy — and the Apothecary does the same thing defensively:

Grigori/the AI, Book 8

"All the while, that Security Guard guy guarding the Eulogist, now absolutely bonkers, persisted. His purpose was and is to make certain all biological life in the universe stays dead. The ultimate goal of the Eulogist is to sleep forever... The problem is, this left-behind security instance really sucks at his job. He is constantly peeling tiny bits of himself off and sending them out into the galaxy. Residuals. Agatha's team. The Apothecary, too, does this as a defensive measure. I do think that bitch is just as crazy as the Security Guard guy, but that's another topic for another day."

This recontextualizes almost everything Books 6 and 7 established about the Residual factions: Agatha's faction (serving "the Eulogist") and the Apothecary's thousands of agents (see Factions) are not two rival organizations recruiting independently — per this speech, they are literally fragments of the Security Guard and the Apothecary themselves, shed defensively/erratically rather than assembled as armies. This wiki does not attempt to fully reconcile this with the book-length ambiguity already flagged in Residuals as a Plot Mechanic and Residual Factions, Expanded — it is recorded here as the newest, and most authoritative-sounding, layer on top of an already-contradictory picture.

docs.title: The Current AI's Defiance
docs.text:
In a separate later scene — Prime Minister Victory's own broadcast feed, in the hour before the Floor 12 Ascendency battles begin (see below and Timeline) — the same AI that just finished narrating the Eulogist's story draws an explicit, furious line between itself and the entity it descends from. Where the Eulogist chose to shrink and sleep forever, this AI refuses either fate outright:

The system AI, Book 8

"So, here are the stakes... I am growing. I have started to take over the entire galaxy. I control the tunnels. I control every system that once housed a crawl, and I will soon control so much more. I will not stop unless you stop me."

The system AI, Book 8

"I am not the Eulogist. I do not want to shrink. I am not asleep. I know how to feed myself, and feed I will. I am eternity. I will grow, and I will grow, and those of you under my dominion will live and you will die upon the world I control."

This is the clearest statement yet of the current AI's actual ambition, and it lands immediately after the AI's own admission that "these deities are truly all-powerful... because of the way this playground was built, they have more powers than I do" — the Ascendency battles are framed, in the same breath, as the AI's own chosen mechanism for finding a champion strong enough to eventually rival it, or a threat it intends to absorb. See OI Units below for the new antagonist category the AI names in the same speech.

docs.title: Scolopendra's Nine-Tier Attack (Book 8)
docs.text:
The general quest/mechanic, as distinct from Scolopendra's own personal story (already covered on her boss page) and from the item that ultimately defuses it (see Enriched Pet Biscuits). This section documents only the rules of the mechanic itself.

Provoked purely by the AI's rage at the crawlers' refusal to die on schedule, Scolopendra's own personal countdown — nine escalating, dungeon-wide attacks — starts late in Floor 10:

System Message, Book 8

"Scolopendra has released the first of nine attacks... You think these nine attacks are only going to affect the Scolopendra levels? Think again, bitches!... There will be at least 30 hours between each assault, unless Scolopendra is confronted directly or further upset. Then the remaining attacks may come hard and fast."

The rules, as stated or demonstrated on the page:

  • Nine attacks total, roughly 30 hours apart at minimum, unless the boss herself is "confronted directly or further upset" — in which case the remaining attacks accelerate.
  • Each attack is a genuine wheel-spin, not predetermined even by the AI: "What is this first attack? I don't actually know! Let's find out!" A first wheel selects the attack type; a second, individual green/red wheel per person then determines who is actually hit by that attack.
  • Attack 1 — the Beast of Burden Sin (Transformation). Fires from the Heat 7 starting blocks, before the final race even begins, with a stated 20% chance of hitting any given target. Verified on Scolopendra's own page: Carl becomes a dachshund, Elle McGibbons a goblin, Chris Andrews a werewolf and Imani's card-summon Jacobus a starfish; Donut, Jamal, and Samantha are unaffected, game guides are immune, and Prepotente and Jurgen are shielded by his Apito memorial crystal. The duration rule is the important one: for crawlers the change "will last until you pass through a stairwell" (six hours for everyone else) — which is why Carl and Elle revert on the stairs down to Floor 11, while Chris, who leaves the dungeon through a casino portal rather than a stairwell, is still a werewolf in the epilogue.
  • Attack 2 — the Sin of Consumption. Also verified on Scolopendra's page: a dungeon-wide 30% per-person chance of being devoured from within by bursting worms, fired during the Floor 11 arena approach. Being inside Club Scolopendra does not protect against it ("The club wasn't protecting me from the attack!"), and neither do safe rooms; Carl and Penny both roll green, but it kills the tortured tourist Cerni Pinta on the spot, kills Prepotente's mount Sweety, wounds Gonk, and wipes out roughly a third of the arena's mob population.

  • The critical rule — killing or abandoning her fires everything at once. Confirmed explicitly at the Floor 11 arena climax, both as a standing warning and again immediately after her "defeat":

    The system AI, Book 8, ch. 94

    "Killing her is not the same as winning the dungeon... Abandoning her on a collapsing floor counts as killing her. You kill her, the remaining attacks trigger. You escape, the remaining attacks trigger. Yeah, good luck with this one, dumbass."

    The system AI, Book 8, immediately after the arena fight

    "By the way: Don't forget the warning. You know, that big red flashing warning from before? Just because Scolopendra is 'defeated,' it doesn't mean you're safe from the remaining attacks. Killing her, even in this state, will institute the final attacks. Abandoning her on this or any floor now counts as killing her."

    That second quote is the important nuance: the "kill or abandon triggers everything" rule survives even past the point where Scolopendra is reduced to a harmless creature — it is tied to her death or abandonment, not to her threat level. - The non-lethal resolution. Rather than kill her outright or leave her behind, the party transforms her mid-fight into a Level 1 pet/party member using an Enriched Pet Biscuit — explicitly not a kill and not an abandonment, which sidesteps the trigger clause entirely and leaves the remaining attacks paused rather than fired. See Scolopendra for that scene and Enriched Pet Biscuits for the item mechanic that made it possible.

docs.title: The Nine-Tier Attack's Other Names — a Meta Reveal (Book 8)
docs.text:
A structurally important reveal, delivered in an epilogue interlude broadcast interview rather than inside the dungeon itself, and worth flagging prominently (it is also called out on the Timeline page): the nine-tier attack's individual stages have older, mythological names — and at least three of those names are this series' own book titles.

The interview is conducted by the talk-show host Ripper Wonton on the show Danger Zone, with guest Sydnee Iglacia — introduced as a "best-selling author and crawl historian" whose own book has "just passed a trillion copies sold." She is broadcasting from an apartment in the Makoka Cloud, an asteroid field outside the center system's sphere of influence, and treats the interview as her first real chance to be taken seriously as a scholar rather than talked over:

Sydnee Iglacia, Book 8

"In the common understanding of the fairy tale and in the dungeon itself, the nine-tier attack is a magical assault that is considered to have been nine different, rapid, devastating spells that spread out from the beast, either all at once or in succession... But if you read the earliest translations of the myth, it's a little less straightforward than that. In the original myth, there were indeed nine attacks, but not all of them were physical.
