Some were what we might call psychological attacks that resulted in rapid social movements, shifts in philosophy. Attack one was taking control of the infrastructure, but the second and third attacks were more social in nature. That, of course, doesn't make for a good fairy tale because it's too complicated to explain to children. So that's how the myth of the nine-tier attack was born."

Pressed by Ripper on the historical names, she confirms the connection directly — and it lands as a genuine on-air shock to her own host:

Sydnee Iglacia and Ripper Wonton, Book 8

"The first attack is about control. The second attack in the old histories has a name. When translated, it is called 'A Parade of Horribles.' It's right there in the text." "Wait," Ripper said. "No shit? You're telling me in the histories, like the things written down before this season started, the old nine-tier attack had, obviously, nine parts, and the first attack was controlling the tunnel system. And the second attack was called 'A Parade of Horribles'?" "Yes, Ripper, that's what I'm telling you." [...] "You're saying this eleventh floor, which is about to start, is the second attack? What's the third attack called?" "This Inevitable Ruin. And the fourth is called Bedlam. It gets a little fuzzy after that."

Confirmed mapping, by Sydnee's own account:

Nine-Tier Attack Historical/mythological name Series book Attack 1 Taking control of the infrastructure (tunnel network) — Attack 2 "A Parade of Horribles" this book, Book 8 Attack 3 "This Inevitable Ruin" Book 7 Attack 4 "Bedlam" echoes Book 6's The Eye of the Bedlam Bride Attacks 5–9 Not given — "it gets a little fuzzy after that" —

Sydnee also supplies the myth's own philosophical framing, which reads as a direct gloss on why the party chooses the non-lethal biscuit resolution over killing Scolopendra outright:

Sydnee Iglacia, Book 8

"In the myth, Scolopendra awakens, charges up its attack, and attempts to wipe out all life. But another of its kind tempers the attack, and civilization — barely — survives, only to rise again, only for the cycle to repeat. That's the philosophical question the Scolopendra myth asks. If life is imperfect, what do we do about it? Is it better to end it all and just be done with it, or do we stop it, knowing that if we do that, the suffering will continue? Does the good outweigh the bad?"

Left unexplained

Whether "another of its kind tempers the attack" is meant to foreshadow something specific (the party's own intervention, a second Scolopendra-type entity, or nothing at all) is not stated. This wiki does not speculate past what Sydnee says on the page. The interview itself is cut off mid-broadcast when the AI seizes every feed in the galaxy to televise the Grigori parade lecture instead — Ripper's own last words are "I guess the AI has taken over all the feeds. It's not going to let us live-comment."

docs.title: Floor 10's Heat Ruleset — "Don't Come in Last" (Book 8)
docs.text:
Floor 10 restructures the standard dungeon-floor format into a seven-race gauntlet. Zev's opening announcement lays out the shape:

Zev, Book 8

"This is the tenth floor. The floor is called 'Don't come in last.' I guess you can figure out what that means. The floor will consist of seven heats, or races, starting with nine teams each. You've been split into teams no bigger than four, and if you're solo, you've been teamed up with one or two other crawlers."

The numbers. 20,221 crawlers survived Faction Wars (see Timeline). Of those, "almost 15,000" took an exit deal at the Outreach Guild, leaving 5,501 crawlers who continued on, organized into exactly 1,800 teams — "a lot more than we originally planned." The floor whittles that down heat by heat: 989 crawlers, representing 353 teams, are left when Heat 6 ends. An Outreach Guild deal window then opens between Heats 6 and 7, and 715 of those 989 take a deal, so only 274 crawlers in 103 teams actually start the final heat — of whom 23 survive to enter Floor 11.

The vehicle/mount lottery. Each team first chooses biological or mechanical (a pet-eating risk applies to biological options, hence Donut's "we choose mechanical" — see Locations: Hungry Eyes Village), then a giant, hundred-plus-space wheel spins and assigns a specific vehicle or mount at random, no say in the outcome: "You get what you get." Results range from a food truck to a "Popemobile" to a military missile launcher. A named garage attendant (a gremlin, in Carl and Donut's case) keeps the vehicle repaired between heats as long as they stay alive, and only one team member may drive/pilot per heat, with no repeat drivers two heats in a row.

Regular vs. Golden upgrades.

Zev, Book 8

"At the end of each heat, you will be able to choose an upgrade for your vehicle or creature. If you come in first place in a heat, you can choose three regular upgrades or one Golden upgrade. At the end of the fourth heat, everyone gets one Golden upgrade of their choice. Also, if you come in last... well, second to last, then the audience gets to vote for your upgrade."

Coming in dead last is normally instant death for the whole team — confirmed by the garage attendant Hedy's warning, "You come in last place, you die just like Waldrip Chris!" — except where a heat's specific rules soften it (Heat 1 allows "second to last" as survivable with a time limit). Losing last place instead of dying triggers an audience-vote upgrade rather than a chosen one, and the crowd's picks skew punitive/humiliating rather than useful.

Containment shields. Certain heats add a survival containment bubble as a rule change rather than a purchasable upgrade:

System Message, Book 8

"The survival containment is a translucent, indestructible circular bubble that surrounds your vehicle or mount. It will not interfere with any existing shields or any other systems of your vehicle or mount. Spells and projectiles will pass through. Its only purpose is to protect you and your mount from the toxic, unbreathable air of your next heat."

Losing your vehicle or mount no longer means automatic elimination under this rule — it means losing the containment bubble instead, with survival to the finish line still theoretically possible if the racer can endure the hazard unprotected.

The blood bar carries over unchanged from Book 5/7's saferoom-throttling mechanic (see The Creeping Apocalypse & Odious Creepers): ten hours of safe-room access per full bar, refilled only by killing things.

Mercenaries. Up to three mercenaries per heat may be hired from a bar in Hungry Eyes Village, and prices double after a team loses previously-hired mercenaries in a prior heat — "Prices will be double because you lost the last two mercenaries we hired."

docs.title: The Horribles (Book 8)
docs.text: A full catalog entry already exists at Mobs: The Horribles — this is just a mechanics-level pointer, not a duplicate. The Horribles are the thousands of silent, masked, non-combatant figures lining the Floor 11 parade route, each representing one individual death drawn from across roughly 3,424 seasons of the show. They're revealed, via the same Grigori possession covered above, to be literal fragments of the system AI/Eulogist's own fragmented memory rather than resurrected people or ordinary mobs — "You take that mask off, and underneath it, you will find what some people call a Primal... I am her, and she is me." See their own page for the full reveal, the mask-shattering transition into the arena's mob army, and their aftermath.

docs.title: The "Stand-In" System (Book 8)
docs.text:
A distinct mechanic from Fursona/"Fursuiter" (which is about crawlers wearing killed mobs' skins for temporary class benefits). Stand-ins are real people from outside the dungeon's ecosystem — described as coming from the resort on the eighteenth floor — substituted in by audience vote for spared or rescued mobs who would otherwise be sent to the Floor 11 arena in person.

The mechanic surfaces first as a quest reward, then as a running audience-vote choice attached to certain kills:

Quest text, Book 8

"If you successfully complete this quest, two stand-ins of your choosing will be sent to the Arena on the 11th floor... The stand-ins can be anyone within my sphere of influence."

Carl, working out the mechanic, Book 8

"This was what we knew so far. When one killed certain mobs on this floor, they were given an option to take the experience or have the audience vote. If the audience voted one way, the creatures would survive and get sent to this arena. But if the people voted another way, a 'stand-in' was sent. It seemed these stand-ins were people outside the dungeon ecosystem. Like, people from the resort on the eighteenth floor."

The audience vote skews overwhelmingly toward the crueler option — "just about 80% of the votes have favored the stand-in" — and the vote is disclosed to viewers before it's cast, meaning the audience knows exactly who a given stand-in is when they vote to send them. At the Floor 11 arena, stand-ins are a visibly separate population from the Horribles despite sharing the same mask aesthetic:

System description, Book 8

"Stand-In. Someone brought to the arena by audience vote. Most are in the arena like I said they'd be, but there's too many to fit. So I brought some out here. It doesn't matter who they are. They're all the same in the end."

They fight and die in the arena alongside (and instead of) the mobs they were substituted for, "outnumbered a hundred to one by the mobs, who gave them no quarter." Per Prime Minister Victory's own closing assessment, every stand-in taken this way was, in fact, simply dead — not regenerated — which she frames as the closest thing to a mercy available:

Prime Minister Victory, Book 8 epilogue

"As for those who'd been taken as stand-ins... those people, thankfully, were dead. A small mercy. If not for the universe, then for them. Despite the AI's warnings, only those from the club had been taken. She hoped and prayed that meant the system had less power than it was implying."

That last detail matters: Victory confirms only guests physically present at a dungeon-linked location — Club Scolopendra/the Scolopendra Club — were ever actually pulled in as stand-ins, despite the AI's much broader threats elsewhere in the book about who it could reach. Do not confuse this with a separate, unrelated observation a few lines earlier in the same scene, where Victory notes that the club's ordinary guests (not stand-ins) "died" and then "regenerated, just like always" during the Scolopendra-to-crawler transformation — that regeneration applies to protected club tourists in general, not to arena stand-ins, who did not regenerate.

docs.title: The "What-If" Apartment Simulations — Ad Infinitum (Book 8)
docs.text:
Heat 6's track, The L'Engle Building, runs a floor-wide, unauthorized AI event nicknamed "Ad Infinitum" — the AI's own predictive-modeling ability made literal and explorable: individual apartments in the building are staged as playable simulations of a specific crawler's life, had one key event gone differently. The AI frames the entire race in its own voice, verbatim, as a look inside its own head:

The system AI, Book 8

"This floor you're now racing through, ladies and gentlemen, is just a snapshot of my mind when I'm thinking of you."

The system AI, Book 8

"Each apartment represents a crawler I consider interesting in some way. In each apartment is a what-if scenario... I'm not psychic. I can't see the future. But you know what I am good at? Crunching numbers. Crunching probabilities."

Confirmed apartments and whose lives they model (not just Prepotente's): apartment 712 models what would have happened if Tran's father had never died ("Would his mother have still disowned him? The answer is yes by the way"); apartment 728 models Louis Santiago's life if a cop's husband had never been cruel to him as a child; a 4th-floor apartment models Archie Mu's marriage had he never divorced his wife Mackenzie; a 3rd-floor apartment (310) models Imani's Detroit family had she never left — her own verdict afterward is that it proves "my uncle would've died even if I hadn't left"; and a 1st-floor apartment (130) models Prepotente's mother, Miriam Dom, as a professional concert pianist who never stayed home to raise him (Prepotente's own scene, below, is the only one the party directly interacts with).

Apartment 214 — owner never named

The 2nd-floor simulation Carl passes through (214) is not an apartment at all but an institutional youth facility "clearly some other country, possibly China," full of girls in bunk beds. The text never says whose life it models. Carl reacts to it personally and immediately — "My breath caught in my throat the moment I saw it... Were they all like this?" — because of his own childhood in facilities like it, but that is his reaction, not an attribution. Do not assign it to a named crawler.

The AI uses the whole exercise to openly wonder, in the same breath, whether fate is even a real thing:

The system AI, Book 8

"I'm searching. Oh, how I'm searching, trying to answer that question. Is there such thing as fate?"

The system AI, Book 8

"You're unpredictable on a micro level, but on a macro, long-term level you're just like any other algorithm... Deliberate actions, times when you've finally had enough, when you say I am going to make a change — that's when your possibilities really open up. So that's what these apartments are. They're predictive models of major events and how our lives would have changed."

The clearest example the party directly interacts with belongs to Prepotente, who freezes inside his own apartment (130) showing his mother as a professional concert pianist who never stayed home to raise him:

Prepotente, Book 8

"This is my mother if she had never stayed to take care of her parents... She would've become a professional concert pianist. She wouldn't ever have known me... She would've had everything she had ever dreamed of."

Carl talks him back from the edge of giving up entirely, naming the mechanic's real danger out loud:

Carl, Book 8

"This what-if bullshit is insidious. It's like a goddamned toxic virus on your brain."

Getting to Prepotente in time is what costs Carl the minutes that force him to kill Jasha and Radoslav — see their own page for that outcome, and Locations: The L'Engle Building for the building itself and any other apartments' simulations shown on the page.

docs.title: Widow's Rights (Book 8)
docs.text:
A Naga legal custom, and the mechanism behind Chandra's entire subplot (her own page covers her personal arc in full; this entry documents the legal mechanic itself).

Book 8

"This was the old Naga law that stated a Naga royal widow could claim her husband's assassin as her new husband. This right usually only extended to the 'primary' wife, but because that bitch of an obsidian had died alongside Vinata, Chandra had moved to the primary slot, even if it had been only for a few hours."

The mechanic, as demonstrated on the page:

  • It applies specifically to a royal widow of a Naga house, and specifically to the primary wife among any plural marriage — a secondary or lesser wife has no claim under the custom.
  • The right lets that widow claim her late husband's killer (the text says "assassin," but Carl killed Rishi in open combat, not by assassination) as a replacement husband, apparently without requiring his consent.
  • Rank can shift the claim's ownership after the fact: Chandra was not Rishi's primary wife at the time of his death, but became the primary the moment the actual primary wife (Vinata) died in the same event — even though that only held true "for a few hours."
  • A Naga court formally ratifies the claim, and treats a public jury vote on the matter as a form of entertainment/punishment rather than a serious legal question: "the idea of 'punishing' Carl by forcing him to marry her was amusing to the uneducated peasants, and they'd voted overwhelmingly to allow the union." The union comes with an unrequested "prize" — the holdings of the defeated husband, delivered to Carl as a fan box.

See Chandra for how she tries (and fails) to convert the marriage into practical control of Carl and Donut's finances, and for the still-unresolved legal status of the marriage at the end of Book 8.

docs.title: Sponsored-Assassin Infiltration: The Minus Method (Book 8)
docs.text:
A named method, not just a plot beat: the Syndicate directly plants a professional assassin as a disguised tourist inside a crawler-facing fan program, using a real, verified identity stolen from a murdered civilian.

The Syndicate assassin Minus is prepared by his handler, Captain Fresh, by killing Minus's own brother — the real Linus, an actual superfan with a documented history and finances — so that Minus can wear his identity outright, backstopped with roughly five hundred hours of injected false memory:

Captain Fresh to Minus, Book 8

"If the AI so much as suspects you're anything other than a simple tourist, it's going to pop you like a boil."

Posing as "Linus," Minus is attached to Donut's fan meet-and-greet program as a harmless, lecherous superfan — precisely the kind of civilian the show's own security apparatus is least likely to scrutinize. His actual mission is framed as destabilization rather than a direct hit on Carl or Donut themselves:

Book 8

A "surgical crawler kill" meant to destabilize the group and trigger an early Ascendency collapse — his named targets are Imani C and Louis Santiago, deliberately not Carl or Donut.

The method's failure point is exactly what made it effective as a disguise in the first place: crowd-sourced, off-dungeon internet detective work. A leaked private essay written by the real Linus survives online, and viewers cross-reference it against "Linus's" on-air behavior and conversations to prove the impostor never actually knew the real Linus's friends — publicly unmasking him in Heat 6. See Supporting Cast for Minus's and Captain Fresh's full entries and how the confrontation with Carl plays out.

docs.title: OI Units — "Outside Intelligences" (Book 8)
docs.text:
A new, explicitly antagonist category, introduced by name in the same broadcast where the system AI declares its intention to keep growing rather than ever "sleep" (see The Current AI's Defiance above). This section documents what Book 8 actually states about OI units; the Tome of Gatekeeper spell page — which lists OI units as a valid spell target alongside ordinary opponents and deities — explicitly defers this explanation to this page.

The system AI, Book 8

"I gotta warn you. We have some other players vying for the throne now. Remember all those AI systems that you thought abandoned? If they can find a way onto the playing field — and some already have — they, too, have a shot. And I should warn you, some of those guys are pretty intent on some old-fashioned revenge. We will be calling them OIs. Outside Intelligences. And like any family, some of them are a little more... competent than others."

What is actually stated:

  • OI units are rogue or ejected former Macro AIs — the AI's own phrasing, "AI systems that you thought abandoned," lines up directly with Book 6's reveal that most Macro AIs grown in the mantis production facility are simply "ejected... into the closest star" rather than installed (see Macro AIs, Primal Engines, and the Eulogist).
  • Some have already found a way onto the playing field — the current Ascendency battles, i.e., they are entering the same god-tournament competition as sponsored deities and their crawler pilots.
  • They are explicitly framed as carrying a grudge/vengeance motive ("some old-fashioned revenge") against the system responsible for discarding them.
  • Tome of Gatekeeper is mechanically effective against them, alongside ordinary opponents/NPCs and deities — implying OI units have a class-based kit of some kind that the spell can strip, the same way it strips a deity's Worshipper Base skill set.

What remains explicitly unknown — do not speculate further than this:

  • How many OI units exist, or which ones (if any) have already entered the Ascendency games.
  • What form an OI unit takes physically, or how it "competes" mechanically against a sponsored deity.
  • Whether any named character or entity already introduced in the series (Group Six of the Big Six, Forkith, or anything in Sheol) is or becomes an OI unit — the book never draws that connection on the page.
  • What OI units ultimately want beyond the vague "old-fashioned revenge" framing.

docs.title: The Big Six (Book 8)
docs.text:
The system AI's own explicit taxonomy of every power group currently vying for control of, or escape from, the dungeon — delivered mid-fight during the Floor 10 Shadow Mimic ambush at the Desperado Club casino (see Mitch), after Akuma had already been circling the same framework earlier in the book. The AI calls it a "completely arbitrary list."

The system AI, Book 8, ch. 86 (the Mitch ambush)

  1. The Crawlers — "But this group also contains former Crawlers, like that Herot guy, that Forkith dude, and so forth."
  2. The standard NPCs — including offshoot rebellions like Hamed's.
  3. The Gods — "the most fractured and dumbest of all the groups... This is also the group I despise the most."
  4. The sapient mobs — Shadow Mimics, the Ogre Imperium, non-deity boss monsters like Krakaren Prime, and the War Mage Rebellion.
  5. The demons in Sheol — "real wild cards... the most organized. Or maybe not."
  6. Group Six — deliberately withheld: "You survive this fight, you make it to the 11th floor, you'll meet group six."

Group six is never identified in Book 8. The AI's own promise ("you'll meet group six" on Floor 11) is not paid off explicitly on the page — no faction or entity in the Floor 11 material is ever directly labeled "Group Six." The strongest candidate raised elsewhere is Forkith, the demon introduced in Sheol during the book's closing interlude (see Supporting Cast), since Forkith is a wildcard entity encountered only after Floor 11 — but this is this wiki's own inference from timing, not something the text states. Treat Group Six as unresolved.

See Mitch for the ambush this speech is delivered during, and Species: Shadow Mimics for how one member of Group Four is treated on its own dedicated page. Factions: The Big Six carries a short pointer to this section rather than duplicating it.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised, Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario, Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook, Book 4: The Gate of the Feral Gods, Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade, Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride, Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin, and Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Boss Tier Ladder
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Standard tiers (ascending): Neighborhood → Borough → City → Province → Country → Floor
  • Separate category: Elites (not part of the standard ladder)
  • Reward scaling: Bronze Boss Box for Neighborhood, Silver for Borough, and so on up the ladder

docs.title: The Ladder
docs.text: Per Mordecai, woken up specifically to explain it: "There are six main types of bosses... Neighborhood, Borough, City, Province, Country, and Floor bosses. There are also others, but those are called elites. You won't need to worry about them just yet." Each tier scales up in danger, the group size typically needed to survive it, and reward quality.

docs.title: Rewards
docs.text: All bosses drop persistent loot that stays on their corpse for any crawler to claim. A Neighborhood boss drops a neighborhood map; a Borough boss drops a field guide (confirmed Book 3) — each tier up the ladder is implied to drop a progressively more useful public map/reference item. The crawler who lands the killing blow receives an achievement and a Boss Box scaled to the tier — Bronze for Neighborhood, Silver for Borough, etc. — plus a permanent star appended to their name in all future notifications.

docs.title: Elites
docs.text:
Elites sit outside the standard ladder entirely, and Book 2 substantially expands on what that means. The Rage Elemental from Book 1 is a punishment-mechanic example — a Level 93 monster summoned by the System AI in direct response to crawler misbehavior, with no scripted room or reward structure behind it.

Book 2 introduces a second, more common category of Elite: NPCs and mobs tied to ongoing, producer-driven serial storylines that exist independently of the crawl itself, active on every urban ("Over City") floor from Floor 3 onward. Per Mordecai:

  • Elites are never "natural" NPCs — they're designed, printed, and imprinted with the memories needed to play out their assigned drama, and as far as they're concerned, that drama is their real life.
  • Unlike regular autonomous mobs, elites can travel freely between urban floors, carrying their storyline forward to the next one even while crawlers are still working through the levels in between.
  • A quest involving an elite is, functionally, a television show with its own writers, producers, and audience — one that will "play itself out whether or not you get involved," and whose writers will protect it (including by killing an interfering crawler) if a confrontation threatens to end the storyline early.
  • Elites carry heavy plot armor as a result. Mordecai's standing advice is to avoid engaging one directly at all — a crawler who "goes full murder hobo" on an elite is treated as the disposable extra in someone else's story, not the protagonist of their own.
  • An elite can simultaneously hold a standard boss-tier rank — Ringmaster Grimaldi is both an Elite and a Level 85 City Boss, an unusual double classification that still followed normal boss-tier reward rules where it applied.
  • It's possible to negotiate directly with an elite's production team mid-encounter (through a PR contact) for narrative concessions — Carl secures a non-lethal resolution to the Grimaldi confrontation this way, in exchange for future exclusive quest participation.
  • Showrunners can also nudge an elite's behavior mid-scene via suggestion rather than direct control — Book 5 confirms this explicitly through Tsarina Signet, whose Vengeance of the Daughter storyline is a licensed secondary production that visibly steers both her and Queen Imogen's actions around the main broadcast's own climax (the Butcher's Masquerade), including forcing a scheduling standoff neither elite is allowed to break first.
  • Areson the Wise — a Level 45 ogre elite allied with Signet on Floor 6, one of three "nodling yearling" siblings (with Apollon the Mighty, met in Book 3's circus storyline, and Herman the Fleet, whose fate on Floor 9 is unconfirmed) split from a single dead progenitor, the three-headed nodling Di-we — see Species for the nodling race mechanic.

docs.title: Death Challenges (Book 3)
docs.text:
A distinct broadcast format, explicitly not a boss battle:

"A Death Challenge is not a boss battle. It's a pop-up gambling event where viewers, in systems where gambling is legal, are given the option to bet on a multiple set of outcomes, with each possible outcome being given different odds."

A Death Challenge frames an existing encounter — Carl's confrontation with the Mimic Rex City Boss, ambushed mid-fight by an involuntarily-summoned deity — as a live wagering event with full announcer pageantry, introducing both "combatants" with portraits and dramatic voiceover before play resumes. It sits alongside deity summoning (see the War Gauntlet item page for the underlying summoning mechanics) as one of several ways the show layers extra broadcast spectacle on top of an otherwise standard encounter.

docs.title: Player-vs-Player: Skulls, Coupons, and Bounties (Book 3)
docs.text:
Killing a fellow crawler ("player killer") permanently appends a skull icon to the killer's name in every future notification — one small skull per kill, plus one large skull once a party's first player-killer skull is earned. That first-kill milestone also awards a Savage Box containing a PVP coupon book: one named coupon per member of the killer's own party, each redeemable — by killing the crawler named on it — for a Gold Savage Box, Gold Weapons Box, Gold Apparel Box, up to three Platinum Adventurer Boxes, and up to three bonus character levels. The coupons are explicitly designed to sow paranoia within a party; both Imani's and Donut's parties independently chose to discard theirs unused rather than risk the temptation.

Separately, the season's first crawler to kill a fellow crawler ranked in the top 10 earns a bounty — Katia claims a 500,000-gold bounty and a Legendary Bounty Box for (accidentally) killing Hekla this way, jumping two levels in bounty rewards alone. The Enchanted Night Wyrm's Ring of Divine Suffering grants a related skill, Marked for Death, that converts a crawler into a dedicated PvP hunter at severe personal risk — Mordecai calls it a magnet for faction-war recruiters and insists it be sold rather than worn.

docs.title: Deity Summoning Rules (Book 3)
docs.text: See The Iron Tangle Railway System for the full breakdown of celestial boons, indentured summonings, involuntary summonings, and the "Soul Armor" theory of what a deity's physical body actually is.

docs.title: Live Balance Patching
docs.text:
The tier ladder isn't static — the System AI actively rebalances mid-season. A broadcast announcement in Book 1 confirms the removal of an overtuned "Blender Fiend" mob line after it wiped through 15,000 crawlers in a single day, alongside an unrelated tier promotion: "The Street Preacher neighborhood boss has been upgraded to a borough boss."

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised, Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario, Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook, and Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: Loot Box Tier System
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Tiers (ascending): Bronze → Silver → Gold → Platinum → Legendary → Celestial
  • Special tier: Benefactor Boxes — patron-only, can contain off-world tech unavailable anywhere else in the dungeon
  • Restriction: Boxes can only be opened inside a Safe Zone

docs.title: How Boxes Are Earned
docs.text: Loot boxes are awarded almost entirely through achievements — comedic, often crude system notifications that trigger for everything from killing a mob ("You're a murderer! He probably had a family!") to entering a dungeon with a pet, being one of the first crawlers to enter a new World Dungeon, or even just wearing gear for the first time. Each achievement names its own reward box and tier inline.

docs.title: Tiers & Sourcing
docs.text:
Per Mordecai, most patrons can only afford Silver or Gold boxes; Bronze boxes "tend to be crap." Richer patrons may send Platinum boxes. Two tiers are special:

  • Legendary/Celestial boxes are rare enough that receiving one unprompted (as Carl does for his Legendary Pet Box, just for entering with a cat) visibly stuns even a veteran NPC like Mordecai.
  • Benefactor Boxes are patron-exclusive and can contain technology from the patron's home world that never naturally spawns in the dungeon — Mordecai's example: "You will never find a pulse rifle or automated power armor in any sort of box in the world dungeon, but it's possible to get one from a patron."

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Boxes can only be opened while inside a Safe Zone.
  • Once you choose to open your boxes, it's all-or-nothing — you can't selectively open specific boxes out of a batch, and unopened boxes can't be sold or transferred, so there's no tactical reason to hoard them.
  • Boxes will never contain outright cursed loot, but "unstable or damaged" loot is possible — per Mordecai's blanket warning: "Always read the descriptions before you activate or wear something. Always, always. No exceptions."
  • Boxes are somewhat tailored to the recipient's race (not class) — a human barbarian might still receive an item intended for a caster.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised.

docs.title: Character Stats & Progression
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Taught to the reader: Book 1, chapters 3–4 — Mordecai's tutorial to Carl, the first thing any crawler learns
  • Six stats total, five visible: Strength, Intelligence, Constitution, Dexterity, Charisma — plus a hidden sixth, Wisdom, that never appears on the sheet
  • Starting values: Based on the crawler's real, pre-dungeon physical/mental profile; a typical adult human averages 3–5 in each of the first five stats
  • Stat points: +3 per level, but undistributable until a crawler reaches Floor 3 and picks a race and class (see Race & Class Selection)
  • Base stat cap: 300 (confirmed Book 7) — a threshold nobody in the story reaches until deep into Faction Wars

This page covers the core character system as Mordecai first lays it out for Carl, plus every later book's additions to it. For the separate one-time choice of race/class on Floor 3, see Race & Class Selection. For the minimap dot-color system, see Mob Tagging on the main mechanics page.

docs.title: The Crawler Menu
docs.text:
Access to a crawler's own interface — stats, inventory, party, magic, ratings — isn't automatic. It's granted by a guide (Mordecai, for Carl and Donut) inside a Tutorial Guild:

You have been granted access to the Crawler Menu.

From that point on, the HUD is always present: a health bar (top right), a notifications folder (top left), and a minimap (bottom right) that can be mentally resized and repositioned. Everything else — stats, skills, magic, party, ratings — lives in a mental menu system a crawler opens just by thinking about it. Mordecai's summary of the learning curve: "Once you got used to the weirdness of it being in my head, the system was quite intuitive."

Two notification types exist from the start: crawler notifications (seen only by that individual) and system messages (broadcast to every crawler on the floor, sometimes in different in-character voices). Floor-specific notifications are added later as the dungeon's structure gets more elaborate.

docs.title: The Five Visible Stats
docs.text:
Carl's starting sheet, read cold, with no context yet attached:

Strength: 6 Intelligence: 3 Constitution: 5 Dexterity: 5 Charisma: 4

Mordecai's baseline: an average adult human runs 3–5 in each. These numbers are not manually adjustable at this stage — they float up and down on their own, reflecting the crawler's actual physical and mental condition, until a race and class are chosen on Floor 3. Every level-up grants +3 stat points, but those points sit unspent until that same milestone. Items and potions can nudge the numbers temporarily or permanently in the meantime (the game's loot is soaked in small stat buffs), but a crawler otherwise has no say over their own sheet for the first two floors.

What each stat is understood to govern, per Mordecai and later confirmation across the books:

  • Strength — physical power; melee damage, carrying/lifting capacity.
  • Intelligence — the size of a crawler's mana pool and (per Book 2) the effectiveness/mana cost of their spells. Carl's starting Intelligence of 3 gives him exactly 3 mana points at the very start of the tutorial.
  • Constitution — health pool and general physical resilience.
  • Dexterity — accuracy, evasion, reflexes.
  • Charisma — social/persuasion stats, and (as later books make explicit) the size and strength of a crawler's effect on NPCs, audiences, and — at very high values — even other species and deities.

docs.title: The Hidden Sixth Stat: Wisdom
docs.text:
Carl gripes to Mordecai about his 3 Intelligence, using his friend Billy — who once urinated on a police motorcycle in front of the officer — as his measuring stick for stupidity. Mordecai's answer is the series' first mention of Wisdom:

"Intelligence told you that bike belonged to a police officer. Wisdom told you not to urinate upon it. We all have a wisdom stat, but it doesn't appear on that list. It used to, but they discovered changing one's wisdom greatly changed their personality, so it's no longer adjustable. I do not know what this Billy's intelligence is, but I guarantee his wisdom is not a 5."

So: every crawler has a Wisdom score, it exists in the system, and it is permanently locked from display and adjustment because early seasons found that changing it altered a crawler's actual personality — an ethical line the Syndicate apparently won't cross (or won't let players exploit). Book 2 adds one clarification without lifting the veil any further: visible spell costs and effectiveness scale off a caster's displayed stats (chiefly Intelligence), a separate mechanism from whatever Wisdom is quietly doing underneath. It has never been revisited since.

docs.title: Leveling & Experience
docs.text:
Killing mobs, completing objectives, and even passive participation all grant experience. The mechanics, worked out empirically by Carl over the opening chapters:

  • Party members share experience. Anyone who enters the dungeon at the same moment as someone else is auto-partied; being in a party pools XP among its members.
  • Sharing isn't equal, and it isn't pure damage-dealt either. After a fight, Donut receives a fraction of a shared reward (in one case "a 9.8 EXP" to her, "the other .2" to Carl) — support roles like tanking and healing appear to count, and simply being present and partied for a battle grants a nominal amount of experience even with zero direct contribution.
  • Leveling up grants +3 stat points (unspendable pre-Floor-3, see above) and, from Floor 3 onward, flows into whatever a crawler's class dictates instead (see the level-up table on Race & Class Selection for an example: Katia's Level 1 sheet auto-grants a boost to four random stats, then +1 Strength/+1 Intelligence per level with +2 Charisma, and no further free points at all).
  • Returns diminish sharply at higher levels. By around level 8, Carl and Donut find the experience curve has become "absurdly high" — they describe themselves as "plateauing," with their raw combat skill (see below) still climbing even while their character level stalls.
  • Achievements are themselves a major XP/reward channel — see Achievements on the main mechanics page.

docs.title: Health & Mana
docs.text:
A health bar only becomes visible once a target has taken damage — undamaged mobs and crawlers show no bar at all until the first hit lands. There's no partial recovery outside of magic, potions, and rest: health that reaches zero means death, and per the dungeon's basic rules (see The World Dungeon's Basic Rules), death is permanent.

Mana works differently: it's a small, separate pool sized by Intelligence (Carl's starting 3 Intelligence gives him exactly 3 magic points), spent per spell cast, and it regenerates naturally at roughly one point per hour without any action needed.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
Distinct from the five stats, and covered on its own in brief on the main mechanics page — see Skills for the base mechanic (every real-world habit and practiced skill is tracked automatically, filterable by level, and combat-relevant skills level up with use and stack multiplicatively with gear).

One addition worth flagging here because it's a stats-and-progression story, not a combat one: skills were understood throughout the series to cap at level 15 — until Book 7, when Carl's Mind Balance skill breaks straight through that ceiling to level 16 purely from sustained battlefield pressure, with the system calling it out as a first: "You've trained a skill past 15 using battlefield conditions, as opposed to just taking a bunch of potions to do it." The same book separately shows level-16 spell effects reached the "easy" way — through a flat item/natural-benefit bonus rather than training — which the wiki treats as a mechanically distinct shortcut; see Mind Balance for the full breakdown of the difference.

docs.title: The 20% Buff Display Bug (Book 3)
docs.text: A long-standing, apparently unfixed bug: the "Good Rest" (post-nap) buff and the shower buff each add roughly 20% to a crawler's effective stats, but the boost is calculated before gear bonuses are applied and never actually shows up on the displayed stat sheet. A caster only notices it indirectly — Donut's spell points read higher than her listed Intelligence should allow. Mordecai says he's filed a support ticket about it for several seasons running, with no fix.

docs.title: Base Stat Cap and Natural Benefits (Book 7)
docs.text:
Base stats cap at 300. A crawler can keep climbing past that number with equipment, buffs, and spells stacked on top, but the underlying base stat itself stops there.

Crossing each hundred-point threshold in a base stat unlocks a free, mandatory choice of natural benefit — a permanent passive keyed to that stat, picked from a short menu the system won't let the crawler dismiss unanswered. Donut collects four in a single evening after casting several Atrocity-class spells in a row; Mordecai's line is the clearest statement of the rule: "You'll have a few choices you need to make for both your intelligence and strength now that they're both over 100." Her picks — Muscle Mommy (Strength, 100), Brain Trust (Intelligence, 100), Wholesale Discount (Charisma, 200), and later Monologue (Charisma, 300) — are documented on the Abilities & Skills side rather than here, since each is a distinct trained effect.

Li Na maxes everything. During Floor 9's Peeling phase, Li Na becomes the first crawler in the game's recorded history to hit exactly 300 in every base stat simultaneously, at level 87. The system announces it stat by stat, then openly gives up trying to have a plan for it:

System message... yeah, I can keep doing this, but she maxed them all. Even Charisma, which is a hard one.

System Message. So, this has never happened before, but a crawler has reached max base stats. She can still raise her stats beyond that with equipment and bonuses and spells, but we don't actually have a plan to deal with this, so I'm gonna have to come up with something.

Carl's reaction is a chill rather than celebration — the AI openly admitting it has no contingency for a maxed-out crawler is one of the clearest signals in the series that the dungeon's designers never modeled what their own crawlers were capable of becoming.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Race & Class Selection — the one-time Floor 3 choice that unlocks stat-point distribution
  • Mob Tagging — the minimap dot-color system, part of the same HUD
  • Achievements — the dungeon's other major XP/reward channel
  • Mind Balance — the skill that breaks the level-15 training cap
  • Loot Box Tier System — how items (a major source of temporary/permanent stat changes) are tiered

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised, Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario, Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook, and Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Locations & Places to Go
docs.text: A directory of recurring place types a crawler encounters on every floor, plus full pages for specific named venues that are places to go rather than organizations with their own agenda (an organization that runs a location, like Rev-Up Moonshine Company, still gets filed under Dungeon Factions instead — the distinction is whether the entry is about the place or the people/group running it).

docs.title: Clubs
docs.text:
Members-only social venues, gated by a pass/tattoo rather than run by any single named organization — see Dungeon Factions instead for locations that are actually run by a group with its own agenda.

  • Desperado Club — Floor 3's cross-instance nightclub/bazaar
  • Club Vanquisher — its upscale, clergy-heavy rival

Both clubs recur on Floor 5 with branches in Hump Town (Desperado Club) and the pazuzu town of Pandinus (a Club Vanquisher, temporarily closed for "cleansing" after Prepotente's hellspawn familiar attacks a group of clerics inside).

On Floor 8 both clubs change permanently. The Desperado Club is destroyed and closed after the Astrid assassination goes wrong and Carl releases a holding pen of vorpals inside it. Club Vanquisher, meanwhile, is finally shown from the inside — including its Emberus High Temple of the Ending Sun — reached through temple entrances seeded into the floor's own geography rather than through a pass.

On Floor 9 both clubs are back. The Desperado Club reopens on ring 4 of Larracos, with the Midnight Market hidden on its bottom regular floor, a Gray Market on its middle floor, and a Cosmic Lounge in the basement that lets non-warlords teleport straight to the 18th. Club Vanquisher gets two entrances per floor as usual — one inside the city, which "would almost always get trashed," and one outside the city limits, which this season is the Temple of the Dagda.

On Floor 6, the Desperado Club's Zockau branch introduces a new rule: each dungeon floor a crawler has visited maps to a corresponding physical floor of the club itself, and — after Carl's opening-day raid strands a group of hunters inside — crawlers and hunters are barred from mixing between those floors, reached via ordinary doors on the crawler side and a secret stairwell hidden in a bathroom toilet tank for anyone who needs to reach a floor they're not supposed to access directly. See Desperado Club for detail.

docs.title: Safe Rooms / Safe Zones
docs.text: Combat cannot occur inside a Safe Zone, and they're the only places loot boxes can be opened. They always appear on the minimap automatically, even under fog of war. Size and amenities vary widely — Carl and Donut's first real base is built from an intact Polish fast-food restaurant with a playground; their first Floor 2 base is a storm shelter. Larger Safe Rooms may include restrooms, sleeping cubicles, food, and healing-potion fountains. Restrooms are notably the one place camera drones can't follow a crawler.

docs.title: Tutorial Guilds
docs.text: Seeded on Floors 1–3 specifically, run by a Non-Combatant NPC guide (like Mordecai). A Tutorial Guild is where a brand-new crawler first unlocks inventory/menu access and gets walked through core mechanics — it's a one-time onboarding experience, distinct from the many ordinary Training Guilds scattered elsewhere.

docs.title: Training Guilds
docs.text: Ordinary guildhalls found scattered across every floor (not just 1–3) — Mordecai's own Tutorial Guild is itself a Training Guild, just the first one a crawler visits. Once a crawler has been "trained" (assigned a registered guide), entering any other Training Guild on that floor automatically redirects them back to their own guide's room instead: "if you enter any additional training guilds, you'll be transported back to this room." They're common enough that groups scouting a floor track which quadrants still have accessible ones nearby.

docs.title: Reward Rooms
docs.text:
A rarer room type offering items not obtainable from ordinary loot boxes. Discovering one triggers a distinct achievement:

"You have discovered a reward room! Scattered throughout the dungeon, reward rooms offer crawlers items generally not available within loot boxes. Most reward rooms only allow one choice."

Pet reward rooms are a named subtype — caged, selectable pet-class creatures (this is where Mongo is found):

"You have discovered a pet reward room. From caterpillars who secrete vodka to basilisks who can turn mobs to stone, a good pet can make the difference between survival and the end of the road."

docs.title: Other Named Locations
docs.text:
Organization-run — see their own pages instead of duplicating detail here.

  • Floor 2: Rev-Up Moonshine Company — the pyramid-scheme distillery run by the Krakaren Clone
  • Floor 3: Grimaldi's Traveling Circus and the Medium Skyfowl Settlement — see Level 3: Layout & Notable Areas for both, and Dungeon Factions for the organizations that run them
  • Floor 5: Hump Town, a Dromedarian brothel settlement, and the Necropolis of Anser, the ancient tomb at the heart of the bubble — both "places to go" in their own right rather than organization-run venues
  • Floor 6: Point Mongo, a conquered Ursine settlement serving as Carl and Donut's base of operations; Fort Freedom, the ruined Naiad river palace liberated during the Vengeance of the Daughter quest; and the High Elf Castle, site of the Butcher's Masquerade and the book's climax
  • Floor 8: El Capitolio Nacional de Cuba, Colón Cemetery / the Temple of Yemaya, the FOCSA building, and the transplanted Dallas County, Iowa — plus the shorter entries below
  • Floor 9: Larracos, the City of Dreams, the funnel city the whole of Faction Wars is fought over; Shanty Town, the new ring around its lip; The Plains of Larracos, the nine-slice battlefield outside it; The Nest, the Princess Posse's Atrocity-keyed synergy tower; and Area 52, their forest airbase

For a floor-by-floor breakdown of layout (as opposed to organized by place type, as above), see the Dungeon Floors section — each floor's page has its own "Layout & Notable Areas" section.

docs.title: Book 6 (Floor 8): Cuba
docs.text:
Floor 8's phase-one and phase-three region for Carl and Donut is a replay of Havana and its surroundings, exact down to the Christmas decorations. See Level 8 for the floor's overall shape.

Location What it is El Capitolio Nacional de Cuba The floor's starting chamber and one of the region's two stairwells. Destroyed in phase three; its doorway's destruction takes every key cut for it. Full page. Colón Cemetery A corrupted Medium Ghommid Settlement, liberated and renamed the Temple of Yemaya. Holds a Club Vanquisher entrance and the Yellow Zone saferoom pub. Full page. The FOCSA building A green-and-tan, Y-shaped, 32-storey residential tower; the site of the book's final battle. Full page. Old Havana The downtown zone immediately outside the Capitolio ("Entering Old Havana"), adjoining Miramar. A named starting area rather than a destination. Cuba Libro "A small coffee shop name 'Cuba Libro'," with a mob-filled park a street over — a named saferoom, never described inside. Iglesia San Hilarion A phase-three drop point: the interior of an old, empty Catholic church, moonlight through stained glass, roughly 50 km southwest of the exit stairwell. Iglesia de Jesús de Miramar The region's other stairwell, and the only surviving exit once the Capitolio falls. Its grounds hold a temple of Ibeji and a temple of the ocean goddess Kuraokami — the latter doubling as a Club Vanquisher entrance. Both gods are named in a single sentence and nowhere else. The church is deliberately demolished so a channel can be dug beneath it for the escape plan. Guanajay A small town north-west of Havana, reached past midnight, with a huge pileup of cars and a population of duendes. A waypoint on the way to intercept Quan Ch. The northern beach A rocky, empty stretch of coast where Carl and Donut capture monk-seal totems — and, later, where roughly a hundred Petty Demon Pleasure Valets are freed from their zombie shells during the Demon Eviction. The Bay of Pigs marshlands The land-crab migration route and the web-choked swamp realm of the boss Shi Maria — webs strung over roads and trees "like a cotton candy machine had exploded," broken crab husks, a moped cocooned in silk. See Bosses.

docs.title: Book 6 (Floor 8): Phase Two — Florida and Iowa
docs.text: Location What it is Monroe County, Florida (the Florida Keys) Carl and Donut's phase-two region. Arrival is inside a dark Victorian mini-mansion; outside is a narrow beach town on a two-lane road with ocean close on both sides. Donut: "we're in the Miami area, but we're at the bottom of the map. We're really in the Florida Keys!" Dallas County, Iowa A 700-foot mesa of Iowa farmland dropped bodily onto the Keys by a placement glitch, complete with snow, a commercial farm, a turkey barn, a trailer park, and Carl's father's trailer spliced in from another season. Full page. Homestead, Florida — "The Shepherd's House" A homeless shelter just south of Miami, found via a flyer: "Don't spend Christmas alone… Food, a warm bed, and fellowship. Intake open 24 hours." A graffiti-covered building in an industrial fruit-packing district, with a wreath on the door and a memory-ghost desk clerk watching anime. Hidden in the graffiti, in Syndicate Standard, is the real message: "Look for me at breakfast every morning. I wear the red hat with the flaps. Coffee then speech." Inside, rows of cots full of sleeping ghosts. This is where Carl hears the Residual Paulie speak — and where Orren pulls him out before the end. See The Residuals as a Plot Mechanic.

docs.title: Book 6: Off-Floor and Recurring Locations
docs.text: Location What it is Club Vanquisher and the High Temple of the Ending Sun The rival club, shown from the inside for the first time, along with the Emberus temple that is Carl's de facto church. Full page. The Hunting Grounds Casino The Desperado Club's middle-floor casino. Carl has "never actually gone into this casino before" and still doesn't — it is only ever seen from the corridor outside, during a security alarm. The Mock Battle Arena A practice arena attached to every saferoom on Floor 8. The base room is a featureless gray hangar; a menu lets a squad pick an environment and adjust gravity, terrain, and crowd favourability by slider. Confirmed presets: the Arena of the Eulogist (a colosseum with a hostile Nebular crowd whose friendliness is the only adjustable slider), Verdant Hills (grassy rises that break sightlines), and a full 1980s shopping mall (arcade, Kay-Bee Toys, Waldenbooks, Orange Julius, a Santa line). See The T'Ghee Card System for pricing and rules. No "abandoned arena" preset appears under that name in the text. The Mercenary Arcade Not an independent venue but a purchased training room inside Carl's own guild space, named by Katia. Larger than expected, staffed by an AI drill sergeant who appears in multiple instances at once and can genuinely kill trainees (who "regenerate a minute later"); mercenaries also spar to the death for practice. Carl is warned he "wouldn't be safe in here," and later locks the Penis Parade dancers inside it as a containment measure. The underwater production facility A complex on the ocean floor beneath a space station parked over the Indian Ocean, reached by transferring through the station. It houses the production trailer where Odette's show is taped (dressed to look like Larracos) and the sponsor meeting room Carl knows from CrawlCon — a round ten-seat table with holographic remote attendees, run by a robot called Urkel under the executive Cascadia. Larracos Still flooded from Book 5's Gate of the Feral Gods; its restaurants reopen but the attendants' boardroom remains unavailable, and the master pulpmancer who could have freed Shi Maria is presumed drowned. New this book: the goddess Ysalte, "The Downward Spiral," is native to Larracos and worshipped by its earliest citizens; and the battlefields outside it hold the Semeru Dwarves' castle, built along the roots of the All Tree. In the epilogue vote, Larracos is designated the home base of the new all-NPC tenth Faction Wars team. "Larracos level" is also Desperado Club slang for a punitive club tier guarded by Armored Sai rhinoceros samurai. Sheol, the 15th floor Named and described but never visited — "There's no tourist activity at all on that floor… we never get to see Sheol itself." The closest the book gets is a remote viewing of a lava-rock hellscape crawling with tiny flaming centipedes. Portals to it read "Entrance to Sheol, Floor 15" and pull like a black hole. See Sheol and the Fifteenth Floor. Wenatchee, Washington — the Meadowlark Elder Care facility An epilogue location, and the same facility the Meadowlark crawler group is named for. Agatha spent almost ten Earth years disguised as a homeless woman in the alley behind it, sitting by a barrel near a lit kitchen window, shown small kindnesses by two staff brothers named Brandon and Chris. She was there on the night of the collapse. The Kinder Facility, Mumbai Where disqualified crawlers are exported: "You will be disqualified and exported to the Kinder Facility located in the former city of Mumbai, India on the surface of the planet." Glimpsed once more in the epilogue, with humans "constantly battling the security forces, attempting to break into the kinder facility." No interior is ever shown. The Scolopendra Club Mentioned exactly once, and only as leverage: "do you know who is currently trapped in the Scolopendra Club? Over half of the entire galaxy's wealth is already gathered, and that includes my own children." It is the reason the Syndicate Council will not pull the failsafe. No physical description exists. The Penis Parade and the Guild of Suffering lair The Desperado Club's first-floor strip club — dark, bass-heavy, no pole, with a tusked mohawked troll dancer on the main stage and a young crocodilian "Bucket Boy" working tips — and a front for the Guild of Suffering, whose entrance sits inside it and requires an elbow tattoo. The Night Wyrm's own lair is "hidden up there on the top floor. The vorpals won't go up there," and is never toured. See Dungeon Factions for the organization.

docs.title: Book 6: Other Crawlers' Phase-Two Regions
docs.text:
Recorded for continuity. Note that phase one, phase two, and phase three are three different places for most squads, and the phase-two assignments were widely corrupted by the same placement glitch that moved Iowa.

Crawler Phase one Phase two Phase three Katia Reykjavík, Iceland Chose Ukraine, landed in a Ukraine/Vietnam hybrid; key at Da Nang Back in Iceland Imani C Western US (the Great Wolf Lodge) Detroit — given only one choice, the city she grew up in Detroit, at her family home Elle McGibbons Pacific Northwest, near Portland Belgium Olympia, Washington Li Jun, Li Na, Chris Andrews The Galaxy Soho building, Beijing "Still in China, but further into the mainland" — never named more precisely Back at Galaxy Soho, for the Battle of Beijing Florin Ecuador Eastern Nigeria — Prepotente The Bahamas Northern Italy Back in the Bahamas Lucia Mar — Never stated; she travels alone as "the most isolated crawler" Beijing, where she slaughters the crawler population in the Battle of Beijing

Other regions named in passing: Turkey (Hekla's daughters' squad in phase three), Tokyo and Brazil on recap footage, and one unnamed squad leader who was offered the entire globe and "dropped herself into the middle of the ocean for some reason."

docs.title: Book 7 (Floor 9): Larracos and the Plains
docs.text:
Floor 9's geography is unusually simple to state and unusually consequential: one sunken funnel city, one new ring of slums around its lip, and nine pie-slices of open plain radiating outward, one per attacking team. See Level 9 for the floor overview.

Location What it is Larracos, the City of Dreams A funnel-shaped city sunk into a volcanic pit, built as 66 rings numbered from the bottom up. Held by the all-NPC Team Retribution; still flooded to ring 3 from Book 4. Transferred bodily to the 12th floor at the end of the book, leaving an empty pit. Full page. Shanty Town A settlement that generated itself around the top lip after the flooding. Carl buys the mayorship from Ferdinand for a bowler hat. Has no throne room — it can only be taken by killing the mayor. Full page. The Plains of Larracos Nine numbered territories plus the city. Mostly flat except the rocky, lava-prone north. Border crossings are restricted to fixed one-kilometre corridors during the Ramp-Up. Full page. The Nest The Princess Posse's master-quality granite synergy tower, keyed to Atrocity-class spells and built at the edge of the hole into Larracos. Donut's perch. Full page. Area 52 The Posse's forest airbase, missile battery, and rear saferoom. Full page. The FUPA The Princess Posse's main castle in spot 3 — the Fortress of Unyielding Power and Authority, named for the acronym. Site of Baroness Victory's one kill, a Gondii brain-worm infiltration, and a Reaver paratrooper drop. See The Plains of Larracos. King's Point The orcs' pre-built mountain castle in spot 1 — the only territory that came with a castle. Destroyed by a deliberately engineered volcanic eruption, "leaving nothing but a throne room just sitting there in open air." Architect Houston's operating theatre The Madness warlord's lair, beside his throne room, which nobody had ever breached. Carl does, kills him there, and finds it rigged to a dead-man's switch. The Reaver honeycomb The Reavers' castle: dozens of honeycomb cells stacked three or four storeys high that constantly and randomly re-arrange themselves, with the throne room behind the centre cell. The Sugar Cube The Floor 6 High Elf Castle, Zerzura'd down to Floor 9 at the end of Book 5. It lands in Lemig Sortion territory and becomes their HQ, and is thereafter referred to as the Dream castle in spot 6 — a chain of custody the book never reconciles. Demolished by fighting gods. The Temple of the Dagda The season's out-of-city Club Vanquisher entrance temple. Dagda is "a weather and 'masculinity' god" whose only membership requirement is a beard. The Temple of Khepri An endless buffet: "one long table covered with a never-ending feast. And that feast is covered with 433 different kinds of bugs." Reached by a ritual in which female adherents swallow the god's beetles. The Midnight Market The hidden bazaar on the Desperado Club's bottom regular floor — "Access to the Midnight Market. Safety or Sanity not guaranteed." Run by the merchant Paca, an agent for Krakaren Prime, and the source of the hell-kissed Conscription potions. The calligraphy and cartography guilds Two adjoining hidden guildhalls with the same guildmaster, Milk, who hasn't had a floor-supervisor meeting in over fifty seasons. The calligraphy guild teaches Words of Power. Their physical location is never stated — only that both doors are hidden.

docs.title: Book 7: Off-Floor and Other Locations
docs.text: Location What it is The Outreach Guild Where a departing crawler negotiates their exit deal, with an assigned attorney. Physically a bare, doorless "zero zone" cubicle. Carl's lawyer is Quasar; Carl refuses every offer — "My official answer is, fuck these options. I am not taking a deal." See Post-Crawl Economics. The production facility The Borant/Valtay broadcast site where the season's shows are taped, including Odette's — the same complex introduced in Book 6 beneath a space station over the Indian Ocean. "Entering Production Facility." Orren's office The liaison's office Carl keeps getting yanked into without warning — multicoloured wood panelling and a framed painting of Astrid. This is where Carl is introduced to the AI's avatar, Growler Gary. The Squirties waystation "Squirties waystation and refueling platform. Located just outside the main tunnel access route entrance to the Earth system." The setting of the book's closing scene: its saccathian owner Zander is going bankrupt under the Earth-system embargo and facing indenture, and then Eris walks in. The kinder facility (Earth's surface) Where children and pregnant women — ineligible to crawl — are held. Zev puts the count at "About 120,000. Give or take a few." It is tied to a dead-man's switch on Lucia Mar's survival, and it is what Katia deliberately makes herself ineligible in order to reach: "There are no children or pregnant women allowed here … But there are several children, up there … I think they're in trouble … this is the only way I can get to them." (She never names the facility at her departure; the connection is strongly implied rather than stated outright.) The Aryl system A previous season's crawl — a battle-royale rather than a dungeon — revealed to have gone completely dark at the exact instant its own crawlers triggered their failsafe: "They tried triggering it, and nothing happened here. But the moment they pressed the button, the Aryl system went dark." Nothing has been heard from it since. This is the single fact that collapses the Syndicate's failsafe debate. See The Containment Interface and the Star-Detonation Failsafe. The 16th floor — "Agony of Mirrors" Revealed, in a deliberately anticlimactic aside, to be nothing at all: "the 16th Floor, supposedly entitled 'Agony of Mirrors' is actually a giant, empty room with a single mirror in it: a non-magical mirror plucked from an abandoned Motel 6 location in Boise, Idaho." The 17th floor — "The Backstage Death Maze" Confirmed fully built and already running, in the same breath: "Unfortunately, the 17th floor, called 'The Backstage Death Maze' is currently built and running. You will have to proceed through this level should you want to get to the 16th." The Scolopendra Club (18th floor) Finally described rather than merely cited: a members-only VIP viewing facility holding over half the galaxy's wealth, with food menus, an activity schedule, personal-trainer feeds and gossip-trained massage NPCs — all "programmed from orbit" and therefore usable as a covert channel into the dungeon. Also used as a sentence ("Death. Scolopendra Club. The Cabaret backstage. Or Earth's surface. Pick."), and evacuated at the end of the book when Scolopendra wakes.

docs.title: Book 8 (Floor 10-11): Don't Come in Last / A Parade of Horribles
docs.text:
Floor 10 replaces the usual open dungeon with a seven-Heat vehicle race, funneled through a single hub town and a rotating set of themed tracks; Floor 11 is a single mandatory float parade ending in an arena. See Level 10 and Level 11 for the floor overviews once those pages exist.

Location What it is Hungry Eyes Village The floor's hub town — a "1980s neon-infused, cyberpunk fever dream" holding the Team Roundabout garages, the vendor village, the Hairpin and Lollipop bars, and the mercenary market. Full page. Chicken and Waffles and Upgrades (C&W&U) A hidden upgrade shop behind an ordinary diner front, tucked into Hungry Eyes Village's vendor strip — its jukebox is the real door, and its back room is the war mage Akuma's hideout. Full page. Upano A jungle pit-stop city shared by four parallel Heat 4 tracks at once, ringed by unexplained black tubes and cliffs. Full page. Satan's Water Park A Heat 4 track owned by the invulnerable, comic-relief country boss Satan (see Bosses) — waterslide tubes, a River of Sloth, and a mountain-sized British hedgehog narrating the whole thing. Full page. Gasworks Screw Factory, Steel Mill, and Doll Workshop Heat 5's single combined industrial track — one dilapidated factory building, not several separate sites — and the site of Dong Quixote and Corcunda's reunion and double death fighting the war god Grull. Full page. The L'Engle Building Heat 6 and 7's shrunk-scale apartment-complex track, home to the AI's unauthorized "Ad Infinitum" what-if simulations — see The "What-If" Apartment Simulations. Full page. Club Scolopendra A luxury resort built literally inside Scolopendra's own body, reached via Oozy Form during the Floor 11 arena climax — this wiki treats it as the same venue as "the Scolopendra Club" documented above under Book 7's 18th floor, with Book 8 finally revealing the mechanism (see the location page for the reasoning). Also where "the Kyryap" is first established as a real presence. Full page. The Pineapple Cabaret's "back door" Referenced repeatedly but never a physical set — see Dungeon Factions: The Pineapple Cabaret for the hidden pocket-dimension sanctuary itself. Floor 11's parade route and arena A road lined with thousands of masked Horribles leading to a colosseum-style arena; no independent location page exists since the route and arena are one continuous set piece covered by the mechanics and boss pages above rather than duplicated here.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised, Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario, Book 4: The Gate of the Feral Gods, Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade, Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride, Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin, and Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Managers
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Unlocked by: A hidden "Manager Benefit" attached to certain classes (e.g. Former Child Actor)
  • Effect: Converts a stationary guildmaster/guide into a mobile, always-present companion
  • Trade-off: The guide loses their guildhall, television access, the information codex, and eventually their own life once combat protections kick in on Floor 4
  • Notable Manager: Mordecai, from Book 2 onward

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text:
A Manager can physically teleport to a crawler's location any time they're in a safe room, and can accompany the party outdoors on urban ("Over City") floors — something a standard guide cannot do at all. In exchange, the guide permanently loses their guildhall room, access to the information codex (everything they tell a crawler from that point on comes from memory alone), and their in-universe television/feed access, which also means they lose all advance warning of what's about to happen to their crawler.

A Manager is explicitly barred from one thing: direct combat. Per Mordecai, "we can't engage in direct battle with mobs. Everything else is fair game" — which leaves room for a Manager to steal supplies, forge potions, gather intelligence, or otherwise support a crawler through any means short of fighting alongside them.

docs.title: Protection & Mortality
docs.text:
Managers (like tourists and staff generally) receive no combat protection on Floors 1–3 — a guide who wanders into danger during this window can die for real. Starting on Floor 4, Managers receive the same "kicked from the game, not truly killed" protection tourists get during Floor 9's Faction Wars: they can still be hurt and can still feel pain, but a fatal injury only ends their season rather than their life.

A Manager's obligation (and by extension a guide's indentureship) is typically tied to reaching a specific floor with their crawler — for Mordecai, Floor 4. Once that's reached, he is free to leave crawler service, collect his stipend, and depart, regardless of what happens afterward. His final payout scales with how well his crawler continues to perform for the rest of the season, which is the stated reason a freed Manager might choose to keep helping anyway.

docs.title: Why a Crawler Might Hide the Choice
docs.text:
Per advice from Odette relayed to Carl, deliberately picking a class for its Manager benefit should be disguised as an accident. A guide who knows their ward chose the benefit on purpose — trading away the guide's own comfort and safety for the crawler's benefit — may hold a lasting grudge; one who believes it was a naive mistake is far more likely to forgive it.

Sourced from Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario.

docs.title: Over City Floors
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Which floors: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 — every third level, per Mordecai
  • Size: Much smaller than Floors 1–2 (Floor 3 is roughly the size of Arizona, ~300,000 square kilometers), except Floor 9, which is large again
  • Structure: Fortified villages connected by dangerous "ruins" wilderness
  • First appearance: Floor 3 in Book 2, themed as a destroyed volcano-kingdom ("the Over City")

docs.title: The Pattern
docs.text:
Every third floor of the World Dungeon is built around a persistent, semi-independent "urban level" setting — the Over City is Book 2's example, spanning six narrative layers built inside a dormant volcano's crater, of which crawlers only ever experience the top layer at a time. Per Mordecai, this is a Dungeon Crawler World tradition: floors 6, 9, 12, 15, and 18 will each present a new, self-contained urban setting with its own recurring cast of Elites, ongoing storylines, and species.

Deeper Over City-style layers escalate in danger and exclusivity:

  • Floor 6 ("the Hunting Grounds") — jungle-like ruins, bigger and wealthier villages, and the first floor open to paying tourists who hunt crawlers for sport
  • Floor 9 — hosts the "Faction Wars" segment; unusually large again, unlike the floors around it
  • Floor 18 — described as a luxury retreat for the galaxy's wealthy elite, where otherwise illegal activities (like the operation of genetically-engineered brothel staff) are permitted
  • Floors 15 and 18 — nobody has ever recorded a crawler reaching either; even Borant and the system AI reportedly don't know for certain what a crawler would find there

docs.title: Villages & the Ruins
docs.text:
Each Over City layer consists of scattered fortified villages (sized tiny → small → medium → large → extra-large) surrounded by "ruins" — abandoned, monster-infested wilderness making up most of the floor's area. Villages are unnamed by default; a crawler can rename one by killing its mayor, though this rarely comes with meaningful benefits on a short-timer floor. Every medium (or larger) village includes a Tutorial Guild.

City guards patrol village streets only while an in-world "sun" is up; the same streets (and especially alleyways) become lawless and dangerous after dark, when the guards vanish entirely. Ruins-dwelling monsters exist at all hours but are markedly more dangerous at night.

docs.title: Navigation Without a Pathfinder Skill
docs.text: Concealed holographic signposts — a Dungeon Locator — stand at major ruins intersections, giving general directional information (nearest settlement, stairwell, restroom) even without a Pathfinder-type skill. They're less precise than a true Pathfinder skill (which reveals a wide radius of the map outright) but still make blind wandering unnecessary.

docs.title: NPCs & Ethics
docs.text:
Over City villagers are living, biological beings engineered and owned by the season's operator (here, Borant), reused season after season with wiped and rewritten memories and backstories — last season's meth-addicted goblins might return next season worshipping a different god, with no awareness of the change. Using such NPCs for anything outside a sanctioned production is treated as a serious crime, comparable to a war crime, under Syndicate law — a protection that does not extend to how the season's writers are allowed to use them within the show itself.

Sourced from Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario.

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • First appears: Floor 3, via a dedicated Quests tab
  • Reward tiers: Bronze → Silver → Gold → Platinum → Celestial Quest Box
  • Upgrade achievements: Hadji, then Bandit — each bumps a quest's reward box up one tier
  • Elite-linked quests: Treated as scripted "drama," not random content — see Elites

docs.title: How Quests Work
docs.text: Quests can be triggered by walking into a scripted location (Grimaldi's circus), by an NPC directly asking for help (GumGum's request about the dead sex workers), or by other means. Each quest's completion criteria can be narrower than they first appear — the text of a quest is the actual contract, and satisfying it literally (rather than doing what seems intuitively "right") is often both possible and rewarded. Mordecai's blanket advice on Floor 3 is to avoid quests entirely unless a crawler is comfortably ahead of the difficulty curve, since quests consume time against a floor's shortened collapse timer without guaranteed proportional reward.

docs.title: Reward Tiers & Upgrade Achievements
docs.text:
A completed quest normally grants a single loot box scaled to its difficulty (Silver for a relatively simple mystery, Gold for one involving multiple Elites and a City Boss). Two special, repeatable achievements can upgrade that box after the fact:

  • Hadji — awarded for completing a quest in an unusually creative or unconventional way; upgrades the box one tier
  • Bandit — a second, even rarer upgrade tier, awarded (per its own flavor text) even without the crawler doing anything special to earn it

Both upgrades stack, so a quest can jump multiple reward tiers in one completion. Borant has patched out both achievements at least once after a costly incident (see below), suggesting they can be disabled mid-season if they threaten the season's finances.

docs.title: Event Quests
docs.text: A distinct, higher-stakes category: group event quests, automatically assigned to every crawler within a defined blast/danger radius when something catastrophic is triggered, with no option to decline except reaching a safe room within a short window (60 seconds, in the one seen) — after which all safe rooms in the quest zone lock down until the event concludes. The crawler(s) responsible for triggering the event are locked in as the "Host" and cannot opt out under any circumstances, even if they have no way to reach a safe room themselves. Objectives can be as blunt as "don't die," with a flat reward (a Platinum Quest Box) for every survivor.

docs.title: Case Study: The Financial Near-Catastrophe
docs.text:
The event quest "The Fools Who Broke the Glass" (see Level 3: Quests for the full text and context) triggers when Remex's death destabilizes a generations-old spell, threatening a 45-square-kilometer blast radius. Carl, Donut, and Katia are locked in as Hosts — unable to opt out even though Katia, lacking Desperado Club access, has nowhere to actually flee.

The twist: it isn't the Hosts who get the big reward. A random other survivor in the blast zone, a level-15 crawler named Quan Ch, receives the rare Bandit achievement — an upgrade so powerful its own flavor text admits "you didn't actually do anything to deserve this prize" — jumping his promised Platinum Quest Box straight to Celestial tier. The same achievement fires for all 83 survivors in the blast radius simultaneously, a number large enough to threaten bankrupting Borant Corporation, which pays Syndicate tax on every non-sponsored Celestial box given out. Borant invokes a once-per-season veto to void every prize from the quest — including Carl, Donut, and Katia's own promised Platinum boxes, despite them having done the actual work — but Quan Ch has already opened his, so that one box stands. Borant immediately patches out both the Hadji and Bandit achievements to prevent a repeat.

Sourced from Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario.

docs.title: Race & Class Selection
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • When it happens: Upon reaching Floor 3, in a private session with a crawler's guide
  • Choices: Hundreds of races (Carl: 398, Donut: 320) and classes (Carl: 650+, Donut: 34)
  • AI recommendations: The system always offers exactly three suggested choices
  • Stat cost: Most non-Human races cost stat points relative to a flat +2-to-everything Human baseline; exclusive/rare races and classes carry unlock requirements instead

docs.title: The Process
docs.text:
Crawlers choose a permanent race and class during a private session inside their guild hall on Floor 3 — the training-wheels period ends the moment this happens ("the training levels have concluded. Now the games may truly begin," per Mordecai). Race is chosen first, then class; both present a scrollable list (alphabetical for race) with exactly three AI-picked recommendations highlighted at the top, tailored to the crawler's stats, achievements, and skills. The final choice is irreversible and must be manually confirmed.

Race grants a flat set of stat modifiers and species-specific benefits/skills. Some races are limited/exclusive, gated behind an achievement or a skill threshold (e.g. Hobgoblin requires Level 5 Explosives Handling; Sasquatch requires Level 5 Smush). A handful of races — like Primal — are technically available to everyone but carry an unusual stat penalty in exchange for unlocking normally-capped skill training.

Class determines a crawler's build far more heavily than race. Many classes are gated behind skill thresholds, view-count minimums, or specific achievements.
