Classes flagged as Earth Classes are an incentive category exclusive to human-world crawlers: choosing one grants an automatic Silver Earth Box and, per the game's own rules, comes with a mandatory Earth Hobby Potion — a legally-required (per "the Indigenous Species Protection Act") random Level 3 skill in an Earth-based hobby, which can be anything from a martial art to jai-alai to competitive stamp collecting.

docs.title: Class-Linked Benefits Worth Knowing
docs.text:
• The Manager Benefit — a hidden perk on certain classes (see Managers) that converts a crawler's guide from a stationary guildmaster into a mobile, always-present companion — at the cost of the guide's own comfort, access, and information.
  • The Character Actor Skill — found on classes like Former Child Actor, it lets a crawler re-pick an entirely new "specialty" class each floor, themed to that floor, with the specific skills/spells granted determined semi-randomly by the system AI. Existing permanent spells/skills are untouched, but a poor specialty roll can temporarily saddle a crawler with mana-cost penalties on their real kit for the length of the floor.

docs.title: Notable Choices (Book 2)
docs.text:
Crawler Race Class Carl Primal Compensated Anarchist Princess Donut Cat (unchanged) Former Child Actor (permanent class, chosen specifically for its hidden Manager benefit — publicly framed as a "mistake" so Mordecai wouldn't suspect it was deliberate); used her resulting Character Actor skill to pick Artist Alley Mogul as her Floor 3 specialty Lucia Mar Lajabless Black Inquisitor General (cleric/mage/warrior triple class) Hekla Amazonian Shieldmaiden

Sourced from Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario.

docs.title: Ratings & Viewership System
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Core stats: Views → Followers → Favorites → Patrons (each stage funnels into the next)
  • Active from: Floor 2 onward — Floor 1 is off-limits to live viewers entirely
  • Why it matters: Patrons are, per Mordecai, the single most reliable path to survival-grade gear

docs.title: Why This Menu Exists
docs.text: Mordecai calls Ratings "the single most important menu in the entire game. Your life depends on these numbers." Floor 1 activity isn't visible to live viewers at all — Borant only releases an edited highlights reel afterward — so a crawler's public numbers only start moving once they reach Floor 2.

docs.title: The Funnel
docs.text:
• Views — accumulated automatically; roughly 8 seconds of someone watching counts as one. Doesn't directly help or hurt, but signals how "interesting" a crawler is.
  • Followers — a viewer has bookmarked the crawler's ID and can check in whenever they want.
  • Favorites — a stronger commitment; favoriting gets a viewer live updates and combat notifications for that crawler. Viewers only get a limited number of favorite slots, so per Mordecai it should be "considered an honor."
  • Patrons — almost always organizations rather than individuals, sponsoring a crawler (usually after seeing a strong favorites count) by purchasing them loot boxes as a form of advertising. Patron-sponsored boxes can outclass anything else in the dungeon (see the Box Tier System's Benefactor Box entry).

docs.title: Playing to the Camera
docs.text:
Mordecai's blunt advice: survival isn't just about combat competence — "You need to stand out... Maybe you can come up with a catchphrase." He credits his own 30-million-follower, four-patron run as a crawler as the reason he survived at all. This incentive structure is the explicit in-universe justification for crawlers' larger-than-life, showboating behavior throughout the series.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised.

docs.title: The T'Ghee Card System
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Floor: 8 ("The Ghosts of Earth") — see Timeline
  • What it is: A collectible-card battle system layered over ordinary combat, in which captured monsters become summonable "totem" cards held by a squad leader
  • Who it binds: Every crawler on the floor, whether or not they ever build a deck — non-leaders are reclassified as minions during a card battle
  • Carried forward: Exactly one card per surviving squad, kept past the floor's collapse

Floor 8's defining mechanic, and the thing every other Floor 8 system eventually routes through. Crawlers are sorted into squads, handed flags, and told to go capture monsters; the monsters become playing cards; the cards become a duel format that overrides normal combat for everyone in range. Carl's first-pass explanation to Donut is the right mental model — "Do you remember when I used to play that Pokémon game on the Nintendo? I think it might be a little like that."

docs.title: Squads and Flags
docs.text:
Announced in the floor's opening broadcast, before any card is ever shown.

Every crawler is placed in a squad of no more than five. Parties of six or more are split into equal squads of fewer than five, and the split is permanent in a way parties are not: "These squads are not able to be broken. If you leave your party, you will not leave the squad."

A squad has six more spots than it has crawlers — a solo crawler gets seven slots total, a five-crawler squad gets eleven. Filling those spots is phase one's entire job, and it is mandatory: a squad that hasn't filled out by the phase-one timer has the remainder filled randomly, which the announcement goes out of its way to warn against.

The squad leader receives twenty flags bearing the squad's auto-generated logo:

"If you plant the flag within the body of a living entity while they are at less than 5% health, they will be transformed into something called a T'Ghee totem, which will be added to the squad leader's inventory."

The 5% threshold is the whole design: capture requires beating something almost to death without killing it. Noncorporeal monsters can be flagged too. Flagged monsters automatically join the squad and become minions of whoever summons them, following orders "to a certain extent, depending on the level difference and nature of the monster" — which is the announcement's way of warning squads against building a roster that outclasses them.

Other flag rules:

  • Flags are not replaced if lost or wasted. Twenty is all anyone gets.
  • A squad may hold more totems than it has squad spaces.
  • Totems may be traded with other crawlers — and stolen from them.
  • Dismissing a squad member means ripping its totem card in two.
  • Cards may only be held and activated by the squad leader.
  • On the start of phase two, every totem not placed in an active deck dissipates.

docs.title: Phase Structure
docs.text:
The floor's three phases each change what the deck is for.

Phase Dates What the deck does One Dec 10 – Dec 24 (14 days) Build it. Capture totems, fill the squad, practice in the mock arena. No exit key is obtainable. Two Dec 24 – Dec 26 (48 hours) Use it. A new region populated by intelligent deckmasters who carry their own decks; beat them for cards and for the region's exit key. Three Dec 26 onward Defend it. Keyholders teleport back to their original region; keyless squads are deliberately dropped onto keyholders' doorways.

Phase two hard-locks the roster: "Once phase two starts, you may never have more or less than six totem cards in your possession." Taking a killed deckmaster's totem therefore means discarding one of your own. Phase three's design is openly adversarial — "you'll be blocking their path. If you can kill them before they exit, you can take the key to save yourself" — and the announcement is frank that this is the point: "the potential of crawler on crawler violence is quite high. Doesn't that sound just great?"

docs.title: Combat Rules
docs.text:
The full rulebook is delivered mid-book by Cascadia and mirrored in each crawler's deck tab.

Activating a deck. "Each squad must have six totems active in their deck. You may activate your deck with as little as six cards total." Six totems is the floor, not the ceiling; observed decks in the back half of the book run fifteen to twenty-two cards.

Starting and ending a fight. "Combat is engaged when a nearby monster's aggro is activated, and they are actively hunting you. Combat disengages when the mobs are dead, rendered neutral, or one of the parties has fled." Crucially, "Overlapping combat with multiple mobs will count as a single session" — you do not get a fresh hand by picking a second fight mid-fight, and most totems cannot be reused once knocked out within a session.

The hand. Four random cards are drawn the moment combat initiates. Spent cards are replaced "at the rate of one card every ten seconds." A single discard is available at the start of combat, and "This ability resets once every thirty seconds." (Ten seconds is the crawler default, not a universal constant — at least one enemy deckmaster is observed drawing on an eight-second cycle.)

The squad leader's handicap. This is the rule that makes the system dangerous:

"Once deck combat is initiated, the Squad Leader loses access to their regular magic abilities and their inventory system. They may still fight using melee attacks. They may use potions, scrolls, wands, etc. as long as the items are physically available to them."

Access returns only when the deck is empty: "Once all cards in your deck are played or discarded, the Squad Leader regains their ability to use their inventory and spells." A spellcaster squad leader in an active card battle is, functionally, an unarmed person holding cards.

Everyone else is a minion. Non-leaders present at a card battle are reclassified, and the system enjoys telling them so:

"By the way, have you realized yet that you're considered a minion during card battles? That's something you should probably pay attention to."

Enemy totems generally cannot strike an opposing squad leader while that leader has a totem of their own active — but minions are fair game, and the system awards an achievement (Smeat!: "Expendable. Cannon fodder.") for the privilege. In a deckmaster duel the win condition is to "Strike a single blow against the deckmaster," and the lose condition is to "Have an enemy totem or deckmaster strike you."

If the leader dies. "If the squad leader dies during deck combat, the deck will transfer to the next in line."

docs.title: Card Types
docs.text:
"There are five types of cards: Totems, which are the summonable monsters. Utility cards, which can only be played on one or more of your summoned totems. Snare cards, which can only be played on an enemy's totem. Mystic cards, which are similar to regular magic spells, and special cards which are usually one-time use."

  • Totem — a captured monster, summonable for a timed duration. Reusable across battles even if the summoned creature dies.
  • Utility — buffs, playable only on your own actively summoned totem. Most persist for the duration of combat "even over multiple summonings." A totem's capacity for utility buffs is limited by its rarity.
  • Snare — debuffs, playable only when an opponent has an active totem. Also persistent across resummonings of the same totem. A totem has one snare slot.
  • Mystic — the disruption layer: "usually have a direct effect on squads, squad leaders, or the squad leader's deck." Some are persistent, occupying a hand slot for as long as they stay active.
  • Special — one-off effects, usually consumable and usually aimed at the caster.

A taxonomy the book breaks itself

The Combo card's own printed face reads "Utility Card," even though the narration and every subsequent use treat it as a Special. Separately, the Worm Fulcrum is explicitly "a combination of a mystic Necro card and a Walking Stick totem" — simultaneously a totem with hit points and a persistent mystic — which Donut correctly protests is not supposed to be possible.

docs.title: Rarity
docs.text:
Seven tiers, weakest to strongest: Common, Uncommon, Rare, Very Rare, Legendary, Mythic, Unique. Mythic cards carry a black border and are "the second highest quality, only behind the orange unique cards."

Rarity governs how many utility buffs a totem can carry. The only figure the system actually states is Donut's: "Carl, it says uncommon totems can only hold two utility cards!" Carl infers from that a clean 1-through-7 scale — Common holds one, Unique holds seven — but that scaling is his guess, not system text, and the book never confirms it.

docs.title: The Mock Battle Arena
docs.text:
A practice facility where a squad can run its deck against generated opposition. Three difficulty tiers at 1,000 / 2,000 / 5,000 gold respectively for an easy opponent, an opponent matched to your deck, and a "challenge." The generated mobs can't hurt you, but the arena environment still can.

Consumables are genuinely spent: a one-time card used in practice is gone, and cards on a long cooldown don't reset just because the fight was simulated. Beating the challenge tier unlocks further options, including a free Secret Challenge Mode — a true deck-versus-deck duel against an AI opponent with its own deck, usable three times.

Prices rise the night before phase two ("Starting tonight, the prices in the mock battle arena are going up"); the middle tier is confirmed to move from 2,000 to 2,500 gold, and the other tiers' new prices aren't given.

docs.title: The Champion Pack
docs.text:
Awarded for defeating a phase-two keymaster:

"Champion Pack. Offered only to those who have defeated the keymaster, the champion pack contains the following items: Backup slot: Allows space for two extra totems to be kept on reserve. With this pack you may now carry a total of eight totems, but you still may only keep six in your active deck. A champion trophy to display in your personal space. A cooler filled with yellow Gatorade… Two Flee cards. Warning: Flee card mechanics will change during the final phase."

The backup slot is the only reserve-totem mechanic in the book; outside this pack, six is six.

docs.title: Carrying a Card Forward
docs.text: "All surviving squads may choose a single T'Ghee card to keep upon the collapse of this floor." In the event, Carl and Donut weigh keeping Lazarus or the Golden Combo and take neither — they spend their choice on ripping Paz Lo's card instead, at Paz's own earlier request.

Consumable; cast on an active totem

docs.title: Notable Totems
docs.text: A partial roster of totems that matter to the plot: the monk seal sentries Yago and Geraldo (Carl and Donut's first captures); Skylar Spinach, a ghommid splitter; Asojano, Uzi Jesus, and Raul the crab; Der Kornwolf and Die Kartoffelwölfin, a phase-two deckmaster's wolves; Jola, Lazarus A-Bang-Bang, Basquiat the Mongolian Death Worm, and the Demon Queen; the parody pair Alpha Male Carl and King Croissant, built from a captured "Carl" mob; the hybrid Worm Fulcrum; and Shi Maria, the Unique totem the book is named after.

docs.title: Crawlers as Cards
docs.text:
The system permits flagging a crawler. Sister Ines does it to her own squadmate Paz Lo rather than let him die to Ogun's smite, over his explicit objection — "Let me go" — and his card afterward reads "Paz Lo. The God Predator. Level 101. Former Crawler." A second card, "Frank," raises the worse possibility Carl names outright: that the dungeon can bring back dead crawlers as cards.

Unique totems can also arrive with obligations attached. Capturing Shi Maria triggers an escort quest, The Bedlam Bride — "Get her crazy ass to the city of Larracos. That's it. That's the quest." The quest survives the card being ripped.

docs.title: In-World: Stolen Sacred Objects
docs.text:
T'Ghee is not a game's brand name. It is somebody's religion. Allister, author of the cookbook's 13th edition, knew T'Ghee as a faith that "had nothing to do with capturing and summoning monsters," and Carl is blunt about what the dungeon has done with it: "Even the cards themselves — T'Ghee cards — were considered sacred to the aliens they stole the idea from. They were never meant to be used like this."

Sister Ines makes the broader version of the argument about the whole floor, whose monsters are drawn from real Earth folklore:

"It is all a mockery of our faiths and legends. They ignore the meanings behind the myths and stories, and they just see the surface, steal it, and use it to make something shiny and pretty and completely devoid of its meaning… These cultures and creatures are holy to people, and they are making jokes of it all."

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: The Iron Tangle Railway System
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Floor: 4 (Book 3), themed as a sprawling subway/rail network
  • Scale: 150,000+ stations, only 9,375 stairwells, spread across dozens of parallel trainyards
  • Central hub: The Abyss — a mile-wide pit where every colored-line train ultimately terminates
  • Corporate operator: see Iron Tangle Management for the org running it

Floor 4 replaces the usual walkable cityscape with a transit maze. Getting anywhere requires understanding the rail system itself — this page covers the mechanics; the company running it is covered separately under Dungeon Factions.

docs.title: Colored Lines vs. Named Trains
docs.text:
• Colored lines (Puce, Vermillion, Mauve, Zomp, Fulvous, Camel, and dozens more, up to ~48 per quadrant) are ordinary subway trains that only travel up the numbered stations, never back down, and never loop.
  • Named trains (the Nightmare Express, Escape Velocity, the Eviscerator, the Raven Blade Unlimited, the Dismemberment Limited) are old-style steam/diesel engines that loop continuously through a fixed set of stations, including some far lower-numbered ones — making them the only way to travel backward down the line. Each pulls dozens of freight cars, some carrying stat-boosted monsters, and each is staffed by a two-person crew (an engineer and, reserved for the harder lines, a war mage — see Levi the Seventh). Only a caboose (entry) and a forward passenger car (exit-only) allow boarding; hijacking one requires killing its engineer for a Steam Engineer's Key, which also grants access to all 400 of the Iron Tangle's steam-type trains.
  • Only station numbers ending in a prime are true transfer stations with a full settlement (restaurant, general store, and often a Desperado Club entrance); non-prime stops are small and often monster-free.

docs.title: Portals, Trainyards, and the Abyss
docs.text:
Every colored-line train eventually reaches its terminus at a DungeonWerx subspace portal, one-way and passable only by a train (or a crawler wearing the free souvenir conductor's hat given out at the floor's start). Passing through separates the train: only the engine car survives, teleported back to a trainyard to be reassembled into a new train from scratch; the passenger and freight cars are simply hurled into the Abyss, a mile-wide, mile-deep pit at the map's center where every line's wreckage and monsters ultimately fall. Dozens of trainyards (lettered E, H, M, Q, and more) ring the Abyss's edge, each a walled compound patrolled by lizard-like Wall Monitors and, once the ghoul-disposal pipeline overloads, flooded with escaped ghouls.

Interdiction carts, small hobgoblin-and-gnoll-crewed maintenance vehicles kept at transfer stations, carry a portable version of the same portal technology on a wide front-mounted "scoop" — anything the moving scoop touches, including other trains, gets teleported to wherever the portal is dialed (a specific trainyard, or the Abyss). A Rapid-Response cart requires two gnolls' left hands on separate control plates to activate — a security measure the crawlers subvert by farming an indestructible gnoll NPC's severed hand.

docs.title: Station Mimics
docs.text: Six enormous Station Mimic City Bosses exist floor-wide, each one large enough to occupy the mass of five or six ordinary stations at once — Mimic Rex is one of the six, encountered at station 433/Terminus. A Station Mimic can't be killed conventionally: severed pieces regrow legs and crawl back to the main body, and only stripping over 50% of its mass at once (with no way to reabsorb it) leaves it briefly vulnerable — the removed pieces keep fighting independently until the main body dies. Mordecai identifies the design as a callback to the H'lene, an extinct species that ran identical ambush "waystations" near the galactic core before being wiped out.

docs.title: The Ghoul-Disposal Pipeline
docs.text: See Iron Tangle Management for the corporate cause. Mechanically, non-undead mob deaths spawn Blister Ghouls (station 72) or Jikininki (station 12); those that congregate in large enough numbers at a stairwell station fuse into a Province Boss — a single conglomerated, many-mouthed monster that fills the entire chamber. Every ghoul generator runs on a soul crystal; killing enough monsters near one at once (or blowing one deliberately) causes it to detonate, destroying everything nearby but permanently ending that generator's output — and Mordecai suspects killing a Province Boss directly would blow every soul crystal on that stretch of line at once.

docs.title: The Mirrored "Noodle" and the Syndicate Logo
docs.text: Katia eventually works out that the entire railway, viewed from above, traces the Syndicate's own overlapping-rings logo — each named-train loop is one ring, tracing back to the wormhole ship Escape Velocity that founded the Syndicate. Each individual colored line, she further deduces, is actually a single "noodle": tracks run along the outside of a tube-shaped tunnel, with an identical, inverted station on the tube's opposite face — meaning digging straight down from any station 59 leads not to open ground but to an upside-down mirror of station 59 on a different line, separated only by a thin escape-tunnel buffer ("the noodle") that the ghoul-disposal conveyor and hidden robot-tended tunnels run through. This is why province bosses often appear in pairs on directly opposite lines, and why plugging a station's central floor with a downward- facing portal (as Carl does with an interdiction cart, suspended by an improvised crane) can redirect an entire incoming horde into the Abyss instead of the room.

docs.title: Subspace Portal Vision
docs.text: A Valtay Corporation Neural Enhancer, delivered as an unsolicited Bronze Benefactor Box gift, permanently grants the ability to identify and see through subspace portals (but not ordinary doors) — including taking a still-photo "visual analysis" of what's on the other side before stepping through. It only functions on true portals, not disguised or magically-locked doorways.

docs.title: Deity Summoning Rules
docs.text:
The cookbook and Mordecai both describe three categories of deity summoning: a celestial boon (a worshipper prays and the god comes willingly), an indentured summoning (a powerful mage compels the god against its will), and an involuntary summoning (an accident, as with Carl's War Gauntlet). Gods are invulnerable below the 12th floor. An involuntary summon lasts (vessel's level + god's level) seconds — a Level-40 Mantaur vessel summoning the Level-250 Grull lasts 290 seconds — and once unsummoned, the same god can be re-summoned immediately with no cooldown; summoning him a second time via a different vessel while already bound will forcibly transfer him to the new vessel. Per one cookbook note, the gods themselves are "Soul Armor" — bodies worn by an alien pilot exactly like the Intellect Hunters and Valtay — meaning in theory a biological-armor-removal spell could strip the alien driver out of a god's body, though no crawler has ever been positioned to try it.

Sourced from Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook.

docs.title: Mobs
docs.text: Regular (non-boss) monster types encountered across the series. Full pages exist for mobs with real recurrence or plot weight in Book 1; everything else is listed in the table below.

docs.title: Full pages
docs.text:
• Brindle Grub — Floor 2's corpse-eating "janitor" mob, matures into Brindled Vespas
  • Tuskling — Orcish Supremacy ruling class; forms the Ball of Swine
  • Rage Elemental — Level 93 elite, bathroom-violation punishment mob
  • Street Urchin — Floor 3's corpse-cleanup "janitor" mob
  • Krasue — undead vampire-women manufactured by Miss Quill
  • Shambling Berserker — undead body-part pile, quadrupled power in darkness
  • Remex — Miss Quill's undead husband, a Soul Leech Capacitor
  • Drek — Floor 4's swarming, demonic-baby horde mob
  • Jikininki — Floor 4's ghoul "janitor" mob, first tier of the Iron Tangle's corpse-disposal system
  • Frenzied Gerbil — Level 11 swarm mob; the System AI's recurring in-joke, from Ralph through Floor 5's gnomish "Live Ammo Balls"
  • Funeral Bell — Floor 6's mushroom-headed town guard, trap-deactivating and faction-agnostic
  • Night Weasel — Floor 6's invisible, paralysis-biting pack hunter
  • Flesher — animated corpse-skin, stage one of the war mage cycle; weaponised at scale on Floor 9
  • War Mage — Level 100, a true dungeon-born entity nobody designed; the Floor 9 wild card
  • Zarogoth — Level 50 soul-generated "sludge ghoul," the swarm mob of the Peeling Phase
  • Hunter Wraith — Floor 10–11 possession monster carrying the Inevitable Ruin curse, the book's title
  • Bijou — tiny fairies that physically carry worship-tendrils between gods and their adherents
  • The Horribles — Floor 11's masked, silent parade avatars; revealed as literal fragments of the system AI's own lost memory

docs.title: Book 6 mob catalog
docs.text: Floor 8's mobs are grouped by region rather than by area, because the floor is a patchwork of recreated Earth locations and crawlers are scattered across all of them. Most of the entries below also double as T'Ghee totem cards — Floor 8 runs on card combat, so a mob's real significance is often what it does once it has been flagged rather than how it fights.

docs.title: Cuba / Havana region (Phase One)
docs.text: Name Level(s) Notable trait The Experience 55 Taino folklore — a dog-bodied creature with an oversized human head in a red beret, guardian of the world of the dead. Drops the magical red beret Donut wears on and off through the floor (a small boost to all stats) Duende 20 Foot-tall rag-men who tackle through the memory ghosts' clothing and hoard the shoes; physically weak and uncoordinated, and the cause of most of the region's car pileups. One is named Mordecai Monk Seal Picket Sentry 70 Caribbean-kung-fu-fighting monk seals sworn to hold the coast against the land crabs. Named individuals: Yago (Sister Ines's totem), Geraldo (Donut's), and Chuy Red Maníseros Land Crab 70 "Cultivators" — peanut-farming crabs, masters of Juego de maní, at war with the seals over their ocean breeding grounds. Named individual: Raul, a "Sun-Kissed Cloud Rank Warrior" and one of Donut's six starting totems Unsettled Ghommid 30 Non-corporeal visitors from the land of the dead, in endlessly varied one-of-a-kind forms — toddler minotaurs, six-legged foxes, bug heads, a naked obese man walking on his hands with flaming Dumbo ears. Their touch inflicts a powerful freezing effect. Driven mad en masse by Asojano's presence Ghommid Splitter 66 A donkey-head-and-snake hybrid ghommid. Named individual: Skylar Spinach, one of Donut's six starting totems. Has the Splitter ability — it breaks into two pieces on a fatal blow and must be killed three times total, and unusually, each iteration is more powerful than the last Spirit Box — A trap, not a creature. Roots the target for sixty seconds, lowers spirit resistance, and summons a random non-corporeal entity from the area to possess them — permanently, if it succeeds La Ciguapa Legendary A hairy woman with backward feet who lures opponents with a charm attack. Per the Bahamas book, she is hard to kill by any means except familiars and pets — never by a crawler directly. Mongo kills the one they find before it fully wakes Pox Slug / Sluggalo 1, then escalating Juggalo-themed slugs that pop out of the boils of anyone infected with SlugPox. Each successive slug is one level higher than the last. Later weaponised: crawlers deliberately infect themselves and rebrand as "Sluggalos," with their leader, Doctor Bones, carrying a superior Super Spreader spell Zombie Turkey 10 Undead farm stock; the Havana region's zombie outbreak also produces zombie cows, pigs, fish and seagulls, all of which spread the infection by bite

docs.title: Book 7 mob catalog (Floor 9)
docs.text: Faction Wars is a war, so Floor 9's "mobs" are mostly soldiers, generated troops and faction hardware rather than wandering dungeon creatures. The five with real plot weight — Zarogoth, Flesher, War Mage, Hunter Wraith and Bijou — have their own pages above.

docs.title: Generated troops and the war mage cycle
docs.text: Name Level(s) Faction Notable trait Zarogoth 50 War Mage Rebellion "Sludge Ghoul" / "Sausage Golem" — a translucent sausage casing full of soul-oil, produced by a soul-crystal generator. Has a pain ray attack and will not die until it has lost 51% of its internal fluid. The primary swarm mob of the endgame Peeling Phase Flesher 1 Any — they attack whatever is flagged an enemy The skin stripped off a corpse by the spell You're Not Done Yet and animated. Seeks out enemies on its own, dissolves their flesh and re-sleeves them; combines with a reanimated skeleton into a symbiote. Immune to fire — symbiotes are not War Mage 100 Skull Empire, then the War Mage Rebellion A symbiote re-sleeved 12+ times until the accumulated magic becomes spontaneously sapient. Nobody designed them; they "just sort of happened." Heads explode ~10 minutes after death — a Sapient Moment of Destruction. Rarely recycled between seasons, so individual war mages can remember prior events

docs.title: Recycled and wilderness mobs (the expanded map)
docs.text:
When the AI enlarges the playing field, the new territory is stocked by recycling and re-levelling mobs from previous floors, with "no rhyme or reason or quests, kind of like the first floor."

Name Level(s) Notable trait Skank Skunk Warrior 45 Peaceful enough individually, but kept in line by their leadership's spells and tricks. Their spray inflicts the Skanked debuff: three hours of unremovable stink, −70% Charisma, and uncontrollable vomiting as a side effect. Not deadly; genuinely awful Fancy Boy 55 A Skank Skunk Battle Wizard — the named leader of the skunk band. Eaten by Jamal the shark mid-berserk Rolling Battle Formation Ball 70 A riff on Floor 1's Ball of Swine: a self-propelled ball of packed mobs bulldozing circles through the forest. Not listed as a boss, despite the smaller Ball of Swine having been a Borough Boss. Distinct from Donut's player-cast spell of the same name — the mob came first, the spell arrives later from a stolen skunk wizard's hat Chilly Goats Unspecified Floor 1 mobs recycled into the expanded map and re-levelled; fought by Imani's team Danger Dingoes (with Kobold riders) Unspecified Floor 2's kobold cavalry, likewise recycled; fought by Jurgen's group Concierge Shark 41 Floor 5's "Death's Welcoming Committee." Appears only as a corpse in a recently drained Larracos alleyway — "Killed by suffocation when the Semeru Warden finally decided to open the drain"

docs.title: Reaver hardware and pets
docs.text: Name Level(s) Notable trait Dumplin' — Juiced Rot Sticker Behemoth 40 Rot stickers raised from babies as genuine, affectionate pets, then caged, injected with size-altering steroids, deliberately infected and fired at enemy positions as biological seeking missiles the size of a Mini Cooper. Warning tags read: the Gurgles, Insanity, "Not Just Rabies, but Eat-Your-Face-Off-Rabies," and "This Pet has been fed a Truck Stop Boner Pill." A level-40 behemoth packs the punch of a stick of goblin dynamite Reaver Security Force Cyborg Drop Trooper 53 Warlord Fang's personal defense deployment; part-organic, part-machine mercenaries in the "light" version of their armor. The System AI apologises at length for the Spelljammer/Warhammer aesthetic and says it has already rejected the Valtay's plans for the eleventh floor Reaver Industries Security Sentry Dog, "The Ditch Digger" Unspecified Latest-model robot guard dog, a tech-based security system with an optional anti-personnel explosive. The larger, lion-sized variants carry Mini Tactical Nukes — the stockpile that levels the Reaver castle and kills Warlord Fang

docs.title: Bloc / Operatic Collective hardware
docs.text: Name Level(s) Notable trait Weeper Unspecified (tank class) The Bloc alliance's armor — "Look like those British Mark V's from the first world war, but with a top turret and a single anti-air tube." Formidable with infantry support. Exploitable flaw: to avoid magical fire control, each tank charges an energy ball moments before firing; a driver who deliberately removes the fire control chamber turns the tank into a bomb. Commander Volteeg does exactly that, killing 10,000 Bloc soldiers and Warlord Hortense Leadership Unit, and eliminating the Operatic Collective from Faction Wars Clockwork mounts Unspecified The Bloc war mages ride "a menagerie of clockwork animals" instead of horses — horse-like creatures, a Mongo-sized dinosaur, a horse-sized panther, a mantid-hunter-like insect — all whirring, clicking and hissing steam

docs.title: Deity-adjacent and special
docs.text: Name Level(s) Notable trait Bijou Unspecified (non-corporeal fairy) Physically carry the invisible worship-tendrils between gods, temples and adherents. Never killed or caught by anyone, though a trap is theoretically possible. Central to the Sepsis Whore's disappearing act (via Travel the Path + Welcome Home) and to Justice Light's climactic trap Ogre Basilica Cleric Guard 125 Worships Taranis, which grants the rare Untouchable status: gods are not allowed to attack them, and they can temporarily bar a deity from crossing a threshold. They guard the Basilica Entrance of Club Vanquisher on the 12th floor — and their absence from that post is exactly why gods are able to wander onto the Floor 9 battlefield at all. A Black Nimbus potion strips the "Un" off Untouchable, at the cost of dozens of instant god-issued marked-for-death flags. Juice Box's changelings later imitate them to hold Harpocrates out of Shanty Town Hunter Wraith Unspecified A Floor 10–11 monster form. Possession lets you puppet a body even if it is dead, and use its inventory — but carries the curse called the Inevitable Ruin, which forces the possessor to see an unwanted truth about whoever they possess. The curse shares its name with the book Eclipse Pyxies Unspecified (demon mob) Fat, fur-covered guinea pigs with bat wings and jagged teeth. Bautista carries a dozen as stuffed animals that switch from toy to live monster in midair Newborn Ursensus 0 — Legendary Creature A brand-new creature type, created for the occasion: Mongo and Kiwi's twin daughters. Four legs, wing stubs, wet brown fur, Mongo-like beaked heads, bulbous mismatched pug eyes, and an unsettlingly human-sounding cry. "Part raptor, part bear, part Scolopendra magic. All adorable." Because of this mob's intelligence level they cannot be used as pets Children of Inpewt Unspecified The Book 5 revenant-curse creature type. Not actually encountered here — Carl notes that anyone squished by the teleported city of Larracos landing on the twelfth floor will turn into one, and expects it to become someone's problem later. Eileithyia confirms the zombies exist and that Odette has taken control of them

docs.title: Book 8 mob catalog (Floors 10-11)
docs.text:
Floor 10's races run through several recycled and satirical Earth-adjacent regions before the Floor 11 finale. The Horribles, the finale's central masked mob, has its own full page above rather than a table row here.

Name Level(s) Notable trait Screeching Death Manatee 90 A theme-park-satire mob populating Heat 1's track: real manatees relocated to a former Land War terraforming world whose bankrupt orcish owner named everything after its worst trait — "the raccoons are Doom Crier Beasts. The cockatiels are called Fuck-Off Cockatiels." Individually named victims (Miss Talulah, Miss Brianna Kim) are killed by the racers' mounts rather than fought directly Sugar Hermit 11 Migratory, skull-wearing swarm creatures — "these horrific little terrors feed off of two things. Brains and bones" — that wear painted Day-of-the-Dead-style skulls "like a snail wears a shell" and migrate toward a kaiju skull blocking the Heat 3 finish line. Not the same mob as any Book 6–7 mock-battle-arena creature; nothing by this name appears before Book 8 Coblyn Corporation "Toddler Cocaine" doll-elementals 12 A deliberately, self-consciously satirical corporate mob: the knockers (small gnome-like miners displaced from their own caves) turn to drug manufacturing for survival, then legitimize into the Coblyn Corporation, then — having run out of adult customers — begin selling low-dose cocaine to children through toy-doll mascots (Sally Speedball, Toot-Toot, and Belushi, together "the Nose Candy Star Dusters"). The dolls themselves become infused Cocaine Elementals with a contagious "pass-through" ability once elemental magic leaks in their factory. The text's own framing is unusually blunt about the satire: "There's not really a lesson here or a point to any of this, just a sad observation" Knocker Unspecified The small, gnome-like miners behind the Coblyn Corporation above; driven from their mineral-rich caves by "larger, stronger, and more powerful creatures," they turn to drug manufacturing and eventually corporate ownership as their only path to survival Great Rusty / Ginger cannibal tribes 99 (Great Rusty, boss) Two warring cannibal settlements (north and south) of pale, mask-wearing "Gingers" living in the Heat 3 jungle track, led by chieftains Great Rusty (south, one-shot killed by Donut, triggering a mandatory kill-quest against his rival) and Maurice (north). The book explicitly, self-consciously flags this content as satire rather than playing it straight: Carl calls the AI's own description "both socially conscious and outrageously racist at the same time," and the description itself frames the joke as being about colonial exploitation cycles rather than the Gingers themselves Zipper Shrew 10 Small, drill-headed rodents infesting Satan's Water Park (Heat 6); swarm the racers' shielded vehicles in the thousands and are weaponized by Donut's Summon Ye, Vermin spell to finish off the Maurice variant hiding among the water park's ginger "season pass holders" Slag Elemental 75 (Neighborhood Boss) Regenerating, molten-metal gorilla-shaped elementals infesting the inverted steel-mill ceiling maze of the Coblyn Corporation factory (Heat 5); a cut-rate security measure that went wrong — "wildly contagious, regenerating, infused, and very pissed-off elementals all over the place." Immortal for practical purposes: "it's pretty much impossible to kill these things" unless the corpse is kept from falling back into the molten metal below

docs.title: Bijou
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Tiny, non-corporeal fairy mob
  • Function: Physically carries the worship-tendrils that connect gods, their temples and their worshipers
  • Where: Everywhere in the dungeon, zipping between floors; invisible to almost everyone
  • Can they be killed? "Nobody has ever killed or caught or stopped the Bijou," though Mordecai believes a certain type of trap should in theory work
  • Plot weight: The mechanism behind the Sepsis Whore's disappearing act, and the mechanism behind Justice Light's climactic trap

docs.title: What They Do
docs.text:
Worship in Dungeon Crawler World is not abstract. It is a physical, whisker-thin thread of invisible light that can penetrate almost any substance or spell — and something has to carry it.

Book 7, ch. 49

"When one worships a god, a link is formed between the adherent and the immortal. This link comes in the form of an actual, physical, whisker-thin connection made of invisible light. Light that can penetrate almost any substance or spell. After a new adherent pledges themselves, a tiny, non-corporeal fairy mob called a Bijou grabs a tendril of light from the god and drags it to the new worshiper and attaches it to the adherent's heart. When a person moves around, other tendrils also grow, connecting the adherent to other temples and in some cases, other worshipers. These connections, too, are facilitated by the Bijou fairies."

Rosetta Thagra reads them as a workaround rather than a design feature — a kludge the original designers used to bolt the deity system onto the game — and the quirk "usually has no impact on anything."

Certain skills can perceive them. The NPC Edgar has a level-15 skill called Sense Movement that catches their motion; upward momentum from the ground means someone nearby has just worshiped a god for the first time. That is the detection method the Princess Posse uses to test Rosetta's theory about the naga escape trick.

docs.title: The Sepsis Whore's Disappearing Act
docs.text:
The bijou tendril is the road. Of the fifteen "light" deities with temples inside Club Vanquisher, six carry Travel the Path, a spell that turns the caster into light and lets them follow a path at light speed — and which the system does not count as teleportation. Four of those six also carry the once-ever skill Welcome Home.

Book 7, ch. 49

"This skill, combined with Travel the Path, would allow the adherent to follow the bijou fairy's light tendril path directly to the strongest connected temple, which was invariably inside of Club Vanquisher."

That combination is how Princess Vinata, the Sepsis Whore, has vanished instantly at the end of every Faction Wars for centuries without ever being killed. Cracking it is what sends Carl into the Temple of Khepri on Operation: Snake Pit.

docs.title: Justice Light's Trap
docs.text:
The skyfowl trap master Justice Light builds the endgame around them. His trap combines a bijou fairy trap with a demon trap, and it uses the fairies' own unbreakable connections as structural cable.

Book 7, epilogue

"The items that fell were a bijou fairy trap, along with the thousands of threads that connected the fairies to the 12th floor, and a demon trap, along with the thousands of evicted demons with the power to open a portal back to Sheol, if only they could find something to latch onto... Four separate planes—all jumbled and confused—folded and moved together as the unbreakable lines of the bijou fairies tightened, creating a flower pattern before the darkness in the center of it all broke apart. System Message: The Bijou Trap has deactivated. All captured Bijou have been freed."

The consequence of that folding is the last thing the book reports: the Nothing draining into Scolopendra's Lair, and Scolopendra awakening.

Scope

Princess Vinata and Justice Light are covered on their own character pages; this page covers the bijou as a creature type and the mechanic they exist to serve.

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Brindle Grub
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Base level: 2 (juvenile) → 3 (Cow-Tailed stage) → adult "Brindled Vespa" (hornet form)
  • Floor: 2
  • Role: Dungeon "janitor" mob — spawns automatically on corpses
  • Danger: Individually trivial; dangerous in swarms and at full maturity

AI Commentary (in-voice, written for this wiki — not a book excerpt)

"Ah, the circle of life — kill a mob, get a grub, ignore the grub, get a flesh-eating hornet the size of a golden retriever. Truly a beautiful ecosystem we've built here. Please recycle your corpses responsibly, folks."

docs.title: Official Description
docs.text:
Per the in-universe monster card:

"Have you ever found a dead, bloated, and decomposing body? Have ya poked it with a stick just to see what would wiggle out?... Here on the second floor, rats are yesterday's news. Brindle Grubs are now all the rage, and janitor duty falls unto them. The more monsters you kill in an area, the more the grubs eat. The more the grubs eat, the bigger they get. Once you start finding them in the pupa stage, you best move on. Grubs are easy to kill. Their older siblings are not."

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
Brindle Grubs are a corpse-cleanup mechanic as much as a monster: every corpse left on Floor 2 spawns more of them, and grubs that eat enough corpses mature — first into Cow-Tailed Brindle Grubs (Level 3, per their card: "finally able to defend itself, kind of like the way a toddler holding a plastic baseball bat is able to defend himself"), then into pupae, and finally into Brindled Vespas: huge hornet-bodied creatures with clawed, grasping arms and an acid-spit attack. This escalation is directly responsible for Carl adopting a strict "always destroy the corpse" policy after learning how the chain works — leaving bodies behind is what turns a nuisance into a real threat later in the same area.

The System AI patches Brindled Vespa numbers down mid-book after their spitting-acid attack proves too aggressive for the current floor's difficulty curve.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised.

docs.title: Drek
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Level: 6
  • Floor: 4 ("The Iron Tangle")
  • Appearance: Fat, wrinkly, grey-skinned, knee-height, demonic-baby-like creatures
  • Behavior: Travel in packs of 50+; can climb walls/pillars like spiders

docs.title: Official Description
docs.text:
Per the in-universe monster card:

"Everybody loves babies, right? What kind of asshole doesn't love babies? How about demonic, ravenous, berserking babies who travel in packs of at least 50? It's rumored these lil' rascals can devour a full-sized elephant down to the bone in less than five seconds. And you're a lot smaller than an elephant."

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: Dreks are the Iron Tangle's most immediate, entry-level threat — a swarming horde mob that packs train station platforms and surges as one toward anything visible through a train's windows. Individually weak (Level 6, easily one-shot), their danger is entirely in numbers and their willingness to climb walls, pillars, and ceilings like spiders to reach prey. One latches onto Carl's bare foot during his first encounter with them, biting down hard enough to cause real pain before he stomps it — exploding "like a tomato soup-filled balloon."

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text:
Dreks are the first monster Carl's party encounters upon arriving on Floor 4, immediately establishing the danger of the Iron Tangle's train-station platforms and forcing the party into an improvised defensive retreat through the train's cars.

Sourced from Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook.

docs.title: Flesher
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Level: 1
  • Floors: First seen on Floor 4 (Book 3, the Dismemberment Limited); mass-deployed on Floor 9 ("Faction Wars")
  • Origin: The skin of a corpse, stripped off by the spell You’re Not Done Yet and animated
  • Behaviour: Autonomously hunts anything flagged as an enemy; dissolves the victim's own flesh and re-sleeves them
  • Resistances: Immune to fire. (Symbiotes, their next stage, are not)
  • Matters because: Twelve or more re-sleevings of a symbiote produce a War Mage

docs.title: The Flesher Cycle
docs.text:
The flesher is stage one of a three-stage escalation that the dungeon never designed and cannot fully control.

Monster description (Book 7, ch. 62)

"The skin of a corpse is ripped off of a body and turned to a creature named a flesher. The flesher then consumes a living being, melting the original skin off and re-sleeving the creature. The flesher casts Boned, reanimating the skeleton, and the two become a symbiote. Symbiotes are extremely attractive targets to other fleshers. And because young symbiotes are slow and awkward, they are oftentimes quickly re-sleeved by fresh fleshers. Each iteration results in a more powerful being."

Twelve or more iterations and the accumulated magic becomes spontaneously sapient — see War Mage.

Physically they read as dark, flat shapes that skitter "like manta rays across the ocean floor," flapping onto a target, wrapping around the legs and moving upward while the victim's flesh dissolves. They burn through cybernetic armor. Carl's reaction to watching a field of them move is "a deep, primal revulsion."

docs.title: Floor 9: Weaponised at Scale
docs.text:
The Princess Posse turns the flesher cycle into a deliberate tactic. Every allied graveyard's corpses are collected by Bodi and the 103rd and dumped on the battlefield, then Princess Donut casts a wide-range, tower-amplified You’re Not Done Yet over them — stripping thousands of skins at once and sending the resulting fleshers sailing across the field at enemy formations. The Madness abandoning that front wastes the first batch; the second batch is the one that matters.

When Donut's Rolling Battle Formation ball forms, the fleshers crawl over and into it, worming through the cracks to find the Dream and Reaver soldiers inside. Because the prisoners are invulnerable while the spell holds, the fleshers simply wait, wrapped around them.

That is the whole design. Rosetta Thagra explicitly vetoes casting Laundry Day to strip them off, because the fleshers are the finisher:

Rosetta, Book 7, ch. 74

"With them both amplified by War Crime, it should separate the enemies all out and drop them into a ring of fire. Fleshers are fire resistant, but symbiotes aren't, so if any enemies resist, they should be pounced upon by the fleshers, turned to symbiotes, and then killed. That's the finisher since War Crime keeps them alive. It'll kill the enemy and any potential baby war mages."

Carl's other standing concern all floor is preventing new war mages from being born in the middle of his own battlefield. When Nami — the influencer piloting the goddess Eris — is ejected from the ball and immediately skinned into a flesher wearing a dromedarian hide "much too big for her frame," two more fleshers attach within seconds. Carl blows the whole cluster up rather than let a twelfth iteration start.

Cross-reference

You're Not Done Yet, War Crime, Rolling Battle Formation and Boned are Spells-pass topics — see Spells.

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin, with background from Book 3.

docs.title: Frenzied Gerbil
docs.text:
Level 11, and one of the System AI's recurring private jokes. Ralph, the Floor 2 boss Carl and Donut kill by stomping him underfoot in a kobold fighting pit, is a Frenzied Gerbil — and the AI has never gotten over how much it enjoyed watching Carl squish him.

The joke resurfaces on Floor 5: dirigible gnome snipers carry bandoliers of Live Ammo Balls, clamshell containers that store a live creature in stasis until impact, fired as a ranged weapon or point-defense munition. After the Wasteland is shot down, Carl and his party loot several intact balls off gnome corpses — and every single one turns out to contain the exact same thing: a Frenzied Gerbil. Carl's refusal to squish one on principle (correctly identifying the pattern as the AI angling for another crowd-pleasing kill) triggers an actual in-game punishment: thousands of gerbils scattered by the Wasteland's wreckage regroup and swarm Hump Town in a mass attack, forcing Carl to kill dozens of them by hand — including, eventually, by foot — before the assault stops on its own. He receives a You're the reason why daddy drinks! achievement (and a Gold box) for "correcting the issue," alongside a warning that the dungeon's underlying "acceleration" punishment system had been quietly threatening to escalate the whole time.

Sourced from Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario and Book 4: The Gate of the Feral Gods.

docs.title: Funeral Bell
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Level: ~90–95 (varies by settlement)
  • Floor: 6 ("The Hunting Grounds")
  • Type: Mushroom-humanoid town guard
  • Role: Standard-issue city/village guard NPC across the floor's non-elf settlements

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Funeral Bells are the mushroom-headed guard race stationed in nearly every town on Floor 6 outside of the High Elf territory — flat, white, emotionless faces, tall bell-shaped caps, and (per Carl, who never once hears one speak to a crawler) an apparent ability to communicate with each other that they simply don't extend to outsiders. They're consistently high-level (90+) even in small settlements, making them far too dangerous for a crawler to fight directly this early in the floor.

Their most useful trait is passive: standing guard automatically deactivates nearby traps set for crawlers, which is why the roads immediately around Funeral-Bell-guarded towns and the caravans that travel between them are safe to walk, while the surrounding wilderness is not.

docs.title: Settlement Guards vs. Conquered Guards
docs.text:
Funeral Bells guard towns regardless of who currently controls them. Once Donut or Carl takes over a settlement (by killing its mayor), the town's existing Funeral Bell garrison switches allegiance automatically and can be issued orders, armed with missile launchers, and assigned to specific entrances — this is how Point Mongo's defenses are built up against the incoming hunters. Individual guards can be renamed by whoever controls the town; Donut renames several of Point Mongo's garrison (Doctor El, Dinallo, Miss Nance, Ice Man) over Mordecai's objections.

Funeral Bells are not involved in the personal-space "three strikes" ejection rule — that's a separate saferoom mechanic: attacking a crawler's own party member/NPC three times inside their personal space forcibly ejects the attacker, stripped of gear, to the nearest monster nest. This is the fate of Edict, a Dark Hive mantis merchant who deliberately provokes his own ejection this way (by attacking Bomo, then Carl, inside Carl's personal space in Zockau — a town with no Funeral Bell garrison at all) for reasons of mantis honor culture (see The Dark Hive).

Sourced from Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: Hunter Wraith
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Ethereal, non-corporeal possession monster
  • Native floors: 10 and 11 — "Those are floor 10 and 11 monsters," per Tipid
  • Core ability: Possession. A wraith-possessed body can be puppeted even if it is dead, and the wraith can use items from the host's inventory
  • The cost: A curse called the Inevitable Ruin, which forces the possessor to see an unwanted truth about whoever they possess
  • Seen in Book 7: Taken on as a form by the changeling Juice Box in ch. 79, to rescue Louis Santiago from the Reaver castle

docs.title: The Form
docs.text:
A hunter wraith is a ghost-like thing — Carl's first sight of one is Juice Box shifting into "an ethereal, ghost-like creature" so fast he misses the change. Tipid recognises it immediately and flags both its usefulness and its price in the same breath: "It's, uh, not going to be a clean getaway. There's something that happens when that particular wraith touches people, but that's more an issue for Juice Box than Louis."

Its combat value is the possession mechanic, which is unusually total:

Book 7, ch. 80

"People wraith-possessed could be moved like puppets even if they were dead, which was terrifying, especially since the wraiths could—and did—utilize items in the crawler's inventory. It was a common, terrifying mob from higher floors."

That is precisely how Warlord Fang of the Reavers dies: Juice Box possesses Louis inside the castle, puppets him into dropping a No Disassemble from his own inventory, and teleports out. The system splits the credit accordingly — 51% to Carl for detonating the bomb, 1% to Louis, 40% to Juice Box, and the remainder to Fang himself "for hiding in the worst possible place, which was inside the dragon."

docs.title: The Inevitable Ruin
docs.text:
The curse is what gives the book its title.

Juice Box, Book 7, ch. 82

"It's also a spell. Or rather, it's a curse, inflicted upon the mind of the Hunter Wraith, which is why they are so bitter. When they possess someone, it ruins something pure. It doesn't change whatever it is. It just tells you the truth. It's difficult to explain, and it manifests itself in different ways. But for me, when I had Louis possessed in order to save him, the curse showed me the truth. And the truth is that he's terrified of me. The truth is he's not in love with me..."

Her verdict afterward: "I wish I hadn't taken on the form of that hunter wraith. It was worth it to save him, but I wish I hadn't."

Thematically central

The Inevitable Ruin is the title of Book 7, and the phrase is used three separate ways across the book: as the High Elf queen's name for the moment you accept you are going to die (Everly's chapter); as Carl's private label for the sense of universal doom that follows Juice Box's warning; and finally as the literal name of this wraith curse. The hunter wraith is where the title lands as a game mechanic.

Scope

Juice Box's arc — why she takes the form, and what the revealed truth costs her — is a Characters-pass topic. See Juice Box and Louis Santiago.

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Jikininki
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Level: 17
  • Floor: 4 ("The Iron Tangle") — the "Janitor's Lair" car type, station 12 and similar stops
  • Role: Corpse-cleanup "janitor" mob — the Iron Tangle's version of a recurring series pattern
  • Appearance: Seven-foot, emaciated, white-skinned ghouls in tattered conductor-style suits and hats

docs.title: Official Description
docs.text:
Per the in-universe monster card:

"Of all the types of ghouls one may find in the Iron Tangle Rail System, the Jikininki is the most common, the most well-behaved, and the most insatiable. Their voracious appetite for flesh makes them the perfect janitors. They'll generally leave you alone as long as you're not bleeding, as long as you don't litter, and as long as you don't trespass into their personal space. It's rude."

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: Jikininki wear tattered double-breasted suits with golden "Janitor" lettering on their conductor-style hats — one has a pinback button reading "How may I hurt you?" — and their mouths chatter up and down "like an industrial shredder." They're found in dedicated "Janitor's Lair" train cars, marked on the map with a question mark until first entered. Despite the threatening description, they're not aggressive by default — a pattern consistent with the Iron Tangle's broader corpse-disposal "ghoul system," which scales up in danger the more bodies accumulate (see Wrath Ghouls and Blister Ghouls, the more dangerous forms this system produces further down the line).

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text:
Two Jikininki are the first real fight Carl's party has on Floor 4, killed via a coordinated double Magic Missile headshot followed by melee finishers, while fleeing a Drek swarm into their car by mistake.

Sourced from Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook.

docs.title: Krasue
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Level: 16
  • Floor: 3 (Medium Skyfowl Settlement)
  • Classification: Ghost-class mob — only harmed by magic or magical items
  • Danger: Requires finding and destroying the physical corpse to kill permanently, not just the flying "head"

docs.title: Official Description
docs.text:
Per the in-universe monster card:

"Said to be the undead shell of a woman who lived a life of sin, Krasue roam the dark places, hiding their hideous true form. They are ravenous, and they devour the blood of the unsuspecting. In other words, these things are flying heads who are also vampires. And, they bring their organs along because... nobody knows why. Probably just because it's really gross. You may kill the head and trailing organs to fend her off, but this mob doesn't truly die until you find and destroy the rest of her corpse. You will not earn experience for killing this mob until it is dead-dead. Not just dead."

docs.title: What They Are
docs.text: Krasue in Book 2 aren't a random spawn — they're deliberately manufactured by Miss Quill from Desperado Club sex workers lured to her settlement with false promises of safe passage to lower floors. By day, the transformation's "successes" appear as ordinary human women working in Quill's administrative building; by night, their heads detach and fly free, trailing their own organs on wet ropes of tissue, to feed and serve as Quill's army. Killing the daytime body (or "corpse," as the game labels it even while it's technically alive) is what actually ends a krasue permanently — decapitating the floating head alone only drives it off temporarily.

docs.title: Notable Appearance
docs.text:
A group of krasue kill the orc NPC GumGum after she starts investigating the deaths of Desperado Club workers, and later ambush Carl and Donut directly. One transformed krasue, Burgundy — a magistrate's-office assistant Carl and Donut had spoken to earlier — survives the destruction of Quill's nest long enough to explain the krasue-creation scheme in detail before begging to be killed while still human, rather than transforming again at nightfall.

Sourced from Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario.

docs.title: Night Weasel
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Level: Unspecified (pack mob)
  • Floor: 6 ("The Hunting Grounds")
  • Type: Invisible pack-hunting weasel/mustelid mob
  • Notable trait: Hunts entirely by sound and smell; inflicts paralysis on contact

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Night Weasels are naturally invisible, pack-hunting predators found across the Floor 6 jungle, both wild and occasionally under the control of a hunter (their original owner, one Hunter Zabit, loses his entire pack to Carl and Donut in the floor's opening hours) or of the High Elves. They hunt in coordinated groups of at least a dozen, attacking from multiple directions at once, and their bite inflicts a paralysis effect strong enough to freeze a crawler in place for a full "Deer in the Headlight-ed" debuff window.

Since they can't be seen directly, the only reliable way to fight them is to track incoming damage and sound — Carl and Donut's usual method is a smoke curtain plus Torch on infrared, or simply letting an immune ally (the were-castors Clint and Holger are immune to the paralysis effect and can smell/hear the weasels perfectly well) tank the fight while everyone else evacuates.

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text:
Night Weasels are the first mob Carl and Donut encounter on Floor 6, ambushing the party at a village gate within minutes of the floor opening — an early demonstration of the Ping spell's value for exposing invisible threats. They recur throughout the book as a background hazard for anyone traveling off the main caravan roads.

Sourced from Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: Rage Elemental
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Level: 93 (vastly above Floor 2's normal range)
  • Classification: Elite — not a standard boss-tier encounter
  • Trigger: Summoned by the System AI as a punishment for public urination/defecation outside designated bathrooms
  • Outcome (Book 1): Kills Yolanda Martinez; ultimately defeated by Carl and Donut via a collapsing-stairwell trap

AI Commentary (in-voice, written for this wiki — not a book excerpt)

"You had one job, humans. One. And instead of finding a toilet, you got Grandpa Jack killed by a screaming, teleporting nightmare with anger issues. Let this be a lesson: hold it, or we will send something that cannot be reasoned with. This has been a public service announcement from Sanitation Compliance."

docs.title: Official Description
docs.text:
Per the in-universe monster card:

"The first recorded summoning of a Rage Elemental, blah, blah, blah. If you are reading this, you likely don't give a shit about the monster's (rather interesting and tragic) history. You're probably running. It's not going to matter. The almost-indestructible Rage Elemental is said to only dissipate after it has claimed 666 souls."

docs.title: Encounter
docs.text:
Announced via a System AI broadcast as a deterrent after repeated bathroom-etiquette violations by human crawlers, the Rage Elemental is dropped directly into Team Meadow Lark's location after elderly resident Jack urinates in a hallway and is shot dead by Yolanda moments before the elemental arrives. A badger-headed, multi-limbed horror that teleports short distances and appears to have near-limitless stamina, it kills Yolanda during the group's escape. Carl and Donut ultimately deny it a real victory by luring it into a collapsing stairwell alongside an explosive, destroying it (or at least driving it off) without it claiming the achievement/XP a normal kill would grant — a deliberate choice to spite the system that sent it.

The event becomes a broadcast segment, and the show frames it as a consequence of "disrespect... regarding the bathrooms" rather than acknowledging it as a design failure.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised.

docs.title: Remex
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Level: 1
  • Classification: Soul Leech Capacitor — a "Bereft Minion" (a minion still animate after its controller's death)
  • Floor: 3 (Medium Skyfowl Settlement)
  • True identity: Miss Quill's undead husband and former magistrate; once a famous crawler himself

docs.title: Official Description
docs.text:
Per the in-universe monster card:

"Have you ever played with a Ouija board and realized that speaking with a lost loved one just wasn't doing it for you anymore? Perhaps you wanted to kick it up a notch? Maybe bring them back to life?... A Soul Leech Capacitor can do that for you. These fragile, but physically strong undead creatures can only be created by a Necromancer or a Dark Cleric. The spell latches onto the most-loved soul of the spell's target and yanks that creature back into existence... A simple scratch from this beast will rip your soul straight from your body. That soul power is stored in the capacitor, allowing the Leech's owner to access huge reserves of mana points."

docs.title: What He Is
docs.text:
Remex was once a real crawler — a "tenner" who reached at least the tenth floor and became famous enough to be recognized by the achievement/views system years later. After his original death (killed by an orc, "years ago," per his own rambling account), his wife Miss Quill resurrected him as a Soul Leech Capacitor, deliberately positioning the ritual next to the town's Swordsman-guard Soul Crystal amplifier so the resulting feedback would also kill and transform the sitting magistrate, Featherfall — all part of Quill's long-term plan.

As a capacitor, Remex channels and stores the enormous soul power generated whenever something dies near the amplifier, including every krasue Quill creates. He exists in a permanent state of grief and confusion, unable to stay on topic, occasionally addressing a dead son who isn't there.

docs.title: Notable Appearance
docs.text:
After Quill's death, Carl and Donut find Remex cowering, harmless and non-hostile, in the Swordsman depot's upper floor. He explains the entire krasue/soul-crystal scheme (see Miss Quill) in a long, rambling confession before the still-building soul energy inside him triggers a massive, unstoppable magical explosion — the climax of the "Sex Workers Who Fell from the Heavens" quest chain. Carl manages to contain and defuse the worst of it using an item that becomes Carl's Doomsday Scenario, though Remex himself is destroyed in the blast, finally free of his half-life.

Sourced from Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario.

docs.title: Shambling Berserker
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Level: 12
  • Floor: 3 (Over City ruins), but also confirmed to exist on Floor 1
  • Aliases: "Mini Grinder," "the Shrilling"
  • Danger: Individually weak in daylight; power quadruples in darkness

docs.title: Official Description
docs.text:
Per the in-universe monster card:

"If you weren't fortunate enough to face one of these neighborhood boss monsters on the first level of the dungeon, fret not! Now's your chance to get in on the fun!... What you see here is a Shambling Berserker, the smallest iteration of this creature. Also known as the Mini Grinder or the Shrilling, this creature consists of extra parts we found after creating the World Dungeon. Waste not, want not... This undead abomination is oftentimes found in groups, summoned as a slow, but very tenacious assassin. The good news is, they're mostly harmless. Unless, of course, you face one in the dark. Their power is quadrupled in the dark. And once they go berserk, there's no putting them down."

docs.title: Appearance & Behavior
docs.text: A shambling, thirteen-foot pile of mismatched human body parts — arms, legs, torsos, and multiple groaning heads — fused together into a single slow-moving, slug-shaped mass, with tentacle-like limbs waving above it. In daylight (or any bright light source) they're slow and fragile, falling apart after a single solid hit. In darkness they become vastly more dangerous and relentless.

docs.title: Notable Appearance
docs.text:
A group of Shambling Berserkers ambush Carl and Donut in full darkness outside an abandoned Over City pool, summoned specifically by Miss Quill as a stalling tactic. Carl, unable to see them, badly misjudges a stick of dynamite that bounces back toward him; he ends up falling into and detonating the rotting corpse of a dead boss monster (The Divider) in the resulting chaos, which does more damage to him than the berserkers themselves.

Sourced from Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario.

docs.title: Street Urchin
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Level: 8
  • Floor: 3 (Over City ruins)
  • Role: Floor 3's "janitor" mob — the Over City's equivalent of Floor 2's Brindle Grubs
  • Danger: Individually low; aggressive toward anything blocking their cleanup work

docs.title: Official Description
docs.text:
Per the in-universe monster card:

"These pokey little puppies only come out at night. Long, long ago, some of the richest citizens of the Over City kept these things as pets... When the cataclysm came, the Street Urchins were transformed into what you see today. Larger, deadlier, and a lot spikier. And after they cleaned the corpses of their former owners, they moved into the ruins and resumed their duties as the janitor mobs of the Over City... The ruin's version of a Roomba, these things only have one purpose: to remove dead bodies and any other refuse left behind by inconsiderate crawlers. They won't bother you if you don't bother them."

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: Squat, knee-high, black, spike-covered creatures that move like rolling tumbleweeds. They're mindless scavengers, not natural predators — they attack only when something (a corpse, debris, an improvised barricade) is blocking access to whatever they're trying to clean up. Their long, piercing spikes can seriously wound anything caught in the middle of that cleanup, as Mongo and a sedated Princess Donut discover when a swarm mistakes Carl's makeshift defensive pile for refuse.

docs.title: Notable Appearance
docs.text:
A swarm nearly kills Mongo while he defends an unconscious Donut (held under Tsarina Signet's Water Lily curse) — the urchins are drawn by the debris Carl piled up as a barricade, not by malice. Removing the debris (and the resulting scattered spikes) causes the swarm to lose interest immediately.

Sourced from Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario.

docs.title: The Horribles
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • What they are: Masked, silent, non-combatant avatars lining the parade route and filling the arena stands at the Floor 11 climax
  • Level: X (unexaminable as a combat threat — "This is a non-combatant")
  • Count: Thousands, described as representing every death across roughly 3,424 seasons of Dungeon Crawler World
  • True nature: Revealed at the Floor 11 finale to be literal fragments of the system AI's own lost memory — remnants of the Eulogist, not monsters at all
  • Floor: Floor 11 ("A Parade of Horribles"), Book 8

docs.title: What They Look Like
docs.text:
The Horribles line both sides of the parade route in a low fog, standing ten deep for as far as the eye can see — thousands of human and humanlike figures of every size, dressed in identical filthy earth-brown rags, arms and legs grimy "as if they'd just been dug up." Every single one, adults and infants alike, wears an oversized, comic-grotesque full-head mask — goblins, trolls, hobgoblins, demons — rendered in the exaggerated style of Mardi Gras or Carnival, "but much more sinister." They do not speak, do not react, and barely move beyond an occasional shift of weight.

Examining one returns a description credited to "a memory from the Eulogist":

Book 8, ch. 91

"A Horrible. Level X. This is a non-combatant. She's not really here because she no longer exists. You take that mask off, and underneath it, you will find what some people call a Primal... I am her, and she is me."

docs.title: The Reveal
docs.text:
Partway through the parade, the AI possesses the fleshmancer mercenary Grigori the Placid to deliver a guided cosmology lecture in five parts (only four of which it claims are "written" yet). The short version, kept deliberately brief here because the full Primal/Eulogist history is a Mechanics-pass topic: the Horribles are literal, remembered avatars of a Primal civilization that eventually meshed its dying members into a single collective consciousness — the same lineage that eventually produced both the system AI and the goddess Apito (called "the Apothecary" in this telling). Each of the thousands of masked figures on the road represents one individual death from across the show's entire 3,424-season history, preserved as an "anonymous inkling" inside the AI's own fragmented memory rather than as an actual resurrected person.

At the arena entrance, in time with the parade's own weapons fire, the Horribles' masks shatter and the figures collapse — only to rise again moments later without masks, their faces transformed into the actual creatures they had represented (a troll, and so on), now the mob army the crawlers must fight through in the arena itself. Examining one at this stage confirms the shift:

Book 8, ch. 92

"Marsh Troll. Level X. This is a non-combatant. This is an avatar of a troll that died during the 3,424th season of Dungeon Crawler World. He isn't really here because he is dead and gone, never to return."

The arena's bleacher seats hold a separate group — living Stand-Ins, tourists and NPCs brought in by audience vote to stand in for crawlers who couldn't be squeezed into the fight directly — distinct from the Horribles themselves, though dressed in the same style of mask.

docs.title: Aftermath
docs.text:
Once the arena fight concludes, the Horribles rise from the fog a final time, stand silently as one, and vanish for good. No mechanical reward, quest, or further encounter is attached to them; they function purely as the book's central image and the delivery vehicle for its cosmology reveal. The full history of the Primals, the Eulogist, and how the two connect to Apito and the system AI itself is left for a future Mechanics page rather than expanded further here.

Sourced from Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Tuskling
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Levels seen: 4 (Knight), 8 (Dominatrix)
  • Floor: 2
  • Faction: Ruling class of the Orcish Supremacy
  • Notable formation: The Ball of Swine borough boss

AI Commentary (in-voice, written for this wiki — not a book excerpt)

"Ladies and gentlemen, the Tuskling Knight — a title that means as much as 'Executive Vice President of Synergy' back on your home planet. Get a few dozen of them drunk and horny enough, and they'll roll into a ball and try to kill you. Frankly, relatable."

docs.title: Official Description
docs.text:
Per the in-universe monster card for a Tuskling Knight:

"When it comes to the Tuskling, their titles are about as accurate as their dating website photos. The once-mighty warriors conquered the Orcish Supremacy hundreds of years ago, defeating all the other clans. They are now shells of the mighty warriors they once were... Knights and their slightly-more dangerous female counterparts, Tuskling Courtesans, are only worthy adversaries when they come together to form an ancient, Tuskling battle formation known as a 'Ball of Swine.'"

docs.title: Appearance & Behavior
docs.text:
Short (roughly 4.5 feet), wide-bodied, warthog-headed humanoids, pink-skinned, with four tusks per individual. Individually weak and largely comedic — drunk, overdressed in formal tuxedos/gowns, and generally more dangerous to themselves than to crawlers — but their mass battle formation, the Ball of Swine, is a genuine borough-tier threat. Variants include Tuskling Courtesans (female, "slightly more dangerous") and at least one higher-level Tuskling Dominatrix (Level 8). Mordecai confirms Tusklings, like the Ball of Swine formation itself, are one of the "real" alien species used by the dungeon rather than a human-actor-driven caricature.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised.

docs.title: War Mage
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Level: 100 (Akuma, the Rebellion's leader, reads at level 100)
  • Floors: Encountered as early as Floor 4 (Book 3, "Dismember the War Mage"); central to Floor 9 ("Faction Wars")
  • Type: A true dungeon-born entity — nobody designed them, and nobody can un-design them
  • Made from: A flesher-symbiote re-sleeved twelve or more times until the accumulated magic becomes spontaneously sapient
  • Signature hazard: Their heads explode roughly ten minutes after death — a "Sapient Moment of Destruction"
  • Spell list: "War mages come with knowledge of hundreds of spells"

docs.title: The Worldbuilding Reveal
docs.text:
Book 7 is where the dungeon explains what a war mage actually is, and the answer is that it is an accident that the showrunners have been exploiting for thousands of years.

Monster description (Book 7, ch. 62)

"Want to know some interesting trivia about war mages? These guys have been around since the very early days of Dungeon Crawler World, but they are one of the few, true dungeon-born entities. They weren't dreamed up by a sweaty, caffeine-addled writer, nor were they developed by one of my kind. They just sort of happened, a result of too many combatants having access to You're Not Done Yet. The final form a war mage takes is entirely dependent on the combination of its first two forms... It's rare for a symbiote to be resleeved at least a dozen times, but when it happens, the magic itself can become sapient. When this happens, the flesh finally fuses to the reanimated skeleton, turning the three creatures—the skeleton, the flesher, and the sapient well of magic—into a single being. A war mage. This process usually takes at least 12 iterations, but there's no hard rule about it. Sometimes it takes up to 15 or 16 iterations. It depends on the latent magic in the skin of the fleshers."

Two consequences follow from being born rather than built.

They all look different. The final form depends entirely on what the first two components were — Akuma, built from "a human crawler from a very long time ago and a high elf," reads as a long-haired, old, wizened elf with a sagging, sneering face. Standing in a group, "even though they were all the same type of creature, they all looked like different monsters," each with a crackling, multi-hued glow.

They remember. Because they are made rather than spawned, they are not routinely recycled between crawl seasons the way ordinary mobs are:

Book 7, ch. 62

"Each war mage one may find in the dungeon was created naturally, meaning they could have been made several seasons previous, and because the showrunners like to use war mages, especially for their precious Faction Wars, they are rarely recycled."
