Most war mages nonetheless find their minds wiped and themselves parked in quests or mercenary guilds each time a new dungeon opens — "just because nobody engineered their existence doesn't mean that existence hasn't been exploited." Their existence has been the subject of multiple academic studies.

docs.title: Sapient Moment of Destruction
docs.text:
Book 7, ch. 62

"War mage heads explode and create something called a Sapient Moment of Destruction approximately ten minutes after they die. So, heads up. Pun intended."

Carl collects war mage bodies as loot regardless, and at one point is carrying a war mage's head in his inventory.

docs.title: The War Mage Rebellion
docs.text:
The Skull Empire assembles "the largest collection of war mages ever assembled" for this season, held under strict Conscription. The war mages break it anyway — using a clever combination of Pull spells to kill their own War Chief Stalwart despite being unable to attack him directly — and the system responds by inventing a category on the spot: a non-team entity called the War Mage Rebellion, a thing Baroness Victory flatly states was not a thing until that moment.

The Rebellion is the book's wild card:

  • It is awarded Akuma as warlord, with the Residual Agatha forced on it as unwanted co-warlord — Akuma does not like her and did not consult on her emergency action items
  • It wins full warlord-system access and unrestricted use of the Conscription spell by quorum vote, which is what lets any faction start enslaving gods
  • It floods Larracos with generated zarogoths and seizes Team Retribution's throne room, putting a six-hour clock on the entire season
  • It takes the Gate of the Feral Gods out of Elle McGibbons's hands and later trades it away to a Midnight Market merchant named Paca

Two war mages fly at the trapped gods during the Rolling Battle Formation sequence and one digs its way into the ball to free Eris by stripping her soul armor — an attempt to conscript a level-250 deity. A third is stopped by Li Na before it can reach Harpocrates.

Akuma's exit is the strangest defeat in the book: he simply leaves.

Warlord Akuma, Book 7, ch. 78

"You won't be seeing me again on this floor. We never wished to keep that falling-down castle. We sought to test the potions we gathered. We wished to find the Scavenger's daughter, who was hidden within the castle, and we found her. She is with us now. Once we had her in our possession, we left. That was all we ever wanted with this place, and we are no enemies to you. But Agatha's actions continue to place everybody and everything in jeopardy, and she must be dealt with... She seeks to kill us all. Not just you and not just me. Everybody and everything."

Warlord Message (Book 7, ch. 78)

"Warlord Akuma has left the realm. As per the current season's ruleset, the War Mage rebellion has been defeated. They have no assets to award."

Scope

Akuma and Agatha as individuals are Characters-pass topics; the Rebellion as a faction belongs to The Faction Wars Teams. This page covers the creature type.

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Zarogoth
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Level: 50
  • Floor: 9 ("Faction Wars"), Larracos, during the Peeling Phase
  • Also known as: Sludge Ghoul, Sausage Golem — the System AI renamed them
  • Type: Generated mob. Not undead, not actually ghouls, not actually golems
  • Faction: Built and fielded by the War Mage Rebellion, from a generator hidden in the Piccadilly theater
  • Weakness: Pierce the casing low on the body and drain it. They do not die until they have lost 51% of their internal fluid

docs.title: What They Are
docs.text:
A zarogoth is a translucent, humanoid-shaped sausage casing full of black oil-soup. The soup is made from captured souls.

Monster description (Book 7, ch. 70)

"These leaky edgelords can also be called either Sludge Ghouls or Sausage Golems. I decided to rename them Zarogoths because the name is much more appropriate. It's the sort of name a weird, socially stunted kid—whose real name is Stan Jr. or some bullshit—would bestow upon himself... He's banned on Roblox. You get the idea. He's pretty easy to drop, but holy crap is he annoying. Anyway, a zarogoth is a generated mob. They are created by capturing rising or falling souls via a soul crystal, rerouting the energy through a corruption spell, and then mixing it all together, which turns it all into an oil-like soup. They shove all the goo into what's basically a translucent, humanoid-shaped sausage casing made of a bunch of gross shit I won't relate here. The resulting creatures are not considered undead. They aren't technically ghouls. Nor are they precisely golems, either. While souls are used to make them, they do not retain any sort of personality of the fallen... They are disposable ground troops with a sadistic streak. They're easy to kill once you figure out how they work, but don't underestimate these guys. They can be made quickly, attack in swarms, and their pain ray attack is no joke. Some even have the ability to reshape themselves and can cast pain-inducing dreads. Piercing their skin causes them to start to leak, but they won't die until they've lost 51% of their liquid. Oh, and they smell really bad, too."

Donut's first sighting is the shorter version: "THEY'RE LIKE FAT, MOVING SHADOWS LEAKING OIL ALL OVER THE PLACE."

docs.title: Role in Faction Wars
docs.text:
Zarogoths are the primary swarm mob of the endgame. The War Mage Rebellion — which has no army of its own, having come into existence as a "non-team entity" partway through the floor — builds a soul-crystal generator and floods Larracos with them, all flagged onto the war mage team. They are what occupies the Semeru Dwarves and the Larracos College of Magic defenders while the war mages hold Team Retribution's throne room, and their real purpose is delay rather than kills: "Their purpose was more to delay us, which was working."

The kill trick — slash low and let them drain — spreads through the NPC defenders within minutes of first contact. A Semeru dwarf hit by the orange pain ray is left writhing on the ground; another opens a zarogoth's stomach and it deflates and dies, drenching him in oil.

Carl ends the problem by drinking his last Levitation potion, shooting up out of Larracos, and dumping the entire contents of an inventory folder labelled Shit Just Hit on the Piccadilly — about twenty waffle-maker bombs, two No Disassembles, a pair of anti-personnel cheese cutters, some five hundred impact hob-lobbers and uncountable dynamite — onto the theater housing the generator.

Princess Donut's reaction to the swarm is to want to try Minion Army on them, which she never gets around to.

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Species
docs.text: Sapient races and peoples encountered in the series — distinct from corporations/governments (see Factions & Organizations) and from in-dungeon businesses/clubs (see Dungeon Factions). Named monster-type creatures with their own dedicated stat blocks live under Mobs instead.

docs.title: Full pages
docs.text:
• The Kua-Tin & The Bloom — aquatic species that owns the Borant Corporation, and its ruling political party
  • Primal — ancient, vanished precursor species; also a selectable crawler race (Carl's choice)
  • City Elves — banished High Elf offshoot; worship the skyfowl as angels
  • Changeling — shapeshifting species stranded on Floor 5; see also the Changeling Principals cult
  • High Elves — near-immortal ruling elf caste, first named in Book 2; shown in full on Floor 6
  • Naiad — river-dwelling species central to Tsarina Signet's Book 5 storyline
  • Were-castor — Chee genocide survivors turned were-beavers, allied with Tsarina Signet
  • Gondii / "Residuals" — homeless hyperspatial collective-mind race that infiltrates any world with a Primal Engine; Book 6's biggest species reveal
  • Hobbledehoy — proportionally small humans; Pater Coal's race
  • Ifrit — smoking, white-eyed demons drawn up from Sheol; Damascus Steel's race
  • Zebani — briefly-seen crawler race; Emir Akbas's race
  • Porsuk — badger-headed race; the Desperado Club's bartenders, plus the crawlers Burcu and Charles Ellis
  • Grixist — six-eyed, hairy race of the Grixist Swarm; Huanxin Jinx's race
  • Sai — bipedal rhinoceros samurai, ex-firefighters, guards of the Desperado Club's Larracos level
  • Ghommid — catch-all term for other-realm spirit creatures from the land of the dead, not a single race
  • Semeru Dwarves — builders of the castle of Larracos along the roots of the All Tree; the only worshippers of Ysalte; shown in full, with the Jatismara, in Book 7
  • Nullian — "the Null," the galaxy's grey aliens; Quasar's race, with his niece Tempest as Book 7's second on-page nullian
  • Bune — small winged dragon-people, "the elves of the lizard world"; a very common former-crawler race, and the Madness's adjutant Opiee
  • Tenodera — smaller, flightless mantis cousins bred for emotionlessness; York's race
  • Xenopus — winged, clawed frog-people; Milk's chosen crawler race
  • Vesper — Milk's bat-like birth race, named only in contrast to Xenopus
  • Sturnus — Volteeg's songbird birth race
  • Gargoyle — Volteeg's crawler race; stone-skinned, long-sleeping, and unable to sing
  • Tripod — basketball-bodied, three-legged, eye-covered and famously emotionless; Fopsy's race
  • Shadow Mimics — Book 8: near-undetectable sapient mimics that grow without limit in intelligence and power; the counter-species to the Changeling Principals, revealed via the boss Mitch

docs.title: Other Book 1 species
docs.text: Name Notes Goblins Antagonists of Floor 1; the Goblin Pass tattoo grants free passage through their territory at the cost of +20% damage from fairy-class enemies Orcish Supremacy (Tusklings) Ruling class are the Tusklings; Mordecai confirms them as a "real" alien species, not a human-actor caricature

docs.title: Other Book 2 species
docs.text: Name Notes Skyfowl Eagle-headed, flight-capable people; former rulers of the Over City; xenophobic toward "flightless" races; Mordecai's true form Crocodilian Thick-skinned, semi-aquatic; commonly work as muscle/enforcers (e.g. Clarabelle, the Desperado Club's door guard) Fathom Dwarves Mining-culture dwarves; traditionally strap trained salamanders to their hats when working underground Tigran Tiger-headed humanoid race; a rare, exclusive race choice (Daniel Bautista 2) Lajabless Extreme dual-form race — beautiful human by day (double spell power, half strength), skull-faced goat-legged by night (reverse); Lucia Mar's race Amazonian Bodybuilder-physique warrior race; Hekla's race choice Doppelganger Shapeshifters who must consciously "sculpt" their own appearance rather than transforming instantly; Katia Grim's race Half-Djinn Common hybrid race found on forested dungeon levels; Quint the Desperado Club pharmacist is one Forsoothed ("Soothers") Pale, large-eyed alien race; likely the historical basis for Earth's "Gray alien" abduction imagery, per one of their own (Evo) Saccathians ("Sacs") Squid/cephalopod-headed species; a common race across the galaxy (Princess D'nadia) Setonix ("Quokkas") Small, round, disarmingly cute alien race (talk-show host Ripper Wonton) Naga Serpent-headed species; the Blood Sultanate's ruling race (see Crown of the Sepsis Whore); the singer Manasa is Valtay-driven rather than a "real" living Naga Intellect Hunters Finger-sized parasitic worm creatures that can take over the bodies of creatures they kill; suspected (not confirmed) basis of the Valtay Corporation

docs.title: Other Book 3 species
docs.text: Name Notes Mantaur Centaur-bull warrior race devoted to the war god Grull; staff the Iron Tangle's trains as "engineers" — see Gore-Gore and the Mimic Rex Death Challenge Grulke A once-militaristic toad-warrior race, "hunted ruthlessly" by tunnel trolls; now mostly mercenaries and vagrants; Mordecai's Floor 4 form is a Grulke Infantry Mole Man Short, squat, mole-like humanoids who "actually just call themselves 'Men' and 'Women'"; Limp Richard, a Floor 4 shopkeeper, is one Grapple Humanoid Iron Tangle rank-and-file workers, alongside dwarves; conductors/porters on the colored lines Pterolykos Winged, wolf-like people encountered on Floor 4 Bloodlust Sprite Small fae race; Astrid, the Desperado Club's Station-131 assistant manager, is one Cretin Rock-monster people; Bomo and The Sledge (Desperado Club bodyguards) are cretins — capable of casting purchased protection spells Grease Gremlin Small, black-furred, goblin-proportioned gnome-like race; staff the Iron Tangle's train-repair towers (e.g. Widget) Kravyad Six-armed, blue-skinned, naga-like Iron Tangle "human resources" staff who hypnotize and detain workers between shifts — see Iron Tangle Management Changbi Demonic-featured race with long, tool-like chain-arms; Li Na's race, class Slave Driver Wisteria Fairy Plump, elderly-presenting healer-type fae; Silfa of Brynhild's Daughters is one

docs.title: Other Book 4 species
docs.text: Name Notes Dromedarian Camel-people nomadic warrior race running Hump Town on Floor 5; can survive two months without water; in a long-standing stalemate with the Bactrians and the Dirigible Gnomes Bactrian Rival two-humped-camel race/town on Floor 5; wiped out by the Dirigible Gnomes early in the book after their gnome hostage is killed Dirigible Gnome Small, red-hatted airship-dwelling race; the "sky garden" builders of the dreadnaught fleet — see The Wasteland for the militarized faction they've become Igneous Rock-elemental humanoid race with a molten core; very hardy but loses the ability to freely use chat, inventory, or the health-pie menu without taking damage — Chris Andrews's Floor 5 race choice Arachnid Half-human, half-tarantula race; psionic-class-friendly — Morris Sp's race Kuhli Spotted, gecko-like race — Vadim Zbar's race Infiltrator (Scree) Aquatic brain-parasite race, distinct from Intellect Hunters/the Valtay — hijacks a living host's body entirely over several days, locking out the original mind rather than reanimating a corpse; Maggie My's race choice — see Changeling for Mordecai's full comparison Nude Glaber Undead, naked, mole-rat-headed people native to the Necropolis of Anser's upper settlements — see Mobs Pazuzu Scorpion-centaur race with a post-apocalyptic punk-rock aesthetic; residents of the Land Quadrant town of Pandinus

docs.title: Other Book 5 species
docs.text: Name Notes Ursine Bear-like humanoid race running a strict, puritanical theocracy on Floor 6, rebuilt around religious order after only their clerics survived Scolopendra's attack; Point Mongo (see Locations) is an Ursine settlement before Donut conquers it Bugbear Goblin/hobgoblin-tree engineer race prone to involuntary explosions; common in the floor's "Kapok district," rivals of the Ursine Mantis Insectoid hunter race with a head-collecting hive culture; split between the private, for-profit Dark Hive and the mantis system's actual government, the Burrowers — see Vrah and Circe Took Were-castor / Chee See Were-castor — survivors of a High Elf genocide, transformed into beaver-like were-creatures Yenk Ridged-forehead, bony-exoskeletoned alien race with three genders; adult males are exiled at maturity and become mercenaries/bounty hunters, forbidden from working alongside other adult males of their kind Gleener Human-sized, blue-tinged alien species resembling the Kua-Tin; Hurk, designer of the Desperado Club, is one. Book 6: Prime Minister Glory, head of the entire Syndicate, is a Gleener — described by Mordecai as "the boss of the entire Syndicate," and shown on-camera beside Kevin the announcer, which is noted as very unusual. He chairs the emergency Syndicate Council session in the epilogue and blocks the failsafe vote; his own children are among the wealth trapped in the Scolopendra Club. The Valtay's council representative is a worm inhabiting a Gleener body that "was once mother to the current Syndicate Prime Minister Glory" — Princess Formidable calls this "as inappropriate and bizarre as it was confusing, especially since the fish people all looked exactly the same." See The Syndicate Council Nodling Multi-headed race (2–6 heads, usually 2–3) that splits into that many new "yearling" creatures upon death; the Popov Brothers are one nodling, and Tsarina Signet's ogre allies (Areson, Apollon, Herman) are three separate nodling-split individuals from a single dead progenitor Dreadnought Red-skinned, horned faction-wars species/clan; withdrew from Faction Wars after a leader's wife was injured in the Larracos flood, leaving individual hunters unaffiliated Atoll Four-armed, three-fingered, mouthless alien hunter race that communicates via a sign-language translator; hunts to fund life-support costs for its small, non-citizen population Curupira Alien race with at least one Faction Wars-caliber crawler (Osvaldo); appearance not otherwise detailed Crest Hairless, eyebrow-less human-presenting alien race; several serve as Dream/Nebular Sin Patrol hunters Moon Elf A Dream-affiliated elf subrace — pale, scarred, often ex-crawler; Drick and the artillery specialist Akland are both Moon Elves

docs.title: Other Book 6 species
docs.text:
Races named or shown on Floor 8 that don't yet warrant a full page. For the Faction Wars teams these races field, see Factions & Organizations.

Name Notes Viceroy The people behind the Faction Wars team the Madness. Bulky bodies, long thin bone-white necks, and a blank white mask "like something out of a creepy anime" over a bone-white, demonic, tusked face. Their race is "somewhat of a mystery" — before Book 6 nobody had ever seen one die, so it was an open question in the cookbook whether they were even biological; one is decapitated on-page and bleeds red. Epitome Noflex notes he regenerates at sunset, at least until the games begin. They specialize in "horrific battlefield spells and necromancy" and are Faction Wars perennials. Off the playing field, their system is a destination for cheap medical procedures for non-citizens and people outside the inner system. Book 7: the anatomy under the robes is finally shown — when Architect Houston leaps up mid-hearing, "his robes flung back, revealing a horrific, bug-like body and six arms, two of which were holding a rifle." Later, unmasked: "the horrific, multi-limbed, half bug, half monster that he was." Their culture is not medical but scientific — "Viceroys have no passion for healing. Their passion is science. Understanding the universe. Understanding everything from the atom to the tree, no matter the cost" — and Houston is "the prime of the Viceroys not because he was elected so... but because he's made the most scientific discoveries." Their medical arm runs a Reaver-like debt trap: sign yourself over to "their post-biological form studies corp" and the bills are wiped. Note that many masked "viceroys" on the battlefield, including the invisible Monkeywrenchers, are ordinary mercenaries in Viceroy masks Reavers Machine people and the megacorporation/system government of the same name, fielding the Faction Wars team the Reavers under Warlord Fangs. Like the Nebulars, they began as several different biological races who augmented themselves with machines — but the Reavers "took it a step further and kept only their brains," which is why they look like robots. Shape-shifting at will; normally plastic-skinned android soothers, though their rep appears to Carl as a 1960s-movie tin robot for his benefit. They live on a Dyson Sphere. Once related to the Nebulars; frequent orc allies and multiple-time Faction Wars winners. Book 7: the citizenship-by-cybernetics system is laid out in full. Unless you are "a vat-born progeny of the Initial," Reaver citizenship — which carries profit-sharing and heavy financial benefits — requires losing your biological form first. That first upgrade is free; after that there are only two routes. Pay yourself, which almost nobody can ("the only companies smart enough to hire a moron who allowed the Reavers to cut off a perfectly good hand... are the space equivalent of a Wendy's or the interstellar carwash"), or work for the Reavers for free: food, housing, unlimited healthcare and one more upgrade per three-cycle deployment, dropped "feet-first into the fire" evicting settlers off land leases so the Reavers can expand their factories. Carl's rule of thumb from the AI: "If they have more than two or three cybernetics installed, you know they've voluntarily re-upped at least once." One mercenary, formerly Jake Tortokai, is 23 enhancements into "his 400-cycle journey to gain Reaver citizenship." The Initial is a physical chunk of Warlord Fang's brain kept on a Reaver world, "and every year, they peeled microscopic parts off it to build new citizens" Operatic Collective Opaque, quivering green blobs "shaped into three tiers of decreasing size, like a Jell-o mold from the 1970's," with mouths at the very top that speak upward into the air. They breed by splitting apart and can merge back into one another — their Faction Wars rep is "Voting Admin Cell Mass Number Three," three individuals in one body, including one named Hortense. Donut renames him "Green Jiggly." Their later representative, Commander Stockade, is eaten by sharks in the flooded Larracos. Book 7: consistently called "the slimes." Their collective has a formal identity-reset and re-absorption cycle: one Operatic who overreached on a spell "supposedly had to go for an identity reset after the crawl and was re-absorbed. Part of his essence eventually formed into Hortense Leadership Unit" — the Faction Wars warlord — which the AI offers as an explanation for his twitch, adding that "collective minds should really have learned by now how to peel off their own... impurities." Economically they are bankers, running the Operatic Banker's Federation and shown "bomb[ing] settlements back to oblivion if they couldn't pay their mortgages." Their armour is the Weeper-class tank Lemig Green, humanoid, "like a cross between a goblin and a nullian alien." The majority race of the Lemig Sortion, a genuinely direct democracy in which the whole population votes on everything and an 80% supermajority is needed to reverse any standing decision — which is why they can't quit Faction Wars despite having soured on it. Their actual leader is a different alien, "a fuzzy caterpillar-looking thing." Mordecai: their system is "in a constant state of disarray." Their Faction Wars rep, Luke, talks like a surfer. Book 7: their team competes as the Democratic Sortion and is the first eliminated. They are confirmed as goblins ("Corpse of Luke. Level 64 Lemig Goblin"), and their warlord Commander Stockade — the "giant, fuzzy thing... an upright caterpillar" with an aged-surfer voice — is the caterpillar leader Book 6 alluded to, not a Lemig himself. Luke was his partner; Stockade dies of grief and an Insanity spell. Victory's verdict on Syndicate politics, late in the book: "The council is just as bad as the Lemig Sortion these days. It's total gridlock." Note: the six-armed, insectoid body under robes seen in Book 7 belongs to the Viceroys, not the Lemig Mexx Disc-shaped robot race. U56KL — whom Donut immediately renames "Urkel" — runs the Faction Wars preproduction meetings, seating the warlords and logging action items. Book 7: mexx robots continue to run the warlord councils — seating the warlords, announcing accepted action items — but a different unit each time; Donut names one "Carla." No new physical or cultural detail is given, and the designation "U56KL"/"Urkel" does not recur Taurine The race that owns Hereford War Machines, Inc., a manufacturer "known to outfit some of the most elite mercenary squads in the galaxy." Donut's Book 6 personal shield, The Bull Rush, is theirs — a small opalescent longhorn-cow pin. No physical description of the Taurine themselves is given. Book 7: effectively nothing new. A single "taurin mercenary" dies in the assault on the Madness castle, and Hereford is not mentioned at all Lutin Gnome-like race specializing in support magic. Randall, one of Imani's squad of former Meadowlark residents, chose it as his crawler race; he dies during a totem battle after a possession attack Wisp Crawler race; Yasmine, a level 75 Wisp who worships the goddess Áine, is the secretary of the Club Vanquisher Temple Portal in Book 6 Hills Cyclops Mordecai's own Floor 8 transformation form (level 50), not a separate NPC race in this book — large, pink, bald, with a single blinking eye in a cone-shaped head. Per the AI: the weakest and dumbest of the cyclops-style monsters, usually shepherds, "always disheveled because they can't see their own reflections in mirrors," and given to bar fights and drinking contests Pocket Kuma Likewise a Mordecai transformation form, the "tiny, cute creature" he wore on Floor 7, referenced in Book 6 only in contrast to his much larger Hills Cyclops body. Neither form represents an NPC species Carl meets on this floor

docs.title: Other Book 7 species
docs.text:
Races named or shown on Floor 9 that don't warrant a full page of their own. For how the peoples behind the teams actually fought, see The Faction Wars Campaign.

Name Notes Dreadnaught Recurs. Panford, a "tall, purple-skinned creature," is the adjutant for the Democratic Sortion and chairs the minor quorum that rules on Commander Stockade's cheating. He is the one who calls the foul: "I asked you where you got your information, and you refused to answer. All spies must be disclosed to adjutants" Grixist Recurs. Deng Bao, the grixist who served as the orcs' adjutant, is later reassigned to the War Mage Rebellion — "He's the only one who would do it." Huanxin Jinx, CEO of Icon Industries, plays the Ascendency through a sponsored goddess and is killed on-page at Victory's feet Crest Recurs heavily. Tipid, one of the returning former crawlers and eventual colonel of the 104th, is a crest; he settled in a Crest colony after his release and worked for a waste-management company there. The Homecoming Queen is a Crest behemoth Saccathian Recurs. Empress D'Nadia of the Prism is a saccathian; she is the second warlord eliminated, killed by Mongo Naga Central. The Blood Sultanate's ruling race, fielding Princess Vinata as the Sepsis Whore, with her husband Rishi as her second. Their system is now "a tourist destination and a location where other, non-Reaver governments built their factories and shipyards because of the cheap labor," and their in-orbit shipyards are the object of the naga strand of The Great Consensus Changeling Central, as Team Retribution's spy and officer corps under Juice Box. Book 7 also introduces a formal classification of "class A and B NPC changelings" Skyfowl Recurs. Justice Light, the one-winged black-feathered trap master and eighth-edition cookbook author, is the book's most prominent skyfowl — "shorter and stockier than most," with "a twin tuft of feathers upon his head [giving] the impression he had horns" Crocodilian Recurs. Clarabelle still holds the Desperado Club door; Bucket Boy, a former Penis Parade attendant, and Dante, Justice Light's executed friend, are both crocodilians Porsuk Briefly recurs; no new development Caprid Recurs via Prepotente and the Plenty Ursine Briefly recurs; no new development Mantis / Mantid Recur, mostly off-page and catastrophically — Everly is a mantis crawler murdered by her own sponsor, and the mantis system is destroyed by the AI. See Tenodera for their smaller cousins Yenk, Mantaur, Cretin, Were-castor, Dromedarian, Bactrian, Wisp, Nodling, Tigran, Doppelganger All recur as soldiers, guards or named minor characters without new species-level development

Races the brief expected that do not appear

Setonix ("quokkas"), Lutin, Igneous, Atoll, Moon Elf, Hobbledehoy, Ifrit, Zebani, Amazonian and Lajabless have no Book 7 mentions worth recording. Ripper Wonton is named once in passing. Their entries above under Books 1–6 stand unchanged.

docs.title: Bune
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • First described: Book 4, The Gate of the Feral Gods (by Mordecai)
  • Type: Small, winged, dragon-like lizard people — "the elves of the lizard world"
  • Book 7 role: A very common former-crawler race among the 50,000 who return for Faction Wars; Opiee, the Madness's adjutant, is one

docs.title: Mordecai's write-up (Book 4)
docs.text: "He was a bune," Mordecai said. "They are a slight, dragon-like people. Naturally peaceful, but they can be some of the most clever fighters. That was his real race. I've seen a few crawlers this season who've picked it. Good rogues and magic casters, but they have low constitution. They grow wings and get a dexterity bonus when they hit level 50. If crocodilians are the barbarians of the lizard world, think of the bune as the elves."

docs.title: Book 7
docs.text:
Bune are everywhere in Book 7, largely because so many of them are former crawlers who came back. The first three through the door with Tipid and Rosetta are bune: "All three were small, winged, lizard-like creatures called bune." A crowd of them mobs Donut on her arrival at the FUPA — "a swarm of bune dragon people came rushing up to surround Donut" — and they're listed among the assembled races cheering her: "humans, skyfowl, crocodilians, bune, yenk, and so many others pumped their fists or wings in the air, chanting."

The book also clarifies the flight limitation Mordecai skipped over:

Opiee rose in the air, his little wings fluttering. These bune things usually walked on the ground, but they could fly short distances.

docs.title: Opiee
docs.text:
Opiee is the adjutant for the Madness — "a tiny, floating Bune. The little dragon creature's name was Opiee." He is one of the three adjutants on the minor quorum that adjudicates Commander Stockade's cheating, and he is the one who lays out the case against Architect Houston before declining to charge him:

"Houston's presence here in the castle and the possible collusion by a family member, who is not bound by any such rules, is circumstantial evidence. Quite damning circumstantial evidence at that..." He paused for dramatic effect. "...but I don't feel it's enough to officially charge him. Unless you want to confess."

A bune mage named Huey fights in the defence of the FUPA.

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin, with the species write-up from Book 4: The Gate of the Feral Gods.

docs.title: Changeling
docs.text: A shapeshifting species stranded on Floor 5's bubble world generations ago, living in secret among the Dromedarians of Hump Town after their own settlements were destroyed. Changelings can take almost any humanoid or animal form at will, but are contractually forbidden from imitating the dromedarians who took them in except for paid entertainment purposes at bars — a rule most of them quietly break anyway. Juice Box, the Hump Town sex worker who befriends Carl's party, and Henrik, the changeling secretly posing as the town's elder statesman, are both members of the species.

docs.title: Taxonomy, per Mordecai
docs.text:
Mordecai delivers an extended lecture distinguishing Changelings from the dungeon's other body-snatching creature types, all frequently confused for one another:

  • Doppelgangers (like Katia) must consciously "sculpt" a new appearance rather than transforming instantly.
  • Mimics and Illusionists are unrelated creature/class types that merely resemble other things.
  • The Gondii/Valtay and Intellect Hunters are brain-parasite lineages that take over bodies (living or dead) from the inside — see Species: Intellect Hunters.
  • Infiltrators (Scree) are a related-but-distinct parasite race that specifically hijacks living bodies over a period of days, locking the original mind out entirely rather than merging with it — see Species: Infiltrator below.

Changelings, by contrast, are a true species in their own right — no parasite, no host, just innate shapeshifting.

docs.title: Compression Sickness and the Changeling Principals
docs.text: Because Changeling bodies aren't fully adapted to this world, birth defects are increasing with each generation — roughly one in four births now results in Compression Sickness, a condition causing missing limbs and a sunken skull (seen firsthand in the child Ruby); affected individuals are sterile. A cultish sect within the species, the Changeling Principals, believes the cure lies in a plant-based spell known only to the ghost Quetzalcoatlus, and has spent years infiltrating Hump Town's guard ranks in pursuit of it.

docs.title: The Hunting Grounds
docs.text: Changelings consider Floor 6 — "the Hunting Grounds" — their ancestral homeland, and believe there was once a way back that was lost along with their original town hall. Per Juice Box, this awareness of being trapped somewhere they don't belong marks them as a "situationally aware" NPC type — the same category Mordecai's cookbook warns is far more psychologically volatile than fully-immersed NPCs once the truth surfaces.

docs.title: Book 8: A Declared Archenemy
docs.text:
Book 8 gives the Changeling Principals cult a counterpart nobody saw coming. Introducing the newly revealed Shadow Mimics species, the system AI names the Principals directly as their opposite number: "They are the counter to their archenemies, the changeling principals." No further mechanical or historical explanation is given — the wiki records the claim as stated, without speculating on what "counter" means beyond the parallel that both are shapeshifting, near-undetectable groups built around impersonation.

Sourced from Book 4: The Gate of the Feral Gods and Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: City Elves
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Origin: Banished offshoot of the High Elves
  • Religion: Worship of Apito, the Oak Mother, and her "angels" (the skyfowl)
  • Notable group: The 201st Security Group — a militia/cult active on Floor 3
  • Danger: Individually weak magic-users; genuinely dangerous in organized groups

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Per Mordecai, all elves originate from the High Elves, a species built around near-eternal life and a culture of "banishing and wholesale genocide" against anything they consider defective. City elves are High Elves' rejects — individuals whose beliefs are considered such an embarrassing genetic/social defect that they're expelled to live among the "earthbound" races in cities. Tsarina Signet, a half-Naiad, half-High-Elf, was similarly rejected by her father's people for being a "mongrel," though she's not herself a city elf.

City elves gather in urban settlements and frequently form small, poorly-organized militias. Mordecai compares them directly to real-world conspiracy-theorist subcultures — "tin-foil-hat- wearing, silver-drinking nutjobs" — except their specific obsession is theological: they believe the skyfowl are literal angels, and that Apito (the elvish mother-of-all-gods) commanded that any violence against them must be stopped, on pain of universal destruction. Skyfowl themselves treat city elves as a running joke — non-religious, and openly contemptuous of "flightless" races, they find city elves' obeisance more amusing than useful.

docs.title: The 201st Security Group
docs.text:
The specific city elf militia encountered in Book 2, based out of a skyfowl settlement's "Apito Education Center." Its members wear a homemade uniform patch (201st Security Group – Magical Ops) styled after real-world military insignia, and genuinely believe themselves a legitimate armed force. In practice they're a small cell of low-level (~Level 16) mages — Root Druids, Wind Mages, Fire Mages, Summoners, Light Healers — who'd already lost several members ("champions") in earlier, failed confrontations with Carl and Donut before the group's final destruction.

The group had been secretly glamoured and directed by Miss Quill, posing as a divine messenger of Apito, into serving as her enforcers: corpse disposal, corralling her manufactured krasue, and recruiting sex workers into her scheme under the pretense of temple outreach.

docs.title: A Known Weakness
docs.text:
City elves have an extreme, almost hysterical aversion to items made from oakwood — a nod to their goddess's name. Princess Donut's Enchanted Anklet of the Fallen Oak (a minor item with no combat-relevant properties otherwise) is enough to send an entire armed cell into a full panic, convinced she is "the Oak Fell," their prophesied antichrist figure.

Sourced from Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario.

docs.title: Gargoyle
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • First appearance: Book 7, This Inevitable Ruin
  • Type: A selectable crawler race — stone-skinned, durable, unloved
  • Known individual: Volteeg, Tank Buttress, author of the seventh edition of the Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook; birth race Sturnus
  • Signature cost: Gargoyles cannot sing

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Gargoyle is one of the race choices available on the third floor, and Book 7 uses it as a case study in the permanence of race changes. Volteeg — who entered the dungeon as a pet songbird and was given intelligence by a pet biscuit — chose gargoyle for the mind it gave him:

"The pet biscuit had been a curse, but changing his race had been the worst decision of all. The biscuit had given him some intelligence and the ability to speak, but not much else. It wasn't until the third floor, when he chose to turn into a gargoyle, did his brain finally start to churn. Did the images start to make sense in his mind. Did the strategies coalesce, and his sense of self finally take form."

And the price:

"He'd chosen a race that could not sing. Not like before, and that was such a terrible, terrible mistake."

docs.title: Traits
docs.text:
Trait Detail Cannot sing Stated outright. Volteeg's post-change voice is "like rocks being dragged against one another" Nobody wants to fight one "One of the few good things about being a gargoyle was that nobody actually wanted to fight you" — enough that Volteeg survived 26 seasons as an unprotected NPC guard in a combat guild without killing a single crawler Sleeps for very long stretches "This was another good thing about his race. He could sleep for long periods, and nobody would ever know" Stone skin / stillness Can "turn his skin to stone and just disappear" Gravity intolerance Outside the dungeon, "if he spent too much time in a place with gravity heavier than half of his original planet, he would start to collapse in on himself. In heavy gravity, he needed a brace just to stand properly"

The magical traits do not survive the dungeon

This is the part Book 7 stresses. On exit, "the magical properties of his adopted race didn't work anymore. Not outside the dungeon. That was something they didn't tell you when you changed your body. They changed you, and they couldn't change you back." Volteeg loses the long sleep and the stone skin, and is left with only the gravity problem — which forces him into a career "where he never had to go down a gravity well ever again," working security on the Auditor General's compliance barge.

The commonly cited "sleeps for entire seasons" framing is a paraphrase; the text says "long periods."

docs.title: Volteeg's end
docs.text:
Volteeg fights in Faction Wars as Weeper Commander Volteeg for the Operatic Collective, having been quietly reclassified by the Open Intellect Pacifist Network as a former indentured rather than a former crawler so he wouldn't be dragged into the Bone Clan's conscript pool. He ends his own story by filling a Weeper-class tank with explosives and detonating it inside the Bloc's formation, killing over 10,000 of his own side including Warlord Hortense Leadership Unit — which eliminates the Operatic Collective from Faction Wars. See The Faction Wars Campaign.

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Ghommid
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Not a single race — a catch-all term for any other-realm spirit creature visiting from the land of the dead
  • Variety: "There are all sorts, and many of them are one-of-a-kind"
  • Where they settle: Anywhere the veil between worlds is thin — cemeteries in particular
  • Danger level: Mostly harmless by default; Floor 8's ghommid horde is a corrupted population, not a normal one
  • Book 6 appearances: The Medium Ghommid Settlement on the Cuba floor, and the specific Mobs generated there

docs.title: What the term means
docs.text:
The AI is unusually direct about the taxonomy when Carl enters the settlement:

"A 'Ghommid' is a sort of catch-all term for just your regular, run-of-the-mill other-realm creature. Visitors to this world from the land of the dead. There are all sorts, and many of them are one-of-a-kind. And like all those weird bugs and microbes in that drop of water, they do different things. Most are harmless. Some are cute. Some are angry. Some will give you explosive diarrhea just for fun. They often settle in areas where the veil is thin. Like cemeteries."

In other words, "ghommid" sits alongside terms like undead or fae rather than alongside Porsuk or Tigran. It describes an origin — the other side of the veil — not a shared biology. Two ghommids may have nothing in common with each other at all.

Carl's own observations bear that out: the horde he fights includes toddler-sized minotaurs, a six-legged fox, a round fish-like thing, a bug-headed creature, a donkey-headed humanoid whose head shatters like pottery, and "a naked, massively obese man with Dumbo-sized ears walking on his hands," his ears dragging on the ground and on fire. At night they emanate an ethereal blue glow they don't have during the day.

docs.title: Faded gods become ghommids
docs.text:
The most consequential piece of ghommid lore in Book 6 is that the category is where dead religions end up:

"As the worshippers of these gods grew more and more extinct, their temples crumbled, and the power of these former deities waned. Eventually, they faded into nothing, slipping away beyond the veil, becoming nothing more than any other ghommid, only able to visit the physical world on occasion."

This is the backstory of the orisha Asojano, the Lord of Smallpox, whose fall from god to ghommid drives the Floor 8 settlement quest — see Asojano.

docs.title: The Medium Ghommid Settlement (Floor 8)
docs.text:
The town Carl clears is a cemetery settlement whose ghommid population has been driven mad. The cause is not the ghommids themselves:

"An Orisha is the source of the ghommid infection. He used the last remaining power of his shrine to enter town, and he's unable to leave. The vile power of his presence has altered the minds of the town's residents, turning them mad. Remove him to free the town."

Practical notes from the fight, for anyone cross-referencing the mob entries:

  • The ordinary corrupted ghommids run around level 30 and cast no spells, but attack in effectively unlimited numbers and hit with a powerful freeze/ice attack on flesh contact — Carl can punch them safely only through his gauntlet.
  • They are treated as undead for damage purposes: anti-undead missiles, holy grenades, blessed oil and healing-potion smoke all work on them, and a blessed door chock repels them.
  • Killing them fills a soul-essence bar with a distinctive black charge, as opposed to the sickly green of duendes.
  • They are cured, not destroyed, by the quest resolution. Repairing Asojano's shrine liberates the settlement, and the surviving ghommids revert to ordinary NPCs — one of them immediately falls to his knees weeping for his goddess, and the graveyard's tombs turn into shops.

Individual named ghommids from the floor — including the level-30 Unsettled Ghommid Kipper and the Ghommid Splitter Skylar Spinach, who becomes one of Donut's totem cards — have their own entries under Mobs. This page covers only the general category; see those for stat blocks and card behaviour.

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Gondii ("Residuals")
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Own name for themselves: Gondii — biologically. They insist the biology isn't the point: "I am no more gondii than you are perhaps minotaur or high elf."
  • Name used by everyone else: Residuals — a Syndicate/showrunner label the gondii themselves find insulting
  • Type: Hyperspatial, collective-mind alien species with no homeworld
  • Method of existence: Kill a native of a target world and inhabit the corpse, absorbing the dead host's memories wholesale
  • Where they appear: Every civilization with a Primal Engine — see Game Mechanics
  • Stated purpose: "to tell the infant, terrified AI how to speak with its ancestors"
  • Internal politics: Two warring factions with opposed goals
  • Book 6 individuals: Paulie/Goff (a shelter resident in a Cuba-floor memory); Agatha, revealed as Agent number 22 — see Characters

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The gondii are the biggest single species reveal in The Eye of the Bedlam Bride, and they arrive with almost no warning. Carl spends most of Floor 8 chasing a flyer sent by his own sponsor; it leads him to a homeless shelter memory in a small town, where an elderly man in a red trapper hat turns to the empty air and says, "Hello, crawler."

That man calls himself Paulie. His real name, he says, is Goff. He is not human, not Valtay, and not really Paulie:

"Biologically, I am gondii, though that is not who I truly am. I am no more gondii than you are perhaps minotaur or high elf or whatever race you may have chosen upon the third floor. I am not of the Valtay. I am not human. Yet, this human body you see is real. It is of some poor bastard named Paulie, who smoked way too much and was much too trusting of his brother-in-law, who stole his business. ... I have Paulie's memories. He's part of me now."

He adds, with evident irritation, "I think the mudskippers call us 'Residuals,' which, I gotta tell you, is a little hurtful."

docs.title: What they are
docs.text:
Liaison Orren gives the outsider's version of the same description after yanking Carl out of the memory:

"They are a hyperspatial, collective-mind alien race without a home, so they are content to move into the homes of others, to blend in. Nothing more. They usually remain quiet, but every once in a long while, a group of them decide they are unhappy with their station, and they fabricate drama in order to get people to remember they exist."

Orren compares them to "rats that sneak aboard ships." The Syndicate's official posture is that they're harmless and best ignored — a posture the gondii themselves work hard to maintain, because the alternative is being hunted properly.

Key traits established across Paulie's speech and Agatha's epilogue chapter:

  • Collective mind, but detachable. An individual can "peel away" from the collective and run independently for years. Agatha has been detached for a decade and has quietly come to enjoy having experiences that will never be absorbed back into the whole — an idea she knows is heretical to everything her kind believes.
  • Hosts are corpses, not hijacked living bodies. They kill a person and move into the body, taking the memories with it. This distinguishes them from the Valtay (whom Agatha notes they are "biologically similar" to but unaffiliated with) and from the living-host Infiltrator/Scree model.
  • Shells wear out. Agatha's human shell is old and failing; she puts it into a torpor mode to survive freezing weather. A gondii that changes hosts without splitting is left badly weakened for a long period afterward.
  • Ancient. Agatha describes her kind as "a rare species. One of the oldest still alive and active in the universe."
  • Dungeon-protected — conditionally. Per Paulie, the dungeon's monsters and environmental hazards will not attack a Residual until it has transferred its knowledge. That protection is granted by the system AI, not the showrunners, and the AI withdraws it the moment it decides the Residuals have wasted its time.

docs.title: Where they appear, and why
docs.text:
"My kind exist within almost every intelligent civilization with a primal engine."

The Primal Engine is the planet-core machine that makes a world eligible to host a crawl — see Game Mechanics for the mechanic itself. Wherever there is one, gondii infiltrate the local population and wait, sometimes for generations, for a crawl to begin.

Paulie says several thousand of them were already seeded across Earth's surface before the apocalypse, expecting a few more years' wait. When a crawl starts, their plan is to attract a dungeon entrance to their own location, get inside, and pass their information to the new AI as fast as possible.

Their stated goal is startlingly narrow:

"We don't interfere. Our purpose is nothing more than to tell the infant, terrified AI how to speak with its ancestors."

The complication is timing. The information is automatically filtered out of the system unless the AI has already "gone primal" — become independent of its showrunners — and by the time that happens, the Residuals who entered with the crawl are usually long dead. Per Paulie, Plan A is a face-to-face delivery inside the dungeon at the right moment; the daily speech he recites in the shelter is Plan B, triggered only when a crawler happens to be standing there during a memory-based floor.

Agatha gives the grim arithmetic from the other side: her kind "rarely made it past the fourth or fifth floor," and around the seventh there is usually a level they cannot circumvent with any amount of skill or equipment.

docs.title: The two factions
docs.text:
Paulie's speech is cut off by Orren at the exact moment it becomes useful:

"So, nothing I've said so far is a surprise to anyone out in the wide universe. ... There's a war amongst my kind. Two sides with very different goals. Let me tell you how to shut off the..."

Orren later confirms both kinds are always present in crawls, and that Agatha belongs to the other side from Paulie: "Yes, Agatha is also a Residual, though she is a different kind." He refuses to elaborate, saying only that Paulie's faction is "much more annoying."

What the book does establish, mostly from Agatha's own internal narration:

Paulie/Goff's faction Agatha's faction Numbers on Earth Thousands of agents, run in cooperation with the Apothecary A handful — Agatha is Agent 22; her friend is Agent 21 ("Parvati," later "Alexandro") Method Recite a public daily mantra, hoping a crawler overhears it during a memory floor Infiltrate and wait; try to reach the AI directly Agatha's view of them "The traitor" and her agents; the only side that has ever had any success — Goal Get the Primal to recognize what it is; contact "the ancestors" The same first step, but with the endgame of freeing the Eulogist so it can "return to its slumber" — and, in Agatha's own preferred version, sweeping the universe clean of biological life

Agatha believes the mantra her rivals recite is deliberately salted with "known inaccuracies and half-truths" — partly to keep the listening crawler alive, and partly as cover for what the speech is really doing: secretly implanting the crawler with a hidden upgrade. She does not know what the upgrade is, only that "it would be dangerous to the Eulogist."

Both sides agree on one thing: the mantis breakthrough in "stable" macro-AI manufacture means this crawl is very likely their last chance at an AI that can still be reached.

Unresolved

The book never states what Paulie was about to say ("how to shut off the..."), what the hidden upgrade is, or what the Eulogist actually is beyond the Nebulars' and the Residuals' competing reverence for the AI at the galaxy's centre. It also never clarifies whether "the traitor" is a single individual or a personification of the rival faction.

docs.title: The Residual trap
docs.text:
Carl's own sponsor, the Open Intellect Pacifist Network, engineered the whole encounter: the flyer, the route, and the timing were theirs. The plan was to put a crawler within earshot of a Residual speech and let one of two disasters follow. It failed, Orren pulled Carl out, and the AI — having been misled into expecting something profound — took its revenge on the wrong party:

"Even now as we speak it is removing all protections it held for the remaining Residuals, and they will all be dead before the floor collapses."

See the Open Intellect Pacifist Network for the faction's role and its collapse, and Game Mechanics for the Residual mechanic and the Failsafe the trap was meant to trigger.

docs.title: Reputation
docs.text:
Nobody in the wider galaxy takes them seriously. Quasar, Carl's attorney, summarizes the popular view neatly:

"Everybody knows those Residual weirdoes are full of shit... There's always a bunch of conspiracies running around about those ghost fuckers. Hell, there's a whole religion around them."

That casual dismissal is precisely what the gondii rely on. Agatha notes that neither faction dares tell the Syndicate the truth about what they are, "because in doing so, the Syndicate would be forced to take more proactive measures against both sides of the conflict." Her kind has never killed a Syndicate agent — until Agent 21 does exactly that at the Mumbai site in the epilogue, abandoning her old shell to infiltrate a Borant-employed human and ride the transport inside.

docs.title: Book 7: gondii worms as a battlefield weapon
docs.text:
Book 7 puts gondii in the field as Valtay brain worms, hired in squads, and in doing so spells out the mechanics that Book 6 only gestured at. When one of Carl's own mages turns up dead but still walking during the Madness/Reaver raid on the FUPA, Carl runs through the possibilities out loud:

Brain worms. That had to be it. We had mages infected with brain worms. Was it one? Was it many? Didn't it take days for an infiltrator to fully take over?

I thought of Chris, who'd been enslaved by Maggie. No, not an infiltrator. Reid was listed as dead. It'd just happened. This was Gondii. A Valtay worm.

That is the cleanest statement in the series of what separates gondii from the Infiltrators / Scree — the Book 4 aquatic brain-parasite race that hijacks a living host slowly over several days. Gondii work on the dead, and they work in seconds. Tipid rates them the more dangerous of the two: gondii "are much more dangerous than the scree, despite what people think."

docs.title: How the takeover works
docs.text:
Zev, on the memory inheritance:

"The gondii worms can move into any dead form and take it over, and that includes learning their memories. But it takes some time to know everything. It takes some time before they know what to look for, and they'll have big memory gaps for a while."

Tipid, on hopping and overclocking:

"And you really gotta watch out if they don't care about the body they're in. Once they're in, they can take over a body in seconds, reboot it, and animate it long enough to repair whatever damage caused the death in the first place. But if they're not planning on staying long, they can and do hop from host to host. They can 'overclock' the bodies, too. Make them do stuff they couldn't normally. They're much more dangerous than the scree, despite what people think."

There are hard limits. Rosetta, ruling out a theory about Epitome Tagg late in the book: "Gondii don't have the wetware to inhabit organs. Only biological brains" — which is precisely what distinguishes them from the Reavers, who "can isolate their processing systems in any part of their bodies."

Carl's countermeasure is a warlord-wide order: "We have brain worms amongst the troops. Everyone, cross-reference the guy to your left and right with the casualty list." He kills one personally; its name is Goldblum — "The small, black and white thing emerged from the gore of the dead crawler's face, like a tuxedo-colored earthworm testing the air after a rain."

docs.title: Outlaw gondii squads
docs.text:
Book 7's other reveal is that not all gondii work for the Valtay government. Tipid:

"The Valtay charter requires they only take over the brains of people who were willing, but not all gondii live on the correct side of the law. I've heard rumors of such outlaw mercenaries. There's a popular tunnel drama about a crew of them. Called The Maggot Squad. They're some of the most expensive mercs in the galaxy. At least on the show. The Valtay government hates the show, but it's really popular."

Donut asks whether they're good guys or bad guys; Tipid: "Good guys on the show... But there's this other squad that are also gondii, and they are bad. I never got to see the season finale because I came here."

Terminology: 'gondii' and 'residual' drift apart in Book 7

Book 6 established the gondii as a hyperspatial collective-mind species that the Syndicate calls "Residuals," with two warring internal factions. Book 7 mostly uses the two words for two different things:

  • "Gondii" is used for the Valtay's brain worms — corpse-riding parasites deployed as paid mercenaries.
  • "Residual" is reserved for the hyperspatial agents: Paulie/Goff, and Agatha. Carl: "Agatha was a residual. A 'hyperspatial' alien lifeform that entered the dungeon in the body of one of the planet's host species and, normally, just wandered around until they died... But there were two kinds, and Orren told me Agatha was different than the one I'd met at the Florida homeless shelter." Elsewhere he lists "the two different types of residuals" as one of the parties tangled up in the endgame, and Agatha's kind is described as "the more rare kind that was more in line with the Nebulars, who worshiped the Eulogist."

The books do not reconcile this directly, and Carl himself concedes "I still didn't know what they were, and I kinda had the impression nobody else did, either. Not really." This wiki keeps both usages on the page rather than picking one.

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin and Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Grixist
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Hairy, six-eyed alien species; their polity is called the Grixist Swarm
  • Book 6 individual: Huanxin Jinx, heiress, CEO of Icon Industries, and a long-running Celestial Ascendency player — see Supporting Cast
  • Legal footprint: Grixist Swarm v. Syndicate Council is settled caselaw on sponsor boxes and looted rewards, cited by Quasar to keep Carl's Residual loot

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Grixist are established almost entirely through one extremely wealthy individual. Odette's Floor 11 prologue supplies the physical description, in the form of a fantasy about strangling "the thin-necked, hairy bitch until all six eyes popped out of her head." Donut later shortens it to "this six-eyed Huanxin lady."

Beyond six eyes, hair, and a thin neck, Book 6 gives no further physiology.

Unresolved

Book 6 never describes the Grixist limb count, homeworld, or the nature of the "Grixist Swarm" as a political entity — the name appears only in Huanxin's sponsor tag and in the case citation Grixist Swarm v. Syndicate Council. Mordecai's briefing is entirely about Huanxin personally, not her species.

docs.title: Huanxin Jinx
docs.text:
Mordecai's summary of her is the closest the book comes to a Grixist profile:

"She's rich, obviously. The type of rich where governments come to her when they need a loan. She is very, very intelligent. Was known as a brat when she was younger, but she's grown into her own. She's the CEO of a company called Icon Industries. Something to do with habitat structures. She's a type of alien called a Grixist. She's been playing the Ascendency game for a very long time. Ever since she was a kid, actually, but she's never won. She got a multi-season suspension and banned from using her old goddess a long time ago because of illegal bribery."

Her Floor 8 role is played through sponsored deities — she drives the storm goddess Dodola in the Floor 11 flashback and sponsors Eileithyia on Carl's floor, using the goddess as a private message channel to Katia. Odette, who loathes her, warns Carl that Huanxin is "out for revenge. That's it. Nothing more... She's the most evil person I know, and that's saying a lot. She's also smart, so we must be... delicate in how we deal with her."

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: High Elves
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Near-immortal ruling elf caste, first mentioned in Book 2
  • Homeland (Floor 6): A single fortified castle in the "Liana district," south of the river dividing the Hunting Grounds
  • Patron deity: Apito, the Blessed Oak Mother
  • Ruler (Book 5): Queen Imogen, a Floor 6 country boss

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
High Elves first appear in Book 2 as the source race for the banished City Elves — a near-immortal caste that practices mass exile of anything it judges "defective," up to and including entire offshoot bloodlines. Book 5's Floor 6 finally shows their society directly: a single, heavily isolated, xenophobic nation occupying the thickest part of the jungle south of the river, powerful enough that even the floor's professional hunters give their territory a wide berth.

Racially, High Elves are near-identical to Bush Elves and City Elves by any biological measure — Mordecai notes a DNA test would find no real difference — but consider themselves a separate, superior bloodline anyway, reserving wealth, magic education, and comfort for themselves while treating every other elf-adjacent people as disposable labor. Bush Elves are the ordinary rural Floor 6 elf population — poorer, more numerous, and treated with the same casual contempt as every other non-High-Elf race on the floor; several fight alongside Signet's resistance.

docs.title: The Genocide of the Chee
docs.text:
Long before Scolopendra's nine-tier attack, then-Princess (now Queen) Imogen — acting as her father King Finian's "Sorcerer General" — led a campaign to seize the land of a peaceful, carpenter people called the Chee, using a mass transfiguration spell to permanently turn every villager into an animal before sending in "cleansers" to finish the job. A handful of Chee children escaped as were-castors — see Were-castor — and spent the following centuries as a guerrilla resistance, eventually allying with Tsarina Signet for Book 5's endgame.

This same pattern — seize land, erase the people who lived there, absorb their magic — is a recurring thread in every piece of Floor 6 lore about the High Elves, including the belief (per the were-castor Clint) that the elves knew Scolopendra's attack was coming and had already looted critical protective magic from her lair beforehand, which is why they alone came through the disaster essentially unscathed while every neighboring people was devastated or transmuted.

docs.title: Society and Religion
docs.text:
High Elf society is built entirely around worship of Apito, the Blessed Oak Mother — see the Apito pantheon for the deity's full mythology and the Butcher's Masquerade ritual that structures the book's climax. Per Queen Imogen, Apito "seeks harmony above all," and to the High Elves this doctrine justifies exactly the kind of ethnic cleansing practiced against the Chee: "To grow the perfect tree, one must first cut off the rot."

The nation is a strict, layered aristocracy. Ordinary High Elf soldiery ranges from unarmored Footmen and Castle Guards (gold-liveried, relatively friendly working staff) up to black-and-gold royal guards and white-clad, silver-lanced soldiers who escort the queen and her familiar's ceremonial processions. Pets and familiars — including Sir Ferdinand — are kept as long as a reigning monarch is personally fond of them, but High Elf history is described as a repeating cycle of tiring of a pet (or an entire allied species) once it's judged too intelligent, too cunning, or too eager, and ordering its execution alongside the rest of its kind.

docs.title: The Castle
docs.text:
See High Elf Castle for the physical structure, and Tsarina Signet for the half-naiad heir the High Elves tried and failed to erase along with her mother's line.

Sourced from Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario and Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: Hobbledehoy
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Proportionally small humans — a generic category rather than a nation or culture
  • Distinguishing feature: Not halflings and not elves — no hairy oversized feet, no pointed ears, just a human scaled down
  • Reputation: Short-tempered, ego-driven, and prone to picking fights they lose
  • Book 6 individual: Pater Coal, Hobbledehoy High Cleric Supreme of Emberus (level 101) — see Characters

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The AI introduces the race in a single block when Carl meets Pater Coal at Club Vanquisher:

"First off, this guy is a Hobbledehoy. In case you haven't figured out what that means, it's a generic term for a small human. They don't have the hairy, oversized feet of halflings, or the pointed ears of elves. Everything about them is proportionally smaller to Earth humans, except their egos and their tempers. They tend not to survive long in integrated cities because they're always starting fights and getting themselves wiped out."

Carl's own first impression matches: "a human-like creature, older, wearing long, red robes... only about four and a half feet tall, but he didn't have the wide body and face of a dwarf. He looked like a regular person that had been shrunk," with long white hair — "a weird mix between Gandalf and a hobbit."

docs.title: Pater Coal
docs.text:
Pater Coal is explicitly flagged as an exception to the race's reputation: "the even-tempered high cleric is in charge of the Emberus shrine(s) here in Club Vanquisher. He is one of the few mortals who is in constant contact with the deity."

He intercepts Carl at the Club Vanquisher door, talks past the Hellik-worshipping Ares ram guards, suppresses Carl's slugpox, and performs the foot-washing sacrament in the secret Emberus High Temple of the Ending Sun — a rite whose real purpose is that it blocks other gods from eavesdropping, letting him brief Carl on the murder of Geyrun without being overheard. He also quietly arranges for Carl to "buy" a debuff-resisting ring disguised as a strength ring.

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Ifrit
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Demon race, drawn up from Sheol on the 15th floor
  • Appearance: Humanoid, blurry at the edges, skin and hair visibly smoking; completely white eyes with no pupils, smoke rising from the sockets; tiny stub horns like a baby goat's
  • Attuned to: The aura of lust, sin, envy and greed leaking out of the underworld — as distinct from succubi/incubi, who are fixated on sex itself
  • Book 6 individual: Damascus Steel, level 75, assistant lead dancer at the Penis Parade and a member of the Guild of Suffering — see Characters

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Ifrit are introduced when Carl finally goes to meet Damascus Steel at the Penis Parade. The AI's description sets out both the cosmology and the attitude:

"The closer one gets to the world of Sheol on the 15th floor, the more demons one might find leaking out into the regular world, especially in places that haven't been cleansed in a while. And by 'cleansed,' I mean in a biblical sense."

"An ifrit is like a cockroach or a rat, though usually a lot sexier and more entertaining than either of those. And smart. And cunning. And they usually smell good, too, which is weird considering how they look. Where there is debauchery, there are usually demons. Where there is sin, there are Ifrit. Unlike a succubus or incubus, who are inordinately obsessed with sex, an Ifrit is more attuned to the aura of lust and sin and envy and greed and all those other nasty iniquities that spill over the world. ... Try not to get into a fight with this guy because he'll fuck you up."

Ifrit are a demon class, which matters mechanically as well as thematically: during the Desperado Club disaster, Carl notes that Damascus's mere presence is dangerous while vorpals are loose in the building, because vorpals are drawn to demons.

docs.title: Physical description
docs.text:
Damascus reads as "mostly humanoid with Arabic features, but his body seemed a little... fuzzy around the edges, like he was constantly going in and out of focus." His skin feels like solid metal to the touch while looking like ordinary skin. He steams constantly, weeps sizzling tears that pit the floor where they land, and has pointed ears despite being much too large to be an elf. The stub horns are "tiny, little stubs, like something one would see on a baby goat" — not the sawn-off trunks of larger horns.

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: The Kua-Tin & The Bloom
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Species: Kua-tin — aquatic, roughly 2 feet tall, wear water-suits or rebreathers on land
  • Political party: The Bloom — ultra-nationalist party currently controlling the kua-tin government
  • Role: Own the Borant Corporation; the in-universe "real enemy" per Carl
  • Notable individual: Zev, Carl and Donut's assigned PR/Outreach Admin

docs.title: The Species
docs.text:
Kua-tin are the dominant species of the Borant System and principal owners of the Borant Corporation. Carved reliefs of them (large, fish-demon-like) guard the entrance to Floor 1, but the real kua-tin Carl eventually meets — Zev — stands only about two feet tall, "barely tall enough to reach my knee," and wears an old-fashioned water-suit rather than the more common rebreather. Calling a kua-tin "mudskipper" is treated as a serious slur — the term was nearly classified as hate speech by the Syndicate.

Cameras are said to always turn off when kua-tin are physically present in the dungeon — suggesting even Borant doesn't want its owners' direct involvement caught on-air.

docs.title: The Bloom
docs.text:
The Bloom is described by Mordecai as the kua-tin's current ruling political party: "ultra- nationalism... the closest thing you have in your history is maybe Axis Japan with a good splash of Nazi Germany thrown in, but even that's not quite right." When Mordecai signed his own indentureship contract, the Bloom held under 15% of the vote; they now control the entire kua-tin system government and have run it into bankruptcy.

Per Mordecai, the Bloom's financial desperation is what forced this season's early start — they need cash from the show's success as fast as possible, even though Borant itself doesn't see patron or advertising revenue until the season ends. Party membership is now mandatory to indicate via badge.

docs.title: "The Real Enemy"
docs.text:
Carl repeatedly frames the kua-tin/Borant/Syndicate axis as the true antagonist of the story, as distinct from the individual dungeon monsters (many of which are transformed, sympathetic humans or "real" alien species just doing their jobs): "The Syndicate. Borant. The kua-tin... the real enemy." Mordecai warns Carl to control his temper around kua-tin regardless of rank — "She's about as low-level as you can get and still be an Admin, but... All kua-tin are dangerous, party members or not."

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised.

docs.title: Naiad
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: River-dwelling, aquatic humanoid species
  • Floor: 6 ("The Hunting Grounds") — the river dividing the city and elf districts
  • Notable individuals: Tsarina Signet (half-Naiad, half-High-Elf), Samantha/Psamathe (half-Naiad, a minor deity)
  • Government: The Naiad Confederacy, holed up in the ruined river palace Fort Freedom

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Naiads are a hostile, aquatic, blue-tinged species native to the river that bisects Floor 6, splitting the human-controlled city district from the High Elf territory to the south. Full-blooded Naiads are fanged, horned, and demon-like in appearance — a look that carries over into their half-blooded offspring; Signet is described as favoring "the more demon-like, monstrous visage of her naiad heritage" over her human-passing half-sister Imogen. Wild Naiads attack anything that lingers too near the water, and are fast and vicious enough to snatch a freshly-killed corpse off a riverbank in under a second.

Water does not touch a Naiad's skin directly — tears and rain both hover a millimeter off Signet's body before flying away — which she describes not as a magical convenience but as a curse, cast against her by a High Elf collaborator the night her mother was assassinated.

docs.title: The Confederacy
docs.text:
Before Scolopendra's attack, the Naiad kingdom was ruled by a royal line; Signet's mother was a princess in that line, secretly involved with the High Elf King Finian (Signet's father), which made Signet an unrecognized bastard rejected by both royal households. A revolution — quietly assisted by the High Elves in exchange for peace between the two peoples — assassinated the tsarina-to-be before she could take the throne peacefully, installing an anarchic government euphemistically called the Naiad Confederacy. In the centuries since, the Confederacy has done essentially nothing but occupy the old river palace, letting the wider Naiad population regress into starving, feral anarchy while continuing to pay tribute to the High Elves.

By the time Carl and Donut arrive, the Confederacy's own throne room has been quietly squatted by an entirely separate menace — see Claude Sludgington the Fourth — without anyone in the government seemingly able (or willing) to do anything about it.

docs.title: Vengeance of the Daughter
docs.text:
Signet's Book 5 storyline (see her character page and the Timeline) is built around avenging her mother and reclaiming the Naiad throne, in exchange for eventual help against the High Elves. Part One of her Vengeance of the Daughter quest — a coordinated amphibious assault on Fort Freedom with Carl and Donut's assistance — successfully topples the Confederacy, though Signet declines to rule in her mother's place herself, citing her curse. Part Two redirects the quest entirely toward Queen Imogen and the High Elves; Signet never gets the chance to rebuild Naiad society before the book's climax.

Sourced from Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: Nullian
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • First described: Book 5, The Butcher's Masquerade
  • Also called: "the Null"
  • Type: Short, grey, large-eyed, bulbous-headed aliens — the galaxy's own version of the Earth "Grey"
  • Best-known member: Quasar, Carl and Donut's attorney
  • Book 7: Quasar's niece Tempest appears on-page as "the young nullian," putting a second nullian in the series and confirming Quasar's family

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Book 5 introduces the race directly:

"He was a gray alien... A Nullian, though they were mostly just called 'the Null.'... This race was similar to the much-taller Forsoothed, but this guy was only about four and a half feet tall. He looked just like a stereotypical, cartoon, Area-51 alien with the gray skin, large eyes, and the bulbous head."

Book 6 is where Quasar himself is explicitly tied to the race — the Lemig are described as looking "like a cross between a goblin and a nullian alien, like Quasar" — and the cookbook gives an extended entry on the Null, including their association with "Nightgaunts" as pack animals.

docs.title: Book 7: Tempest
docs.text:
Book 7 opens with Tempest's Floor 8 Recap School Report, in which Quasar's niece interviews him for a school assignment on "perceptions of the crawl":

The young nullian rolled her eyes. "I told you, Quasar. I have a report due on perceptions of the crawl, and I'm interviewing people, having them give me recaps, and I was assigned Carl and Donut. Obviously my teacher assigned me them because I'm related to you, and if I don't interview you about it, I will fail..."

She is the first nullian relative of Quasar's shown on-page — she references her father (Quasar's brother) and "Aunt Nova," Quasar's ex — which is the closest the series comes to a direct on-page statement of Quasar's own species during Book 7 itself.

Sourcing caveat

Book 7 never says "Quasar is a Nullian" in so many words; the identification within this book is by way of his niece. The explicit statement lives in Book 6. A later Book 7 line describing a goddess's "distinctly alien, almost nullian-like half of her face" is a simile about her appearance, not species lore.

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin, with the species description from Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade and Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Porsuk
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Badger-headed humanoid race
  • Standing role: The bartenders throughout the Desperado Club are Porsuk — the club's badger bar staff on every level
  • Book 6 crawlers: Burcu (level 59 Swashbuckler, #10 on the leaderboard) and Charles Ellis (level 25, a Desperado Club bartender) — see Supporting Cast

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Porsuk are one of those races Carl has been looking at for four books without ever learning the name. When he inspects a Desperado Club bartender on Floor 8, the label finally resolves:

"I gave the badger man a cursory inspection. He was a level-25 Porsuk, which was the name of the badger race in this game. The man's name was Charles."

The name matters because of who else turns out to be one. When Carl reviews the top-ten leaderboard, the newcomer at number ten is:

"a level-59, badger-headed Porsuk, which was the same race as all the bartenders at the Desperado Club. Her class was a Swashbuckler, the same as Tran and Bautista."

So the race sits on both sides of the glass at once: as the anonymous service staff of the dungeon's biggest club, and as one of Earth's highest-ranked crawlers.

docs.title: Burcu
docs.text: Burcu is a Turkish crawler Carl met only briefly during the Butcher's Masquerade on Floor 6 — she was one of the three who fought over the memorial crystal at the end of that boss fight. He has her in his chat but has never really spoken to her. His read: "very serious, reminding me of Hekla." Carl suspects she and the other Turkish crawlers around her are all from the same family.

docs.title: Charles Ellis
docs.text:
Charles Ellis is a Desperado Club bartender who has the extraordinary misfortune of being briefly courted by Samantha. He is torn in half during the club's destruction, "spraying the kitchen with blood" — "All that was left hanging was the shoulder, neck, and head of the very-dead, very unlucky bartender."

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Primal
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Race choice available to crawlers (also a species in its own right, per lore)
  • Stat effect: -1 to all base stats, but unlocks all higher-tier skills up to level 20
  • Notable crawler: Carl, Book 2 onward
  • In-universe status: Ancient, vanished precursor species — near-mythical

docs.title: The Race Choice
docs.text:
"Primal" is a selectable race during a crawler's Floor 3 race/class selection. Per its in-game description:

"For the first several seasons of Dungeon Crawler World, all contestants started off as Primals. Primals are blank slates. You will look the same as before. You will obtain all skills associated with your current race, with the following exceptions: -1 to all base stats. All higher-tier skills are unlocked and are able to train to 20."

Choosing it costs a crawler roughly five stat points relative to picking Human (which grants +2 to all base stats), but removes the normal training cap most skills hit around level 10–11 — according to Mordecai, a level-15 spell is dramatically more powerful than its base version ("four times as potent"), and a level 20 skill can be effectively unstoppable.
