It's a high-risk, high-ceiling choice most crawlers avoid; Mordecai notes only a rare few who pick it ever successfully train a skill past 15.

docs.title: The Lore
docs.text: Per Mordecai, Primals are the setting's deep-lore precursor race — "the progenitors, the first known species to conquer the universe... the boogeymen of the cosmos." Nobody knows what they actually looked like; they vanished after a galaxy-spanning war of unknown origin, leaving only ruins. When someone discovers an abandoned Primal site, the site's resident AI reportedly takes on the appearance of whoever found it — which is offered as the in-universe explanation for why a crawler who picks Primal "looks the same as before" rather than transforming. Some cultures worship Primals as gods; mothers invoke them to frighten children; it's said they will one day return.

docs.title: Notable Crawlers
docs.text:
Carl chooses Primal as his race on Floor 3, largely because it pairs with his intended Compensated Anarchist build and its emphasis on training a small set of skills as high as possible, rather than because of the lore attached to it.

Sourced from Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario.

docs.title: Sai
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Bipedal rhinoceros people; "steampunk samurai" in presentation
  • Size: Roughly seven feet tall and heavily built
  • Former profession: Firefighters, until war-zone firefighting nearly wiped them out
  • Current role: The Armored Sai — the standing guards of the Larracos level, the bottom floor of the Desperado Club

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Carl hears about the Sai before he ever sees one. Reading up on the Desperado Club's Larracos level, he notes that its psionic management keeps "rock creatures, lizard creatures, and 'The Armored Sai'" in line, and that "the sai were the regular guards of the Larracos level, though I'd never seen one. Apparently they were like samurai rhinoceroses."

They turn up in person during the club's destruction, when a demon breaks loose in the restaurant:

"a whole stampede of bipedal, rhinoceros samurai dudes dashed from the room, screaming as they rushed the demon in the restaurant. They were decked out like steampunk samurais, complete with swords and blades at the end of sticks. Each stood about seven feet tall and were huge. The ground shook as they charged."

docs.title: The AI's write-up
docs.text:
"The Sai are quite serious about their guard duties, mostly because it's the only gig they can really get. They used to be firefighters, but firefighting in a war zone is a good way to make yourself almost extinct. So, they migrated into the Desperado Club and now are known as the ever-present guards of the bottom floor of the Desperado. Focusing on their duties distracts them from all those urban legends about their armor being too itchy. These creatures aren't really known for their intelligence, but they're generally good guys, loyal until the end. That's what makes them good guards. They don't care about rules or laws or morals. They just do what they're told."

Carl explicitly distinguishes them from the ordinary rhinoceros mounts elsewhere in the series — Sir Ferdinand's rhino mount is "more like the real deal than these guys, who walked on two feet."

docs.title: Book 7: what happened to the guards
docs.text:
The destruction of the Desperado Club has a direct cost to the Sai as a people. When the club reorganizes under its new management, the survivors lose the only job their species reliably gets. Carl meets one of them as a prisoner — a duct-taped mercenary sergeant named Toyotomi, level 70, "Sai Outpost Guard Mercenary Leader," working castle security for the Prism:

"Toyotomi was once an honorable, experienced leader of Sai. He has since lost his way. His entire squad was killed during an unfortunate incident at the Desperado Club that you may or may not have been partially responsible for. During the club's reorganization, the few Sai survivors were relegated to the mercenary markets, where he was quickly snatched up."

Carl draws the line himself: "I remembered what Clarabelle had told me earlier. All the sai and cretin guards had been fired and replaced." Other Sai turn up in the Bone Clan's army — "There were quite a few of the Sai rhino guards in their midst, along with several of the Bactrian and Dromedarian camels."

docs.title: Edifice Shield
docs.text:
Toyotomi's introduction also gives the Sai a signature ability. It is a fortification buff, and notably it is scale-limited — it works on outposts, not palaces:

"I was hired to help protect this castle, but my magic is for outposts, not primary palaces. If your castle is bigger than this place, I won't be able to cast my Edifice Shield spell. Therefore, I am useless to you."

Carl finds a use for it anyway. Toyotomi joins the Princess Posse and becomes part of the defence of the Nest, Justice Light's tower:

"And as soon as the men up there place the last block and the tower is complete, the bonus will activate and the strength will increase to 200%. And after that, I will cast Edifice Shield which doubles that. With Princess Donut's Sentry and Flak spells, most incoming fire should get deflected."

Toyotomi is killed defending it — "cleaved right in half with a spell... Toyotomi was dead-dead." Book 6's read on the species holds up: they are not clever, and they are loyal until the end.

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin and Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Semeru Dwarves
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Dwarven people of the ninth floor
  • Built: The castle of Larracos, raised along the roots of the All Tree
  • Religion: The only worshippers of the goddess Ysalte anywhere in the dungeon; she has a single temple in the entire crawl
  • Book 6 status: Holding the castle submerged and sealed off after the Larracos flood, letting nobody near that part of the city

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Semeru are a Floor 9 people who become relevant to Book 6 in advance, because Carl's team floods Larracos and then inherits the consequences. They are named in the quest text that ushers in the book's endgame:

"This usually happens here in the dungeon, but only upon the battlefields outside Larracos, where the Semeru Dwarves built their castle along the roots of the All Tree, seeking the very gods who disdain them."

"The very gods who disdain them" is the whole character of the people in one clause. They built at the roots of the world-tree specifically to be near deities who want nothing to do with them.

docs.title: The All Tree
docs.text: The All Tree is carried over from Book 5: per Tsarina Signet, it is a massive tree that "grew through all the worlds at once, connecting everything," and her husband Grimaldi — transformed into a vine by Scolopendra — is now connected to it. Carl makes the link himself on Floor 8 when a tree motif comes up in a quest.

docs.title: Ysalte
docs.text:
The Semeru are the reason Ysalte exists as an encounter at all. Per the Bahamas book:

"The Semeru Dwarves of the ninth floor all only worship a single goddess, who inevitably makes an appearance near the end of the battles as the final teams approach the gates of the castle of Larracos. She only has a single temple in the entire dungeon. I have never seen or heard of a crawler worshiping her. I don't know if that's even possible."

The AI adds that "the earliest citizens of Larracos always worshipped Ysalte," and that she takes no new worshippers beyond the citizens of Larracos. She is the Goddess of Hopelessness and Insanity — formerly of the Dirt, then of Tears — and is better known to crawlers as The Downward Spiral or The Vinegar Bitch.

That exclusivity has a hard consequence in Book 6. When the crawler Paz Lo kills Ysalte on Floor 8, the system announces that all worshippers of Ysalte have permanently been inflicted with the Despondent debuff — which, given the Semeru are her only worshippers, lands squarely on the entire people whose castle Faction Wars is about to be fought over.

docs.title: Book 6 posture
docs.text:
Odette's report on the state of Larracos after the flood:

"The Semeru aren't letting anyone near that part of the city, and they're keeping the castle submerged. Mercenaries and players alike are getting fed into that pit on the daily."

docs.title: Book 7: the Semeru on-screen
docs.text:
Book 7 is where the Semeru stop being a rumour. Carl meets War Leader Arief, Commander of the Larracos Defense Force Infantry, at the foot of a tower on the campus of the Larracos College of Magic, and gets the series' first proper look at one:

"This was the first time I'd gotten a chance to really examine a Semeru dwarf. All the dwarves we'd met so far were more like the traditional, angry Scottish variety. His body was squat and wide, but that's where the similarities ended. This guy was darker complected, Asian looking, with a round face and flat nose. Thick, black hair peeked out from under his large hat. He did not have a beard, though he did have a long, thin mustache."

Their war gear is the other surprise:

"His armor was almost samurai-like, but not quite. It was like a wide, open-chested metallic vest with flared shoulders. The bottom of the metal vest moved outward, like a bell, ending just below his waist. His squat legs were covered in what looked like chainmail with loose, flowing, red and yellow fabric strips along the sides."

"His helmet was a rounded skull cap, but it was decorated with multiple feathers of various kinds, reaching straight up into the air. In the front of the helmet was a metallic ornament, featuring a wide-leafed fern, which curled at the tip, making the helmet look a little ridiculous. His whole getup made him appear as if he was getting ready for a parade, not a battle."

"The wide sickle slung over his shoulder was no joke, however. And everything the dwarf wore was enchanted. Everything, including the individual feathers in his helmet, all let off a glow of various colors."

The narration later calls the look by name: "A group of Semeru dwarves, all with their ornate parade armor, stood at the front gate to the college, pushing back a rush of the shadowy mobs who were trying to fight their way inside." Sickles are standard issue — elsewhere a running formation jogs past "carr[ying] hammers and sickles over their shoulders."

docs.title: The full history
docs.text:
The AI finally tells the story properly, and it is the bleakest origin in the series:

"Anyway, of all the peoples in this story, there's an argument to be had that the Semeru had it the worst. This land, the volcanic level in which Larracos stands, was once a haven for their people... The Semeru people lived here in relative peace. They farmed. They mined. They learned."

They dug toward the gods out of love for Ysalte; a city grew in the pit; scholars came from everywhere and Larracos became "a rich, cultural paradise." What they found at the bottom was not gods but the roots of the All Tree — and they stopped:

"They built their castle at the very bottom, along the thick roots. But it's more than a castle. It's a monument. An apology. In discovering these roots, they had an epiphany... Some things are best left alone. Some things should never be woken up."

Then Scolopendra's nine-tier attack:

"When Scolopendra's nine-tier attack came, the Semeru got it the worst of all. It wasn't their fault. But they were there, and they were mortal, and they were devastated. They numbered in the millions before that day. Today, there are less than 10,000 left."

"And in the ultimate irony, their great structures weren't even touched... The remaining dwarves, defeated, took it upon themselves to be stewards of the great, empty city."

docs.title: The Despondent debuff, in numbers
docs.text:
The consequence of Ysalte's death in Book 6 is now quantified. Every Semeru Carl meets has it blazing over their head:

Warning: This NPC is Despondent because his goddess is dead. He is unable to worship another deity, and all of his stats have taken a 15% hit. In addition, those who worship other deities inflict 10% more damage against him.

Carl: "That despondent debuff was pretty brutal. Still, it didn't seem to bother him too much." Arief greets the two crawlers who flooded his city by bowing deeply and calling it an honour to have them within his borders — Donut, watching: "CARL DOES THIS GUY KNOW YOU AND KATIA ARE THE ONES WHO FLOODED THE CITY IN THE FIRST PLACE? HE'S BEING REALLY NICE."

docs.title: The Jatismara
docs.text:
Book 7 introduces a term for Semeru who carry memory across crawl seasons. Arief, asked whether he remembers previous seasons:

"I don't remember this, but there are some with the memory quickened. I believe I am new, as are most of us. But some have persisted. My uncle remembers dozens of seasons now. Not as many as Juice Box, but he's one of the Jatismara, and he sits upon her war council."

One sentence is all there is

That quotation is the only occurrence of "Jatismara" in the series, and the only occurrence of "quickened" in this sense. What can be said with confidence: some Semeru retain memory of past crawl seasons, they are called the Jatismara, and at least one of them sits on Juice Box's war council. Anything beyond that is unsupported.

docs.title: Dwarven diggers
docs.text:
The Semeru pilot enormous excavation machines that become a major asset for Team Retribution during the siege:

"The massive dwarven digger, which was basically a boxy, god-sized robot covered in all directions with spiral digging arms and goblin-murder-dozer-like spinning wheels, sat idle. A pair of Semeru stood atop it, doing something inside a control panel on the shoulder of the thing. They looked like bugs standing upon it."

The floor is honeycombed for them: "They had passages like this intersecting the entire floor. They were built so the massive, dwarven diggers could get from point A to B quickly."

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin and Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride, with All Tree background from Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: Shadow Mimics
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Sapient mob species; one of the "Big Six" power groups vying for control of the dungeon, per the system AI's own taxonomy (see Factions & Organizations)
  • Growth mechanic: Unbounded — "one of the few entities in the dungeon who grow significantly in intelligence and strength and power as they age with no limit"
  • Detection: Functionally undetectable to most spells; described by Mordecai as "like one of Carl's level 15 traps. All but invisible"
  • Declared archenemy: The Changeling Principals — per the system AI, Shadow Mimics are "the counter to their archenemies, the changeling principals"
  • First confirmed individual: Mitch ("Mitch Fiorelli"), an Adolescent Shadow Mimic, level 120 — killed on Floor 10 (Book 8)
  • Confirmed infestation sites: The Desperado Club casino (Floor 10, Book 8) and the Pineapple Cabaret (a Book 8-revealed pocket dimension)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Shadow Mimics are Book 8's biggest species reveal: a mimic subtype the system AI singles out, mid-fight, as one of the true power players of the dungeon's endgame rather than just another monster type. They are introduced through Mitch, an ambush boss disguised as the Desperado Club's Wheel of Fortune croupier, and confirmed independently as an infestation problem inside the Pineapple Cabaret, the hidden NPC/mob sanctuary the party spends the back half of the book trying to access. Between the two locations, Shadow Mimics touch nearly every major thread of the book's second half.

docs.title: What They Are, Per the System AI
docs.text:
The AI delivers its lore dump on Shadow Mimics mid-ambush, treating the reveal as a scheduled checkpoint in Carl's education about "the true bad guys of the dungeon":

Book 8, Chapter 86

"There are a few dozen types of mimics in the dungeon, from your basic treasure-chest-impersonating mimic to the prostitute-imitating, vagina-as-mouth demon mimics, to the behemoth-sized mimic rex. Shadow Mimics are a whole other Popsicle stand. They are the counter to their archenemies, the changeling principals. They are one of the few entities in the dungeon who grow significantly in intelligence and strength and power as they age with no limit."

Three features distinguish them from every other mimic variety on the ladder — including the treasure-chest mimics, the "vagina-as-mouth demon mimics," and the behemoth Mimic Rex — none of which share these traits:

  • No growth ceiling. Unlike a normal boss or mob, which levels within a fixed band, Shadow Mimics simply keep growing "in intelligence and strength and power" for as long as they survive. The text never specifies the underlying mechanism (feeding, aging, or something else) beyond "as they age" — this is stated as fact, not explained further.
  • Prone to "ideation breaking." The AI's own gloss: "Because of the nature of how they're designed, they're especially prone to ideation breaking. That's a technical term some of you crawlers call 'becoming self-aware.'" A floor designer who understands what a Shadow Mimic is "knows not to mess with them" — implying their self-awareness is an accepted occupational hazard of the species, not a rare glitch.
  • Near-total stealth. "What's even more insidious is that they're almost impossible to detect." Mordecai independently confirms this after Mitch's death: "They have a special ability to avoid most detection spells. They're like one of Carl's level 15 traps. All but invisible... They can mimic crawlers, and the system will label them as such until you discover them."

Mitch himself is offered as a data point on the growth curve, not the ceiling: "Mitch here, the strongest of the mimics in this room right now—hint, hint—is still a baby. He's level 120, and he's pretty damn strong." The implication, left unstated but pointed, is that older, stronger Shadow Mimics exist elsewhere in the dungeon.

docs.title: Counter to the Changeling Principals
docs.text: The AI names Shadow Mimics as the direct opposite number to the Changeling Principals — the Floor 5 cult of disguised Changelings — without elaborating on what "counter" means mechanically or historically. No further explanation is given in Book 8; the parallel (both are near-undetectable species built around impersonation, at opposite philosophical poles) is left for the reader to draw and for a future book to potentially confirm.

docs.title: Mitch and the Desperado Club Infestation
docs.text:
The species' first on-page confirmed member is Mitch, who spends most of Floor 10 disguised as the Desperado Club casino's new Wheel of Fortune croupier before revealing himself — along with the entire casino floor's furniture — as a coordinated ambush. See Mitch's own page for the full fight, his death by the Eye of the Bedlam Bride and a point-blank Magic Missile, and what became of the real Mitch (a "Wall Rat" — an NPC who figured out how to escape the standard dungeon-wipe-and-rewrite cycle — eaten by his impersonator).

Mitch, while dying, claims the Shadow Mimics "needed" crawlers "for the Cabaret" — that the war mages, "the ogres," and a third faction he calls "Cock-A-Doodle-Do" are locked in a three-way struggle to control "the dungeon back door," and that possessing captured crawlers would have given the mimics leverage in that fight. He also states he was "sent up here by \<redacted> to fuck Hamed's shit up," implying the Desperado Club infestation was a deliberate operation against Hamed, the club's current owner, rather than incidental squatting — though the employer behind the redaction is never named.

The aftermath is a permanent status change for the club itself:

Mordecai, Book 8

"If the Desperado Club is infested, you guys can't go back. Those things are almost impossible to root out. The whole place will need to be fumigated. ... You should all devise safe words and quiz each other every day from now on."

See Desperado Club for the location's own updated status.

docs.title: The Pineapple Cabaret Infestation
docs.text:
Independently of Mitch, Akuma reveals that the Pineapple Cabaret — the hidden pocket-dimension sanctuary built by the former crawlers Herot and Menerva — has also been overrun:

Book 8

"That Cabaret place was currently overrun. Akuma had been a little... fuzzy... on who the bad guys were. He mentioned something called the Ogre Imperium, which was a long-forgotten plotline that had gotten binned because the ogres were made too intelligent and they had immediately figured out that they were trapped in a dungeon. And there was a shadow mimic infestation, which was just as bad."

This makes the Cabaret a second, separate Shadow Mimic presence from the Desperado Club one — the text never confirms whether the two infestations are coordinated, though Mitch's dying claim about crawlers being wanted "for the Cabaret" suggests at least some overlap in planning. See The Pineapple Cabaret for the full three-way contest over the space.

docs.title: As One of the "Big Six"
docs.text:
The system AI explicitly places Shadow Mimics inside Group Four: the sapient mobs of its own "Big Six" taxonomy of dungeon power factions, delivered in the same breath as the Mitch reveal — alongside the Ogre Imperium, non-deity boss monsters like Krakaren Prime, and the War Mage Rebellion:

Book 8

"The sapient mobs. This is the group our friends the Shadow Mimics are a part of. But we also have the Ogre Imperium and a few other non-deity boss monsters in here, like Krakaren Prime. The War Mages, of course, are also part of this group... within this group, the Shadow Mimics are one of the strongest."

See Factions & Organizations: The Big Six for the taxonomy in full — treated there as a stub pointer to a future Mechanics-pass page rather than duplicated here.

docs.title: Open Threads
docs.text:
• Who sent Mitch. The system's own examine text calls Mitch "an Enforcer for the \<Redacted>," and the AI itself declines to name the employer beyond confirming they're "still in their early stages of planning." Whether this is the same faction contesting the Pineapple Cabaret, a different Shadow Mimic leadership structure entirely, or something else is not resolved in Book 8.
  • "Cock-A-Doodle-Do." Mitch's name for the third faction fighting the war mages and the Ogre Imperium over "the dungeon back door" is never explained or repeated elsewhere in the book. Treated here as an unresolved, possibly jokey, dying declaration rather than a confirmed faction identity.
  • The growth mechanic's actual trigger. "As they age" is the only stated condition for a Shadow Mimic's growth; whether feeding, successful impersonation, or something else accelerates it is never addressed on-page.

Sourced from Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Sturnus
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • First appearance: Book 7, This Inevitable Ruin
  • Type: Small songbird people — Volteeg's birth race
  • Status: Named exactly once in the series, on Volteeg's character sheet

docs.title: What the text actually says
docs.text:
"Sturnus" appears in Book 7 in a single place — the closing sheet of Volteeg's POV chapter:

Class: Tank Buttress — Race: Gargoyle — Birth Race: Sturnus — Top Level: 71

Everything else about the race is inferred from Volteeg's own history, told in the same chapter before he became a Gargoyle.

docs.title: The bird Volteeg was
docs.text:
Volteeg entered the dungeon as a pet, belonging to Mistress Henspar. His pre-transformation life is described in small-bird terms throughout: he perches on her shoulder at the market, she "scritched under his wing," he bites a shopkeeper's finger over a berry, and he dreams afterward "only of berries and fire and the warmth of the hearth."

Above all, he could sing:

"When he felt that love, he would sing. He knew not to sing in the market, because that was a secret, and he was protecting her just as much as she was protecting him. But later, when they were back outside and his belly was full, he would sing for Mistress Henspar. He would sit on her shoulder and sing, and she would have salty-tasting tears spring down her cheeks."

A pet biscuit gave him intelligence and speech. On the third floor he chose to become a gargoyle, which gave him a working mind — and cost him his voice:

"He'd chosen a race that could not sing. Not like before, and that was such a terrible, terrible mistake."

'Songbird' is an inference

The word songbird never appears in the text. The identification rests on the real-world genus Sturnus (starlings), on Volteeg's perching-and-singing pet life, and on his later inability to whistle — "his voice was like rocks being dragged against one another." The wiki treats it as a reasonable reading, not a stated fact.

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Tenodera
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • First appearance: Book 7, This Inevitable Ruin (the epilogue)
  • Type: A smaller, flightless cousin species to the mantids
  • Known individual: York, the tenth-edition cookbook author and sole crew aboard the Homecoming Queen
  • Defining trait: Ancestral warrior castes were deliberately bred to feel nothing

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The tenodera are introduced in Book 7's epilogue through York, who spends the entire chapter alone aboard the Homecoming Queen writing bad poetry and trying to feel something. His character sheet is unusual among the cookbook authors in that it records no race change at all:

Class: Advocate. Race: Tenodera. Birth Race: Tenodera.

docs.title: Relationship to the mantids
docs.text:
The tenodera are mantis-adjacent and, in the mantids' eyes, a contamination risk:

"The larger mantids hated his race, the tenodera. They were similar, but York and his kind were much smaller physically. Flightless. And not nearly as aggressive and violent. Most mantids openly spoke of exterminating him and his kind, as they could crossbreed, and they feared what would happen should the tenodera mix en masse."

York's reaction to the destruction of the mantis Hive Re-Population Center 51 is, accordingly, "a strange, empty sense of satisfaction" — and he tries the words "That's what you deserved" out loud without feeling them.

docs.title: Bred numbness
docs.text:
The species' central trait is a heritable emotional flattening:

"And then, somewhere around the 9th floor, a numbness spread. He knew this was something locked deep in his tenodera DNA. His warrior ancestors had been specifically bred to be without emotion. This was before they'd all become civilized, before all their wars were fought with tanks and bombs and drones, the military hardware substituting for the chemicals their queens of old would drill into their brains."

"This lack of emotion would be required of any soldier whose duty it was to crack into an enemy hive and kill all the children within."

York's arc turns on exactly that: he volunteers to destroy an orc yacht full of children — "he'd looked forward to it... He wanted to do it because he wanted to feel something afterward" — and it doesn't work. He finally feels something only at the very end of the book, when the Homecoming Queen's weapons come online and Porthus's resistance broadcast airs.

York entered the dungeon with his whole hive, and "recalled — vaguely recalled — the anger he'd felt at how they'd been picked off one by one. And not just at that, but at the realization that he'd never really fit in. And because of his own individuality, he never was part of a team, despite being part of a hive."

New in Book 7

"Tenodera" does not appear anywhere in Books 1–6. The name York does — he's cited in Book 3 as the author of the tenth cookbook edition — but his species and history are new here.

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Tripod
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • First appearance: Book 7, This Inevitable Ruin
  • Type: Round, basketball-bodied aliens balanced on three long jointed legs, covered in eyes
  • Reputation: Famously, completely emotionless
  • Known individual: Fopsy — adjutant for the Dream, and a former Syndicate Prime Minister

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text:
Carl meets his first one when a second adjutant teleports into an adjudication:

"The thing was a round, basketball-like creature standing upon three, long, multi-jointed legs. The round ball was covered in black dots that might be eyeballs. I was pretty sure this was a type of alien called a 'tripod.' I'd heard of them, but I'd never seen one before. They were supposedly completely without emotion, like extra asshole versions of Spock from Star Trek."

The eyes are functional and expressive in their own way: "All the eyes on the adjutant's round body twinkled as he moved through his menus, glittering like a disco ball." Donut's field identification is blunter: "IT'S THAT WEIRD ALIEN WHO LOOKS LIKE A BASKETBALL ON STILTS. FOPSY."

Prepotente supplies the only other data point in the book, complaining about a harem: "One of the harem girls was one of those tripods, like the adjutant for the Dream. It would be like having sexual congress with the Sputnik satellite!"

docs.title: Fopsy
docs.text:
Fopsy is the only named tripod in the series so far, and he is considerably more than a bit part. He is the Dream's Faction Wars adjutant and a former Prime Minister of the Syndicate — a combination that becomes politically explosive when Prime Minister Glory falls. Victory, on the no-confidence vote: "if the vote goes a certain way, this guy here might actually be the Prime Minister again, which is doubly interesting because he's the Dream's adjutant. You'd think he'd know if his client was a robot." Fopsy: "I had no idea. No inkling whatsoever, but it does make sense now considering some clues."

He is ultimately passed over — "as people weren't certain of former Prime Minister Fopsy's relationship to the Dream, he was passed over for the newly-vacated position" — and Baroness Victory becomes acting Prime Minister instead. See The Syndicate Council.

Fopsy also supplies two of the book's key pieces of exposition: he traces the war mages' trade of the Gate of the Feral Gods to the Midnight Market, and he theorises about Agatha's real motive for seizing the War Mage Rebellion.

Emotionless, but not useless

The "completely without emotion" line is the reputation Carl has heard, and Fopsy's dialogue is consistent with it — his stock response to catastrophe is "Interesting." The book never tests the stereotype directly.

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Vesper
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • First appearance: Book 7, This Inevitable Ruin
  • Type: Milk's birth race — bat-like, winged
  • Status: Named three times in the whole series, always in contrast to Xenopus, the race Milk chose as a crawler

docs.title: What the text actually says
docs.text:
Vesper exists in the books entirely as the "before" half of Milk's race change. Every mention:

"Yes, I am a xenopus, but before I came into the dungeon, I was a vesper."

Race: Xenopus — Birth Race: Vesper

"...she'd written extensively about the differences between the wings of her chosen race, the Xenopus, and those of her birth race, the Vesper."

Carl describes Milk as a "half frog, half bat creature," and the bat half is the Vesper inheritance — but the book never independently describes what an unchanged Vesper looks like, where they come from, or anything else about them.

Deliberately thin

There is no standalone description of the Vesper as a people anywhere in Books 1–7. The bat-like reading is an inference from Carl's "half frog, half bat" phrasing plus the wing comparison; the wiki does not extend it further.

docs.title: Why the race change matters
docs.text:
Milk's birth race / chosen race split is one of a matched pair in Book 7. The other is Volteeg, whose birth race was Sturnus and who chose Gargoyle — and whose entire tragedy is that gargoyles cannot sing. Both characters are cookbook authors, both chose a race for utility, and both carry the consequence permanently: "That was something they didn't tell you when you changed your body. They changed you, and they couldn't change you back."

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Were-castor
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Were-creature race (beaver-based transformation), formerly the Chee
  • Floor: 6 ("The Hunting Grounds")
  • Named individuals: Clint Smashgrab, Holger, and four unnamed brothers; their teacher Nadine (a transformed Bearded Sage Caterpillar); their village leader, the child golem "young Clint"
  • Allied with: Tsarina Signet

docs.title: The Chee
docs.text: Before High Elf Queen Imogen — then a princess and her father's Sorcerer General — led a campaign to seize their land, the Chee were a peaceful people of carpenters and teachers on Floor 6. Imogen's forces cast a mass transfiguration spell on the entire village and sent in "cleansers" to finish the job; the only survivors were a handful of children, transformed into new forms that stuck permanently. Six boys became were-castors — human-sized were-beavers, capable of shifting between a short, stocky "Chee" humanoid form and a fully furred, buck-toothed beaver form with a lisp — while their teacher, a woman named Nadine, became a Bearded Sage Caterpillar (see the description on her page in-book as a giant, intelligent, tree-dwelling insect who raised the six boys to adulthood in hiding).

docs.title: In the Story
docs.text:
Two of the six, Clint Smashgrab (bald, missing a leg below the knee, replaced with a metal bar) and Holger (recognizable by his mullet), are Carl and Donut's primary contacts among Signet's forces — bickering, foul-mouthed, and quick to violence with each other but fanatically loyal fighters, immune to the paralysis effect of Night Weasels and strong enough in constitution to tank sustained mob damage without much visible injury. Both fight alongside Carl and Donut at Point Mongo and during the assault on Fort Freedom.

Clint and Nadine are both killed during the Fort Freedom assault — Nadine to a stray lightning bolt from Claude Sludgington the Fourth, Clint on the opposite shore to Big Tina. Signet has Edgar the tortoise tattoo both of their memories onto her own skin that same night, using a needle dipped in Nadine's remains — the resulting "blood and ink elemental" recreates not just Nadine but a small, tattooed version of Clint as he appeared as a child, since Nadine's memory of him was strong enough to bring his likeness along without a body to draw from.

Holger survives through the book's end, present at the Butcher's Masquerade fighting alongside Carl's group.

Sourced from Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: Xenopus
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • First appearance: Book 7, This Inevitable Ruin
  • Type: Winged, clawed, frog-like people
  • Known individual: Milk, guildmaster of the Cartography and Calligrapher's guilds and author of the sixth edition of the Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook — a chosen crawler race, not her birth race (see Vesper)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Xenopus is a crawler race, and the book has fun with the fact that its name is borrowed straight from Earth taxonomy. When the vampire crawler Miriam asks Milk what she is —

"A xenopus is the genus name of a type of clawed frog," the caprid said as he handed the woman a magical salve. "Common throughout the world. Disgusting creatures. The earth versions do not have wings."

— the correction is Prepotente's, and it's the only physiological detail the text gives outright: the dungeon version does have wings.

Milk answers for herself:

"Yes, I am a xenopus, but before I came into the dungeon, I was a vesper."

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text:
Carl's first sight of her, when he discovers she is his sister:

"But I barely registered this as I stared at the half frog, half bat creature. The guildmaster met my gaze... My eyes moved to the wings of the creature. She'd written extensively about the differences between the wings of her chosen race, the Xenopus, and those of her birth race, the Vesper."

The "half bat" half of that composite is Milk's Vesper inheritance showing through; the wings of the two races are different enough that she wrote about the contrast at length in the cookbook.

docs.title: Milk's sheet
docs.text:
Class: Cartographer — Race: Xenopus — Birth Race: Vesper — Top Level: 73

Dungeon Exit: took a deal on the tenth floor. Runs both the Cartography guild and Calligrapher's guild. Will not be freed until her services are used at least 333 times in the dungeon. Times used so far: 6.

Author of the sixth edition of the Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook. Current status: Indentured within the dungeon.

For the guilds themselves, see Dungeon Factions.

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Zebani
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Humanoid crawler race, seen exactly once in Book 6
  • Book 6 individual: Emir Akbas, a level 55 Ghazi — see Supporting Cast

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Zebani appear in a single scene. During the Floor 8 "Royal Court" storyline, Carl tries to recruit a four-crawler squad he runs into, and the one who pushes back is a Zebani:

"His race was a Zebani, and he was a level 55 Ghazi named Emir Akbas. I had no idea what either a Ghazi or Zebani was, but the tall guy had huge arms and a curved sword over his shoulder."

That is the whole of it. Carl reads him as tall, heavily built, in his fifties, with an extraordinarily thick monobrow, and carrying a curved sword. The squad's crawler numbers are similar enough that Carl guesses they are all from one family.

Unresolved

Book 6 gives no physiology, homeworld, culture, or political affiliation for the Zebani, and the AI never provides one of its usual species write-ups. Both Zebani (the race) and Ghazi (the class) go unexplained on the page — Carl himself says he doesn't know what either is. Do not read anything further into the name without a later-book source.

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Spells
docs.text: Catalog of spells encountered across the series — how they're learned (tome vs. scroll), their effects, and notable uses. Full pages exist for spells with real plot weight in Book 1; everything else is listed in the table below. Any full page should include a Scaling section whenever the book describes how the spell's effect changes with skill level. Any spell named in a full-page character's Quick Facts box must itself have a full page here, not just a table row.

docs.text:
• All Eyes on Me — Donut's Legendary Diva mass-charm song (Book 5)
  • Astral Paw — Donut's giant-cat's-paw spell; crushed a car in Book 8, first seen combined into War Crime (Book 7)
  • Bad Attitude — Donut's mass Int drain and resistance reduction; pairs with Carl's Fear (Book 6)

  • Black Nimbus — Carl's item-granted involuntary abjuration, strips a deity's blessing (Book 6)

docs.title: Book 8 spell/scroll catalog
docs.text:
Floors 10–11, "Don't Come in Last" and "A Parade of Horribles." Spells with full pages are listed above; everything else Book 8 names is catalogued here.

Name Caster Effect Temporary Macaroni Princess Donut, from her Banquet Fit for a Princess book Casts a giant, solid tube of pasta (15 ft tall, 20 ft wide) as an instant barrier; at level 15 (base 14 + Brain Trust) the caster can choose the size, shape, and pasta type, and chain casts into a continuous tunnel. Only 10 mana per cast. Used to shield the race truck from a hail of exploding sugar-hermit skulls Gutter Bumper Carl, via a page eaten from Carl's Book of Boom Focuses the area of effect of another spell along a chosen path ("gutter"), rather than the spell's normal shape. Combined with Donut's Ice Slick to freeze an entire winding river instead of a single cone, extending the ice's reach by roughly 50% Big-Ass Magnet Princess Donut, from her Feast book Cast on a chosen object; pulls every loose piece of a matching material (screws, in practice) within 200 meters toward that object, intensifying for about 15 seconds after casting. Used both as a planned car-snatching tool and, in the event, to arm Dong Quixote's lance with a wave of screws for his final charge against the god Grull — see Corcunda for that scene in full Fresh into Salt Princess Donut, from her Champion of Nekhebit title Turns a body of water into salt; used on an entire river to wipe out a swarm of level-50 flying piranhas in one cast Summon Ye, Vermin Princess Donut Instantly draws every rodent in the area to the caster; used as a finisher to send a wave of drilling "zipper shrews" through a river's worth of frozen enemies, and to kill the boss Maurice
