docs.title: Celestial Thorn Room — the shrine rewards not taken
docs.text:
Only one of the seven orisha shrines could be repaired, and the party chose Yemaya. The spells offered by the others were forfeited:

Shrine Spell offered Also offered Legba Confusing Fog, level 15, to everyone 50% chance to avoid all future smites Shango Lightning, level 15, to everyone — trainable to 20, with a pointed "Hint, hint that spell might come in handy later" — Oshun Heal Party, level 10, to everyone Protection from the next five fatal blows; +50% Charisma

docs.title: All Eyes on Me
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: Book 5, Chapter 1 — granted automatically as part of her starting kit the moment she picks Legendary Diva as her Character Actor floor specialty in the Floor 6 class-selection room (see Standing Ovation for the acquisition scene); the "All Eyes on Me" name is only attached to it later, when she performs it at the Masquerade
  • Class requirement: Legendary Diva (Bard floor specialty, Floor 6)
  • Type: Mass charm / attention-focusing song

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: A sung charm spell that focuses everyone within earshot's attention onto a subject of the caster's choosing. The charm itself is minor and doesn't compel action, but its effective range scales directly with the caster's Charisma — a sufficiently high-Charisma cast can affect an entire room, including crawlers, hunters, elves, and even attending deities, all at once.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: Not given as an explicit numeric curve, but the spell's area of effect is described as Charisma-dependent; with her benefactor tiara doubling her Charisma to 276+, Donut's cast affects literally everyone in the Butcher's Masquerade's ballroom simultaneously, Queen Imogen included.

docs.title: Role in the Story — Book 5
docs.text: Donut headlines the Butcher's Masquerade's talent competition by singing "All Eyes on Me" — the same nonsensical lullaby her original owner, Beatrice, used to sing to her. The number was already planned as part of the group's escape choreography before Tsarina Signet decides, only moments earlier, to sacrifice herself instead of following through on her own riskier plan; Carl times her cue to the song regardless. The spell locks the entire ballroom's attention onto the stage (and, immediately after, onto a dancing Big Tina), giving Signet the unnoticed opening she needs to perform her Ink Marauder ritual at the edge of the room.

docs.title: Book 8: Cast by Spoken Word Alone
docs.text:
At the Floor 10 stage-performance guild, Donut casts All Eyes on Me without singing at all:

Donut was casting the spell All Eyes on Me, which under normal circumstances required a song. But because her charisma was now so high, she could now cast it with spoken words. After just a few seconds of her talking, they wouldn't be able to keep their eyes off of her.

No specific Charisma threshold is given for when the song requirement drops away — the text credits it generally to her Charisma being "now so high," consistent with the score already in the 276+ range by Book 5. Treat the exact cutoff as unconfirmed.

Sourced from Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade and Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Astral Paw
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: Book 4, Chapter 2 — a spellbook from Donut's Floor 5 "spellbook-of-the-floor club" mailbox prize, read back at the personal space right after the Grull/mantaur fight ("Carl, Carl, I got a good one this time!"). The same chapter's box-opening session also gives her Wall of Fire
  • Type: Melee-shaped area spell; manifests as a giant translucent cat's paw
  • First seen: Book 4, as a mailbox-delivered utility spell; first shown at battlefield scale in Book 7, combined into War Crime's only cast

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: Astral Paw manifests as an enormous, glowing, translucent cat's paw that can crush, sweep, or pin whatever it lands on — scaling from a battlefield-sized effect (combined with War Crime) down to a single, close-range strike.

docs.title: Acquisition — Book 4, Chapter 2
docs.text:
Donut grabs her monthly mailbox spellbook the moment the party returns to the personal space and reads it before Carl can stop her. Mordecai identifies it once she describes it:

"Astral Paw," Mordecai said. "Not as good as Astral Hand because there's no thumb to manipulate and hold things. But there's more force to it, especially at higher levels, and it can be used as a weapon. She can grow claws on it at level five. At level 10, she can make the paw a lot bigger. At level 15, her skills and abilities will translate directly to the paw... Anyway, she can manipulate items at a distance as if she was physically touching them. Distance grows with level-up. At level one, it's about 10 meters."

docs.title: Book 7: The War Crime Finisher
docs.text:
Donut's only lifetime cast of War Crime combines Bijanbi and Astral Paw. The paw appears at massive scale, hovering over the hole of Larracos:

Then I saw it, hovering above the hole of Larracos, right outside the tower. It was the massive, glowing outline of a cat's paw. The paw was absolutely enormous.

It catches thousands of frozen elves, gnolls, and Reaver cyborgs — plus the god Meatus — beneath it, covered in fleshers. The finisher isn't automatic: Donut has to close the paw herself, manually, once Li Na's chain lattice fails to do the job:

"I shouldn't have picked Astral Paw," she said. "I have to do it myself."... She closed her eyes, and she swiped downward with three quick baps.

See War Crime for the complete scene; it isn't repeated here.

docs.title: Crushing a car
docs.text:
At the Floor 11 climax, with Chris's truck and the APV knocking down a fleeing Cadillac's shield, Donut casts Astral Paw at point-blank, close-combat scale rather than the battlefield scale seen in Book 7:

In that moment, as the shield was down, Donut cast Astral Paw. She smashed the car where it stood, crushing it like a tin can. The Cadillac simply ceased to exist.

The whole exchange — Donut's shout to the car's destruction — takes less than a second, and costs her three new player-killer skulls (the vehicle's occupants were fellow crawlers).

docs.title: Decapitating a unicorn — not this spell
docs.text:
Exact-verification note

Book 8 also shows Donut removing the racer Dwight the unicorn's head "in a single swipe of Donut's claw" during the Heat 7 starting-line massacre. The text attributes this explicitly to her claw, not to Astral Paw — no spell name is given for that strike, and it reads as the newly celestial-boosted Claw skill (glowing, functionally indestructible claws, broken past its training cap to level 17 this same book) rather than as an Astral Paw cast. Treat the car-crushing feat above as the confirmed Astral Paw moment, and the decapitation as a Claw feat instead — see that page for the full context.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: Per Mordecai's original Book 4 explanation: manipulation range starts at roughly 10 meters at level 1 and grows with level-up; the paw grows claws at level 5; the paw itself gets noticeably bigger at level 10; and at level 15, Donut's own skills and abilities translate directly onto the paw. No further per-level formula is given past that. What's observable in play: at Nest-tower/War Crime scale it's large enough to sweep up thousands of combatants and a god; at ordinary combat scale (unassisted, Book 8) it's still powerful enough to crush a car "like a tin can" in under a second.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Wall of Fire — acquired in the same Book 4, Chapter 2 box-opening session
  • War Crime — the spell it was combined with for its only recorded battlefield-scale use
  • Claw — the skill actually responsible for the Book 8 unicorn kill
  • Bijanbi — the other component of the War Crime cast

Sourced from Book 4: The Gate of the Feral Gods, Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin, and Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Bad Attitude
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: Granted automatically with her Floor 8 Character Actor class, Master Telephone Psychic
  • Type: Mass debuff
  • Effect: Drains Intelligence and lowers resistances across a group
  • Designed to combo with: Carl's Fear

docs.title: Effect
docs.text:
Mordecai's introduction of the spell is also the instruction manual for how the party is meant to use it:

"Bad Attitude is similar to Carl's Fear spell, but it'll be a lot more potent in your hands. If you work it together, it'll be a great combo. Fear tends to affect dexterity while Bad Attitude drains intelligence and lowers resistances."

The two spells are explicitly complementary rather than redundant. Fear wrecks a group's Dexterity; Bad Attitude wrecks its Intelligence and strips its resistances, which opens the same targets up to everything else Donut can throw — including her nipple-ring-amplified fire spells, whose damage the reduced resistances directly multiply.

"A lot more potent in your hands" is a Charisma note: Donut's Charisma is far above Carl's, and charm- and morale-based effects scale with it.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: No numeric formula is given, and unlike its single-target sibling Brain Freeze — which gains blindness at level 10 — Bad Attitude has no stated level breakpoint. Donut does not report a starting level for it. What the text does establish is that its area and potency ride on the caster's Charisma, which is the stat Donut has in surplus.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Brain Freeze — the single-target version, which adds a health drain
  • Fear — Carl's Dexterity debuff, the intended pairing
  • Why Are You Hitting Yourself? — the third spell from the same class grant

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Bang Bro
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Carl
  • Obtained: A Boss Box tome, Book 3 (Floor 4)
  • Cost: 5 mana
  • Duration: 5 minutes + 1 minute per spell level; 5-minute cooldown

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A tome-taught spell that temporarily enchants an equipped item with combined fire and electrical damage:

"Adds both fire and electrical damage to any currently-equipped item. May not be cast on flesh. Well, actually it can be cast on (your own) flesh, but I really wouldn't recommend it. May inflict Burn and Shock on targets. Can also be used to cook hotdogs and other items."

Carl casts it on his War Gauntlet — Mordecai confirms it works well there, but warns against using it on the Xistera given how Carl loads it, and cautions (unnecessarily, since Carl declines) against casting it on his own foot even with an invulnerability buff active.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
Duration scales directly with spell level: base 5 minutes, +1 minute per level (per the tome's own text: "Duration: 5 minutes + 1 minute per level of spell. Requires 5 minute cooldown."). No explicit damage-scaling formula is given anywhere in the text, and no book ever states Carl's actual Bang Bro skill level. The spell stays in continuous, unchanged use through Book 8 — most notably electrifying his gauntlet to kill a parasite that had latched onto it after a skull exploded in the FUPA's cab — with no new numbers, effects, or level references appearing at any point after the Book 3 grant. This is a genuinely thin scaling picture; the text simply doesn't give more to work with.

Sourced from Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook and Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Bear Witness and Bring Forth the Witnesses
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Eris, goddess of chaos
  • Type: The Ceremony of Chaos — a divine ritual, not a crawler spell
  • Uses: Once. Ever. Per Mordecai, this is a hard limit on the goddess herself
  • Bear Witness: Freezes every mortal outdoors on the floor, marks them Witness, and makes them invulnerable
  • Bring Forth the Witnesses: Teleports all of them into a single enormous pile at the goddess's location
  • Side effect: The level-20 cast causes a floor-wide magical backlash — no long-range teleport spells for an hour

The ceremony is normally a 12th-floor event. Eris casts it on Floor 9, out of what Mordecai reads as panic, and in doing so hands Donut the setup for Rolling Battle Formation.

Exact-verification note

No tome or system description block exists. The quoted material below is system warnings plus Mordecai's explanation.

docs.title: The Warnings
docs.text:
You are invulnerable until the completion of the Chaos Ritual.

Warning. The Goddess Eris has cast Bear Witness in a wide area around her current position. This will only affect those outside of structures. The area of effect is marked on your map, but it's pretty much the whole floor.

Your Mind Balance has negated Bear Witness.

Then the second half:

Warning: The Goddess Eris has cast Bring Forth the Witnesses.

Warning: The effects of a level-20 Bring Forth the Witnesses has caused a magical backlash over the entire floor. No long-range teleport spells will work for the next hour.

docs.title: What It Looks Like
docs.text:
Everyone outdoors freezes as if a boss battle had just started, eyes gone completely white, with the word Witness floating over their heads next to a symbol Carl describes as "two Cs back to back with a flaming lance through the middle."

Then they leave:

everyone in the army just rocketed up into the air like they'd all been launched out of trebuchets… ascended into the air and disappeared like it was the goddamned rapture.

docs.title: Who Was Immune
docs.text:
Two categories escaped, and the second one is a surprise.

Indoors. The spell explicitly "will only affect those outside of structures." Anyone under a roof was untouched.

Otherwise immune:

Who Why Carl Mind Balance negated it outright — see Mind Balance Dong Quixote, Bigs the Sluggalette, and the sluggalos Per Li Na, "anyone who was once a tattoo… Same with the sluggalos" Rend, Gonk the yak, Jamal the shark Pets Samantha —

Carl's level-16 Mind Balance — trained past the cap by battlefield conditions in the same chapter — stopping a level-20 divine ceremony is the clearest demonstration of what that skill is worth.

docs.title: What It Is For
docs.text:
Mordecai's explanation in chapter 66 is the only account of the mechanic's purpose:

This is exclusive to Eris, and she usually does this on the 12th floor. I'm not sure why she did it now, but it sounds like she's panic casting things and doesn't know what she's doing. Some gods can only claim the Ascendent throne if there are no mortals present, so Eris sometimes causes chaos by summoning mortal witnesses to the ceremony. It's called the Ceremony of Chaos. The witnesses are protected from the gods during this, hence the invulnerability, and she can keep them in the Witness state as long as she wants. She can also turn the invulnerability off early if she wants. They're brought to her in a giant pile. It's... it's a thing. They're usually NPCs since most crawlers never make it to the 12th floor. She can only cast this once. Ever.

So it is a spoiler mechanic: certain gods cannot take the Ascendent throne with mortals watching, and Eris's counter is to teleport in an audience. It is meant to be used at the throne, on the 12th floor, against rivals. Using it on Floor 9 wastes it.

docs.title: The Consequence Nobody Planned
docs.text:
The giant pile of frozen mortals is sitting in the middle of a god fight. Donut, intending only to move them somewhere safer, casts Rolling Battle Formation on the entire pile — and accidentally scoops up both Eris and the feral god Meatus along with tens of thousands of people.

That turns out to be the thing that saves them. Eris later turns her Witness spell off, removing the invulnerability she had granted and leaving everyone exposed on an active battlefield. Rosetta, chapter 68:

"She turned off her Witness spell and just removed everyone's invulnerability, but they're still invulnerable anyway. The Rolling Battle Formation spell keeps them immobile and invulnerable. But they'll be exposed the moment the ball breaks!"

Carl's assessment to Donut in chapter 75: "If you hadn't done it, half of everyone would be dead by now."

The teleport ban is its own minor disaster — an hour with no long-range teleportation, in the middle of a war, imposed by a goddess who by Mordecai's read did not think it through. Carl separately complains that his lava-abatement work "had been interrupted by the Bear Witness spell."

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: Bring Forth the Witnesses is cast at level 20 — a number well outside the crawler scale, and the reason for the floor-wide backlash. The area of Bear Witness is nominally "a wide area around her current position" and in practice "pretty much the whole floor."

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Rolling Battle Formation — what Donut does with the pile
  • Mind Balance — the only thing that negated it
  • Pied Piper — Eris's other intervention in Carl's book, a coin flip

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Bijanbi (formerly "Heel")
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: Tattooed onto her right flank by Edgar in chapter 74 — see The Toraline Ink Tattoo System
  • Original owner: A cleric of the god Wepwawet who fell defending the FUPA. The spell was granted to him through worship
  • Effect: A wide-area drag — pulls multiple enemies toward a designated location
  • Level: Arrives at 2; boosted temporarily to 15 by Milk's Words of Power calligraphy
  • Renamed: "It used to be called Heel, but apparently the translation makes it sound like another spell, so this season it's called Bijanbi."

Exact-verification note

There is no system description block for this spell anywhere in Book 7. The only definition is Carl's inference by comparison, quoted below. The text also spells it "Binjabi" in chapter 76, where the spell is actually used; "Bijanbi" in chapter 74 is the spelling Rosetta gives when naming it. Both spellings appear once each.

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text:
Carl works it out by triangulating against two spells he already knows:

Hamzo was a spell that stunned and then summoned an enemy to your location. Katia had it. Dinner Bell was similar, but it worked in a wide range over multiple enemies at once, and you could designate a location. It didn't stun them. I didn't know, exactly, what Bijanbi did, but it was clearly something that dragged enemies toward you.

Rosetta calls it "a Dinner Bell variant," so the working definition is: mass, ranged, targeted drag, no stun.

docs.title: Why Donut Needed It
docs.text:
Purely as ammunition for War Crime. The endgame plan requires two component spells, each at level 8 or higher, and Donut's arsenal has no mass-drag effect at all. Rosetta explains the substitution in chapter 74:

"We were going to go with Hamzo, but even with the Synergy tower's effect tied in with the bonus from the War Crime spell, it won't be a wide enough area. So we went with a Dinner Bell variant from a cleric who fell defending the FUPA. It's a spell that came from him worshiping his deity, but it appears it's going to work. Edgar extracted it properly, and with some ink tips from Milk, we don't need the toraline anymore to do what we need."

This is also the first demonstration of Edgar's new ink, which can pull an ability from a corpse — something the original toraline ink, which required a living donor, could not do.

docs.title: The Tattoo
docs.text:
Edgar picks the placement and Donut objects at volume: "You will not be shaving my ass!" He needs "a spot about as big as my foot" on her right flank, and works fast enough that the artwork is not his best. The result:

It was a simple, rather adorable line art tattoo of a dog. As I watched, the tattoo did, indeed, move. It lifted its leg and started to lick itself.

Edgar's professional assessment: "I do not believe the art is sentient, as it hasn't been imbued with anything other than the spell itself. I imagine this is all it can do."

The full negotiation, including Donut's condition that Carl get a matching one, is on The Toraline Ink Tattoo System.

docs.title: Levels 2 to 15
docs.text:
The transfer lands short. Donut, immediately after:

"I did, but it's only level two! My word... this is quite a good spell. It says it came from a god called 'Wepwawet.' What kind of name is that? It gives me the option to worship him now." She gasped. "Carl, Carl, it says he's in the 'Court of Nekhebit!' and I can worship Odette now, too!"

Level 2 is useless for War Crime, which requires 8. Milk fixes it by writing calligraphy directly over the finished tattoo:

"Not quite yet, child. We must get it temporarily above level eight. This may sting a little," Milk said. She came forward and produced a pen, dripping with black ink… She wrote some words atop the tattoo with a flourish as Donut hissed with pain. I didn't recognize the script, but when I examined the characters, the system simply said, Words of Power.

"It's a magic style that I haven't seen used often in the dungeon. The calligraphy guild teaches it."

The overshoot is dramatic — "The spell went up to level 15!" — and explicitly temporary: "As the ink fades, the power will decrease, but if you practice using the spell at that high of a level, it will assist greatly with training."

docs.title: Use — Chapter 76
docs.text:
Bijanbi is one of the two component spells Donut feeds into War Crime from the Nest tower, the other being Astral Paw. Combined and tower-amplified, the two produce the effect that ends the battle of Larracos: thousands of frozen enemy soldiers, plus the feral god Meatus, dragged up off the field and gathered beneath a colossal glowing cat's paw.

Per the War Crime rules, Donut loses access to both component spells for the remainder of the floor, and gains the permanent ability to chain them together for a single cost on later floors.

docs.title: Side Effects
docs.text: The transfer comes with unwanted extras. Donut receives "two very rude achievements. One called me a traitor and another just gave me something called a stolen catalytic converter as a prize" — consequences of taking a spell that belongs to a god she does not worship. It also opens Wepwawet as a worship option, which turns out to matter: he sits in the Court of Nekhebit, and Donut is named Champion of Nekhebit at the end of the same sequence.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: No stated per-level formula. The observable facts are that level 2 is too low to be combined into War Crime (the floor is 8), and that the level can be inflated well past the donor's own by overlaying Words of Power, at the cost of the boost decaying as the ink fades.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• The Toraline Ink Tattoo System — how it was acquired
  • War Crime — the only thing it was acquired for
  • Enchanted Prison Tattoo Kit

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Bitch, What? (Fire Berserker)
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: Item-granted by the Enchanted Nipple Ring of the Superior Fire Demon's Hand Maiden — "User may cast Bitch, What? Once a day"
  • Type: Berserking spell + partial invulnerability
  • Target: Self only
  • Cost: Item-based (no mana)
  • Duration: 20 seconds
  • Cooldown: Once every 30 hours
  • System's internal name: Fire Berserker

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Bitch, What?

Type: Berserking Spell + partial invulnerability.

Target: Self only. Cost: Item based.

Duration: twenty seconds. Cooldown: Once every 30 hours.

Effect: You ever seen an angry, on-fire weasel tossed into a room full of chickens?

The nipple ring is unambiguously a good item and Mordecai says so, but the granted spell is the one thing he stops Carl to talk about before Donut equips it. He and Carl have both seen the state before without realising it:

"I have, and so have you. Remember that rage elemental? They're perpetually in that state. It's actually called Fire Berserker. They've been changing the names a lot more than usual."

A Rage Elemental is, mechanically, a creature permanently locked in this spell. That is the reference point for what twenty seconds of it looks like.

His one instruction is the important one: "Donut, only cast it when you're by yourself." The combination of berserk state and partial invulnerability means she will attack whatever is nearest and cannot reliably be stopped, while being hard to stop safely.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: No level. The three numbers — 20-second duration, 30-hour cooldown, once a day — are fixed by the item, and the spell has no training path. The 30-hour cooldown is deliberately longer than a day, so it cannot be reliably banked against a daily schedule.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text:
Carl uses this spell as his own benchmark for danger. On receiving Self-Immolation from Emberus, his immediate assessment is: "Yikes. That was just like Donut's Bitch, What? berserking spell. It was something I wouldn't be able to cast with anybody nearby." Both are extremely powerful, once-per-cycle, self-targeted fire effects that are functionally unusable in a party formation.

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Black Nimbus
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Carl
  • Obtained: Granted by the Enchanted Nipple Ring of the Defiler
  • Type: Involuntary Abjuration
  • Cost: Item-based (no mana)
  • Cooldown: Once every hour
  • Target: Single target
  • Duration: Instantaneous cast; the target suffers the effect for (30 + [Caster's Intelligence + Constitution] − [Target's Intelligence / 2]) seconds

docs.title: Effect
docs.text:
Has the same effect as wearing a shirt for the band Cattle Decapitation to church. Instantly removes target from the blessing of their deity and all associated buffs and effects. Will make it so target is unable to physically enter church or temple while the spell is in effect. Higher levels of this spell increase the possibility of forcing a smite upon the target.

Warning! You probably don't want to cast this on members of the same religion more than two or three times in a row.

Three distinct effects, then: strip the deity's blessing and every buff riding on it; lock the target out of temples for the duration; and — at higher spell levels — a growing chance of calling down a smite on them outright. The closing warning is unexplained, but the implication is that repeatedly defiling the same faith draws that faith's attention back to the caster.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: The duration formula is the only hard number: it scales up with the caster's Intelligence + Constitution and down with half the target's Intelligence, meaning it holds far longer on a brute than on a mage. The smite chance is stated to rise with spell level, but no per-level table is given, and Carl never trains it.

docs.title: Notable Use — Ogun's Judgement (Chapter 17)
docs.text:
Carl's only on-page cast is a rescue attempt that fails in an instructive way. After the party repairs Yemaya's shrine instead of Ogun's, the level-250 god Ogun arrives in person to punish his two worshippers, Paz and Anton. Carl reasons that if Black Nimbus temporarily removes all the benefits of worshipping a god, it might also remove Anton from the god's reach — but he can only cast it on one of the two men, and casting anything at all risks drawing the god's eye. He describes the odds as "like trying to stop a train by stepping in front of it."

He casts it on Anton anyway, following with two Heal scrolls. Ogun notices, and corrects him without much anger:

"Black Nimbus," the god said. He sounded more curious than angry. "That was a good attempt. But all you have done is removed this man from my protection. From my mercy. Not from my wrath."

The spell does exactly what it says on the label. It severs the connection to the deity — which also severs whatever mercy that deity might have extended.

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Book of Rhymes
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Sister Ines Quiteria, Cat Girl Poet Laureate
  • Type: Bard skill
  • Level: 15
  • Source: Her patron, the Nebulars — newly granted during Floor 8
  • Effect: Enhances her other bard spells

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Book of Rhymes is a force multiplier rather than a spell in its own right. Sister Ines receives it from her patron partway through the floor, at level 15, and its entire function is to make the rest of her bard kit hit harder.

Most bards operate on the patron system rather than the cleric/deity system — a patron supplies money, spells, and equipment in exchange for entertainment, and unlike a god, a patron cannot smite you. Doctor Bones explains the arrangement to Carl in almost exactly those terms. Ines's patrons are the Nebulars, who are also her sponsors, and they invest in her heavily: they fund both this skill and the push that takes Word Weaver to level 15.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
The one on-page application is decisive. Per the broadcast recap:

"...crawler Sister Ines Quiteria used her level-15 Book of Rhymes bard skill, which she just got from her patron, to enhance her Word Weaver spell to charm this creature, a level-125 city boss."

Without Book of Rhymes, Word Weaver does not reach a level-125 city boss. With it, Ines charms the Madre de Aguas and inherits its regional control over every creature in the area — the single most consequential act by any non-party crawler in the book, and the chain of events that eventually drags a prince of Sheol onto Floor 8.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: No per-level detail is given; the skill is granted at 15, the maximum standard level, and is only ever seen operating there. What the book does establish is that the enhancement applies to her bard spells generally, not to Word Weaver alone — Ines is also a cleric-style support caster, buffing allies and throwing afflictions, and Carl notes she "mostly fought like Imani did."

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Word Weaver — the spell it boosts

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Brain Freeze
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: Granted automatically with her Floor 8 Character Actor class, Master Telephone Psychic
  • Starting level: 8 — unusually high for a newly-granted spell
  • Type: Single-target debuff + damage-over-time
  • Effect: Drains Intelligence, lowers resistances, and drains health

docs.title: Effect
docs.text:
Brain Freeze is the single-target sibling of Bad Attitude. Mordecai explains both in the same breath, immediately after Donut lists her new class spells in chat:

"Bad Attitude is similar to Carl's Fear spell, but it'll be a lot more potent in your hands. If you work it together, it'll be a great combo. Fear tends to affect dexterity while Bad Attitude drains intelligence and lowers resistances. Brain Freeze does the same thing, but it targets only one mob and drains health. It also makes them temporarily blind if you can get it up to 10."

So: the same Intelligence drain and resistance reduction as Bad Attitude, narrowed to one target, with health drain added on top.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
Level Behaviour 8 (starting level) Intelligence drain, resistance reduction, health drain on a single target 10 Additionally inflicts temporary blindness

Donut reports that it "started at level 8," and Mordecai's response is immediate: "Good. You'll want to train that one." The two-level gap to the blindness threshold makes this the class spell he wants prioritised.

docs.title: Notable Use
docs.text: Against Raul, the 150-Intelligence ninja crab, during the ambush on the moving truck: Carl drops a Fear-inducing smoke curtain into the cargo hold while Donut — still dangling from a rope — casts "her health-draining, resistance-lowering Brain Freeze" on him. The crab starts whimpering and scrambling backwards with his health already at half. Raul is subsequently recruited as one of Donut's totems.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Bad Attitude — the mass-target version
  • Fear — Carl's Dexterity-affecting debuff, designed to stack with these

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Clockwork Triplicate
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: From the mailbox spellbook-of-the-month club, on Floor 3
  • Mana cost: 26 points per cast
  • Type: Illusion / decoy summon (pets and minions only)

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: Creates two duplicate copies of a bonded pet or minion (Donut first tests it on Mongo). The duplicates are physically real for the duration — they can move independently, have their own apparent "minds," and can absorb hits — but are revealed as clockwork constructs (gears, servos, electric parts) when the spell ends, disintegrating in a puff of smoke.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: At level 1 (its level when learned), the duplicates last about one minute. No further scaling data given yet in Book 2.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Can only be cast on pets/minions, not on Donut or Carl themselves ("no clockwork Carl")
  • Expensive relative to Donut's early mana pool (26 of a ~29-point pool)
  • Doesn't appear to gain experience/level up while cast inside a Safe Room

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text: First used for training/entertainment with Mongo, then used tactically in the fight against Signet's mold lions — Donut reanimates two lions with Second Chance and casts Clockwork Triplicate on one of the undead minions to multiply the party's numbers mid-fight.

docs.title: Notable Use — Book 3
docs.text: Reused on Hekla's own reanimated corpse immediately after her death, tripling the body into three to stall the rest of Brynhild's Daughters while Carl and Katia loot the remains — see Second Chance.

docs.title: Notable Use — Book 5
docs.text: Donut casts Clockwork Triplicate on the mercenary cretin Sledge to create decoy duplicates during a saferoom teleport-trap ambush, successfully fooling both Lucia Mar and the hunter Vrah's allies into attacking the wrong target — one clockwork double is teleported directly into the midst of the hunters and detonates, the other draws Lucia's attack away from the real party. She also magically charms and re-classifies Queen Imogen's cat familiar, Ferdinand, as her own minion, specifically to make him eligible for this spell in the future.

docs.title: Notable Uses — Book 8
docs.text:
Reused twice during the Floor 10 vehicle race, both times to extend a Second Chance reanimation past its timer rather than for combat decoys:

  • On the reanimated toad corpse Olga, mid-race, to buy roughly twenty more minutes of a driver before the original timed out: "I'm going to cast Clockwork Triplicate before it times out."
  • On Mongo, mid-fight against the ambushing Shadow Mimics at the Desperado Club, creating two duplicates as Donut flips clear of a grab.

The Olga use directly echoes the Book 3 Second-Chance-into-Clockwork-Triplicate combo on Hekla's own corpse — the same pairing of spells, a different corpse, and a race-logistics problem standing in for a combat stall.

Sourced from Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario, Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook, Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade, and Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Conscript
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Doctor Bones, the skin-skellie bard and Desperado Club strip-show announcer, hired into Carl's mercenary barracks after Astrid's death
  • Type: Military charm
  • Effect: Forces the target to fight on the caster's side
  • Duration: "If they're weak, it pretty much lasts forever" — permanent on the weak-minded, shorter or ineffective on stronger subjects
  • Limitation: Does not work on anyone already pledged to a specific army

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Carl catches Doctor Bones practising "that mind control thing" in the mercenary arcade and asks what it is. The skeleton's answer is matter-of-fact: "It's a type of military charm. It only works on the weak minded. That is why I am training with it." He is deliberately honing it upward so it will hold against stronger subjects.

Asked how it compares to Donut's Minion Army, Doctor Bones draws the line cleanly: Minion Army is battlefield sabotage — effective, but slow to cast and temporary. Conscript is neither. It is slow to train and hard to land, but when it lands on the right target it simply never wears off.

docs.title: Why It Matters: Faction Wars
docs.text:
Carl's reaction to hearing the name is "a sudden sense of revulsion," because he already knows the spell from the Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook. This is the spell used against crawlers on the ninth floor:

It was used quite a bit against crawlers on the ninth floor. It wouldn't work if they'd already pledged themselves to a specific army. Most factions spent a lot of resources making sure they had somebody who could cast that spell at level-15. Part of the reason why we bought the Faction Wars team was to negate their ability to basically enslave crawlers to their cause.

That last clause retroactively explains one of the book's biggest expenditures. Buying the Princess Posse's own Faction Wars team slot was never only about getting a seat at the table — a crawler pledged to a faction is immune to Conscript, so owning a team is the only reliable defence against the other nine factions simply charming the remaining crawlers into their own armies.

docs.title: Carl's Sluggalo Infantry
docs.text:
Having learned what the spell does, Carl immediately turns it around. He locks Doctor Bones and the "strippers" — the Club Vanquisher dancers hired as mercenaries — into the mercenary arcade together and has the bard Conscript a squad of slug mobs born inside the arcade, building an infantry force of roughly forty hatchet-wielding sluggalos out of nothing. He buys the five-million-gold barracks upgrade (20 → 100 slots) to hold as many of them as possible.

His own assessment of what he's bought is not flattering:

The Conscript spell is far from perfect. It makes them fight on our side, sort of. It doesn't really change their attitude, and they can be rebellious. It's kinda like turning them into totems. We'll probably have to kill the highest level ones, but the rest are going into our infantry.

This is borne out at the FOCSA tower, where the entire sluggalo squad ignores the plan, screams "Chop, chop, bitches!" and charges a mass of demons unprompted, then routs and runs back into the city. Carl notes one thing the cookbook authors before him — including Priestly — apparently never knew: during an actual Faction Wars, a warlord can open the warlord menu and force conscripted troops back into line, which would have prevented exactly that.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: No numeric formula. Level matters in two stated ways: factions invest heavily in having a level-15 caster, which is treated as the practical ceiling; and the target's mental strength sets whether the effect is permanent, temporary, or fails outright. Doctor Bones' training is aimed squarely at raising the tier of subject he can hold.

docs.title: Book 7: Level 18, and It Works on Gods
docs.text: Book 6 set Conscript up as the reason Carl had to buy a Faction Wars team at all. Book 7 makes it one of the central plot mechanisms of Floor 9 — and blows past the level-15 ceiling the previous book treated as the limit.

docs.title: The ordinary spell on Floor 9
docs.text:
Faction Wars conscription in practice, as Book 7 documents it:

  • Any crawler not already recruited when the ceasefire ends is vulnerable (ch. 1)
  • The effect is control, not loyalty: conscripts "wouldn't be able to attack officers directly. We could force them to follow orders. We would get a notification if they ran away" (ch. 27)
  • Conscripted crawlers show as a light blue glow on the map (ch. 68)
  • Refusing to fight while conscripted inflicts "a nasty, no-healing debuff" — Tuba nearly bleeds out from it (ch. 68)
  • Carl knows workarounds: "The Conscription spell was far from perfect, and I knew of several tricks one could employ to hinder an army's efforts even with the debuff active" (ch. 58)
  • The war mages break their own allegiance with "a clever combination of Pull spells" to kill Prince Stalwart (ch. 63)
  • Non-combatants — King Rust's harem, for instance — cannot be conscripted at all (ch. 82)

The one hard personal defence Carl has is Mind Balance, from his Enchanted Toe Ring of the Well-Balanced: "Mind Balance, Level 5. Allows protection from Enslavement and Conscription."

A Faction Wars ruling in chapter 68 also extends the spell to a new claimant:

"Action item two. 'The War Mage Rebellion be given full access to the Conscription spell and all its benefits.' … This request has been granted. The Conscription spell will now allow unaffiliated players to be conscripted into the War Mage Rebellion."

docs.title: The Hell-Kissed Potion, level 18
docs.text:
The escalation arrives as a potion, not a spell, and it is the only verbatim description Book 7 gives for anything in this family. See Hell-Kissed Potion of Conscription for the full item page.

Hell-Kissed Potion of Conscription, level 18.

This works like a regular potion of Conscription, but it has been hell-kissed. At level 18, it will work against pretty much any non-affiliated entities, regardless of their protections, including most deities. Most. It was brewed in the dark recesses of the Nothing by Krakaren Prime, who is said to yearn for domination, which was why she'd been banished there in the first place. She prepares for a war she considers inevitable. There's an irony that the in-dungeon version of Krakaren has supplied these potions to the War Mages…

Conscription potions only work on the 9th, 12th, 15th, 17th, and 18th floors.

Baroness Victory's read on the risk, which is the reason this is not simply a free win:

"They're using potions, not the spell. They'll have to be hell-kissed versions. Those will be level 18. But, it also means using the potion is likely suicide for the caster if the level disparity is too high."

docs.title: Three gods conscripted
docs.text:
Deity Chapter By whom Outcome Yarilo 69 An unnamed war mage Worked — and "the moment he cast the spell, the war mage guy just blew up!" Lucia Mar 71 Carl, smashing the potion against her head Worked. Under Orders appears over her; she is physically prevented from attacking him Harpocrates 72 Li Na Worked, and she survived. "Warlord Message: Harpocrates has been successfully conscripted. Harpocrates, level 250 is now a member of the Princess Posse."

Carl gets his potion because Li Na duplicated the one looted from the war mage who attacked Harpocrates, using Li Jun's scroll of potion duplication. She used the original herself.

Carl's read on Lucia afterward: "There were ways to break conscription, as the war mages figured out, but it was all but impossible during the first few days. Especially with this version of the Conscription spell." And the hard limit: "The conscription only lasts until the end of this floor."

Chapter 74 shows the strain — Li Na is "literally riding Harpocrates like he was a mount… the god was clearly enraged by this, but so far the conscription held" — and the practical constraint: "I think Harpocrates is fighting the Conscription, so we need to do this now… he's harder to control when I'm not near him."

Exact-verification note

Book 7 contains no system description block for the Conscript spell itself. The level-18 potion's description is the only quoted text. The spell's own rules in Book 7 are reconstructed from scattered prose.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:

  • Mind Balance — the personal counter
  • Enchanted Toe Ring of the Well-Balanced

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride and Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Entourage
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: Book 5, Chapter 1 — granted automatically as part of her starting kit the moment she picks Legendary Diva as her Character Actor floor specialty in the Floor 6 class-selection room (see Standing Ovation for the acquisition scene)
  • Class requirement: Legendary Diva (Bard floor specialty, Floor 6)
  • Type: Illusion / decoy

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: Creates multiple illusionary duplicates of a target — Donut initially only ever manages a single, semi-transparent duplicate of Carl when singing off-key, but a full, in-key cast produces several solid-seeming copies at once.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: Casting quality is tied directly to whether Donut holds pitch: an out-of-tune, low-monotone cast produces one weak, visibly fake duplicate; a properly sung cast produces multiple convincing ones.

docs.title: Role in the Story — Book 5
docs.text:
Donut's first successful full-power cast comes mid-battle against Lucia Mar: she overlays herself onto the middle of five simultaneous illusionary copies lining a burning treehouse wall, then stacks an invisibility potion and a Hole spell cast under her own feet on top of it in the same instant — so when Cici the rottweiler lunges and bites down on the "middle" illusion, her jaws close on nothing, and the real Donut has already dropped straight through the floor to the ground below, unseen. (It's the same single Hole, not a second cast, that finishes the job moments later: when Cici sticks her head down through that hole hunting for Donut, Donut simply snaps the still-active spell shut from below, decapitating the dog.)

Sourced from Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: Fear
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Carl
  • Obtained: Granted automatically by the Compensated Anarchist class on Floor 3
  • Mana cost: 3 points per cast
  • Type: Debuff / crowd control

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: Casts a fear effect on a target, intended to make it flee or falter. Mordecai advises Carl to use it in nearly every fight once he obtains it.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
Confirmed, in-order data points from across the series:

Level Book / ch. What's confirmed ~1 (just granted) Book 2, ch. 11 3 mana per cast; simple flee-or-falter effect 3 Book 2, ch. 12 Trained up via the "Panic" play; text states the dexterity debuff on a mob that stands its ground "was lowered by an increasing amount each level" — a confirmed per-level scaling formula for the dexterity debuff, though no exact number is ever given 5 (stated threshold) Book 2, ch. 12 Same passage: "at level five, it would work on groups of mobs" — a forward-looking statement about an area effect unlocking at 5 5 (plateau) Book 5, ch. 4 Confirmed stalled at level 5 "despite constantly using it," going into the Floor 6 Magic Workshop training push 10 Book 5, ch. 8 "Your Fear spell has been upgraded five levels! It is now level 10!" — a flat +5 correction from a Platinum Asshole's Box, explicitly framed by the system as fixing an undertrained stat rather than a bonus. At 10: 2% paralyze chance, wide-area casting instead of single-target, and it can now be imbued into smoke curtains/explosives (risking "Dud" status on the item) 11 Book 6, ch. 42 "I cast Fear, zeroing out my mana points to cast the level-11 spell at full strength" — confirms level 11 by this point in Book 6, and reveals a separate mana-intensity dial: spending more than the 3-mana base apparently casts a stronger version ("full strength"). No formula or exact mana-to-power ratio is given — this is the only data point for that mechanic

Unresolved discrepancy in the text

Book 2 ties the area/group effect to level 5 ("at level five, it would work on groups of mobs"), but the level-10 upgrade in Book 5 is the point where Carl actually gains "wide area" casting on-page. The book never reconciles this — it's possible the level-5 line was Carl's own expectation rather than a confirmed mechanic, since he never demonstrates a group-cast at level 5. Both quotes are reported here rather than silently picking one.

No level-15 mention and no indication Fear was ever trained past 15 or hit a stated cap.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
Explicitly does not work on high-tier or "scary-ass" mobs — confirmed when Carl tries to cast it on the boss-tier monster Terror the Clown and receives an on-screen warning that such mobs are immune to Fear effects entirely.

Sourced from Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario, Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade, and Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Fireball
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: Granted by the Enchanted Obsidian Bracelet of the Raggle Rouser, looted on Floor 6
  • Cooldown: Once every twenty minutes (an item-granted limitation, not an innate spell cooldown)
  • Type: Area fire damage

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: Launches a beachball-sized, slow-moving orb of fire that explodes on impact, igniting the target and anything flammable nearby. Explicitly an outdoor spell — Mordecai warns against casting it in enclosed spaces.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: Granted at a flat level 10 by the bracelet; no independent training or leveling shown.

docs.title: Role in the Story — Book 5
docs.text:
Donut's first cast finishes off the rooted-in-place Eryops boss Claude Sludgington the Fourth, punching a hole clean through its stomach and setting the wound alight — an accidental demonstration of the spell's power that also nearly gets Carl killed moments later, when the Protective Shell holding the flaming, bent-back trees in place finally collapses and springs the dying boss's body back down at him. She casts it again indoors, cornered inside Lucia Mar's treehouse pub, blasting Lucia into the back wall and setting the whole pub ablaze — almost certainly the source of a "Did-You-Really-Just-Cast-Fireball-in-a-Room-This-Small" achievement box Donut mentions receiving, prompting Mordecai's irritated aside ("We still need to have a discussion about that"); Carl and Donut go on to watch this exact fight play out on a recap broadcast shortly afterward, which is also where Mordecai separately warns that Fireball is "an outdoor spell" — well after the fact, since Donut had already cast it indoors twice by then.

She separately kills a dryad mayor with a Fireball to the back while conquering a village, accidentally setting the pub behind him ablaze and burning half the town. She is not shown casting it again at the Butcher's Masquerade — Katia's own scouting report on Queen Imogen specifically notes nobody hits her with a fireball, since Imogen can reflect magical fire back at the caster.

Sourced from Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: Gloom Wraith Phase
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • User: Carl
  • Type: Technically a skill, but it costs mana — the description says so explicitly
  • Obtained: Chapter 4, from a Hell-Kissed Celestial Skill Potion of the Prince of Woe
  • Level: 13 on acquisition
  • Cost: Each burst halves the user's current mana. Minimum 2 mana to initiate
  • Effect: A non-corporeal lunge that passes through unenchanted matter and "scrambles" unarmored flesh
  • Notable kill: Architect Houston (chapter 68)

Carl's third Celestial item, per Kevin the announcer, after the Scavenger's Daughter and ahead of the Hairbrush of the Beefmaster.

docs.title: The Potion
docs.text:
Hell-Kissed Celestial Skill Potion of the Prince of Woe.

In case you haven't figured this out yet, we're trying to kick things up a notch this year. If we're gonna do this, we want all of you fuckers as deadly as possible. Hence, this prize.

It's time to bring out your inner demon.

Drinking this potion will give you a random level 10 to 15 Celestial-tier skill. The skill will be combat based, and it will be something you don't already have.

This skill potion is hell-kissed. That means this skill will be any combat-based skill from any Sheol-level mob level 200 or higher.

Go ahead and drink it. Do it. Do it.

After a flash-vision of Sheol and a demon-skull button:

You have gained a skill.

You have gained the level-13 ability, Gloom Wraith Phase.

docs.title: The Description
docs.text:
Gloom Wraith Phase.

This scary-ass skill allows for non-corporeal, intangible bursts of speed. You and all your equipped items become non-corporeal during a lunge attack, allowing you to pass through unenchanted weapons and flesh and obstacles with ease. Mirrors that of multiple phase skills and spells, effectively combining both Path of Destruction and Rush.

Upon activation, you become non-corporeal and rush forward. Any biological entity that is unarmored against non-corporeal attacks is... scrambled. Yeah. This is a good, gnarly spell. It's really fucking gross, but holy shit.

Note: While this is a skill, it still requires mana to utilize. Each burst will halve your mana points. You must have at least two mana points to initiate a burst.

At level 5, you have the option to designate a weapon or item that can remain corporeal as you rush forward.

At level 10, you have the option to remain non-corporeal up to five seconds at a time with a cooldown of thirty seconds between bursts.

At level 15, the cooldown lowers to six seconds between bursts.

Mordecai's reaction to Carl and Donut's chapter-4 haul, taken together: "You two are both some seriously scary bastards now."

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
Level Behavior 5 May designate one weapon or item to remain corporeal during the rush 10 May sustain the phased state for up to five seconds, with a 30-second cooldown 13 Carl's level on acquisition — he has the level-10 tier, not yet the level-15 cooldown 15 Cooldown drops to six seconds

The mana cost is unusual in that it is proportional rather than flat: each burst halves whatever mana is currently in the pool. A full bar buys many more bursts than the first one suggests, but the pool never quite empties and never quite refills between uses in a long fight.

Book 8 uses the skill twice more (chapters covering the Floor 10 race and the Floor 11 climax) with no new level, cooldown, or effect mentioned — Carl is never shown reaching level 15 with it on-page, and there's no record of it being trained past the cap the way Mind Balance was.

docs.title: The Shi Maria Problem
docs.text:
The skill's most consequential appearance in Book 7 is a use that never happens. Buried in Carl's suppressed notification spam, discovered in chapter 14:

Gloom Wraith Phase failed to activate. Mind Balance prevented activation.

Your attempt to disable Mind Balance was prevented by Mind Balance.

Your Mind Balance has risen to level nine.

There are hundreds of these entries. Shi Maria, sealed in the tattoo on Carl's chest, has been trying to cast his own skills without his permission, over and over, and Mind Balance — from the Enchanted Toe Ring of the Well-Balanced — has been silently stopping her every time. The specific attempt logged here would have killed the ogre Carl was fighting and set off his non-magical bombs in the process, which would have killed Donut.

docs.title: Speedster
docs.text:
Chapter 57 pairs the skill with the Speedster benefit from the Hairbrush of the Beefmaster, and the combination is better than either part:

And best of all, I could combine it with my Gloom Wraith Phase, allowing the distance I could travel while phased to be much further.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Chapter 14 — escaping a cloud attack
  • Chapter 15 — combined with Walk on Air: "I activated Walk on Air and rushed upward, like I was running up a set of stairs"
  • Chapter 68 — killing Architect Houston. "For my part, I activated Gloom Wraith Phase the very moment my feet touched the ground." The escape is messier than the kill: "I'd cast Gloom Wraith Phase to escape the room, but I'd hit something magical on the way out, which had injured me." The skill passes through unenchanted matter only, and enchanted obstacles hurt. "Either way, Architect Houston was dead. Burcu was dead. I'd barely escaped."
  • Chapter 71 — dodging the gale tower on the run to the Nest

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Mind Balance — the skill that keeps blocking it
  • Speedster — the range multiplier
  • Walk on Air — frequently chained with it
  • The Eye of the Bedlam Bride — the thing trying to cast it

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin and Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Graupel
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Elle McGibbons
  • Obtained: A loot box at the end of Floor 5, after the party's first fight with the Maestro in Grull form
  • Type: Outdoor-only war spell — a devastating hailstorm
  • Spell level: 5
  • Cooldown: One week
  • Casts before Book 6: One, used to defeat the air quadrant in their bubble on Floor 5

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: Graupel (the meteorological term for soft hail) pulls a sheet of fist-sized ice down out of the sky over a wide area in front of the caster. Mordecai had warned that it was a war spell, meant only to be cast outside, and the single Book 6 casting demonstrates why: the thunderclap knocks the whole party off their feet, steam and smoke swallow the street, black asphalt explodes under each impact, and the ground rumbles like an earthquake.

docs.title: The FOCSA Tower Cast (Chapter 65)
docs.text:
Elle uses it as a last resort against the demon horde massed outside the FOCSA building — grumbling, "This spell has a one week cooldown, but I guess I gotta use it now. Don't know if this is going to make things better or worse" — while Donut is still rooted four minutes deep into her own Minion Army cast.

It goes wrong immediately, in the party's favour. The blue glow around Elle keeps intensifying and she shouts a warning mid-cast: "Guys, it says it's casting more powerful than usual. Holy shit, head's up!" When the steam clears, the street is a field of mangled demon corpses as far as Carl can see, almost every red dot on his map has turned to an X, and Elle has gained six character levels in one go, settling at level 72.

Her own reaction is confusion, not triumph:

"What the hell? That spell is strong, but it's not usually that strong. It's only level five. It said it cast at level 16. I just got a bunch of achievements."

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
Level 5 is the spell's actual trained level; 16 is the effective level it inexplicably cast at. No per-level numbers are given, but the jump from "strong" to "wipes a street full of thousands of demons and awards six levels" gives a rough sense of the curve between the two.

Unexplained in the text

The book never explains the amplification. Samantha — herself glowing with the same bluish-white light — is asked directly and does not know, spinning in circles and talking to herself: "Elle is part earth, part water mage. She's on the four seasons path. I... but how did that happen? I am stronger too. I didn't do that. It's the tree, I think. Or maybe. It's all there. He's opening a path through the river, the water, and the tree, the earth. It's good she's not fire yet, but maybe the prince's spell enhanced her." She then snaps out of it and has no memory of having said any of it. Nothing in Book 6 confirms or resolves any of these guesses; Amayon's presence, the Havana setting, and Elle's elemental path are all raised and none is settled. Do not treat Samantha's mumbling as an answer.

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Heal Critter
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: Starting Bronze Pet Box, Book 1
  • Type: Single-target heal (pet-class targets only)

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: Heals a pet-class creature. Wastes itself with an on-screen error if cast with no valid pet target in range — a limitation discovered by Carl and Donut before Donut had actually bonded a pet of her own.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: No skill-level scaling described.

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text:
Becomes genuinely useful once Mongo joins the party — Donut uses it to stabilize him mid-fight after he's caught in the Over City's opening magical-mortar barrage on Floor 3.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised and Book 2: Carl's Doomsday Scenario.

docs.title: Hole
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Owner: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: Spellbook-of-the-month mailbox subscription, Book 3
  • Effect: Creates a temporary hole in a chosen surface
  • Duration: ~5 minutes at low levels; can be toggled off early at will

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Donut receives this spell via her recurring mailbox subscription and is initially unimpressed — she's outgrown Magic Missile and wants something flashier, like Fireball. Mordecai talks her into reading it anyway. Per his explanation: "It makes a temporary hole on a surface of her choosing. She'll need to level it up before it's too helpful, as a level one isn't thick enough to get through most doors, but it's a useful spell. Especially if you're creative with it."

Carl immediately sees the tactical potential, and the spell earns its keep — used to open shortcuts through non-reinforced doors, and, most memorably, to decapitate a war mage mid-battle (a clip the broadcast splices misleadingly to make Carl look unstable). It cannot be cast on Safe Room doors.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: Depth scales directly with skill level: a level 1 cast produces roughly a 1-inch-deep dimple; by level 2, it reaches about 2 inches deep (precisely 6 centimeters, or 3 cm/level — the dungeon uses metric internally), enough to punch through most non-reinforced doors. It does not work on mobs directly, but it does work on the ground beneath a mob standing on a surface.

docs.title: Book 5 Notable Uses
docs.text:
Donut opens a Hole directly under her own feet mid-battle against Lucia Mar's rottweiler Cici, using it to drop safely out of a burning treehouse pub — then snaps the hole shut the instant Cici follows her head-first through the gap, decapitating the dog outright. Later, at the Butcher's Masquerade, she casts a much deeper Hole through three stacked floors between the two identical "goodwill ballrooms" hosting hunters and crawlers, which is what actually causes Mongo to end up in the same physical (rather than illusory) room as the hunters' side, and which she uses again as a last-resort collapse plan ("Escape Plan C") to drop the whole party out of a sealed ballroom.

Sourced from Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook and Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: I Need My Personal Space
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Katia
  • Obtained: Granted by an Apothecary-sponsored knit beanie, given to Katia on Floor 6
  • Type: Area knockback

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: A violent, area-of-effect blow that knocks back everyone caught in it — allies and enemies alike, with no exceptions for party members.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: Not described.

docs.title: Role in the Story — Book 5
docs.text:
Katia never casts the spell herself in the text. She gives the beanie granting it away to Carl mid-battle at the Butcher's Masquerade so he can use its knockback to clear a path through the nymphs to Donut — leaving her own head bare. That turns out to matter far more than the spell itself: with no headgear occupying the slot, there's nothing to stop the reforming Crown of the Sepsis Whore from landing on Katia's head later in the same battle, after she kills Eva Sigrid. Carl uses the spell itself only once, clearing a knot of mantis nymphs off himself while fighting toward the goddess Diwata.

Sourced from Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: Laundry Day
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: A separate, ordinary spell gifted by Donut's Floor 6 "spellbook-of-the-floor club" — not part of her Legendary Diva bard kit, and not sung
  • Type: Armor-stripping debuff

docs.title: Effect
docs.text:
A spell that strips a target's equipped armor away. Its scaling thresholds are explicit:

Spell level Effect 5 Strips a target's chest armor 10 Strips a target's entire outfit 15 Can strip multiple targets at once

Crucially, when cast on a mortal host possessed by a god, the spell can treat the god's own presence/possession as the target's equipped "armor" rather than trying to strip gear off the god directly. Stripping actual equipment off the god itself would need the spell at level 20 (which Donut can never reach, capped at 15) and simply isn't feasible — but treating the god as the "armor" worn by the person underneath only requires the ordinary level-15 threshold for stripping a person's gear. That distinction is the whole trick: the level-15 cast leaves the god itself completely unharmed while banishing it from its host and exposing the now-unprotected mortal underneath.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: Donut trains the spell to level 9 on her own through Book 5, then uses a Pawna's Cries potion (+3 to a chosen spell) to push it to 12, and finally, during the climactic battle, a rarer Pawna's Tears potion (+5) to reach level 17 — overshooting the level 15 actually needed, following an explicit instruction from Carl's sponsor to use exactly this combination for a specific upcoming fight.

docs.title: Role in the Story — Book 5
docs.text: At the Butcher's Masquerade's climax, Donut casts Laundry Day (boosted to level 17) on the possessed form of Circe Took, who is wearing the goddess Diwata as a borrowed divine "armor." The spell strips Diwata's protection away from Circe's mortal mantis body without harming the goddess herself, forcing Diwata to return to the Halls of the Ascendency and exposing Circe to be killed moments later by her own children.

docs.title: Book 6: Half of "Phantasm"
docs.text:
By Floor 8 the spell sits at level 15 and acquires a permanent partner. The moment Donut reads the tome for Legionnaires of the Damned, Mordecai spots the combination: strip the armor off a group of mobs with Laundry Day, then reanimate that same armor with wailing spirits and set it on them — "they will tear through the unarmored monsters like wildfire."

Carl names the two-spell move Phantasm. Donut objects to the name every time he says it. Its signature use is the Asojano fight, where the "armor" stripped is a purpose-built Scrapheap Breastplate Carl assembled out of loose metal and trash-tier daggers and put on the cretin mercenary Bomo — engineering a room full of freshly-unequipped, individually-animatable pieces on demand.

A totem's version of the same effect appears later in the book: Jola the Yule Cat's Fashion Critic!, which explodes every item off a target at once. Carl's assessment is that it's "pretty much the same spell as Donut's Laundry Day except the cat was going to literally eat the clothes if we let him."

docs.title: Book 8: Ejecting the Maestro from Grull
docs.text:
Corrected — not Emberus

An earlier draft of this catalog's brief misremembered this scene as involving Emberus. It does not. The god possessed/ridden in this scene is Grull, and the possessing entity ejected is an orc called the Maestro — not a mortal wearing a god's power like Circe Took in Book 5, but the reverse: an orc apparently lodged inside the god's own chest.

Cornered by Grull mid-race on Floor 10, with the god about to kill the mantaur Corcunda for breaking faith, Donut casts Laundry Day directly on the god himself:

Grull raised his axe over his head. "I'm gonna enjoy this, Meat!" Bubbles started to form around his shoulders. "After all this time, and you're going to die like the little bitch that you . . . Gah!"

Donut finished casting Laundry Day.

The orc was ejected from the god's chest. He dropped like a rock into the river of metal below.

The Maestro can't be killed here — Floor 10's rules don't allow tourist deaths on this floor, so he simply regenerates a few minutes later, presumably back at Grull's own quarters. Grull himself is entirely unharmed and unslowed by the cast; the spell only strips the orc riding inside him, buying the party a brief window rather than ending the fight. This is functionally the same armor-vs-possession distinction established in Book 5 (stripping a god's presence from a host without harming the god) run in reverse — here it's the god's own body that gets something stripped out of it, rather than a mortal host losing a god's protection.

Sourced from Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade, Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride, and Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Legionnaires of the Damned
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: A Legendary De-Sleeving Box (awarded for what the party did to the goddess Diwata at the end of Floor 6), opened in the Floor 8 saferoom
  • Type: Summoning spell
  • Mana cost: 25
  • Duration: (spell level × 2 + Intelligence) seconds
  • Cooldown: One minute; only one active instance at a time
  • Target: Recently-unequipped armor or weapons only; total number of targets "varies based on multiple factors"

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The tome arrives chained shut, "squishy and warm," wriggling like a puppy and hopping on the table — Mordecai notes that "happens sometimes with the more powerful tomes. Especially summoning ones." It screams when Donut reads it.

The spell reanimates physical weapons and armor pieces with "an undead, wailing spirit plucked straight from the river of falling souls," turning each piece into a temporary minion of the caster. The system's own description spirals off into an unnerving aside before catching itself:

There are a lot of angry souls out there. Like, a lot. It's said if one has the ability to actually see all the wailing souls that filter through the edges of our world, one would go quite insane.

(The AI gave an unsettling giggle.)

Quite, quite insane, actually. All that death, spiraling down, down, down into the drain. Where do they go? Why are they always screaming?

In practice a purple rent tears open in midair and dozens of shrieking white ghosts pour out, flowing down into whatever loose metal is lying on the floor.

docs.title: The Catch
docs.text:
Two hard limits shape every use:

  1. The gear must have been recently equipped on a combatant or a corpse — friend or foe doesn't matter, but a pile of loose inventory items won't work. Carl's original plan to simply dump a mountain of scrap on the ground and animate it is killed by this rule.
  2. The gear is usually destroyed. "In most cases, armor and weapons utilized with this spell will disintegrate upon the completion of this spell." Cursed and enchanted items "may react in an unpredictable manner" instead.

docs.title: "Phantasm" — the Laundry Day Combo
docs.text:
Mordecai spots the combination the moment Donut reads the tome. With Laundry Day now at level 15, she can strip the armor off a whole group of mobs and then animate that same armor against them: "they will tear through the unarmored monsters like wildfire." Carl names the two-spell move Phantasm; Donut objects to the name every single time he calls it.

Carl then builds a delivery system for it. Rather than relying on enemies to be wearing armor, he sews dozens of individual metal chunks and trash-tier daggers onto a fabric undershirt at his armorer's table — the game registers the result as a "Scrapheap Breastplate" — and repeats the process for arms, legs, and the rest of the outfit. He puts the whole getup on Bomo, the cretin mercenary bodyguard, who is big enough to carry it.

Against the orisha boss Asojano in the ruined temple, Donut casts Laundry Day on Bomo; the armor detonates off him "like a fragmenting grenade," filling the room with dozens of separate, legally-recently-equipped metal pieces (one of which lodges in Carl's arm). Legionnaires of the Damned then animates all of them at once. Carl calls it an exploit and isn't sure the showrunners will let it stand, but it works — and because the animating spirits are non-corporeal, the swarm hurts non-corporeal monsters even though none of the individual pieces are enchanted. The reanimated daggers also do the fight's decisive non-combat work, cooperating to carry a floating skull gem across the temple to Yemaya's shrine.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
Duration is explicitly level-scaled: (spell level × 2 + Intelligence) seconds, so the spell gets meaningfully longer both as Donut trains it and as her Intelligence climbs. The strength of the summoned "symbiotes" and the number of targets allowed both "vary based on multiple factors" that the book never spells out. Mordecai's framing is that the spell is only as good as the caster's ability to produce loose, recently-worn gear — which is what makes the Laundry Day pairing the real unlock.

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Li Na's Dreads
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • User: Li Na
  • Type: Dreads — hostile auras, activated at will
  • The four: Dark Purpose, Defile Soul, Bleeding Horror, Succulent Decay
  • Why they matter: Dreads are not classified as offensive magic, so they remain legal during the Ramp-Up phase's magic restrictions (see the Mechanics pages for the Faction Wars Ramp-Up rules)
  • Delivered by: The clocktower Extend Aura synergy tower, plus Mistress Tiatha's wire hack
  • Result: All four trained to or near level 15 in the course of a single assault

Exact-verification note

None of the four has a system description block. Defile Soul and Succulent Decay have no described mechanics at all — they are named and nothing more. Everything below is prose, party chat, and observed effect.

docs.title: Auras, Blessings and Dreads
docs.text:
Book 7 formalises a mechanic the series had only gestured at. Carl's own summary:

The aura mechanic wasn't normally something I needed to worry about. We only had two crawlers in the guild who used it. One was Imani, who had a wide variety of aura effects imparted by touching her wings. Some were persistent, and she couldn't turn them off. The other aura effects, like some of her more specialized healing and protection spells, were called Blessings, and they could be turned on at will. Blessings drained her mana while they were active.

The other crawler who used auras was Li Na.

Hers were very, very different.

The ones she could activate at will were called Dreads.

The counter exists too — Mordecai brews a potion that produces:

You have been Closed Off! You are no longer susceptible to aura effects, both Blessings and Dreads. This will not cancel existing effects nor will it negate your own auras.

That potion is also what finally makes Li Na recruitable: without it, her own party could not stand near her.

docs.title: The Legality Loophole
docs.text:
This is the whole reason the Dreads matter strategically. During the Faction Wars Ramp-Up phase, offensive magic is banned. Dreads are auras.

Best of all, dreads didn't count as offensive magic.

The delivery mechanism is a second exploit stacked on the first. The clocktower's Extend Aura synergy — "one of the few synergy towers that could be used during the offensive magic ban" — is combined with Mistress Tiatha's wire hack: dozens of wires dangling from the clock arms, run into Club Vanquisher as an improvised antenna. Anyone within about 20 meters of the wires catches the aura.

Li Na's Dreads normally have almost no reach — Dark Purpose only affects someone physically touching her. The tower and the wires turn a contact-range debuff into building-wide saturation.

docs.title: Dark Purpose
docs.text:
The one they chose, and by a wide margin the one the book actually shows.

When we'd first discussed this next part of the plan, Li Na stated she had several dreads that would be effective if they were allowed to fill Club Vanquisher.

We settled on one called Dark Purpose.

Normally, this was a fairly small-area aura, and it would only affect someone if they were physically touching Li Na. Now, with the tower mixed with Tiatha's wire hack, anyone within about 20 meters of the wires would get hit with the effect.

Mordecai said he'd never even heard of this particular dread. According to Li Na, it was basically the same thing as Donut's Why Are You Hitting Yourself? The feeling normally only lasted a moment, but it accelerated the longer one was touching Li Na. But because we were using the wires to amplify the signal, it would be almost impossible to escape.

Li Na's own comparison undersells it badly. Carl's verdict once it is running: "This was not the same thing as Why Are You Hitting Yourself? This wasn't even close."

What it does. After roughly a minute's delay, everyone in range begins destroying themselves. Mork the ram pulls out his own eyes and reinserts them backward. A mantaur stabs himself in the throat. Hundreds of taxidermied trophy heads and the rugs on the walls come alive and scream. Mork then tries to rip out his own heart.

Then the part that makes it a dread rather than a charm: ethereal white chains rise out of the floor and drag the ghosts of the dead down through it.

Warning: This area of Club Vanquisher has been defiled.

The club's own PA system responds with what amounts to a demonic-incursion alarm:

"Shelter in place! Shelter in place! Demonic activity has been detected within the club! Security to the lobby! All hands! All hands! Implement Aura protections before you venture out!"

docs.title: Training on the Job
docs.text:
The assault doubles as a training montage. Li Na cycles Dreads deliberately, burning each one up the level track and moving to the next:

Li Na: Dark Purpose was level 4 when I cast. It is not meant to be used like this, and it leveled even more rapidly than we anticipated. It hit level 15, and I moved to a different dread. I am cycling my dreads and rapidly leveling them all. Right now I am using Defile Soul. Next I will train Bleeding Horror.

Level 4 to 15, in a single engagement, on an aura that normally requires skin contact to work at all.

docs.title: Defile Soul
docs.text: Named, activated in sequence after Dark Purpose hits 15, and never described. Contextually it is what is running during and after the ghost-chain sequence, and the "This area of Club Vanquisher has been defiled" warning may relate to it rather than to Dark Purpose — the text does not say which.

docs.title: Bleeding Horror
docs.text:
Li Na's own explanation, chapter 52 — and note she has never made it work before:

Li Na: I've never gotten it to work before, but if someone with bloody hands gets near me, and I have the dread active, it's supposed to turn their blood against them. And then the blood would turn on my enemies. I've never gotten it past level two because they're usually dead within moments of coming near me. It takes a lot of mana.

Li Na: … When mantaurs extend their claws, they bleed. That should be enough when the dread trains high enough. It is already level 5 and rising. You are marked as an ally. The blood won't hurt you, but if the new guards have aura protection, this will be better because the blood already under my control will still attack them.

That last clause is the tactical point: blood already under her control keeps fighting even against targets who are warded against auras. It routes around the counter.

Observed: a ram's own blood swirls "like liquid mercury" and pours into his mouth and nostrils, and "what appeared to be a sentient pool of blood rushed across the wall" — Prepotente jars a sample.

Naming inconsistency

The text calls this "Bleeding Horror" when Li Na announces her training plan and "Blood Horror" in her later message reporting it at level 15. Both refer to the same dread.

docs.title: Succulent Decay
docs.text:
The fourth and last, activated in chapter 52:

Li Na: I am ready. My Blood Horror is now level 15. I am turning on the last of my dreads, and I do not know how it will react. It is called Succulent Decay.

Carl: Jesus. Okay.
