The Khepri temple door opens immediately afterward and the point of view moves inside. No effect is ever described. "I do not know how it will react" is the last word the book gives on it.

docs.title: Collateral
docs.text:
Dreads do not distinguish carefully between targets in a building. Chapter 57 records one casualty found afterward: "The bearded cleric within the temple had apparently boiled himself alive in his own stew, collateral damage from one of Li Na's dreads during the assault on Club Vanquisher."

There is also a downstream consequence for loot. In chapter 58 Li Na is offered the Necklace of Indelible Woe and turns it down "especially now that she had several level-15 dreads that she could possibly lose if she used the necklace." Having four maxed Dreads makes any spell-swapping item too dangerous to touch.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
No per-level tables. What the book establishes:

  • Dark Purpose — effect "accelerates the longer one is touching" the caster; range is normally contact-only
  • Bleeding Horror — requires nearby bleeding targets to train at all, which is why it had been stuck at level 2 for Li Na's entire career; high mana cost
  • All four trained from low levels to 15 (or near it) inside one extended engagement, because the tower let them run continuously against a full building

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Why Are You Hitting Yourself? — Li Na's own comparison, and an understatement
  • Profane Iron — her chain skill, lent to Carl as a tattoo
  • Necklace of Indelible Woe — declined because of these

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Magic Missile
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: Self-taught from a Tome of Magic Missile in her starting Silver Adventurer Box
  • Mana cost: Flat 5 mana per cast early on; from skill level 5 onward, scalable 3–6 points per cast depending on chosen "power"
  • Type: Ranged single-target damage

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: Magic Missile fires as a visible bolt ("laser blasts," in Carl's words) from Donut's eyes.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: Spell skill level Behavior 1–4 Flat 5-mana cast, fixed damage, no choice in power 5+ Caster can choose a "power" from 3–6 mana per cast, trading efficiency for damage — a 6-power cast can vaporize a mid-tier single target outright (drops a level-2 Troglodyte Pygmy in one hit), while a 3-power cast only handles weaker mobs 8 (reached by end of Book 1) Combined with Intelligence climbing from 11 to 20+ (which governs mana pool size), lets Donut fire many casts before needing a Mana Potion

docs.title: Progression Through Book 1
docs.text:
• First cast: kills nothing, alerts a Bad Llama on the first floor
  • Used as the party's primary ranged damage source throughout — softening bosses (the Juicer, Krakaren clones) before Carl closes in for melee

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Mana regenerates slowly (roughly 1 point/minute for Donut early on) and potions have a punishing ~2-minute cooldown between uses, so Magic Missile runs dry fast in extended encounters — a recurring tactical problem the duo has to plan around
  • Donut is reluctant to rely on melee (calling it "inelegant"), so running out of mana mid-fight is a recurring moment of real danger, not just inconvenience

docs.title: Notable Use — Book 3
docs.text: Donut's Prism Industries Capacitating and Focusing Goggles let her fire multiple full-power Magic Missile bolts at once — a "Double Shot" headshots two Jikininki ghouls simultaneously in one encounter — and separately let her store a full-power charge in the goggles for later release as its own "double shot," used against a (fully awake) province boss during a cart-lift ambush. Earlier in the book, an accidental Magic Missile meant for a group of ghouls instead hits Katia — friendly fire that becomes tangled up in Hekla's manipulation of Katia shortly before Hekla's death.

docs.title: Book 4: Glass Cannon
docs.text: On Floor 5, Mordecai steers Donut toward Glass Cannon as her Character Actor "floor specialty" class specifically because it sharply increases spell training speed and power across the board. The choice is confirmed accurate in play: her Magic Missile is repeatedly described as noticeably stronger for the rest of the floor, and the same boost supercharges her other spells — most visibly Second Chance, whose range and duration both roughly double for the floor. The one cost is that Donut never receives Glass Cannon's usual +15 Constitution bonus, leaving her exact mechanical downside somewhat unclear even after the floor ends.

docs.title: Book 5 Notes
docs.text: Donut continues relying on Magic Missile as her core damage spell through Floor 6's hunter war, training it toward level 12 by the book's end; a full-powered cast is enough to stagger even a level-70+ hunter elite (Vrah) mid-fight. Carl deliberately holds off giving Donut the Pawna's Cries potion boost meant for her Laundry Day spell instead, planning to let Magic Missile top off naturally once it hits level 12.

docs.title: Book 6: Reclassified as a Fire Spell
docs.text:
Conflict resolved

This page previously carried a note claiming that a new Book 6 class grants Donut Fireball and Wall of Fire alongside Magic Missile, which conflicted with Book 4 (where she already casts Wall of Fire twice with no indication it's new). That note was wrong. No class is involved.

The actual text is Mordecai speaking in chapter 2, right after the AI reads out the description of Donut's new Enchanted Nipple Ring of the Superior Fire Demon's Hand Maiden:

"Donut, only cast it when you're by yourself. You have three fire spells now. Fireball, Magic Missile, and Wall of Fire. All three of them are going to be much more intense. So, be very careful."

He is listing spells Donut already has and explaining that a new item will amplify all three. The ring's relevant line is: "All spells with a fire attack now deal (Intelligence)% more damage." It empowers; it teaches nothing. (The "only cast it when you're by yourself" warning attaches to the ring's separate Bitch, What? berserking spell.)

The one piece of genuinely new information in the exchange is the classification: this is the first time Magic Missile is stated to be a fire spell, which means Donut's whole Intelligence-stacking build now feeds her core damage spell twice over — once through mana pool and once through the ring's percentage bonus. She continues to use it as her primary ranged attack throughout Floor 8, frequently paired with Mute ("Here we go. Mute first, then Magic Missile").

docs.title: Book 7: Level 16, and It Now Vaporizes People
docs.text:
The "advanced targeting" comes from a third tiara, the Tiara of a Thousand Lights — the targeting itself doesn't originate with the tiara, though; it's absorbed into it from the Targeting skill on a boonie hat that ships with Donut's new Deathbed Hellcat class.

The payoff line, chapter 61:

It was Donut casting Magic Missile. With her tiara's advanced targeting skills and Donut's elevated position, along with her Deathbed Hellcat class, she could hit anything she could see with any of her long-range spells.

Floor 9 is where Magic Missile stops being a workhorse and becomes an execution tool. Three things stack in the same book:

  1. Range. The Deathbed Hellcat class quadruples the range of all Donut's existing spells before anything else is applied. The boonie hat's Targeting skill adds more range on top, and also lets her zoom in and examine targets at distance. Absorbed into the tiara, that becomes permanent and hat-independent.
  2. Level. The spell reaches 15 by chapter 74 — "My Magic Missile is level 15 now… It tripled in power!"
  3. Brain Trust. Donut takes the Brain Trust natural benefit when her Intelligence tops 100, which makes every spell she casts operate one full level above its trained level. Magic Missile therefore fires at an effective level 16 — a number the series had previously treated as effectively unreachable.

The result, chapter 80:

This was the effect of Donut's Brain Trust upgrade. It made all spells operate at one full level higher than before. Not a huge deal, except her Magic Missile was now 15, meaning she was firing these things at level 16. Apparently that evaporated the targets completely.

A Reaver sentry dog hit with one "literally evaporated, having been turned into a rapidly expanding group of atoms."

There is also a tactical cost attached to the tiara that carries it: it glitters so brightly that by chapter 73 it "glowed like a lighthouse beacon," advertising the exact position of Donut's head from the top of a sniper tower. Carl hates it. Donut loves it.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Tiara of a Thousand Lights — the source of the targeting
  • Targeting — the absorbed skill itself
  • Brain Trust — the +1 effective level

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised, Book 4: The Gate of the Feral Gods, Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride, and Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Minion Army
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Tome owner: Princess Donut — obtained Book 1, first successfully cast in Book 6
  • Obtained: Silver Beguiler Box (reward for charming the goblins during the meth-war setup)
  • Mana cost: 50
  • Type: Battlefield sabotage — turns a percentage of an enemy force against its own side
  • Casting time: Five minutes base (four with Donut's Charisma boosts); caster is Rooted in Place and visibly glowing the entire time

docs.title: Effect
docs.text:
Per the Book 1 text: "caused hostile enemies to fight for you instead of against you." Doctor Bones, the skeleton bard who casts the related spell Conscript, gives the sharper Book 6 definition: "Minion Army is a battlefield sabotage spell, and it's quite effective, but it has a long casting time, and it is temporary."

It only works on intelligent mobs. It does not recruit an army so much as poison one: a percentage of the enemies inside the casting area simply turn on their comrades.

docs.title: Book 1: Out of Reach
docs.text: Donut's mana pool never reaches 50 during Book 1 (she peaks in the 20s–30s), so the tome sits unread for most of the book. The attempt reveals a rule that holds across the series: a crawler cannot self-teach a spell from a tome unless they already have enough mana to cast it. Donut tries anyway with 24 mana and the system simply refuses. Carl reassures her they'll either trade it for something more immediately useful or hold onto it until she can actually cast it.

docs.title: Books 1–5: Learned, Never Cast
docs.text: Donut does eventually learn the spell, but it goes uncast for five books — not for lack of mana but because of what casting costs. The spell is "designed for war," and the caster is frozen, glowing, and completely defenseless for four straight minutes. There is almost never a moment in a dungeon crawl where that trade is survivable. As late as Book 6's midpoint Carl still describes it to Doctor Bones as the spell "she hasn't tried yet."

docs.title: Book 6: The First Cast (Chapter 65)
docs.text:
The FOCSA tower assault in Havana is the first situation that actually fits the spell. Thousands of demon zombies are massed in the street between the party and the building, and most of them are standing frozen and unaware.

Donut positions herself at the edge of an alley inside the basket of a taxi bike, low enough that only her eyes show — invisibility is useless because the spell makes her glow regardless. Elle raises the obvious objection ("You said it only works on intelligent mobs, and zombies ain't too smart") and Carl answers: "It's demon zombies. They're intelligent."

The numbers are stated plainly. The spell is only level one. At that level it turns two percent of the enemies in the casting area against their comrades. With both Imani and Samantha enhancing it, that two percent should rise to about five percent. Carl thinks that sounds far too low; Mordecai and Doctor Bones both insist it will create utter chaos. Donut's Charisma is high enough that she can select the entire mass outside — "Even some of the birds!" — and it trims the cast from five minutes to four.

The result is muddied by luck rather than by the spell: while Donut is still rooted, Elle's Graupel misfires upward into level 16 and annihilates most of the ground force before Minion Army even lands. Donut's immediate reaction is outrage ("Wait, so I cast that giant spell for nothing? Elle, you stole my experience!"). It isn't wasted — her casting area had included the lower edge of the demon-bird tornado circling the tower, which the hail never reached, and those birds and bats spend the next stretch of the fight tearing each other apart and raining corpses into the street while Donut collects the experience for every one that dies.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: The only hard datapoint is the level-1 baseline: 2% of enemies in the area, roughly 5% with two spell-enhancers stacked on the caster. No per-level table is given. Area size is governed by the caster's Charisma — Donut's is high enough at level 57 to blanket a street full of thousands of demons plus part of an aerial formation, and she specifically laments not still having her Charisma-doubling tiara from the previous floor. Casting time also shortens with Charisma (five minutes → four).

docs.title: Future Enhancements
docs.text:
Open — Books 7+

The spell finally works, at level 1, in a set-piece designed for it. Whether Donut trains it higher, and what 2% becomes at level 10 or 15, is not established in Book 6.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised and Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Mute
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: The floor-8 spellbook delivery, waiting in the guild mailbox at the start of the floor (Donut is furious that only one spellbook arrived — the Floor 7 delivery was forfeited when the party skipped that floor)
  • Type: Anti-caster interrupt
  • Effect: Stops a target from casting spells

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Donut's first reaction to the spellbook is "That sounds boring." Mordecai's is immediate and flat: "Good. That's on our list. You can stop monsters from casting spells. Learn it and practice it." He is right and she is wrong — Mute becomes one of the two or three most-used spells in the book.

Mechanically it is a slow-moving yellow bolt that has to physically travel to the target and disappear into them, which means it can be dodged, beaten by a faster cast, or simply arrive too late. The effect lasts roughly a minute against ordinary mobs, but Carl notes it "would only last a handful of seconds" against a boss-tier monster.

docs.title: Notable Uses
docs.text:
• Practice on Floor 8's ghommids — the very first outing, alongside Why Are You Hitting Yourself?, while the party is still learning what Donut's new class gave her
  • The Asojano fight — the whole plan depends on Donut holding Mute in reserve so the orisha can't inflict the party with disease. It half-works: Asojano gets a shield up before she can stop him the first time, but her second cast lands and kills a spell mid-formation
  • Raul the crab — Hole drops him into a truck's cargo hold and Mute lands as Donut jumps, shutting down a 150-Intelligence caster before he can retaliate. Carl's chat plan for that whole sequence is simply: "Here we go. Mute first, then Magic Missile."
  • As the thing Carl misses most — planning the Astrid assassination inside Club Vanquisher without Donut, Carl's chat message lists everything that makes the target dangerous and then ends: "It's too bad we can't get Donut to help with the fight. Her new Mute spell would really come in handy."

The spell is also shown in enemy hands: during a card battle the crawler Zeynep casts Mute on her own teammate to stop him attacking Carl with a spell.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
No numeric formula is given on-page. What the book does establish is that duration scales inversely with target power — roughly a minute on ordinary mobs, "a handful of seconds" on a boss — so the spell stays useful at high level only as a timed interrupt, not as a lockout.

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Oozy Form
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Carl
  • Obtained: Chapter 7, from a spellbook delivered via the safe room mailbox — a "special edition" that Mordecai says trains faster than normal
  • Type: Slime/ooze transformation — travel, escape, and camouflage
  • Comparable to: Phase, and to Donut's Smoke Form (her own Assassin of Sekhmet-class equivalent)

docs.title: Acquisition
docs.text:
The spellbook arrives already animated, oozing and scurrying like an escaped rat before the safe room's cleaner bot catches it and drops it in Carl's arms:

"What the hell?" I said, holding it out. I examined it. "It's a spell book called Oozy Form."

Mordecai's summary on the spot:

"It's a great spell... It's a special edition, so it'll train faster, too. You can do all sorts of things with it. You can slip between cracks. Turn into a puddle on the floor. It's great as a defensive and camouflage spell. But it's kinda like Phase, too. Just make sure you're someplace safe when it runs out. At level 15, you can stay in the form indefinitely, but before then, be careful."

Donut is offered the same spell in the same delivery and declines it outright ("That is absolutely disgusting, and I am never going to use it"), instead relying on her own class-granted Smoke Form for the same travel/camouflage niche.

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: Transforms the caster into a mobile slime/ooze form capable of squeezing through gaps and cracks too small for a normal body, and of lying flat and unnoticed as a puddle. It functions as a Phase-style escape and infiltration tool rather than an attack spell.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
Level Effect Below 15 Time-limited; the caster must return to a safe location before the form expires, or risk being caught mid-transformation 15 Duration becomes indefinite — the caster can remain in Oozy Form for as long as they like

The book doesn't give Carl's actual skill level at any point it's used, so it isn't established whether he's reached the level-15 threshold by the time of his Book 8 uses below. Mordecai's "special edition, so it'll train faster" line is the only stated modifier to its leveling speed, and no number is ever attached to how much faster — no formula, just the claim. There's no mention anywhere of Oozy Form being trained past 15; level 15 here is a stated cap on the spell's own downside (indefinite duration), not the wiki's separate skill-training cap discussed elsewhere.

docs.title: Notable Uses — Book 8
docs.text:
Chapter 10 — sharing the effect. Discussing a baby-backpack item for carrying the pig Penelope, Carl notes the harness lets a passenger share his phase effects: "If I wear it with you buckled in, I can use my Phase or Oozy spell, and you'll Phase, too." This is confirmed in practice at the Floor 11 climax below, where Penelope rides through Scolopendra's body with him.

First use — planting the bomb (ch. ~76). Carl uses Oozy Form for the first time to slip, unnoticed, into Jasha and Radoslav's cul-de-sac while Samantha distracts the two bugbears, so he can swap one of their beer cans for a duplicate hiding a fail-safe explosive. The bomb is what later kills them both, deliberately, to save Prepotente — see Jasha and Radoslav for that outcome.

We'd had Samantha roll into the cul-de-sac earlier and distract the two bugbears while I used my Oozy Form spell for the first time.

Entering Scolopendra's own body (Floor 11 climax). With Emberus and Taranis both drawn into the arena and Club Scolopendra sitting inside the Dungeon Boss's own physical form, Carl casts Oozy Form to slime his way through Scolopendra's interior — organs, tissue, and all — toward the club entrance, carrying the pig Penelope along as a passenger via her oxygen-ring "carrier":

"Hang on," I called as I cast Oozy Form.

Splatch!

I'd only done this once, and the sensation wasn't like anything I'd ever experienced. I lost my eyes and my ears, and my vision was suddenly all around, and I could see perfectly in the dark... I aimed for the building wall and slimed my way toward it, pushing through and around and over strange, giant, pulsing organs.

This is the clearest demonstration of the spell's range: full darkvision while transformed, and enough structural integrity to travel through a living dungeon boss's tissue under a hard countdown (Scolopendra's third nine-tier attack) without being digested or dissolved.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• The Eye of the Bedlam Bride — used moments later in the same infiltration
  • Scolopendra — the dungeon boss Carl slimes his way through
  • Jasha and Radoslav — the outcome of the spell's first use

Sourced from Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Ping
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Carl
  • Obtained: Book 4 — a platinum quest box tome, awarded after saving Hump Town from the Wasteland's bombardment
  • Mana cost: 5 mana per cast
  • Type: Detection/hunting utility, not offensive

docs.title: Effect
docs.text:
Also nicknamed "Here piggy, piggy" or "The Night Dread," Ping sends out an audible pulse that reveals the distance and location of every non-crawler, non-red-tagged mob in range — including targets outside the caster's normal minimap radius. Anyone hit by the ping hears an audible noise but can't tell where it came from.

"Sends out an audible ping that gives the distance and location of all non-crawlers and non-red-tagged mobs in a circle around you. It will mark targets beyond the range of your map."

The spell is popular among the elven gunnery officers of a faction called the Dream, and — per the tome's own description — is dreaded by anyone hiding in a trench, since it reveals their position without ever revealing the caster's.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
• Range: 1 kilometer around the caster, plus 500 meters for every 10 points of Intelligence (environmental factors and obstacles can increase or decrease this) — confirmed again in Book 5, ch. 22: "My Ping spell had a reach of one kilometer plus 500 meters for every ten points of intelligence." Book 6, ch. 4 reconfirms the resulting range as "a little more than three kilometers" by that point, consistent with the same Intelligence-scaling formula, though Carl notes city terrain (tall buildings) shrinks the effective range in practice
  • Duration: Instantaneous; the pulse travels at the speed of sound
  • Cooldown: 5 minutes (confirmed again Book 5, ch. 32: "I cursed myself for having wasted my Ping spell when the map was down. It had a five-minute cooldown.")
  • At skill level 5+, the caster may imbue the ping with Fear — per the tome's own text at acquisition; Carl explicitly plans around this threshold in Book 5, ch. 8 ("Once I trained it up to five, I'd be able to combine the two spells"), tracking Ping at only level two at that point. No later book states the moment he actually crosses level 5

No formula or number is ever given for how Ping's effective radius scales with its own skill level (as opposed to Intelligence) — every range figure on record traces back to the Intelligence formula above, not to a stated per-level bonus.

The spell explicitly does not work on mobs or crawlers, making it most useful against NPCs — Carl notes it's primarily intended for locating elites and hunters on Floors 6 and 9, rather than anything on Floor 5 itself.

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text: Carl receives the tome as part of a Book-4 platinum quest box and picks it up specifically with Floor 6's hunting grounds in mind, anticipating the wave of bounty hunters he expects after publicly declaring war on them at the end of the floor.

docs.title: Book 5: In Regular Use
docs.text: Carl casts Ping extensively on Floor 6 exactly as anticipated — locating hidden hunters, confirming a stuck bounty hunter's exact position in a tree, and coordinating multiple raid-and-ambush operations against Zockau's satellite towns. He also discovers a countermeasure: casting a Major Charlie ("Brain Juice") intelligence potion beforehand temporarily extends Ping's range to a full three kilometers, at the cost of a subsequent five-minute Intelligence penalty once the potion wears off. The spell fails entirely at least once when an unrelated magical dampening field blankets an entire village, confirming it can be blocked by area effects.

docs.title: Book 6 and Beyond
docs.text:
Ping stays in regular rotation through Floor 8 (Book 6), used the same way — locating NPCs and checking whether an area is clear — but with no further mechanical changes shown. By Book 7, the spell has spread beyond Carl entirely: Florin describes staffing border towers with "a group of four or five folks with proper observation and Ping spells" as a standard Faction Wars scouting tactic, confirming it is a known, teachable spell rather than something unique to him. Carl's own Floor 9 hunting plans for it, floated when he first obtained the tome in Book 4, are never shown paying off on-page in the specific way he originally anticipated.

Sourced from Book 4: The Gate of the Feral Gods, Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade, Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride, and Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Profane Iron
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Original owner: Li Na
  • Borrowed by: Carl, via a chain-shaped dragon tattoo on his right forearm, inked by Katia in chapter 40
  • Level: 13
  • Frequency: Once a day
  • Effect: A dozen-plus prehensile chains erupt from the user's own flesh
  • Classified as: A defensive skill. Nobody uses it that way

Exact-verification note

No system description block exists for this ability in Book 7. The narration of its one use, quoted in full below, is the only description the book gives.

docs.title: Acquisition
docs.text:
Profane Iron is the first ability transferred by the toraline ink tattoo system, and the transfer that establishes its rules. Li Na gives blood freely, which makes the copy temporary and costs her only a reversible five levels:

"She says it didn't hurt at all. It's not permanent, unlike what happened with her brother. She lost five levels temporarily, but she can still use it. Intention matters."

Because the source ability is level 13, the tattoo has to be large: "Since this is a level-13 skill, it has to be pretty big. I have to use almost all the ink in the vial, otherwise you won't get it at full strength." Carl picks the design himself — "It has to be a chain. A chain shaped like a dragon" — and the system grades Katia's first-ever tattoo as expert quality, the second-highest rating available.

Donut, following by Voodoo book, is unimpressed: "You're starting to look like one of those white rapper doodle notebook guys, Carl. And it's a little crooked!"

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text:
Carl activates it exactly once, in chapter 55, in a corridor full of mantaurs:

I pulled two more Black Nimbus potions as I activated the skill I'd received from Li Na.

Profane Iron.

I felt my own skin tear as dozens of chains ripped from my flesh. I took a tiny bit of a hit to my own health. Two of the chains reached down and plucked the potions from my hands. Each one shot out in a different direction and smashed into a different mantaur… A third chain wrapped around the neck of another, and a fourth tripped two more. Two more struck, scorpion-like at the closest, piercing directly into the guard's flesh at his clavicles…

The fight is over in seconds, which is fortunate, because the skill does not last long. The comparison against the original owner is the useful part:

Li Na had several chain spells and skills, and this was different from her regular ones. This was a once-a-day, multiple chains at once skill. I could only do it for about thirty seconds. She said she could now do it for about a minute and a half. I could only truly control two of the chains. She could control ten. She used it to attack multiple enemies at once, but it was actually designed as a defensive skill, like a type of shield.

That paragraph is the clearest statement in the series of what a borrowed ability actually costs. Carl has the same skill at the same level and gets roughly a third of the duration and a fifth of the control. The chains all appear; only two of them do what he tells them to. The rest thrash.

It also damages the user on activation — the chains tear out through his own skin — which is a small health hit but a permanent feature of the ability, not a side effect of borrowing it.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: No per-level table is given, and the spell is never mentioned again after chapter 55 — including no appearance anywhere in Book 8. What the text establishes is that level is not the whole story: at identical level 13, the owner and the borrower get materially different results in duration and number of controllable chains. Practised familiarity, not skill level, is the variable, and there's no stated formula connecting level to either duration or chain-count — just the one paired data point (Carl vs. Li Na, both level 13) above. No level-15 cast or cap-break is recorded for this skill.

docs.title: Intended Use vs. Actual Use
docs.text: The last line of Carl's assessment — "it was actually designed as a defensive skill, like a type of shield" — is worth holding onto. Li Na uses it offensively. Carl uses it offensively. Nobody in the book uses it as a shield. The original plan for the tattoo, before events overtook it in chapter 55, was explicitly offensive too: "to activate Li Na's tattoo skill—which I still hadn't used—to kill all the nagas."

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• The Toraline Ink Tattoo System — how it was transferred
  • Enchanted Prison Tattoo Kit
  • Li Na's Dreads — her other signature abilities

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Protective Shell
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Carl
  • Granted by: Enchanted BigBoi Boxers (item-based spell — see item page)
  • Mana cost: None — item-based, but has a 30-hour cooldown once the underlying item is unequipped or used
  • Effect radius: 3-meter sphere centered on the caster's right hand, +50cm per point of Intelligence (4.5m for Carl at the time he first casts it)
  • Duration: 5 seconds + 1 second per spell level (20 seconds at first cast)

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: Protective Shell creates a static, glowing dome that blocks physical mob attacks and presence for its duration. Critically, the dome does not move with the caster once cast — it remains fixed in space, filling the area it was cast in "floor to ceiling" regardless of what happens around it. It offers no protection against magic or non-corporeal attacks.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
The Enchanted BigBoi Boxers grant a fixed level-15 cast of this spell — Carl doesn't level it up independently, since it's tied to the item rather than his own spell list. At that fixed level:

  • Duration: 5 seconds base + 1 second per spell level = 20 seconds (matches the level-15 grant exactly)
  • Radius: 3-meter base sphere + 50cm per point of Intelligence — 4.5m for Carl at the time he first casts it

Since the level is locked to the item, any future growth in this spell's effect would only come from Carl's Intelligence stat increasing the radius, not from the duration or a higher cast level.

docs.title: The Rage Elemental Save
docs.text: This spell is the reason Carl survives the level-93 Rage Elemental's first charge in Book 1. Cast in a corridor at the exact moment the elemental attacks, the dome physically repels the creature — its claws bounce off even though its head can partially pass through. Mordecai notes he had the same spell during his own crawl and that it "saved him more than once," specifically because its static nature means a caster can use it to block a hallway or doorway rather than just personally shield themselves.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The long 30-hour cooldown makes it a true last-resort, one-per-crisis tool, not a repeatable defense — this cooldown directly forces Carl to improvise an entirely different (and much riskier) plan to permanently deal with the Rage Elemental rather than simply waiting to recast it
  • Because the dome is static rather than caster-following, timing and positioning are everything — cast too early or in the wrong spot, and it does nothing

docs.title: Future Enhancements
docs.text:
Book 5, ch. 32 confirms the mechanic that makes future growth possible after all: the Nest's tier-four combined training room lets Carl train item-granted spells directly, and doing so upgrades the underlying item itself rather than a separate spell-list entry:

"My regular spells were listed as trainable along with spells associated with equipment, like my Protective Shell. Apparently, if I upgraded the spell in the training room, the associated armor — my boxer shorts in the case of Protective Shell — the equipment itself would actually be what got upgraded."

This directly supersedes the Book 1-era assumption that only Intelligence could grow the spell's radius. That said, Carl never actually spends training time on it — the one scene that reveals the mechanic has him pick trap-table and explosives training instead, and every later confirmation of the spell's level (see Scaling above) still shows a flat 15. Donut's Book 7 Size-Up scan of King Rust notes, in the same breath as spotting his Tripper, that "he has that same Protective Shell as you, but it's level 15!" — the same number Carl has had since Book 1, so the mechanic is confirmed to exist but is never shown being exercised on this particular spell.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised, Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook, Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade, and Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Puddle Jumper
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: Bronze Boss Box (reward from The Juicer)
  • Mana cost: 20
  • Cast delay / cooldown: 10-second delay, 5-hour cooldown between casts

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: Teleports Donut and up to three others to any location within her line of sight — per Mordecai, "especially useful if you come across rivers of lava or other impassable locations." Not viable as a combat spell given its 10-second delay, but valuable for utility and escape.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: Per Mordecai: "Higher levels of the spell allow her to go further. If she manages to hit level 15 with the spell, it works almost as well as Teleport" — one of the most powerful spells in the dungeon. The book doesn't give a level-by-distance formula beyond this benchmark.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text: The two biggest practical problems, per the text: the 5-hour cooldown (once cast, no second use for the rest of most encounters) and the 20-mana cost against Donut's small early mana pool, compounded by a punishing 2-minute cooldown between mana potions.

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text: Used both tactically (infiltrating the Rev-Up filling room via Plan Pied Piper) and as an emergency escape tool later in the book.

docs.title: Book 8: Level 17, Almost Any Distance
docs.text:
The Book 7 Cloak of the Benevolent Champion grants Donut a one-time bonus: one spell already raised to level 15 by the Cloak may be pushed to level 16. Facing a shortlist that includes Wall of Fire and Heal Critter, she picks Puddle Jumper:

"They already all activate at level 16 because of your Brain Trust skill," Mordecai said, sounding awed. "...Puddle Jumper at level 17... I don't know, Donut. I don't even know what level 16 of that spell can do."

"That's what I picked," she said... "Puddle Jumper. It's now officially level 16."

With Brain Trust adding its usual +1 to effective spell level, the true level-16 spell casts at an effective level 17 — one level past Mordecai's own original Book 1 benchmark ("if she manages to hit level 15... it works almost as well as Teleport").

Used twice at this level in Book 8: once mid-race to recover Donut and a knocked-out mantaur half-brother back to the truck, and once at the Floor 11 climax to escape Emberus's arena immediately after Carl renounces his god:

"Toodles," Donut said as she jumped to my shoulder and activated Puddle Jumper.

At level 17, the spell had the ability to return her to any place she'd recently visited at almost any distance. In this case, she took us outside to the entrance of the arena.

docs.title: Scaling — Book 8 Note
docs.text: At effective level 17, Puddle Jumper can return the caster (plus passengers) to any recently-visited location, at almost any distance — no longer limited to line-of-sight, and well past the level-15 "works almost as well as Teleport" benchmark Mordecai gave back in Book 1.

docs.title: Future Enhancements
docs.text:
Confirmed — Book 8

See above. The spell's Book 1 level-15 benchmark ("works almost as well as Teleport") is exceeded at the effective level 17 reached in Book 8.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised and Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Rolling Battle Formation
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Princess Donut
  • Type: Atrocity
  • Obtained: Absorbed from a defeated skunk battle-wizard's hat — "the stinky wizard hat"
  • Effect: Balls thousands of creatures, friend and foe alike, into a single enormous sphere that is immobile, invulnerable, and steerable by the caster
  • Duration: Until the ball sustains enough damage
  • First cast: Chapter 66, on the pile of mortals Eris had just teleported into one place

This is the spell that accidentally saves half the floor.

Exact-verification note

No system description block exists for this spell. Everything below comes from a mob entry, Donut's all-caps chat explanations, and other characters' observations.

docs.title: Origin of the Name
docs.text:
The spell is named after a mob the party fought earlier in the book, in the expanded map area — a skunk-themed riff on Book 1's Ball of Swine:

Rolling Battle Formation Ball. Level 70.

You don't want to get in this thing's way. It would really stink.

I hope you have some hydrogen peroxide, soap, and baking soda ready.

Carl notes it is not listed as a boss. Donut later acquires the spell from that creature's hat — presumably via her Tiara of a Thousand Lights charge pillow, though the text never says so explicitly.

docs.title: The Cast — Chapter 66
docs.text:
The setup is not Donut's doing. The goddess Eris has just cast Bear Witness / Bring Forth the Witnesses, freezing every mortal outdoors on Floor 9 and teleporting the lot of them into a single colossal pile as witnesses to her Ceremony of Chaos. Donut's intention is modest: move the pile away from a god fight.

System Message: Warlord Princess Donut has committed an atrocity.

Donut: WELL, I NEVER. THAT WAS VERY RUDE.

Carl: What was that?

Donut: IT'S A TWO-PART PLAN. FIRST I GOTTA MOVE THE PILE TO WHERE ALL THE DEAD BODIES ARE PILED. IT'LL GET THEM AWAY FROM THE GOD FIGHT, TOO.

What she has actually done takes a moment to register on everyone else:

Donut: MEATUS GOT PULLED IN, TOO! AND SINCE HE IS STILL WRAPPED AROUND ERIS, SHE'S ALSO PART OF IT! IT SAYS THE GODDESS IS UNCONSCIOUS!

Rosetta: Ball?

Mordecai: Donut, what the hell did you do?

Donut: ROLLING BATTLE FORMATION. I GOT THE SPELL FROM THAT SKUNK'S HAT! YOU KNOW, THE STINKY WIZARD HAT? IT'S AN ATROCITY SPELL, AND THE TOWER MAKES IT REALLY POWERFUL. I DIDN'T KNOW IT WAS GOING TO BE THAT POWERFUL! BUT I CAN TELL IT WHERE TO ROLL! I CAN DRIVE IT LIKE A REMOTE CONTROL. IT'S, UH, REALLY, REALLY, REALLY BIG.

Carl: How long does it last?

Donut: IT SAYS UNTIL IT SUSTAINS ENOUGH DAMAGE!

Mordecai: Wait, wait, wait. Are you telling me you just made a ball of swine, but out of everyone? Including two gods? There has to be tens of thousands of people in that thing! And the system just let you do it?

Donut: IN MY DEFENSE, I DIDN'T KNOW THE DINK WAS GOING TO BE SUCKED INTO THE SPELL, TOO. THE BACK END IS JUST SLOPPED OUT THE BACK LIKE THE BALL FORGOT TO ZIP UP.

Two gods — the feral god Meatus and the goddess Eris herself, wrapped up with him — are inside the ball. Eris is registered as unconscious.

docs.title: Mechanics, as Established in Play
docs.text:
Property Detail Targets Everyone in the area, indiscriminately. Friend, foe, NPC, deity State The contents are immobile and invulnerable for the spell's duration Control The caster steers the ball remotely — "I can drive it like a remote control" Duration Until the ball sustains enough damage to break Range Enormously extended by casting from an Atrocity-synergy tower (the Nest) Sound The ball screams; it is a mass of conscious, trapped people

The invulnerability clause turns out to matter more than anything else. Eris had granted her Witnesses invulnerability for the ceremony and then turned it off; Rosetta, chapter 68:

"She turned off her Witness spell and just removed everyone's invulnerability, but they're still invulnerable anyway. The Rolling Battle Formation spell keeps them immobile and invulnerable. But they'll be exposed the moment the ball breaks!"

Donut cast an atrocity to tidy up a pile and, in doing so, overrode a goddess's decision to leave tens of thousands of people to die. Carl's verdict is delivered to her in chapter 75:

"You saved them by casting the Battle Formation spell. If you hadn't done it, half of everyone would be dead by now."

docs.title: Aftermath
docs.text: The ball is a standing feature of the battlefield for roughly ten chapters, rolled around by Donut and swarmed on the outside by the fleshers from You're Not Done Yet. Carl uses Ping to locate Tagg and Fang inside it. When the ball finally breaks apart, the party has Bounce House pre-cast below the hole of Larracos to catch the falling crawlers. In chapter 82, once "the Battle Formation spell was dispelled," King Rust's harem women flee into the city.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: No level and no stated formula. The two real variables are how many bodies are in range and whether it is being cast from a synergy tower — and Donut's own testimony is that she badly misjudged the second one.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Bear Witness / Bring Forth the Witnesses — what made the pile
  • You're Not Done Yet — Donut's other Atrocity, cast onto the same field
  • War Crime — her third, and the one that ends the floor

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Run, Little Günter, Run
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Carl
  • Obtained: Chapter 40, from the Legendary 1914 box — the same box that gave Donut War Crime
  • Type: Special Edition spellbook — learned at level 5, trains faster than normal
  • Cost: Variable, minimum 20 mana
  • Cooldown: Once every ten hours
  • Effect: Summons a one-hit-point child-like creature who stores an attack and carries it to a target

The spell is a delivery system. Carl's own framing is that it is "like sending explosive robot spiders after Samantha on floor 6," except the spider is a small crying boy in lederhosen who runs away from you as fast as he can.

Like War Crime's tome, this book has the odd property of not registering on the map at all.

docs.title: The Description
docs.text:
Spellbook of Run, Little Günter, Run.

This spellbook is a Special Edition. This means you will learn this spell at level 5, and it will train up faster than usual.

Run, Little Günter, Run.

Cost: Variable. Minimum 20 mana.

Target: This is a summoning spell. It will summon a small, hominid creature named Little Günter. He will appear directly in front of caster.

Duration: Once activated, Little Günter will last 20 seconds plus one second per mana point added above the minimum. Higher spell levels decrease mana cost per second. You must activate Little Günter within 30 seconds of summoning him, otherwise he will dissipate.

Cooldown: You may cast this spell once every ten hours.

This spell summons a small, fat, child-like creature named Little Günter. Little Günter only has a single point of health and will remain in front of you until you cast a spell, use a skill, or otherwise attack him. Attacking Günter activates him. The effects of the attack will be temporarily "stored" until Günter times out. Once activated, Günter will run away from you as fast as he can.

If you designate a target, Günter will run toward your target. The stored attack will trigger once he reaches the target or times out.

If you do not designate a target, Günter will try to flee from you in a random direction.

Higher levels of this spell will decrease cooldown, increase Günter's speed, and lower the mana cost per second. At level 10, Günter can split into a second creature after activation. This second Günter can target another enemy. At level 15, Günter can split into five different Günters.

Warning: Once activated, Günter's constitution will increase to that of the caster. If a second attack kills Little Günter before he reaches his target or times out, he will immediately trigger the stored attack.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The sequence is: summon → hit him → he runs → the hit lands on someone else.

  1. Cast the spell. Günter appears directly in front of you and stands there.
  2. You have 30 seconds to activate him, or he dissipates.
  3. You activate him by attacking him. A spell, a skill, or a punch — whatever you hit him with is absorbed and held.
  4. Designate a target and he sprints toward it. Don't, and he flees in a random direction, which is a considerably worse outcome for everyone nearby.
  5. The stored attack fires when he reaches the target or when he times out, whichever comes first.

The warning clause is the tactical hinge in both directions. Günter starts with one hit point, which makes him trivially killable — but the moment he is activated his Constitution rises to match the caster's, so he becomes as durable as Carl. And if someone does manage to kill him early, the stored attack detonates immediately, wherever he happens to be standing.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
Level Behavior 5 Carl's starting level (Special Edition). One Günter 5+ Each level decreases cooldown, increases Günter's speed, and lowers mana cost per second 10 Günter can split into a second Günter after activation, targeting separately 15 Günter can split into five

Duration is bought with mana: 20 seconds base, plus one second per mana point above the 20-point minimum.

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
Carl immediately starts thinking about loading Günter with the Daughter's Kiss — a charged melee finisher delivered by a courier who cannot be reasoned with. Katia asks in chapter 40 whether Donut could store a trigger spell on him instead, which the description permits but the book never shows.

The spell is cast in chapter 54, as part of the Khepri temple assault at Club Vanquisher: "At the same moment, I cast Run, Little Günter, Run."

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• War Crime — Donut's book from the same 1914 box
  • Soul Reaper / The Daughter's Kiss — the payload Carl wants to use

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Second Chance
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: Mailed automatically via the "Dungeon Book of the Floor Club" (a perk from a Boss Box) upon reaching Floor 2
  • Mana cost: 10
  • School: Necromancy

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: Second Chance raises a dead monster to fight temporarily on the party's behalf.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
Spell skill level Duration Reanimation level cap 1 1 minute Target must be lower level than caster 3 3 minutes Target must be lower level than caster 5+ 10 minutes Can raise monsters up to 5 levels higher than caster

Reanimated mobs are tagged Undead Minion of Crawler [caster name] and appear as a distinct, lower-level version of the original creature. They follow simple verbal commands from the caster (e.g., "rip up the dead bodies of your friends" — used as a demonstration/intimidation tactic against a group of clurichauns).

docs.title: Donut's Reaction
docs.text: Donut finds the spell genuinely disturbing to use — despite loving showmanship, she's visibly repulsed by controlling a moaning, decaying corpse, and needs to be talked into casting it more than once. This is one of the few spells in her kit she doesn't enjoy showing off.

docs.title: Tactical Uses in Book 1
docs.text:
• Distraction/decoy: sending a reanimated clurichaun corpse to walk into a boss chamber holding a lit incendiary jug, drawing fire away from Carl and Donut
  • Free combat practice: Carl uses reanimated clurichauns as target practice for his slingshot training, since they pose minimal threat at level 1
  • Skill training synergy: raising Second Chance's level (to 5 by late Book 1) both extends minion duration and raises the level cap of what can be reanimated

docs.title: Notable Use — Book 3
docs.text: During the mid-battle death of Hekla, Donut casts Second Chance on Hekla's own corpse and immediately follows it with Clockwork Triplicate, tripling the reanimated body into three to hold off the rest of Brynhild's Daughters while Carl and Katia loot the remains — one of the spell's more tactically ruthless uses to date. She reuses the same Second Chance → Clockwork Triplicate combo later in the floor against exploded Krakaren clone corpses.

docs.title: Book 5 Notable Use
docs.text: Donut casts multiple Second Chance spells on the severed heads mounted on hunter Vrah's own carapace — trophies of fallen crawlers, including the archer Langley — reanimating them just long enough for them to bite down on Vrah's exposed neck in a coordinated distraction that lets Carl land a killing blow with a poisoned arrow.

docs.title: Future Enhancements
docs.text:
Confirmed — Book 4

In Book 4 (The Gate of the Feral Gods), the spell's normal level-10 caps (reanimate up to 10 levels above caster, for up to 15 minutes) are explicitly stated — and then her Glass Cannon class pushes them further: up to 20 levels above her own, for up to 30 minutes. Full detail to be filled in once Book 4 is processed.

docs.title: Book 8: Comedic Reuse — Reanimated Race Car Drivers
docs.text:
Donut spends much of the Floor 10 vehicle race keeping a rotating cast of corpses reanimated as temporary drivers, since neither she nor Carl can safely drive and steer at the same time during combat. At level 11 (level 12 with Brain Trust), each reanimation lasts up to fifteen minutes:

Donut's Second Chance spell was currently at level 11, which brought it up to level 12 with her Brain Trust skill. The spell brought the dead corpse back to life for a maximum of fifteen minutes.

Two corpses are used as drivers this way in the same race: Olga (a toad, head caved in, driven by shouted directions and eventually multiplied with Clockwork Triplicate to buy extra time), and Joel, a dead Bactrian camel too large for the driver's seat, wrangled into position by Carl physically pushing the seat back through the corpse's own chest cavity. Both are steered entirely by voice command while Carl and Donut fight off the track's mobs, continuing the same undead-chauffeur gag the spell has been good for since its first appearances.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised, Book 3: The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook, and Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Self-Immolation
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Carl
  • Obtained: Granted at the Devotee worship rank of Emberus, God of Sun and Ash (achievement "Baptism by Fire"), alongside upgraded Burn immunity and a tithe increase from 5% to 10%. Devotee is the highest rank Carl can reach, since he is neither a Cleric nor a Paladin
  • Granted at level 10
  • Cost: Nothing — but requires being in Emberus's good graces to cast
  • Target: Self only
  • Duration: Instantaneous; the fire burst lasts up to three seconds
  • Cooldown: Once a day, resetting with the obeisance countdown rather than from the moment of casting

docs.title: Effect
docs.text:
The spell wraps the caster in a non-static sphere of Sheol Fire with a one-foot buffer from every body part, so Carl himself is untouched. Everything else inside the sphere is not.

Casts a non-static sphere of Sheol Fire around the caster with a 1-foot buffer from all body parts of caster. Fire expands in a distance of .15 meters per level of spell until it reaches level 15, at which time the distance increases exponentially and may be controlled.

The system's explanation of Sheol Fire is one of the book's better warnings:

You know how when you were a kid, you'd take a lighter and pass your finger over the flame really fast, and it wouldn't hurt you? Don't try that with this stuff. It's fire with rabies. Wood turns instantly to ash. Rock to lava. Flesh... well. Just be careful. Or don't, if you're looking to go out with some char-scented gusto.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
Spell level Sphere radius Per level +0.15 m 10 (as granted) 1.5 m in every direction — "up, down, left, and right" 15 The per-level distance "increases exponentially" and becomes controllable

The downward expansion is the part Carl fixates on: at level 10 the sphere reaches 1.5 m below his feet as well, so casting it on solid ground leaves him standing in a pool of fresh lava. Level 15's controllable radius is what would make the spell safe to use near allies, and Carl never gets there in Book 6 — and Self-Immolation is never mentioned again in Book 7 or Book 8 (unsurprising, since Carl publicly renounces Emberus at the Floor 11 climax, which is presumably what ends his access to it). No level-15 cast, and no indication it was ever trained past the cap, appear anywhere in the series.

docs.title: The Cooldown Quirk
docs.text:
Carl flags the reset behaviour as unusual and useful: most of his spells (he compares it to Protective Shell) don't start their cooldown until they're cast, but Self-Immolation resets on the same daily cycle as the Emberus shrine and his obeisance countdown — generally around the daily recap episode. Cast it late in one cycle and early in the next and you effectively get two uses close together. See Deity worship for the obligations attached to the rank.

Carl's own summary when he reads it: "That was just like Donut's Bitch, What? berserking spell. It was something I wouldn't be able to cast with anybody nearby."

docs.title: The One Cast (Chapter 71)
docs.text:
He's right, and the single on-page use proves it — badly. During the Ysalte/Amayon climax, Shi Maria takes control of Carl's body while summoned as a totem. Needing extreme heat to brew tattoo ink on the spot, she rifles his magic menu, makes him warn everyone to step back ("I won't warn you again. Step back now."), and casts Self-Immolation with the party standing around him.

He snaps it off within a second. It is still enough to burn a hole clean through the floor and drop him into the apartment below, leaving the building melting around him. Donut's message arrives immediately: "CARL, YOU HURT MONGO AND KATIA!" Katia is "grievously injured"; Mongo loses his entire right wing and most of the scales and feathers down his right side. Both survive — one of the potions Shi Maria upgrades on her way out will regrow the wing — but Carl wakes up looking at the damage and thinking Oh no. I did that.

Sourced from Book 6: The Eye of the Bedlam Bride.

docs.title: Standing Ovation
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: Book 5, Chapter 1 — granted automatically as part of her starting kit the moment she picks Legendary Diva as her Character Actor floor specialty in the Floor 6 class-selection room; she announces the pick, and the songs it came with, over chat immediately afterward ("I SING SONGS AND THEY CAST SPELLS. I GOT A BUNCH OF THEM.")
  • Class requirement: Legendary Diva (Bard floor specialty, Floor 6)
  • Type: Buff song

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: A sung buff spell that grants nearby allies a Dexterity boost and makes the party's own regular spells more powerful. Like all of Donut's Legendary Diva songs, it requires the caster to sing "in key" to reliably take effect — failed or off-key casts simply don't work.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: Not described in detail; the were-castor Holger identifies it as a good beginner song to practice on.

docs.title: Role in the Story — Book 5
docs.text:
Donut attempts to cast Standing Ovation mid-combat against a pack of invisible night weasels, hoping to buff her were-castor allies Clint and Holger, but fails to hold pitch amid the chaos of battle — Holger gently tells her afterward that she needs vocal lessons or magical assistance before trying it again in combat. She later trains the spell using a hired vocal coach installed in the party's personal space.

Sourced from Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: Tome of Gatekeeper
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: Floor 11, from a loot box opened just before The Parade Begins countdown
  • Type: Advance Reader Copy — installable now, unusable until the 12th floor
  • Cost: 75 mana
  • Target: Any opponent, NPC, deity, or OI entity
  • Duration: (5 minutes + 1 minute per level of spell) × [caster's Intelligence / (target's Constitution + Charisma)]

docs.title: The Advance Reader Copy
docs.text:
Donut receives the spellbook as a paperback — unusual in itself, since it doesn't resemble any other spell book she's owned — with a cover illustration of a gate and an angry human woman standing in front of it. She hands it to Carl unread, unable to make sense of "the duration formula" in "nerd math." The book's own description opens with an explicit release-date restriction:

Tome of Gatekeeper.

This is an Advance Reader Copy. Street date: 12th floor.

Cost: 75 Mana.

Target: Any opponent or NPC or deity or OI entity.

Duration: (5 minutes + 1 minute per level of spell) × [Your Intelligence / (Target's Constitution + Charisma)]

The AI's voice narrates a lengthy, self-aware digression about "gatekeeping" in the internet sense before getting back to mechanics:

Anyway... this is an Advance Reader Copy. That means you can install the spell now, but it won't work until a specific floor. In this case, the 12th floor.

So the spell can be learned and installed in Book 8, but is confirmed unusable — not merely untrained, but flatly inert — until the party reaches Floor 12. This page documents it now, ahead of that floor, because it's acquired here; expect it to actually see use starting in Book 9's coverage of Floor 12.

docs.title: Effect
docs.text:
This spell removes the target's ability to use any skills or abilities associated with their class for a short period.

If this spell is cast on a deity, they will temporarily lose access to their Worshipper Base Associated skill and spell set. You probably don't know what that means yet. It's basically most of their spells and skills, but if it's a god made of lava, they'll probably still be able to fuck you up with lava. Get it? No? Don't worry, you'll figure it out.

The duration formula scales directly with the caster's Intelligence relative to the target's Constitution plus Charisma — meaning it hits weaker-willed, lower-Constitution targets far harder and longer than tough or charismatic ones, independent of the target's raw level or class.

docs.title: Targets: Deities, and "OI Units"
docs.text:
The spell's target line is unusual for a crawler-tier spell: it explicitly names deities as a valid target (stripping their class-based "Worshipper Base" kit, though not any innate elemental power — the lava-god caveat above), and a third category neither Carl nor Mordecai recognizes:

Carl: Mordecai, what's an OI unit?

Mordecai: In what context?

Carl: It's a spell target for Donut's Gatekeeper spell. It says opponents, deities, and OI units.

Mordecai: I have no clue.

"OI units" are not explained anywhere in Book 8. What they are is a Mechanics-pass topic; this page notes only that Tome of Gatekeeper works on them by name, alongside ordinary opponents/NPCs and deities.

docs.title: Setup for Floor 12
docs.text: Between the Advance Reader Copy's explicit 12th-floor lock and the spell's ability to strip a deity's class kit, Tome of Gatekeeper reads as direct, deliberate setup for the Celestial Ascendency fight the party is already bound for on Floor 12 (see The Celestial Ascendency for the general mechanic). A spell that can neutralize a god's or an OI unit's class-based kit for a duration the caster can stack Intelligence against is exactly the kind of tool a fight against ascending divine/OI contestants would call for — and the book is unusually explicit that it can't be used a single floor early.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Deity Mechanics — the general rules deities play by
  • The Celestial Ascendency — the Floor 12 event this spell is plainly built for

Sourced from Book 8: A Parade of Horribles.

docs.title: Torch
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: Bronze Boss Box (reward from The Hoarder)
  • Type: Utility — light source

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: Per Mordecai's description: "It makes a curl of light follow you around." Donut applies it to herself automatically without reading the description first, and is initially furious to have gotten "a stupid spell" instead of something flashier.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: Per Mordecai: "The more she uses it, the more powerful it'll become" — the book doesn't give an exact curve, but the spell is explicitly usage-based rather than tied to character level.

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text: Despite Donut's initial disdain, Torch proves genuinely useful — it lights the party's way through at least one pitch-black corridor without needing to carry a physical light source.

docs.title: Book 5: A Weapon
docs.text: Torch reaches skill level 13–14 by Floor 6, strong enough at full brightness to function as a genuine offensive tool: turned all the way up, it stuns vampire-infected creatures at full strength and sets their heads on fire outright, killing a vampiric pterodactyl-like Northropi boss alongside a fistfight from Carl. Donut also uses it at low, controlled settings to safely illuminate dark areas without alerting nearby vampiric wildlife.

docs.title: Future Enhancements
docs.text:
Not yet researched

Later books haven't been checked yet for whether this spell gets upgraded or replaced.

Sourced from Book 1: The Apocalypse Will Be Televised and Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade.

docs.title: Travel the Path and Welcome Home
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Type: Light-god worship spells — granted on worship, not learned from tomes
  • Available from: 6 of the roughly 15 light deities in the Ascendency pantheon grant Travel the Path; 4 of those 6 also grant Welcome Home
  • Travel the Path: Turn into light and travel an existing path at the speed of light for a few seconds. Not classified as teleportation by the system
  • Welcome Home: Once ever. Combined with Travel the Path, follow a Bijou fairy's worship tendril directly to the strongest connected temple
  • Why it matters: This pair is the mechanism behind the Sepsis Whore's legendary disappearing act

Exact-verification note

Neither spell has a system description block. Everything here comes from Carl's chapter-49 25th-Edition notes, which are the party's reconstruction of how the trick works.

docs.title: The Bijou Mechanic
docs.text:
Neither spell makes sense without the infrastructure they run on, and Book 7 explains that infrastructure for the first time.

When one worships a god, a link is formed between the adherent and the immortal. This link comes in the form of an actual, physical, whisker-thin connection made of invisible light. Light that can penetrate almost any substance or spell. After a new adherent pledges themselves, a tiny, non-corporeal fairy mob called a Bijou grabs a tendril of light from the god and drags it to the new worshiper and attaches it to the adherent's heart.

Here's the important part. This line isn't direct. It goes from the god to the strongest temple on the floor and from the temple to the worshiper. This whole process takes about two minutes. From the third floor until the 11th floor, the strongest temple will almost always be inside of Club Vanquisher.

When a person moves around, other tendrils also grow, connecting the adherent to other temples and in some cases, other worshipers. These connections, too, are facilitated by the Bijou fairies.

This strange, little quirk of the game usually has no impact on anything, and Rosetta seems to think it's actually some sort of workaround the original designers developed to add the whole deity aspect to the game. Nobody has ever killed or caught or stopped the Bijou, though Mordecai says in theory it should be possible to catch one with a certain type of trap.

The Bijou fairies themselves are covered on the Species/Mobs pages. What matters mechanically is that worship leaves behind a physical route from the worshiper to a temple, and that route runs through Club Vanquisher.

Edgar is how the party detects them. His level-15 Sense Movement skill lets him see non-corporeal motion:

In Edgar's case, he can catch their movement. He can see upward momentum from the ground. This is a sign that someone nearby has just worshiped a god for the first time.

docs.title: Travel the Path
docs.text:
There were approximately 15 different deities in the Ascendency pantheon who were gods and goddesses of light. All 15 of those immortals had temples inside of Club Vanquisher, and, unique amongst the light gods and goddesses, was a powerful spell called Travel the Path. It looked and acted like a mix between a phase and a teleportation spell. It was neither. It allowed someone to temporarily turn into light and follow a path. They could usually only do it for a few seconds, but they could follow that path at the speed of light, making travel almost instantaneous. It was a dangerous spell to use and oftentimes ended with the caster getting splattered or cut in half by an unexpected shadow blocking their route. It was not considered teleportation by the system.

Of those 15 gods, six gave their adherents some version of this spell immediately upon worship.

Two clauses carry all the weight:

  1. It is not teleportation. Which means every teleport ban, teleport suppression field and anti-teleport ward in the dungeon simply does not apply to it.
  2. A shadow across the route is lethal. The path has to be clear of obstruction the whole way, at the speed of light, with no ability to react.

docs.title: Welcome Home
docs.text:
Of those six, four also included a skill called Welcome Home. This could usually only be used once. Ever. This skill, combined with Travel the Path, would allow the adherent to follow the bijou fairy's light tendril path directly to the strongest connected temple, which was invariably inside of Club Vanquisher.

Even if we destroyed the entrance to the temple, the spell would work.

So the combination is: worship a light god, receive a permanent light-tendril route to Club Vanquisher, and hold a one-shot ability to ride that route there instantly, through walls, immune to teleport bans, from anywhere on the floor.

That is a perfect escape hatch, and it is the answer to a question the party has been chewing on for most of the book.

docs.title: The Sepsis Whore's Disappearing Act
docs.text:
Princess Vinata, the reigning Sepsis Whore, has never been killed in a Faction Wars game. Not once, across every season the naga have played and lost. The party needs to know how she leaves.

Rosetta's theory is the light-god escape. Two problems have to be solved for it to hold:

  • Nobody ever sees the sultana worship a god, which implies the worshiper is somebody else — the always-conveniently-absent guard
  • Seven naga escape on a single worship event, which a one-person spell does not explain

The answer to the second is a church-recruitment quest. Two of the four candidate deities issue a quest requiring a new worshiper to bring someone in, via a "Prospect Congregation" day pass — which works like a party: everyone piles into the worshiper's pocket and transfers together. Carl's description of the experience is that prospects cannot leave the temple for at least an hour, making it "the dungeon equivalent of going to a timeshare pitch."

That narrows the field to two gods. Theia is sponsored, and a sponsored deity would smite Vinata for the abuse, which leaves Khepri — and Khepri's temple inside Club Vanquisher becomes the target of the assault that eventually gets Vinata killed.

The twist, in chapters 52–53: "To my surprise, I saw Vinata was actually the one who'd worshiped Khepri, which was a break in tradition." She had not delegated it this time. She had summoned Khepri into his own temple, as a trap for the party.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: No levels given for either spell. The only stated limits are Travel the Path's duration ("usually only… a few seconds"), its lethal intolerance of obstruction, and Welcome Home's single lifetime use.

docs.title: Coda: The Bijou Trap
docs.text:
Mordecai's throwaway line that it "should be possible to catch one with a certain type of trap" pays off on the last page of the book. In chapter 87 a bijou fairy trap is deployed along with "the thousands of threads that connected the fairies to the 12th floor," and "the unbreakable lines of the bijou fairies tightened, creating a flower pattern." Then:

System Message: The Bijou Trap has deactivated. All captured Bijou have been freed.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Crown of the Sepsis Whore — Vinata, and how she is eventually killed
  • Zerzura — the other non-teleport mass-transit trick in the book

Sourced from Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Tripper
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Carl
  • Type: Trap-detonation utility — item-based spell, no mana cost
  • Source: Drakea's Enchanted Kerchief of Disorder (the bandana), Book 4 — "Wearer may cast a level-15 Tripper spell once every five hours"
  • Item-granted level: Flat 15, fixed to the item, 5-hour cooldown
  • Underlying spell level: Trained independently to 7 by Book 7, discovered only when the bandana came off — 10-minute cooldown at that level
  • Also lent out: Tattoo-transferred to Imani in Book 7 at an effective level 9 (15 − 6, both numbers stated on-page; the resulting "9" itself is simple arithmetic, not a quoted figure)

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: Instantly triggers every trap within the spell's area of effect at once — landmines, alarm modules, snare traps, and any other device, regardless of who placed it or whether a target has stepped on it. It works just as well on traps Carl never set himself: he uses it to clear a path through an unfamiliar minefield of hunter-planted alarm traps around the Zockau stairwell on his very first day on the floor, and later to blow through a nest of naiad castle traps he'd never seen before while riding in Miriam Dom's cart.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
Tripper turns out to have two separate levels running at once — a discovery Carl doesn't make until Book 7, ch. 47:

Level Book / ch. What's confirmed 15 (item-granted, flat) Book 4, ch. 28 (grant); reconfirmed Book 7, ch. 33 The bandana's own text: "Wearer may cast a level-15 Tripper spell once every five hours." At level 15 the radius is described as "very wide." This level is fixed to the item and doesn't reflect Carl's own trained skill 7 (underlying spell, trained) Book 7, ch. 47 "when I took off the bandana, I learned my Tripper spell had raised on its own to level 7" — Carl's actual spell-list entry had been training up independently the entire time, invisible behind the item's flat-15 display. Cooldown at this level is 10 minutes, versus the item's 5 hours — the two versions can't share cooldowns 90% detonation chance (external data point) Book 7, ch. 33 Not Carl's own cast, but the same spell at the same flat level: King Rust's level-15 Tripper gives "each trap a 90% chance to blow anyway" even against traps built to resist it — the clearest number the text gives for what a level-15 cast can do against hardened defenses

Confirmed formula: none stated

Unlike Wisp Armor or Bang Bro, no per-level radius or duration formula is ever given for Tripper — level 15's "very wide radius" and the 90% figure above are the only concrete numbers on record, and there's no stated rate connecting level 7 to level 15's performance.

docs.title: The Imani Transfer (Book 7, ch. 47)
docs.text:
When Katia's toraline tattoo system makes borrowing possible, Carl can't just hand over the bandana (fairy-class crawlers can't wear it), so he tattoos the spell onto Imani instead:

"I couldn't give Imani the item, but I could still let her borrow the spell in the form of a tattoo. Since it was a lower level spell, the tattoo didn't need to be big. When I drank the associated potion and selected the spell, I lost six levels when Katia drew the blood. That was irrelevant because the bandana itself brought the spell up to 15 either way."

Carl's own item-independent copy drops from 15 to 9 (a flat –6 on the blood draw, both numbers stated on-page — the "9" is arithmetic, not a quote) but the bandana's flat grant papers over the loss for him personally. Imani receives that computed level-9 copy, which "would slowly lose potency" and eventually fade entirely, while Carl's own dip "heals" back over four days. This is the same borrowing mechanic documented on Profane Iron, and it's the clearest confirmation that Tripper's two levels (item-flat-15 vs. trained-spell-7) are tracked completely separately by the system.

docs.title: Role in the Story — Book 5
docs.text:
Carl casts Tripper repeatedly on Floor 6 as an offensive weapon, most notably during raids on hunter-held towns: cast alongside Ping, it sets off dozens of alarm and landmine traps simultaneously to disorient a group of hunters right before Carl's seeker spider automatons move in. He also uses it mid-escape from his opening solo raid on Zockau, deliberately triggering an unavoidable alarm trap along with every other trap nearby rather than being caught by just the one. While riding in Miriam Dom's cart toward a village, Prepotente warns of a set of decapitation traps guarding the town's entrance — and insults Carl in the same breath — prompting Carl to cast Tripper on the spot, both clearing the traps and startling Prepotente into a scream.

By Book 7, Faction Wars has turned it into a recognized threat rather than just Carl's personal trick: border defenses are built specifically to be "Tripper-proof," Florin recruits a trap-master NPC explicitly to counter it, and Carl still runs into traps flagged "This trap is Tripper proof" when the system decides it should fail.

docs.title: Level Cap — Not Broken
docs.text:
Neither of Tripper's two tracked levels ever exceeds 15, and Carl's own trained copy (level 7) never gets close. Contrast this with Mind Balance, which the wiki documents as the first skill in the series pushed past the level-15 training cap by sustained battlefield conditions — Tripper is a useful case of the opposite: an item quietly holding a skill artificially at the cap while the "real" version underneath trains up slowly and separately, never threatening to overtake it on-page.

Sourced from Book 4: The Gate of the Feral Gods, Book 5: The Butcher's Masquerade, and Book 7: This Inevitable Ruin.

docs.title: Twinkle Toes
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: Book 4 — a platinum quest box tome
  • Type: Buff, movement speed

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: Twinkle Toes dramatically increases the movement speed of Mongo — or any other bonded minion — for a duration scaling with Donut's Intelligence. Donut is visibly delighted by the spell, describing it as one of her favorite acquisitions of the floor.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: The book doesn't give an exact formula, but the duration is explicitly tied to Donut's Intelligence stat, consistent with how her other minion/pet-support spells (like Heal Critter) scale.

docs.title: Role in the Story
docs.text: Donut receives the tome late in Book 4 and doesn't get a dedicated combat showcase for it before the floor ends, but immediately adds it to her active repertoire alongside Clockwork Triplicate as another way to support Mongo in a fight.

docs.title: Future Enhancements
docs.text:
Pending

Not yet confirmed how Twinkle Toes gets used on Floor 6 or beyond.

Sourced from Book 4: The Gate of the Feral Gods.

docs.title: Wall of Fire
docs.text:
Quick facts

  • Caster: Princess Donut
  • Obtained: Book 4, Chapter 2 — a 15-mana spellbook from Donut's Platinum "That Wasn't Too Smart, Was It?" Box, awarded for attacking the Province Boss during the mantaur/Grull fight. She reads it back at the personal space in the same box-opening session that also gives her Astral Paw, before either of the notable Book 4 uses below
  • Type: Area-effect fire damage/barrier

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: Wall of Fire conjures a burning barrier capable of igniting anything that passes through it. In practice this cuts both ways: it reliably kills or damages enemies forced through it, but it can also ignite the caster's own allies or environment if used carelessly in an enclosed space.

docs.title: Acquisition — Book 4, Chapter 2
docs.text:
Back at the personal space after the Grull/mantaur fight, Donut runs through a stack of boss and achievement boxes — including a Platinum "That Wasn't Too Smart, Was It?" Box for attacking the Province Boss. Mordecai narrates it as she reads:

Donut's final, platinum box contained another magic book. It was a 15-mana spell called Wall of Fire.

"That's an escape spell," Mordecai said. "It's about a 10 meter wide, two meter high wall of fire that lasts 15 seconds at level 1. It's a common spell. Powerful later on, but it's also fire. Fire tends to spread. When the magic goes away, if it's cast on something flammable, it stays on fire... Fire gets out of control very easily."

Donut's own reaction is dismissive — "It's not Fireball," she grumbles, "That's what I really want" — before glowing as she reads the book anyway. This is the same chapter-2 box-opening session that gives her Astral Paw, and it precedes both notable Book 4 uses below.

docs.title: Notable Uses — Book 4
docs.text:
• Cast to trap the sand-ooze boss Mrs. Ghazi and its summoner Ghazi inside a burning room during the Mad Dune Mage encounter — the fire catches Ghazi's cluttered lab alight and traps him on the far side of the flames, forcing him to grab his only prized possession and flee toward Carl and Katia instead of hiding
  • Cast defensively against a swarm of thousands of exploding Live Ammo Ball gerbils outside Hump Town — backfires when the leaping gerbils ignite on contact with the flames, turning into miniature fireballs that still manage to set several dromedarian defenders on fire before dying

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: At level 1: roughly 10 meters wide, 2 meters high, lasting 15 seconds, for 15 mana. No further per-level formula is given beyond Mordecai's level-1 baseline and the Book 8 effective-level-16 datapoint below.

docs.title: Book 6: Empowered, Not Granted
docs.text:
Conflict resolved

This page previously flagged a conflict with the Magic Missile page, which claimed a new Book 6 class grants Donut Fireball and Wall of Fire. That was a misread, and the prediction recorded here was correct: Book 6 empowers an already-known spell, it does not teach it.
